- The Jews, led by Ibn Ṣūriyā, called Jibrīl (Gabriel) their enemy and Mīkāʾīl (Michael) their friend, and used this as a pretext to reject the Qur'an.
- Jibrīl is a messenger acting only by Allah's command (19:64, 26:192-194), so enmity to him is enmity to all messengers and to Allah.
- ʿAbdullāh ibn Salām's three questions, answered through Jibrīl, led him to Islam and exposed the Jews' lies, as al-Bukhārī records.
- The Book Jibrīl brought confirms earlier Scripture and is guidance and good news for believers (41:44, 17:82), and "to your heart" means words as well as meanings, received by the heart as the true perceiver.

98.text:
Verse 98 widens the principle. "Whoever is an enemy of Allah, His angels, His messengers, Gabriel, and Michael, then ˹let them know that˺ Allah is certainly the enemy of the disbelievers". Loyalties among the angels cannot be divided, because they all serve one Lord.

### Phrase by phrase

**"Whoever is an enemy of Allah, His angels, His messengers"**. Whoever takes Allah, His angels and His messengers as enemies has made himself Allah's enemy. His messengers include both angels and men, for Allah selects messengers from both angels and people (22:75). Whoever believes in one messenger must believe in all, and whoever rejects one has rejected them all. Allah pronounced those who deny Him and His messengers and say "we believe in some and disbelieve in others" to be disbelievers (4:150), and the same applies to those who take Jibrīl (Gabriel) as an enemy.

**"Gabriel, and Michael"**. Both are angels who serve as messengers, but Jibrīl and Mīkāʾīl (Michael) are singled out. The verse supports Jibrīl, who conveys Allah's messages to His Prophets. The Jews had declared him an enemy while claiming Mīkāʾīl as a friend. Allah's reply is that an enemy of either one is an enemy of the other, and of Allah. The two names are a particular added to a general, "His angels". Several readings of the names are recorded: Jibrīl, Jabrīl, Jibraʾīl, Jabraʾīl, Mīkāl, Mīkāʾīl. Mīkāʾīl also sometimes descended to Allah's Prophets. Jibrīl did so far more frequently, as this was chiefly his task. Isrāfīl is entrusted with the Trumpet announcing resurrection on the Day of Judgement. The Ṣaḥīḥ records that whenever the Messenger of Allah ﷺ woke at night he would pray: "O Allah, Lord of Jibrīl, of Mīkāʾīl and of Isrāfīl, Creator of the heavens and the earth, who knows the seen and the unseen, it is You who judge between Your servants in what they differ over. Guide me by Your leave to the truth about which they differ, for You guide whom You will to a straight path."

**"then ˹let them know that˺ Allah is certainly the enemy of the disbelievers"**. Allah says "of the disbelievers" rather than "of them" to make their status plain. Hostility to Allah's friend amounts to hostility to Allah. The person finds Allah against him and suffers loss here and in the Hereafter. Al-Bukhārī records from Abū Hurayrah that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ related Allah's words: whoever takes a friend of Mine as an enemy, I have declared war on him. So Allah was angry with those who took Jibrīl as an enemy. Allah is the rival of the disbelievers among the Jews and among others, just as Jibrīl, Mīkāʾīl and all the believers are enemies of those who oppose them, and certain defeat awaits whoever has Allah as his rival. Those who deny or oppose the angels and the prophets will meet their due punishment in the other world.

### ʿUmar among the Jews

Ash-Shaʿbī related that ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb said: "I used to go to the Jews while they studied the Torah, amazed at how the Qur'an agreed with the Torah and the Torah with the Qur'an. Once they said to me, 'ʿUmar, there is no one we like more than you.' I asked why, and they said it was because I visited them and mixed with them. I told them I came only out of amazement at how the parts of the Book of Allah strengthen one another, the Qur'an agreeing with the Torah and the Torah with the Qur'an. One day as I sat with them, Allah's Messenger ﷺ passed behind me. The Jews said, 'There is your man, go to him. He has just reached an alley of Madinah.' I turned to them and said, 'I adjure you by Allah and by the Scripture revealed to you, do you know that he is Allah's Messenger?' Their chief told them, 'He has implored you by Allah, so tell him.' They said, 'You are our chief, you tell him.' The chief said, 'We know he is Allah's Messenger.' I said, 'Then you are headed for the worst destruction, knowing that he is Allah's Messenger and refusing to follow him.' They said, 'Among the angels we have one enemy and one ally.' I asked who, and they said, 'Our enemy is Jibrīl, the angel of harshness and coarseness, burden and hardship, and our ally is Mīkāʾīl, the angel of tenderness, gentleness and ease.' I said, 'Then I bear witness that Jibrīl cannot be at enmity with the allies of Mīkāʾīl, nor can Mīkāʾīl be the ally of the enemies of Jibrīl. Both of them, and all who are with them, are enemies of whoever takes either as an enemy, and allies of whoever takes either as an ally.'" The verse was revealed in confirmation of this.

### Hostility to the angels is hostility to Allah

Hostility to angels or prophets amounts to hostility to Allah Himself. That includes opposition to Jibrīl and Mīkāʾīl. By identifying Allah as the disbelievers' enemy, the verse describes those opponents as disbelievers. The devotional reading reflects on the honour this confers. The Jews claimed that Jibrīl brought no good and that they did not love him, and that had it been Mīkāʾīl they would have believed. The Real exposed their lie, for what good is greater than the Qur'an that came down through him? Then He declared that whoever is an enemy to Jibrīl and Mīkāʾīl has God for an enemy. The messenger sent by the Beloved to His highly esteemed beloved, Muḥammad ﷺ, has a noble station and a weighty rank. The enmity of the disbelievers does no harm to Jibrīl, for the Real is his protector (walī), and whoever is Jibrīl's enemy has God as his enemy. How mighty and glorified is that station, and how grand is His exaltedness!

### In short

- Enmity to Allah, His angels or His messengers, angelic or human (22:75), is a single enmity, since believing in some and rejecting others is disbelief (4:150).
- Jibrīl and Mīkāʾīl are named because the Jews tried to set one against the other, and Allah answers that an enemy of either is an enemy of both and of Him.
- ʿUmar confronted the Jews with their own knowledge of the Prophet ﷺ and refuted the Jibrīl-Mīkāʾīl excuse before the verse came down.
- Allah declares war on whoever makes an enemy of His friend, as the ḥadīth in al-Bukhārī says, and the enemies of the angels cannot hurt them, for Allah is their protector.

99.text:
Verse 99 answers the complaint that the Prophet ﷺ had brought no proof. "Indeed, We have sent down to you ˹O Prophet˺ clear revelations. ˹But˺ none will deny them except the rebellious". The signs were there for anyone willing to see them, so denial could only come from defiance.

### Phrase by phrase

**"Indeed, We have sent down to you ˹O Prophet˺ clear revelations"**. Ibn ʿAbbās said this verse was revealed in reply to Ibn Ṣūryā (also written Ibn Suwriyā), who said to Allah's Messenger ﷺ: "Muḥammad, you have brought nothing that we recognise, and no clear sign has been revealed to you on account of which we should follow you." The Jews used to say, in denying the Prophet ﷺ, that no evidence of his prophethood had come to him of a kind they could recognise and accept. The Holy Qur'an answers that Allah has revealed many very clear signs of his prophethood, signs which they themselves know and understand very well. Imām Abū Jaʿfar ibn Jarīr explained the phrase as "We have sent you clear signs that testify to your prophethood", signs contained in the Book of Allah itself. The Qur'an narrates the secret knowledge the Jews possessed and concealed, the stories of their earlier generations, and the texts of their own Books known only to the rabbis and scholars, including the places where they altered and distorted the rulings of the Torah. That Allah mentioned all this in the Book revealed to His Prophet ﷺ should be evidence enough for anyone honest with himself and anxious not to destroy himself through envy and transgression. Human nature too testifies to the truth he was sent with and to the clear signs he brought, which he neither learned nor acquired from any human being. Aḍ-Ḍaḥḥāk reported Ibn ʿAbbās putting it this way: day and night you recite this Book to them and convey it, you who are unlettered and never read a book, and yet you tell them what their own Books contain. Allah made this a lesson, a clear sign and a proof against them, if only they knew. One early gloss adds that the signs came through Jibrīl (Gabriel) and expound commands and prohibitions. The word for "clear" describes the state in which the revelations came down.

**"˹But˺ none will deny them except the rebellious"**. The wicked, the unbelievers and the Jews who reject the signs, those who have abandoned Allah's path. Their denial does not stem from any lack of recognition or knowledge but from their habitual disobedience, for as a rule no one rejects such evidence except the wilful and the stubborn.

### Why clear signs are still denied

The devotional reading observes that a person disbelieves in Allah's clear signs only when his eyes are blocked from perceiving and his lot from God has already been determined as unfortunate. There is no reasoning with someone who denies that day is day, and likewise there is no union for anyone who has not been aided by lights and insights from the Real.

A modern reflection traces the perversion of the People of the Book to a single cause. They come to believe that uttering words and performing lifeless rituals will earn them salvation, when salvation can only be earned by righteous action. In this stage of decline superstition is valued above good deeds, and people expect mysterious benefits from senseless rites. What begins as a theory of salvation ends by dominating the whole policy of the community, and a realistic outlook gives way to a superstitious one. Those who make only an outward show of religion are inevitably averse to responding in earnest when pure, unadulterated religion is proclaimed, because they see the call as a threat to the worldly honour and status their worldly version of religion secures for them. Out of this negativity they put forward objections that look correct on the surface but are meaningless in reality. The coming of the angels and the messengers was wholly part of the divine plan. Every argument shows that the Arab Prophet ﷺ received the same message that was sent to Ibrāhīm (Abraham), Mūsā (Moses) and ʿĪsā (Jesus), and that his revelation tallied exactly with the predictions of the earlier scriptures, which proves beyond doubt that it came from God Himself. People make many protestations of faith, but when these are hollow they have nothing to do with true faith and piety.

### In short

- To Ibn Ṣūryā's claim that the Prophet ﷺ had brought no recognisable sign, Allah answers that the Qur'an itself is a clear sign, revealing to the Jews the secrets of their own Books through an unlettered man.
- Only the rebellious deny such evidence, so the Jews' denial was wilful disobedience, not ignorance.
- Eyes blocked from the Real cannot see, and a religion reduced to ritual resists the true call because its worldly interests are at stake.

100.text:
Verse 100 turns to the Jews' record with promises. "Why is it that every time they make a covenant, a group of them casts it aside? In fact, most of them do not believe".

### Phrase by phrase

**"Why is it that every time they make a covenant"**. After the Messenger of Allah ﷺ had been sent, Allah reminded the Jews of their covenant with Him, and in particular of the part concerning Muḥammad ﷺ. Mālik ibn aṣ-Ṣayf said: "By Allah, Allah never made a covenant with us about Muḥammad, nor did He ever take a pledge from us." Allah then revealed this verse. The Torah itself reports that Allah had made the Jews pledge to believe in the Prophet ﷺ when he appeared, and when reminded of it they flatly denied ever having given such a pledge. The covenants in question include the pledge to believe in the Prophet ﷺ when he came and the pledge not to help the idolaters against him. One early gloss applies the verse to the covenants that the Jewish leaders made with Muḥammad ﷺ.

**"a group of them casts it aside?"**. They reject it, repudiate it and break it. There is no promise they make that they do not break and abandon, making a promise today and breaking it tomorrow. The question is a rebuke. The Holy Qur'an points out that this was no isolated case, for the Jews had never kept even the pledges they acknowledged, and one group or another among them was always breaking the compacts they had entered into, especially in religious matters. Their corrupt state meant that some group would always break any commitment, including the duty to believe in what the Torah had revealed about Muḥammad's prophethood.

**"In fact, most of them do not believe"**. The particle marks a transition: the truth is that most of them are disbelievers, or, as one gloss says, all of them in fact. It can even be said that most of those guilty of such gross violations did not believe at all in the compacts they made with Allah. Breaking a pledge is a sin and a transgression, but having no faith in the pledge one gives to Allah is outright unbelief. Faith leads to keeping and honouring commitments and promises, so a people who keep none have little of it.

### Why "a group", not all

The Qur'an deliberately speaks of one group or another breaking the pledge, not of all the Jews, because some among them did keep their pledges, and in the end many Jews recognised Muḥammad ﷺ as a true prophet and took their place among the Muslims. The devotional reading adds that their predetermined lot confounded them and their subsequent contrivances broke their covenant, and God prevails over His affair.

### In short

- Reminded of the covenant about the Prophet ﷺ, Mālik ibn aṣ-Ṣayf denied it ever existed, and the verse came down.
- A group among the Jews broke every covenant they made, and not believing in a pledge given to Allah is worse than merely breaking it.
- The verse blames "a group", not all, since some kept faith and many eventually embraced Islam.

101.text:
Verse 101 gives the latest and most relevant instance of the habit just described. "Now, when a messenger from Allah has come to them—confirming their own Scriptures—some of the People of the Book cast the Book of Allah behind their backs as if they did not know".

### Phrase by phrase

**"Now, when a messenger from Allah has come to them"**. Namely Muḥammad ﷺ, a prophet from Allah.

**"confirming their own Scriptures"**. Confirming what they possess of the Book, conforming in traits and description to what the Torah said of him. The Torah had given the Jews the good tidings of his coming, and he came with every sign it had indicated, so that he fitted its description and confirmed their sacred Book. As-Suddī explained what happened next. When Muḥammad ﷺ came, the Jews wanted to contradict him and dispute with him using the Torah, but the Torah and the Qur'an confirmed each other. So the Jews gave up on the Torah and turned instead to the Book of Āṣaf and to the sorcery of Hārūt and Mārūt, neither of which agreed with the Qur'an.

**"some of the People of the Book cast the Book of Allah behind their backs"**. A party of those given the Scripture flung the Torah behind them. They did not act on what it said about belief in the Messenger and other matters, and they disbelieved in what it contained of Muḥammad's traits and description and did not expound them. Great numbers of them refused him recognition as a prophet, and in refusing it they were in fact denying the Torah itself. They turned away from the scripture that pointed to him, unmindful of it, drawing no benefit from its truth and guidance.

**"as if they did not know"**. As though they were ignorant people who knew nothing of what it contained about his being a true Prophet, or about its being the Book of Allah. Qatādah said that they knew the truth but abandoned it, hid it and denied that they even possessed it. They behaved as if they knew nothing of the prophecy, or of the Torah being a Book of Allah, and so were guilty of unbelief (kufr) even by the Torah's own terms. They acted, as one commentary puts it, like fools.

### The habit and its latest instance

The previous verse showed how breaking pledges and disobedience had become a settled habit with the Jews. This verse presents the freshest example and the one most relevant to the context. Everything that follows in the passage, the turn to sorcery and the tale of what the devils recited in the reign of Sulaymān (Solomon), flows from this moment of throwing the Book away. A people who abandoned the Scripture that confirmed the Messenger would look for something else to set against him, and they found it in books that had nothing to do with revelation.

### Denying the messengers within and without

The devotional reading sees a double denial. The messengers of the Real that reached their hearts as intuitions (khawāṭir) they denied, and the messengers who came to them outwardly they called liars. What ignorance, without a sliver of deeper knowledge (ʿirfān)! What deprivation, with disappointment (khidhlān) for its companion!

### In short

- When the Messenger ﷺ came matching the Torah's own description, a party of the People of the Book threw the Torah behind their backs rather than follow where it led.
- As-Suddī relates that, unable to use the Torah against the Qur'an, they fell back on Āṣaf's book and on the sorcery attributed to Hārūt and Mārūt.
- Qatādah: they knew the truth, abandoned it, hid it and denied having it, which is unbelief even by the Torah's standard.
- Rejecting the inner promptings of the Real goes hand in hand with rejecting His outward messengers.

102.text:
Verse 102 explains what the Jews turned to once they had thrown the Book of Allah behind their backs. "They ˹instead˺ followed the magic promoted by the devils during the reign of Solomon. Never did Solomon disbelieve, rather the devils disbelieved. They taught magic to the people, along with what had been revealed to the two angels, Hârût and Mârût, in Babylon. The two angels never taught anyone without saying, “We are only a test ˹for you˺, so do not abandon ˹your˺ faith.” Yet people learned ˹magic˺ that caused a rift ˹even˺ between husband and wife; although their magic could not harm anyone except by Allah’s Will. They learned what harmed them and did not benefit them—although they already knew that whoever buys into magic would have no share in the Hereafter. Miserable indeed was the price for which they sold their souls, if only they knew". It is one of the longest verses in the surah, and it raises three questions at once: where the sorcery of the Jews came from, who Hārūt and Mārūt were, and what Islam says about magic.

### Phrase by phrase

**"They ˹instead˺ followed the magic promoted by the devils during the reign of Solomon"**. The verb "followed" continues the previous verse: having cast the Scripture away, they took up what the devils used to recite in the days of Sulaymān's (Solomon's) kingdom, and acted on what the devils had written against his kingdom. As-Suddī told the background. Before Sulaymān's time the devils used to climb up towards heaven and eavesdrop on the angels discussing what was about to happen on earth, deaths, events and other matters of the unseen. They passed this on to the soothsayers, the soothsayers passed it on to the people, and the people found it came true. Once the soothsayers trusted them, the devils began to lie, mixing falsehood into the true news until there were seventy lies for every truth. People wrote these sayings down in books, and soon the Children of Israel were saying that the jinn knew the unseen. When Sulaymān was sent as a prophet he gathered up these books, locked them in a chest and buried it beneath his throne, and any devil who came near the chest was burned. He declared that he would cut off the head of anyone he heard claiming that the devils knew the unseen. After Sulaymān died, and the scholars who knew the truth about him had passed away, a new generation arose. A devil appeared to some of the Israelites in human form and offered to show them a treasure they could never exhaust. He led them to the throne and told them to dig beneath it, but refused to come closer himself, saying they could kill him if they found nothing. They dug up the buried books, and Satan told them that this was the magic by which Sulaymān had ruled men, devils and birds. The rumour that Sulaymān had been a sorcerer spread, and the Israelites adopted the books. When Muḥammad ﷺ came, these were the books they used to argue against him.

ʿImrān ibn al-Ḥārith heard Ibn ʿAbbās tell the same story more briefly: a devil would bring down one true word from heaven and, once trusted for it, add seventy lies that won people's hearts. Sulaymān seized the material and buried it under his throne. After his death a devil stood in the street and offered to guide people to a guarded treasure of Sulaymān's that had no equal. They dug it up and said, "This is magic", and nation after nation copied it. Al-Kalbī gave a different version. The devils wrote out magic and talismans and attributed them to Āṣaf ibn Barakhiyā, heading the text "This is what Āṣaf ibn Barakhiyā taught King Sulaymān", and buried it under his place of worship without his knowledge, at the time when he was stripped of his kingdom. After his death they unearthed it and told people that Sulaymān had left it for them to learn. The scholars of the Children of Israel said, "Allah forbid that this should be Sulaymān's knowledge", but the common people said it was, sought it out, and abandoned the scriptures of their prophets. Sulaymān was blamed for this until Allah sent Muḥammad ﷺ and cleared him in His own words. One of the readings in this verse's wider commentary says the books were buried when his kingdom was taken from him, and that those who found them said, "Your kingdom was only thanks to what is in here", then took to studying them and rejected the Scriptures of their prophets. Khuṣayf added a tale that Sulaymān used to ask every newly sprouted tree what disease it cured, until the carob tree answered that its purpose was the destruction of his sanctuary, and confirmed that it would indeed destroy it.

One early gloss says the devils had written of the collapse of Sulaymān's kingdom and of forty days of sorcery and white magic. A modern reading places the story in the decline of the Jewish people. When superstition and apathy set in, certain individuals exploited the mood for commercial gain by supplying success-seekers with magical prescriptions. To make their trade flourish they attributed their art to Sulaymān, claiming that the extraordinary powers he exercised over the spirits and the winds really rested on his knowledge of magic, and that the spirits had handed this knowledge on to them. This claim to authority did much to spread sorcery, which became a highly popular art among the Jews.

**"Never did Solomon disbelieve, rather the devils disbelieved"**. The Jews had the impertinence, and the folly, to pin magic and sorcery on a prophet. They said: "Look at this Muḥammad, he counts Sulaymān among the prophets when he was nothing but a sorcerer." So while condemning them for learning the black arts of the devils, the Qur'an inserts a parenthesis to deny this vile allegation. Sulaymān never practised magic out of disbelief, and never wrote this sorcery and white magic. It was the devils who disbelieved, teaching people sorcery, and it is said that the Jews in turn taught it to others. The devils lied about Sulaymān's kingdom, claiming it was established through black magic. Allah declared his innocence.

**"They taught magic to the people, along with what had been revealed to the two angels, Hârût and Mârût, in Babylon"**. Babylon (Bābil) is a town in lower Iraq. The names Hārūt and Mārūt stand in place of "the two angels", or explain who they were. Here scholars differ sharply. Al-Qurṭubī related the view that the verse denies anything was sent down to the two angels, the negation covering both halves: Sulaymān did not disbelieve, and nothing was sent down to the two angels. On this reading the Jews had claimed that Jibrīl (Gabriel) and Mīkāʾīl (Michael) brought magic down to the two angels, and Allah refuted the claim. Ibn Jarīr reported through al-ʿAwfī that Ibn ʿAbbās said of this clause, "Allah did not send magic down", and ar-Rabīʿ ibn Anas said the same. Ibn Jarīr judged this the correct explanation, taking the whole verse to mean that what the devils recited in Sulaymān's reign was magic, that Sulaymān did not disbelieve, and that Allah did not send magic with the two angels, Jibrīl and Mīkāʾīl, as the Jewish sorcerers alleged when they said that Allah had sent magic to Sulaymān son of Dāwūd by their words. The devils disbelieved and taught magic to the people of Babylon through the agency of two men, Hārūt and Mārūt, who on this view were ordinary human beings. These were the words of aṭ-Ṭabarī, but other scholars found this explanation implausible. Ibn ʿAbbās is also quoted as saying that the two were sorcerers who taught people magic, and a variant reading has al-malikayn, "the two kings", instead of "the two angels".

Many of the early generations held that the two were real angels, who descended from heaven to the earth and did what the verse describes. To reconcile this with the angels' immunity from error, scholars answer that Allah knew from eternity what these two would do, just as He knew what Iblīs would do while still counting him among the angels when He said "Prostrate before Adam" and all did so but Iblīs (20:116). What Hārūt and Mārūt did was in any case less evil than what Iblīs did. Al-Qurṭubī traced the angel view to ʿAlī and Ibn Masʿūd, to Ibn ʿAbbās and Ibn ʿUmar, and to Kaʿb al-Aḥbār, as-Suddī and al-Kalbī. Another gloss has it that the angels themselves were not taught sorcery, and offers the alternative that the devils taught people what the angels had been inspired with. One modern reading draws a comparison: when angels came to the people of Lūṭ (Lot), who practised homosexuality, they came as handsome boys in order to test them, and in the same way angels were sent to the Jews in Babylon in the dress of holy men to teach them magic, while making it perfectly clear that this was only a test and a knowledge not to be practised. The Jews ignored the warning, practised magic with fervour and even turned it to illicit ends.

**"The two angels never taught anyone without saying, “We are only a test ˹for you˺, so do not abandon ˹your˺ faith.”"**. Ibn ʿAbbās, through Qays ibn ʿAbbād and ar-Rabīʿ ibn Anas, described how it worked. Whenever a would-be learner of magic approached the angels, they tried to put him off, saying, "We are only a test, so do not fall into disbelief." They knew good from evil and belief from disbelief, and they knew that magic was a form of disbelief. If the man insisted, they would direct him to a certain place where Satan would meet him and teach him. Once he had learned it, the light of faith would leave him and he would see it shining as it flew away into the sky, and he would cry out, "O my sorrow! Woe to me! What shall I do?" Al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī said the angels were sent with magic so that those whom Allah willed to test would be tested, and Allah made them promise to teach no one before announcing, "We are a test for you, do not fall into disbelief." Ibn Abī Ḥātim recorded this, and Qatādah said the same. As-Suddī's account is that when a man ignored their warning they would tell him to go to a certain heap of ashes and urinate on it. When he did, a light, the light of faith, would leave him and shine until it entered heaven, and then a black smoke-like thing would come down and get into his ears and the rest of him, and that was the anger of Allah. When he reported what had happened, they would teach him. One gloss has the angels say "we have been tried by calling people to this in order to lighten the torment inflicted on ourselves", and explains "do not disbelieve" as "do not learn it or act on it".

Ibn Jurayj commented that no one dares practise magic except a disbeliever, and that the "test" (fitnah) involves trial and freedom of choice. Whoever learns it is a disbeliever, and whoever renounces it is a believer. Scholars who hold that learning magic is disbelief rely on this verse, and also on the ḥadīth which Abū Bakr al-Bazzār recorded from ʿAbdullāh: whoever goes to a soothsayer or a sorcerer and believes what he says has disbelieved in what was revealed to Muḥammad ﷺ. This ḥadīth has an authentic chain and other reports support it.

**"Yet people learned ˹magic˺ that caused a rift ˹even˺ between husband and wife"**. From the two angels, though not taught by them directly in one reading, people picked up the means of separating spouses, people who are closer and more intimate than any others. This is the devil's work. Muslim recorded from Jābir ibn ʿAbdullāh that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said that Satan sets his throne on the water and sends out his emissaries among mankind, and the nearest to him in rank is the one who causes the greatest discord. One comes back and reports that he kept at a man until he said such and such, and Iblīs replies, "By Allah, you have done nothing." Another reports that he kept at a man until he had separated him from his wife, and Satan draws him close, embraces him and says, "Yes, you have done well." The separation happens because each spouse begins to see the other as ugly or ill-mannered, so that the husband finds a pretext to leave his wife, or hatred is sown between them.

**"although their magic could not harm anyone except by Allah’s Will"**. Sufyān ath-Thawrī glossed this, "except by Allah's appointed term". Al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī said that Allah lets magicians affect whomever He wills and saves whomever He wills from them, and sorcerers never harm anyone except by His leave. The doctrinal point is important: causes in themselves cannot produce the effects usually associated with them, for it is Allah who creates the effects just as He creates the causes.

**"They learned what harmed them and did not benefit them"**. It harms their religion, and harms them in the Hereafter, and brings no benefit worth the harm in this world or the next. One gloss notes that the devils, the Jews and the sorcerers all learn it from one another.

**"although they already knew that whoever buys into magic would have no share in the Hereafter"**. The Jews who preferred magic to following the Messenger of Allah ﷺ knew that those who chose it would have no khalāq in the Hereafter. Ibn ʿAbbās, Mujāhid and as-Suddī explained khalāq as "share", a portion in Paradise. Some take "they knew" to refer to the angels, some to the Jews who knew it from their own Book, and some to the devils. The Jews knew very well that dabbling in black magic was not only a sin but involved unbelief, and they could see that it would do them no good even in this world, since their sorcery could harm no one unless Allah willed it. Their practice contradicted their knowledge, and they made no use of their understanding to notice the contradiction.

**"Miserable indeed was the price for which they sold their souls, if only they knew"**. Evil was what they chose in place of faith and following the Messenger, if only they would take the advice. They exchanged the revelation and the sacred law of Allah for black magic. The verse first says that they "knew" and then takes the knowledge away again with "if only they knew". Knowledge that is neither acted upon nor properly thought through is no better than ignorance. One gloss reads the ending as "but they do not know", another as "and they did know it from their own Book". Had they believed in Allah and His Messenger ﷺ and kept away from what is forbidden, Allah's reward would have been far better for them than what they chose, as the next verse goes on to say, and as those with knowledge said in another passage: Allah's reward is far better for those who believe and do good (28:80).

### Why angels, and why not prophets?

Scholars have related in connection with this verse certain Jewish traditions that have raised doubts, particularly among Muslims with a Western outlook. Among them is a long and well-known story about a woman named Zuhrah, which rests on no sound Islamic transmission. Scholars who find that it breaches the rules of the Sharīʿah dismiss it as fiction, while those who think it can be interpreted in line with the Sharīʿah have not thrown it out altogether. Whether it is true or false, a proper understanding of the verse does not depend on it in any way. The devotional literature knows the same story, saying that Hārūt and Mārūt, deceived by the disobedience they had grown used to, blamed their fall on the disobedience of the children of Ādam, that their own appetites and the promptings of temptation plunged them into sin, and that, as the storytellers relate, they hang upside down until the Day of Resurrection, their punishment destined to last even longer were it not for God's gentleness towards them.

A clearer account of the angels' mission has been offered by Thānavī. There was a time when black magic had become very popular in the world, and in Babylon especially. Seeing its astonishing effects, ignorant people confused it with the miracles of prophets and supposed the two were of one kind. Some even regarded magicians as holy men worthy of obedience, and others began learning and practising magic as though it were a pious act with divine sanction. Something similar happened in the West after the mid-1960s, and since 1968 the study of magic has even found its way into universities, above all in America. This exaggerated reverence for magic and magicians had become a potent source of misguidance. To root it out, Allah sent two angels to Babylon to inform people of the true nature of magic and its various forms, so that they could tell it apart from the miracles of prophets, stop obeying magicians and stop practising magic themselves. Just as the prophethood of prophets is confirmed by miracles, signs and arguments, the angelic nature of Hārūt and Mārūt was confirmed by signs and arguments of its own, so that people would listen to them attentively and follow their guidance.

Why was this task not given to prophets? For two reasons. First, the need of the hour was to draw a line between prophets and magicians, and since the prophets were in a sense one party to the dispute, it was fitting that a third party should arbitrate. Second, the distinction could not normally be made clear without quoting and reporting the verbal formulas magic uses. Merely reporting heretical speech is not itself heresy, a rational principle the Sharīʿah accepts, so the prophets could have been permitted to quote them. But because the prophets are the embodiment of divine guidance, Allah did not assign them this work and chose two angels instead. Allah's commands are of two kinds, those belonging to takwīn, the order of creation and the cosmos, and those belonging to tashrīʿ, the order of legislation, and the two may sometimes appear not to agree. The created order is woven of good and evil alike, and it is the angels who carry out divine commands in that sphere. So angels are made to do things which in the cosmic perspective always serve the general good, yet which involve some partial disorder and so appear evil, such as the growth and preservation of a tyrant or a dangerous beast, each right within the order of creation and wrong from the standpoint of the law. Prophets, by contrast, are entrusted only with the legislative order, which is nothing but good in its general and particular applications. Reporting the formulas of magic did ultimately serve the legislative order, but there was a real risk, which in fact materialised, that reporting them would encourage the practice. Allah therefore preferred not to make the prophets even an indirect means of so reprehensible an activity. The prophets served the main purpose in their own way, by announcing the basic rulings of the Sharīʿah on magic without the detailed subsidiary rules, since even those might have led to temptation. An analogy makes it clear. The prophets have told us that taking a bribe is forbidden and have explained what bribery is, but they did not spell out the methods by which bribes are given and taken, since such detail would only have taught people how to do it. Or take a branch of magic: a certain formula, it is claimed, will make a man find money under his pillow or in his pocket when he rises in the morning. The Sharīʿah makes plain that such a practice is in principle illegitimate, but it does not tell us what the formula is.

So the two angels came down to Babylon and set about their task. They would explain the basic principles of magic, its forms and its specific formulas, and then dissuade people from involving themselves in these things or with magicians. Their work resembled that of a scholar who, finding that uneducated people sometimes utter heretical phrases out of ignorance, collects in his lectures or writings all the phrases in circulation and tells them what to avoid. People of every kind started coming to the angels to learn the nature and formulas of magic, so that ignorance would not lead them astray in belief or in practice. To teach correctly and protect people from error, the angels took care to warn each enquirer of the dangers of the information they were giving. They made it clear that in permitting them to pass on this knowledge Allah intended to test His servants, to see who would use it to protect his faith by recognising evil and avoiding it, and who would fall into misguidance by adopting an evil he now knew to be evil, a choice that can easily lead to unbelief in practice or in doctrine. They repeatedly urged people to seek this dangerous knowledge only with a good intention, to remain firm in it, and never to misuse it so as to earn perpetual damnation.

The angels could hardly have been more honest. They explained the principles and even the details of magic to everyone prepared to pledge that he would hold fast to his faith. If anyone broke the pledge and fell into transgression or unbelief, that was his own affair and the angels could not be blamed. Some kept their word, but many did not, and used their knowledge of magic to harm people, which is in itself sin and transgression, while some forms of magic involve unbelief. Through misuse of this knowledge some became sinners and others unbelievers. It bears repeating that the angels taught magic to reform people and keep them on the straight path, and that those who misused the teaching did so out of their own perversity. Compare a man who goes to a master of the Islamic sciences, expert in the traditional disciplines and in philosophy too, and a man who practises what he knows. The pupil asks to be taught philosophy, ancient and modern, so that he can defend himself against the doubts philosophers raise about Islamic beliefs and answer those who raise them. Fearing that the pupil may prove insincere and end up pressing philosophy into the service of anti-Islamic ideas, the master warns him, the pupil promises not to misuse what he learns, and the master then trains him thoroughly. If the pupil later breaks his promise and accepts the false theories of the philosophers as truth, no one would hold the teacher responsible. In just the same way there is no room to doubt the integrity of the two angels. Allah alone knows how matters stood, but one may suppose that once they had finished their assigned work they were recalled to the heavens.

### What magic is

According to the authoritative dictionary al-Qāmūs, siḥr means an effect whose cause is hidden, whether the cause lies in something with a luminous quality, such as the effect of certain phrases, or in beings of an extra-sensory reality, such as the effects produced by jinn and devils, or in the power of imagination, as in hypnotism, or in things that are physical but concealed, such as a hidden magnet drawing iron, drugs secretly administered, or the influence of the stars and planets. Since the causes are many, so are the forms of magic. In everyday speech magic means practices that use the cooperation of jinn and devils, or the power of imagination, or particular words and phrases. Ancient philosophers and some modern ones accept, and observation and experiment confirm, that words and phrases possess a certain efficacy of their own, and that reciting or writing certain letters, words or phrases a set number of times produces specific results. Similar results are sought by using a person's hair, nails or clothing, the practice usually called preparing charms. All of this is commonly called magic.

In the terminology of the Qur'an and the ḥadīth, however, siḥr refers to those unusual happenings brought about with the active help of the devils, who are won over by practices that please them. There are several ways of pleasing them: singing their praises, reciting heretical formulas that deny Allah or associate partners with Him, worshipping the stars and planets, and committing certain evil deeds, such as making a charm with the blood of someone unlawfully killed, refusing the prescribed modes of bodily purification, or deliberately living in a constant state of filth and impurity. Just as the help of the angels is won only by speech and conduct they love, remembrance of Allah, fear of Him, obedience to His commands, cleanliness and purity, avoidance of every kind of dirt, physical and otherwise, and good deeds generally, so the cooperation of the devils is obtained by speech and conduct that pleases them. That is why success in black magic comes only to those who are habitually unclean, who neglect purification and the remembrance of Allah, and who are given to evil deeds, and it is claimed that women become effective in it chiefly during menstruation. This is black magic in the exact sense. Sleight of hand, mesmerism, hypnotism and the tricks of jugglers are called magic only by extension or metaphor.

### Kinds of magic

Imām Rāghib al-Iṣfahānī, in his Mufradāt, cites the magic of Pharaoh's sorcerers as an example of magic that works on the imagination. The Qur'an says they "deceived the eyes of the people, stunned them, and made a great display of magic" (7:116), and that their ropes and staffs "appeared to him—by their magic—to be slithering" (20:66). The verb in the second verse shares its root with khayāl, imagination, which shows that the ropes and sticks neither became serpents nor moved at all. It was the imagination of Mūsā (Moses) that was affected so that he saw them running about as serpents. The Qur'an also points to the other way of working on the imagination, with the help of the devils, when it asks on whom the devils descend and answers that they "descend upon every sinful liar" (26:221-222).

A third kind of magic is said to change the very nature of a thing, turning a man into an animal or a stone. Imām Rāghib and Abū Bakr al-Jaṣṣāṣ deny that magic can alter a thing's nature entirely, limiting its power to the imagination and to deceiving the onlookers' eyes, and this was also the Muʿtazilah position. Most scholars, however, hold that neither the Sharīʿah nor any rational argument rules out transformation, a living body becoming a stone for instance. The well-known philosophical principle that essences cannot change concerns only the three categories of the impossible, the possible and the necessary: the impossible cannot become possible, nor the possible impossible. And the fact that the Qur'an describes the Egyptian sorcerers' magic as an effect on the imagination does not mean that all magic is of that kind. Some scholars see support for the possibility of transformation in a saying of Kaʿb al-Aḥbār that Imām Mālik records in the Muwaṭṭaʾ from al-Qaʿqāʿ ibn Ḥakīm: "Were it not for these phrases that I recite regularly, the Jews would have turned me into a donkey." Although "donkey" is a common metaphor for a fool, there is no need to leave the literal sense for a figurative one without reason, so the saying means what it says: without the protection of the phrases, the Jewish sorcerers would have turned him into a donkey. It thus establishes two things, that turning a man into a donkey is possible, and that the phrases he recited had the property of neutralising the sorcerers' magic. Asked what they were, Kaʿb taught this prayer: "I seek refuge in Allah the Great, than whom none is greater, and I seek refuge in the perfect words of Allah which no man, righteous or wicked, can overstep, and I seek refuge in all the Beautiful Names of Allah, those I know and those I do not know, from the evil of everything Allah has created, brought into being and spread abroad." In sum, all three forms of magic are possible and do occur.

### Miracles and magic

Through prophets and saints events occur that never happen in the ordinary course and are therefore called kharq al-ʿādah, a breach of the habitual. The miracle of a prophet is called muʿjizah and that of a saint karāmah. A muʿjizah is an unusual event that occurs at the hands of a prophet, purely by Allah's act, the prophet's own will playing no part in producing it, and those who witness it are obliged to believe in it. A karāmah is likewise Allah's act, appearing at the hands of a man of Allah. The basic difference is that the one who performs a muʿjizah announces himself as a prophet, whereas the man of Allah makes no such claim. In both, the usual link of cause and effect is absent and there is usually a complete transformation in the nature and behaviour of things. A general belief in them is required. Allah chooses whom He wills for them, and no amount of rigorous discipline can give anyone the power to make the unusual happen. Irhāṣ is a kind of karāmah that heralds the coming of a prophet and usually occurs at the hands of someone closely related to him: the unprecedented events in the life of Maryam, mother of ʿĪsā (Jesus), or the unusual things that happened to and around Āminah, the blessed mother of the Prophet ﷺ, who felt no pangs of birth and towards the end of her term heard strange voices greeting her though she saw no one. Such events of irhāṣ as the Qur'an mentions must be believed, together with the general truth that irhāṣ accompanies the coming of a prophet.

The effects of miracles sometimes look like the effects of magic, and the resemblance leads ignorant people to confuse the two and to revere magicians quite wrongly. The difference lies first in their natures and second in the signs that accompany each. As to nature, results produced by magic depend on the law of causality just as ordinary events in the physical world do. The only distinction is that in ordinary events the causes are plain or easily observed, while in magic they are hard for the common man to detect. Where causes are evident, effects are traced straight back to them and nothing seems astonishing. Where causes are hidden, the effects provoke wonder, and those ignorant of the causes readily believe that the habitual laws of the universe have been broken. What they fail to realise is that such happenings have their causes just as habitual events do, the cause in extraordinary cases often being the activity of a jinn or a devil. Suppose a letter suddenly drops in front of a man and he finds it was written that very day ten thousand miles away. Onlookers would call it supernatural, not knowing that Allah has given jinn and devils the power to do such things. Once the means is understood, the event no longer looks supernatural or even contrary to habit. In short, everything achieved by magical practices is in fact the work of physical causes, and it wears the illusory appearance of the supernatural only because those causes are hidden from ordinary people. In the West such events are labelled "supernatural", although the Latin natura, like the Greek phusis, originally covered everything created, whether within the field of empirical science or beyond it.

Miracles, on the other hand, happen directly by divine command without the intervention of physical causes. The Qur'an tells how Ibrāhīm (Abraham) was thrown into a blazing fire by the tyrant Namrūd (Nimrod), and how Allah commanded the fire to be cool for him, though not so cool as to harm him, and the fire obeyed, offering him safety instead of scorching him. That was a direct divine act and therefore a miracle. We sometimes hear of men who coat their bodies with certain chemicals and walk into fire unscorched. That is no miracle, because a physical cause, the chemicals, is at work, and people unfamiliar with it are deluded into thinking the performance supernatural. The Qur'an leaves no doubt that a miracle is Allah's own act. At the Battle of Badr the Prophet ﷺ scooped up a handful of pebbles and flung them towards the unbelieving army, and their eyes were blinded, and the Qur'an says of it: "Nor was it you ˹O Prophet˺ who threw ˹a handful of sand at the disbelievers˺, but it was Allah Who did so" (8:17). The miraculous effect of a handful of pebbles was not the Prophet's ﷺ doing but Allah's.

How then is the common man to tell them apart, when the results look the same? Allah has given each its distinguishing marks. First, miracles appear through people whom everyone knows to be clean in body, pure in conduct and God-fearing, while magic works through those who are unclean in body, foul in conduct, and estranged from the worship and remembrance of Allah, a difference anyone can see with his own eyes. Second, Allah has so arranged matters that if a man claims prophethood and claims to work miracles, and yet tries to practise magic, his magic never works. He can be effective in magic only so long as he makes no claim to prophethood.

Can magic affect prophets? It can. Magic works through physical causes, and prophets are not immune to physical causes. Just as they feel hunger and thirst, fall ill and recover through ordinary causes, the hidden workings of magic, which are physical too, can affect them as well. Being affected by magic no more detracts from the dignity of prophethood than hunger or thirst does. Authentic ḥadīths report that the Prophet ﷺ was affected by a spell cast by the Jews, that he learned of it through revelation, and that he took steps to free himself of its effects. The Qur'an likewise tells how Mūsā felt magic's effect when the sorcerers bewitched his eyes, so that their ropes and sticks looked to him like running serpents, so that he was genuinely frightened (20:66).

### The rulings of the Sharīʿah on magic

In the language of the Qur'an and the ḥadīth, siḥr means only those practices in which one seeks the help of jinn and devils by pleasing them through words or deeds that involve unbelief (kufr) and association (shirk), or sin and transgression, and thereby produces extraordinary events. The magic of Babylon mentioned here was exactly this, and this is the form the Qur'an condemns as kufr, as al-Jaṣṣāṣ explained. According to Abū Manṣūr, the soundest view is that not every form of magic is unconditionally unbelief, but only the form that uses actions or speech contrary to the tenets of faith (īmān). The Qur'an and the ḥadīth repeatedly command Muslims to treat the devils as enemies, to hate and curse them, so seeking to please them and win their friendship is in itself a sin. They are pleased only by kufr or shirk, which forfeits faith altogether, or at least by disobedience and transgression that displeases Allah and His angels, such as wallowing in filth and impurity, which adds a further sin. If magic is then used to harm a human being unlawfully, that is one sin more. What the Qur'an and ḥadīth call siḥr, therefore, is never free of unbelief either in belief or in action. One who adopts speech or acts of kufr or shirk to please the devils commits real unbelief in matters of faith, and one who avoids these but indulges in other sins does not escape unbelief in matters of action. This is what the verse means in calling magic kufr. In sum, magic that uses acts or speech of unbelief, such as seeking the devils' help, believing that the stars and planets act of themselves, or claiming prophethood by passing off magical results as miracles, is unbelief by consensus, while magic that involves no act of unbelief but only sinful acts is a major sin.

Five subsidiary rulings follow. First, since magic is rarely free from unbelief in faith or in action, it is forbidden to learn it, teach it or practise it, though some jurists permit learning it in order to protect Muslims from harm, and then no more than is necessary. Second, charms and amulets prepared with the help of jinn and devils fall under siḥr and are forbidden, and so are charms whose words are obscure if one suspects they are invocations of idols or devils. Third, forms of magic other than the Babylonian kind condemned by the Qur'an and ḥadīth are also forbidden if they involve kufr or shirk in any way. Fourth, a form of magic that uses words, actions or other elements to which the Sharīʿah does not object is permissible, provided it is not used for a purpose the Sharīʿah forbids. Fifth, it is permissible to use verses of the Qur'an, the Divine Names or the words of the ḥadīth in charms and amulets, or as recitations and invocations seeking Allah's help towards a desired end, but using the sacred texts for a reprehensible purpose, such as harming someone without just cause, is forbidden even so.

### The inner allusion

The devotional reading finds in the story a portrait of a type. Whoever is torn apart by his whims (ahwāʾ) falls from one heedlessness (ghaflah) into the next, and every kind of ignorant business comes to greet him. Those long absent from the Beloved turn into a warning for others and a temptation for anyone who follows their road, and whoever imitates their transgression joins their company and becomes one of them. So it was with Hārūt and Mārūt, who became a temptation and a warning for mankind. Whoever listens to such people without reckoning with their ignorance will share their trial (balāʾuhumā) and suffer their distress (ʿanāʾuhumā, as the text has it) in the Hereafter. The allusion is to the man on the spiritual path (ṭarīqah) who inclines to affectation, deception and pretension. He gathers followers whom he leads to the Fire by his falsehood, and by the evil of his darknesses he blocks them from the way of right direction. Those who take heed cross safely over its bridges, while the one disgraced (tahattaka) by his leaning towards falsehood finds his veils (astāruhu) torn and his faults (ʿawāruhu) laid bare to anyone with eyes.

### In short

- After abandoning the Torah the Jews took up the sorcery the devils had attributed to Sulaymān, books of eavesdropped half-truths and seventy-fold lies dug up from beneath his throne, or forged under the name of Āṣaf ibn Barakhiyā. Allah declares Sulaymān innocent of disbelief.
- Hārūt and Mārūt in Babylon are, in the view of most early authorities, two angels sent as a trial, who warned every enquirer "we are only a test, do not disbelieve", while Ibn Jarīr read them as two men and the clause as a denial that Allah ever sent down magic.
- The angels' mission, on Thānavī's explanation, was to teach people to distinguish magic from prophetic miracles, a task given to angels rather than prophets so that guidance would never become even an indirect cause of sorcery.
- Magic that works through the devils is unbelief, magic that involves only sin is a major sin, learning or teaching it is forbidden except as needed for protection, and nothing it does can harm anyone except by Allah's leave.
- Miracles come directly from Allah through the pure, magic through hidden physical causes and the impure, and those who buy into it have sold their souls for a miserable price with no share in the Hereafter.

103.text:
Verse 103 closes the long passage on the sorcery of the Jews by pointing to the road they could have taken. "If only they were faithful and mindful ˹of Allah˺, there would have been a better reward from Allah, if only they knew". Having described what they bought and what it cost them, Allah states what they refused, and why the refusal was so foolish.

### Phrase by phrase

**"If only they were faithful and mindful ˹of Allah˺"**. The Jews are meant. Had they believed in Muḥammad ﷺ and the Qur'an, and been fearful of Allah's punishment, turning from Judaism and sorcery and giving up acts of disobedience to Him, of which sorcery was the prime example, the outcome would have been altogether different. Faith here means really having faith in Allah, and mindfulness means taking care to obey His sacred law and not to rebel against it. The grammarians note that the answer to the conditional "if only" is left unspoken. It is understood to be "they would have been rewarded", and the rest of the verse makes that plain.

**"there would have been a better reward from Allah"**. Had they believed in Allah and His Messenger ﷺ and avoided what He prohibited, the reward He gives for such deeds would have served them far better than the thing they chose and preferred. It would have been better than Judaism and sorcery, and better than the thing for which they sold their souls in the previous verse (2:102). The Holy Qur'an makes the same point elsewhere through the people of knowledge who rebuked those dazzled by Qārūn's wealth: "Allah’s reward is far better for those who believe and do good" (28:80). The phrase is framed as an oath, "verily a reward from Allah", with "would have been better" as its predicate. The reward is the subject, and the comparison is deliberately open, since nothing they could have gained by magic bears comparison with it.

**"if only they knew"**. Had they known that this is better, they would never have preferred the other thing to it. One gloss reads the ending as "if only they believed in Allah's reward, but they neither know nor believe", while another says that they did in fact know all this from their own Book. Both readings fit the pattern of the preceding verse, which first says that the Jews "knew" that the buyer of magic has no share in the Hereafter and then ends with "if only they knew". Knowledge that is neither acted upon nor thought through properly counts for nothing, and so it is treated as if it did not exist. If they had truly grasped what would benefit them they would never have done anything so disgraceful and so plainly misguided.

### What the whole passage comes to

Read together, verses 102 and 103 set out an exchange. On one side is the magic the devils fathered on Sulaymān (Solomon), the books dug up from beneath his throne, the formulas the two angels in Babylon explained only under protest and with a warning, and the spells that broke up marriages. On the other side is faith in the Messenger who confirmed the Torah, and the God-fearing life that follows from it. The Jews of al-Madinah chose the first and threw the second behind their backs, although they knew the price. This verse says that the price was not only miserable but needless, since a far better reward stood ready for them in return for belief and piety. The faith and the fear of Allah it mentions are precisely the things that sorcery destroys, for magic in the strict sense is won by pleasing the devils through unbelief, impurity and sin, and no one keeps both. That is why the verse joins "faithful" and "mindful" and sets the pair against the sorcery of the previous verse as its exact opposite.

The modern reflection on the passage observes that once superstition and apathy had settled on the declining community, the profiteers who sold magical prescriptions in Sulaymān's name found a ready market, and even the angels' plain warning that they were only a test did not stop people practising magic eagerly and for illicit ends. The remedy was never more knowledge of the formulas. It was belief in the clear signs that had come, and a fear of Allah that kept people away from what they had been told to shun.

### The treasure of the two abodes

The devotional reading sees in the verse the whole difference between turning towards God (iqbāl) and being distracted from Him (ishtighāl). Had they only preferred drawing near to God over being preoccupied with other things, they would have gained the treasure of both abodes (dhukhr ad-dārayn) and reached the glory of both worlds (ʿizzat al-kawnayn). Instead the blows of subjugation pressed down upon them and held them fast in the lands of abandonment (mawāṭin al-hajr). Reward "from Allah" is set against everything that distracts from Him, and the one who sells his soul for the lesser thing ends up losing both.

### In short

- Had the Jews believed in the Prophet ﷺ and the Qur'an and feared Allah enough to abandon sorcery and disobedience, Allah's reward would have been far better than anything they gained.
- The unspoken answer to "if only" is "they would have been rewarded", and the reward is framed as an oath that admits no comparison (28:80).
- "If only they knew" repeats the lesson of the previous verse: knowledge not acted upon is as good as none.
- Turning towards God wins the treasure of both worlds, while being distracted from Him leaves a people in the lands of abandonment.

104.text:
Verse 104 turns from the Jews to the believers, and teaches them to watch their words. "O believers! Do not say, “Râ’ina.” [Herd us!] But say, “Unẓurna,” [Tend to us!] and listen ˹attentively˺. And the disbelievers will suffer a painful punishment". Behind a single word lies a story of mockery, and a lasting rule about not giving enemies an opening.

### Phrase by phrase

**"O believers!"**. Those who believe in Muḥammad ﷺ and the Qur'an are addressed directly, because the fault being corrected had crept into their own speech.

**"Do not say, “Râ’ina.” [Herd us!]"**. Rāʿinā is an Arabic imperative from murāʿāh, meaning "be mindful of us", "attend to us" or "look after us", and the Arabs used it freely when asking a speaker to give them his attention. In the language of the Jews, however, a word of the same sound was a term of vile abuse, connected with ruʿūnah, thoughtlessness, and carrying the sense of "fool". Ibn ʿAbbās, in the narration of ʿAṭāʾ, told what happened. When the Jews heard the Arabs addressing the Prophet ﷺ with this word they were delighted, since in their own tongue it was a curse. They said to one another: until now we have abused Muḥammad in secret, now we can abuse him openly, because the word is part of their speech. So they would come to the Prophet ﷺ, say "Muḥammad, rāʿinā", and laugh. Saʿd ibn ʿUbādah of the Anṣār, who knew the Jews' language well, saw what they were doing and said: "Enemies of Allah, may Allah's curse be on you. By Him in whose hand is Muḥammad's soul, I will cut off the head of any one of you who says this word." They protested: "Do you not say the same thing to him yourselves?" Then Allah revealed the verse. Some Muslims had indeed begun to use it with the Prophet ﷺ in its innocent Arabic sense, to the great glee of the Jews, who had found a way to insult him openly and had even tricked the Muslims into joining in.

Aḍ-Ḍaḥḥāk reported from Ibn ʿAbbās that the Jews used to say to the Prophet ﷺ "arʿinā samʿak", a form of the phrase they intended as an insult, and the same was related from Abū al-ʿĀliyah, Abū Mālik, ar-Rabīʿ ibn Anas, ʿAṭiyyah al-ʿAwfī and Qatādah. A modern writer explains the trick of pronunciation: said properly, rāʿinā means much the same as unẓurnā, but drawing out the second vowel turns it into "our shepherd", and drawing out the first turns it into "idiot". The Jews would twist the word when they themselves addressed the Prophet ﷺ, corrupting it to mean "foolish" or "evil". Mujāhid gave two further explanations, that "do not say rāʿinā" means "do not dispute", and that it means "do not say, we hear from you and you hear from us". ʿAṭāʾ said it was simply an expression in the dialect of the Anṣār which Allah forbade. As-Suddī said that Rifāʿah ibn Zayd, a Jew of Qaynuqāʿ, would visit the Prophet ﷺ and say "Hear, may you hear nothing", and that some Muslims, imagining that prophets were greeted and honoured with this sort of speech, began to say the same. The Holy Qur'an records the Jews' habit elsewhere, in Sūrat an-Nisāʾ: "Some Jews take words out of context and say, “We listen and we disobey,” “Hear! May you never hear,” and “Râ’ina!” [Herd us!]—playing with words and discrediting the faith" (4:46). After that Allah forbade the believers to use the word at all. ʿAbd ar-Raḥmān ibn Zayd ibn Aslam said the same.

**"But say, “Unẓurna,” [Tend to us!]"**. The two words mean the same in Arabic, "look at us", "watch over us", "regard us and hear us", but unẓurnā carried no second meaning and gave no one anything to laugh at. By commanding the believers to use it Allah frustrated the Jews' design. Allah forbade His believing servants to imitate the speech and conduct of the disbelievers, for the Jews used devious words that concealed what they really meant. The ḥadīths record the same habit in their greetings: they would say "as-sāmu ʿalaykum", "death be upon you", which is why Muslims were commanded to answer "wa ʿalaykum", "and upon you", so that the supplication of the Muslims against them would be answered rather than theirs against the Muslims. Imām Aḥmad narrated from Ibn ʿUmar that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "I have been sent with the sword before the Hour, so that Allah alone is worshipped without partner. My provision has been placed beneath the shade of my spear. Humiliation and lowliness have been decreed for whoever opposes my command, and whoever imitates a people is one of them." Abū Dāwūd narrated the Prophet's ﷺ words, "Whoever imitates a people is one of them." With their threats and warnings these ḥadīths show that Muslims may not imitate the disbelievers in their sayings, deeds, dress, festivals or acts of worship, in anything of theirs that was not legislated for us.

**"and listen ˹attentively˺"**. Give ear to what you are commanded, be ready to accept it, and obey. Muslims were told to avoid ambiguous words and to speak plainly, shunning above all words with a mocking shade of meaning. They were also to attend closely to the Prophet's ﷺ words and work at understanding them for themselves, without excessive questioning, meeting his instructions with receptiveness rather than obstinacy, for this was the way to gain faith, and the strengthening of faith was the thing to be sought.

**"And the disbelievers will suffer a painful punishment"**. For the Jews who insulted the Prophet ﷺ and tried to be clever with him there is the Fire, a torment that will reach into their hearts. The verse calls these insolent Jews disbelievers (kāfirīn), which shows that deliberate disrespect towards a prophet, even by indirect means, is itself unbelief.

### Closing the door to harm

The verse establishes a principle of law. If a perfectly legitimate act on one's part gives others room to commit illegitimate acts, that act ceases to be lawful for one. A scholar's permissible deed, for instance, becomes forbidden for him if it is likely to lead the ignorant into error and induce them to do forbidden things, provided the deed is not something the Sharīʿah requires or counts among its objectives. The Qur'an and the ḥadīth supply many examples. Before Islam the Quraysh, rebuilding the Kaʿbah, had departed from the design laid down by Ibrāhīm (Abraham). A ḥadīth reports that the Prophet ﷺ wished to pull down the existing structure and rebuild it on the Abrahamic plan, but refrained, since ignorant people might have been led by such a step into misunderstanding and error. In the vocabulary of legal theory rulings of this kind are called sadd adh-dharāʾiʿ, blocking the means to wrongdoing. All the jurists accept the principle, and the Ḥanbalī school applies it with particular care, as al-Qurṭubī notes.

The devotional reading draws the same line in the language of friendship and enmity. The aims of enemies in all their states (fī jamīʿi aḥwālihim), in their deeds and words alike (min aʿmālihim wa aqwālihim), are malicious, since they stay bound to their own ways in what they do and leave undone. The way of the friends of God is to avoid resembling them and to walk a path that is not their path.

### In short

- The Jews turned the innocent Arabic request rāʿinā into a hidden curse and laughed when Muslims used it to the Prophet ﷺ, so Allah told the believers to say unẓurnā instead and to listen attentively.
- Saʿd ibn ʿUbādah exposed the trick, and the verse, with 4:46, records the Jews' habit of playing with words, including the greeting "death be upon you".
- Deliberate disrespect to a prophet, even indirect, is unbelief, and a painful punishment awaits it.
- Believers must not imitate disbelievers in word or deed ("whoever imitates a people is one of them"), and a lawful act becomes unlawful when it opens the door to wrong, the principle of sadd adh-dharāʾiʿ, as the Prophet's ﷺ decision not to rebuild the Kaʿbah shows.

105.text:
Verse 105 moves from how the Jews treated the Prophet ﷺ to how they felt about the Muslims. "The disbelievers from the People of the Book and the polytheists would not want you to receive any blessing from your Lord, but Allah selects whoever He wills for His mercy. And Allah is the Lord of infinite bounty".

### Phrase by phrase

**"The disbelievers from the People of the Book and the polytheists"**. Among the People of the Scripture this means Kaʿb ibn al-Ashraf and his companions, and among the idolaters of Arabia Abū Jahl and his companions. The "from" is explanatory, and the polytheists (al-mushrikīn) are joined to the People of the Book for emphasis, to make the point that the Jews can no more be well-wishers of the Muslims than the idolaters can, the two being alike in their hatred of them.

**"would not want you to receive any blessing from your Lord"**. Whenever the Muslims urged their Jewish allies to believe in Muḥammad ﷺ, the Jews would answer: "What you are inviting us to is no better than what we have. We only wish it were better." Allah revealed this verse to give them the lie. Some Jews used to assure the Muslims of their sincerity, pretending they would dearly have liked the Muslims to receive from Allah teachings and laws superior to their own, so that they too could accept them, but that Islam, sadly, did not appear to be the better religion. The Holy Qur'an rejects their claim to be well-wishers and declares that the unbelievers, Jews and idolaters alike, are so jealous of the Muslims that they cannot bear the thought of their receiving any blessing from Allah whatsoever, big or small. The blessing in question is revelation itself, that Allah should send Jibrīl (Gabriel) down to their Prophet with the good of prophethood, Islam and the Book. Their motive is envy.

These Jews made two claims, that Judaism was a better religion than Islam and that they wished the Muslims well. The first they could never support with any valid argument, and it remained an empty assertion. In any case the difference between Islam and Judaism does not turn on which is better. When something new comes to abrogate something older, the older is given up as a matter of course, and Allah sent Islam to abrogate all earlier religions. Because this is so obvious, the Qur'an says nothing in refutation of the first claim and deals only with the second. In describing the deep enmity of the polytheists and the People of the Scripture, whom the believers had just been warned against imitating, Allah teaches the Muslims to keep no intimate friendship with them. At the same time He reminds them of what He has given them, the perfect Law He legislated for His Prophet Muḥammad ﷺ.

**"but Allah selects whoever He wills for His mercy"**. He chooses for His religion, His prophethood, Islam and the Book whoever deserves to be chosen, and He singled out Muḥammad ﷺ for the office of His Prophet. Out of His mercy He grants prophethood, revelation and faith to those of His servants whom He wills. Their jealousy can do the Muslims no harm, for Allah is Beneficent and All-Powerful and showers His special blessings on whomever He chooses.

**"And Allah is the Lord of infinite bounty"**. His favour in granting Muḥammad ﷺ prophethood and Islam is great indeed. Allah's bounty is vast, no one in creation receives any good except from Him, and it is of His bounty that He sent His Prophet and revealed His Book to us.

### Envy that cannot prevail

The believers were themselves told not to be jealous of another person's precious possession, for it was God who bestowed that blessing on His servant. God decreed that the Prophet ﷺ should receive divine revelation, and anyone earnest about learning from him could share in the blessing he received. The devotional reading observes that the hostility of enemies towards the steady decency of the friends of God never ceases, but the envier does not prevail (al-ḥasūd lā yasūd) and never obtains what he seeks. The special qualities of mercy are enough for the friends, even while the enemies are abased and the very borders of the lands where they once rejoiced are laid waste.

### In short

- Kaʿb ibn al-Ashraf's party and Abū Jahl's party alike hated to see any good, above all revelation, come down to the Muslims.
- The Jews' pose as well-wishers who merely found Islam no better than Judaism is exposed as envy, and the claim of Judaism's superiority is left unanswered as an empty assertion, since the later revelation abrogates the earlier.
- Allah chooses whom He wills for His mercy and chose Muḥammad ﷺ for prophethood, and His bounty is boundless.
- The envier does not prevail, and whoever learns sincerely from the Prophet ﷺ shares in the blessing given to him.

106.text:
Verse 106 answers an objection that the Jews, and some idolaters with them, had begun to press on the Muslims. "If We ever abrogate a verse or cause it to be forgotten, We replace it with a better or similar one. Do you not know that Allah is Most Capable of everything". It is the Qur'an's own statement of the principle of abrogation (naskh), and the foundation of a whole branch of Islamic learning.

### Phrase by phrase

**"If We ever abrogate a verse"**. At first the Muslims prayed facing the Bayt al-Maqdis in Jerusalem, and later Allah commanded them to face the Kaʿbah. Certain other rulings too were withdrawn altogether or replaced by others. The Jews, and some of the idolaters, seized on this to taunt the Muslims, saying that the changes were the Prophet's ﷺ own work and not Allah's. The Quraysh said: "Muḥammad, why do you command us to do something and then forbid it?" The disbelievers mocked that one day Muḥammad ﷺ enjoined something on his Companions and the next day forbade it. The aim was to plant doubt in Muslim minds about whether the Qur'an was revealed by Allah at all. Their argument ran like this: if everything Allah reveals is good, as the Muslims say, why should one ruling be replaced by another? That would mean one of the two was good and the other bad, and no divine revelation can be bad, so the Qur'an cannot be a revealed book. The campaign became so intense that some simple-minded Muslims were affected and started raising the question with the Prophet ﷺ. The People of the Book regarded prophethood as their exclusive right. They could not conceive of a prophet among another people and tried every means of discrediting the Arab Prophet ﷺ. One theological objection concerned abrogation. Did replacing a command imply a mistake in Allah's earlier revelation?

The verse refutes the whole line of reasoning. Abrogation does not mean replacing good with bad or bad with good. Everything Allah reveals to His prophets is good, and what is abrogated is as good as what abrogates it. Naskh has two lexical meanings, to write or copy, and to abolish or repeal. All exegetes agree that the second sense, repeal, applies here. In Qur'anic and ḥadīth terminology, naskh therefore means establishing a ruling in place of an earlier one. The later ruling may simply cancel its predecessor or replace it with another regulation. Ibn ʿAbbās, through Ibn Abī Ṭalḥah, glossed the phrase as "whatever verse We abrogate". Mujāhid said "whatever verse We erase", and in another narration, related from the companions of ʿAbdullāh ibn Masʿūd, "We keep the words but change the meaning", which Abū al-ʿĀliyah and Muḥammad ibn Kaʿb al-Quraẓī also said. As-Suddī said "We erase it", and some took it to mean erasing and lifting the wording itself, as happened with the former verses "the married man and the married woman who commit adultery, stone them", and "if the son of Ādam had two valleys of gold he would seek a third". Ibn Jarīr defined it as repealing the ruling of a verse, making the permitted forbidden or the forbidden permitted. Naskh applies only to commands, prohibitions, permissions and the like, never to narratives. Whether the wording is withdrawn, or the ruling, or both, it is called naskh. The abrogation may be of the verse together with its recitation, or of its ruling only while the recitation continues.

**"or cause it to be forgotten"**. The word is read in two ways. Read nunsiʾhā, from "to postpone", it means that Allah defers a verse, withholding its ruling or its recitation, or keeps it in the Preserved Tablet. ʿUbayd ibn ʿUmayr, Mujāhid and ʿAṭāʾ said it means "We delay it", that is, we leave it unabrogated, and ʿAṭiyyah al-ʿAwfī, as-Suddī and ar-Rabīʿ ibn Anas said "We delay repealing it". Ibn ʿAbbās glossed the pair as "whatever verse We repeal or leave standing unchanged", and the companions of Ibn Masʿūd read it as "We keep its wording and change its ruling". Read nunsihā, from "to forget", it means "We make you forget it, erasing it from your heart". Qatādah said that Allah made His Prophet ﷺ forget what He willed and abrogated what He willed. At times Allah did cause the Prophet ﷺ and the Companions to forget a verse entirely, and several instances are related, the purpose usually being to repeal a particular regulation. Between them the two phrases cover every form in which a verse can be abrogated.

**"We replace it with a better or similar one"**. "Better" refers to the benefit of those addressed. Ibn ʿAbbās explained it as a ruling more beneficial and easier for you. As-Suddī said a better verse, or one like the one repealed. Qatādah said a verse that is easier, or that permits, commands or forbids. The replacement is more beneficial for Allah's servants either because it is lighter to carry out or because it carries greater reward, or it is the like of the first in obligation and reward. Allah sends Jibrīl (Gabriel) with what is more profitable and easier to act on, or equal in reward, benefit and practice, more beneficial for the moment or for later. If Allah chooses to withdraw the ruling of a verse while keeping the verse in the Qur'an, or to remove a verse from people's memories altogether, there is nothing objectionable in it.
