He alone knows the wisdom of His choice, He makes such changes for people's good, and He always sends another verse or ruling better than or at least equal to what He withdrew.

**"Do you not know that Allah is Most Capable of everything"**. The question is an affirmation: you know, O Prophet, that Allah has power over all things, including abrogating and substituting verses, over what is abrogated and what is left standing. He does as He wills and rules as He wishes. Being all-powerful and all-knowing, He has the authority to change His commands as He pleases, and He knows what is good for people at any given time and changes His commands accordingly.

### Why abrogation happens

Allah is reminding His servants that He alone owns His creatures and does with them as He wills. His is the supreme authority and all creation is His. His will governs creation and the distribution of happiness and misery, health and sickness, success and failure. He judges His servants and determines what is permitted or forbidden. Nobody can overturn His judgment. He is not questioned about His acts, although His servants are questioned about theirs. Through naskh He tests His servants' obedience to His Messengers. He commands something containing a benefit known to Him, and then in His wisdom forbids it, so that perfect obedience lies in holding to His commands, following His Messengers, believing whatever they bring, carrying out their orders and avoiding what they prohibit.

Making laws and repealing them in favour of new ones is routine in human governments. Human laws are changed sometimes because the lawmakers misjudged the situation when they framed the law and must correct their mistake, and sometimes because a law that suited conditions when it was made no longer suits them after unforeseen change. Neither of these can apply to divine commands. There is a third kind. A lawmaker makes a law knowing full well that circumstances will change so that it will no longer be suitable, and when the change he foresaw arrives he replaces it with the new law he had in mind from the start. A physician knows the patient's present condition requires one medicine. After two days, the anticipated change will require another. The initial prescription and its later replacement are therefore planned together. He could hand the patient written instructions for the whole course with every change marked, but that would overburden an already weak patient and risk harm through error or misunderstanding. This third kind is the only abrogation that can occur, and has occurred, in divine commands and divine Books. Every new Sharīʿah and revealed Book has abrogated many rulings of the earlier one, and within a single Sharīʿah too a law has often been in force for a time and then replaced by divine wisdom with another. Aḥādīth related by Muslim say that there was never a prophethood that did not abrogate some rulings. The principle is not hard to grasp. Only certain Jews, malicious and ignorant, mixed up the divine abrogation of rulings with the two kinds of repeal to which human laws are subject, and these two verses were revealed in reply to their taunts.

### Has abrogation actually occurred?

Some of the Muʿtazilah, apparently wishing to deny the enemies of Islam any occasion for such taunts, tried to explain the whole question away. Abrogation of divine commands is rationally possible, they argued, but it has not actually happened in the Qur'an: no verse abrogates another (nāsikh) and none is abrogated (mansūkh). This view is attributed to Abū Muslim al-Iṣfahānī, and the scholars at large have always rejected it. The people of all revealed laws, it has been said, agree on both the validity of abrogation and its actual occurrence. Only the Jews, apart from their ʿĪsawiyyah sect, denied its possibility, and only Abū Muslim denied its occurrence while granting its possibility. Imām al-Qurṭubī wrote that understanding abrogation is essential, that great benefits flow from it which no scholar can do without, and that none but the ignorant and the dull deny it. He related an illuminating incident. The fourth Caliph (Khalīfah) ʿAlī saw a man preaching in the mosque and asked what he was doing. Told that he was preaching, ʿAlī said that he was doing nothing of the kind, only announcing to the people who he was and whose son he was so that they would know and remember him. He called the man over and asked whether he knew which rulings were abrogated and which had abrogated them. When the man admitted he did not, ʿAlī expelled him from the mosque and forbade him ever to preach there. Numerous sayings of the Companions and their Successors affirm actual abrogation in Qur'anic and ḥadīth rulings. Ibn Jarīr and ad-Durr al-Manthūr gather some with evidence for their soundness. Less strongly attested reports are still more numerous. Hence the consensus of the scholars on naskh, with the exception of Abū Muslim and a few other Muʿtazilah whose position Imām ar-Rāzī exposed in detail.

The word naskh also needs to be used with care. Technically it means changing a ruling and putting another in its place, but the change may be the total repeal of one ruling and its replacement, such as fixing the Kaʿbah as the qiblah instead of the Bayt al-Maqdis, or it may be the retention of a ruling with added conditions and provisos. The scholars of the earliest period used the word in this broad sense, covering total repeal and partial modification alike, which is why they listed some five hundred verses as abrogated. Later scholars counted as naskh only a change that cannot in any way be reconciled with the earlier ruling, which greatly reduces the number. As-Suyūṭī, for instance, counts only twenty such verses. Later still Shāh Walīyullāh, reconciling abrogated rulings with the earlier ones wherever possible, brought the number down to five, the cases where the later ruling cannot be squared with the earlier without far-fetched interpretation. This effort is highly commendable, since the basic presumption behind a ruling is its permanence and abrogation runs against that presumption, so it is improper to assume abrogation in a verse whose ruling can reasonably be shown to be still in force.

The argument rejects a modernist inference from these reduced counts. Reduction does not make abrogation a defect that scholars spent fourteen centuries trying to remove. Shāh Walīyullāh's count of five is not presented as a final discovery on that supposed course. Nor does it imply that later thinkers should bring the number to zero. May Allah forgive the reproduction of such a blasphemy. Such an approach serves neither Islam nor the Qur'an, cannot erase the profound investigations of the Companions, their Successors and the scholars of fourteen hundred years, and will not silence the enemies of Islam. All it does is hand a weapon to present-day detractors and rebels, who would say that what the scholars of the Ummah maintained for fourteen centuries has at last been proved wrong. Open that door and every kind of disorder enters, and every ruling of the Sharīʿah falls under suspicion, with no guarantee that the results of this "modern" research will not themselves prove wrong tomorrow. Certain recent writings revive Abū Muslim's argument through the word mā. They read it as conditional "if" rather than relative "whatever". In their interpretation, "if We abrogate a verse" expresses only a supposition. They compare it with hypothetical sentences introduced by law: "Had there been other gods besides Allah in the heavens or the earth, both ˹realms˺ would have surely been corrupted" (21:22). Another example is "If the Most Compassionate ˹really˺ had offspring, I would be the first worshipper" (43:81). On this basis they argue that abrogation is possible but never occurred. Such writers show little intimate knowledge of Arabic grammar, for a condition expressed by mā is very different from the imaginary situation introduced by law. More to the point, it is on the strength of this very verse that the Companions affirmed the occurrence of abrogation and cited many instances, as did their Successors and all the reliable exegetes, and in the face of such unanimity the new interpretation cannot be accepted. Even Shāh Walīyullāh, while reducing the number, never dreamed of denying the fact. All authoritative scholars from the Companions to the present, including without exception the scholars of Deoband, have affirmed both the possibility and the actual occurrence of abrogation. The detailed rules of naskh are too many and too intricate for a commentary and belong to the books of legal theory.

### The allusion of the mystics

The devotional reading hears in the verse a promise to the Prophet ﷺ himself: We never make you advance beyond the station of servanthood without setting you down in the courtyards of freedom, and never remove one of the attributes of mortal nature from you without making you abide through one of the marks that bear witness to the Divinity. It addresses him as the paragon of the horizons, the messenger to jinn and men, the quintessence of predetermination, the luminous full moon, the totality of perfection, the qiblah of prosperity, the one whose branch of union is in bloom and whose star of exaltedness never stops shining, the one whose good fortune has passed beyond the clouds of being. What others wear as crowns, he wears as sandals, and the sandals thrown from his steed's feet became the crowns of sultans. Even the stations beyond which he is advanced, which are the beautiful deeds of all the friends of God, count as ugly deeds for him while he remains in them, and when he passes beyond them he is to ask forgiveness for them. So the Prophet ﷺ, al-Muṣṭafā, said: "My heart becomes clouded, and I ask forgiveness of Allah seventy times a day." Abū Bakr aṣ-Ṣiddīq said, "Would that I could witness the thing for which God's Messenger asked forgiveness!" Others read the verse as a rule of the spiritual life: the servant is never moved out of one state without being given what lies above and beyond it. In the image, a removed trace of worship gives way to a light of servanthood. That light may in turn give way to a moon of servitude. The servant rises through these stages until an attraction from the Real seizes him. One such attraction outweighs all the deeds of jinn and men.

### In short

- The verse answers the Jews' and idolaters' taunt that changing rulings, such as the qiblah, proved the Qur'an was Muḥammad's ﷺ own work. Abrogation never replaces good with bad, since both the abrogated and the abrogating rulings are from Allah and good.
- Naskh means repealing a ruling, with or without its wording, and "cause it to be forgotten" covers deferral and actual forgetting, so that every form of abrogation is included. The replacement is always better for people or equal to the old.
- Divine abrogation is like a physician's planned change of medicine, foreseen from the start, not a correction of error, and every prophethood abrogated some earlier rulings.
- The Companions, their Successors and the scholars unanimously affirm that abrogation has actually occurred. Only Abū Muslim al-Iṣfahānī and a few Muʿtazilah denied it, and recent attempts to revive their view by reading "if" for "whatever" misread the grammar. The count of abrogated verses ranges from five hundred in the broad early sense to twenty (as-Suyūṭī) or five (Shāh Walīyullāh) in the strict sense.
- Allah's power over all things includes the power to replace His commands, and for the mystic each abrogated station gives way to a higher one.

107.text:
Verse 107 grounds the right to abrogate in the right of ownership. "Do you not know that the kingdom of the heavens and the earth belongs ˹only˺ to Allah, and you have no guardian or helper besides Allah". The One who owns everything may command His subjects as He sees fit, and those who object will find no one to shield them from the consequences.

### Phrase by phrase

**"Do you not know that the kingdom of the heavens and the earth belongs ˹only˺ to Allah"**. O Prophet, you know that the heavens and the earth and all their stores belong to Allah, and that His rule in them is whatever He wills. He commands His servants with whatever He wills because He knows best what is good for them, instructs and forbids as He pleases, establishes the sacred law as He wishes and abolishes what He wishes. Imām Abū Jaʿfar ibn Jarīr paraphrased: "Do you not know, Muḥammad, that I alone own the heavens and the earth and decide in them whatever I will? I forbid what I will, change and repeal whichever of My earlier rulings I will, whenever I will, and I keep in force whatever I will." He added that although Allah addressed this statement of His greatness to His Prophet ﷺ, He was also giving the lie to the Jews, who denied that any ruling of the Torah could be abrogated. The Jews likewise denied the prophethood of ʿĪsā (Jesus) and of Muḥammad ﷺ because they disliked what they brought from Allah, including the change of certain rulings of the Torah by His command. Allah therefore declares His ownership of the heavens and earth and all authority within them. His subjects are His creatures, required to obey His commands and prohibitions. He can establish, repeal or retain any ruling as He wills.

**"and you have no guardian or helper besides Allah"**. Addressed to the Jews, this means that apart from Allah they have no one close enough to benefit or protect them from His torment and no one able to prevent their punishment. For believers, Allah alone is the protector who cares for them. No other helper can keep harm away. He is the Walī, who guards and protects everyone, and His power encompasses everything. As friend, Allah keeps people's good in view when He lays down commands. As helper, He protects the obedient against their enemies. Their blessings in the next world outweigh the harm suffered here. Their enemies' apparent dominance therefore cannot determine their ultimate condition.

### Abrogation in the earlier scriptures

The Jews' refusal to admit abrogation is nothing but unbelief and rebellion. Sound reason does not deny that Allah's commands can be abrogated, since He decrees what He wills just as He does what He wills. And abrogation did occur in the earlier Books and laws. Allah permitted Ādam to marry his daughters to his sons and later forbade it. After the Ark came to rest He permitted Nūḥ (Noah) to eat every kind of animal and later prohibited some foods. Marrying two sisters at once was permitted to Isrāʾīl and his children and later forbidden in the Torah. Allah commanded Ibrāhīm (Abraham) to sacrifice his son and withdrew the command before it was carried out. He commanded the Children of Israel to kill those who had worshipped the calf and then lifted the command so that they would not all be wiped out. There are many other examples which the Jews themselves admit yet ignore. It is well known, too, that their Books foretold Muḥammad ﷺ and commanded them to follow him, so that by their own scriptures they were bound to follow him and no good deed of theirs would be accepted unless it conformed to his Law. He brought another Book, the Qur'an, the last revelation from Allah. These two verses therefore refute the denial of abrogation and expose the unbelief behind it. The discussion rejects the claim that sound reason makes abrogation impossible. Some also alleged that divine texts excluded it. The argument treats these objections as ignorance and arrogance.

### From kingdom to essence

The devotional reading finds in the verse the stages of the spiritual journey. God's way with His friends is to draw them from witnessing what He possesses (milk) to beholding His kingdom (mulk), and from there to witnessing His truth (ḥaqq). Next they are moved on from seeing His signs (āyāt) to seeing His attributes (ṣifāt), and at last from the attributes to the witnessing of the essence (dhāt) itself.

### In short

- Because the whole kingdom of the heavens and the earth is Allah's, He commands, forbids, repeals and retains as He wills, and His subjects have only to hear and obey.
- Ibn Jarīr: the statement, though addressed to the Prophet ﷺ, rebuts the Jews who denied that the Torah's rulings could be abrogated and rejected ʿĪsā and Muḥammad ﷺ for changing them.
- The earlier scriptures themselves record abrogations, from the marriages of Ādam's children and the food of Nūḥ to the sacrifice of Ibrāhīm's son and the killing of the calf-worshippers.
- Apart from Allah no one can protect from His punishment or help against His enemies, so the believer's only guardian is Allah Himself.

108.text:
Verse 108 warns the believers against a habit that had ruined earlier communities. "Or do you ˹believers˺ intend to ask of your Messenger as Moses was asked before? But whoever trades belief for disbelief has truly strayed from the Right Way".

### Phrase by phrase

**"Or do you ˹believers˺ intend to ask of your Messenger"**. Allah forbids the believers to pester the Prophet ﷺ with questions about matters that have not yet arisen, as He says elsewhere: "O believers! Do not ask about any matter which, if made clear to you, may disturb you. But if you inquire about what is being revealed in the Quran, it will be made clear to you" (5:101). Ask about a matter once it has been revealed and it will be explained, but do not ask about what has not happened, for it may become forbidden on account of your asking. The Ṣaḥīḥ records that the greatest offender among the Muslims is the one who asks about something not forbidden and it becomes forbidden because of his question. That is why the Messenger of Allah ﷺ disliked the question put to him about a husband who finds another man with his wife, who would be making public a grave matter if he spoke and staying silent about a grave matter if he did not, until Allah later revealed the ruling of liʿān, the mutual oaths of the spouses (24:6-9). The Two Ṣaḥīḥs record from al-Mughīrah ibn Shuʿbah that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ forbade hearsay, "it was said" and "he said", the wasting of wealth, and asking too many questions. Muslim records that the Prophet ﷺ said: "Leave me alone so long as I leave you alone. Those before you were destroyed only by their excessive questioning and their disputing with their prophets. So when I command you something, do as much of it as you can, and when I forbid you something, keep away from it." He said this after telling the Companions that Allah had commanded them to perform ḥajj. A man asked, "Every year, Messenger of Allah?" The Prophet ﷺ did not answer, and the man repeated the question three times, until the Prophet ﷺ said: "No. Had I said yes it would have become obligatory, and you would not have been able to do it." Anas ibn Mālik said that they were forbidden to question the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, and so were delighted whenever a bedouin came and asked him while they listened.

Not all the questions in view were sincere. Muḥammad ibn Isḥāq related from Ibn ʿAbbās that Rāfiʿ ibn Ḥuraymilah or Wahb ibn Zayd said: "Muḥammad, bring us a Book sent down from heaven that we can read, and make rivers flow for us, and then we will follow you and believe in you." Allah sent down this verse in answer. Ibn ʿAbbās also said that it was revealed about ʿAbdullāh ibn Abī Umayyah and a group of the Quraysh who said: "Muḥammad, turn aṣ-Ṣafā into gold, widen the land of Makkah for us and make rivers gush out all through it, and if you do, we will believe in you." The Makkans asked him to enlarge their city and make aṣ-Ṣafā solid gold. Other reports add that the Jews and the idolaters put all sorts of demands to him. Some said, "Bring us a whole Book from heaven as Mūsā (Moses) brought the Torah." ʿAbdullāh ibn Umayyah al-Makhzūmī said, "Bring us a Book from heaven that reads: from the Lord of the Worlds to Ibn Abī Umayyah, know that I have sent Muḥammad to mankind." Others said, "We will not believe in you until you bring the angels as guarantors." Hostility to the Prophet ﷺ had become so habitual to the Jews that they were forever making insolent demands, once asking him to produce the whole Qur'an at a single stroke, as the Torah had been revealed.

**"as Moses was asked before?"**. Before Muḥammad's ﷺ time the Children of Israel asked Mūsā to let them see their Lord, to hear His speech, and other things of that kind. The Qur'an records in Sūrat an-Nisāʾ that they said, "Show us Allah openly." Allah here censures those who question the Messenger of Allah ﷺ merely to be difficult, just as the Israelites questioned Mūsā out of stubbornness, rejection and rebellion. In such cases the Jews' intention was never to seek guidance, resolve doubts or strengthen faith, but only to cast aspersions on a prophet or call Allah's wisdom into question. Such demands are improper because there is a reason for everything Allah does, but divine wisdom alone knows it. The creature has no right to dictate the precise form his Creator's acts should take. He should not even ask why and wherefore, but accept and submit to the Divine Will. Read as addressed to the Muslims, the verse warns them against making improper demands of the Prophet ﷺ, and against resisting and quarrelling with the revelation as the people of Mūsā did with their prophet.

**"But whoever trades belief for disbelief"**. Whoever prefers disbelief to faith, taking the one in place of the other by declining to reflect on the clear proofs already given and demanding others instead. The verse brands this behaviour as kufr.

**"has truly strayed from the Right Way"**. He has left the straight path for the path of ignorance and misguidance and relinquished the way of guidance. The word for "right" (sawāʾ) basically means the middle, so he has lost the balanced, even road. This is the state of those who turned away from accepting and obeying the prophets and kept putting needless questions to them in defiance and disbelief, of whom Allah said: "Have you not seen those ˹disbelievers˺ who meet Allah’s favours with ingratitude and lead their own people to their doom? In Hell they will burn. What an evil place for settlement" (14:28-29). Abū al-ʿĀliyah summed it up: they exchanged comfort for hardship.

### Awe in the Messenger's presence

The Children of Israel wearied Mūsā, and the Muslims were forbidden to follow their precedent. They were commanded to be mindful of the Messenger's ﷺ modesty as far as they could, so that in his presence they kept an awed silence, as Allah said of him: "support and honour him" (48:9). Beauty of conduct (adab) in outward dealings is the pattern for beauty of conduct with God within. Needless questioning is thus not a small matter of manners. Those before us perished by it, rulings were made harder by it, and the verse places it on the road that leads from belief to disbelief.

### In short

- Believers must not press the Prophet ﷺ with needless questions or demands for signs, as the Israelites pressed Mūsā to show them Allah openly.
- The occasion was the demands of Rāfiʿ ibn Ḥuraymilah or Wahb ibn Zayd and of ʿAbdullāh ibn Abī Umayyah and the Quraysh for a Book from heaven, rivers, and aṣ-Ṣafā turned to gold.
- Excessive questioning destroyed earlier nations and can turn a permitted thing into a forbidden one, so the Prophet ﷺ said, "leave me alone so long as I leave you alone", and the Companions welcomed the bedouin who asked on their behalf (5:101).
- To demand new proofs instead of reflecting on those given is to trade faith for disbelief and to lose the middle road (14:28-29), and reverent silence before the Messenger ﷺ (48:9) is the model of adab with God.

109.text:
Verse 109 names the motive behind the Jews' campaign against the young Muslim community, and tells the believers how to respond for the time being. "Many among the People of the Book wish they could turn you ˹believers˺ back to disbelief because of their envy, after the truth has been made clear to them. Pardon and bear with them until Allah delivers His decision. Surely Allah is Most Capable of everything".

### Phrase by phrase

**"Many among the People of the Book wish they could turn you ˹believers˺ back to disbelief"**. According to Ibn ʿAbbās, the verse came down concerning some Jews who, after the Battle of Uḥud, told the Muslims: "Can you not see what has happened to you? If you were really following the truth you would not have been defeated. Come back to our religion, it is better for you." Ibn Abī Ḥātim records an account conveyed by ʿAbdullāh ibn Kaʿb ibn Mālik from his father. Kaʿb ibn al-Ashraf, a Jewish poet, satirised the Prophet ﷺ in verse. He also used poetry to incite Quraysh's disbelievers against him. The account describes severe harm from al-Madinah's idolaters and Jews when the Messenger ﷺ and his Companions first arrived. Allah commanded His Prophet ﷺ to endure it all and to forgive them, and this passage was revealed about them. One early gloss names Kaʿb ibn al-Ashraf and his companions and Finḥāṣ ibn ʿĀzūrāʾ and his companions as the ones who longed to make the believers abandon their religion, and ʿAmmār ibn Yāsir, Ḥudhayfah ibn al-Yamān and Muʿādh ibn Jabal as those they worked on. "If only", the wording implies, they could make you unbelievers after your faith in Muḥammad ﷺ and the Qur'an, back to worshipping idols as you did before. Allah warns His believing servants against following the ways of the People of the Book, who harbour enmity and hatred for the believers openly and in secret and envy them, even while recognising the merit of the believers and their Prophet ﷺ. Some of the Jews, posing as well-wishers of the Muslims, were forever devising new schemes to turn them from Islam, and did not give up despite repeated failure. Having set their minds against Islam as worthless, they were alarmed by the heartfelt welcome many were giving it. They regarded themselves as the only ones entitled to rule on truth and falsehood, so how could others be allowed to believe what they had chosen to reject? Their first step was to incite the polytheists against the Muslims, and their second was to unsettle the converts with doubts about their new religion in the hope that they would go back to the faith of their fathers.

**"because of their envy"**. The envy sprang from their own souls, which is to say that their wicked souls prompted them to it. Ar-Rabīʿ ibn Anas glossed "from their own selves" as "of their own making". It was resentful envy, arising not from anything the Muslims did but spontaneously from within. Aḍ-Ḍaḥḥāk related Ibn ʿAbbās's explanation: an unlettered Messenger came to the People of the Scripture confirming what their own Books say about the messengers and the signs of Allah, and believing in all of it as they did, yet they rejected him out of disbelief, envy and transgression. After Allah had made the truth plain to them, so that none of it was hidden from them, their envy still drove them to deny the Prophet ﷺ, and for this Allah censured, rebuked and condemned them. Against this He laid down what His Prophet ﷺ and the believers should hold to: belief, faith, and acceptance of the revelation sent to them and of what was sent to those before them, a gift of His generosity and great kindness.

**"after the truth has been made clear to them"**. Abū al-ʿĀliyah explained it this way. Once it was plain to them that Muḥammad ﷺ was Allah's Messenger, the one described in their Torah and Injīl, they still rejected him, in disbelief and transgression, for the sole reason that he did not belong to them. Qatādah and ar-Rabīʿ ibn Anas said the same. The truth about the Prophet ﷺ, his description and his traits, stood in their own Book. A modern writer adds that accepting the truth means negating the self, something people of high standing always find hard, and hardest of all for the People of the Book, who thought prophethood their exclusive right.

**"Pardon and bear with them until Allah delivers His decision"**. Leave them be, keep away from them and make no move against them, pardoning what they do and overlooking their ignorance and whatever is bad in them, until Allah's command about them comes. The command meant fighting them, and it came in the form of Islam, the jizyah or the sword. One gloss has it that the decision was the punishment Allah brought on Banū Qurayẓah and Banū an-Naḍīr by killing, captivity and expulsion. The instruction resembles Allah's words, "you will certainly hear many hurtful words from those who were given the Scripture before you and ˹from˺ the polytheists. But if you are patient and mindful" (3:186). Ibn ʿAbbās, through ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭalḥah, said this pardon was abrogated by "kill the polytheists ˹who violated their treaties˺ wherever you find them" (9:5) and by "Fight those who do not believe in Allah and the Last Day, nor comply with what Allah and His Messenger have forbidden, nor embrace the religion of truth from among those who were given the Scripture, until they pay the tax, willingly submitting" (9:29). Abū al-ʿĀliyah, ar-Rabīʿ ibn Anas, Qatādah and as-Suddī likewise said it was abrogated by the verse of the sword, and the words "until Allah delivers His decision" themselves point that way. Ibn Abī Ḥātim also records Usāmah ibn Zayd's account. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ and his Companions regularly forgave the disbelievers and the People of the Book, obeying Allah's command. He remained patient until permission to fight came. Allah then brought about the killing, through the Prophet's ﷺ forces, of those Quraysh chiefs whose deaths He had decreed. The chain of this text is ṣaḥīḥ, and though its wording is not found in the six collections, its basis is in the Two Ṣaḥīḥs from Usāmah ibn Zayd.

The Muslims were asked not to give way to a justified anger at such misconduct but to forgive and wait for a fresh command on the matter. The verse thus hints that Allah would soon lay down a law for preserving peace and order on earth that would guide the Muslims in dealing with mischief-makers, namely the permission to make war on the enemies of Islam. The command of forbearance suited the Muslims' situation at that time. Later Allah fulfilled the promise by revealing the ruling on jihād. The account applies it to the Jews and other troublemakers alike. The Muslims fought to prevent disorder and establish peace. Those causing mischief were killed, exiled or required to pay jizyah. This levy applies to non-Muslims under the Islamic state's protection and exempts them from military service. The provocation was natural, but God told the believers it was not the moment for a violent reaction. Patience keeps a person from negative retaliation in the heat of the moment.

**"Surely Allah is Most Capable of everything"**. The Muslims knew their own weakness and the strength of their enemy and might have wondered how they could ever act on such a law, so the verse reminds them that Allah's power covers everything, small or great, ordinary or extraordinary, including the death and expulsion of their enemies. He is able to do all things, and their plotting does not touch Him.

### Envy and the traveller

The devotional reading says that the heedless who have lost all understanding wish that not a single star would rise over those who live in peace and safety (salāmah), and that the envious would like the sun to stop shining on those they envy. These are the attributes of disbelievers, and God abases and humbles them. The allusion is to the state of those with spiritual desire (irādah) when they first set out on their travels. Without the help of good companionship, they may remain among people concerned only with externals. Such people obstruct their journey through repeated "advice". They frighten the seekers with weakness and poverty. Eventually they divert them into heedlessness and sever their spiritual desire. Such people are truly God's enemies, overcome by the enmity of the moment, and their punishment is to be denied the least scent of the fragrance of sincerity (ṣidq). "Pardon and bear with them", because the aspirant's way is to guard his innermost self from everything other than God, to show his best nature to everyone, and to spare no effort in kindness, for the Real will soon open the way before him.

### In short

- After Uḥud, and from the day the Prophet ﷺ arrived, Jews such as Kaʿb ibn al-Ashraf and Finḥāṣ ibn ʿĀzūrāʾ worked to turn the believers back to unbelief, incited Quraysh and sowed doubts among converts.
- Their motive was envy from within themselves, not any wrong done to them, and it operated after the truth about the Prophet ﷺ stood plain in the Torah and the Injīl.
- The command to pardon and bear with them was for that stage only. Ibn ʿAbbās and others say it was abrogated by the verses of fighting (9:5, 9:29), when Allah's decision came as Islam, jizyah or war.
- Allah's power over all things answered the Muslims' sense of weakness, and for the spiritual traveller the verse teaches patience with those who would frighten him off the path.

110.text:
Verse 110 tells the believers what to do while they wait. "Establish prayer, and pay alms-tax. Whatever good you send forth for yourselves, you will ˹certainly˺ find ˹its reward˺ with Allah. Surely Allah is All-Seeing of what you do".

### Phrase by phrase

**"Establish prayer, and pay alms-tax"**. Having commanded them to forgive and be patient until His help and victory came, Allah commanded the believers to perform the prayer perfectly and to pay the zakāh, and urged them to keep up these righteous deeds. Establishing prayer means perfecting the five daily prayers with all their parts, obligatory and recommended. Paying the alms-tax means giving the poor their due from one's wealth, zakāh to those entitled to it. Until the law of jihād came down, the Muslims were to go on praying and paying zakāh, and when it came they could add fighting in Allah's cause to the good deeds they were already doing. They were not to imagine that until they could take part in jihād mere prayer and fasting would fail to earn the spiritual merit they longed for. Steadfastness in prayer brings a person closer to God, and never failing in the prescribed alms builds a society in which the rich share willingly with the poor, a society founded on compassion with a real sense of togetherness among its members.

**"Whatever good you send forth for yourselves, you will ˹certainly˺ find ˹its reward˺ with Allah"**. Whatever righteous deeds, alms and charitable works you lay up for yourselves, and whatever acts of obedience such as maintaining kinship ties and giving charity, you will find their reward with Allah. Every good act done in life before death becomes a treasure whose reward will be found with the Lord on the Day of Judgement. Allah encourages the believers to busy themselves with deeds that will profit them and earn reward on the Day of Resurrection, prayer and zakāh above all, so that they gain His help in this life and on "the Day the wrongdoers’ excuses will be of no benefit to them. They will be condemned, and will have the worst outcome" (40:52). Not a particle of anyone's good deeds will be lost.

**"Surely Allah is All-Seeing of what you do"**. He knows your intentions and sees what you spend in charity and zakāh. He is never unaware of anyone's deeds and never lets them go to waste. Righteous or evil, every deed will be requited exactly as it deserves.

### The aspirant's obligation

For the devotional reading, the aspirant's duty is to perform the acts of intimate communion (muwāṣalāt) and to keep seeking access to God through every kind of act that draws near (qurubāt), trusting that what he offers in sincere, strenuous effort (mujāhadāt) will bear fruit in the final states (ḥālāt). What is sent ahead in this world is found again in the next.

### In short

- While pardoning their enemies, the believers were to perfect their prayers and pay zakāh, the deeds that would later be joined by jihād.
- Whatever good a person sends ahead is stored up with Allah and found again on the Day when excuses will not help (40:52).
- Allah sees every deed and intention and lets none of it be lost.

111.text:
Verse 111 confronts a claim that both communities of the People of the Book made against everyone else. "The Jews and Christians each claim that none will enter Paradise except those of their own faith. These are their desires. Reply, ˹O Prophet,˺ “Show ˹me˺ your proof if what you say is true.”".

### Phrase by phrase

**"The Jews and Christians each claim that none will enter Paradise except those of their own faith"**. The Jews said no one would enter Paradise unless he died a Jew, and the Christians made the same claim for themselves. The Jews of al-Madinah and the Christians of Najrān both said this when they argued before the Prophet ﷺ, each party separately reserving Paradise for its own members. The Arabic word for Jews here, hūd, is the plural of hāʾid. Allah lays bare the confusion of the two communities, who likewise claimed, as the Qur'an reports in Sūrat al-Māʾidah, "“We are the children of Allah and His most beloved!” Say, ˹O Prophet,˺ “Why then does He punish you for your sins?" (5:18). Allah refuted that claim and told them they would be punished for their sins, just as He rebuked their earlier claim that the Fire would touch them only for a few days before they were admitted to Paradise. The Jews used to tell new converts that if they must leave their ancestral religion they should become Jews or Christians, since those descended from saints and prophets through history were the ones bound for heaven. Hostile not only to the Muslims but to each other, both groups had forgotten the essence of religion, which is holding true and sound beliefs and performing the good deeds the Sharīʿah prescribes, and had reduced it to membership of a racial or social community. Each claimed an exclusive right to Paradise without a single argument to support it.

**"These are their desires"**. Abū al-ʿĀliyah said these were wishes they hoped Allah would grant them, with no foundation. Qatādah and ar-Rabīʿ ibn Anas said the same. They are false passions, vain wishes and imaginings, things they want from Allah even though nothing in their Books supports them. The Qur'an dismisses such pretensions as fancy and self-delusion. No one earns entry into heaven by belonging to a particular community. Everyone will be judged by his own actions, and national standing counts for nothing in the sight of God.

**"Reply, ˹O Prophet,˺ “Show ˹me˺ your proof if what you say is true.”"**. Say to both parties: bring your burhān, your proof. Abū al-ʿĀliyah, Mujāhid, as-Suddī and ar-Rabīʿ ibn Anas explained burhān as proof, and Qatādah as the evidence that supports your statement. The proof was to come from their own respective Books, if they were truthful in their claim. The Qur'an does not simply contradict them. It asks for evidence, and the demand is itself the refutation, since none was forthcoming.

### Guessing is not proof

The devotional reading remarks that every party (ḥizb) smooths things over for itself, convinced that salvation belongs to it and claiming Paradise as its portion. But mere supposition (ḥusbān) without the verification of proof (burhān) yields no result and is of no use. The next verse supplies the standard that applies to everyone alike.

### In short

- The Jews of al-Madinah and the Christians of Najrān each claimed Paradise for their own community exclusively, as they also claimed to be Allah's children and beloved (5:18).
- Such claims are wishes with no basis in their Books, the product of reducing religion to communal membership.
- Allah's answer is a demand for proof, and supposition without proof settles nothing.

112.text:
Verse 112 replaces the communal claims of the previous verse with the only standard that counts. "But no! Whoever submits themselves to Allah and does good will have their reward with their Lord. And there will be no fear for them, nor will they grieve".

### Phrase by phrase

**"But no!"**. It is certainly not as they claim. Others too will enter Paradise, and the door is defined by two conditions rather than by lineage or label.

**"Whoever submits themselves to Allah"**. Literally, whoever submits his face to Allah. The face is mentioned because it is the noblest part of the body, so that once it has submitted the other members have all the more reason to follow. Abū al-ʿĀliyah and ar-Rabīʿ said it means whoever is sincere with Allah, and Saʿīd ibn Jubayr said it means being sincere in one's religion. It is to perform one's deeds purely for Allah without partner, to make one's religion and works sincere for Him, and to adhere to His commands. The same expression appears when Allah tells His Prophet ﷺ: "So if they argue with you ˹O Prophet˺, say, “I have submitted myself to Allah, and so have my followers.”" (3:20).

**"and does good"**. He is a muḥsin, one who does what is beautiful in word and deed, who affirms Allah's oneness and follows the Messenger ﷺ. Two conditions must be met for a deed to be accepted: it must be done for Allah's sake alone, and it must conform to the Sharīʿah. A deed that is sincere but does not conform to the Sharīʿah is not accepted. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said, in a ḥadīth recorded by Muslim, that whoever does a deed that is not in accordance with our religion will have it rejected. For this reason the good deeds of the priests and rabbis are not accepted even when done sincerely for Allah alone, because they do not follow the way of the Messenger ﷺ, who was sent to all mankind. Of such cases Allah said: "Then We will turn to whatever ˹good˺ deeds they did, reducing them to scattered dust" (25:23), and "As for the disbelievers, their deeds are like a mirage in a desert, which the thirsty perceive as water, but when they approach it, they find it to be nothing" (24:39), and "On that Day ˹some˺ faces will be downcast, ˹totally˺ overburdened, exhausted, burning in a scorching Fire, left to drink from a scalding spring" (88:2-5). Conversely, a deed that conforms to the Sharīʿah outwardly but is not done sincerely for Allah is also rejected, as with the hypocrites and those who act to be seen: "Surely the hypocrites seek to deceive Allah, but He outwits them. When they stand up for prayer, they do it half-heartedly only to be seen by people" (4:142), and, in Sūrat al-Māʿūn, "So woe to those ˹hypocrites˺ who pray, yet are unmindful of their prayers, those who ˹only˺ show off, and refuse to give ˹even the simplest˺ aid" (107:4-7). Hence Allah's words: "So whoever hopes for the meeting with their Lord, let them do good deeds and associate none in the worship of their Lord" (18:110).

This is the general principle, accepted by the followers of every revealed Book. The essence of religion, whether Islam, Christianity or Judaism, lies in two things. One should obey Allah in belief and in action, and this obedience should spring not from expediency but from a sincere surrender to divine commands. Nor is it enough, to merit Paradise, to have a sincere intention to obey and then to invent the forms of obedience according to one's own fancy. Worship and obedience must take the forms Allah appointed through His prophets. Since the revelation of the Qur'an, this means accepting and following the Islamic Sharīʿah. For the first principle the Qur'an uses the word aslama, total submission to Allah, and for the second muḥsin, one who does good deeds in accordance with the Sharīʿah. Paradise is therefore open to others besides the Jews and Christians, to all who in their own time followed the Sharīʿah of their own prophet and who, now that the Qur'an has abrogated the earlier Books, follow the Islamic Sharīʿah. Whoever sincerely turns to Allah, does good, serves Him and follows what the Prophet ﷺ brought will enter Paradise whatever group he comes from. And whatever a person's original religious community, Jew, Christian, idolater or other, submission to Allah is now valid before Him only by becoming Muslim, after the coming of Muḥammad ﷺ. Having laid down the two principles, the Qur'an invites the disputants to see who is actually acting on them. One who goes on following a ruling after it has been abrogated cannot be called obedient, so the Jews and Christians no longer qualify. After abrogation, obedience means acting on the new ruling that replaced the old, and only the Muslims, who accepted the last Prophet and his Sharīʿah, fulfil this condition. The condition of sincerity excludes the hypocrites as well, whom the Sharīʿah counts among the unbelievers and assigns to Hell. To be sincere in faith is to become so devoted to God that everything else becomes secondary, so that prejudice, personal loyalties and worldly interests never stand in the way of answering the call of truth.

**"will have their reward with their Lord"**. The reward of their deeds, which is Paradise. Allah guarantees them their recompense and safety from what they fear.

**"And there will be no fear for them, nor will they grieve"**. No fear of what lies ahead in the Hereafter, no fear of staying for ever in Hell, and no grief over what they left behind, no grief at the prospect of missing Paradise or over what passed them by in life. Saʿīd ibn Jubayr said: no fear in the Hereafter, and no grief at the approach of death. On the Day of Judgement they will have nothing to fear and nothing to mourn, for the angels will bring them good news.

### A warning for Muslims too

These verses warn the Muslims as well, lest they delude themselves like the Jews and Christians and suppose that merely belonging to the Muslim community, and being able to call themselves Muslims, excuses them from obeying Allah and following the Sharīʿah while still entitling them to the rewards promised to true Muslims. Even Muslims have no right to hope for those rewards until they submit totally, in thought and deed, to the commands of Allah and His Prophet ﷺ.

### Purified, not merely purifying

The devotional reading calls the work described here the work of the purifiers, the good fortune of the truthful, the conduct of the pure, and the hard cash in their purse. Today their seat is the carpet of service, lit by recognition, and tomorrow it will be the carpet of companionship, with the joy of union. Allah says of such people, "We truly chose them for the honour of proclaiming the Hereafter" (38:46). He made them pure and brought them through testing in purity. They were thereby fitted for the Presence. The Pure Presence admits only the pure, and Allah is good and accepts only what is good. Nothing avails there but pure action and pure speech, and then one must become so purified even of that pure action that one no longer seeks it in this world or the next, and so reach God pure: "And he will indeed have ˹a status of˺ closeness to Us and an honourable destination" (38:40). Abū Bakr az-Zaqqāq put the secret of it this way: the defect in every purifier's purity is that he sees his own purity, and if God wishes to purify a man's self-purification He removes from it his seeing of it, so that he becomes "purified" (mukhlaṣ) rather than "purifying" (mukhliṣ). Your sincerity is pure when it is pure of your watching it. This sincerity, moreover, is not in your hands or within your power. It is a secret of the Lord deposited by the Glorified, which no one knows and no one else can reach. The One says: it is one of My secrets that I place in the hearts of those of My servants whom I love. I choose a servant, approve him for My love and lay My deposit in the core of his heart, where Satan cannot reach to destroy it, nor the soul's caprice see it to change it, nor the angel reach it to write it down.

### In short

- Paradise belongs not to a community but to whoever submits himself wholly to Allah and does good, the two conditions being sincerity and conformity to the Sharīʿah of the final Prophet ﷺ.
- A sincere deed outside the Prophet's ﷺ way is rejected (25:23, 24:39, 88:2-5), and a correct deed done for show is rejected too (4:142, 107:4-7). Both conditions are joined in 18:110.
- After the Qur'an abrogated the earlier Books, only the Muslims meet the test of obedience, but Muslims who rely on the name alone are warned just as sternly.
- Such people have their reward with their Lord, with no fear ahead and no grief behind, and the highest sincerity is to be purified even of seeing one's own purity.

113.text:
Verse 113 shows that the two communities who each claimed Paradise for themselves could not even agree with each other. "The Jews say, “The Christians have nothing to stand on” and the Christians say, “The Jews have nothing to stand on,” although both recite the Scriptures. And those ˹pagans˺ who have no knowledge say the same ˹about people of faith˺. Surely Allah will judge between them on the Day of Judgment regarding their dispute".

### Phrase by phrase

**"The Jews say, “The Christians have nothing to stand on” and the Christians say, “The Jews have nothing to stand on”"**. Allah exposes the disputes, hatred and obstinacy the People of the Book direct at one another. Muḥammad ibn Isḥāq reported from Ibn ʿAbbās that when the Christian delegation of Najrān arrived to see the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, the Jewish rabbis turned up and started arguing with them in his presence. The debate grew so heated that they shouted at each other. Rāfiʿ ibn Ḥuraymilah said, "You follow nothing", and declared his disbelief in ʿĪsā (Jesus) and the Injīl, and a Christian of the Najrān delegation answered, "No, it is you who follow nothing", and declared his rejection of Mūsā's (Moses') prophethood and the Torah. Then Allah revealed this verse. The Jews of al-Madinah said the Christians had no religion from God and that there was no true religion but Judaism, and the Christians of Najrān said the Jews had no religion from God and that there was no true religion but Christianity. Each party asserted out of malice that the other's religion had nothing to support it.

**"although both recite the Scriptures"**. Each party could read in its own Book the confirmation of the very thing it denied. The Jews reject ʿĪsā although they have the Torah, in which Allah took their covenant through Mūsā to believe in ʿĪsā, and the Christians reject Mūsā although the Gospel contains ʿĪsā's affirmation that Mūsā's prophethood and the Torah came from Allah. Yet each disbelieved in what the other had. The Jews read the Torah and the Christians read the Gospel, and they could easily have seen that the two Books confirm each other and that both command faith in all the prophets without distinction. Both parties read the Book, failed to believe in it, and then claimed things it never says. The clause describes their state: they say this while reciting the Scripture.

**"And those ˹pagans˺ who have no knowledge say the same ˹about people of faith˺"**. Allah thus exposes the ignorance of the Jews and the Christians in what they said, by likening them to those without knowledge. Who these are is disputed. Ar-Rabīʿ ibn Anas and Qatādah said the Christians said the like of what the Jews said. Ibn Jurayj asked ʿAṭāʾ who "those who have no knowledge" were, and he answered that they were the nations of old, earlier than the Jews and the Christians and earlier than the Torah and the Gospel. As-Suddī said they are the Arabs, who said that Muḥammad ﷺ followed nothing. Abū Jaʿfar ibn Jarīr preferred to take the verse generally, since no evidence singles out any one of these explanations, and the general reading is better, and Allah knows best. The ignorant among the Arabs and others said to every person of religion, "You have no basis." The polytheists, for all their ignorance, seized the excuse the two communities gave them and said the same of both religions. One gloss explains "those who have no knowledge" as people who knew Allah's oneness only through their forefathers, or who knew Allah's Book only at second hand. In this they resemble people who know nothing at all, who worship others beside Allah and reject every prophet and scripture. For the Israelites, truth was measured by their link with the prophets and the saints, and so their own community was right and every other wrong. The Christians thought themselves unique because God's "beloved son" had been sent to them. Even the polytheists of Makkah thought themselves superior as guardians of God's Sacred House. Every nation had set up its own self-made religious standard by which it inevitably came out right and everyone else wrong, while their actions did nothing to bear out their claims.

**"Surely Allah will judge between them on the Day of Judgment regarding their dispute"**. Allah will gather them all on the Day of Return and judge between them justly, for He wrongs no one by so much as an atom's weight. He will admit the one who confirmed the truth to Paradise and the one who denied it to the Fire. The verse resembles His words in Sūrat al-Ḥajj: "Indeed, the believers, Jews, Sabians, Christians, Magi, and the polytheists—Allah will judge between them ˹all˺ on Judgment Day. Surely Allah is a Witness over all things" (22:17), and "Say, “Our Lord will gather us together, then He will judge between us with the truth. For He is the All-Knowing Judge.”" (34:26). In truth the question has already been settled, by what Allah revealed in His Books and by rational argument. The judgement of the Last Day will be the visible kind, when the followers of truth are sent to Paradise and the followers of falsehood cast into Hell. Through His perfect and just judgements Allah teaches His servants that no one succeeds without believing in all that He revealed.

### The friends who quarrel

The devotional reading turns the verse's apparent sense on its head. Today God's enemies disown one another as they always have, but the friends of God do something of the kind as well. The saying goes that the Sufis stay in a good state only so long as they quarrel and decline to accept one another, since acceptance would make them settle down with each other instead of turning to God.

### In short

- When the Najrān Christians met the rabbis before the Prophet ﷺ, each side declared the other's religion baseless, the Jews denying ʿĪsā and the Gospel and the Christians denying Mūsā and the Torah.
- Each denied what its own Scripture confirms, since the Torah pledges faith in ʿĪsā and the Gospel affirms Mūsā.
- The ignorant pagans, Arabs or earlier nations, said the same of everyone, and Ibn Jarīr took the phrase generally.
- Allah will judge all parties on the Day of Judgement (22:17, 34:26), a judgement already settled in substance by revelation and reason.

114.text:
Verse 114 turns from the quarrels of the People of the Book to a wrong that idolaters and others had committed against the houses of Allah. "Who does more wrong than those who prevent Allah’s Name from being mentioned in His places of worship and strive to destroy them? Such people have no right to enter these places except with fear. For them is disgrace in this world, and they will suffer a tremendous punishment in the Hereafter". It is at once a condemnation, a prophecy and the basis of several rulings about mosques.

### Phrase by phrase

**"Who does more wrong than those who prevent Allah’s Name from being mentioned in His places of worship"**. No one does greater wrong. The places of worship are where Allah's Name is invoked in prayer and praise, and barring them means stopping the prayer, the remembrance of Allah and the recitation of the Qur'an within them. Ibn Jarīr reported from Ibn Zayd that the verse concerns the idolaters of Quraysh, who stopped the Prophet ﷺ entering Makkah from al-Ḥudaybiyyah, so that he slaughtered his sacrificial animals at Dhū Ṭuwā. He then made a peace treaty with them and said to them that no one before had ever barred people from the House: a man might see the killer of his own father or brother there and still not keep him from the House of Allah. They answered that whoever had killed their fathers at Badr would never enter it while one of them was alive. Ibn Abī Ḥātim recorded from Ibn ʿAbbās that the verse was revealed when Quraysh stopped the Prophet ﷺ praying at the Kaʿbah inside al-Masjid al-Ḥarām. Having rebuked the Jews and the Christians, Allah now rebukes the idolaters who drove the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and his Companions out of Makkah and kept them from praying in the Sacred Mosque, which they reserved for their idols and their polytheism. Allah said of them: "And why should Allah not punish them while they hinder pilgrims from the Sacred Mosque, claiming to be its rightful guardians? None has the right to guardianship except those mindful ˹of Allah˺, but most pagans do not know" (8:34), its rightful guardians being the God-fearing (al-muttaqūn), and "It is not for the polytheists to maintain the mosques of Allah while they openly profess disbelief. Their deeds are void, and they will be in the Fire forever" (9:17), and "They are the ones who persisted in disbelief and hindered you from the Sacred Mosque, preventing the sacrificial animals from reaching their destination" (48:25).

A second view relates the verse to earlier history. It was revealed, some say, to tell of the Byzantines' destruction of the Holy House in Jerusalem. One early gloss names Ṭīṭūs son of Asipanos the Roman (ar-Rūmī), king of the Christians, who destroyed Jerusalem, barred Allah's sanctuary there to the declaration of His oneness and the call to prayer, and strove to ruin it by having carrion thrown into it, a state of affairs that lasted until the reign of ʿUmar. On this reading "such people" are the Romans, who could enter Jerusalem only in hiding from the believers for fear of being killed, their worldly disgrace being the ruin of their cities, Constantinople, Amorium and Rome, and their punishment in the Hereafter harsher than anything they suffered here. A modern reflection widens the charge to every community of the time. All of them, though sworn to the divine scriptures, had split into sects, and each seized every chance to deny others the right to enter places of worship, claiming to be protecting their sanctity. In truth they were ruining them, for a place of worship falls derelict when people are refused the right to worship there. A worshipper with the right attitude never denies that right to those who come to pray and never persecutes those who come to serve the Lord. Whoever is truly conscious of God's greatness and his own helplessness before Him shows his humility in his dealings with others, and will not harm his fellow men in any way, let alone deny them the basic right to worship God.

**"and strive to destroy them?"**. Through demolition, and through keeping people away. The idolaters were preventing those who kept the mosques alive with Allah's remembrance and who came to His House for ḥajj and ʿumrah. Allah said: "The mosques of Allah should only be maintained by those who believe in Allah and the Last Day, establish prayer, pay alms-tax, and fear none but Allah. It is right to hope that they will be among the ˹truly˺ guided" (9:18). If believers of this description are barred from the mosque, what ruin could be worse? Maintaining mosques does not mean beautifying them. It means remembering Allah in them, establishing His Sharīʿah in them, and purifying them of the filth of shirk. If the verse was revealed at the Peace of al-Ḥudaybiyyah, when the idolaters of Makkah barred the Muslims from the Sacred Mosque, then it is obvious that laying a mosque waste does not only mean pulling it down. It also means not letting it be used for the purpose it was built for, the prayer (ṣalāh) and the remembrance (dhikr) of Allah.

**"Such people have no right to enter these places except with fear"**. The phrase is a statement that also works as a command: frighten them with the threat of war so that not one of them enters feeling secure. Do not let the disbelievers into the mosques except under the terms of a truce or treaty. When the Messenger of Allah ﷺ had conquered Makkah, he had it proclaimed at Minā in the ninth year that after that year no idolater would perform ḥajj and no naked person would circle the House in ṭawāf, except that whoever had a treaty would be allowed to see it out to its term. This agrees with the verse: "O believers! Indeed, the polytheists are ˹spiritually˺ impure, so they should not approach the Sacred Mosque after this year" (9:28). Those who tried to destroy Allah's houses should enter them only fearfully, with trembling hearts, after their disbelief and their obstruction of worship. It has also been said that the verse brings the Muslims good news from Allah that He will give them al-Masjid al-Ḥarām and all the mosques and disgrace the idolaters, so that soon no idolater would enter the House except in fear of being seized or killed, unless he accepted Islam. Allah fulfilled the promise and later decreed that idolaters be kept out of the Sacred Mosque. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ declared that two religions should not remain in the Arabian Peninsula. He also directed the expulsion of the Jews and Christians. These rulings are presented as protecting the Sacred Mosque's honour and purifying the land of his mission. Allah sent him there to warn and bring good news to all mankind.

**"For them is disgrace in this world"**. Debasement through being killed, taken captive and made to pay the jizyah, shame and humiliation on earth at the hands of the believers. The punishment matched the deed. As they had kept the believers out of the Sacred Mosque, they were kept out of it in turn, and as they had expelled the believers from Makkah, they were expelled from Makkah themselves.

**"and they will suffer a tremendous punishment in the Hereafter"**. The Fire, because they violated the sanctity of the House and defiled it, setting up idols around it, calling on others besides Allah and circling it naked. Here belongs the ḥadīth on seeking refuge from disgrace in this world and torment in the next. Imām Aḥmad recorded from Busr ibn Arṭāh that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ used to pray: "O Allah, make the end of all our affairs good, and save us from disgrace in this world and the punishment of the Hereafter." This ḥadīth is ḥasan.

### Rulings drawn from the verse

The verse lays down, or allows us to infer, several important rulings. First, all the mosques in the world deserve respect alike. Just as it is a grave sin to desecrate the Bayt al-Maqdis, the mosque around the Kaʿbah or the mosque of the Prophet ﷺ in any way, the same prohibition protects every other mosque. The three do enjoy a higher rank and a special reverence. One prayer in al-Masjid al-Ḥarām equals a hundred thousand prayers elsewhere, and a prayer in the Prophet's ﷺ mosque or in the Bayt al-Maqdis equals fifty thousand. Travelling far to pray in one of these three is a meritorious act that earns a special blessing (barakah), whereas the Prophet ﷺ forbade setting out on a long journey to pray in any other mosque in the belief that doing so is meritorious.

Second, it is forbidden to hinder people in any way from praying or remembering Allah in a mosque. The obvious form is to refuse someone entry, or to stop him praying or reading the Qur'an there. A subtler form is to make noise inside the mosque or play music nearby, disturbing people at prayer or in remembrance. Likewise, reciting the Qur'an or making dhikr aloud so as to disturb those offering voluntary prayers (nawāfil), reading the Qur'an or remembering Allah silently is the same sin, and the jurists (fuqahāʾ) have forbidden it, though when no one else is present one may recite or make dhikr aloud. By the same principle it is forbidden to beg or collect donations, even for a religious purpose, while people are busy praying or making dhikr.

Third, every form of laying a mosque waste is forbidden, not only demolishing it but also creating conditions that leave it deserted, for a mosque is laid waste when few come to pray in it. A mosque flourishes not through the beauty of its architecture or decoration but only when it is full of people who come to pray and remember Allah, as 9:18 indicates. The Prophet ﷺ foretold that as the Day of Judgement draws near the mosques of the Muslims will be beautifully built and decorated and apparently full, yet in reality deserted, because few will go there to pray. ʿAlī, the fourth Caliph, said that six things befit a man, three at home and three on a journey. At home: to read the Qur'an, to populate the mosques, and to gather friends who wish to serve Allah and His religion. On a journey: to spend on needy companions of the road, to be courteous to everyone, and to be cheerful with fellow travellers within the limits the Sharīʿah allows. By "populating" the mosques he meant entering them humbly with the fear of Allah in one's heart and then busying oneself with prayer, recitation or dhikr. The opposite, laying them waste, is when few pray in them or when circumstances are allowed to arise that make it hard for those present to attain the proper humility.

### A note on the verse that follows

The verse that comes next (2:115) says that wherever one turns there is the Face of Allah. Since Allah is not confined to any direction or place, the Muslims who face the Kaʿbah do not worship it. The orientation was fixed for other reasons. For sixteen or seventeen months after the Hijrah the Prophet ﷺ and the Companions were commanded to face the Bayt al-Maqdis in prayer, a practical demonstration that Allah can be found in every direction and that His attention embraces all directions and dimensions at once. The ruling on voluntary prayers (nawāfil) gives permanent expression to the same truth. One who wishes to pray them while riding a horse or a camel need not face the qiblah at all. He may face the direction in which his mount is moving and pray by gestures of the head and arms, and some scholars hold that 2:115 lays down exactly this rule. The concession applies only to travel on animals, where turning to the qiblah is difficult. In a train, ship or aeroplane, facing the qiblah is not difficult. The proper orientation must therefore be adopted even for voluntary prayers. If the train or aeroplane changes direction and there is no room to adjust, the prayer may be completed as it stands. Similarly, if a person cannot tell the direction of the qiblah, because of the darkness of night or some other valid reason, and can find no one to inform him, he may follow his best estimate and face the direction that seems most likely, and that direction serves as his qiblah. If after the prayer he discovers he was wrong, the prayer remains valid and need not be repeated.

### The three homelands

The devotional reading asks, by way of allusion: who does greater wrong than one who ruins the homeland of worship with appetites, the homeland of recognition with attachments, and the homeland of contemplation by glancing at others? The first homeland, that of worship, is the renunciant's soul. The second, that of recognition, is the heart of one who knows God. The third, that of contemplation, is the secret core of His friends. Whoever keeps his soul from appetites makes the homeland of his worship flourish, and his name is entered in the register of the renunciants. Mālik ibn Dīnār lived forty years in Basra and died without ever eating or tasting its dates, fresh or dried, and when asked about it said that the possessor of appetite is veiled from his Lord. Whoever keeps his heart clear of attachments makes the homeland of his recognition flourish and joins the ranks of the recognisers. A companion of Ibrāhīm ibn Adham told how, on a journey, hunger overtook them. After they had settled in a mosque Ibrāhīm brought out some sections of the Qur'an he carried and told him to go and pawn them for something to eat. On his way out he was met by a man leading a fully laden mule and asking for a fair-skinned man named Ibrāhīm ibn Adham. Asked what he wanted, the man said he was the slave of Ibrāhīm's father and that the goods belonged to Ibrāhīm. Brought into the mosque, he placed his head and hands on the ground and kissed Ibrāhīm. He announced the death of Ibrāhīm's father. He had brought forty thousand dinars as the inheritance. He added, "I am your slave, command me as you wish." Ibrāhīm replied: "If you are telling the truth, then you are free for the sake of God, and everything you have with you is a gift to you. Leave us." The man who had just sent his Qur'an to be pawned for bread gave away a fortune on the spot rather than let an attachment settle in his heart, and the mosque in which he sat remained, in the allusive sense, a flourishing house of God.

### In short

- The verse condemns those who bar Allah's houses to His remembrance and work to ruin them, above all the Quraysh who kept the Prophet ﷺ from the Sacred Mosque at al-Ḥudaybiyyah (8:34, 9:17, 48:25), and by another view the Romans who devastated Jerusalem.
- Ruining a mosque includes keeping it from its purpose, and only believers who pray, pay zakāh and fear Allah truly maintain it (9:18).
- The idolaters were to enter only in fear, and after the conquest were excluded from the Sacred Mosque altogether (9:28). Their disgrace mirrored their deed, and a tremendous punishment awaits them in the Hereafter.
- All mosques are inviolable, though the three great mosques rank highest. Hindering worship, even by noise or collecting money during prayer, is forbidden, and a mosque lives by its worshippers, not its decoration.
- In allusion, appetites, attachments and glancing at others lay waste the inner sanctuaries of worship, recognition and contemplation, as the examples of Mālik ibn Dīnār and Ibrāhīm ibn Adham show.

115.text:
Verse 115 answers those who made the direction of prayer a weapon, and comforts those who had been driven away from the House they loved. "To Allah belong the east and the west, so wherever you turn you are facing ˹towards˺ Allah. Surely Allah is All-Encompassing, All-Knowing".

### Phrase by phrase

**"To Allah belong the east and the west"**. That is, the whole earth, since these two directions stand for its two sides. Allah has authority over the entire world and instructs His servants as He wills. This ruling was a comfort to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and his Companions, expelled from Makkah and forced to leave the precincts of al-Masjid al-Ḥarām, the Sacred Mosque. In Makkah the Messenger ﷺ used to pray towards the Bayt al-Maqdis with the Kaʿbah between him and his qiblah. After the Hijrah to al-Madinah he kept facing the Bayt al-Maqdis for some sixteen or seventeen months, until Allah directed him to the Kaʿbah. Ibn ʿAbbās, through ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭalḥah, said that the first thing in the Qur'an to be abrogated was the qiblah. When the Messenger of Allah ﷺ migrated to al-Madinah, a city of Jews, he was first commanded to face the Bayt al-Maqdis, which pleased the Jews, and he did so for some ten months. But he loved the qiblah of Ibrāhīm (Abraham) and used to look up to the sky and pray, until Allah revealed: "Indeed, We see you ˹O Prophet˺ turning your face towards heaven. Now We will make you turn towards a direction ˹of prayer˺ that will please you. So turn your face towards the Sacred Mosque" (2:144). The Jews were disturbed and asked what had made the Muslims abandon the qiblah they had been facing, and Allah revealed, "Say, to Allah belong the east and the west". The new command delighted the Muslims, but the Jews in their habitual malice taunted them with having abandoned the way of the earlier prophets, and tried to plant doubts which, had they taken root, would have led to denial of the Prophet ﷺ and the abandonment of the prescribed prayer, thereby laying waste the Prophet's ﷺ own mosque. This was one of three incidents in which the three groups hostile to Islam were each guilty, in one way or another, of hindering worship in Allah's mosques and laying them waste. The second was the Romans' invasion of Jerusalem, when the ignorant among them defiled the Bayt al-Maqdis so that no one could pray there. The Christians regarded the Romans more or less as their ancestors, and the Jews' humiliation pleased them, so by refusing to condemn the Romans' deed they shared indirectly in the ruin of that mosque. The third was the Peace of al-Ḥudaybiyyah, when the idolaters refused the Prophet ﷺ entry to Makkah for the pilgrimage. Ibn ʿAbbās related the previous verse (2:114) to the second incident, and Ibn Jarīr accepted that, while others followed Ibn Zayd in preferring the third. The Holy Qur'an, however, speaks generally of "the mosques of Allah" so as to lay down a permanent law for all peoples covering every case of desecrating mosques or hindering the remembrance of Allah, calling those who do it "unjust" and threatening them with humiliation.

**"so wherever you turn you are facing ˹towards˺ Allah"**. ʿIkrimah related Ibn ʿAbbās's gloss: wherever you face, east or west, there is Allah's direction. Mujāhid said: wherever you are, you have a qiblah to face, namely the Kaʿbah. Whichever way you turn your faces in prayer, at His command, there is Allah's Face, that is, the direction of prayer He is pleased with, and the prayer is performed in His good pleasure. Wherever you turn you will find Allah, who surrounds His creation. Whether the instruction is to face Jerusalem or the Kaʿbah, and whether you mistake the direction or are unsure of it, there is no problem, since every direction belongs to Allah. One gloss reads the opening clause as the direction of prayer for someone who does not know the correct one, and another takes it to mean that east and west alike, all their peoples, have one qiblah, the Sacred Precinct, so that "the Face of Allah" means the direction of prayer towards Him.

Several occasions of revelation are recorded, and scholars disagree about them. It has been said that the verse came down before the command to face the Kaʿbah. Ibn Jarīr related the view that it was revealed to permit the one offering voluntary prayers to face wherever he wishes, east or west, while travelling, in fear, or when facing the enemy. Ibn ʿUmar used to face whichever way his mount was heading and say that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ did the same, citing this verse in explanation. Saʿīd ibn Jubayr related from Ibn ʿUmar that the verse was revealed so that one prays towards whatever direction one's mount takes when offering voluntary prayers. This ḥadīth was collected by Muslim, at-Tirmidhī, an-Nasāʾī, Ibn Abī Ḥātim and Ibn Marduwayh, and the Two Ṣaḥīḥs contain its basis from Ibn ʿUmar and ʿAmr ibn Rabīʿah, without the verse being mentioned. In his Ṣaḥīḥ, al-Bukhārī recorded from Nāfiʿ that whenever Ibn ʿUmar was asked about the prayer of fear he would describe it and then add that when the fear is worse than that, one prays standing or riding, facing the qiblah or not. Nāfiʿ added that he thought Ibn ʿUmar attributed this to the Prophet ﷺ. Others say the verse concerns those who cannot find the direction of the qiblah in the dark or under cloudy skies and so pray the wrong way by mistake. Jābir ibn ʿAbd al-Malik told of a military expedition on which it was so dark that the men could not determine the qiblah. Some said it lay to the north and prayed that way, drawing lines on the ground, and others said it lay to the south and did the same. When the sun rose they found their lines pointed away from the qiblah. On their return they asked the Prophet ﷺ, who gave no answer until Allah revealed this verse. ʿAbdullāh ibn ʿĀmir ibn Rabīʿah related from his father a similar account: they were praying with the Prophet ﷺ on a journey on a dark night, each man faced the direction he thought right, and when they told the Prophet ﷺ in the morning the verse came down. An early gloss likewise says it was revealed about a group of Companions who prayed in the wrong direction while travelling after doing their best to determine it.

In his commentary on this verse al-Ḥāfiẓ Ibn Marduwayh recorded from Abū Hurayrah that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "What lies between the east and the west is the qiblah for the people of al-Madinah, ash-Shām and Iraq." At-Tirmidhī and Ibn Mājah recorded it with the wording, "What lies between the east and the west is a qiblah."

**"Surely Allah is All-Encompassing, All-Knowing"**. Ibn Jarīr explained that Allah encompasses all His creation by providing for their needs and by His generosity and favour, and that "Knowing" means He knows their deeds, nothing escapes His watch, He is unaware of nothing, and His knowledge embraces everything. His bounty embraces all things, He knows how to manage His creation, He covers His creatures with His mercy and ease, and He knows their intentions and all that they do. He is all-embracing with regard to the direction of prayer, and all-knowing of what the worshippers intend.

### Why a fixed qiblah at all?

The verse has two facets: an answer to the Jews' objection, and comfort to the Prophet ﷺ and his Companions. Had Allah been confined to one direction, a fixed and permanent orientation would have been necessary in order to worship Him. Being infinite and beyond every limitation, He is Lord of the east and the west and of every conceivable direction, everywhere, surrounding everything. Wherever a person turns he finds Allah "facing" him, ready to accept his prayer and shower His bounty on him. It follows that neither the Bayt al-Maqdis nor the Kaʿbah has any inherent or inalienable superiority. Either acquires a privileged position only by divine appointment. What matters is to obey Allah's command, which alone makes a person worthy of His grace, and to win His pleasure one must orient oneself as He has determined. If, despite being free of all limitation, Allah has fixed a particular orientation, it is because He is all-knowing and knows what is best in a given situation and for a given people. The fixing of a definite direction for prayer has an obvious rationale even if no one can fully grasp the wisdom in every divine command. Whichever way one turns one would find Allah "facing" one, but having to choose a direction every time one prays would scatter one's attention, and when several people pray together it would be absurd for each to face a different way. A single orientation helps individual and congregation alike to concentrate and to feel a shared purpose. This also disposes of the objection of certain opponents who accuse the Muslims of worshipping the Kaʿbah. If they reply that they too keep idols before them while meditating or worshipping for the sake of concentration, the claim does nothing to strengthen their accusation, and an impartial look at the two frames of mind shows how genuine the Muslims are in worshipping none but Allah and how doubtful the others' position is. Even granting that idols or icons are only a means to an end, using them as a "support" would still require a ruling from a Sharīʿah that has not been abrogated, and today only the Muslims possess one. A modern reflection adds that one of the errors of the opponents was to liken God to man. Since a human being cannot be in two places at once, people imagine that God too is found only in a particular place. But God is everywhere. He has prescribed a direction for us to face in worship, yet this is purely an organisational requirement of prayer and does not mean He is found in one direction and not another.

A caution is in order. The verse speaks of "the Face of Allah" and of Allah being All-Encompassing. Wisdom lies in not probing needlessly into the meanings of such statements.
