Just as a creature cannot fully comprehend the Being (Dhāt) of Allah, it is equally impossible to grasp the essential reality of His Attributes (Ṣifāt). What is required is a general faith in the realities of the divine order, not an inquiry into particulars that lie wholly beyond human reach.

### The east and west of the heart

The devotional reading finds here an allusion to the eastern and western regions of the believers' hearts. A heart has its rising lights (shawāriq) and its night visitors (ṭawāriq). The visitors of the night are the murmurings (hawājis) of the lower self, which come in the darkness of desire and carnal passion. The lights that rise are the stars of the various sciences, the moons of presence, the suns of gnosis. While those lights are rising, the heart's qiblah stays clear and visible. Once the realities take over, the lights lose their authority and are hidden, as the stars are at sunrise. When the Real appears there is destruction and subjugation. No trace is witnessed any more, no sensation or comprehension is left, neither the power of intellect and knowledge nor the illumination of deeper knowledge, because all such qualities last only as long as human nature does, and once those who bear attributes are effaced, how can any attribute of theirs remain? Hence "wherever you turn you are facing towards Allah". Yet as long as even a sliver of sensory perception and the ability to differentiate remain, the qiblah should be aimed at, and if it is not known it should be sought. The scholars hold that when the landmarks in every direction are obscure and the qiblah is unknown, all directions are equally permissible for prayer, since none can be preferred for the intention (niyyah).

### In short

- Allah owns every direction, so the change of qiblah from the Bayt al-Maqdis to the Kaʿbah (2:144) gave the Jews no ground for their taunts and consoled the Muslims cut off from the Sacred Mosque.
- The verse is also applied to voluntary prayers on a mount facing any direction, as Ibn ʿUmar did following the Prophet ﷺ, to the prayer of fear, and to Companions who prayed the wrong way in the dark, whose prayer was accepted.
- "What lies between the east and the west is a qiblah" for the people of al-Madinah, ash-Shām and Iraq.
- A fixed qiblah is an organisational aid to concentration and unity, not a limit on Allah, who is everywhere, and the Muslims worship Him alone, not the Kaʿbah.
- The "Face of Allah" and His encompassing are to be believed in generally, not probed, and for the heart the qiblah stays visible as long as its lights are rising.

116.text:
Verse 116 confronts the gravest error the surrounding communities had made about Allah. "They say, “Allah has offspring.” Glory be to Him! In fact, to Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and the earth—all are subject to His Will".

### Phrase by phrase

**"They say, “Allah has offspring.”"**. "They" are the Jews, the Christians and those who claimed that the angels are Allah's daughters. Certain Jews called ʿUzayr (Ezra), a prophet, the son of God. The Christians said the same of ʿĪsā (Jesus), and most still do, and the idolaters of Makkah held the angels to be God's daughters. The word is read either as "and they say" (wa-qālū) or simply "they say" (qālū). This verse and the next refute the Christians and their like among the Jews and the Arab idolaters, all of whom claimed that He had begotten a son.

**"Glory be to Him!"**. Allah exalts Himself above such a thing. He is holier and more perfect than their claim, far too exalted to have a son or a partner. Of His creation He has no need, and having a son is a mark of need. Only those with needs beget children, and God is above every such imperfection and limitation, complete in Himself. Such beliefs do not come from God. People invented them.

**"In fact, to Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and the earth"**. The truth is not as the disbelievers claim. The kingdom of the heavens and the earth is Allah's, together with everything and everyone in them, on them and between them. He is the supreme authority in the heavens and the earth, the Creator, Provider and Sustainer who decides the affairs of creation as He wills. All creatures are His servants and His possessions, so how could one of them be His son? A son is born of two comparable beings, and nothing is Allah's equal or peer in His grace and greatness. Having no wife, how could He have a son? Allah said: "˹He is˺ the Originator of the heavens and earth. How could He have children when He has no mate? He created all things and has ˹perfect˺ knowledge of everything" (6:101), and "They say, “The Most Compassionate has offspring.” You have certainly made an outrageous claim, by which the heavens are about to burst, the earth to split apart, and the mountains to crumble to pieces, in protest of attributing children to the Most Compassionate. It does not befit ˹the majesty of˺ the Most Compassionate to have children. There is none in the heavens or the earth who will not return to the Most Compassionate in full submission. Indeed, He fully knows them and has counted them precisely. And each of them will return to Him on the Day of Judgment all alone" (19:88-95), and "Allah—the Sustainer ˹needed by all˺. He has never had offspring, nor was He born. And there is none comparable to Him" (112:2-4). In these verses Allah declares Himself the supreme Master without equal or rival, the Creator of everything and everyone, so how could He have a son from among them? The particle "whatever" (mā) is used so as to include all of creation, rational and non-rational, and this sovereignty is incompatible with having a child. Al-Bukhārī recorded in the commentary on this verse that Ibn ʿAbbās reported the Prophet ﷺ saying that Allah said: "The son of Ādam has denied Me, and he had no right to. He has insulted Me, and he had no right to. His denial of Me is his claim that I cannot restore him as he was. His insult to Me is his claim that I have a son. Glory be to Me, far be it from Me to take a wife or a son." The Two Ṣaḥīḥs record the Messenger of Allah ﷺ saying that no one is more patient under insult than Allah: they attribute a son to Him, and He still grants them provision and health.

Reason itself shows the impossibility of offspring for God. Were it possible, the offspring would have to share the father's genus or belong to a different one. If to a different genus, that is plainly a defect, and God must be free of all defects, as reason requires and as this verse affirms. If to the same genus, that is a contradiction in terms, since God has no equal and no existent can share His genus. God alone is the Necessary Being (adh-Dhāt al-Wājib) and therefore necessarily possesses the Attributes of Perfection peculiar to Him alone, which cannot exist in anyone else. To deny a being its necessary attribute is to deny its existence, so nothing other than God can be a necessary being, and since necessity is the very essence of the Ultimate Reality, or an inseparable quality of it, nothing other than God can share that Reality. To claim that anything belongs to His genus is a plain contradiction. Having refuted the Jews, the Christians and the idolaters, the two verses go on to show why the Attributes of Perfection belong to Allah alone. First, everything in the heavens and the earth belongs to Him. Second, everything is subservient to Him, in that nothing can interfere with His omnipotence, His power to create and to destroy, even if some people are lax in obeying His law. Third, He is the Creator and Inventor of the heavens and the earth. Fourth, His creative power is such that when He wishes to do something He needs no instruments or helpers but simply says "Be", and it becomes what He wishes. None of these four qualities is found in anyone but Allah, and even those who attributed offspring to Him acknowledged them, so their claim refutes itself.

**"all are subject to His Will"**. All are qānitūn to Him. Ibn ʿAbbās explained the related word qānitīn in "stand in true devotion to Allah" (2:238) as "they pray to Him". ʿIkrimah and Abū Mālik said qānitūn means bound to Him in servitude, Saʿīd ibn Jubayr said it means sincerity, ar-Rabīʿ ibn Anas said standing before Him on the Day of Resurrection, and as-Suddī said obedient on the Day of Resurrection. Mujāhid said it means obedient: He says "be a human" and it becomes a human, "be a donkey" and it becomes a donkey. Mujāhid also said that the disbeliever's obedience is when his shadow prostrates while he himself hates it. Ibn Jarīr preferred Mujāhid's explanation because it gathers all the meanings together: qunūt is obedience and submission to Allah, and it is of two kinds, legislated and decreed, as Allah said, "To Allah ˹alone˺ bow down ˹in submission˺ all those in the heavens and the earth—willingly or unwillingly—as do their shadows, morning and evening" (13:15). All obey His will, each submitting to what is required of it, with the emphasis here falling on rational beings, bound to Him by servitude and by the declaration of His oneness. As His servants they are dealt with as He wills.

### Two further lessons

First, if Allah has chosen to assign certain tasks to certain angels, such as sending rain or bringing creatures their sustenance, or has chosen to work through causes, materials and physical forces, He has done so in His wisdom. It is therefore neither permitted nor proper to regard those angels, causes or forces as effective agents in themselves and to turn to them for help in need. Second, al-Bayḍāwī remarked that, Allah being the First Cause of things, the earlier sharīʿahs had allowed the title "Father" to be used of Him, but the ignorant so misunderstood and distorted the sense of "fatherhood" that to hold such a belief, or to apply the title to Allah, has now been declared unbelief (kufr). Because the practice can lead to every kind of doctrinal disorder, it is no longer permissible to use this word or any similar expression of Allah.

### The one Lord

The devotional reading answers the claim with a litany. He is pure and without fault, incomparable, the one Lord: one in forbearance, so that when the servant does harm He does not cut him off, one in loyalty, so that when the servant inclines to another He does not incline away, one in love, so that when the servant breaks the covenant He does not break it. He is one in Essence and one in attributes, free of causes, praised by every expression, fitting for every allusion, who created time and the hours and determines every instant and moment. No defect mars His artisanry, no contrivance His determining, no likeness His description. He is Powerful and Knowing, Alive and Desiring, Hearing and Seeing, clothed in majesty, too holy to have an equal, beyond all opinion and talk. Lord without associate or partner, king without equal or need, He makes no false promise and bears no metaphorical name. Withholding's door is shut, and the door of His generosity stands open. He forgives sins and caresses the faulty, knows without cause and is able without artifice, alone without poverty, outside number, an artisan without toil, self-subsisting to the Endless, hallowed beyond envy. His names are the Subtle, the Self-Standing, the Self-Sufficient, who "has never had offspring, nor was He born. And there is none comparable to Him" (112:2-4). So present is He face to face in the heart and so hidden from the eyes that no describer can describe Him: He is as He is. Ears are open to His name, hearts captive to His message, the voicers of tawḥīd caught in His snare and the yearners drunk with love from His cup. No one in the universe matches His loving kindness. The disobedient and the destitute hope in Him, and the poor rejoice in the subsistence of His majesty.

### In short

- Jews who called ʿUzayr God's son, Christians who said it of ʿĪsā, and Arabs who called the angels His daughters all attributed offspring to Allah, and Allah declares Himself glorified above it.
- Everything in the heavens and the earth is His property and His servant, so none of it can be His son, and a son requires a mate and a peer, which He has not (6:101, 19:88-95, 112:2-4).
- The ḥadīth qudsī calls the claim an insult to Allah, who nonetheless keeps providing for those who make it.
- Reason rules out offspring of the same or a different genus, and the four marks of ownership, subjection, origination and creation by "Be" belong to Him alone.
- All creatures are qānitūn, obedient and submissive by law or by decree (13:15), and after the distortion of "fatherhood" the title may no longer be used of Allah.

117.text:
Verse 117 completes the refutation by describing how Allah actually brings things into being. "˹He is˺ the Originator of the heavens and the earth! When He decrees a matter, He simply tells it, “Be!” And it is".

### Phrase by phrase

**"˹He is˺ the Originator of the heavens and the earth!"**. The Badīʿ created them when nothing resembling them existed, with no exemplary precedent and out of nothing. Mujāhid and as-Suddī said this is the linguistic sense, for every new thing is called a bidʿah. Muslim recorded the Messenger of Allah ﷺ saying that every innovation in religion is a bidʿah. Bidʿah is thus of two kinds, the religious kind named in the ḥadīth "every innovation is a bidʿah, and every bidʿah is misguidance", and the linguistic kind, as when the Commander of the Faithful ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb gathered the Muslims for the Tarāwīḥ prayer in congregation, something the Prophet ﷺ had himself done earlier, and said, "What a good bidʿah this is." The scholars define the Originator as the One who gives the entity (ʿayn) existence with no model before Him (lā ʿalā mithāl). For the people of allusion the name says that nothing is like Him, denying at once any likeness (mithl) to His essence and any model (mithāl) for His acts. He is al-Aḥad, the One, comprised by no quantity. He is aṣ-Ṣamad, the Eternal, cut off by no end-point in time. He is al-Ḥaqq, the Real, whom no imagination pictures, and al-Mawjūd, the Existent, whom no understanding grasps. Nothing in creation resembles Him. Ibn Jarīr drew the two verses together: Allah is far too glorious to have a son, for He owns everything in the heavens and the earth, all of which testifies to His oneness and its own submission to Him. He is their Creator and Maker, who shaped the creatures in their present forms without any created precedent, and He bears witness to His servants that ʿĪsā (Jesus), whom some called His son, is among those who testify to His oneness. Having created the heavens and the earth from nothing and without precedent, He likewise created ʿĪsā the Messiah by His power and without a father. This explanation is very good and correct.

**"When He decrees a matter, He simply tells it, “Be!” And it is"**. This displays His perfect power and tremendous authority. Once He has decided a matter, a single order to be brings it into existence, and nothing stops His command and decree. Allah said: "All it takes, when He wills something ˹to be˺, is simply to say to it: “Be!” And it is" (36:82), and "If We ever will something ˹to exist˺, all We say is: “Be!” And it is" (16:40), and "Our command is but a single word, done in the blink of an eye" (54:50). So Allah created ʿĪsā merely by saying "Be": "Indeed, the example of Jesus in the sight of Allah is like that of Adam. He created him from dust, then said to him, “Be!” And he was" (3:59). When He wants to create a child without a father, like ʿĪsā, He says "be a child without a father", just as Ādam was without father or mother. The verb is read fa-yakūnu, "and it is", or in a variant fa-yakūna in the subjunctive as the response to the command. Whatever He decides, no preordained thing (maqdūr) opposes it and no created thing (mafṭūr) can break away from His decree.

### "Be" and the mystery of creation

For those drawn to Western philosophy, Christian theology or the writings of the Orientalists, a note on the command "Be" is in order, with the warning that this is a mystery in the original sense: a reality beyond human understanding, and one which even when partly grasped must not be handed to those without the aptitude to receive it, so that silence is often the better part. What is revealed, and when, is a matter of spiritual etiquette rather than of liberalism or egalitarianism. The theologians (mutakallimūn) approach it in two ways. For the Ashʿarīs, "Be, and it is" (kun fa-yakūn) is a metaphor. The phrase does not mean that Allah actually addressed an existent thing and commanded it to be. It is an allegorical picture of His omnipotence, suggesting that no interval separates His act of will from its realisation. Al-Bayḍāwī took this view, and the kalām debate turns on it. For the Māturīdīs the phrase means literally what it says, which raises a difficulty. A command is addressed only to something that exists. How can Allah address what does not exist at all, and why command what already exists to be? Two considerations resolve the problem. First, this command does not belong to the order of legislation (tashrīʿ), which requires an addressee that actually exists and understands, but to the order of creation (takwīn), which gives existence to non-existents. Second, there is the question that has muddled so much Western thought, creation "out of nothing" (ex nihilo). Existence (wujūd) is usually set against non-existence (ʿadam), yet it has also been said that non-existence does not exist. Allah is omniscient, and His knowledge comprehends all that has been, is or will be, so that what does not yet exist by our reckoning already exists in His knowledge. Everything past, present or future has its pure, subtle counterpart in divine knowledge. One may call these prototypes, numbers, essences, ideas or archetypes, provided the terms are given a higher and more refined meaning than Pythagoras or Plato ever gave them. The Sufis call them al-aʿyān ath-thābitah. When Allah wishes to create a thing, He says "Be" to its essence, which is already present in His knowledge, and it comes to be, that is, it is actualised in the world. Creation therefore does not arise out of nothingness. Before a thing exists as an actuality in the world it exists as a potentiality in divine knowledge, and it is this potentiality that the command "Be" addresses. Hence it is equally true to say that the essences do not exist, from the standpoint of created knowledge, and that they do exist, from the standpoint of divine knowledge. Once again, no good comes of meddling with such delicate questions needlessly, least of all for the sake of a new sensation.

### In short

- Allah originated the heavens and the earth without model or precedent, which is the linguistic root of bidʿah, a word that is blameworthy in religion but neutral in language, as ʿUmar's remark about Tarāwīḥ shows.
- Whatever He decrees He brings about simply by saying "Be" (36:82, 16:40, 54:50), and so He created ʿĪsā without a father as He created Ādam (3:59), which is why ʿĪsā cannot be His son.
- Ashʿarīs read "Be" as a metaphor for instant omnipotence, Māturīdīs literally as a creative command addressed to essences already present in Allah's knowledge, the Sufis' al-aʿyān ath-thābitah, so that creation is not strictly from nothing.
- Such matters are a mystery to be believed, not a puzzle to be probed for novelty.

118.text:
Verse 118 records yet another demand from those who would not believe. "Those who have no knowledge say, “If only Allah would speak to us or a sign would come to us!” The same was said by those who came before. Their hearts are all alike. Indeed, We have made the signs clear for people of sure faith".

### Phrase by phrase

**"Those who have no knowledge say, “If only Allah would speak to us or a sign would come to us!”"**. Muḥammad ibn Isḥāq reported from Ibn ʿAbbās that Rāfiʿ ibn Ḥuraymilah said to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ: "Muḥammad, if you are truly a Messenger from Allah as you claim, ask Allah to speak to us directly so that we hear His speech", and Allah revealed the verse. Abū al-ʿĀliyah, ar-Rabīʿ ibn Anas, Qatādah and as-Suddī said it was in fact the saying of the Arab disbelievers, and that "those who came before" were the Jews and the Christians. That the Arab idolaters said such things is confirmed by other verses: "Whenever a sign comes to them, they say, “We will never believe until we receive what Allah’s messengers received.”" (6:124), and "They challenge ˹the Prophet˺, “We will never believe in you until you cause a spring to gush forth from the earth for us" down to "or until you have a house of gold, or you ascend into heaven—and even then we will not believe in your ascension until you bring down to us a book that we can read.” Say, “Glory be to my Lord!" (17:90-93), and "Those who do not expect to meet Us say, “If only the angels were sent down to us, or we could see our Lord!” They have certainly been carried away by their arrogance" (25:21), and "In fact, each one of them wishes to be given a ˹personal˺ letter ˹from Allah˺ for all ˹to read˺" (74:52). Many other verses attest the Arab idolaters' disbelief, transgression and obstinacy, and their needless questions asked in disbelief and arrogance. One gloss takes "those who have no knowledge" to be the Jews, who did not know Allah's oneness, demanding that Allah speak to them directly or send a sign confirming Muḥammad's ﷺ prophethood, "for then we would surely believe". Another takes them to be the disbelievers of Makkah, the Quraysh, asking that God tell them Muḥammad ﷺ was His Messenger, or send the kind of sign they had requested as proof of his sincerity. They were the ignorant among the People of the Scripture and the idolaters, speaking out of stubbornness against the truth.

The Jews, the Christians and the idolaters denied the prophethood of Muḥammad ﷺ, some out of sheer malevolence, and to feel triumphant in their obstinacy they made absurd and impossible demands, two of which are mentioned here. First came the insistence that Allah speak to them Himself, directly as He does to the angels, or through angels as He does to the prophets, and either proclaim His commands to them Himself, making a new prophet unnecessary, or at least announce that He had sent Muḥammad ﷺ, so that believing in him would be easy. Should Allah decline, they had a second demand ready: that He send them a sign or proof confirming his prophethood.

**"The same was said by those who came before"**. The demand of the Arab idolaters echoed earlier nations. Those earlier peoples included recipients of the two Scriptures and adherents of other religions. Allah said: "The People of the Book demand that you ˹O Prophet˺ bring down for them a revelation in writing from heaven. They demanded what is even greater than this from Moses, saying, “Make Allah visible to us”" (4:153), and "And ˹remember˺ when you said, “O Moses! We will never believe you until we see Allah with our own eyes,” so a thunderbolt struck you while you were looking on" (2:55). Past communities said the like to their prophets in their obstinacy and demands for signs, and so did their forefathers. Allah dismisses the demand as a foolish custom practised unthinkingly by ignorant people in every age.

**"Their hearts are all alike"**. The hearts of the Arab idolaters are just like the hearts of those before them, full of disbelief, obstinacy and injustice, as Allah said: "Similarly, no messenger came to those before them without being told: “A magician or a madman!” Have they passed this ˹cliché˺ down to one another? In fact, they have ˹all˺ been a transgressing people" (51:52-53). Their words and their hearts are the same. All disbelievers are alike even when they belong to different times and places. The verse traces the demand to a distortion of the heart in which the ignorant of every age are alike, which is why the same demand is repeated parrot-fashion down the centuries. The observation is meant as consolation for the Prophet ﷺ.

**"Indeed, We have made the signs clear for people of sure faith"**. We have made plain the arguments proving the truth of the Messengers, so that those who believe, follow the Messengers and understand what Allah sent them with need no further questions or proofs. Those who are certain know that these are God's signs and believe in them, and to ask for other signs would be sheer obstinacy. The signs include the commands and prohibitions and the Prophet's ﷺ description in the Torah. As for those whose hearts and hearing Allah has sealed and whose eyes He has covered, "those against whom Allah’s decree ˹of torment˺ is justified will not believe—even if every sign were to come to them—until they see the painful punishment" (10:96-97). The first of the two demands was silly on its face, for with all the coarseness of their minds and hearts they had the audacity to put themselves on the level of angels and prophets, so the Qur'an treats it as unworthy of reply. To the second Allah answers that He has sent not one but many clear signs and proofs establishing the prophethood of Muḥammad ﷺ, which help only those who sincerely wish to know the truth and attain certainty. For those not seeking truth but content to wallow in malice and obstinacy there is no help. One may wonder why Allah calls the Jews and Christians, People of the Book, some of them learned, "those who have no knowledge". The answer is that despite the many clear signs and definite proofs sent to establish his prophethood they persisted in denial, and that is the mentality and conduct of the ignorant.

### The ear of comprehension

The devotional reading notes that God's speech (kalām) reaches every created thing, its entity (ʿayn) and its traces (āthār), by way of the creative command "Be" (amr at-takwīn), and to those charged with the law through the prescriptive command (amr at-taklīf). Whoever lacks the ear of comprehension is deaf to the Real. He did address some of the People of the Book, and they heard but could not bear it, and after recognising the enormity of the signs they fell to distortion and alteration. Among the signs He made manifest were those that remove the defect of everything other than Him and quench the thirst with what is better. But what proofs, however plain, could suffice those whose portion is wretchedness, and whose wretchedness has already arrived?

### In short

- Rāfiʿ ibn Ḥuraymilah, and the Arab idolaters with him, demanded that Allah speak to them directly or send them a sign of their own choosing (6:124, 17:90-93, 25:21, 74:52).
- Earlier peoples made the same demands of their prophets, asking Mūsā to show them Allah (4:153, 2:55), because the hearts of the obstinate are alike in every age (51:52-53).
- The first demand, to be addressed like angels and prophets, is beneath reply. The second is answered by the many clear signs already given, which suffice people of sure faith but never the sealed heart (10:96-97).
- Learned deniers are still "without knowledge", for persisting in denial against clear proof is the conduct of the ignorant.

119.text:
Verse 119 turns to the Prophet ﷺ himself with reassurance about the limits of his task. "We have surely sent you with the truth ˹O Prophet˺ as a deliverer of good news and a warner. And you will not be accountable for the residents of the Hellfire".

### Phrase by phrase

**"We have surely sent you with the truth ˹O Prophet˺"**. With Islam, the Qur'an and the declaration of Allah's oneness, the guidance and the religion of truth in which there is no doubt. The previous verse (2:118) implied that those who persisted in denying the Prophet ﷺ did so from sheer malice and ignorance and could not be expected to reform. Since he was sent as a mercy to all the worlds, the thought that they were incorrigible was bound to sadden him on their account, so here Allah consoles him. He has been sent to mankind bearing the truth and the genuine faith.

**"as a deliverer of good news and a warner"**. Good news of Paradise for those who believe in what he brought and respond to the guidance, and a warning of the Fire for those who disbelieve and do not respond. His task has two sides: glad tidings for those who accept the truth, and a warning of dire punishment for those who deny it.

**"And you will not be accountable for the residents of the Hellfire"**. You will not be asked about the unbelief of those who rejected you, nor why they failed to believe, because delivering the message is the whole of your responsibility. Allah said likewise: "your duty is only to deliver ˹the message˺. Judgment is for Us" (13:40), and "So, ˹continue to˺ remind ˹all, O Prophet˺, for your duty is only to remind. You are not ˹there˺ to compel them ˹to believe˺" (88:21-22), and "We know best what they say. And you ˹O Prophet˺ are not ˹there˺ to compel them ˹to believe˺. So remind with the Quran ˹only˺ those who fear My warning" (50:45), among many similar verses. A variant reading, lā tasʾal with the final vowel dropped, makes it an imperative, "do not ask about the inhabitants of the Fire", and one gloss explains that it is not fitting for him to ask about the people of Hell, or that he should not ask forgiveness for them. Ibn ʿAbbās said that one day the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said, "Would that I knew what became of my parents", and the verse came down in answer, though this applies only on the imperative reading. Muqātil said the Prophet ﷺ remarked that the Jews would have believed had Allah sent His harm upon them, and Allah revealed the verse in response. Muḥammad ﷺ is assured that he will not be held responsible or called to account for those who willingly take the road to Hell. All he must do is keep performing his own function, without worrying about who accepts the truth and who does not.

### His description in the Torah

Imām Aḥmad recorded that ʿAṭāʾ ibn Yasār met ʿAbdullāh ibn ʿAmr ibn al-ʿĀṣ and asked him to describe the Messenger of Allah ﷺ as the Torah describes him. He answered: "Yes, by Allah. He is described in the Torah with some of the same qualities as in the Qur'an: O Prophet, We have sent you as a witness, a bearer of good news, a warner, and a refuge for the unlettered. You are My servant and My Messenger. I have named you al-Mutawakkil, the one who relies on Allah. He is not harsh or rough, nor loud in the markets. He does not repay evil with evil but forgives and pardons. Allah will not take him until through him He has set the crooked religion straight, so that people declare that there is no god but Allah, and through him He opens blind eyes, deaf ears and sealed hearts." Al-Bukhārī alone recorded this.

### Under his banner

The devotional reading hears Allah telling His Prophet ﷺ that He has singled him out with qualities He gave to no one else, so that all people stand under his banner. The accepted are those in conformity with him and the rejected those who oppose him (al-maqbūl man wāfaqaka wa-l-mardūd man khālafaka). He will not be questioned about the states of others, and he will not be turned away on anyone's account.

### In short

- The Prophet ﷺ was sent with the truth to bring good news of Paradise and warning of the Fire.
- He is not answerable for those who choose Hell. His duty is to deliver the message, not to compel belief (13:40, 88:21-22, 50:45).
- On the imperative reading, "do not ask about the people of the Fire", connected with his words about his parents or about the Jews.
- The Torah's description of him, witness, bringer of good news, warner, refuge of the unlettered, al-Mutawakkil, gentle in the markets and forgiving of wrongs, matches the Qur'an's.

120.text:
Verse 120 tells the Prophet ﷺ plainly what lies at the bottom of the opposition he faced from the People of the Book. "Never will the Jews or Christians be pleased with you, until you follow their faith. Say, “Allah’s guidance is the only ˹true˺ guidance.” And if you were to follow their desires after ˹all˺ the knowledge that has come to you, there would be none to protect or help you against Allah".

### Phrase by phrase

**"Never will the Jews or Christians be pleased with you, until you follow their faith"**. Ibn Jarīr explained: the Jews and the Christians will never be happy with you, Muḥammad, so do not seek what pleases or appeases them, but hold to what pleases Allah by calling them to the truth He sent you with. The Jews of al-Madinah and the Christians of Najrān are meant, and "their faith" is their religion and their direction of prayer. Two occasions are reported. According to one, they used to ask the Prophet ﷺ for a truce, giving the impression that if he granted them respite they would follow him and believe in him, and Allah revealed the verse. Ibn ʿAbbās, however, said it was revealed about the qiblah. The Jews of al-Madinah and the Christians of Najrān had hoped that the Prophet ﷺ would go on praying towards their qiblah, and when Allah directed him to the Kaʿbah they were disappointed and despaired of his ever following their religion. Anxious to save as many people as possible from misguidance and damnation, the Prophet ﷺ took great pains to convince the deniers and was especially gentle and lenient with the People of the Book. Allah explains their denial through pride and self-satisfaction, not a lack of convincing proof. Each group regarded its religion alone as genuine. Neither could therefore be pleased without his accepting its religion. Both faiths had once been genuine, laid down by Allah Himself, yet each community went on to twist its own religion out of shape. In any case, once Islam came as the final Sharīʿah, Allah abrogated every earlier code, so that Islam alone is now acceptable to Him and the only real guidance in this last of the ages. A modern reflection adds that when the Jews and Christians declined, their religion shrank into a set of ethnic customs. Piety lay in belonging to the community and impiety in standing apart from it, and the one test of truth and falsehood became a person's relation to his own group. This sectarian attitude kept them from accepting genuine, unadulterated religion when it was offered. Every preacher of truth has met the same reaction. People ask why God's envoy is not blessed with worldly treasures, because they think only in worldly terms and cannot conceive of a messenger of God without worldly grandeur. How, they wonder, could the great God whose kingdom spans the earth and the furthest heavens choose so ordinary a man? Yet the lives and teachings of the prophets were exactly where God's signs showed themselves: because their words and deeds rested on truth, those words and deeds were His signs in human form. Materialistic minds recognised greatness only through tangible, visible signs. They could not discern these signs in the prophets. Their negative outlook also kept them from grasping the preacher's forceful arguments. True religion can be accepted only by those alive to their own true human nature, not by those who have suppressed it and traded natural religion for artificial dogmas.

**"Say, “Allah’s guidance is the only ˹true˺ guidance.”"**. Say, Muḥammad, that the guidance Allah sent me with is the true guidance, the straight, perfect and comprehensive religion. Islam is the religion Allah has chosen, the Kaʿbah is the direction He has fixed for prayer, and whatever lies outside that guidance is error. Qatādah described this reply as a true argument: Allah taught it to Muḥammad ﷺ and to his Companions, and with it they answered the people of misguidance. Qatādah also related that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ used to say: "A group of my Ummah will never cease fighting upon the truth, prevailing, unharmed by those who oppose them, until the decree of Allah comes." This ḥadīth is in the Ṣaḥīḥ, narrated from ʿAbdullāh ibn ʿAmr. Because of the distorted state of the earlier religions, and above all because they have been abrogated by divine command, the verse equates them with ahwāʾ, the plural of hawā, personal desires, private opinions and baseless conjectures. Since the deniers will not free themselves from their desires and fancies, there is no pleasing them short of accepting their opinions, which a Messenger of Allah can never do. Even a friendlier approach must be answered plainly. The only true guidance comes from Allah. He has already made clear that Islam is now the guidance He accepts.

**"And if you were to follow their desires after ˹all˺ the knowledge that has come to you"**. The particle is that of an oath, and the case is hypothetical: were you to follow the whims to which they are calling you, their religion and their qiblah, after the divine revelation that has come to you, after knowing that Islam is Allah's religion and the Kaʿbah His qiblah. For the Muslim Ummah the verse is a stern warning: once people have knowledge of the Qur'an and the Sunnah, they must not copy the ways and methods of the Jews and Christians, may Allah protect us from such conduct. Though the words are addressed to the Messenger ﷺ, the ruling applies to his whole Ummah. Were he, or anyone who follows him, to act in that way after the clear truth had come, Allah would give them neither protection nor help, which shows the gravity of abandoning the truth and following the people of falsehood.

**"there would be none to protect or help you against Allah"**. No friend (walī) to benefit you or shield you from His punishment, and no helper to defend you against Him. Supposing, purely for the sake of argument, that he were to accept their fancies despite having received the truth by revelation, he would find no one to save him from divine wrath. Other verses establish beyond doubt that Allah is pleased with the Prophet ﷺ and will remain so, and that he can never be an object of divine wrath. Since wrath necessarily follows the acceptance of baseless fancies, and no one can be the object of divine pleasure and divine wrath at once, it follows that he could never, in logic, adopt the opinions of the Jews and Christians. They for their part will never be pleased with him unless he follows their wishes, so no change of heart can be expected from them, and the purport of the verse is to advise the Prophet ﷺ not to worry too much about them. The warning is addressed to him on the surface but is really aimed at the deniers, to make them realise the dire consequences of their vanity. Indeed divine wrath is already visible in the fact that the warning reaches them obliquely rather than directly, a mark of the contempt in which Allah holds them.

### Free of them, through Him

The devotional reading paraphrases the verse as Allah's counsel: do not concern yourself with pleasing the enemies once you have received Our good pleasure (riḍāʾ), for nothing short of following their religions will please them, and that is impossible. So declare yourself quit of them, make your difference plain and show them your opposition. Know, too, that when people lean on whatever they find pleasing, that leaning is what brings endless wretchedness. Do not trouble yourself. Call your community to free themselves from them and from their path, and be for Us and through Us, free of everyone but Us, trusting that Our help is enough, for through Us and from Us is all that you are.

### In short

- Neither the Jews nor the Christians will ever be satisfied with the Prophet ﷺ short of his adopting their religion and qiblah, so he is told to stop seeking their approval.
- Allah's guidance, Islam, is the only guidance now that the earlier religions are distorted and abrogated, which is why they are called mere "desires".
- Following their whims after revelation would leave even a prophet without protector or helper against Allah, a warning aimed through him at his whole Ummah and at the deniers themselves.
- A group of this Ummah will always stand victorious upon the truth until Allah's decree comes.

121.text:
Verse 121 turns from the hopeless opponents among the People of the Book to those of them who were honest and just. "Those We have given the Book follow it as it should be followed. It is they who ˹truly˺ believe in it. As for those who reject it, it is they who are the losers".

### Phrase by phrase

**"Those We have given the Book"**. Scholars differ about who they are. Qatādah, in the narration of Maʿmar through ʿAbd ar-Razzāq, said they are the Jews and Christians, which was also the view of ʿAbd ar-Raḥmān ibn Zayd ibn Aslam and the choice of Ibn Jarīr. In the narration of Saʿīd, Qatādah said they are the Companions of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, in which case the Book is the Qur'an. Ibn ʿAbbās reported that the verse was revealed when forty Christians arrived from Abyssinia and accepted Islam, and it is likewise said to concern a group of Ethiopians who presented themselves to the Prophet ﷺ and embraced Islam. One early gloss identifies them as those among the People of the Book who believed, naming ʿAbdullāh ibn Salām and his companions, Baḥīrā the monk, and the Negus with his followers, and it takes the Book to be the Torah. On the first reading, the verse describes those Jews and Christians who, having recognised the truth, affirmed the Prophet ﷺ and accepted Islam, and explains how they were able to change themselves so radically. The Christians, no less than the Jews, had received a Book from Allah, and unlike most of their co-religionists these people gave that Book the reading it deserved.

**"follow it as it should be followed"**. Literally, they recite it with its true recitation (ḥaqqa tilāwatihi), as it was revealed. Abū al-ʿĀliyah relates Ibn Masʿūd's explanation, given under an oath by the One who holds his soul. True recitation permits what the Book permits and forbids what it forbids. It recites the Book as Allah revealed it, without moving its words from their places or giving it an improper interpretation. Ibn ʿAbbās, through Abū Mālik and as-Suddī, said: they permit what it permits, forbid what it forbids, and do not alter its wording. ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb said they are those who, when they recite a verse of mercy, ask Allah for it, and when they recite a verse of punishment, seek refuge with Allah from it. The same is attributed to the Prophet ﷺ, who used to ask for mercy when he recited a verse of mercy and seek refuge when he recited a verse of punishment. ʿUmar is also reported, by Ibn Abī Ḥātim, to have said that reading the Book with the right of its recitation requires that on reaching a description of Paradise one pray to be granted it, and on reaching a description of Hell one seek Allah's protection from it. Reading it rightly also means pronouncing each word correctly and clearly, keeping the fear and love of Allah present in the heart while reading, and resolving to follow divine guidance and obey divine commands. One gloss explains that they describe the Book as it is and do not alter it, setting out its lawful and unlawful, its commands and prohibitions, to whoever asks, acting on what is clear and unambiguous and believing in what is ambiguous. These people distorted neither the words nor the meanings, and neither misinterpreted nor concealed the prophecies of the Prophet's ﷺ coming. They used their intellect to understand the meanings and their will to accept the truth and follow it.

**"It is they who ˹truly˺ believe in it"**. This clause explains the one before. Those among the People of the Book who adhered perfectly to the Books revealed to the earlier prophets will believe in what Allah sent Muḥammad ﷺ with, and in Muḥammad ﷺ and the Qur'an. Acknowledging the Qur'an affirms their own Books and acts on them. Those Books explicitly foretell the Last Prophet and Allah's final Book. Finding the signs of his coming in their scriptures, they believe in him at once. Allah said: "And had they observed the Torah, the Gospel, and what has been revealed to them from their Lord, they would have been overwhelmed with provisions from above and below" (5:66), and "Say, ˹O Prophet,˺ “O People of the Book! You have nothing to stand on unless you observe the Torah, the Gospel, and what has been revealed to you from your Lord.”" (5:68), which means that if they adhere to the Torah and the Gospel properly, believe in them as they should, and accept what those Books report about Muḥammad ﷺ, that is, his prophethood, the description given of him and the order to follow him, help him and stand by him, then they will be led to truth and righteousness in this life and the next. Allah also said: "˹They are˺ the ones who follow the Messenger, the unlettered Prophet, whose description they find in their Torah and the Gospel" (7:157), and "Say, ˹O Prophet,˺ “Believe in this ˹Quran˺, or do not. Indeed, when it is recited to those who were gifted with knowledge before it ˹was revealed˺, they fall upon their faces in prostration, and say, ‘Glory be to our Lord! Surely the promise of our Lord has been fulfilled.’" (17:107-108). These verses show that what Allah promised concerning Muḥammad ﷺ was bound to come about. He said further: "˹As for˺ those ˹faithful˺ to whom We had given the Scripture before this ˹Quran˺, they do believe in it. When it is recited to them, they declare, “We believe in it. This is definitely the truth from our Lord. We had already submitted ˹even˺ before this.” These ˹believers˺ will be given a double reward for their perseverance" (28:52-54), and "And ask those who were given the Scripture and the illiterate ˹people˺, “Have you submitted yourselves ˹to Allah˺?”" (3:20).

**"As for those who reject it, it is they who are the losers"**. Whoever disbelieves in the revealed Book by distorting it, or disbelieves in Muḥammad ﷺ and the Qur'an, is among the losers, duped out of both this world and the next and destined for a Fire made everlasting for them. As Allah said: "˹Can these people be compared to˺ those ˹believers˺ who stand on clear proof from their Lord, backed by ˹the Quran as˺ a witness from Him, and preceded by the Book of Moses ˹which was revealed˺ as a guide" (11:17), where whoever of the factions disbelieves in it is promised the Fire. The Ṣaḥīḥ records that the Prophet ﷺ said: "By Him in whose hand is my soul, no one of this community, Jew or Christian, hears of me and then dies without believing in what I was sent with, but will be among the people of the Fire." Those who persist in denial suffer the greatest loss, for they have refused the last revelation and have shown little real belief in their own Books either, having ignored the guidance those Books give on this very point.

### The rightful due of recitation

For the devotional reading, the rightful due of recitation is to recite the Qur'an with burning and need. The heart must be limpid and the belief pure. The tongue must remember, the heart must believe, the spirit must be limpid. The tongue is in remembrance, the heart in grief, the spirit in love. The tongue is in loyalty, the heart in limpidity, the spirit in shame. The tongue is at the work, the heart in the mystery, the spirit in joy. The Pīr of the Ṭarīqah said that in remembrance the servant reaches a point where the tongue arrives at the heart, the heart at the spirit, the spirit at the secret core, and the secret core at the Light. The heart tells the tongue to be silent, the spirit tells the heart to be silent, the secret core tells the spirit to be silent, and then God says to the traveller: "My servant, you have been speaking for a while. Now I will speak, and you listen."

### In short

- "Those given the Book" are either the honest Jews and Christians who read their scriptures rightly and so believed in the Prophet ﷺ, such as the forty converts from Abyssinia, ʿAbdullāh ibn Salām and the Negus, or the Companions reading the Qur'an.
- True recitation means permitting what the Book permits, forbidding what it forbids, keeping its words in place, interpreting it rightly, and responding to verses of mercy and punishment with prayer and refuge, as ʿUmar and the Prophet ﷺ did.
- Faithful adherence to the Torah and Gospel leads straight to faith in Muḥammad ﷺ (5:66, 5:68, 7:157, 17:107-108, 28:52-54), while rejecting him after hearing of him is loss in both worlds (11:17).
- Inwardly, the due of recitation is reached when tongue, heart and spirit fall silent and God Himself speaks.

122.text:
Verse 122 closes the long address to the Jews that began many verses earlier, and it closes it with the very words that opened it. "O Children of Israel! Remember My favours upon you and how I honoured you above the others". A similar verse has already come near the beginning of the surah. The whole account of the Israelites' conduct, their favours, their lapses and their punishments, was framed by this one statement. It stood at the start as the thesis, the verses in between were the detailed demonstration, and now it returns as the summary.

### Phrase by phrase

**"O Children of Israel!"** The Children of Yaʿqūb (Jacob), who is Israel. There is a point in the form of address. Allah's way with the people of Mūsā (Moses) is to call them by their proper name, "O Children of Israel", whereas He addresses the community of Muḥammad ﷺ by a title of honour, "O you who believe".

**"Remember My favours upon you"**. The blessings, sacred and worldly, that were given to their forefathers: deliverance from Pharaoh and his people, and all the bounties and benefits that followed. They are told to recall how Allah blessed them in their daily life and in their religion. Among those favours is the knowledge they were given of the unlettered Prophet, who is described in their Books by his characteristics, his name, the good news of his coming and the description of his Ummah (community). The reminder is also a warning against concealing that knowledge.

**"and how I honoured you above the others"**. Over the people of their own time, with prophethood and authority, and, on one reading, with Islam itself, the religion of submission to Allah. The Children of Israel were chosen for a special task: to call other nations to Allah and to impress on them that they would answer to their Lord for their actions. To help them in that task Allah raised countless prophets from among them, Ibrāhīm (Abraham) and Yaʿqūb before them, then Yūsuf (Joseph), Mūsā, Dāwūd (David), Sulaymān (Solomon), Zakariyyā (Zachariah), Yaḥyā (John the Baptist) and ʿĪsā (Jesus), to name only some.

### Why the opening statement is repeated

Over the centuries the community degenerated. It took its privileged position, which was due solely to the lofty task entrusted to it, as a sign of ethnic superiority, and so it lost its right to represent the religion of Allah on earth. The coming of the Arab Prophet ﷺ marked the replacement of the Children of Israel by the Children of Ismāʿīl (Ishmael) as the people charged with carrying Allah's word to the nations. The genuinely pious among the Israelites soon realised that what Muḥammad ﷺ taught came from the same origin as the message of the earlier prophets. Those who denied him did so out of prejudice, refusing to accept that any nation but their own could be chosen. The verse is repeated here to stress how much depends on following the unlettered Prophet, and to tell them not to envy their cousins, the Arabs, because the Final Messenger is an Arab. Envy must not drive them to oppose him, deny him or hold back from following him.

There is also a reason of method. A basic, general statement is easy to keep alive in the mind, and because it applies readily to particular cases it helps the details to be remembered too. Good speakers and writers state their basic ideas briefly before a long discussion and repeat them at the end by way of summary. The statement here, which encourages the Israelites to return to the Straight Path by reminding them of Allah's blessings, and (in the next verse) warns them by depicting the Day of Judgement, is of exactly that kind, repeated so that the two ideas sink deep.

### In short

- The verse repeats the statement that opened the address to the Israelites, so that the whole account is framed by a reminder of favour and a warning of judgement.
- Their favours included rescue from Pharaoh, a line of prophets, authority, and knowledge of the Prophet ﷺ described in their Books.
- They were preferred over the people of their time for a task, not for their race. Having turned the task into a claim of superiority, they were replaced by the Children of Ismāʿīl, and they are told not to let envy of the Arabs keep them from the Prophet ﷺ.

123.text:
Verse 123 completes the repeated statement with its warning half. "And guard yourselves against the Day when no soul will be of any help to another. No ransom will be taken, no intercession accepted, and no help will be given". Where verse 122 recalled favours, this verse depicts the Day of Judgement, so that the Israelites are both encouraged back to the Straight Path and warned of what their lapses lead to.

### Phrase by phrase

**"And guard yourselves against the Day"**. Fear the torment of that Day, the Day of Return, and protect yourselves from it by following Allah's instructions and keeping away from what He has forbidden.

**"when no soul will be of any help to another"**. No soul will be requited for another or ward anything off from it. This has been understood in several ways: no unbelieving soul will be able to drive anything away from another unbelieving soul, or no righteous soul from another righteous soul, or no father will be able to turn Allah's punishment away from his son and no son from his father.

**"No ransom will be taken"**. No compensation or ransom will be accepted from a soul, however great the payment offered.

**"no intercession accepted"**. No intercessor will intercede for it, not a close angel, not a sent messenger, not a righteous servant, and no plea on its behalf will benefit it, however high the position of the one who pleads.

**"and no help will be given"**. They will not be defended against Allah's punishment or kept from what they are about to face. Apart from Allah, no helper will be left to any soul on that Day.

### Why the Israelites needed this warning

In this world a person can sometimes bear another's burden. Intercession is sometimes accepted, a man can sometimes free himself by paying compensation, and a helper is often at hand in a difficult situation. In the next world none of these mitigating factors will come into play. Allah's justice will apply to everyone equally. The Israelites, who thought that their descent guaranteed them salvation, are warned through the Arab Prophet ﷺ that in the next world value attaches only to true faith borne out by earnest deeds, and that no ethnic group holds a monopoly over the Hereafter.

### Whose intercession, and for whom

As for the enemies of Allah, nothing will be accepted from them, no payment and no plea. As for His friends, the Prophet ﷺ said: "Protect yourself from the Fire even if it be by half a date" given in charity. The intercession of the intercessors will not benefit the disbeliever, for that has been settled for each community with its prophet. The believers, on the other hand, will benefit in particular from the intercession of the Prophet ﷺ. On that Day everyone will be saying "My soul, my soul", but our Prophet ﷺ will say "My community, my community".

### In short

- The Day of Judgement allows none of the escapes of this world: no one can stand in for another, no ransom, no intercession for the deniers, no helper.
- The verse answers the Israelites' belief that belonging to a chosen people would save them. Only faith proved by deeds will count.
- Intercession is denied to the disbelievers, while the believers will have the Prophet's ﷺ intercession, and he will be pleading for his community when everyone else pleads for himself.

124.text:
With verse 124 the surah turns from the history of the Israelites to the man they, the Christians and the Arab idolaters all claimed as their father. "˹Remember˺ when Abraham was tested by his Lord with ˹certain˺ commandments, which he fulfilled. Allah said, “I will certainly make you into a role model for the people.” Abraham asked, “What about my offspring?” Allah replied, “My covenant is not extended to the wrongdoers.”" Allah tells of the honour of Ibrāhīm (Abraham), His close friend (al-Khalīl), whom He made an imām, a leader and model for people to follow, because of how he conducted himself and held to tawḥīd, the oneness of Allah. The honour came when he carried out Allah's commands and prohibitions. The verse says, in effect: Muḥammad, remind the idolaters and the People of the Book, who pretend to follow the religion of Ibrāhīm while in reality they do not, that you and your followers are his true followers, and remind them of the commands with which Allah tested him.

The passage that begins here answers the Jews in an indirect way. They were proud of descending from Yaʿqūb (Jacob) and Ibrāhīm, believed that as the chosen people they alone could lead humanity, and held that prophethood could not go to anyone outside their race. The story of Ibrāhīm and his elder son Ismāʿīl (Ishmael) suggests several answers. Only a person who is not unjust, who has passed the trial Allah set him, can guide humanity, and the Jews did not meet that condition. The Kaʿbah, which the Muslims face in ṣalāh (prayer) and which the Jews would not accept, was built by Ibrāhīm, so the Muslims' qiblah (direction of prayer) is his. The way of Islam is the way of Ibrāhīm, and the Muslims alone really follow him. Ibrāhīm himself prayed for the Last Prophet to be sent, so whoever wants to follow him must accept Muḥammad ﷺ. And Ibrāhīm had two sons, Ismāʿīl and Isḥāq (Isaac), and prayed for Allah's grace on both (as Genesis, chapter 17, also records), so that the superiority once enjoyed by the children of Isḥāq has passed to the children of Ismāʿīl. Whoever wants a share in Allah's grace must therefore accept the last and now the only valid form of the Abrahamic way. Ibrāhīm is the patriarch of both the Arabs and the Jews. He was granted leadership only after very severe tests, and the rule applied to him applies to every generation: a share in Allah's covenant goes to those who prove themselves worthy, and those who do not will meet the fate of any other offender, whatever nation they belong to.

### Phrase by phrase

**"˹Remember˺ when Abraham was tested by his Lord"**. The name is read Ibrāhīm, and in another reading Ibrāhām. The trial raises an obvious question: a trial tests someone's aptitude for a task, but Allah knows everything that exists inside out, so what was its purpose? The clue is the word Rabb, Lord. Of all the Divine Names the verse uses the one that denotes bringing a thing to its perfection gradually, stage by stage. The trial was not punishment for a crime, nor a way of discovering a hidden aptitude. It was part of the nurturing of a prophet, by which his inherent qualities were made to show themselves to the world so that he could be led, step by step, to the station his Lord had already chosen for him. Although Allah's knowledge and will choose a man for prophethood, he does not assume that station until his worthiness has been shown openly for people and angels to witness, just as happened with Ādam (Adam) before the angels earlier in this surah. In the Arabic the object, Ibrāhīm, is placed before the subject, his Lord, a word order that signals his glorious rank among the prophets.

**"with ˹certain˺ commandments"**. Literally "with words", kalimāt. Here it means laws, commands and prohibitions, which is how most scholars understood it. The word "words" is used in the Qur'an in more than one way: for what Allah has willed, as when Maryam "testified to the words of her Lord" (66:12), for His law, as in "The Word of your Lord has been perfected in truth and justice" (6:115), and for truthful news or a just command or prohibition. Here it is the last sense: the orders Ibrāhīm was charged with. One gloss takes it as ten traits he was commanded to fulfil, five concerning the head and five the body. Another view says it means every single word with which he prayed to Allah. These trials were not academic tests of mental capacity or theory. They tested readiness to obey Allah and steadfastness in submitting to His commands, which shows that what has value in Allah's sight is deeds, inward and outward, not theoretical hair-splitting.

**"which he fulfilled"**. He carried out all of Allah's orders, performing them thoroughly and completely. He was truthful and obedient to Allah's legislation, which is why the Qur'an says of "Abraham, who ˹perfectly˺ fulfilled ˹his covenant˺" (53:37), or, in another rendering, who paid his debt in full. That is the measure of his success in the trials. Elsewhere he is called a model of excellence, devoted to Allah and upright, not a polytheist (16:120-123). The Prophet ﷺ is told to say that his Lord has guided him to the Straight Path, the faith of Ibrāhīm the upright (6:161), and Ibrāhīm "was neither a Jew nor a Christian" but one who submitted in uprightness (3:67-68).

**"Allah said, “I will certainly make you into a role model for the people.”"**. The word is imām, which lexically means a leader, chief or guide: a vicegerent and exemplar in religion whose conduct and path people imitate. Since the verse concerns Ibrāhīm, the word means above all a prophet, though it includes leadership in the general sense, and also the title of patriarch that the Jews and Christians give him. The honour was a reward for his good deeds, for keeping the commands and avoiding the prohibitions. Prophethood cannot be won by personal effort, yet a prophet must display his perfection in the qualities that tested Ibrāhīm, and people of lower rank must possess them in their own degree to deserve leadership of any kind. The Qur'an says plainly: "We raised from among them leaders, guiding by Our command, when they patiently endured and firmly believed in Our signs" (32:24). That verse sums up all those qualities in two words, ṣabr (patience), the perfection of practice, and yaqīn (certainty), the perfection of knowledge.

**"Abraham asked, “What about my offspring?”"**. Make leaders from among my descendants too, whom people will follow. Allah accepted the prayer. The proof is in Sūrah al-ʿAnkabūt: "reserved prophethood and revelation for his descendants" (29:27). So every prophet Allah sent after Ibrāhīm came from his offspring, and every Book Allah revealed was revealed to them.

**"Allah replied, “My covenant is not extended to the wrongdoers.”"**. The covenant is prophethood and leadership, My promise to you and the honour and mercy I bestowed on you. Allah told him that there would be unjust people among his descendants, polytheists and wrongdoers, and that they would not benefit from His promise. They would neither be imāms nor be imitated, even though they are children of Allah's Khalīl. The righteous among his children are the ones who profit from his prayer. The clause implies that the covenant reaches only those who are not wrongdoers. One reading restricts the wrongdoers to the disbelievers among them. Another view holds that the covenant will not include the wrongdoers in the Hereafter, though in this life it does include them. Ibn Jarīr said the verse shows that the unjust are not to be leaders of people. Ibn Khuwayz Mindād al-Mālikī went further: an unjust man does not qualify to be a khalīfah, a ruler, a giver of religious verdicts, a witness, or even a narrator of hadith. To hold the station of guide and leader is, in a way, to be a vicegerent of Allah, and that rank cannot be given to a rebel against Him. It follows that Muslims, in so far as they have a choice, should not appoint as their ruler or representative a man who rebels against Allah or disobeys Him.

### What were the words he was tested with?

Scholars differ about this, and several opinions are attributed to Ibn ʿAbbās himself. ʿAbd ar-Razzāq related from him that Allah tested Ibrāhīm with the rites of Hajj, and Abū Isḥāq reported the same. ʿAbd ar-Razzāq also related from Ibn ʿAbbās that He tested him with ṭahārah, bodily purity: five things on the head and five on the body. On the head: rinsing the mouth, drawing water into the nose and expelling it, using the siwāk (tooth-stick), parting the hair and cutting the moustache. On the body: trimming the nails, plucking the underarm hair, shaving the pubic hair, circumcision and washing with water after answering the call of nature. Ibn Abī Ḥātim said that a similar statement was reported from Saʿīd ibn al-Musayyib, Mujāhid, ash-Shaʿbī, an-Nakhaʿī, Abū Ṣāliḥ, Abū al-Jald and others. Imam Muslim narrated something similar from ʿĀʾishah, that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said that ten things belong to the fiṭrah (the natural constitution): trimming the moustache, growing the beard, using the siwāk, drawing water into the nose and expelling it, cutting the nails, washing between the fingers, plucking the underarm hair, shaving the pubic hair and washing with water after relieving oneself, and the narrator said he had forgotten the tenth, which he thought was rinsing the mouth. The Two Ṣaḥīḥs record from Abū Hurayrah that the Prophet ﷺ said five things are of the fiṭrah: circumcision, shaving the pubic hair, trimming the moustache, cutting the nails and plucking the underarm hair, this being Muslim's wording. These ten characteristics of the fiṭrah have been made permanent injunctions for all later communities too, and the Last Prophet ﷺ insistently commanded his followers to keep them.

Muḥammad ibn Isḥāq reported a different list from Ibn ʿAbbās: the words Allah tested Ibrāhīm with, and which he carried out, were leaving his disbelieving people when Allah commanded it, disputing with Nimrod, the king of Babylon, about Allah, being patient when he was thrown into the fire despite how traumatic that was, migrating from his homeland at Allah's command, bearing patiently the material cost of hosting guests by Allah's order, and Allah's command to slaughter his son. When he had been tested with all of this and was ready for the major test, Allah said to him "Submit", and he answered "I submit to the Lord of all worlds" (2:131), even though this meant defying his people and standing apart from them.

Some said the injunctions were ten, others thirty, but there is no real conflict between these views, since everything mentioned in this connection served in one way or another as a test, and this is what Ibn Jarīr and other leading scholars held to be the truth of the matter. Ibn ʿAbbās is reported to have said that thirty elements make up the whole of Islam: ten are mentioned in Sūrah 9 (al-Barāʾah, also called at-Tawbah), in the verse that lists those who repent, worship, praise, fast, bow, prostrate, enjoin good, forbid evil and keep Allah's limits (9:112), ten in Sūrah 33 (al-Aḥzāb), in the verse about the men and women who submit, believe, obey, are truthful, patient, humble, charitable, fasting, chaste and much in remembrance of Allah (33:35), and ten in Sūrah 23 (al-Muʾminūn), in its opening description of the believers who will prosper (23:1-11). Ibrāhīm was tried in these too, and he fulfilled them all with equal faithfulness. In the devotional tradition it is related from al-Ḥasan that Allah tried him with the stars, the moon and the sun, and he spoke beautiful words in that, because he knew his Lord was constant and never ceasing, and that He tried him with the sacrifice of his son, and he was patient and did not fall short.

### The great trials, in order

Because Allah intended to raise Ibrāhīm to an especially exalted station and to give him the title Khalīlullāh, the Friend of Allah, his trials were very severe. Not only his people but his own family were sunk in idol-worship. Against their creed and customs he was given ad-Dīn al-Ḥanīf, the pure religion, and sent to bring them back to the Straight Path. He obeyed without flinching, waged war on idolatry and called them to worship the One God alone. This drew down on him the anger of his people and of their king Namrūd (Nimrod), who decided to burn him alive. Seeking only the pleasure of his Lord, he let himself be thrown onto the pyre. Having passed that test, he heard Allah's command: "O fire! Be cool and safe for Abraham!" (21:69). The command was addressed to fire as such, not to one particular fire, so every fire in the world grew cold, Nimrod's among them. Since extreme cold is as painful and deadly as heat, and Hell itself has a region of extreme cold called Zamharīr, Allah in His grace added the word salāman, "and safe".

The second trial was the command to leave his homeland and migrate to Syria with his family. Then he was told to leave even that country, and he set out at once with his wife Hājirah (Hagar) and his infant son Ismāʿīl, led by the archangel Jibrāʾīl (Gabriel). Whenever they passed through fertile land he wished to settle there, and each time the angel told him Allah did not want it. At last they reached the barren desert that was to be the site of Makkah, where the Kaʿbah would be built, and there he was told to stop. Then came a harder trial: he was ordered to leave his wife and son in that desert and return to Syria. So completely had the Friend of Allah given up his own will that he let no moment pass between the command and its execution. He started back without telling his wife. When she saw him going she called after him and got no reply, not even when she asked why he was abandoning them in so vast and lonely a place. But she was the wife of the Friend of Allah and could see how matters stood, so she asked whether he had received a divine command. Only then did he answer that it was so. She said calmly: go, then. The Lord who commanded you to part from us will Himself look after us and will not allow us to be destroyed.

She sat back in the desert, full of trust and peace, with the infant on her lap. In time thirst, her own and above all her suckling child's, drove her to go looking for water. She climbed up and down the hills of aṣ-Ṣafā and al-Marwah seven times and came back without success. It is to commemorate this that running seven times between the two hills was made an obligatory rite of Hajj and ʿUmrah. When she returned to her son, Allah's mercy came in the form of Jibrāʾīl, who made a spring of fresh water gush from the parched ground, the spring now called Zamzam. Within a day or two the water drew animals, and the animals drew men. Little by little the necessities of life became available, and the future city of Makkah began to take shape. Under divine permission Ibrāhīm came now and then to see how his wife and son were faring.

Then came the greatest trial of all. The boy had grown up in those unpromising conditions, deprived of constant fatherly care, and now the father was commanded to slaughter him with his own hand: "Then when the boy reached the age to work with him, Abraham said, “O my dear son! I have seen in a dream that I ˹must˺ sacrifice you. So tell me what you think.” He replied, “O my dear father! Do as you are commanded. Allah willing, you will find me steadfast.”" (37:102). Ibrāhīm took his son to the wilderness of Minā and, as far as his own part went, carried out the command. But Allah never meant the son to be slaughtered, only the father to be tested. The words of the Qur'an show that in his dream he had seen the act of slaughtering, not its completion, and that much he performed. Perhaps this is why the revelation came as a dream picturing the act rather than as a spoken order to kill his son. Allah therefore praised him: "You have already fulfilled the vision" (37:105). In return for this total submission Allah sent down a ram from heaven to be sacrificed in Ismāʿīl's place, and the yearly sacrifice of animals became an act of worship in memory of Ibrāhīm's way. The demand made of him was the hardest sacrifice there is, his son's life, and when Allah intervened before the blow fell it was because Ibrāhīm had already shown his perfect willingness to give whatever Allah asked, however great or terrible. One who is ready to make such soul-searing sacrifices for Allah's cause shows the utmost dedication to it, and it is only just and natural that he should lead his people. Besides these rigorous trials a number of further restrictions were laid on him in the form of injunctions, which he kept with the same devotion.

### Why the covenant excludes wrongdoers

The word ẓālim, wrongdoer, carries a further lesson stated very explicitly: every prophet is wholly sinless, as much before he becomes a prophet as after. Certain expressions in the Qur'an that seem to suggest otherwise, for example in the case of Ādam, are used metaphorically, not in the literal or technical sense of sin. To read them as technical sin is a grave doctrinal error, and insisting on it opens the way to further errors.

A note has also been made about a modern misreading. Since the Second World War the writings of the Danish thinker Kierkegaard, and particularly his book "Fear and Trembling", which treats Ibrāhīm's trial in the manner of a psychological novel, have fascinated many in the West and are said to have set off several existentialist philosophies and much modern Protestant theology. Three objections are raised. Ibrāhīm was, by the admission of Jews and Christians too, a prophet, not the average sensual man who is the subject of novels, psychology and that theology. He did not merely pass through emotional stress, a problem of conscience or a crisis of identity, the fear and trembling of the title, but was equally tried in faithfully observing divine injunctions. And when he knew Allah had chosen him he did not become silent, secretive and lonely, as the novelist's fancy would have it, but proclaimed the fact, without which he could not have functioned as a prophet at all. It is even said that the Friend of Allah would not take his daily meal until he had found a guest to share it. In short, prophethood is a degree of reality that can be understood only partially, and only with the help of the Divine Books, and it is not a field where human fantasy may roam at will.

### The inner reading of the trial

Al-Ḥasan's words about the stars, the moon and the sun are taken up in the devotional reading. The shining stars and the brilliant sun were adorned, and Ibrāhīm was tested, "so that the one tried would know, not that the one trying him was ignorant": to show him what came from him and how he walked on the road of servanthood. He came through it virtuous, fortunate and felicitous. When he said "This is my Lord" (6:76), it is said that there is an ellipsis: he meant, these estranged people say that this is my God, but it is not, for it is one of the low things that are taken down, and "I do not love the low ones". Well done, Ibrāhīm. It rose up from below, and he knew that the Lord is high, beyond His servants, and when it set he turned from it, saying that what sets is not worthy of Godhood.

The lords of realisation voice another allusion. From the first, Ibrāhīm's clay was mixed with the water of bosom friendship, his secret core burned with the fire of passion, his spirit lit with the love of eternity, and an ocean of passion stirred within him. Then at dawn, when the passionate take their morning draught, when drunkards shout for joy and the heart-lost raise their uproar, he opened his eyes, still giddy from the wine of friendship and the drunkenness of passion, and said "This is my Lord". As the lovers say: your image has so filled my eyes that wherever I look I fancy it is you. Drunkenness and passion are both paths of trial. Passion alone threw Yūsuf (Joseph) of Canaan where it did, and drunkenness alone did what it did to Mūsā (Moses) of ʿImrān, and in Ibrāhīm the two were joined. It is no wonder, then, that heart-lost drunkenness should make him gaze at the moon and the stars and say "This is my Lord". A drunkard does not know what he says, for if he knew, how would he be drunk? The one who says "I am drunk" does not know drunkenness.

As for his trial by the sacrifice of his child, it came because he gazed on the beauty of Ismāʿīl and began to pay regard to him, and the sword of that beauty wounded his heart. The command came: O Bosom Friend, did We preserve you from Āzar and the idols of Āzar so that you could gaze on Ismāʿīl's face? The stamp of bosom friendship with Me cannot be combined with glancing at others, whether at Āzar's carvings or at Ismāʿīl's face. Any talk that keeps you back from the road, call it unbelief or faith, and any picture that holds you back from the Friend, ugly or beautiful, is the same. Soon a sword was placed in his hand with the words: sacrifice Ismāʿīl, for two friends will not fit in one heart. With two qiblahs no one walks straight on the road of tawḥīd: it is either the Friend's approval or your own caprice. The outward story of the sacrifice is known and famous. In the tongue of allusion it means: cut off your heart's attachment to your child with the sword of truthfulness, for truthfulness is Allah's sword in His earth, and it cuts whatever it is laid on. Ibrāhīm heard the command and with that sword cut his heart off from his child, separating the love of Ismāʿīl from it. Then the call came, "You have already fulfilled the vision" (37:105). His state was saying: I separated from creatures to sharpen my love for You, and I made my child an orphan in order to see You.

### In short

- Ibrāhīm was tested by his Lord with commands, which he carried out completely (53:37), and as a reward was made an imām, a prophet and model for people to follow.
- The trials were a nurturing by the Rabb, not a punishment or an enquiry, and they showed his worthiness openly, as Ādam's had been shown before the angels.
- The "words" are explained as the rites of Hajj, the ten traits of the fiṭrah, the thirty qualities of 9:112, 33:35 and 23:1-11, or the great trials of leaving his people, Nimrod, the fire (21:69), migration, hospitality and the sacrifice of his son (37:102, 37:105), and there is no real conflict between these lists.
- Leadership was promised to his descendants (29:27), but never to wrongdoers, which bars the unjust from being imām, ruler, giver of verdicts, witness or narrator, and shows that prophets are sinless.
- The passage answers the Jews' claim to inherited privilege: Ibrāhīm is the father of Arabs and Jews alike, and the covenant goes only to those who prove worthy. Inwardly, his trials taught that two friends will not fit in one heart.

125.text:
The story of Ibrāhīm (Abraham) now reaches the building of the House of Allah. "And ˹remember˺ when We made the Sacred House a centre and a sanctuary for the people ˹saying˺, “˹You may˺ take the standing-place of Abraham as a site of prayer.” And We entrusted Abraham and Ishmael to purify My House for those who circle it, who meditate in it, and who bow and prostrate themselves ˹in prayer˺". The Jews denied the Prophet ﷺ on the assumption that prophethood could not go outside their own clan, scoffed at the Muslims for turning towards the Kaʿbah in prayer, and regarded the Hajj as no more than a custom of the ignorant Arabs. The previous verse had shown that leadership could never go to the unjust, even among Ibrāhīm's descendants, which knocks away the basis of their vanity. This verse reminds them that the Kaʿbah was built under divine command by Ibrāhīm himself with the help of his son Ismāʿīl (Ishmael).
