The Hajj and the facing of the Kaʿbah were therefore instituted by Allah, and the Prophet ﷺ, a direct descendant of Ibrāhīm and Ismāʿīl, is reviving the Abrahamic way, which the Jews too must follow.

In a few words the verse sketches the history of the rebuilding of the Kaʿbah, the qualities of the House of Allah and of the city of Makkah, and the respect that must be paid to this sacred place. The Qur'an returns to the subject again and again, and the chapter devoted to the pilgrimage gives the fullest account, where Allah appointed for Ibrāhīm the place of the House, told him to associate nothing with Him, to purify the House for those who circle it, stand, bow and prostrate, and to proclaim the pilgrimage so that people would come from every distant pass (22:26-27).

### Phrase by phrase

**"And ˹remember˺ when We made the Sacred House a centre"**. Remember, Muḥammad, when We appointed the House, the Kaʿbah. The word rendered "centre", mathābah, comes from a root that means to come back, and it denotes a place to which people return again and again. Ibn ʿAbbās explained that people do not stay at the House. They visit it, go home, and come to visit it again. It is a place of visitation to which people flock from every direction, a place to which they turn and for which they long, a means of connecting their hearts to Allah. Al-Qurṭubī reports Mujāhid as saying that no one ever has enough of visiting the Kaʿbah. Each time a person comes back with a greater longing to return and see it again. Some scholars remarked that one sign of an accepted Hajj is that the pilgrim finds in his heart, on returning home, a stronger desire to present himself at the House again, and those who have been there confirm it: each visit increases the thirst instead of quenching it. Makkah has no beautiful landscape, no easy access and no worldly comforts to offer, yet its power to draw millions of people to itself every year is nothing short of a miracle. This is because Allah accepted the prayer of His Khalīl (close friend) Ibrāhīm when he asked Him to make people's hearts eager to visit the House.

**"and a sanctuary for the people"**. A place of safety from the injustice and attacks that befall other places. Abū al-ʿĀliyah said: safe from enemies and armed conflict. In the Jāhiliyyah (the age of ignorance before Islam) people were often victims of raids and kidnapping, while those living around the Sacred Mosque were safe and nobody was carried off from there. Mujāhid, ʿAṭāʾ, as-Suddī, Qatādah and ar-Rabīʿ ibn Anas all explained the phrase as meaning that whoever enters it is safe. A man might come across his father's killer there and still not raise a hand against him. Those who visit the House are safe even if they had committed evil acts, and this honour flows from the honour of the one who first built it, the Khalīl of ar-Raḥmān. "The House" here means not only the Kaʿbah itself but the whole area of the Mosque around it, which is called the Ḥaram. The Qur'an uses "Kaʿbah" and "House of Allah" in this wider sense elsewhere: the phrase about "an offering to reach the Kaʿbah" (5:95) must mean the Ḥaram, since the verse concerns animal sacrifice and no sacrifice may be offered inside the Kaʿbah itself. So the verse means that the whole Ḥaram is a place of peace, in which shedding blood and taking revenge are forbidden. In the devotional reading, everyone who seeks refuge at that House in veneration and respect, repenting of his sins, is secure from the punishment of the Hereafter as well.

**"˹You may˺ take the standing-place of Abraham as a site of prayer"**. The verb is read as a command, ittakhidhū, and also as a statement, ittakhadhū, "they took". It is addressed to the community of Muḥammad ﷺ: take the Maqām of Ibrāhīm as a place of prayer, the stone he stood on while building the House, the founding stone, so that you perform two units of prayer there after circling the Kaʿbah. One early gloss paraphrases it as "a place by which you turn in prayer". The stone miraculously received the print of his foot, as al-Bukhārī's collection records. Ibn ʿAbbās is also reported to have said that the whole Ḥaram is the Station of Ibrāhīm. He probably meant that the two rakʿahs (units of prayer) which this verse enjoins after ṭawāf (circling the Kaʿbah) may validly be offered anywhere within the Ḥaram, and most of the jurists accept this. The Prophet ﷺ himself explained the command by word and deed on his last Hajj. After finishing his ṭawāf he reached the Station, which stands some yards from the Kaʿbah, recited this very verse, and prayed two rakʿahs on the far side of the stone with his face towards the Kaʿbah, as Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim records. From this the jurists inferred that a person who cannot find room close to the Station may stand at any distance from it, so long as the Kaʿbah and the Station are both in front of him. The verse shows that the two rakʿahs after ṭawāf are wājib (necessary), as al-Jaṣṣāṣ and Mullā ʿAlī al-Qārī held, while offering them specifically behind the Station is a sunnah (the Prophet's ﷺ practice). There is no bar to praying them elsewhere in the Ḥaram, for the Prophet ﷺ is reported to have offered them near the door of the House, and so did Ibn ʿAbbās, as al-Jaṣṣāṣ notes. In his "al-Manāsik" Mullā ʿAlī al-Qārī says that someone unable to pray them behind the Station may validly pray them wherever he can within the Ḥaram, or even outside it. That is exactly what happened to Umm Salamah, one of the Prophet's ﷺ wives: on her last Hajj she could not pray them inside the Ḥaram and did so only once she was outside the city of Makkah. Most jurists, apart from Imam Mālik, hold that someone compelled to pray them outside the Ḥaram owes no animal sacrifice in compensation.

**"And We entrusted Abraham and Ishmael"**. Literally, We made a covenant with them, We gave Our ʿahd. Al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī said this means Allah ordered them to purify it of every filth and impurity, so that none should ever touch it. Ibn Jurayj asked ʿAṭāʾ what Allah's ʿahd is, and he answered: His command. The command to settle near the House and keep it clean, mentioned in the pilgrimage chapter (22:26-27), had at that time been addressed to Ibrāhīm alone, because his son was still an infant, and its purpose then was not to begin rebuilding the Kaʿbah but to place his wife and son in that locality so that a human settlement would take shape. This verse repeats the command to keep the House clean, and now it is addressed to Ismāʿīl as much as to his father, for the son had grown into a young married man and could share in the task.

**"to purify My House"**. From idols and graven images, said Ibn ʿAbbās in the report of Saʿīd ibn Jubayr. Mujāhid and Saʿīd ibn Jubayr added: from idols, sexual activity, false witness and sins of every kind. The command covers physical and outward dirt as much as inner filth, kufr (unbelief) and shirk (associating partners with Allah), and impurities such as greed, lust, envy, pride, vanity and hypocrisy. People come to this place to remember Allah in an atmosphere of peace and solitude, so everything contrary to that purpose is banned. The expression "My House" shows that the command applies to mosques generally, for all mosques are the houses of Allah, "houses which Allah has ordered to be raised" (24:36), and many hadiths order that mosques be kept pure and free of filth. The Prophet ﷺ said that mosques are established for the purpose they were built for, the worship of Allah alone. Al-Qurṭubī reports that the second caliph ʿUmar once heard a man shouting in the mosque and rebuked him for forgetting where he was. Due respect to a mosque means not speaking loudly and above all not saying anything the Sharīʿah forbids. Those who enter must keep body and clothes free of dirt, filth and even bad smells, and keep their hearts free of shirk, hypocrisy, pride, malice and greed. The Prophet ﷺ told people not to enter a mosque after eating raw onion or garlic, and forbade very small children and the insane to be brought in, for fear of their polluting it.

**"for those who circle it, who meditate in it, and who bow and prostrate themselves ˹in prayer˺"**. Ṭawāf around the House is a well-established rite. Saʿīd ibn Jubayr said "those who circle it" are the strangers who come from outside Makkah, while "those who meditate in it", those who stay in retreat (iʿtikāf), are the people who live in the area of the Sacred House, and Qatādah and ar-Rabīʿ ibn Anas explained it the same way. "Those who bow and prostrate" are those who pray, and the two words are the plurals of rākiʿ, one bowing, and sājid, one prostrated. Ibn ʿAbbās said that once it is a place of prayer it includes everyone described as bowing and prostrating, and ʿAṭāʾ and Qatādah gave the same explanation. One gloss reads it as those who perform the five daily prayers, whatever country they come from. Here the faithful bow and prostrate themselves, and their greatest mark of respect for their Creator is the circling of the Kaʿbah. For those who come from outside to perform the Hajj, ṭawāf carries greater merit than prayer. The verse also makes clear that it is entirely permissible to pray inside the House of Allah, whether the prayer is farḍ (obligatory) or nafl (voluntary), as al-Jaṣṣāṣ observed.

### How Makkah came to be a sanctuary

Several hadiths say that Allah made Makkah sacred before He created the heavens and the earth. The Two Ṣaḥīḥs record from ʿAbdullāh ibn ʿAbbās that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: Allah made this city a sanctuary on the day He created the heavens and the earth, so it is a sanctuary until the Day of Resurrection by Allah's decree. Fighting in it was not lawful for anyone before me, and it was made lawful for me for a few hours of one day. Its thorny shrubs are not to be uprooted, its game not to be chased, nothing dropped in it to be picked up except by someone who announces it publicly, and its trees are not to be cut. Al-ʿAbbās said: except the idhkhir, the lemon-grass, Messenger of Allah, for our goldsmiths and our graves. He replied: except the lemon-grass. That is Muslim's wording. The Two Ṣaḥīḥs have a similar hadith from Abū Hurayrah, and al-Bukhārī one from Ṣafiyyah bint Shaybah.

Abū Shurayḥ al-ʿAdawī told ʿAmr ibn Saʿīd, when the latter was sending armies against Makkah: Commander, allow me to tell you something the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said on the day after the conquest of Makkah. My ears heard it, my heart took it in and my eyes saw him as he said it. He praised and thanked Allah and said that Allah, not the people, made Makkah a sanctuary, so no one who believes in Allah and the Last Day may shed blood in it or cut down its trees. If anyone argues that fighting there is permitted because the Messenger fought in it, tell him that Allah permitted His Messenger and did not permit you. Allah permitted me only for a few hours of that day, and today its sanctity is as it was before, and let those present inform those absent. When asked what ʿAmr had answered, Abū Shurayḥ said: he told me, "I know this better than you, Abū Shurayḥ. The Sacred House gives no protection to a sinner, a murderer or a thief." Al-Bukhārī and Muslim both collected this.

Ibn Jarīr narrated from Jābir ibn ʿAbdullāh that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said that Ibrāhīm made Allah's House a sacred area and a safe refuge, and that he himself had made what lies between the two sides of al-Madīnah a sacred area, so that its game may not be hunted nor its trees cut. An-Nasāʾī and Muslim also recorded this. There is no contradiction between the hadiths that say Allah made Makkah a sanctuary when He created the heavens and the earth and those that say Ibrāhīm made it one, because Ibrāhīm conveyed Allah's decree that Makkah is a sanctuary before he built the House. In the same way the Messenger of Allah ﷺ was recorded as the Final Prophet when Ādam (Adam) was still clay, and yet Ibrāhīm prayed, "Our Lord! Raise from among them a messenger" (2:129), and Allah accepted the prayer although He knew in advance that it would come about by His decree. When the Companions asked the Prophet ﷺ how his prophethood began, he said: I am the supplication of my father Ibrāhīm and the good news of ʿĪsā (Jesus) son of Maryam, and my mother saw a light go out from her that lit up the castles of ash-Shām (Syria).

### What the sanctuary protects, and what it does not

The ban on bloodshed in the Ḥaram was one of the remnants of the way of Ibrāhīm that survived into the Jāhiliyyah. Every kind of fighting or bloodshed, individual or collective, was held forbidden inside the sanctuary, so much so that a man would not take revenge even if he met the killer of his brother or father there. The Islamic Sharīʿah preserved this rule. It was lifted only for the Prophet ﷺ on the day Makkah was conquered, only for a few hours, and was reimposed for ever straight afterwards, as he himself announced in his address that day, which al-Bukhārī records. Here no one may harm even the lowliest living creature, for Makkah has been made a sacred place of worship for all time.

A man who commits, inside the precincts, a crime for which the Sharīʿah lays down a fixed punishment (ḥadd) or allows retaliation (qiṣāṣ) gets no sanctuary from the Ḥaram. By consensus, as al-Jaṣṣāṣ and al-Qurṭubī record, such a criminal is duly punished, for the Qur'an itself says that if they fight you inside the Sacred Mosque, fight them (2:191). The jurists differ about a man who commits a crime outside and then takes refuge in the Ḥaram. Some would punish him there in the prescribed manner. Imam Abū Ḥanīfah held that if such men could escape punishment this way the Ḥaram would become an easy refuge for every kind of criminal and disorder would prevail, yet out of regard for the sanctity of the place the criminal is not punished inside it. He is forced to come out, and then the prescribed punishment is carried out.

### The stone Ibrāhīm stood on

Saʿīd ibn Jubayr said that the Maqām is the stone on which Ibrāhīm, Allah's Prophet, stood, and a mercy from Allah: he stood on it while Ismāʿīl handed him the stones for the Kaʿbah. As-Suddī said it is the stone that Ismāʿīl's wife placed under Ibrāhīm's feet when she washed his head. Al-Qurṭubī mentioned this but considered it unauthentic, though others preferred it, and it was reported from al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī, Qatādah and ar-Rabīʿ ibn Anas. Ibn Abī Ḥātim reported Jābir's description of the Prophet's ﷺ Hajj: when the Prophet ﷺ had performed ṭawāf, ʿUmar asked him, "Is this the Maqām of our father?" He said yes. ʿUmar said, "Should we take it as a place of prayer?" and Allah revealed the words of this verse. Al-Bukhārī headed a chapter with this phrase, explaining "centre" as meaning that they return to it repeatedly, and under it he gave the report of Anas ibn Mālik about ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb's saying that he agreed with his Lord in this matter. Ibn Jarīr narrated from Jābir that after the Messenger of Allah ﷺ kissed the Black Stone he went round the House three times at a fast pace and four times at a slow pace, then went to the Maqām of Ibrāhīm, keeping it between himself and the House, and prayed two rakʿahs. This is part of the long hadith that Muslim recorded in his Ṣaḥīḥ. Al-Bukhārī recorded that ʿAmr ibn Dīnār heard Ibn ʿUmar say that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ went round the House seven times and then prayed two rakʿahs behind the Maqām.

All these texts show that the Maqām is the stone Ibrāhīm stood on while building the House. As the walls rose, Ismāʿīl brought his father a stone to stand on and handed him the building stones. Ibrāhīm would set them on the wall, and whenever he finished one side he moved to the next, until the House was complete. His footprints remained visible in the stone, and the Arabs knew this in the Jāhiliyyah, which is why Abū Ṭālib said in his poem known as al-Lāmiyyah that Ibrāhīm's footprint, made with his bare feet on the stone, was still to be seen. The Muslims saw them too. Anas ibn Mālik said that he saw the Maqām with the print of Ibrāhīm's toes and feet still visible in it, but that the prints wore away because people rubbed the stone with their hands. In earlier times the Maqām stood close to the wall of the Kaʿbah. Today it stands next to al-Ḥijr, on the right of those entering through the door. When Ibrāhīm finished building he either placed the stone beside the wall or simply left it where it last stood, and he was commanded to pray next to it after ṭawāf, so it is understandable that the Maqām should stand where the building of the House ended. The Leader of the Faithful, ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb, moved it back from the wall during his caliphate. He is one of the two men the Messenger of Allah ﷺ meant when he said to imitate the two who come after me, Abū Bakr and ʿUmar, and he is the one whose view about praying at the Maqām the Qur'an confirmed, which is why none of the Companions objected when he moved it. ʿAṭāʾ said that ʿUmar moved the Maqām back, and Mujāhid said he was the first to move it to where it now stands. ʿĀʾishah is reported, through an authentic chain, to have said that in the time of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and of Abū Bakr the Maqām was right beside the House, and that ʿUmar moved it during his reign.

### Was the Kaʿbah built from nothing?

Ibrāhīm was living in Syria when he received the revelation that Allah would show him the site of the Kaʿbah, which he was to build and keep clean for those who would gather there for the Hajj and the prayer. The earlier verse told how Jibrāʾīl (Gabriel) led him to the desert where Makkah now stands, where the remains of the earlier structure of the Kaʿbah survived only as a mound, and how he was commanded to leave his wife and infant son there and return to Syria. He left at once, but was naturally anxious for them, so when he was out of earshot he prayed for them with the prayer recorded in the chapter named after him: "My Lord! Make this city ˹of Mecca˺ secure" (14:35), and further that he had settled some of his offspring in a barren valley near the Sacred House so that they might keep up prayer, asking Allah to make people's hearts incline to them and to provide them with fruits so that they would be thankful (14:37). He knew that the command to keep the House clean meant freedom from inner filth, shirk and kufr, as much as from outward dirt, so on leaving he prayed first that the place be made safe and peaceful and second that he and his children be protected from idol-worship. The Friend of Allah had reached that degree of knowledge where a man sees himself as nothing and makes no move without realising that everything, even his inclinations, rests in Allah's hand, so he turned to Allah for help in carrying out the command itself. There is a further subtlety: since Allah had commanded respect for His House, some people might one day, out of sheer ignorance, begin to worship the Kaʿbah itself, and that is why he prayed specifically for protection from shirk. Out of love for his wife and son he then prayed for them to be provided with fruits in that uncultivable land. A hadith in al-Bukhārī's collection tells in detail how Jibrāʾīl made the spring of Zamzam flow, how people of the tribe of Jurhum came and settled there, and how Ismāʿīl married a woman of that tribe. The full story is told under the verse about raising the foundations.

Every verse of the Qur'an on the Kaʿbah either says that Allah Himself indicated its location or reports the command to keep the House clean. None suggests that a new House was to be built in a new place, which itself shows that the Kaʿbah already existed in some form. Hadith and history confirm it. The earlier structure had either been destroyed in the Flood of Nūḥ (Noah) or raised into the heavens, leaving its foundations buried, so Ibrāhīm and Ismāʿīl were not its original founders but raised a new building on the old foundations. As to who founded it first and when, there is no fully authenticated hadith. Certain narrations coming from the People of the Book say that the angels founded it even before Ādam came down to the earth, and that Ādam built it a second time or renovated it. That structure stood until the Flood destroyed it and left it a mound, which is how Ibrāhīm and Ismāʿīl found it. Since then the Kaʿbah has undergone alterations but has never been completely demolished. Before the Prophet ﷺ was commissioned, the Quraysh of Makkah rebuilt it afresh, and he himself took part in that work.

### A House of stone that draws hearts

In the devotional reading, it is a House that Allah created from stone yet attached to eternity. Whoever looks at the House with the eye of creation is cut off, while those who look with far-reaching vision arrive and connect. It is said that the House was built of stone, but of a stone that attracts hearts as a magnet attracts iron. What kind of house is it? A house whose shade keeps whoever comes to it in the courtyard of security. A house that gives whoever glances at it the good news of forgiveness. A house around which subtleties circle the heart of whoever circles it, one circling answering another, for "Is there any reward for goodness except goodness?" (55:60). A house on which nothing spent to reach it is lost, and from which nothing withheld brings profit. Whoever visits it forgets every other place of visitation and leaves his own country behind. No distance to it counts as too far, and visiting it is not to be neglected for fear of unpleasant events or harmful attacks, for the House holds no harm for the lifeblood of the poor. Whoever holds back from visiting it lacks noble-heartedness (futuwwah) or is deficient in love (maḥabbah), and the heart of one who stays away from it is harder than stones. When the rays of its lights fall on someone he forgets suns and moons. The wonder is not those who stay away but how those who come to it can bear to leave. As for the Station of Ibrāhīm, a servant was raised up on his feet for the sake of Allah, and his footprints were made a qiblah for all Muslims, to honour him for all time until the Resurrection.

### In short

- The Kaʿbah was built under Allah's command by Ibrāhīm with Ismāʿīl, so the Hajj and the Muslim qiblah are Abrahamic institutions, and the Prophet ﷺ is their rightful heir, which answers the Jews' scorn.
- The House is a "centre", a place people return to with ever greater longing, and a sanctuary: the whole Ḥaram is a place where blood may not be shed, a rule Allah decreed from the creation of the heavens and the earth, which Ibrāhīm proclaimed and which was lifted only for the Prophet ﷺ for a few hours on the day of the conquest.
- The sanctuary shelters no criminal: a crime committed inside is punished by consensus, and for one who flees there after a crime outside, Abū Ḥanīfah held that he is forced out and then punished.
- The Maqām is the stone Ibrāhīm stood on while building, marked with his footprints. The Prophet ﷺ prayed two rakʿahs behind it after ṭawāf, which is wājib wherever it is offered and sunnah at that spot, and ʿUmar, whose suggestion the verse confirmed, later moved the stone back from the wall.
- Ibrāhīm and Ismāʿīl were commanded to purify the House of idols, sin and inner filth for those who circle it, stay in it and pray in it, a command that extends to every mosque.

126.text:
Verse 126 records the prayer Ibrāhīm (Abraham) made for the place where he had left his family, and Allah's answer to it. "And ˹remember˺ when Abraham said, “My Lord, make this city ˹of Mecca˺ secure and provide fruits to its people—those among them who believe in Allah and the Last Day.” He answered, “As for those who disbelieve, I will let them enjoy themselves for a little while, then I will condemn them to the torment of the Fire. What an evil destination!”" Ibrāhīm always carried out Allah's commands without losing a moment and was ready for every kind of sacrifice in His way, of worldly goods, of wife and children, of his own likes and dislikes. Yet love for one's family is not only a natural urge but a divine command, and here he prays for the well-being of his family in this world as much as in the next.

### Phrase by phrase

**"And ˹remember˺ when Abraham said, “My Lord"**. Remember, Prophet, when Ibrāhīm prayed to his Lord. The prayer opens with the word Rabb, which means the One who gives nurture, and this teaches the proper way of praying, for the address itself draws Allah's mercy and grace on the one who prays. In ancient times Arabia was the most arid land on earth, its sands and bare rocks unfit for any cultivation and wholly exposed to attack from outside. Four thousand years ago Ibrāhīm was commanded to take his family into an uncultivable valley in the part of Arabia known as the Ḥijāz and settle them there, and he bowed to the will of Allah without the slightest hesitation. Having done so, he prayed in effect: my Lord, I have done as I was commanded. Now hear the call of Your servant.

**"make this city ˹of Mecca˺ secure"**. Free of fear and disturbance, a place where no one meets with evil: safe from slaughter and plunder, from calamities, and from the domination of unbelievers. The first thing he asked was that the barren desert where he had left his family under divine command become a city, so that his wife and son would not feel lonely and their daily needs would be easily met. The same prayer occurs in the chapter named after him: "My Lord! Make this city ˹of Mecca˺ secure, and keep me and my children away from the worship of idols" (14:35). There, however, the Arabic says "the city", al-balad, while here it says "a city", baladan. The difference probably arises because the prayer reported here was made when the place was still a desert and Ibrāhīm wished a city to grow in it, before the Kaʿbah was built, whereas the prayer in the other chapter was made a second time after the House had been built and people lived around it. Near the end of that chapter he says, "All praise is for Allah who has blessed me with Ishmael and Isaac in my old age" (14:39), which shows that the second prayer came after the birth of Isḥāq (Isaac), who was born thirteen years after Ismāʿīl (Ishmael).

**"and provide fruits to its people"**. Different kinds of fruit, all types of crops, bestowed on those who live there. The surrounding land could grow nothing, and before this the place had neither vegetation nor water.

**"those among them who believe in Allah and the Last Day"**. Those who believe in the resurrection after death. The phrase stands in place of "its people" and singles out the believers for mention in the request, in keeping with Allah's earlier words that His covenant does not reach the wrongdoers. This is an example of Ibrāhīm's rectitude. The opening of his prayer for the prosperity of the people of Makkah seems to include unbelievers as much as believers. But when he had earlier prayed for all his descendants without distinction, asking for the position of imāmah (leadership), Allah had answered that the prayer would be granted for the faithful but not for the unjust, the mushrikūn, those who associate partners with Him. The fear of Allah and the anxiety to obey Him completely were so deeply rooted in the heart of His Friend that even while praying for his people's prosperity the earlier proviso came to his mind, and he at once added that he was asking only for the believers. Ibn Abī Ḥātim narrated that Ibn ʿAbbās explained it in these terms: Ibrāhīm asked Allah to grant sustenance to the believers only.

**"He answered, “As for those who disbelieve, I will let them enjoy themselves for a little while"**. Allah was pleased with his rectitude and told him that worldly prosperity would be given to the disbelievers too. Ibn Jarīr related that Ubayy ibn Kaʿb said these are Allah's words, not Ibrāhīm's, and Mujāhid and ʿIkrimah explained it the same way. In Ibn ʿAbbās's account Allah revealed: I will also provide for the disbelievers just as I provide for the believers. Would I create something and not sustain and provide for it? I shall allow the disbelievers a little delight and then force them to the torment of the Fire, and what an evil destination. Ibn ʿAbbās then recited: "We provide both the former and the latter from the bounty of your Lord. And the bounty of your Lord can never be withheld" (17:20). Ibn Marduwyah recorded this, and similar statements from ʿIkrimah and Mujāhid. The verb is read both umtiʿuhu and umattiʿuhu, and the enjoyment is sustenance in this life, a little, for the length of his life. The Qur'an says the same elsewhere: those who fabricate lies against Allah will never succeed, theirs is a brief enjoyment in this world, then their return is to Allah and He will make them taste the severe punishment for their disbelief (10:69-70). The Prophet ﷺ is told not to let their disbelief grieve him, for "We allow them enjoyment for a little while, then ˹in time˺ We will force them into a harsh torment" (31:23-24). And were it not that people might all become one community of disbelievers, Allah would have given the homes of those who disbelieve silver roofs and stairways, gates and thrones and ornaments of gold, "Yet all this is no more than a ˹fleeting˺ enjoyment in this worldly life. ˹But˺ the Hereafter with your Lord is ˹only˺ for those mindful ˹of Him˺" (43:33-35).

**"then I will condemn them to the torment of the Fire. What an evil destination!”"**. After the delight the disbeliever enjoyed in this life, I will force him and drive him to the Fire in the Hereafter, with no escape, and an evil place of return it is. In the next world only the faithful will prosper, while the disbelievers receive nothing more than the punishment due to them. The verse shows that Allah gives the disbelievers respite and then seizes them in a manner that befits His greatness and power: "Many are the societies whose end We delayed while they did wrong, then seized them. And to Me is the final return" (22:48). The Two Ṣaḥīḥs record that no one is more patient than Allah on hearing abuse: people attribute a son to Him while He grants them sustenance and health. The Ṣaḥīḥ also records that Allah gives the unjust person respite until, when He seizes him, He never lets him go, and the Prophet ﷺ then recited, "Such is the ˹crushing˺ grip of your Lord when He seizes the societies entrenched in wrongdoing. Indeed, His grip is ˹terribly˺ painful and severe" (11:102).

### How the prayer for security was answered

Allah granted the request. He made Makkah a sanctuary in which no human blood is shed, no injustice is done to anyone, no prey is hunted, and no part of which is ever deserted. He said, "Whoever enters it should be safe" (3:97), and "Have they not seen how We have made ˹Mecca˺ a safe haven, whereas people ˹all˺ around them are snatched away?" (29:67). Muslim recorded that Jābir said the Messenger of Allah ﷺ forbade anyone to carry weapons in Makkah, and the hadiths forbidding fighting in the sacred area are given under the previous verse. Makkah became a thriving city, which Muslims now visit as pilgrims in their millions every year, and no unbeliever has ever conquered it or held sway over it. The Qur'an itself tells the story of the People of the Elephant (Aṣḥāb al-Fīl), who were destroyed for venturing to invade it. The city has also been safe from slaughter and plunder. Even before Islam, the Arabs of the age of ignorance, for all their unbelief and idolatry, respected the Kaʿbah and its surroundings as a matter of creed. Vengeful as they were, they would never take revenge while the enemy remained inside the Ḥaram. The people of Makkah were respected throughout Arabia, and the caravans trading between Makkah and Syria or Yemen were never molested. Allah gave security even to the birds and animals of the Ḥaram by forbidding all hunting there, and birds and animals visibly feel safe inside it and are not frightened of people. Islam emphasised and enforced this sanctity still further. As for the bloodshed that took place in the Ḥaram at the hands of al-Ḥajjāj ibn Yūsuf or the Qarāmiṭah, that was the work of people who called themselves Muslims, not an invasion by unbelievers. If a man sets fire to his own house it does not disprove the rule that the house is secure against outsiders. Such incidents have been very rare since the days of Ibrāhīm, and the dreadful fate of those who dared to pollute the House of Allah is known. In short, Allah made the city so secure in answer to this prayer that even the Dajjāl (the Antichrist) will have no power to enter it. The land of the Ḥijāz has remained an abode of peace and plenty to the present day.

### How the prayer for fruits was answered

Although the land around Makkah cannot be cultivated, Allah in answer to the prayer made the neighbouring city of Ṭāʾif very fertile and rich in fruit, which began to come to Makkah. According to certain Israelite traditions, Ṭāʾif was originally situated in Syria and was moved to its present place by the archangel Jibrāʾīl (Gabriel) at Allah's command. Fruits also arrived with travellers from as far away as Syria.

There is wisdom in the form of the prayer. Ibrāhīm did not ask for the land of Makkah to be made fertile. He asked, in effect, that fruits be brought to it from elsewhere. He probably intended that his descendants should not become absorbed in agriculture, because his purpose in founding the settlement, as his other prayer says, was that his people should keep up the prayer. He wanted the essential work of his descendants to be guarding the House of Allah and devoting themselves to worship. Otherwise he could as easily have prayed for Makkah itself to be fertile, and Allah would have granted it. The point is clearer still in the word thamarāt, the plural of thamarah, fruit, which appears again where Allah asks whether He has not established for them "a safe haven ˹in Mecca˺ to which fruits of all kinds are brought as a provision from Us" (28:57). If the fruits of trees are meant, the word "brought" is enough to show that Allah did not promise to grow them in Makkah but to send them from other places. But that verse does not speak of the fruits of all kinds of trees. It speaks of the fruits of all kinds of things, and in ordinary usage "fruit" means the product of a thing or an activity. The word therefore covers not only the produce of trees but the products of every craft and industry, everything needed to sustain human life. Anyone can see that Makkah has neither agriculture nor industry, yet enjoys the benefits of both as much as any prosperous city in the world.

### Why this prayer was granted

In the devotional reading, the request was answered because it was not adulterated by the servant's worldly concern. Ibrāhīm was not asking for his own portion (ḥaẓẓ) but for the right (ḥaqq) of his Lord. Because he observed the required courtesy in seeking provision, asking it for those who believed, it was granted to them, and to those who did not believe as well. When, on the other hand, he spoke about leadership and asked for his offspring without permission, that request was refused and he was told that the covenant does not reach the wrongdoers.

### What the verse asks of a believer

The believer's whole life should be an act of worship. In whatever far corner of the world he lives he should remember at all times that one day he must return to his Lord. He should harm no one, and should treat the earth he lives on as a place of worship, kept free of all pollution. Physically in this world, his heart and mind should stay fixed on Allah, and his life should revolve around Him alone in submission. True religion makes demands on everyone, and sometimes it even requires that one's children be taken to a place as arid as Ibrāhīm's valley. Whatever it entails, a person should faithfully carry out Allah's commands first, and only then pray that his efforts be made to succeed. It may well be that Allah will make springs gush from a dry desert and lush crops rise from barren land. Whatever splendour one is granted in this life does not of itself mean that Allah considers one fit to lead mankind. Everything given to a person is a means of testing him, and no one is exempt from Allah's trial. Leadership means being chosen by Allah to represent Him among the nations, and it belongs only to those He has found fit to represent His religion on earth.

### In short

- Ibrāhīm prayed that the barren valley become a secure city with fruits for its believing people, and Allah granted both: Makkah became a sanctuary no unbeliever has ever conquered (3:97, 29:67), and its fruits come to it from Ṭāʾif and beyond (28:57).
- Remembering that leadership had been denied to the wrongdoers among his offspring, he limited his request to the believers. Allah replied that He provides for the disbelievers too (17:20), but their enjoyment is brief and ends in the Fire (10:69-70, 31:23-24, 43:33-35, 22:48, 11:102).
- Ibrāhīm asked for fruits to be brought rather than for fertile land, so that his descendants would be keepers of the House rather than farmers.
- The prayer was granted because it sought Allah's right and not the servant's own portion.

127.text:
Verse 127 shows Ibrāhīm (Abraham) at work on the House itself, and shows what was in his heart as he worked. "And ˹remember˺ when Abraham raised the foundation of the House with Ishmael, ˹both praying,˺ “Our Lord! Accept ˹this˺ from us. You are indeed the All-Hearing, All-Knowing". Allah tells the Prophet ﷺ: remind your people how Ibrāhīm and Ismāʿīl (Ishmael) built the House and raised its foundations while saying these words. In obedience to Allah, Ibrāhīm had left the fertile land of Syria and settled his wife and child in a barren desert, and now he took up the labour of building the House of Allah. A man who had borne such hardships might be expected to feel satisfied with himself and relax in self-congratulation. But the Friend of Allah recognised the Majesty of Allah and knew that no creature can worship or obey his Creator as is His due, only within his own limited powers. So he knew that in performing the hardest and greatest tasks a person should not be proud of his achievement but should humbly pray that Allah accept the little effort he has been able to make, an effort made with Allah's own grace. That is exactly what he did as he began, with his young son, to build the Kaʿbah.

### Phrase by phrase

**"And ˹remember˺ when Abraham raised the foundation of the House with Ishmael"**. He raised up the supports or walls of the House, building it, and Ismāʿīl was with him. In the Arabic "and Ishmael" is joined to "Abraham" as a second subject, and "of the House" attaches to the verb "raises". Ibrāhīm built while Ismāʿīl helped, which is the order the names themselves suggest: the builder of the Kaʿbah is Ibrāhīm and his son's role is that of a helper. When they started digging, the earlier foundations became visible, and it was on these that they raised the walls.

**"˹both praying,˺ “Our Lord! Accept ˹this˺ from us"**. Receive from us this building of Your House. Al-Qurṭubī mentioned that Ubayy and Ibn Masʿūd used to recite the verse with the word "saying" added, and what follows, "Our Lord! Make us both submit", confirms that reading, since it continues the same prayer. The two prophets were performing a good deed, and yet they asked Allah to accept it from them. Ibn Abī Ḥātim narrated that Wuhayb ibn al-Ward recited this verse and wept, saying: O Khalīl of ar-Raḥmān, you raise the foundations of the House of ar-Raḥmān and still fear that He will not accept it from you? This is the way of sincere believers, whom Allah described as "those who give whatever they give" (23:60), that is, who give charity and perform acts of worship, "with their hearts fearful" (23:60), afraid that their good deeds may not be accepted. There is an authentic hadith of ʿĀʾishah on this point. In the devotional reading, the success of a request lies in the sincerity of the supplication: when the two of them humbly sought help in prayer, He helped them and granted what they asked.

**"You are indeed the All-Hearing, All-Knowing"**. The Hearer of words and of our prayer, the Knower of deeds and of the answer to this prayer, or, as it is also explained, the Knower of our intention in building Your House. Allah hears what people say and knows their intentions and all that they do.

### How the House was built, in the Prophet's ﷺ own account

Al-Bukhārī recorded from Ibn ʿAbbās the story of how all this came about. Ibrāhīm took Ismāʿīl and his mother and travelled with them until he reached the site of the House, where he left them under a tree above the place of Zamzam, in the upper part of the Mosque. She was still nursing the child. Makkah was then uninhabited and had no water, and he left them with a bag of dates and a skin of water. As he turned to go, Ismāʿīl's mother followed him and asked to whom he was leaving them in a valley with no people in it. She repeated the question several times and he did not answer. Then she asked whether Allah had commanded him to do this. He said yes, and she said: then He will not abandon us. Ibrāhīm went on until, out of their sight near Thaniyyah, he faced the House, raised his hands and prayed that he had settled some of his offspring in a barren valley by the Sacred House, down to the words about giving thanks (14:37).

She went back, drank from the skin and nursed the boy, and when the water ran out both of them grew thirsty. Unable to bear the sight of him suffering, she went to the nearest hill, aṣ-Ṣafā, climbed it and looked in vain for anyone. Coming down into the valley she lifted her garment and ran like an exhausted person until she reached al-Marwah, where again she saw no one, and she went back and forth seven times. Ibn ʿAbbās reported that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said this is why people make the trip between aṣ-Ṣafā and al-Marwah. On al-Marwah she heard a voice, said "hush" to herself, listened, heard it again and called out, "I have heard you. Do you have relief?" She found the angel digging with his heel, or his wing, at the place of Zamzam until water gushed out. Astonished, she began scooping it with her hands into the water-skin. The Prophet ﷺ said: may Allah have mercy on the mother of Ismāʿīl. Had she left the water alone, it would have run as a stream over the surface of the earth. She drank, her milk returned for the child, and the angel, Jibrīl (Gabriel), told her not to fear abandonment, for a House of Allah would be built here by this boy and his father, and Allah does not abandon His people. At that time the site of the House stood higher than the ground around it, and floods passed to its right and left.

Later some people of the tribe of Jurhum, passing through Kadāʾ, camped at the bottom of the valley. They noticed birds circling and said that birds are only found where there is water, though they had never known water in that valley. They sent one or two scouts, who found the spring and reported back, and they all came to Ismāʿīl's mother and asked leave to settle beside her. She agreed, on condition that they would have no exclusive right to the water, and they accepted. The Prophet ﷺ remarked that she welcomed human company. They settled and sent for their relatives. The boy grew up among them, learned Arabic from them, and because they admired the way he had been raised they gave him one of their women in marriage. Then his mother died.

Some time afterwards Ibrāhīm came to visit the family he had left. He did not find Ismāʿīl, who had gone hunting, and asked his wife how they lived. She complained of misery and poverty. He told her to greet her husband and tell him to change the threshold of his door. When Ismāʿīl returned he sensed a visitor had come, heard what had been said, and told her: that was my father, and you are the threshold. He was telling me to part with you. He divorced her and married another woman. When Ibrāhīm came again he found Ismāʿīl out hunting once more, and this wife praised Allah and said they were well. Asked what they ate and drank, she said meat and water, and he prayed: O Allah, bless their meat and their drink. The Prophet ﷺ explained that they had no grain then, or Ibrāhīm would have prayed for a blessing on that too, and that no one outside Makkah can live on meat and water alone. Ibrāhīm told her to greet her husband and tell him to keep the threshold of his door, and Ismāʿīl understood: that was my father, and he commanded me to keep you.

On a third visit Ibrāhīm found Ismāʿīl near the well of Zamzam, under a tree, mending his arrows. They greeted each other as father and son do, and Ibrāhīm said that his Lord had commanded him to do something and asked whether Ismāʿīl would help. Ismāʿīl said: obey your Lord, and I will help you. Ibrāhīm said that Allah had commanded him to build a house for Him there, pointing to a mound that stood above the ground. The two of them rose and raised the foundations of the House. Ibrāhīm built while Ismāʿīl passed him the stones, and both kept saying, "Our Lord! Accept ˹this˺ from us. You are indeed the All-Hearing, All-Knowing". So they built, part by part, going round the House and repeating that prayer.

### The Quraysh rebuild the Kaʿbah

Muḥammad ibn Isḥāq ibn Yasār relates in his Sīrah that when the Messenger of Allah ﷺ was thirty-five years old the Quraysh gathered to rebuild the Kaʿbah and give it a roof, though they were afraid to demolish it. At that time its walls were barely higher than a man's shoulder, and they wanted to raise them and build a ceiling. Its treasure, which used to be kept in a well in the middle of the Kaʿbah, had been stolen beforehand. It was later found with a man called Duwayk, a freed slave of Banū Mulayḥ ibn ʿAmr of Khuzāʿah, and the Quraysh cut off his hand, though some said the real thieves had left it with him. Then a ship belonging to a Roman merchant was wrecked at Jeddah, and they took its timber for the ceiling, a Coptic carpenter in Makkah preparing what they needed. When they decided to begin the demolition, Abū Wahb ibn ʿAmr ibn ʿĀʾidh ibn ʿAbd ibn ʿImrān ibn Makhzūm took hold of a stone of the Kaʿbah, and it slipped from his hand and returned to its place. He said: people of Quraysh, spend on rebuilding the House only what has been earned from pure sources. Let no money from a prostitute, from usury or from injustice go into it. Ibn Isḥāq notes that people also attribute these words to al-Walīd ibn al-Mughīrah ibn ʿAbdullāh ibn ʿAmr ibn Makhzūm.

The Quraysh organised the work so that each subtribe was responsible for a particular part, but they still hesitated to pull the building down. Al-Walīd ibn al-Mughīrah said he would begin. He took an axe, stood by the Kaʿbah and said: O Allah, no harm is meant, we seek only to do good. Then he began to break away the stones. The people waited through the night, saying that if something struck him they would stop and rebuild it as it had been, and if nothing happened then Allah approved of what they were doing. Next morning al-Walīd went back to work and the others joined him. When they reached the foundations laid by Ibrāhīm they uncovered green stones lying one upon another like a pile of spears. Ibn Isḥāq was told that a man of Quraysh put his shovel between two of these stones to lever them up, and when one of them moved the whole of Makkah shook, so they left those stones undisturbed.

Each tribe collected stones separately and the building rose until it reached the point where the Black Stone had to be set in place. Then a dispute broke out, every tribe wanting the honour for itself, and it nearly came to fighting among the leaders of Quraysh beside the Sacred House. Banū ʿAbd ad-Dār and Banū ʿAdī ibn Kaʿb ibn Luʾayy pledged to each other to fight to the death. After four or five days Abū Umayyah ibn al-Mughīrah ibn ʿAbdullāh ibn ʿAmr ibn Makhzūm, the oldest man of Quraysh, intervened and proposed that the first man to enter through the door of the Mosque should judge between them. They agreed, and the first to enter was Muḥammad ﷺ. When they saw who it was they all said: this is al-Amīn, the trustworthy one. We accept him. This is Muḥammad. When he reached them and heard the dispute, he asked for a cloak and spread it on the ground, placed the Black Stone on it, and had the leader of each tribe hold an edge so that they all lifted it together to its place. Then he took the Stone himself, set it in position and built around it. The Quraysh had called him al-Amīn even before revelation came to him.

### Ibn az-Zubayr, al-Ḥajjāj, and what the Prophet ﷺ had wished

Ibn Isḥāq says that in the Prophet's ﷺ time the Kaʿbah was eighteen cubits high and was covered with Egyptian linen, and later with a striped cloth, and that al-Ḥajjāj ibn Yūsuf was the first to cover it with silk. It stayed as the Quraysh had built it until it was burned during the reign of ʿAbdullāh ibn az-Zubayr, after the year 60 of the Hijrah, at the end of the reign of Yazīd ibn Muʿāwiyah, when Ibn az-Zubayr was besieged in Makkah. He then pulled it down and rebuilt it on the foundations of Ibrāhīm, bringing al-Ḥijr inside it, and gave it an eastern door and a western door at ground level, because he had heard his aunt ʿĀʾishah, the Mother of the Believers, relate that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ had wished for this. It remained so until al-Ḥajjāj killed Ibn az-Zubayr and, on the orders of ʿAbd al-Malik ibn Marwān, rebuilt it as it had been before.

Muslim recorded ʿAṭāʾ's account. The House was burned in Yazīd's reign when the people of ash-Shām (Syria) attacked Makkah. Ibn az-Zubayr left it untouched until the pilgrims came, wishing to stir them against the Syrians, and asked the people whether he should pull it down and rebuild it or only repair the damage. Ibn ʿAbbās advised him to leave the stones that had stood when the people became Muslims and the Prophet ﷺ was sent, and to rebuild it as it then was. Ibn az-Zubayr answered that if one of their own houses burned down its owner would not rest until he rebuilt it, so how much more the House of Allah, and said he would seek his Lord's guidance for three days and then act. After three days he resolved to demolish it. People held back, fearing that the first to climb onto it would be struck down, until one man went up and threw down some stones and came to no harm, and then the rest joined in and brought it down to the ground. Ibn az-Zubayr hung curtains from pillars round the site so that the House stayed screened until the walls were up. He then said he had heard ʿĀʾishah relate that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: were it not that your people have only recently left unbelief, and that I lack the money to spend on it, I would have brought five cubits of al-Ḥijr into the House and given it one door for entering and another for leaving. Ibn az-Zubayr said he had the money and did not fear the people. So he added five cubits from al-Ḥijr, which showed clearly as a rear part of the House, raised the walls to eighteen cubits, and thinking that still too low added ten cubits at the front, and made two doors, one to go in by and one to come out by. When he was killed, al-Ḥajjāj wrote to ʿAbd al-Malik ibn Marwān about it. ʿAbd al-Malik replied that he did not approve of what Ibn az-Zubayr had done: the height could stay, but what he had added from al-Ḥijr was to be pulled down and the House rebuilt as before, and the extra door closed. Al-Ḥajjāj did so. An-Nasāʾī in his Sunan collected the Prophet's ﷺ words from ʿĀʾishah, without the rest of the story.

The correct sunnah agreed with what Ibn az-Zubayr did, since it was what the Prophet ﷺ had wished but had held back from, fearing that the hearts of the newly converted could not bear it. This was not clear to ʿAbd al-Malik, and when he learned that ʿĀʾishah had narrated it he said: I wish we had left it as Ibn az-Zubayr made it. Muslim recorded that al-Ḥārith ibn ʿAbdullāh came to ʿAbd al-Malik during his reign, and ʿAbd al-Malik said he had not believed that Abū Khubayb, meaning Ibn az-Zubayr, had really heard from ʿĀʾishah what he claimed. Al-Ḥārith said that he had heard it from her himself: the Messenger of Allah ﷺ had told her that her people had rebuilt the House smaller, that had they not been so close to the time of shirk he would have restored what they left out, and that if her people ever thought of rebuilding it he would show her what they had left out, and he showed her about seven cubits. One of the narrators, al-Walīd ibn ʿAṭāʾ, added that the Prophet ﷺ said he would have made two doors at ground level, one east and one west, and asked her whether she knew why her people had raised the door. When she said no, he explained: so that only those they wished could enter, and when a man they did not want climbed up to the door they would push him down. ʿAbd al-Malik asked al-Ḥārith whether he had really heard ʿĀʾishah say this, and when he said yes, ʿAbd al-Malik said: I wish I had left it as it was.

### The Kaʿbah will be destroyed before the Last Hour

The Two Ṣaḥīḥs record from Abū Hurayrah that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said the Kaʿbah will be destroyed by Dhū as-Suwayqatayn, a man with two thin legs, from Ethiopia. Al-Bukhārī recorded that Ibn ʿAbbās reported the Prophet ﷺ saying: it is as if I can see him now, a black man with thin legs plucking the stones of the Kaʿbah one after another. Imam Aḥmad ibn Ḥanbal recorded in his Musnad that ʿAbdullāh ibn ʿAmr ibn al-ʿĀṣ heard the Messenger of Allah ﷺ say that Dhū as-Suwayqatayn from Ethiopia will destroy the Kaʿbah, loot its ornaments and strip its covering, and that he could almost see him, bald and thin-legged, striking it with his axe. This will happen after the coming of Gog and Magog, for al-Bukhārī recorded from Abū Saʿīd al-Khudrī that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said there will still be Hajj and ʿUmrah to the House after Gog and Magog appear.

### What the prayer meant for the world

Allah ordained that a universal centre for the call to Islam be established in the Ḥijāz, and chose Ibrāhīm and his family to found it and provide for its working. The words the two of them spoke while building were prayers, but they were also a sign of their unwavering loyalty to Allah's plan, and prayer of that kind pleases Him most. He accepted it, and a permanent fountain of spiritual life for the whole world gushed forth from the barren desert of Arabia. Its name was Islam.

### In short

- Ibrāhīm, helped by Ismāʿīl, raised the walls of the Kaʿbah on its ancient foundations, and the two of them kept praying that Allah accept the work, the mark of sincere believers who fear their deeds may be refused (23:60).
- Al-Bukhārī's account from Ibn ʿAbbās tells how Hājar and the infant were left at the site, how Zamzam sprang up, how Jurhum settled there, how Ismāʿīl married, and how father and son built the House together.
- The Quraysh rebuilt the Kaʿbah when the Prophet ﷺ was thirty-five, and he settled their quarrel over the Black Stone by having every tribe lift it on a cloak and then placing it himself.
- Ibn az-Zubayr later rebuilt it as the Prophet ﷺ had wished, including al-Ḥijr and two doors at ground level, and al-Ḥajjāj restored the Quraysh form, which ʿAbd al-Malik later regretted.
- Near the end of time a thin-legged man from Ethiopia will demolish the Kaʿbah, after the coming of Gog and Magog.

128.text:
Verse 128 continues the prayer of Ibrāhīm (Abraham) and Ismāʿīl (Ishmael) as they built the House. "Our Lord! Make us both ˹fully˺ submit to You and from our descendants a nation that will submit to you. Show us our rituals, and turn to us in grace. You are truly the Accepter of Repentance, Most Merciful". The prayer springs from the same fear and awe, and the same knowledge, as the request that the building be accepted. Ibrāhīm had spent his whole life in exemplary obedience, yet he prays to be made obedient, because the more a person grows in knowledge of the Divine Majesty, the more he realises that he is not as faithful and obedient as he should be.

### Phrase by phrase

**"Our Lord! Make us both ˹fully˺ submit to You"**. Make us compliant and obedient to You, sincere in not ascribing any partner to You and in worshipping You alone. Ibn Jarīr said that they meant: make us submit to Your command and obedience, associating no one with You in obedience or worship. ʿIkrimah related that Allah answered, "I shall do that." In the devotional reading, "submitting" means yielding to Your decree so completely that not one vein of ours throbs without Your good pleasure.

**"and from our descendants a nation that will submit to you"**. Make of our progeny a people submissive to You. The Arabic "from our descendants" is partitive, some of them, in keeping with Allah's earlier words that His covenant does not reach the wrongdoers. Again ʿIkrimah related the answer, "I shall do that." It is significant that Ibrāhīm included his descendants. The men of Allah, who never hesitate to sacrifice themselves and their children in His way, still love their children deeply, but they know what parental love really requires. Ordinary people suppose that their children's well-being lies in physical health and comfort alone and spend all their care on providing that. Those favoured by Allah are far more anxious about their children's spiritual welfare and about what becomes of them in the next world. There is a further benefit: experience shows that when respected people and their descendants keep to the right path, they are held in esteem and their conduct moves others to reform. Allah heard this prayer too, and among the descendants of Ibrāhīm there has always been a group obedient to Allah and firm on the Straight Path. Even in the Jāhiliyyah, when the whole world and Arabia in particular lay in the darkness of idolatry and shirk, there remained men of his line who believed in the One God and the next world and obeyed Him, such as Zayd ibn ʿAmr ibn Nufayl and Quss ibn Sāʿidah, and it is reported that ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib ibn Hāshim, the Prophet's ﷺ grandfather, shunned idol-worship. This prayer is like the prayer Allah reports from His believing servants who ask for spouses and children who will be a comfort to their eyes and to be made leaders of the righteous (25:74). Such a prayer is permitted, because wanting offspring who worship Allah alone is a sign of complete love for Allah. That is why, when Allah told Ibrāhīm He would make him a leader, he asked at once for his offspring, and the answer that the covenant excludes wrongdoers is explained by his own words elsewhere, "keep me and my children away from the worship of idols" (14:35). Muslim narrated in his Ṣaḥīḥ from Abū Hurayrah that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said that when a person dies his deeds come to an end except for three: a continuing charity, knowledge that goes on being of benefit, and a righteous child who prays for him. The devotional reading contrasts the one who seeks an heir for his wealth with the one who seeks a deputy to carry on acts of obedience after him. Ibrāhīm asked for successors who would take his place in upholding Allah's rights.

**"Show us our rituals"**. Teach us our ceremonies of worship, the rites of our pilgrimage. Manāsik, the plural of mansik, means the different actions of the Hajj and also the places where they are performed, such as ʿArafah, Muzdalifah and Minā, and both meanings are intended. Ibrāhīm wanted the rites explained and their locations pointed out. The verb is arinā, "show us", and seeing is done through the eyes and through the heart, so the sites were shown to him by the archangel Jibrāʾīl (Gabriel) and the rulings of Hajj were explained in detail. Inwardly, the request means that there is no way to know what conforms to Allah's will except by the path He grants, through His giving of success and His communication.

**"and turn to us in grace"**. Relent towards us, overlook our shortcomings and forgive our faults in carrying out what You commanded. They asked Allah to turn to them despite their moral impeccability, out of humility and in order to teach their descendants. In the devotional reading, they asked for this after carrying out all they were commanded so that they would not look at what they had done or left undone, but would turn back to Him from witnessing their own actions, leaving no room for the hidden shirk of imagining that anything came from them or through them.

**"You are truly the Accepter of Repentance, Most Merciful"**. The One who overlooks shortcomings and turns to those who ask forgiveness, and the One who is merciful towards the believers and compassionate to His creation.

### How Jibrīl showed Ibrāhīm the rites

Saʿīd ibn Manṣūr related, through ʿAttāb ibn Bashīr and Khaṣīf, that Mujāhid said: when Ibrāhīm prayed "show us our rituals", Jibrīl came down, took him to the House and told him to raise its foundations, and Ibrāhīm raised them and completed the building. Then Jibrīl took him by the hand to aṣ-Ṣafā and said that this was among the rituals of Allah, and to al-Marwah and said the same. He took him on to Minā, and at al-ʿAqabah they found Iblīs standing by a tree. Jibrīl told him to say the takbīr, "Allah is the Greatest", and throw pebbles at him, and he did. Iblīs moved to the middle jamrah, and as they passed Jibrīl told him again to say the takbīr and throw, and he threw. The devious Iblīs was trying to add some evil to the rites of Hajj, but he failed. Jibrīl then led him to al-Mashʿar al-Ḥarām and to ʿArafāt and asked him three times, "Have you learned (ʿarafta) what I showed you?", and Ibrāhīm said that he had. Similar reports come from Abū Mijlaz and Qatādah.

### The fruit of the prayer

Allah made the people of that desert, the offspring of Ismāʿīl, enthusiastic champions of the cause of Islam and enabled them to carry His word far and wide. Through them He taught mankind how to please their Lord so that He would turn to them in mercy. It was to the Children of Ismāʿīl that the final Prophet ﷺ was sent, and for the first time in history the whole prophetic pattern was recorded for posterity, so that later generations could follow it.

### In short

- Ibrāhīm and Ismāʿīl asked to be made fully submissive and for a submissive nation among their descendants, and Allah answered "I shall do that" to both.
- Praying for righteous offspring is a sign of complete love for Allah (25:74, 14:35), and a righteous child who prays for a parent is one of the three deeds that outlive a person.
- The manāsik are the actions and the places of Hajj. Jibrīl showed them to Ibrāhīm one by one, from aṣ-Ṣafā and al-Marwah to the stoning at Minā and ʿArafāt.
- Asking Allah to turn to them after perfect obedience taught humility and guarded against the hidden shirk of crediting oneself.

129.text:
Verse 129 is the last part of the prayer Ibrāhīm (Abraham) and Ismāʿīl (Ishmael) made while building the House, and it is a prayer for the Prophet ﷺ himself. "Our Lord! Raise from among them a messenger who will recite to them Your revelations, teach them the Book and wisdom, and purify them. Indeed, You ˹alone˺ are the Almighty, All-Wise.”" Ibrāhīm had asked security and provision for the people of the sacred land, and he perfected the prayer by asking Allah to send a Messenger from his own offspring. The prayer was accepted, in keeping with what Allah had already decreed: that Muḥammad ﷺ be sent among the unlettered Arabs and to all non-Arabs, to jinn and to mankind. Ibrāhīm was thus the first to speak of the Prophet ﷺ to people, and from then on he was known, until the last prophet sent to the Children of Israel, ʿĪsā (Jesus) son of Maryam, mentioned him by name: "O children of Israel! I am truly Allah’s messenger to you, confirming the Torah which came before me, and giving good news of a messenger after me whose name will be Aḥmad" (61:6). This is why the Prophet ﷺ said that he was the supplication of his father Ibrāhīm and the good news of ʿĪsā son of Maryam, a hadith Imam Aḥmad reports in his Musnad. He also said that his mother saw a light go out from her which lit up the palaces of ash-Shām (Syria). It is said that she saw this while she was pregnant with him and told her people, and the story became well known among them.

The Prophet ﷺ is the messenger Ibrāhīm prayed for. The words of this prayer are repeated in two other places in the Qur'an, once in Sūrah Āl ʿImrān and once in Sūrah al-Jumuʿah, and both passages speak of the prophethood of Muḥammad ﷺ. All three say the same thing about him in the same words: they define why he was sent and what his functions as a prophet are. According to a hadith, in accepting the prayer Allah promised that this prophet would be sent in the last of all ages, as Ibn Jarīr and others relate.

### Phrase by phrase

**"Our Lord! Raise from among them a messenger"**. Send among the people of this House, the offspring of Ismāʿīl, a messenger of their own lineage. Allah granted this petition by sending Muḥammad ﷺ. Why did Ibrāhīm, praying for the good of his descendants in both worlds, ask for a prophet from among them? For two reasons. The appearance of a prophet from among them would itself be an honour and a blessing. And since the prophet would be one of their own, they would know his past, his present and his ways thoroughly, and so find it easy to trust him and benefit from his guidance. One gloss adds that these are the very words with which Allah tried Ibrāhīm, and he fulfilled them by asking Allah for them in his prayer.

**"who will recite to them Your revelations"**. The verses of the Qur'an. The verb yatlū comes from tilāwah, which in the dictionary means to follow and obey, but in the usage of the Qur'an and hadith means reciting the Qur'an or a divine Book, since whoever reads a divine Book is also required to obey it fully. The word also implies that the Qur'an must be read exactly as Allah revealed it, without adding or omitting a word or even altering the pronunciation of a word, which in Arabic can change its meaning. In his "Mufradāt al-Qurʾān" ar-Rāghib al-Iṣfahānī says that in current idiom tilāwah cannot be applied to reading any book other than the Word of Allah. The first task of Allah's messenger is to set out His signs, the proofs of His greatness and power. Allah has placed countless signs in human nature and in the outside world so that people may know their Creator, but these signs have to be unveiled by His messenger, who shares his divinely given insight so that people may glimpse Allah's glory.

**"teach them the Book and wisdom"**. The Book is the Qur'an. "Wisdom", ḥikmah, is the Sunnah, the Prophet's ﷺ way, as al-Ḥasan, Qatādah, Muqātil ibn Ḥayyān and Abū Mālik affirmed. It has also been explained as comprehension in religion, and both meanings are correct. In Arabic the word carries several senses, such as arriving at the truth, justice and exact knowledge, as al-Qāmūs records. Ar-Rāghib al-Iṣfahānī says that when used of Allah it means total and perfect knowledge of all that exists together with flawless creation, and when used of anyone else, sound knowledge of things together with good deeds. Maulānā Maḥmūd al-Ḥasan rendered it here as profound truths or subtle realities, and Maulānā Ashraf ʿAlī Thānavī as the art of understanding properly. The Companions and their successors, whose explanations come directly from the Prophet's ﷺ teaching, gave various accounts: the commentary and exegesis of the Qur'an, the proper understanding of the religion, the injunctions of the Sharīʿah, or the commands of Allah received through the Prophet's ﷺ words. Despite the variety of expression these all come to the same thing, the Sunnah and the hadith, which is the explanation reported from Qatādah by Ibn Jarīr. Other glosses take wisdom as the judgments the Book contains, or as the lawful and the prohibited.

**"and purify them"**. Cleanse them of idolatry, of worshipping others alongside Allah, and of every evil. ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭalḥah related that Ibn ʿAbbās explained it as purifying them through obedience to Allah. One gloss says: from sins, through the declaration of Allah's oneness.

**"Indeed, You ˹alone˺ are the Almighty, All-Wise"**. Allah is able to do everything and nothing escapes His power. He is the Victor, and He is wise in His decisions and actions, putting everything in its rightful place through His perfect knowledge, wisdom and justice. He is mighty in His essence and wise in what He does and decrees. One gloss reads the Mighty as the One who takes vengeance on whoever does not answer the Messenger He sent, and the Wise as wise in sending him.

### Why reciting and teaching are named separately

The verse treats reciting the Qur'an and teaching it as two things. Reciting concerns the words and teaching concerns the meanings, so the distinction shows that the words of the Qur'an matter in themselves no less than their meanings, and that reciting and preserving the words is obligatory and an act of worship. The point is sharper when one remembers who the first listeners were. The Prophet's ﷺ immediate disciples knew Arabic perfectly and were eloquent speakers, some of them poets. For such an audience a recitation without commentary should have been teaching enough, and reciting and teaching should in practice have been one and the same. Why then are they named as two distinct functions?

Two conclusions follow. First, the Qur'an is not like other books, in which the meaning is the real object and the words are only a vehicle that can tolerate small changes as long as the sense survives. With a man-made book it would be frivolous to go on reading the words without attending to the meaning. With the Qur'an the words are as essential a part of the intention as the meanings, and the Sharīʿah lays down rulings specifically about them. That is why the science of the principles of jurisprudence (uṣūl al-fiqh) defines the Qur'an as comprising both words and meaning. If its meanings are expressed in another language, or even if other Arabic words are substituted for the revealed ones, the result is not entitled to the name "Qur'an" however intact the meaning may be. Reciting such a version in ṣalāh would not make the prayer valid, reading it would not earn the reward promised in hadith for reciting the Qur'an, and none of the rulings attached to the Qur'an would apply to it. The jurists have therefore forbidden printing a translation of the Qur'an without the Arabic text, and it is quite wrong to speak of an "Urdu Qur'an" or an "English Qur'an", since no translation into any language can properly be called the Qur'an.

The word yatlū therefore leaves no doubt that reciting the verses is an end in itself, for one recites words, not meanings. It goes without saying that Allah sent the Qur'an to be understood and followed, and to be content with memorising the words while ignoring the meanings shows ignorance of the nature of Allah's Book and ingratitude. But many people today suppose the Qur'an is like other books and think it a waste of time to read or memorise words whose meaning they do not know. Against this widespread error it cannot be stressed enough that reciting the words of the Qur'an is in itself a regular act of worship that brings great reward. The practice of the Prophet ﷺ and his Companions proves it. They understood the Qur'an as no one else can, yet they never thought that once they had understood and acted on it nothing more was required. They went on reciting it all their lives. Some Companions recited the whole Book in a single day, some in two days, some in three, and reciting it in a week has always been a common practice among Muslims, as the division of the Qur'an into seven stages (manāzil) shows. By making recitation an act of worship with its own reward, and a separate prophetic function, Allah showed great mercy to Muslims who cannot yet understand the meanings, saving them from indifference to the words and so from being wholly cut off from the blessings of His Book. Such Muslims should still keep trying to understand the meanings too, so that they receive the blessings in full and the ultimate purpose of the revelation is realised.

### Why the Book needs a teacher

Second, since teaching the Book is a prophetic function distinct from reciting it, knowing Arabic is not enough to understand the Qur'an. It also requires the Prophet's ﷺ teaching. To learn any science or art, medicine or engineering or something as ordinary as cookery, it is not enough to read a book or know a language. If it were, anyone could master every subject on which books exist in a language he knows. Even the humblest craft needs the regular guidance of a teacher. How then could anyone hope to understand unaided the Qur'an, which speaks on the hardest subjects imaginable, from theology to philosophy and physics? Had competence in Arabic been sufficient, scores of Jewish and Christian scholars and men of letters in Arab countries today would rank among the greatest exegetes, and so would Abū Jahl and Abū Lahab in the Prophet's ﷺ own day. By separating the teaching of the Book from the recitation of the verses, the Qur'an underlines that even those who know Arabic very well cannot understand the Book of Allah properly just by hearing it recited. That understanding comes only through the Prophet's ﷺ teaching, and to divide the one from the other and attempt interpretation on one's own is self-delusion. If it had not really been necessary to explain and teach the meanings, why would Allah have sent a Messenger at all, when there were many other ways to convey His Book? But Allah knows all things and is All-Wise. He knows that understanding His Book depends on a teacher's guidance far more than the human sciences do, and not an ordinary teacher but one who himself receives guidance directly from Allah through revelation (waḥy), the one called in Islamic terms a nabī (prophet) and a rasūl (messenger). The Qur'an says that Allah sent him precisely to explain the Book: "And We have sent down to you ˹O Prophet˺ the Reminder, so that you may explain to people what has been revealed for them" (16:44).

Teaching the Book includes teaching wisdom, and since the Companions and their successors understood wisdom here as the Sunnah, the prophetic function includes teaching the principles and methods of spiritual discipline. The Prophet ﷺ said that he had been sent only as a teacher. It follows that his followers are required to be disciples, and that every Muslim man and woman should be a lifelong student eager to learn what the Prophet ﷺ taught. Whoever cannot master the sciences of the Qur'an and the Sunnah must at least acquire a sound knowledge of the basic doctrines of Islam and the fundamental rulings of the Sharīʿah that no Muslim can do without.

### Purification: knowing is not enough

Purifying the people is also an essential prophetic function. Tazkiyah means cleansing a person or thing of every kind of filth, inward as well as outward. The outward kinds are plain, and the Sharīʿah has defined them. The inward kinds include, on one side, false beliefs such as kufr (unbelief), shirk (associating partners with Allah) and total reliance on anyone other than Allah, and on the other side pride, vanity, malice, jealousy and love of worldly things. The Qur'an and the Sunnah have fully explained how evil these beliefs and tendencies are. Yet by making purification a separate prophetic function the verse indicates that, just as knowing words and technical terms does not make someone master of a science or art, so knowing and even properly understanding its principles does not by itself make him perfect in it. To reach any degree of perfection one must also learn to put the principles into practice and realise them in oneself, and that again requires the supervision of an authentic teacher and guide. In the Ṣūfī path (ṭarīqah) the role of the spiritual guide, the shaykh, is to help the disciple obey the Qur'an and the Sunnah so thoroughly that obedience becomes not an effort but a habit, almost his nature.

A warning is added here about the modern habit of calling Islam "the religion of action", with the implication that action is the opposite of thought and practice the opposite of theory, as if the two could hardly be reconciled and a self-respecting person must choose action over thought. Such formulations are no older than four centuries and grew out of dilemmas particular to the Christian West. They cannot belong to a religious or metaphysical way of seeing things. Any activity that is specifically human is not automatic but preceded by thought, so all practice is governed by some theory and all action by some principle, good or bad, including the actions of those who promote the dichotomy. In Islam no action, however good, has the slightest merit or spiritual efficacy unless it carries divine sanction, so the first duty of a Muslim is to learn the divine commands and then to obey them. One may call the first theory and the second practice, but there is no dichotomy and no choice between them. No practice is valid unless informed by theory, and no theory is of much use unless put into practice. Theory gives practice its meaning, and only through practice does one truly come to know theory. They are not two things but two ways of looking at one reality, and what finally matters is realisation, making the essential truths real to oneself. Even in the West, as late as the end of the Middle Ages, people knew that theōria and prāxis went together in the language of spiritual discipline. The Greek word itself says it: although "theory" in modern European languages has come to mean speculation, supposition or fancy, the Greek verb theōreō meant to see and theōros meant the man who sees, so theōria was not a fancy but a truth that could be seen and actively realised.

### A Book and a man: the two means of guidance

From the days of the first prophet to the days of the last, it has been Allah's way to guide people and show them the Straight Path by sending them not only His Books but His prophets as well. This points to a general principle: for their guidance people need both a divine teaching revealed as a Book and a human teacher in the form of a prophet who trains and disciplines them until they absorb that guidance fully. Not one or the other, but both, for only a man can be the teacher of another man, and a book serves only as an aid. That is why Islam began with a Book and a Prophet, and the two together produced a society of people unparalleled in history for their rectitude. For later generations the same two principles continue to work in the form of the Sharīʿah and the men of Allah. The Qur'an stresses this again and again: "O believers! Be mindful of Allah and be with the truthful" (9:119), and the verse that sums up the qualities of the truthful (aṣ-ṣādiqūn) ends, "It is they who are true ˹in faith˺, and it is they who are mindful ˹of Allah˺" (2:177). Al-Fātiḥah is the essence of the Qur'an, and the essence of al-Fātiḥah is guidance to the Straight Path (aṣ-ṣirāṭ al-mustaqīm). Yet to indicate that path the Qur'an does not call it the path of the Qur'an, or of the Prophet ﷺ, or of the Sunnah, but speaks of the men of Allah who can show it to the seeker: "the Path of those You have blessed—not those You are displeased with, or those who are astray" (1:7). Another verse specifies who they are: those blessed by Allah are "the prophets, the people of truth, the martyrs, and the righteous" (4:69). The Prophet ﷺ likewise named for all later generations the people to be followed in religion.
