He said he was leaving two things behind, and whoever held fast to them would never go astray: the Book of Allah, and his descendants and family, as at-Tirmidhī reports. A hadith in al-Bukhārī says to follow Abū Bakr and ʿUmar after him. A third says to hold to his Sunnah and the way of al-Khulafāʾ ar-Rāshidūn, the four rightly guided caliphs.

In religion as in the sciences and arts, real knowledge comes from authentic books and authentic teachers together. In religion, however, people are liable to lean excessively or exclusively on one of the two, which does them more harm than good. On one side are those who neglect the Book of Allah and come to adore their scholars and spiritual masters without troubling to find out whether those masters obey the Sharīʿah. This has been the characteristic sickness of the Jews and Christians, of whom the Qur'an says, "They have taken their rabbis and monks as well as the Messiah, son of Mary, as lords besides Allah" (9:31). It is the royal road to shirk and kufr, on which millions have perished and go on perishing. On the other side are those who claim that the Book of Allah is enough for them by itself and that they need no teacher, scholar or guide to understand it. This too is misguidance, for interpreting the Book of Allah on one's own without reliable specialists draws a person into every kind of error, makes him a slave of his own desires, and can in some cases lead him right out of Islam. What is required is to give each of the two means its proper place and benefit from both. The basic principle is clear: the authority to command belongs to Allah alone, and it is Allah alone whom people are called to obey. The Prophet ﷺ is the means by which they learn how Allah is to be obeyed, and he is obeyed because obeying him is obeying Allah. Beyond that, when one meets difficulty in understanding or acting on the Qur'an and hadith, one should turn willingly and respectfully to the words and deeds of the masters of these subjects, and treat that as the key to the door of salvation.

### The Sunnah is preserved along with the Book

A second conclusion follows from the fact that teaching the Book is a prophetic function. Allah has promised to protect the Qur'an Himself: "It is certainly We Who have revealed the Reminder, and it is certainly We Who will preserve it" (15:9). So every word, every consonant and every vowel of the Qur'an has remained intact to this day and will remain so as long as the world lasts. Since the verse makes the Prophet's ﷺ teaching indispensable for understanding the Qur'an and acting on it in any real sense, it follows that his teaching must also enjoy divine protection in its own degree and remain intact as a whole until the end of the world, for otherwise preserving the words alone would not fully serve the purpose for which Allah revealed them. His teaching is what is called the Sunnah or the hadith. Allah has not promised the hadith the same degree of protection as the Qur'an, and the words of the Sunnah have not been preserved in exactly the same way, yet by this verse the prophetic explanations too must remain intact, and taken as a whole they have. Whenever anyone has tried to distort a hadith or invent a spurious one, the specialists of the science have exposed the fraud. In fulfilment of the prediction implicit in this verse, Allah has preserved the Prophet's ﷺ teaching from the days of the Companions to the present through fully authentic collections of hadith and through the masters of the subject, and this protection will continue to the last day. The Prophet ﷺ himself assured his Ummah that until the end of the world there would always be a group of authentic scholars guarding the Qur'an and the hadith against distortion and misrepresentation. The Two Ṣaḥīḥs record his words that a group of his community will always remain on the truth, undeterred by those who fail them or oppose them, until the command of Allah comes while they are so, and al-Bukhārī adds in his Ṣaḥīḥ that they will be in ash-Shām. The light that the Prophet's ﷺ mother saw shining over ash-Shām pointed to the firm establishment of his religion there, which is why at the end of time ash-Shām will be a refuge for Islam and its people, and ʿĪsā son of Maryam will descend there, by the eastern white minaret in Damascus. This hadith also gives the lie to some contemporary writers who, in order to discredit the rulings of the Sharīʿah, have tried to spread the notion that the whole body of hadith is inauthentic and unreliable. Anyone with eyes can see the stratagem: if the hadith cannot be trusted, the text of the Qur'an can no longer be trusted either, and that is exactly what the Westerners and their local allies want, to turn the Muslims away from the Qur'an.

### The prayer fulfilled

The three prophetic functions that Ibrāhīm named in his prayer, and that the Prophet ﷺ was sent to perform, were accomplished in his own lifetime. To grasp the transformation that the recitation of the Qur'an, the Prophet's ﷺ teaching and his purifying influence worked in people, it is enough to read what the Qur'an says in praise of his Companions: "And those with him are firm with the disbelievers and compassionate with one another. You see them bowing and prostrating ˹in prayer˺, seeking Allah’s bounty and pleasure" (48:29).

### In short

- Ibrāhīm's prayer for a messenger from his own offspring was answered in Muḥammad ﷺ, whom ʿĪsā later announced by name (61:6), and who called himself the prayer of his father Ibrāhīm and the good news of ʿĪsā.
- The messenger's three functions are to recite the verses, to teach the Book and wisdom, which is the Sunnah, and to purify people of shirk, sin and inward vices.
- Recitation is named separately from teaching because the words of the Qur'an are themselves an object of worship and reward, and no translation is the Qur'an.
- Teaching is named separately because knowing Arabic cannot replace the Prophet's ﷺ explanation (16:44), which implies that the Sunnah, like the Qur'an (15:9), is preserved, guarded by a group of his community that will never cease.
- Guidance needs both a Book and men of Allah (9:119, 2:177, 1:7, 4:69), and the Companions described in 48:29 show what the three functions achieved.

130.text:
After telling the story of Ibrāhīm (Abraham) and the House, the surah draws the conclusion. "And who would reject the faith of Abraham except a fool! We certainly chose him in this life, and in the Hereafter he will surely be among the righteous". The earlier verses set out the basic principles of Ibrāhīm's religion, called people to it, and refuted the claim of the Jews and Christians to be its followers, showing that Islam alone is now faithful to the Abrahamic tradition and that this tradition has in essence been the religion of every prophet. Here Allah rejects the innovations of the disbelievers, who set up partners beside Him and so defied the religion of Ibrāhīm, the imām of the upright. Ibrāhīm worshipped Allah alone, with sincerity, and never called on anyone else. He did not commit shirk (associating partners with Allah) even for an instant. He disowned every deity worshipped instead of Allah and defied his whole people over it: "O my people! I totally reject whatever you associate ˹with Allah in worship˺. I have turned my face towards the One Who has originated the heavens and the earth—being upright—and I am not one of the polytheists" (6:78-79). He told his father and his people that he was free of whatever they worshipped, except the One who originated him and would guide him (43:26-27). When it became clear that his father was an enemy of Allah he broke with him, tender-hearted and forbearing though he was (9:114). And Allah describes him as a model of excellence, devoted and upright, not a polytheist, grateful for Allah's favours, chosen and guided to a straight path (16:120-122).

### Phrase by phrase

**"And who would reject the faith of Abraham"**. Who turns away from it, abandoning his path, his way and his method, and the practices he taught. The form of the question means "no one". The verse was revealed, according to Abū al-ʿĀliyah and Qatādah, about the Jews. They had invented a practice which Allah never sent down and which went against Ibrāhīm's religion, and the words "Abraham was neither a Jew nor a Christian" (3:67-68) bear this out. The message of Muḥammad ﷺ was exactly the message of Ibrāhīm, yet the People of the Book, who prided themselves on following Ibrāhīm, led the opposition to him. The reason is that the religion Ibrāhīm handed down to his offspring, and that the Prophet ﷺ taught, was Islam, total submission to Allah, while what the People of the Book practised as religion had nothing to do with submitting totally. Having lapsed into permissiveness and being unwilling to change, they had let their religion sink into a set of hollow rituals which they fondly believed would get them into Paradise. In the religion the Prophet ﷺ taught, salvation comes only through one's own actions. The People of the Book thought that belonging to a nation of saints and prophets would be enough to redeem them. True religion means accepting the guidance Allah reveals through His prophets. Theirs rested on a national legacy, a pile of traditions accumulated over generations.

**"except a fool!"**. Literally, one who makes a fool of himself. The Arabic can be rendered three ways: he is stupid in himself, he has besotted himself and allowed himself to become stupid, or he is ignorant of his own self. So he is the one who wrongs himself by turning from the truth to wickedness, the one who ignores that his soul was created for Allah and is bound to worship Him, or who treats his soul with frivolity and degrades it. He does not know his own worth and is content with humiliation. He has ruined himself and lost his mind. Only someone with no understanding, or who has wholly lost it, can turn from this religion, because it alone is the religion of human nature, and no one can deny it while his nature in the essential sense remains intact. Such a person defies the path of the man who was chosen in this life as a true imām from his youth until Allah made him His Khalīl (close friend), and who will be among the successful in the next life. Is there anything more insane than leaving this path for the path of misguidance? Is there a greater injustice? Luqmān told his son that associating partners with Allah "is truly the worst of all wrongs" (31:13).

**"We certainly chose him in this life"**. Allah elected him in this world for prophethood and for friendship, taking him as His Khalīl, or, as it is also explained, by giving him prophethood, Islam and goodly offspring. The superiority of his religion is shown by the fact that Allah honoured him in both worlds on account of this very religion, and his own spiritual station and glory arise from it. His greatness in this world is known to all: Namrūd (Nimrod) with all his might could not impress him, he gladly accepted being thrown into the fire rather than abandon the worship of Allah alone, and the Lord of the worlds made the fire a garden for him, so that believers and unbelievers alike came to recognise his uprightness and pure faith. The idolaters of Arabia were his descendants and, idol-worship notwithstanding, always held him in the highest esteem and even claimed to follow him. Remnants of his religion survived among them, distorted by their ignorance: the Hajj, the yearly sacrifice of animals, hospitality and the like. All of this shows the special grace that made the Friend of Allah an imām for people (2:124).

**"and in the Hereafter he will surely be among the righteous"**. With his forefathers, the messengers, in Paradise, among those of the highest stations, the righteous who fulfilled what Allah required of them and so reached the highest levels. Having spoken of his greatness in this world, the verse announces the exalted rank Allah has given him in the next.

### The Friend and the Beloved

In the devotional reading, one of these two verses praises the Bosom Friend, Ibrāhīm, and the other praises the Beloved, Muḥammad ﷺ. Both are cherished and worthy prophets adorned by the Lord's generosity, yet there is a difference between a friend and a beloved. The Friend is the desirer and the Beloved is the desired. The desirer is the one who wants, the desired is the one who is wanted. The desirer is a traveller, the desired is one snatched away. The desirer stands in the station of service as he travels, while the desired stands on the carpet of companionship, pulled along by the Real. Whoever travels by his own travelling finds that his road is not free of deception. That is why the Friend's road, for all the greatness of his state, was not free of it: when the star of deception rose on his path he said "This is my Lord" (6:76), and Lordship went on opening ambushes of deception by means of the moon and the sun, until protection took the reins of his friendship and pulled him out of the world of deception, and he said that he had turned his face to the Originator of the heavens and the earth, upright (6:79). Muṣṭafā ﷺ, by contrast, was in the pull of the Real. No ambush of deception could make his road steep. On that night, everything that had once not been and then came to be sought his help against deception and took refuge in the lights of his Sharīʿah. He was so confirmed by the Real's pull that he did not glance at any of it from the corner of his eye: "The ˹Prophet’s˺ sight never wandered, nor did it overreach" (53:17). The difference between the Friend and the Beloved is the difference between the traveller and the one snatched away. The Friend had the attribute of servants at the threshold of Lordship, standing on his own feet.

### In short

- Ibrāhīm never associated anything with Allah for a moment (6:78-79, 43:26-27, 9:114, 16:120-122), so turning from his religion, as the Jews did with their invented practices, is to make a fool of oneself and to commit the worst of wrongs (31:13).
- The "fool" is one who does not know what his soul was made for, or who degrades it, abandoning the religion of human nature itself.
- Allah chose Ibrāhīm in this world for prophethood and friendship, as Nimrod's fire and the Arabs' lasting reverence for him both show, and gave him the highest station among the righteous in the next.
- Inwardly, Ibrāhīm is the Friend who travels and must pass through deception, while Muḥammad ﷺ is the Beloved who is drawn, and whose sight never wandered.

131.text:
Verse 131 gives the foundation of Ibrāhīm's (Abraham's) religion in a single exchange. "When his Lord ordered him, “Submit ˹to My Will˺,” he responded, “I submit to the Lord of all worlds.”" Allah commanded Ibrāhīm to be sincere to Him, to obey Him and to surrender to Him, and Ibrāhīm complied perfectly. His Lord asked him to submit himself, and he agreed willingly and gladly to submit himself to the Lord of the worlds.

### Phrase by phrase

**"When his Lord ordered him, “Submit ˹to My Will˺,”"**. Obey Allah and devote your religion purely to Him. The word of command is aslim, from the same root as Islam. No single English word matches it exactly, for it means to obey, to submit oneself, to surrender one's will. Several settings are reported for the command. One says it came when Ibrāhīm came out of the pit of fire, in the sense: say specifically "there is no god but Allah". Another says that when he called his people to accept that Allah is One without partner, his Lord told him to make his religion and his works sincere to Allah. A third says the words came as he was thrown into the fire. Allah chose him because of the swiftness with which he surrendered, telling him to be faithful to Him in worship and to carry out humbly whatever He instructed.

**"he responded, “I submit to the Lord of all worlds.”"**. I submit to the Lord of all the worlds, and I declare that there is no god but Allah, who has no partner. Or: I comply, and make my religion and my works sincere to Allah, Lord of all the worlds, the One who created His servants, provides for them and takes care of their affairs. One would have expected him to answer "I submit myself to You". Instead he said, more fully, "to the Lord of all worlds". That form of reply expresses the respect and awe the occasion called for. It also contains the praise that the honour of being addressed by Allah demanded. And it acknowledges something else: in submitting to the Lord of the worlds he was doing no more than the basic duty a servant owes the Master of all, and he was doing it for his own good. The reply shows that the whole principle and essence of Ibrāhīm's religion is contained in one word, Islam, total obedience and willing self-surrender to Allah. He was made to pass through all his trials before reaching his exalted station precisely so that the world could see how perfectly he adhered to this principle. Islam, submission to Allah, is what the world was created for, and the end that every prophet and every divine Book was sent to serve.

### One religion of all the prophets

This verse teaches that the religion common to all the prophets, the point at which they all meet, is Islam. From Ādam (Adam) to the Last Prophet ﷺ every messenger of Allah called people to Islam alone and told his followers to keep to this Straight Path. The Qur'an is explicit: "Certainly, Allah’s only Way is Islam" (3:19), and "Whoever seeks a way other than Islam, it will never be accepted from them, and in the Hereafter they will be among the losers" (3:85). To put this in perspective: every religion that any prophet brought had divine sanction behind it, was instituted by Allah Himself and was, in its own time, accepted by Him. Each of them, whether one calls it Judaism, Christianity or anything else, must therefore in its essence have been Islam in the general sense of total submission to Allah.

The religion of Ibrāhīm has a distinguishing feature: he gave his religion the name Islam and his followers the name Muslims. In his prayer under verse 128 he asked that he and his son be kept submissive (muslimayn) and that his descendants be a submissive community (ummah muslimah), and in the next verse he will advise his descendants not to die without being sure that they are Muslims. After him this distinction, of being called specifically Muslims and the Islamic Ummah, passed by his own instruction to the community of the Prophet ﷺ, whom the Qur'an addresses as following "the way of your forefather Abraham. ˹It is Allah˺ Who named you ‘the ones who submit’ ˹in the˺ earlier ˹Scriptures˺ and in this ˹Quran˺" (22:78). When the Qur'an was revealed, the Jews, the Christians and even the idolaters of Arabia each claimed to follow the religion of Ibrāhīm. The Qur'an and its followers have made plain that, in this final phase of human history, only the religion of the Prophet ﷺ is the religion of Ibrāhīm, the religion of pure human nature (al-fiṭrah).

### What submission demands

Islam is the essence of every divine Book, every Sharīʿah and the teaching of every prophet: turning away from one's own desires in order to obey Allah's commands, and giving up private opinion in order to submit to His guidance. It is painful that so many Muslims today have forgotten this basic truth. They want to chase their own desires and call it Islam. The interpretation of the Qur'an and hadith that attracts them, or rather the misinterpretation, is whatever flatters those desires. In effect they are twisting the Sharīʿah to fit their fancies, and doing it with enough cleverness that the idols they actually serve come out dressed as religion. People like this are trying to outwit Allah Himself. He knows every particle of the universe and sees into the deepest corners of the heart. Before the Almighty nothing is of any use except complete surrender.

What Islam asks of a person is that he put every desire and inclination aside and, in everything he does, seek his Lord's pleasure. He can find that pleasure only when he knows his Lord's commands and carries them out exactly as prescribed. That is what ʿibādah, worship, really means. The perfection of this obedience, submission and love is the final stage of spiritual development, the Station (maqām) of ʿAbdiyyah, servanthood. At this station Ibrāhīm received from Allah the title Khalīlullāh, the Friend of Allah, and the Last of the Prophets ﷺ received the title ʿAbdunā, Our Servant. On the lower levels of the same station stand the abdāl, the aqṭāb and the awliyāʾ, the men of Allah, the saints of this Ummah, each in his degree. This is the essence of tawḥīd, the realisation of Allah's oneness, on reaching which all one's fears and hopes become bound to Allah and to no one else. Islam, then, means total obedience to Allah, and that obedience is possible only by following the Sunnah, the way of the Prophet ﷺ, as the Qur'an states in the plainest terms: "By your Lord, they will never be ˹true˺ believers until they accept you ˹O Prophet˺ as the judge in their disputes, and find no resistance within themselves against your decision and submit wholeheartedly" (4:65).

### The Friend's three tests

The devotional reading tells the story behind the verse. When the Bosom Friend set out on his journey, the command came from the Exalted Presence: Ibrāhīm, whoever wants Me must belong to Me completely. As long as a sliver of mortal desire and resistance of the soul is left in you, you will not move from the pain of striving to the ease of being drawn. The ransomed slave remains a slave so long as a single dirham is still owed. If you want Me, you must want what I desire and leave yourself aside entirely. The Friend answered: Lord, Ibrāhīm no longer has any self-governance or free choice. On the feet of poverty, in a state of brokenness, I have come to see what You command. I submit. I have overthrown myself, handed my affair to You and returned to You entirely. The command came: that is a very great claim, Ibrāhīm, and every claim must have a meaning and every right a reality. Now be on guard for the testing.

The tests came in three forms: through what was other than himself, by a part of himself, and by his whole self. The test by what was other than himself concerned his abundant possessions. They say he had seventy thousand sheep in seven thousand herds, and each herd had a dog with a gold collar round its neck. He was commanded to cut his heart loose from all of it and throw it away in Allah's path, and he did, keeping nothing. The traditions relate that when the call "And God took Abraham as a bosom friend" (4:125) went out in the world of the Dominion, the angels said: Lord, ever since that call our spirits have been spinning in a whirlpool and our gall-bladders melting at this special favour. How is the Friend worthy of such generosity? The call came: Jibrīl (Gabriel), spread your peacock feathers, go down from the Lote Tree's top to that mountain's summit and put him to the test. Jibrīl came down in the form of a human being, stood beside the mountain and cried out, "O Holy One!" The Friend fainted from the pleasure of hearing it. When he came round he said: servant of Allah, say that name again and this herd is yours. Jibrīl cried it out again, and the Friend rolled in the dust like a half-slaughtered bird, saying: say it again, and another herd is yours. Like the lover who said, you spoke of Him to me and increased my madness, so speak of Him more, he kept begging, and each time gave away a herd with its dog and its gold collar, until he had given everything and lost everything. Then the knots tightened, passion and destitution joined, and he said: servant of Allah, recite the name of the Friend once more, and my spirit is yours. Wealth and gold one gambles away for nothing, and when the matter reaches the spirit, gamble that away too. Jibrīl rejoiced and spread his feathers. He said: He was right to take you as His bosom friend. If anything falls short, it is our eyes. Your passion is perfect. When he showed himself, he said he had no use for the sheep, and the Friend replied that even so, chivalry does not allow taking back a gift. So they agreed to scatter them in the deserts and wildernesses to graze as they pleased, for the benefit of the world's people until the Resurrection. The mountain sheep now scattered across the world all come from that lineage, and whoever hunts and eats one until the Resurrection is a guest of the Friend, eating at the table of that majestic angel's beautiful deed. The test by a part of himself was that he was shown in a dream the sacrifice of his child and instructed to carry it out, a story told in its own place. The test by his whole self was that the rebellious Nimrod was persuaded to light a fire and build a mangonel to hurl him into it, and the divine address came to the fire: "O fire! Be cool and safe for Abraham!" (21:69).

### In short

- Allah commanded Ibrāhīm to submit and he answered at once, "I submit to the Lord of all worlds", a reply full of awe, praise and the recognition that submission is a servant's duty and his own good.
- Islam, total surrender to Allah, is the religion of every prophet (3:19, 3:85). Ibrāhīm named it Islam and its people Muslims, and that name passed to the Ummah of Muḥammad ﷺ (22:78).
- Submission means putting aside one's desires to obey Allah's commands exactly as the Sunnah shows (4:65), the station of servanthood at which Ibrāhīm became the Friend and Muḥammad ﷺ "Our Servant".
- Inwardly, the Friend was tested through his wealth, his son and his own life, and gave each away for the sake of the Friend's name (4:125, 21:69).

132.text:
Verse 132 shows what Ibrāhīm (Abraham) cared most to leave behind him. "This was the advice of Abraham—as well as Jacob—to his children, ˹saying˺, “Indeed, Allah has chosen for you this faith; so do not die except in ˹a state of full˺ submission.”" These verses show how anxious the prophets were to give their own descendants religious and spiritual guidance.

### Phrase by phrase

**"This was the advice of Abraham—as well as Jacob—to his children"**. The verb is read waṣṣā and also awṣā, both meaning to enjoin. Ibrāhīm commanded his offspring to follow this religion, Islam, for the sake of Allah. Yaʿqūb (Jacob) enjoined the same creed on his sons. "This" may also refer to the words of the previous verse, "I submit to the Lord of all worlds". These prophets loved those words so much that they kept them until the moment of death. They charged their children to hold to them afterwards, as Allah says elsewhere of Ibrāhīm, "And he left this enduring declaration among his descendants, so they may ˹always˺ turn back ˹to Allah˺" (43:28). One gloss says that what he enjoined, when he was dying, was that there is no god but Allah. Yaʿqūb, the son of Isḥāq (Isaac), may well have been among the children present when Ibrāhīm gave this counsel. It appears, and Allah knows best, that Isḥāq was granted Yaʿqūb while Ibrāhīm and Sārah were still alive. The good news given to her includes them both: "We gave her good news of ˹the birth of˺ Isaac, and, after him, Jacob" (11:71). If Yaʿqūb had not been alive then, there would be no point in naming him specifically among Isḥāq's children. In Sūrah al-ʿAnkabūt Allah says that He blessed Ibrāhīm with Isḥāq and Yaʿqūb (29:27), and again, "We blessed him with Isaac ˹as a son˺ and Jacob ˹as a grandson˺, as an additional favour" (21:72), which indicates that this happened in Ibrāhīm's lifetime. Yaʿqūb also built Bayt al-Maqdis, as the earlier books testify. The Two Ṣaḥīḥs record that Abū Dharr asked the Messenger of Allah ﷺ which mosque was built first. He said al-Masjid al-Ḥarām, the Kaʿbah. Abū Dharr asked which came next, and he said Bayt al-Maqdis. Asked how many years lay between them, he said forty. The counsel Yaʿqūb gave his own children, related in the next verse, confirms that he was among those who received this advice.

**"“Indeed, Allah has chosen for you this faith"**. The religion of Islam, the true religion of submission to Allah. These words were good news. They strengthened the sons' desire to meet the demands of submission. Once they knew that Allah had chosen them for it, they were certain He would help them and make it easy to give submission its due. Though the laws of these prophets differed in details, they were of one origin, and the spring of tawḥīd (Allah's oneness) is not divided in two.

**"so do not die except in ˹a state of full˺ submission.”"**. Hold fast to Islam until you die as Muslims, sincere to Allah in your worship and in your declaration of His oneness, surrendering inside and out. The command forbids them ever to abandon submission. It tells them to cling to it until death overtakes them. Ibrāhīm advised his sons also to say, "I have surrendered to the Lord of the worlds", and Yaʿqūb told his sons the same. In effect he made his descendants promise that before they died they would make sure they had been Muslims. That means following the teaching of Islam steadfastly all through life, so that by Allah's grace one remains a Muslim to the last breath.

### Dying on the path one lived on

The instruction means: do righteous deeds while you live and stay on this path, so that Allah will grant you the favour of dying on it. As a rule a person dies on the path he lived on, and is raised according to what he died on. A number of hadiths say the same: one dies in the state one kept up in life, and rises from the grave on the Day of Resurrection in that state. This is Allah's usual way with people. When His servant resolves to do good and strives as best he can, Allah, the Most Generous, helps him and makes it easy for him to stay on the righteous path.

This does not contradict the authentic hadith about the last stretch of a life. A man may do the works of the people of Paradise until only an outstretched arm's length or a cubit separates him from it. Then the Book, his destiny, overtakes him, and he does the works of the people of the Fire and enters it. Another may do the works of the people of the Fire until only an arm's length or a cubit separates him from it. Then the Book overtakes him, and he does the works of the people of Paradise and enters it. Some versions of this hadith add the proviso "as it appeared to people". The first man seemed to onlookers to be doing good while in reality he was doing the opposite. The second had been doing from the start what makes a person worthy of Paradise, although people took him for a sinner. Allah says: "As for the one who is charitable, mindful ˹of Allah˺" and believes in the best reward, "We will facilitate for them the Way of Ease", while for the one who is stingy, thinks himself self-sufficient and denies the best reward, "We will facilitate for them the path of hardship" (92:5-10). The person who has been steadfast in good deeds should therefore trust the divine promise. He should rely on Allah's usual way with His creatures, and hope that by His grace he will leave this world in that blessed state.

### In short

- Ibrāhīm, and after him Yaʿqūb, made Islam the one legacy they pressed on their children, enjoining the declaration of Allah's oneness to the end of their lives (43:28).
- Yaʿqūb was probably present at Ibrāhīm's counsel, since Sārah's good news named him (11:71, 29:27, 21:72), and he later built Bayt al-Maqdis forty years after the Kaʿbah.
- "Do not die except as Muslims" means living on the path so as to die on it. One dies as one lived, and the hadith about a last-minute reversal speaks of how things appeared to people (92:5-10).

133.text:
Verse 133 lets Yaʿqūb (Jacob) and his sons speak for themselves. "Or did you witness when death came to Jacob? He asked his children, “Who will you worship after my passing?” They replied, “We will ˹continue to˺ worship your God, the God of your forefathers—Abraham, Ishmael, and Isaac—the One God. And to Him we ˹all˺ submit.”" The verse was revealed about the Jews, when they said to the Prophet ﷺ: do you not know that when Yaʿqūb was about to die he charged his sons to follow Judaism? Allah thus settles the dispute among the Jews about what religion Yaʿqūb left to his children, and the verse carries His criticism both of the Arab idolaters descended from Ismāʿīl (Ishmael) and of the disbelievers among the Children of Israel, the descendants of Yaʿqūb son of Isḥāq (Isaac) son of Ibrāhīm (Abraham).

### Phrase by phrase

**"Or did you witness when death came to Jacob?"**. Were you present, assembly of Jews, to hear what he enjoined on his children, whether Judaism or Islam? The opening "or" works like a question that denies: you were not there at his death, so how can you ascribe to him what does not befit him? When death approached, Yaʿqūb called his sons together and charged them to worship Allah alone.

**"He asked his children, “Who will you worship after my passing?”"**. What will you worship after I die? The question is the test of what he had taught them.

**"They replied, “We will ˹continue to˺ worship your God, the God of your forefathers—Abraham, Ishmael, and Isaac"**. Ismāʿīl was Yaʿqūb's uncle, not his father, so calling him a father is a figure of speech. The father figures are mentioned together, and the standing of an uncle is like that of a father. An-Naḥḥās said that the Arabs call the uncle a father, as al-Qurṭubī records. This phrase shows that the word "father" includes the grandfather, and Ibn ʿAbbās deduced from it that in inheritance the grandfather is treated like the father. The verse serves as evidence that the grandfather is called a father, and that when his son dies he inherits in place of the brothers. This was the view of Abū Bakr, as al-Bukhārī relates on the authority of Ibn ʿAbbās and Ibn az-Zubayr, adding that there was no opposing opinion. ʿĀʾishah the Mother of the Believers, al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī, Ṭāwūs and ʿAṭāʾ held the same. Mālik, ash-Shāfiʿī and Aḥmad held that grandfather and brothers divide the inheritance between them, which is also reported from ʿUmar, ʿUthmān, ʿAlī, Ibn Masʿūd, Zayd ibn Thābit and a number of scholars among the Salaf (the early generations) and after them. In the devotional reading, the sons did not say "our God" out of respect for Yaʿqūb's special status, accepting his superiority and seeing themselves as attached to his station, and by adding "to Him we submit" they declared themselves followers of Ibrāhīm, Ismāʿīl and Isḥāq.

**"the One God"**. "One God" stands in place of "your God". We single Him out in divinity and associate nothing and no one with Him.

**"And to Him we ˹all˺ submit.”"**. In obedience and submission, bound to Him alone, declaring that there is only one true God. Allah says likewise that all in the heavens and the earth submit to Him, willingly or unwillingly (3:83). Islam is the religion of all the prophets, even though their laws differed: "We never sent a messenger before you ˹O Prophet˺ without revealing to him: “There is no god ˹worthy of worship˺ except Me, so worship Me ˹alone˺.”" (21:25). Many verses and hadiths say the same, among them the Prophet's ﷺ words that the prophets are brothers from different mothers, with one religion. All of them followed one way in declaring Allah's oneness and in submission, inheriting it one from another, and they were the people of the house of intimacy, whom Allah made deserving of nearness and purified in truth.

### Why the prophets took such care over their children

Whether one calls it the religion of Ibrāhīm or Islam, it is meant for the whole world. Why then does the passage single out the descendants of Ibrāhīm and Yaʿqūb, and why were these two prophets so particular in counselling their sons? Because love for one's children and concern for their welfare is in no way incompatible with prophethood, or even with being the Friend of Allah. Ibrāhīm, who on one occasion was not only willing but glad to sacrifice his son at Allah's command, on another occasion prayed for his descendants' good in both worlds, and as he left this world wanted to give them what was in his eyes the greatest blessing of all, Islam. Prophets love their children too. The difference is that ordinary people think only the good things of this world worth having and try to leave their children as much of them as they can, while for the prophets and their true followers nothing counts except īmān (faith) and good deeds, in a word Islam, and it is this eternal wealth they strive to pass on whole to their descendants.

This gives parents a specific guidance. As keen as they are to secure their children's worldly comfort and happiness, they should give equal if not greater attention to disciplining their outward and inward conduct according to the Sharīʿah. Is it reasonable to strain every nerve to shield one's children from the heat of the sun and leave them exposed to the fire of Hell? The prophets' example also teaches that it is the parents' duty and the children's right that one should care first for the spiritual health of one's own children and only then worry about others. Three considerations support this. First, because of their special relationship, children are likely to accept counsel more readily and completely than others, and may later be a great help in one's efforts for Islam. Second, the easiest and most effective way to bring the truth to a whole people is for the head of each family to take on the teaching and training of its members. In current terms this localised, decentralised method spreads the responsibility over many individuals, and teaching the families one by one ends up teaching the whole society. The Qur'an lays down the principle: "O believers! Protect yourselves and your families from a Fire whose fuel is people and stones" (66:6). The Prophet ﷺ himself, Allah's Messenger to all humanity, whose guidance holds until the last day, was commanded to carry the truth first to his own family: "And warn ˹all, starting with˺ your closest relatives" (26:214), and "Bid your people to pray, and be diligent in ˹observing˺ it" (20:132), and he always did so. Third, if a man's close relatives and household do not back what he teaches, or do not seem to act on it, his teaching does not succeed so well with others. When the Prophet ﷺ began his mission, his hearers usually answered that he ought first to convince the Quraysh, his own clan, and only then turn to others. When his own clan had accepted Islam, a process completed at the conquest of Makkah, the world saw, as the Qur'an reports, "the people embracing Allah’s Way in crowds" (110:2).

The main cause of the ignorance of Islam and indifference to it so widespread among Muslims today is that even parents who are themselves good Muslims leave their children to themselves and let the social environment shape them as it will. Their one worry is to see the children prosper in this world, and they never think of what will become of them in the next. May Allah in His mercy grant everyone concern for the other world, and help in making a real effort to acquire the only wealth that lasts: faith and rectitude.

### In short

- The Jews claimed Yaʿqūb died commending Judaism. The verse answers that they were not there, and records his sons' pledge to worship the One God of Ibrāhīm, Ismāʿīl and Isḥāq in submission.
- "Father" here covers an uncle and a grandfather, from which the jurists drew the rule on a grandfather's inheritance, with Abū Bakr, ʿĀʾishah and others giving him the father's place and Mālik, ash-Shāfiʿī and Aḥmad dividing with the brothers.
- All the prophets shared one religion of submission (3:83, 21:25), brothers of one faith from different mothers.
- The prophets' care for their children teaches parents to put their children's faith before their comfort, to begin teaching at home (66:6, 26:214, 20:132), and shows why the Prophet's ﷺ success with the Quraysh preceded the crowds of 110:2.

134.text:
Verse 134 closes the account of Ibrāhīm (Abraham) and his family with a principle that cuts the ground from under inherited pride. "That was a community that had already gone before. For them is what they earned and for you is what you have earned. And you will not be accountable for what they have done". No one's link to prophets or righteous ancestors will help him unless he does good deeds of his own that bring him real religious benefit.

### Phrase by phrase

**"That was a community that had already gone before"**. "That" refers to Ibrāhīm, Yaʿqūb (Jacob) and his sons, and is feminine in the Arabic to agree with "community". They were a group of people who lived before your time and have passed away.

**"For them is what they earned and for you is what you have earned"**. They have the reward of what they did, good or evil, and you, the Jews who are being addressed, have what you have earned. This begins a new sentence in the Arabic. They have their deeds and you have yours.

**"And you will not be accountable for what they have done"**. On the Day of Judgement you will not be asked about what they did or said, just as they will not be asked about what you do, the second statement confirming the first. No one is held to account for another's disobedience, and everyone is rewarded for his own actions. One should not be distracted from attending to one's own conduct by looking at what those before did. Nothing will benefit a person except his own good actions. As a hadith puts it, whoever is held back by his deeds will not be moved forward by his lineage.

### What the principle rules out

The good deeds of one's forefathers will not suffice if one has not done good oneself, and in the same way no one suffers for his forefathers' misdeeds if his own account is clean. It follows that the children of mushrikīn (idolaters) and kāfirīn (unbelievers) who die before coming of age will not be punished in the next world for their parents' unbelief. The verse also refutes the Jews' claim that whatever they did they would enter Paradise on the strength of their forefathers' good deeds. Attaching oneself to saints and prophets, living or dead, lulls a person into a false sense of security. He imagines that as he was attached to them in this life he will stay attached in the next, and that their surplus of good deeds will cover his shortfall. The People of the Book were so immersed in this wishful thinking that they invented a dogma of ancestral salvation and pinned all their hopes on the holiness of their elders. To think that one person will be given the reward of another's actions is sheer self-deception. Everyone reaps the reward and bears the punishment of his own deeds, and no one shares in what is awarded to another for what he did on earth.

Let this be a warning to Muslims who, being descendants of the Prophet ﷺ or of a saint, delude themselves that their sins will go unpunished because of that privileged position. The Qur'an is explicit and insistent: "No one will reap except what they sow. No soul burdened with sin will bear the burden of another" (6:164). Addressing his own clan, the Prophet ﷺ said: beware, Banū Hāshim, lest on the Day of Judgement others come bringing their good deeds while you, having neglected good deeds, bring only your trust in being my relatives, for on that day I will not be able to save you from Allah's wrath. Another hadith says that a man whose deeds pull him back will not be pushed forward by his ancestry.

Whoever submits to Allah finds that he must face all kinds of difficulties in this life, and his worldly hopes will not necessarily be fulfilled. Yet one who is firm in faith is not put off by adversity. He perseveres and makes sure he leaves this world a believer, so that he can look forward to Allah's blessings in the next. In the devotional reading, the Real assigned each community its place and singled out for each its status by His decree. No news remains of their outward forms, and no trace of what distinguished one group from another. Each one is a king in his own region, and each has his own celestial sphere turning in felicity.

### In short

- Ibrāhīm, Yaʿqūb and his sons have passed on with their own deeds, and the Jews, like everyone else, will answer only for theirs (6:164).
- Descent from prophets or saints saves no one, as the Prophet ﷺ warned his own Banū Hāshim, and deeds that hold a person back cannot be offset by lineage.
- The same justice means that children of unbelievers who die young are not punished for their parents' unbelief.

135.text:
The earlier verses defined the religion of Ibrāhīm (Abraham) and established that its present form is Islam. Now the surah records what the two communities who claimed him actually said. "The Jews and Christians each say, “Follow our faith to be ˹rightly˺ guided.” Say, ˹O Prophet,˺ “No! We follow the faith of Abraham, the upright—who was not a polytheist.”" For all their pretension to be his followers, the Jews and the Christians did not in fact follow his religion. Instead of accepting Islam, each group kept asking the Muslims to accept its own religion as the way to true guidance.

### Phrase by phrase

**"The Jews and Christians each say, “Follow our faith to be ˹rightly˺ guided.”"**. The Arabic literally says, "Be Jews or Christians, then you will be guided." The "or" spells out the two claims. The first is what the Jews of Madinah said, the second what the Christians of Najrān said. Ibn ʿAbbās reports that the verse came down about four Jewish leaders in Madinah, Kaʿb ibn al-Ashraf, Mālik ibn al-Ṣayf, Wahb ibn Yahūdhā and Yāsir ibn Akhṭab, as well as about the Christians of Najrān. When they argued with the Muslims about religion, each party claimed a better right to Allah's religion than anyone else. The Jews said: our Prophet Mūsā (Moses) is the best of prophets, our Scripture the best of Scriptures, our religion the best of religions, and they rejected ʿĪsā (Jesus), the Gospel, Muḥammad ﷺ and the Qur'an. The Christians said: our Prophet ʿĪsā is the best of prophets, the Gospel the best of Scriptures, and our religion the best, and they rejected Muḥammad ﷺ and the Qur'an. Both parties told the believers that there was no true religion except theirs and invited them to join it. In another report, also from Ibn ʿAbbās, ʿAbdullāh ibn Ṣūriyā al-Aʿwar said to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ: guidance is only what we Jews follow, so follow us, Muḥammad, and you will be rightly guided. The Christians said the same kind of thing, and Allah sent down this verse.

**"Say, ˹O Prophet,˺ “No!"**. Tell them: it is not as you claim. We have no need of the Judaism or the Christianity you call us to. In its own day, and for its own day, each of these two religions was genuine. But both had since been distorted, and both had been abrogated by Allah. So Allah tells the Prophet ﷺ to declare, for himself and for his followers, that they are and will remain firm on the religion of Ibrāhīm.

**"We follow the faith of Abraham, the upright"**. We follow the creed of Ibrāhīm the ḥanīf. The word describes one who inclines away from every other religion towards the upright religion, one who turned from false ways of life to the way of truth. Muḥammad ibn Kaʿb al-Quraẓī and ʿĪsā ibn Jāriyah explained it as being on the straight path. Abū Qilābah said that the ḥanīf is what the messengers, from the first to the last, believed in. One gloss reads: follow the religion of Ibrāhīm, the upright, the Muslim, the sincere, and only then will you be guided. Ibrāhīm shunned every form of shirk (associating partners with Allah), adored the One God alone and obeyed no one else. His religion therefore did not carry a trace of distortion.

**"who was not a polytheist.”"**. He did not worship others alongside Allah as some do, and he did not follow the religion of the Jews or of the Christians.

### Why they turned against the Prophet ﷺ

The religion the Prophet Muḥammad ﷺ taught was the religion of Ibrāhīm, the very religion the Jews and Christians claimed as their own. Why, then, did they turn away from him? Because the religion he brought taught people to take on the colour of Allah and to devote themselves to Him entirely. For the People of the Book religion had come to mean something else. It had shrunk to a badge of national pride. The Prophet's ﷺ message wounded that pride, so they turned against him. People who hold their own race superior cannot accept the truth when it appears in a nation other than theirs. They will believe in prophets who come from their own stock, but not in those raised among other peoples. The only figures they acknowledged were those of their own race. Those who see religion as the worship of Allah, by contrast, recognise the truth of every piece of wisdom Allah sends down, whoever teaches it. For the learned men of these communities, realising that the Prophet ﷺ was Allah's final messenger was no insuperable difficulty. Nothing stopped them seeing that his religion was true. They should have declared what, deep in their hearts, they knew. They refused to accept him as the final prophet, as Allah had commanded, for the simple reason that their own position and prestige mattered more to them.

In the devotional reading, the verse is addressed to the Prophet ﷺ: when the parties contended with you, they demanded that you fall in with them. Stand firm against what they call you to, and turn your attention more and more to Us. Follow the way of the Friend, who withdrew from the crowd, whether it was his own father or anyone else out of step with his Protector. As he told his father, "As I distance myself from ˹all of˺ you and from whatever you invoke besides Allah, I will ˹continue to˺ call upon my Lord ˹alone˺" (19:48). The ḥanīf, on this reading, is the one who leans towards the straight truth on the path of truth, free from any defect of created things, in agreement with the truth through the Truth Himself.

### In short

- The Jews of Madinah and the Christians of Najrān each told the Muslims that their own religion was the only road to guidance, each claiming the best prophet, the best Scripture and the best religion.
- The Prophet ﷺ is told to answer that the Muslims need neither, since both had been distorted and abrogated, and that they follow Ibrāhīm, the ḥanīf, who turned from every false way and never associated anything with Allah.
- The People of the Book rejected a message identical to Ibrāhīm's because religion had become national pride for them, and the truth had appeared outside their race.
- Inwardly, the believer is told to stand firm against the pull of the crowd, as Ibrāhīm withdrew even from his father (19:48).

136.text:
Having rejected the Jewish and Christian invitations, the Muslims are now told what to declare instead. "Say, ˹O believers,˺ “We believe in Allah and what has been revealed to us; and what was revealed to Abraham, Ishmael, Isaac, Jacob, and his descendants", the verse begins, "and what was given to Moses, Jesus, and other prophets from their Lord. We make no distinction between any of them. And to Allah we all submit.”" Allah directs His believing servants to have faith in what came down to them through His Messenger Muḥammad ﷺ, and in what the earlier prophets received in general. Some prophets He names, and many others He leaves unnamed. He tells the believers to believe in all of them and not to differentiate between them. In this way He teaches them the path of Allah's oneness, so that the Jews and Christians could see what that oneness means.

### Phrase by phrase

**"Say, ˹O believers,˺"**. The address is to the believers, and the answer is for the Jews and Christians who make these baseless claims.

**"“We believe in Allah and what has been revealed to us"**. In Muḥammad ﷺ and the Qur'an.

**"and what was revealed to Abraham, Ishmael, Isaac, Jacob, and his descendants"**. In Ibrāhīm and his Scripture, the ten scrolls, in Ismāʿīl, Isḥāq and Yaʿqūb (Jacob) and their Scriptures, and in the sons of Yaʿqūb and theirs. The Arabic calls Yaʿqūb's descendants al-Asbāṭ, the Tribes. Abū al-ʿĀliyah, al-Rabīʿ and Qatādah said that al-Asbāṭ are the twelve sons of Yaʿqūb, each of whom had a community of people descended from him, which is why they bear this name. Al-Khalīl ibn Aḥmad and others said that the Asbāṭ among the Children of Israel are what the tribes are among the children of Ismāʿīl. So the word means the different tribes of Israel, to whom Allah sent a number of prophets. Mūsā (Moses) told the Children of Israel to remember Allah's favour "when He raised prophets from among you, made you sovereign" (5:20), and Allah says, "We divided them into twelve tribes—each as a community" (7:160). Al-Qurṭubī said that a sibṭ is a group of people, or a tribe, all descended from the same ancestors. Yaʿqūb had twelve sons, and the offspring of each formed a tribe. Allah blessed his seed so richly that Yūsuf (Joseph) and his brothers entered Egypt as a group of twelve men, yet their line flourished, and when the Israelites left Egypt with Mūsā they numbered in the thousands. Another form of this blessing was the large number of prophets Yaʿqūb's progeny produced.

**"and what was given to Moses, Jesus, and other prophets from their Lord"**. In Mūsā and the Torah, in ʿĪsā (Jesus) and the Gospel, and in all the prophets and the Books and signs they received. Qatādah said that Allah ordered the believers to believe in Him, in every Book of His and in every messenger. Sulaymān ibn Ḥabīb said that they were commanded to believe in the Torah and the Injīl as originally revealed, not to put them into practice.

**"We make no distinction between any of them."**. We do not believe in some and reject others, as the Jews and Christians do. Allah sent every one of them as a prophet to teach His oneness. The believers must not imitate those whom Allah describes as wishing "to make a distinction between Allah and His messengers, saying, “We believe in some and disbelieve in others,” desiring to forge a compromise", of whom He says, "they are indeed the true disbelievers" (4:150-151).

**"And to Allah we all submit.”"**. We acknowledge that we worship Him, declaring that there is only one true God, and we humbly surrender to Him alone.

### The creed in five points

This verse sets out the basic tenets of the religion of Ibrāhīm in its present form. First, Muslims believe in Allah and in the guidance He sent them through the Prophet ﷺ. Second, they believe in all the prophets Allah sent from age to age, some of whom are named here. Third, some prophets may in certain respects be superior to others, but a Muslim must believe in every one of them without discriminating between them. Fourth, Muslims hold that the Sharīʿahs of all the prophets named here were instituted by Allah Himself, but have now been abrogated, so they follow the Sharīʿah of the Prophet ﷺ, which alone remains valid. Fifth, Muslims obey Allah alone in the end and submit themselves totally to Him.

Two hadiths show how the Prophet ﷺ himself used this verse. Al-Bukhārī relates from Abū Hurayrah that the People of the Book would read the Torah in Hebrew and then explain it to the Muslims in Arabic. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: neither believe the People of the Book nor call them liars, but say, "We believe in Allah and what has been revealed to us." And Muslim, Abū Dāwūd and an-Nasāʾī record from Ibn ʿAbbās that in the two voluntary rakʿahs before Fajr the Messenger of Allah ﷺ would mostly recite this verse, "We believe in Allah and what has been revealed to us", and the words of the disciples of ʿĪsā, "We believe in Allah, so bear witness that we have submitted" (3:52).

### Truth is personal, not ancestral

Just as the people of old received their due as individuals, so later generations will receive what they themselves deserve, for truth is an individual matter, not an ancestral one. The mistake of the People of the Book was to imagine that the good deeds of their ancestors would earn a reward for the present generation and those to come. The Christian idea of original sin implied the reverse, that sins pass from one generation to the next. Neither belief has any basis in truth. Allah rewards each person according to his own actions, and no one answers for the deeds of others.

In the devotional reading, because our Prophet ﷺ believed in everything revealed before him, he was honoured with everything Allah had conferred in honour on the prophets before him. When Allah proclaimed the harmony of all the prophets' messages, He placed everything in existence under his banner, and he said that Ādam (Adam) and all others would be under his banner on the Day of Resurrection. When his community believed in all that Allah had revealed to His messengers, dividing none of them from the rest, it drew the highest share of honour and took precedence over every other community.

### In short

- The believers are told to declare faith in the Qur'an and in everything revealed to Ibrāhīm, Ismāʿīl, Isḥāq, Yaʿqūb, the twelve Tribes, Mūsā, ʿĪsā and all the prophets, without picking and choosing (4:150-151).
- The Tribes are the communities descended from Yaʿqūb's twelve sons (5:20, 7:160), a line that grew from twelve men in Egypt to thousands and produced many prophets.
- The creed has five points: faith in Allah and His final guidance, in all prophets, without distinction, with only the last Sharīʿah in force, and total submission to Allah alone.
- The Prophet ﷺ taught Muslims to answer the People of the Book with this verse and recited it, with 3:52, in the two rakʿahs before Fajr.
- Reward is personal, and the community that accepted all the messengers took precedence over all others.

137.text:
From the start of Sūrah al-Baqarah up to this point, verse after verse has explained the nature and essence of īmān (faith), sometimes briefly and sometimes at length. Verse 137 defines it in one short phrase. "So if they believe in what you believe, then they will indeed be ˹rightly˺ guided. But if they turn away, they are simply opposed ˹to the truth˺. But Allah will spare you their evil. For He is the All-Hearing, All-Knowing". The phrase is simple, yet so comprehensive that every possible detail and explanation is already contained in it.

### Phrase by phrase

**"So if they believe in what you believe"**. If the disbelievers among the People of the Book, and the other disbelievers, believe in all of Allah's Books and messengers without differentiating between any of them. The Jews and the Christians, that is, can find guidance only if they believe just as you believe, in all the prophets and their Scriptures. The word "like" in the Arabic ("the like of what you believe") is for emphasis.

**"then they will indeed be ˹rightly˺ guided."**. They will have grasped the truth and been directed to it, guided out of error by following the religion of Muḥammad ﷺ and Ibrāhīm (Abraham), the way of life that Allah is pleased with.

**"But if they turn away"**. From truth to falsehood after the proof has been set before them, refusing to believe in all the prophets or in some of them.

**"they are simply opposed ˹to the truth˺."**. They are in schism, in conflict with the true religion and in opposition to you.

**"But Allah will spare you their evil."**. Allah will protect you, O Prophet, from their harm and give the believers victory over them. He will lift their burden from you by their being killed and expelled. Allah did suffice him against them, by the killing of Qurayẓah, the expulsion of Naḍīr and the taking of the jizyah from them. The verse points out that the enemies of Islam may still remain unconvinced out of sheer obstinacy and malice, and asks the Prophet ﷺ not to be sad about them, since Allah Himself will deal with them and keep His Prophet safe. The promise is made more explicitly elsewhere: "Allah will ˹certainly˺ protect you from the people" (5:67), and later events showed it fulfilled.

**"For He is the All-Hearing, All-Knowing"**. He hears what they say and knows their circumstances, their intentions, their actions and the punishment that awaits them.

### The faith of the Prophet ﷺ and his Companions as the standard

The immediate addressees of "you believe" are the Prophet ﷺ and his Companions. In matters of belief above all, their īmān is thereby set before us as the model. The verse is in effect a divine command laying down a fundamental principle: the only īmān acceptable to Allah is the one the Prophet ﷺ and his Companions held, and beliefs that deviate from it in the slightest are neither valid nor acceptable to Him. One must believe in Allah and His attributes, in the angels, in His Books, in His messengers and prophets and what they taught, exactly as the Prophet ﷺ and the Companions did. Nothing may be added or taken away on one's own account, and no private interpretation may distort the authentic meaning of these doctrines. Nor may one assign to the angels or the prophets a rank higher or lower than the one given them by the Prophet's ﷺ word or deed. One's faith must also be sincere and pure, since the opposite would be nifāq (hypocrisy).

This helps us see in true proportion the position of the heterodox sects among the Muslims, who make tall claims about the genuineness of their faith but lack faith in the full sense. The idolaters of Arabia, after all, proclaimed the authenticity of their faith, as the Jews and Christians still do, and as heretics have done in every age. Because their beliefs about Allah, the prophets, the angels and the Day of Judgement did not conform to the Prophet's ﷺ faith, Allah rejected them out of hand. Some of the Arab idolaters denied the very existence of angels, while others took them for daughters of God. Among the Jews, some groups would not obey the prophets and hated them so much that they murdered several of them, while other Jewish and Christian groups revered the prophets so extravagantly that they identified them with God, set them on His level or called them His sons. These two attitudes are the two extremes of deviation, and this verse shows both to be forms of misguidance.

Under the Sharīʿah every Muslim is bound to respect and love the Prophet ﷺ, and whoever falls short in this does not possess faith in the true sense. All the same, it must be clearly understood that making him Allah's equal in an attribute like knowledge or power is misguidance and shirk (associating partners with Allah). According to the Qur'an, shirk in its essence is to make someone besides Allah His equal in a divine attribute, as the idolaters confess in Hell: "when we made you equal to the Lord of all worlds" (26:98). Some Muslims consider the Prophet ﷺ all-knowing and present everywhere like Allah Himself, and congratulate themselves on showing the respect and love required of a Muslim, while in fact they disobey him and go against his teaching. They should learn from this verse that the respect and love Allah demands for His Prophet ﷺ is exactly the kind his Companions had, neither more nor less, for either would be a deviation and a sin.

At the other extreme are people who deny the plain and unambiguous declaration of the Qur'an that Muḥammad ﷺ is the last of all the prophets, and who try to make room for a new prophet. To serve this purpose they have manufactured exotic kinds of prophethood out of their own fantasy and given them fanciful names such as burūz (incarnation) and ẓill (manifestation). This verse exposes that fraud too, because the faith of the Prophet ﷺ and his Companions shows no trace of belief in prophets of this kind, and anyone who professes such a belief is an open heretic.

Then there are people whose minds are so fogged by modern materialism and so-called rationalism that they struggle to accept the idea of the other world and what belongs to it. They then subject these matters to crooked interpretations, which they suppose make Islam more acceptable to the modern mind and so count as a great service to it. Insofar as such interpretations break the rule indicated here, in that they do not conform to the faith of the Prophet ﷺ and his Companions, they are wholly false and must be rejected. A Muslim is obliged to believe without demur in whatever the Qur'an and hadith tell us about the other world. It is quite inadmissible, for instance, to hold that on the Day of Judgement people will be raised only "spiritually" and not bodily, that the reward and punishment of the next world will be "spiritual" rather than physical, or that the "weighing of deeds" is merely a metaphor. All such interpretations are doctrinally false and unacceptable to Allah, as this verse establishes.

### Belief in truth for its own sake

What was so special about the Companions' faith was that it amounted to accepting the truth at an abstract level, belief in truth for the sake of truth. That had become rare in a society which revered the words of the ancient prophets and treated as truth whatever centuries of tradition had sanctified. Continued belief in such "truth", embellished with myth and legend, had become a matter of national pride, and to view it in any other light would have meant denying a great legacy from the past. Unlike the ancient prophets, great figures celebrated in their nations' histories, the Prophet Muḥammad ﷺ came fresh to the world, with no accumulated tradition behind him to give his words weight. In his time truth stood on its own, with neither history nor tradition to support it, so those who accepted it did so purely and simply because it was true. Belief of this kind is what Allah recognises and accepts, and only faith of this strength and purity is acceptable to Him.

In the devotional reading the verse is an address to the Prophet ﷺ, the master of east and west and the messenger to men and jinn: We have laid these tasks on your path and commanded the world's people to follow you. We have written the Compact of Love for those who serve you and brought them under Our gaze. We have thrown your opponents down into the lowland of abasement. Whoever opposes you stands with the enemies, and whoever serves you stands with the friends. If someone wants you, We want him and let him reach Us, and if someone turns away, We burn him and cast him down: "Whoever obeys the Messenger has truly obeyed Allah" (4:80). So do not let your heart grow tight at these estranged people's turning away and speaking ill. We will take care of their business and remove their torment from you.

### In short

- Guidance for the People of the Book lies in believing exactly as the Prophet ﷺ and his Companions believed, in all of Allah's Books and messengers without distinction. Anything else is schism.
- Their faith is the binding standard for belief in Allah, the angels, the Books, the prophets and the Hereafter, ruling out both those who belittle the prophets and those who raise the Prophet ﷺ to Allah's level (26:98), those who invent new kinds of prophethood, and those who explain away the realities of the next world.
- The Companions believed in truth for its own sake, without the support of tradition, which is why their faith is the model.
- Allah promised to protect His Prophet ﷺ from his opponents (5:67, 4:80), and He did.

138.text:
Verse 138 gives Islam a striking name. "This is the ˹natural˺ Way of Allah. And who is better than Allah in ordaining a way? And we worship ˹none but˺ Him". The Arabic word is ṣibghah, a dye or colouring: "the colouring of Allah". The verse presents Islam as the colouring of Allah and explains that colouring as unalloyed worship of Him and total submission to Him.

### Phrase by phrase

**"This is the ˹natural˺ Way of Allah."**. Ibn ʿAbbās, as aḍ-Ḍaḥḥāk reports, explained "the ṣibghah of Allah" as the religion of Allah, and the same explanation is given by Mujāhid, Abū al-ʿĀliyah, ʿIkrimah, Ibrāhīm, al-Ḥasan, Qatādah, aḍ-Ḍaḥḥāk, ʿAṭiyyah al-ʿAwfī, al-Rabīʿ ibn Anas, as-Suddī and others. Grammatically the word restates the earlier "we believe", as if to say, "Allah has dyed us". It denotes His religion, the one He made human beings naturally inclined to, which leaves its mark on a person just as a dye leaves its mark on a garment. The believers are told to hold tightly to this religion, their natural way of life, inside and out. The Qur'an calls it "the natural Way of Allah which He has instilled in ˹all˺ people" (30:30), and directs Muslims to hold to it.

**"And who is better than Allah in ordaining a way?"**. Who has a better colouring than Allah? No one. No way of life is better than Allah's path. It agrees with our nature, benefits us in every way and protects us from evil and corruption.

**"And we worship ˹none but˺ Him"**. We are monotheists. We acknowledge that we worship Him, declare that there is only one true God, and worship nothing apart from Him.

### Why "colouring"?

Verse 135 identified Islam with the religion of Ibrāhīm (Abraham). Put verses 135 and 138 together and it becomes clear that Islam, or any authentic religion for that matter, is essentially the religion of Allah, and that linking a religion to a prophet's name can only be symbolic.

The expression carries several levels of meaning. The immediate allusion is to a Christian ceremony. On the seventh day after birth they would bathe an infant in coloured water, probably yellow, as a substitute for circumcision, supposed to guarantee the child's outward and inward purification, a fast and indelible "colouring" of Christian faith, so to speak. The verse suggests that this colour washes away with the water, leaving no trace outside or inside, and that such a baptism neither serves the purpose of circumcision nor cleanses a person of physical impurity. The only colouring worth the name is that of a genuine, unabrogated religion, Islam, the one colouring that guarantees physical and spiritual purification and the only one that will last.

The word has a deeper meaning too. Just as a colour is plainly visible to anyone who looks, so the signs of genuine, pure faith should shine through a Muslim's face, movements, habits and behaviour. In this sense the verse commands Muslims to dye themselves, outwardly and inwardly, in Allah's colouring: to offer unalloyed worship to Him alone, to submit totally to His commandments and to accept His will gladly.

### The colour that is colourlessness

In the devotional reading the verse says: We will bring a people who have come out in the colour of tawḥīd (Allah's oneness), adorned with the attribute of love and clothed in Allah's colour, which is colourlessness. Whoever is pure of the colour of the colour-mixers is coloured with Allah's colour. He who has painted a thousand worlds with colour, why would He buy my colour or yours, O bankrupt man? When someone reaches Allah's colour and falls back on Him, He colours him in His own colour, just as the elixir turns copper and iron to its own colour and makes them precious. Should the estranged fall back on Him, they become His familiars, and should the disobedient fall back, they become obedient.

Many stories of the shaykhs are told on this point. Ibrāhīm al-Khawāṣṣ related that he once went into the desert and met a Christian with his sash round his waist, who asked to travel with him. They walked for seven days. Then the Christian said: O monk of the unswerving folk, bring out what you have of expansiveness, for we are hungry. Ibrāhīm prayed, "O Allah, do not disgrace me before this unbeliever," and saw a tray with bread, roast meat, dates and a pitcher of water. They ate and drank and walked another seven days. Then Ibrāhīm, growing hasty, said: O monk of the Christians, now bring out what you have, since my turn is over. The man leaned on his staff and supplicated, and there appeared two trays holding double what Ibrāhīm's tray had held. Bewildered and upset, Ibrāhīm refused to eat. The man insisted, and finally said: eat, for I have two pieces of good news for you. The first is that I bear witness that there is no god but Allah and that Muḥammad ﷺ is Allah's messenger, and he took off the sash. The second is that I said, "O Allah, if there is any danger here, let me begin with this," and so he began. They ate, walked on, performed the Hajj and lived in Makkah for a year. Then the man died and was buried in al-Baṭḥāʾ, may Allah have mercy on him.

### In short

- The "colouring of Allah" is His religion, Islam, the natural disposition He instilled in people (30:30), which marks a person as a dye marks cloth.
- Set against the Christian baptismal "colouring" that washes away, it is the only colouring that truly purifies and lasts, and Muslims are commanded to let it show in their whole conduct.
- "We worship none but Him" is the declaration of pure monotheism, and in the devotional reading Allah's colour is colourlessness, which can turn even a stranger into a familiar, as the story of the Christian traveller shows.

139.text:
Verses 139 to 141 close the section of the surah that has refuted certain claims of the Jews and the Christians. "Say, “Would you dispute with us about Allah, while He is our Lord and your Lord? We are accountable for our deeds and you for yours. And we are devoted to Him ˹alone˺". The claims in question were that Ibrāhīm (Abraham), Ismāʿīl (Ishmael), Isḥāq (Isaac), Yaʿqūb (Jacob) and the prophets of his line were Jews or Christians, and that the Jews and Christians were the chosen people who alone would go straight to Paradise, a privilege denied to the Muslims. Earlier verses showed that all these prophets followed Islam in the general sense of the word, that the earlier Sharīʿahs are now abrogated, and that the title "Islam" has been specially given to the religion of Muḥammad ﷺ. Allah directs His Prophet ﷺ here to pre-empt the arguments of his opponents.

### Phrase by phrase

**"Say, “Would you dispute with us about Allah"**. The occasion is recorded. The Jews told the Muslims: we are the people of the first Book, our qiblah is the more ancient one, and no prophet was ever sent from the Arabs, so had Muḥammad been a prophet he would have been one of us. The answer begins: do you argue with us about the religion of Allah, about His oneness, about obedience and submission to Him and keeping away from what He forbids, and about His choosing a prophet from among the Arabs? The Arabic question form expresses rejection. If the People of the Book argue that they have more right to Allah and His religion because their way of life is older and their Scriptures came first, it will do them no good.

**"while He is our Lord and your Lord?"**. He has full control over us and over you, and He alone deserves worship, without partners. It is for Him to choose whom He wills. Allah is the Lord of everyone, not of one group alone. Being the Lord of all, He cannot show special favour to one particular set of His creatures. On the Day of Judgement He will assess Jews, Christians and Muslims alike by what each believed and how each behaved, a principle the People of the Book themselves accepted.

**"We are accountable for our deeds and you for yours."**. We have our religion and you have yours. We will be requited for our deeds and you for yours, so it is hardly improbable that some of our deeds will earn us honour. You will not be asked about our actions nor we about yours, and everyone will be rewarded according to what he has done. The sense is also: we disown you and whatever you worship, as you disown us. Allah said elsewhere, "If they deny you, then say, “My deeds are mine and your deeds are yours. You are free of what I do and I am free of what you do!”" (10:41), and, "So if they argue with you ˹O Prophet˺, say, “I have submitted myself to Allah, and so have my followers.”" (3:20). Of Ibrāhīm He said, "And his people argued with him. He responded, “Are you arguing with me about Allah, while He has guided me?" (6:80), and He recounts the dispute of a king with Ibrāhīm concerning the Lord. The king relied on the authority Allah had granted him, but "the disbeliever was dumbstruck" (2:258).

**"And we are devoted to Him ˹alone˺"**. Sincere to Him in worship and submission, in religion and in deed, unlike you, so we are more worthy to be chosen. We acknowledge that we worship Him and that there is only one true God, doing as He instructs and worshipping nothing besides Him. The Muslims are thus told to announce that they recognise no god but Allah and have purified their religion of every trace of shirk (associating partners with Allah). The Jews and Christians, by contrast, hold ʿUzayr (Ezra) and ʿĪsā (Jesus) respectively to be "the Son of God", and their religions have in any case been abrogated. Here at least Muslims stand above them.

### Ikhlāṣ, the mark of this Ummah

This verse brings out the essential and distinctive characteristic of the Islamic Ummah: it has purified itself of every possible admixture of shirk and devoted itself, outwardly and inwardly, to Allah. The Arabic word is mukhliṣūn, plural of mukhliṣ, "one who has purified himself", related to ikhlāṣ, purifying oneself. Saʿīd ibn Jubayr defined ikhlāṣ as worshipping Allah alone, associating no one with Him, and doing good deeds solely to obey Him rather than to win people's admiration. Certain spiritual masters have said that ikhlāṣ is a deed that neither men, nor angels, nor Satan can identify, a secret between Allah and His servant.

Ikhlāṣ is usually translated "sincerity", and mukhliṣ "sincere", but it is doubtful whether "sincerity" ever carried the full range of the Arabic word in any Western language. In current usage, moreover, the sense of "sincerity" has become not merely perverted but at times inverted. The word used to imply harmony between outward action and inner inclination, with the tacit assumption that the action was at least socially acceptable to some degree. As used today it suggests compliance with one's emotions, or even one's instincts, so that "sincerity" is invoked to justify fornication or even murder. Such an idea is the exact opposite of ikhlāṣ. One cannot reach even the lowest degree of ikhlāṣ without a clear intention to obey the injunctions of the Sharīʿah rather than be led by instinctual urges or emotional inclinations, whereas the fashionable "sincerity" requires one to ignore the Sharīʿah, and even worldly considerations, and obey the impulse of the moment, reducing a human being to an automaton at the mercy of his reflexes.

There is a further, related notion of "sincerity" which has troubled the peace of many pious people in the past and has become devastating in our own days. It demands fixity and unbroken continuity in an emotional state, which is simply not possible for human beings as they are made. Some pious people, once they begin seeking this kind of "sincerity" in their prescribed prayers, find they cannot keep up unbroken concentration, and are so frightened by the lapse that they sometimes give up praying altogether, believing such worship "insincere" and therefore invalid. Let it be clear once and for all that the Sharīʿah requires only that we have the correct intention and attitude when we begin our prayer or any other good deed. That alone is the prerequisite of ikhlāṣ, which in any case is not a matter of emotions and feelings. Islam asks us to perfect the quality of ikhlāṣ as the Sharīʿah defines it, not to chase "sincerity" in the Western sense, ancient or modern. For a fuller treatment see Tarbiyat al-Sālik by Maulānā Ashraf ʿAlī Thānavī.

In the devotional reading: how can dispute with strangers be fitting? They are covered by absence and shaded by concealment, while unveiling and the bright noon of witnessing light up the friends.
