When is the state of one made bankrupt by his absence equal to that of one whose selection, sincere devotion and immersion in acts of drawing near have already been decreed? It is preposterous. There is no equality.

### In short

- The Jews argued that their Book, their qiblah and their prophets were older, so no Arab could be a prophet. The answer is that Allah is the Lord of everyone and chooses whom He wills, and that each party will answer only for its own deeds (10:41, 3:20), as Ibrāhīm himself answered those who argued with him (6:80, 2:258).
- The Muslims declare that they are devoted to Allah alone, free of the shirk of calling ʿUzayr or ʿĪsā the son of God.
- Ikhlāṣ, the Ummah's distinctive mark, means worshipping Allah alone and acting only to obey Him. It is a matter of correct intention under the Sharīʿah, not of emotional "sincerity" or unbroken concentration.

140.text:
Verse 140 turns the People of the Book's claim about the patriarchs into a question they cannot answer. "Do you claim that Abraham, Ishmael, Isaac, Jacob, and his descendants were all Jews or Christians?” Say, “Who is more knowledgeable: you or Allah?” Who does more wrong than those who hide the testimony they received from Allah? And Allah is never unaware of what you do". Allah criticises them for claiming that Ibrāhīm (Abraham), the prophets who came after him and the Tribes followed their religion, whether Judaism or Christianity.

### Phrase by phrase

**"Do you claim that Abraham, Ishmael, Isaac, Jacob, and his descendants were all Jews or Christians?”"**. The Arabic "or" at the start carries the force of "nay". The verb is read both "do you say" and "do they say". The question is put to the Jews and the Christians: do you say that Ibrāhīm, Ismāʿīl (Ishmael), Isḥāq (Isaac), Yaʿqūb (Jacob) and the children of Yaʿqūb, the prophets of his descendants, were Jews or Christians, as you claim?

**"Say, “Who is more knowledgeable: you or Allah?”"**. Do you know their religion better, or does Allah? Allah knows best, and He has stated that they were neither Jews nor Christians: "Abraham was neither a Jew nor a Christian; he submitted in all uprightness and was not a polytheist" (3:67). By this He dissociated Ibrāhīm from both groups, and those named with him were his followers in belonging to neither. If the People of the Book claim they were Jews or Christians, the claim is false, because these prophets had been sent, and had died, before the Torah and the Gospel came down. So their claim is a lie against Allah and against His Prophet ﷺ, and it shows that they have hidden the truth of what was revealed to them. If, on the strength of their link with the earlier prophets, the People of the Book still insist on their own rectitude, the Muslims may put this basic question to them: who knows the truth better, Allah or they? In the Last Revelation Allah has announced the truth finally and definitively, and the People of the Book know themselves that the earlier prophets' religion was Islam.

**"Who does more wrong than those who hide the testimony they received from Allah?"**. No one is more unjust in his disbelief, or more insolent and daring towards Allah, than one who conceals from people a testimony he received from Allah. These are the Jews, who concealed Allah's testimony in the Torah about Ibrāhīm's pure faith and about the prophethood of this Prophet ﷺ. Al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī said that they used to recite the Book Allah sent them, which stated that Islam is the true religion and Muḥammad ﷺ Allah's Messenger, and that Ibrāhīm, Ismāʿīl, Isḥāq, Yaʿqūb and the Tribes belonged neither to the Jews nor to the Christians. They bore witness to these facts and yet hid them from people. No one does greater wrong than someone who hides firm evidence he has from Allah, as some of the People of the Book did. They were trying to conceal the truth, and were being unjust in the gravest sense of the term.

**"And Allah is never unaware of what you do"**. He is not heedless of your concealing your testimony. This is a threat and a warning: His knowledge encompasses everyone's deeds, and He will reward each accordingly. He will judge them by their own deeds, not by the deeds of their ancestors.

### Measuring the prophets by oneself

In the devotional reading, whoever looks out from himself at creation forms an image of each thing from his own character and takes everything to be something like himself. When these people, being outsiders to the Real, judged the prophets by their own state, the Real threw their conjecture back on them and left them to their own opinion. Are those drawn away from their own testimony like those whom it veils? Is the one snatched away from all of it equal to the one thrown back on what resembles himself? That is the conjecture of those who disbelieve, and what misery is theirs!

### In short

- The People of the Book claimed the patriarchs as Jews or Christians. Allah, who knows better, has declared Ibrāhīm neither (3:67), and these prophets lived and died before the Torah and the Gospel existed.
- Their scholars knew from their own Book that the true religion is Islam, that Muḥammad ﷺ is Allah's Messenger and that the patriarchs belonged to neither sect, yet they hid this testimony, the gravest injustice.
- Allah is aware of the concealment and will judge each by his own deeds.

141.text:
The section ends by repeating, word for word, the warning given in verse 134. "That was a community that had already gone before. For them is what they earned and for you is what you have earned. And you will not be accountable for what they have done". At the close of this long passage against the claims of the Jews and the Christians, the verse warns them of the consequences of their vanity and pretension, and advises them to look after themselves rather than rely on ancestral glory.

### Phrase by phrase

**"That was a community that had already gone before."**. A group of people who existed before you and have passed away.

**"For them is what they earned and for you is what you have earned."**. They have what they earned of good, and you have what you earn of good. They bear their deeds and you bear yours. They earned for themselves by their own actions, and you earn by yours.

**"And you will not be accountable for what they have done"**. On the Day of Judgement you will not be asked about what they did in this world, and they will not be asked about what you do. Being their relatives will not be enough for you unless you imitate their good deeds. Do not be deceived by being their descendants unless you follow them in obeying Allah's commands and in following the messengers He sent as warners and bringers of good news. Whoever disbelieves in even one prophet has disbelieved in all the messengers, above all if he rejects the master and final Messenger sent by Allah, the Lord of the worlds, to all mankind and the jinn. No one is held accountable for another's disobedience, and no one benefits from another's deeds. Each person receives his reward according to what he himself did. Allah knows what the People of the Book have been doing, and He will judge them by their own deeds, not those of their ancestors.

### A repetition with a purpose

That the same verse appears twice in the space of a few lines is a sign of how central its principle is. Verse 134 closed the account of Ibrāhīm (Abraham), Yaʿqūb (Jacob) and his sons. Here it closes the argument with those who claimed these prophets as their own while refusing the religion the prophets actually taught. In both places the point is the same: a nation's record belongs to that nation, and no later generation can draw on it as capital.

In the devotional reading, fate's barriers came between you and them. They built their structures on separation and heedlessness, whereas you have pitched your tents on closeness and connection. The one freed by Our favour is not like the one driven out by Our force.

### In short

- Ibrāhīm and his family have gone with their own deeds, and the People of the Book, like everyone else, will be judged only by theirs.
- Descent from the prophets counts for nothing without following them in obedience, and rejecting even one messenger, let alone the final one, is to reject them all.
- The verse repeats 134 to seal the refutation of ancestral pride.

142.text:
With verse 142 the surah turns to the change of the qiblah, the direction of prayer, an event that shook Madinah in the second year after the Hijrah. "The foolish among the people will ask, “Why did they turn away from the direction of prayer they used to face?” Say, ˹O Prophet,˺ “The east and west belong ˹only˺ to Allah. He guides whoever He wills to the Straight Path.”" The verse announces the objection before it was made, and supplies the answer. Having spent many verses on the religion of Ibrāhīm (Abraham), the Qur'an now turns the Muslims towards his House.

### Phrase by phrase

**"The foolish among the people will ask"**. The ignorant among the Jews, the Arab idolaters and the hypocrites. The Arabic verb carries a prefix that marks the future and so informs of the unseen: Allah tells the believers what will be said before it is said. When the qiblah was changed, those afflicted with hypocrisy and doubt, and the disbelieving Jews, lost their bearings and fell into confusion. The Qur'an reports their objection and adds that only stupid people could make it, just as earlier in the surah those who turned from Ibrāhīm's religion were described as making fools of themselves. In the devotional reading, the disbelievers' eyes were weak, so the correct view of the believers' affairs never became apparent to them. They looked with an eye for finding fault and loosed their tongues against everything the believers did or would do. They never saw anything new without producing a new objection to it, and the shift of the qiblah to the Kaʿbah was one more occasion.

**"“Why did they turn away from the direction of prayer they used to face?”"**. What has turned the Prophet ﷺ and the believers from Bayt al-Maqdis (Jerusalem), the direction they used to face in prayer? What is the matter with these people, who face one direction one day and another the next? Or, as some took it: there was no reason to leave the direction they had been praying in. The Jews added that the Muslims must want to return to the religion of their ancestors. Before Islam people had prayed towards Jerusalem, and the old qiblah had come to seem sacred and beyond change. How, some asked, could any other place be the qiblah when Jerusalem had held that position from time immemorial? The opponents of Islam used the change to spread every sort of rumour. Earlier prophets always faced Jerusalem, they said, so how could this prophet go against them? It showed that the whole purpose of his mission was to spite the Jews. Some poured scorn on his claim to prophethood: he seemed to be in two minds about his own mission, facing Jerusalem one moment and Makkah the next. Others said that if the Kaʿbah was the real qiblah, then all the prayers the Muslims had offered towards Jerusalem had been wasted. If their qiblah was correct, the objectors asked, what could turn them from it?

**"Say, ˹O Prophet,˺ “The east and west belong ˹only˺ to Allah."**. All directions are His. The command, the decision and the authority belong to Allah alone, so He orders His servants to face whichever direction He wills, and no objection is possible. The prayer towards the Kaʿbah and the prayer formerly offered towards Jerusalem were both by Allah's command. As He has said, "To Allah belong the east and the west, so wherever you turn you are facing ˹towards˺ Allah" (2:115), and, "Righteousness is not in turning your faces towards the east or the west. Rather, the righteous are those who believe in Allah, the Last Day, the angels, the Books, and the prophets" (2:177). The best act is to keep to Allah's commands. Wherever He tells us to face, we face. Since obedience means carrying out His orders, if He commanded us to face a different place every day we would do so, for we are His servants and at His disposal. Their stupidity lies in failing to see that east and west alike belong to Allah, and that He guides whom He likes to the straight path.

**"He guides whoever He wills to the Straight Path.”"**. He establishes whom He wills on a straight religion and a straight prayer direction, the religion of Islam, free of distortion and misguidance, and you are among those He has guided. The verse fully answers the enemies of Islam. The Straight Path is the readiness to obey Allah's command without demur, and that path was granted to the Muslims by His grace. There is also a hint that where the injunctions of the Sharīʿah are concerned, rectitude lies in obeying each divine command unquestioningly, without being too curious about its rationale, since those who go hunting for a rationale usually do so because they wish to deny, belittle or disobey.

### How the qiblah was changed

Al-Bukhārī relates from al-Barāʾ ibn ʿĀzib that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ prayed facing Bayt al-Maqdis for sixteen or seventeen months, while wishing he could face the Kaʿbah. The first prayer he offered towards it was ʿAṣr, with a group of people. One of those who had prayed with him then went out and passed some people bowing in prayer in a mosque. He said: by Allah, I bear witness that I have prayed with the Prophet ﷺ facing Makkah. On hearing this they turned towards the House just as they were, still bowing. Some Muslims who had prayed towards the old qiblah had died or been martyred before the change, and the Companions did not know what to say about them, so Allah sent down the words, "And Allah would never discount your ˹previous acts of˺ faith" (2:143). Muslim recorded the same report by another chain. In another version from al-Barāʾ, the Messenger of Allah ﷺ used to pray towards Bayt al-Maqdis but kept looking up at the sky, awaiting Allah's command, until the words came down, "Indeed, We see you ˹O Prophet˺ turning your face towards heaven. Now We will make you turn towards a direction ˹of prayer˺ that will please you" (2:144). A Muslim then said: we wish we knew about those of us who died before the qiblah was changed, and about our own prayers offered towards Bayt al-Maqdis, and 2:143 was revealed. And the foolish among the people, the Jews and Christians, said, "What made them change the qiblah they used to face?", and this verse came down. Al-Bukhārī also records the report through ʿAbd Allāh ibn Rajāʾ and Abū Isḥāq from al-Barāʾ, which names the Jews as the foolish ones.

Ibn ʿAbbās, in the report of ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭalḥah, said that when the Messenger of Allah ﷺ migrated to Madinah, Allah commanded him to face Bayt al-Maqdis, and the Jews were delighted. He faced it for over ten months, but he loved the qiblah of Ibrāhīm, and he would supplicate and look up to the sky, until Allah revealed the command to turn towards the Sacred Mosque. The Jews disliked the change and asked what had turned the Muslims from their former qiblah, and Allah answered, "The east and west belong ˹only˺ to Allah."

Many other hadiths deal with the subject. In summary: the Messenger of Allah ﷺ was commanded to face Bayt al-Maqdis, and in Makkah he would pray towards it standing between the two corners of the Kaʿbah, so that the Kaʿbah lay between him and Bayt al-Maqdis. After the migration to Madinah that was no longer possible, and Allah commanded him to face Bayt al-Maqdis, as Ibn ʿAbbās and most scholars hold. Some scholars say that when ṣalāh was first made obligatory, the qiblah appointed for him was the Kaʿbah, which had already been the qiblah of his ancestor Ibrāhīm, and that some time after the Hijrah, or as others maintain shortly before it, he was commanded to turn to Bayt al-Maqdis. This particular command is not reported in the Qur'an at all, which shows the hollowness of the claim that the Qur'an can be fully understood without the help of hadith. The spot in the mosque at Madinah where he prayed facing Bayt al-Maqdis is still marked, as al-Qurṭubī notes.

The Prophet ﷺ was obedience personified. He went on praying towards Bayt al-Maqdis as commanded, but he longed for the Kaʿbah, the qiblah of Ādam (Adam) and Ibrāhīm, to be made his qiblah as well. Allah's way is to grant, in His grace, the wishes of servants who have found His favour. So the Prophet ﷺ hoped this wish too would be granted. The Qur'an describes him turning his face to heaven and promises him a qiblah he would like (2:144). That verse speaks not of the "Kaʿbah" or "the House of Allah" but of al-Masjid al-Ḥarām, the Sacred Mosque. This indicates that those far from Makkah need not have the Kaʿbah itself exactly in front of them while praying, and that facing in the direction of the House is enough. Those present in the Sacred Mosque, or able to see the Kaʿbah from a distance, must have the Kaʿbah or some part of it directly in front of them, failing which the prayer is not valid.

Al-Bukhārī records that the news reached some of the Anṣār while they were praying ʿAṣr towards Bayt al-Maqdis, and they at once turned to face the Kaʿbah. The Ṣaḥīḥayn (the collections of al-Bukhārī and Muslim) record from Ibn ʿUmar that while the people in the mosque of Qubāʾ were praying Fajr, a man came and said that Qur'an had been revealed to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ that night commanding him to face the Kaʿbah, so they should face it. They had been facing ash-Shām (Syria), and they turned towards the Kaʿbah. At-Tirmidhī adds that they were bowing at the time and changed direction without rising, and Muslim reports this last detail from Anas. The believers who were praying with the Prophet ﷺ when the command came turned, still in prayer, from Jerusalem to Makkah, a turn of about 160 degrees from north-west to south. All these hadiths show the Companions' perfect obedience to Allah and His Messenger ﷺ and their compliance with every command. They also prove a legal point: an abrogating text takes effect for a person only once he knows of it, even if it has already been revealed and announced. That is why these Companions were not told to repeat the ʿAṣr, Maghrib and ʿIshāʾ prayers they had offered towards Jerusalem after the qiblah had in fact been changed. Allah knows best.

### Why one qiblah at all?

Qiblah means the direction one turns one's face. In every form of worship a true Muslim turns to Allah alone, and Allah is not confined to any direction. He transcends all dimensions. Logically, then, everyone might have been left free to choose whatever orientation he liked and to change it as suited him. Divine Wisdom found it more fitting that all worshippers turn the same way, to a fixed orientation. Worship takes several forms. Some concern the individual alone, such as fasting and dhikr (remembrance of Allah), which can be performed in private. Others, such as ṣalāh and the Hajj, are performed openly and in congregation. These have a secondary function besides worship: they give Muslims a social and collective discipline. The basic principle of any social organisation is the unity and integration of its individuals. On the firmness of that unity its strength depends, whereas an improper stress on individuality encourages disintegration and splintering.

As to what should serve as the principle of unity, people have chosen differently at different times: race or colour, homeland or region, language. All such considerations are arbitrary and accidental. Instead of bringing people together they divide them, producing, as the newspapers show every day, convulsions across the world. The revealed religions and the Sharīʿahs of the prophets, whose collective name is Islam, have paid no unnecessary regard to such accidental factors. They have founded unity and integration on the only basis that can possibly be valid: unity of mind arising from unity of belief. Islam calls on people not to scatter in the worship of a thousand false gods but to join in worshipping the True God, the One without equal, the only worship that can gather people from the four corners of the earth, of the past, the present and the future, into one body of the faithful. To give this inner unity a visible form, and to reinforce it, certain outward expressions of unity were also prescribed. In both cases the governing principle is the same. Unity must not be forced by circumstances. It should spring from a free act of will and choice, and give rise to a spiritual brotherhood.

Accidental factors like race, colour and birthplace are given their proper place in social life, but none is allowed to usurp the centre. Only in the field where the human will can exercise its power of choice has Islam sought to establish unity, inner and outer. A further consideration behind the relevant rules is that whatever serves as a point of unity should be something every human being, man or woman, literate or illiterate, townsman or villager, can adopt with equal ease. That is why the Sharīʿah has not imposed a single rigid mode of dress, food or housing on all the peoples of the world. Climates, needs and even tastes differ from region to region, and such uniformity would have made life hard. Had a certain minimum of dress been prescribed, it would have been inconvenient for some, offended against moderation and amounted to rejecting Allah's bounties, while a more elaborate compulsory dress would have been impossible for the poor. So instead of a uniform, the Sharīʿah permits the modes of dress current among different peoples and lays down only necessary restrictions: the dress must cover a specified area of the body, defined separately for men and women, it must not be chosen out of extravagance or vanity, and it must not be worn in order to imitate non-Muslims. In short, Islam has fixed as points of unity only things that can be freely chosen, are easy to adopt and involve no undue hardship or expense, such as straightening the rows in congregational prayer, following the imām's movements strictly, and wearing a single form of dress during the Hajj.

Among these the qiblah is one of the most important. Allah Himself is free of all dimensions, but a single definite qiblah gives people an easy and concrete unifying principle. Had the choice been left to human beings, it would itself have become a source of dissension and conflict, so a matter of such weight had to be settled by Allah. In fact the angels had laid the Kaʿbah's foundation, the House of Allah, before Ādam was ever sent down to the earth, and it was the first qiblah of mankind: "Surely the first House ˹of worship˺ established for humanity is the one at Bakkah—a blessed sanctuary and a guide for ˹all˺ people" (3:96). As noted under verse 125, it remained the qiblah until the time of Nūḥ (Noah), when the Flood destroyed it. Ibrāhīm and Ismāʿīl (Ishmael) rebuilt it by divine command and it became their qiblah. Afterwards Bayt al-Maqdis in Jerusalem was appointed the qiblah for the Hebrew prophets and their people. Even so, according to Abū al-ʿĀliyah, as al-Qurṭubī records, those prophets would pray in Bayt al-Maqdis in such a way as to face not only the Rock (the Ṣakhrah) but the Kaʿbah as well.

### What the change teaches

The qiblah has to do with the form of worship rather than its reality. A direction is appointed so that prayer may take an organised pattern, and Allah can change it as He pleases, for whichever way one turns, one faces Him. Whatever direction He lays down is the one to face, whatever it may be. Neither the Kaʿbah nor Bayt al-Maqdis possesses any exclusive merit of its own in this respect. It is the divine command alone that confers the distinction of being the qiblah, and Allah could as easily have chosen some other place. The only merit in adopting a particular qiblah lies in obeying the divine command and submitting wholly to Allah's will, which is the basic principle of the religion of Ibrāhīm, the builder of the Kaʿbah. The verses already cited, 2:177 and 2:115, define the matter clearly: the place chosen has no merit in its own right, its special merit arises from Allah's having chosen it, and turning towards it is meritorious only insofar as it shows readiness to obey. The very reason for changing the Prophet's ﷺ qiblah may well have been to show people visibly that a qiblah is no idol to be worshipped. It is a concrete expression of a divine command, and may therefore be changed whenever Allah wills. The next verse says explicitly that the earlier appointment of Bayt al-Maqdis was meant to show who was willing to obey the Prophet ﷺ and who was not. True believers, those not caught up in the externals of religion, were not disturbed by the change. They understood that what mattered was not the direction but Allah's command. He could lay down any qiblah whenever He liked, and whatever He prescribed must be followed.

Allah's care and kindness towards His servant and Messenger Muḥammad ﷺ and his Ummah is profound. He guided them to the qiblah of Ibrāhīm, His Khalīl (close friend), and commanded them to face the Kaʿbah, the most honoured house on the face of the earth, built by Ibrāhīm in the name of Allah, the One without partner. Aḥmad relates in his Musnad from ʿĀʾishah that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said of the People of the Book that they envy the Muslims for nothing so much as for three things. The first is Friday, Jumuʿah, to which Allah guided us and from which they were led astray, for when every community was told to set aside one day of the week for worship, the Jews chose Saturday, the Christians chose Sunday, and the Muslims were given Friday, the day Allah favoured. The second is the true qiblah, to which He directed us and from which they strayed. The third is our saying "Āmīn" behind the imām.

In the devotional reading, the servants worship in whatever region and direction He wills. In the same way, the companions of absence, veiled from witnessing how the Real grants free scope to His friends, seize on isolated aspects of an affair and bring their own states to bear on them. Had they seen the whole picture with a single vision, they would have been spared the pain of divided thinking, the distraction of accursed thoughts and the claims of broken conjecture. But Allah guides whom He wills to His light.

### In short

- Allah foretold that the Jews, idolaters and hypocrites would mock the Muslims for leaving Jerusalem for the Kaʿbah, and answered that every direction is His, so the only thing that matters is obeying His command (2:115, 2:177).
- The Prophet ﷺ prayed towards Bayt al-Maqdis for sixteen or seventeen months while longing for Ibrāhīm's qiblah, until 2:144 came down. Companions who heard the news mid-prayer turned at once, and those who had prayed unaware were not told to repeat, since abrogation binds only once it is known.
- A single qiblah is one of the easy, freely chosen outward points of unity Islam prescribes, founded on unity of belief rather than race, land or language. The Kaʿbah was the first House (3:96), the qiblah of Ādam and Ibrāhīm, before Jerusalem served the Hebrew prophets.
- The change showed that a qiblah is an expression of Allah's command, not an idol, and the People of the Book envy the Muslims for Friday, the qiblah and saying Āmīn.

143.text:
Verse 143 explains the change of the qiblah by setting it inside a larger gift. "And so We have made you ˹believers˺ an upright community so that you may be witnesses over humanity and that the Messenger may be a witness over you. We assigned your former direction of prayer only to distinguish those who would remain faithful to the Messenger from those who would lose faith. It was certainly a difficult test except for those ˹rightly˺ guided by Allah. And Allah would never discount your ˹previous acts of˺ faith. Surely Allah is Ever Gracious and Most Merciful to humanity". Just as Allah gave the Muslims a qiblah superior to every other orientation, so He gave the Ummah of Islam the unmatched distinction of being moderate, balanced and just, the honour of the central place among all religious communities.

### Phrase by phrase

**"And so We have made you ˹believers˺ an upright community"**. "And so": just as We honoured you with the religion of Ibrāhīm (Abraham) and his qiblah, and guided you to it, so We have made you, O community of Muḥammad ﷺ, a wasaṭ nation. The Arabic adjective means moderate, middle or central, and is normally applied to the best of a kind. Allah changed the qiblah to that of Ibrāhīm and chose it for this Ummah so as to make it the best nation ever. For that reason it will bear witness over the other nations on the Day of Resurrection, when all of them will agree about its excellence. To say that Quraysh is "wasaṭ" among the Arab tribes means the best of them. To say the Messenger of Allah ﷺ was wasaṭ in his people means he came from the best branch. The ʿAṣr prayer is called al-wusṭā, the middle prayer, meaning the best, as the authentic hadith collections report. Because Allah made this Ummah the wasaṭ, He endowed it with the most complete legislation, the best method and the clearest way, as He says: He "has chosen you, and laid upon you no hardship in the religion—the way of your forefather Abraham" (22:78). At-Tirmidhī relates from Abū Saʿīd al-Khudrī that the Prophet ﷺ himself explained the word as ʿadl, just, in the sense of the best, as al-Qurṭubī notes. The Ummah was chosen to be a good, just and balanced nation among all communities in its beliefs, its worship and its dealings, excellent and upright.

**"so that you may be witnesses over humanity and that the Messenger may be a witness over you."**. Witnesses on the Day of Resurrection that the messengers delivered the message to their peoples, with the Messenger ﷺ bearing witness that he delivered it to you and that you are upright and on the straight path. This distinction will appear in its full splendour on the Day of Judgement. Those among the earlier nations who denied their prophets will pretend on that day that they never received a Book from Allah and that no prophet ever guided them. The Ummah of Islam will then be called to testify that prophets came from Allah in every age and guided every people. The earlier nations will object. This Ummah did not exist at the time, they will say, and cannot know what happened before it came into being, so its testimony against them cannot stand. The Ummah will answer that although it did not witness those events, it received an authentic report from the most reliable source there could be: the Last Prophet ﷺ and the Last Book of Allah. The Prophet ﷺ will then be called as a witness. He will confirm his Ummah's testimony. Aḥmad relates from Abū Saʿīd that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: Nūḥ (Noah) will be called on the Day of Resurrection and asked whether he conveyed the message, and he will say yes. His people will be summoned and asked whether Nūḥ conveyed it to them, and they will say that no warner came to them and no one was sent. Nūḥ will be asked who testifies for him, and he will say, "Muḥammad and his Ummah." The Prophet ﷺ then said that "wasaṭ" means ʿadl, just: you will be summoned to testify that Nūḥ conveyed his message, and I will attest to your testimony. Al-Bukhārī, at-Tirmidhī, an-Nasāʾī and Ibn Mājah also recorded it. In another report from Abū Saʿīd al-Khudrī, also in Aḥmad, the Prophet ﷺ said that a prophet will come on the Day of Resurrection with only two or more followers. His people will be asked whether he conveyed the message and will say no. He will be asked whether he conveyed it and will say yes, and when asked who testifies for him he will name Muḥammad and his Ummah. They will be summoned and asked whether he conveyed it, and will say yes. Asked how they know, they will say that their Prophet came to them and told them that the messengers had conveyed their messages. Aḥmad also relates from Abū al-Aswad that he came to Madinah during an epidemic that was killing many people, and sat with ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb when a funeral passed and the people praised the dead man. ʿUmar said, "Wajabat," it has become binding. Another funeral passed and the people spoke ill of the dead man, and again ʿUmar said, "Wajabat." Abū al-Aswad asked what he meant. ʿUmar replied that he was saying what the Messenger of Allah ﷺ had said: any Muslim for whom four people testify that he was righteous, Allah admits to Paradise. They asked about three, and he said three as well. They asked about two, and he said two as well. They did not ask him about one. Al-Bukhārī, at-Tirmidhī and an-Nasāʾī recorded this too.

**"We assigned your former direction of prayer only to distinguish those who would remain faithful to the Messenger from those who would lose faith."**. We prescribed for you, O Muḥammad ﷺ, facing Bayt al-Maqdis (Jerusalem) at first and then changed it to the Kaʿbah, in order to find out who would follow and obey you and face whatever you face, and who would turn on his heels, reverting to his religion. Allah of course knew already. "That We might know" means that the knowledge might become manifest and the distinction be seen. The change showed who accepted Allah's decree gladly, did what He instructed and followed the Messenger ﷺ, and who abandoned his religion to chase his own desires instead of Allah's sacred law. On one reading "the direction you were facing" is the Kaʿbah itself, which the Prophet ﷺ had faced in Makkah before being commanded, on emigrating, to face Jerusalem so as to win over the Jews' hearts. He prayed towards it for sixteen or seventeen months, or nineteen months in one account, before the direction changed. Some doubted the religion and thought the Prophet ﷺ confused about the matter, and a number of people apostatised because of it. History records that after this verse came down, those weak in faith, or merely hypocrites, left Islam, and even accused the Prophet ﷺ of going back to the ways of his own people, the idolaters.

**"It was certainly a difficult test except for those ˹rightly˺ guided by Allah."**. The Arabic particle is softened: "though it was indeed a grave thing". Changing the qiblah from Bayt al-Maqdis to the Kaʿbah weighed heavily on hearts, except those whose hearts Allah guided and protected. These believe with certainty in the truthfulness of the Messenger ﷺ and that whatever he brought is true beyond doubt. They believe that Allah does and decides whatever He wills, gives His servants whatever commands He wills, and abrogates whichever of them He wills, with perfect wisdom and conclusive proof in all of it. They were certain that whatever He decrees for His servants carries far-reaching wisdom and underlying reasons. Those with a disease in their hearts are different. Whatever happens breeds doubt in them, while the same event increases the believers in faith and certainty. Allah says: "Whenever a sûrah is revealed, some of them ask ˹mockingly˺, “Which of you has this increased in faith?” As for the believers, it has increased them in faith and they rejoice. But as for those with sickness in their hearts, it has increased them only in wickedness upon their wickedness" (9:124-125), and, "We send down the Quran as a healing and mercy for the believers, but it only increases the wrongdoers in loss" (17:82). Those who stayed faithful to the Messenger ﷺ, obeyed him and faced whatever Allah commanded, with neither doubt nor hesitation, were the foremost of the Companions. Some scholars say that the early Emigrants and the Anṣār were the ones who prayed towards both qiblahs.

**"And Allah would never discount your ˹previous acts of˺ faith."**. The reward of your earlier prayers towards Bayt al-Maqdis will not be lost with Allah. Abū Isḥāq as-Sabīʿī relates in the Ṣaḥīḥ from al-Barāʾ that people asked about those who had prayed towards Bayt al-Maqdis and died before the change, and this phrase came down. At-Tirmidhī recorded the same from Ibn ʿAbbās and graded it ṣaḥīḥ. In Ibn Isḥāq's report, Ibn ʿAbbās explained that the phrase covers both your prayer towards the first qiblah and your belief in your Prophet and obedience to him in facing the second: Allah will reward you for all of it. "Faith" here can be taken in its usual sense. When the qiblah changed, some foolish people thought the Muslims had abandoned Islam and that their faith was now null and void, and the verse assures the Muslims that Allah will not let their faith go to waste and tells them to ignore such senseless conjecture. On the basis of certain hadiths, some early commentators took "faith" to mean ṣalāh. On that reading Allah assures them that the change does not touch the validity of the prayers they offered towards Bayt al-Maqdis, which were valid and have been accepted. Al-Bukhārī relates from al-Barāʾ ibn ʿĀzib, and at-Tirmidhī from Ibn ʿAbbās, that when the Kaʿbah was appointed people grew anxious about Muslims who had prayed towards Bayt al-Maqdis and died before they could pray towards the Kaʿbah. Another explanation: Allah does not thwart your faith as it stood before the abrogation of legal rulings. His purpose is only to abrogate the rulings that govern your faith. He did not nullify your prayers towards Jerusalem, He abrogated the ruling that required them. Allah will not let your faith in Him go to waste, nor your good actions, those prayers included.

**"Surely Allah is Ever Gracious and Most Merciful to humanity"**. Gentle with the believers and merciful in not letting their deeds go to waste. The first word denotes intense mercy, and is placed first for the sake of the rhyme with the preceding verse. He is kind and compassionate with people, does not overburden them, and does not deprive them of the reward of their actions. The Ṣaḥīḥ reports that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ saw a woman among some captives who had been separated from her child. Whenever she found an infant boy among the captives she would clasp him to her chest, searching for her own. When she found him she embraced him and gave him her breast. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ asked his Companions whether they thought this woman would willingly throw her son into the fire. They said no, and he said: by Allah, Allah is more merciful to His servants than this woman is to her son.

### The most moderate of all people

The quality that gives the Ummah of Islam its superiority, according to this verse, is being wasaṭ, variously rendered midmost, moderate, just, intermediary, middle, central or justly balanced. To explain it, commentators have usually used the adjective muʿtadil, moderate or temperate, and the noun iʿtidāl, being equal, both from the root ʿadl, to be equal or to make equal. Why should the superiority of a human group or individual depend on moderation? Begin with a tangible fact. Every system of medicine, old or new, agrees that the health of the body depends on the temperateness of the elements that compose it, and that illness comes from a disturbance of this balance. In the ancient Greek medicine that the Muslims developed further, these elements or humours are four, blood, phlegm, yellow bile and black bile, and they produce four states in the body, heat, cold, wetness and dryness. While the four are properly balanced the body is healthy. As soon as any one of them increases or decreases immoderately the body falls ill, and if the balance is not restored in time it may die. In the ethical and spiritual sphere, likewise, health depends on temperateness and inner equilibrium, and illness arises from intemperance and imbalance which, if allowed to grow, ends in spiritual death. Anyone with eyes to see will also discover for himself where the essence of being human lies. What sets man at the head of all created beings is not the physical states of his body, which he shares with the animals, but something higher and subtler: spiritual perfection. As the great Sufi poet Rūmī put it, manhood does not reside in the flesh, the fat or the skin, but only in seeking to please the Friend. Of those who ignore this essential attribute and let it be destroyed in themselves he said that the people one sees all around are not human. They are not men, they only wear the masks of men.

It follows that only one who has reached ethical and spiritual equilibrium along with physical equilibrium deserves the title al-Insān al-Kāmil, the Universal Man. All the prophets were specially granted this quality, and the Prophet Muḥammad ﷺ received it in its most perfect form, which makes him the Universal Man par excellence. For humanity in general Allah created, on the one hand, a stable and complex system of medicines, instruments and physicians for physical well-being. On the other hand He sent His prophets with divine guidance, equipped also with a measure of physical force, so that they could establish this law of equilibrium and moderation in the world. The Qur'an defines the purpose of sending messengers and Books: "We sent Our messengers with clear proofs, and with them We sent down the Scripture and the balance ˹of justice˺ so that people may administer justice. And We sent down iron with its great might" (57:25). The Book is meant to produce inner equilibrium and temperateness in people, and the Balance to produce equilibrium in their social conduct and economic dealings. The Balance may also stand for the Sharīʿah of each prophet, which defines what equilibrium really means as it applies to the various spheres of human life, and which serves to set up justice in the world.

The verse under discussion characterises the Ummah of Islam as wasaṭ, and the Qur'an says elsewhere, "And among those We created is a group that guides with the truth and establishes justice accordingly" (7:181). The Ummah displays its spiritual equilibrium in three ways. It abandons the pursuit of personal desires and interests so as to follow divine guidance. It tries to bring others to do the same. And it settles every kind of dispute in the light of divine law, without being swayed by the vested interests of any person or group. Another verse is more specific still: "You are the best community ever raised for humanity—you encourage good, forbid evil, and believe in Allah" (3:110). It is the best Ummah because it was given a unique Prophet ﷺ who taught it to respect all the other prophets, and a Book which is the most comprehensive and perfect of the divine Books. The Ummah itself is endowed with temperateness and balance to a degree no other enjoys. It was destined to receive the subtlest modes of knowledge, and to outshine others in every form of faith and practice, most of all in fearing Allah. Its field of action is not limited to one country or race. It extends across the world and into every sphere of human existence. "Raised for humanity" indicates that the very purpose of its existence is to work for people's good and help them find the way to salvation and Paradise. Its function, its very insignia as an Ummah, is to guide people towards good deeds and turn them from evil ones. A hadith sums up this role: religion is to have the good of others at heart, especially one's fellow Muslims. The good deeds it guides others towards are those the Sharīʿah defines as good. The evil it turns them from includes kufr (disbelief), shirk (associating partners with Allah), bidʿah (innovation in religion), sins of every kind, illegitimate customs, transgression of divine commands and immoral or indecent acts. Dissuading people from evil may take different forms, sometimes requiring the tongue, sometimes the hand, sometimes the pen and sometimes the sword, so that it includes every form of jihad. In the breadth and depth of this quality no other Ummah compares with the Ummah of Islam.

### Moderation seen in practice

How far do the facts bear out this moderation? A full comparison of the beliefs and practices of all the communities is not possible here, but a few examples will establish the point.

Take doctrine first. Among the earlier communities, some took their prophets to be sons of Allah and worshipped them: "The Jews say, “Ezra is the son of Allah,” while the Christians say, “The Messiah is the son of Allah.”" (9:30). Others, having recognised and acknowledged their prophet on the strength of his repeated miracles, refused to obey him when he called them to a holy war and told him bluntly, "So go—both you and your Lord—and fight; we are staying right here!" (5:24). There was even the spectacle of prophets tortured by their own followers. The Ummah of Islam, by contrast, loves the Prophet ﷺ so deeply that Muslims in every period of their history have counted it the greatest blessing to give up their lives at his call, and even those of their wives and children. Yet it has never crossed the limit. It has placed him in the station of a prophet, not the station of Allah. Though it knows him to be the most perfect of the prophets, it has gone on calling him "the servant of Allah and His messenger". The doctrinal position, as the famous Arabic poem the Qaṣīdah al-Burdah puts it, is that short of attributing "the sonship of Allah" to him, which the Christians do with Christ and which is disbelief, whatever one says in his praise will be correct. A Persian poet addressed him in a single line: in short, after God, you are the greatest.

Turn from doctrine to worship and rites, and the same excesses appear among the earlier communities. On one side their religious scholars misinterpreted or altered the injunctions of their Sharīʿah, going so far as to distort the Sacred Books for a handful of silver, and devised every kind of ruse to escape the rites Allah had ordained. On the other side people renounced the world altogether and shut themselves in monastic cells. They refused their share of the blessings of the physical world, which Allah had not only given to man but permitted him to enjoy. They believed that imposing hardship on oneself carried the highest merit and was worship par excellence. The history of the Ummah of Islam presents a wholly different picture. It never made monasticism the highest form of religious life, something Islam in fact forbids. At the same time, through its readiness to sacrifice property and life, children and all, for the commands of Allah and His Prophet ﷺ, it established its sway, politically too, over a considerable part of the world. It has demonstrated in practice, as no other community has, that religion is meant to be lived in the marketplace and the halls of power as much as in the mosque and the contemplative retreat. It is this Ummah that showed the world how those poor in spirit can walk about in kings' robes, and how kings in spirit can hide in beggars' garb, because king and beggar alike know that the greatest dignity lies in being Allah's servant.

In human and social relations too, the earlier communities fell into excess one way or another. On one side there was indifference to human rights, above all an utter disregard of the rights of women, and a general pursuit of individual interests and desires regardless of right and wrong. On the other side there was an exaggerated sentimentality that forbade eating animal flesh although Allah had made it lawful, and frowned on killing an insect even by accident. It was the Ummah of Islam and its Sharīʿah that established equilibrium and a just order in human relations. It laid down a clear code of human rights, extended them to women, and prescribed that enemies too, not only in peace but on the battlefield itself, enjoy certain inalienable rights. It demarcated every right and every duty and counted every falling short of the prescribed mark, and every overstepping of it, as a crime. It also taught that one should try to fulfil all one's obligations to others, but that when one's own rights suffer one should show patience and forgiveness.

In the economic sphere the other communities have likewise been prey to excesses. In our own age there is, on one side, the capitalist system, which ignores the distinction between lawful and unlawful, is blind to the welfare of the people and treats the piling up of wealth as the highest virtue. On the other side stand economic systems with no respect for personal property. In reality these two hostile systems share one essence: worldly things pursued as the whole purpose of human life. The Sharīʿah of Islam brings the conflicting elements into balance and gives each its proper place. It does not let the piling up of wealth become the final aim of human effort, nor does it make human dignity depend on money, rank or office. At the same time it lays down principles for distributing wealth in a balanced way, so that no member of society is deprived of the basic necessities of life and no individual or group appropriates all the available wealth. Things that all members of a society can share have been placed under public or joint control, while the right to private property is fully respected in certain specific things. It drew a clear line between ḥalāl (lawful) and ḥarām (unlawful) possessions, insisted on the spiritual merit of lawful possessions and laid down the rules for using them.

### Standing between Allah and the people

The prophets acted as intermediaries, receiving guidance from Allah and conveying it to the people. That process went on for thousands of years until the Prophet Muḥammad ﷺ, with whom prophethood ended. But even after prophethood ended, the conveying of Allah's message to people had to continue, and still does. Generation after generation, countless people are born, and before they die someone must tell them about the reality of life and about the divine commandments. After the Prophet's ﷺ death this duty fell to the Muslims. With the end of prophethood the whole Muslim community stands between Allah and the people, in the position the prophets once held. This is no reward for superiority but a massive responsibility, which means all the Muslims' social and communal planning must necessarily be oriented to daʿwah, the call. Muslims should be most eager to carry out this mission, make it their principal goal and be ready to sacrifice everything for it. The change of qiblah was a sign that Allah had removed the Children of Israel from spiritual leadership and appointed the followers of Muḥammad ﷺ in their place. From then until the end of time the Kaʿbah is to remain the rallying point for the call of the divine religion and a centre for all true believers in Allah, with the Muslims acting as a "middle nation", intermediaries between Allah and humanity. It is for them to communicate the word of Allah to their fellow human beings, as the Prophet ﷺ did in his time, a duty incumbent on the Muslim community for ever. Their success in this world and in the Hereafter depends on how effectively they discharge it.

### Witnesses, trustworthiness and consensus

Several rulings follow from the verse. First, Allah has made the Ummah equitable and just, and hence trustworthy, "so that" it may qualify to bear witness. From this the jurists infer that a person who is not ʿādil, trustworthy as the Sharīʿah defines the term, is not acceptable as a witness in court.

Second, according to al-Qurṭubī this verse establishes ijmāʿ, the consensus of the Ummah, as one of the four deciding authorities in legislation. Since Allah Himself has accepted this Ummah as a trustworthy witness over the other communities, the consensus of the Ummah is decisive in legal matters and acting on it is wājib (obligatory). So the consensus of the Companions must be accepted by their successors, and that of the successors by the generation after them. Al-Tafsīr al-Maẓharī draws from the verse the principle that whatever deeds and practices of this Ummah have been approved by consensus are all commendable, because if a consensus on error were possible the Ummah could not be called moderate and just. Al-Jaṣṣāṣ adds that the reliability of consensus is not confined to the age of the Prophet ﷺ or the Companions. The consensus of the Muslims in any age whatever is equally trustworthy, because the verse addresses the whole Ummah, which includes not only the Prophet's ﷺ contemporaries but every succeeding generation of Muslims until the Day of Judgement. Muslims living in any age therefore qualify as Allah's witnesses, whose agreement on a point becomes decisive in legislation, and who cannot reach a consensus on anything that would be an error or a deviation. It should not be forgotten, however, that consensus in this context does not mean a sort of referendum by adult franchise. It means the agreement of the majority of those scholars who fulfil the conditions for pronouncing judgement in matters of the Sharīʿah, those who possess the authority of ijtihād. Once such a consensus is reached, the bulk of the Ummah naturally accepts it and holds to it.

### Which qiblah came first?

The Companions and their Successors differed over whether it was the House of Allah at Makkah or Bayt al-Maqdis at Jerusalem that was appointed as the qiblah when the five daily prayers became obligatory in Makkah, before the Hijrah. According to ʿAbdullāh ibn ʿAbbās the first qiblah was Bayt al-Maqdis, and it remained so for some sixteen or seventeen months after the Hijrah, and only then did Allah command that the House of Allah be taken as the qiblah. The Prophet's ﷺ practice in Makkah, on this view, was to pray between al-Ḥajar al-Aswad (the Black Stone) and al-Rukn al-Yamānī (the Yemeni corner), so that his face was turned towards the House of Allah and Bayt al-Maqdis at the same time. That was no longer possible after the migration to Madinah, hence his keen desire that the House of Allah be made the new qiblah. Other Companions hold that when the five prayers were made obligatory in Makkah, the House of Allah served as the qiblah of the Muslims, as it had for Ibrāhīm and Ismāʿīl (Ishmael). The Prophet ﷺ kept this qiblah as long as he stayed in Makkah. After the Hijrah Allah ordained a change, and Bayt al-Maqdis became the qiblah for sixteen or seventeen months. Then a new command came and the House of Allah was restored as the qiblah. Al-Qurṭubī, relying on Abū ʿAmr, prefers this second view.

On the second view the reason for the changes is this. On coming to Madinah the Prophet ﷺ had to deal with the Jews, and to familiarise them with Islam he adopted their qiblah under divine command. Little by little it became clear that so stubborn a people would not easily give up their hostility, so Allah allowed him to return to the original qiblah, which as the qiblah of his forefathers Ibrāhīm and Ismāʿīl was naturally dearer to him. In fact the mosque of Ṣāliḥ was oriented towards the House of Allah, as an incident al-Qurṭubī reports from Abū al-ʿĀliyah al-Riyāḥī shows. He once debated with a Jew over the orientation adopted by Mūsā (Moses). The Jew insisted that Mūsā prayed towards the Ṣakhrah, the Rock in the sanctuary at Jerusalem, while Abū al-ʿĀliyah maintained that he stood near the Rock with his face turned towards the House of Allah. He finally suggested settling the dispute by looking at the mosque of Ṣāliḥ, on a hill below Bayt al-Maqdis, and when they visited it they found it oriented towards the House of Allah. Those who prefer the first view explain the matter differently. In Makkah it was necessary to distinguish the Muslims from the idol-worshippers and to stress the difference. So Bayt al-Maqdis was appointed the Muslims' qiblah instead of the House of Allah, which was then the qiblah of the mushrikīn. After the Hijrah a new need arose in Madinah, to highlight the distinction between the Muslims and the Jews, so the Jews' qiblah was given up and the House of Allah adopted.

Because of this difference, "your former direction of prayer" has been read in two ways. On the first view it can only be Bayt al-Maqdis, the first and earlier qiblah. On the second it can also be the Kaʿbah, the earliest and first qiblah. The real import is the same either way. The command changing the orientation was a test of the faith of those who claimed to follow the Prophet ﷺ. It openly demonstrated the difference between those who genuinely obey Allah and His Messenger ﷺ and those who follow their own opinion.

### Rulings drawn from the change

First, the verse shows that an injunction based on the Sunnah is sometimes abrogated by the Qur'an. As al-Jaṣṣāṣ points out in his Aḥkām al-Qur'ān, the Qur'an nowhere states that the Prophet ﷺ was ever commanded, before the Hijrah or after it, to face Bayt al-Maqdis. The evidence is found only in the hadith and the Sunnah. A practice established by the Sunnah was thus abrogated by this verse of the Qur'an appointing the House of Allah as the qiblah.

Second, the verse shows that the hadith of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ cannot, in a certain respect, be separated from the Qur'an, and that the Qur'an recognises the legitimacy of injunctions that find no mention in it but rest on hadith alone. For the verse states plainly at its end that the prayers offered towards Bayt al-Maqdis, as the Prophet ﷺ had commanded, are wholly valid and accepted by Allah.

Third, the verse helps to resolve a delicate question of jurisprudence about the khabar al-wāḥid, a hadith reported by only one or two persons. Can such a hadith abrogate an injunction laid down in the Qur'an or otherwise definitely established? The Ḥanafī school holds that it cannot, while the reports about this verse suggest that it can, provided strong indications establish the hadith's authenticity. Al-Bukhārī, Muslim and nearly all the authentic collections report from several Companions that when the command changing the qiblah came down, the Prophet ﷺ prayed ʿAṣr, or according to other reports Ẓuhr, facing the House of Allah. Some Companions leaving the mosque passed the mosque of the Banū Salamah and found them praying towards Bayt al-Maqdis. They called out that the qiblah had changed and that they had just prayed with the Prophet ﷺ facing the House of Allah. On hearing this, those people changed their orientation at once, in the middle of the prayer. Nuwaylah bint Muslim relates that the women in the back row came forward, so that after the turn the men were again in front and the women behind. The Banū Salamah thus adopted the new qiblah the same day, while the news reached Qubāʾ the next day during Fajr, as al-Bukhārī and Muslim report from Ibn ʿUmar, and the people of Qubāʾ too turned towards the House of Allah during their prayer. From these reports al-Jaṣṣāṣ draws a conclusion. Although this hadith is essentially a solitary report, its general acceptance and the strong indications of its authenticity have raised it to the status of a hadith related by many trustworthy reporters in unbroken succession, which always yields certainty. The Ḥanafī jurists agree. They then face a further question: the hadith gained general acceptance only much later, so how could the news conveyed to the Banū Salamah suffice at the time? Al-Jaṣṣāṣ answers that not only they but all the Companions already knew that the Prophet ﷺ wished the House of Allah to be made the qiblah and had been praying for it. They had come to regard it as quite probable that the command to keep Bayt al-Maqdis would not remain in force. This probability had made the continuation of Bayt al-Maqdis as the qiblah somewhat uncertain rather than definite, and in view of that uncertainty a solitary report was enough to abrogate the earlier command. Otherwise a solitary report cannot justifiably abrogate a definite and final injunction of the Qur'an.

Fourth, the verse helps settle a controversy about the imām using a microphone in leading ṣalāh. Is it legitimate for the congregation to follow his call in their movements, and if they hear nothing but the sound from the loudspeaker, are their prayers invalid? Al-Bukhārī's hadith from ʿAbdullāh ibn ʿUmar tells how the people of Qubāʾ turned towards the House of Allah in the course of their prayer as soon as they heard of the change. Commenting on it, the great Ḥanafī scholar al-ʿAynī says that this hadith establishes a rule: a person who is not praying may teach or instruct a person engaged in prayer. Elsewhere in his ʿUmdat al-Qārī he adds that al-Ṭaḥṭāwī derived a further rule from it. If someone engaged in prayer hears words spoken by someone not praying, his prayer is not invalidated. Ḥanafī jurists generally do hold that if a person at prayer obeys the call of someone outside the prayer, his prayer becomes invalid. What they mean is that obeying someone other than Allah during ṣalāh invalidates it. If one is in fact obeying a divine command and the other person is merely the means of conveying it, the prayer is not invalidated at all. An example makes this clear. If a man joining the congregation finds no room in the first row and would stand alone in the second, the jurists say he should pull someone back from the first row to join him. On the face of it the man who lets himself be pulled back is obeying someone other than Allah during prayer, which ought to invalidate it, but it does not. The most authoritative Ḥanafī text, al-Durr al-Mukhtār, rules that his prayer is perfectly valid, and al-Ṭaḥṭāwī explains why: he has not really obeyed the newcomer but followed a divine command conveyed to him by the Prophet ﷺ. There are, then, two ways in which a person at prayer may answer the call of someone outside it. He may wish to please that person and obey him, in which case the prayer becomes invalid. Or he may obey a command of the Sharīʿah which the other person conveys to him, in which case he is essentially obeying a divine command and his prayer remains valid. This resolves the microphone question. Technical experts hold that the sound from a loudspeaker is exactly the sound the imām produces, and if so there is no question of invalidity. Suppose, though, that the transmitted sound were not the imām's own voice but an imitation of it, or a report of what he said. Even then it would be wrong to suspect the worshippers of obeying the microphone. They are plainly obeying the Prophet's ﷺ command to follow the imām's movements. The microphone merely informs them that the imām has bowed or prostrated, and in acting on that information they obey the imām, not the instrument, and it is a divine command that requires following the imām in congregational prayer.

### The chosen of the chosen

In the devotional reading, it is the wise Lord and knowing King whose power brings beings into existence. The created things exist through His exaltedness and through His making them manifest, and the earth and heavens stand by His keeping. He created the newly arrived things and chose the animals from among them. From the animals He chose the children of Ādam (Adam), from them the faithful, from the faithful the prophets, and from the prophets Muḥammad ﷺ. And he chose his community above those before it. This is why Muṣṭafā ﷺ said that he had been brought forth from the best generation of Ādam's children, one generation after another, until he came to be in his own. He also said that Allah chose his Companions above all the world's people except the prophets and envoys, and from his Companions chose four and made them the best, though there is good in all of them: Abū Bakr, ʿUmar, ʿUthmān and ʿAlī. He chose his community over the other communities and sent him forth in the best generation, after which come the second and the third in succession, then the fourth, one after another. From this report it is understood that Muṣṭafā ﷺ is the best of the children of Ādam and the chosen from among the world's people. He is the leader of creatures and adornment of the world, the weighty one of the age, the earth's lamp and heaven's full moon. He is the shelter of the disobedient and intercessor for sinners, the master and seal of the messengers. After him the best of creatures is Abū Bakr, the sincerely truthful, whose cushion of imamate the Lord of the Worlds set on the throne of Muṣṭafā's ﷺ Sharīʿah. He made self-purification and truthfulness the lodging of his servanthood, and set trust and certainty to guard the rank of his friendship. Next in excellence is ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb, in whose capable hand the Lord of the Worlds placed the reins for lowering and raising the legal rulings, drawing the robe of his rulership over the creed's forehead. Through his sternness and awe the smoke of associationism was subdued by its own misfortune.

### In short

- As Allah gave the Muslims the best qiblah, He made them the wasaṭ, the just and best nation, witnesses on the Day of Judgement that every prophet delivered his message, with the Prophet ﷺ confirming their testimony (22:78). The hadiths of Nūḥ, of the prophet with two followers, and of ʿUmar's "wajabat" illustrate this.
- The first qiblah was a test that separated those who follow the Messenger ﷺ from those who turn back. It was heavy except for the guided, whose faith grows where the sick at heart find doubt (9:124-125, 17:82).
- No prayer offered towards Jerusalem was lost, for Allah is more merciful to His servants than a mother to her child.
- Wasaṭ means moderation and balance, the health of body and soul alike. The Ummah was raised to guide humanity (57:25, 7:181, 3:110), and in doctrine, worship, social relations and economics it holds the middle between the extremes into which earlier communities fell (9:30, 5:24).
- With prophethood ended, the Ummah stands between Allah and people as bearer of the call. The verse grounds the rule that only the trustworthy may testify and the authority of the Ummah's consensus.
- Scholars differ over whether the Kaʿbah or Jerusalem was the first qiblah. The change shows that the Qur'an can abrogate the Sunnah, that rulings based on hadith alone are valid, that an accepted solitary report may abrogate in conditions of uncertainty, and that a worshipper may act on information from outside the prayer, which settles the microphone question.

144.text:
Verse 144 is the command itself, the moment the qiblah changed. "Indeed, We see you ˹O Prophet˺ turning your face towards heaven. Now We will make you turn towards a direction ˹of prayer˺ that will please you. So turn your face towards the Sacred Mosque ˹in Mecca˺—wherever you are, turn your faces towards it. Those who were given the Scripture certainly know this to be the truth from their Lord. And Allah is never unaware of what they do". It opens by describing how much the Prophet ﷺ wanted the Kaʿbah as the qiblah of the Muslims, and then grants the wish in the same breath.

### Phrase by phrase

**"Indeed, We see you ˹O Prophet˺ turning your face towards heaven."**. The Arabic opens with a particle of affirmation: We have indeed seen you. The Prophet ﷺ kept looking up at the sky, searching for revelation and longing for the command to face the Kaʿbah, waiting for Jibrīl (Gabriel) to come down and announce the change. Ibn ʿAbbās, in the report of ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭalḥah, said that the first thing abrogated in the Qur'an concerned the qiblah. When the Messenger of Allah ﷺ migrated to Madinah, the Jews were the majority there, and Allah commanded him to face Bayt al-Maqdis (Jerusalem). This delighted the Jews. He faced it for ten months and more, but he loved the qiblah of Ibrāhīm (Abraham), and he would supplicate to Allah and look up to the sky, until this verse was revealed. The Jews disliked the ruling and asked what had turned the Muslims from their former qiblah (2:142). Allah had already said that east and west belong to Him (2:115), and He explained that the first qiblah had been a test (2:143).

His inclination has been explained in several ways, and the explanations do not conflict. Before prophethood he already followed, by the prompting of his own nature, the way of Ibrāhīm, and once revelation began the Qur'an itself described his Sharīʿah as fully in accord with the Abrahamic way. The qiblah of Ibrāhīm and of Ismāʿīl (Ishmael) had been the Kaʿbah, so it was natural for him to want it as the qiblah of the Muslims. A further factor was that the Arab tribes, idolaters though they were, at least claimed to follow the way of Ibrāhīm and acknowledged the Kaʿbah as their qiblah, in contrast to the Jews. Once the Kaʿbah became the Muslims' qiblah, the Arabs could be expected to find Islam more acceptable. The hope that adopting Bayt al-Maqdis would draw the Jews closer to Islam had meanwhile been dashed by the events of the preceding sixteen or seventeen months, for their hostility, fed by vanity, had only grown. Whatever the motive, the Prophet ﷺ was very keen on the change. Prophets stand as close to Allah as a human being can, and that station teaches them a strict spiritual etiquette: they never put a request before Allah until they have been given leave to do so. This suggests that he had already been permitted to pray for his wish and hoped the prayer would be granted. So he turned his face again and again to the sky, anxiously awaiting the angel who would bring the ruling he longed for. Allah describes this state of His Prophet ﷺ with appreciation.

**"Now We will make you turn towards a direction ˹of prayer˺ that will please you."**. A qiblah that you will love, the qiblah of Ibrāhīm, the Sacred House of Allah instead of the direction you now face. The promise is given and then immediately fulfilled by the command that follows. Here is a subtle working of divine grace: the Prophet ﷺ was first granted the joy of hearing a promise made, and straight after it the greater joy of seeing the promise kept, as al-Qurṭubī, al-Jaṣṣāṣ and al-Maẓharī note.

**"So turn your face towards the Sacred Mosque ˹in Mecca˺"**. Face the Kaʿbah when you pray. Al-Ḥākim related from ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib that the phrase means its direction, and he judged the chain authentic though al-Bukhārī and Muslim did not include it. Abū al-ʿĀliyah and Mujāhid hold this view, as do ʿIkrimah and Saʿīd ibn Jubayr. Qatādah, al-Rabīʿ ibn Anas and others also give it.

**"wherever you are, turn your faces towards it."**. This addresses the whole Muslim community: wherever you are, on land or at sea, east, west, north or south, face the Kaʿbah in your prayers. There are exceptions. A voluntary prayer (nafl) offered while travelling may be prayed in whatever direction one's body is facing, with the heart intending the Kaʿbah. When battle is raging, one prays however one can. And a person unsure of the direction who prays the wrong way, believing it to be the qiblah, is excused, for Allah does not burden a soul beyond its capacity.

**"Those who were given the Scripture certainly know this to be the truth from their Lord."**. The Jews and Christians know well that the change of direction is the truth from their Lord, because their Scripture describes how the Prophet ﷺ would re-orient himself to the Kaʿbah, and that the Sacred Precinct is the qiblah of Ibrāhīm. They conceal this. The Jews who resented the change from Bayt al-Maqdis already knew that Allah would command him to face the Kaʿbah. They read in their Books their prophets' description of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and his Ummah, and that Allah had honoured him with the complete and noble legislation. Yet the People of the Book deny these facts out of envy, disbelief and rebellion. The prophets who arose among the Jews had been told that Allah would one day alter the qiblah, and they passed that knowledge on, so the Jewish scholars should have expected it. Only a few, such as ʿAbdullāh ibn Salām and Mukhayrīq, confirmed the command and acknowledged that Allah had revealed the truth through the Prophet Muḥammad ﷺ.

**"And Allah is never unaware of what they do"**. He is not heedless of what they conceal. This is a threat. He will reward those who turn from the truth according to their deeds. On another reading the verb is "what you do", addressed to the believers when they obey His command.

### Why "the Sacred Mosque" and not "the Kaʿbah"

Allah is not confined to any direction (2:115). To create a visible unity among Muslims scattered across the world, Divine Wisdom assigned them one definite orientation, and Bayt al-Maqdis could have served that purpose as well as any other place. The Kaʿbah was chosen in accordance with the Prophet's ﷺ wish, and the ruling announced here. One would have expected the words "turn your face towards the Kaʿbah" or "towards the House of Allah". Instead the Qur'an says "towards the Sacred Mosque", al-Masjid al-Ḥarām, and this choice of words settles several important questions.

Strictly speaking the qiblah is the House of Allah, the Kaʿbah. But one can face it exactly only while one can see it. For people at a distance, facing it exactly would be an impossibly rigorous obligation, since in distant towns an exact bearing is hard and uncertain even with instruments and calculation. The Sharīʿah always aims at ease. So the Qur'an names as the qiblah not the Kaʿbah but the Sacred Mosque, which covers a far wider area and is easy to face even from far away. A further facility lies in the word shaṭr. It means "the half of a thing" or "the direction in which a thing lies", and there is agreement that the second sense is meant here. The word itself therefore establishes that for places far from Makkah it is not even necessary, for the prayer to be valid, to face the Sacred Mosque exactly. Facing in its direction is enough, as al-Baḥr al-Muḥīṭ explains.

An example makes the rule clear. For countries east of Makkah, such as Pakistan and India, the direction of the Sacred Mosque is the west, and anyone who faces west has prayed validly. Because the sun sets at one point in summer and another in winter, the jurists have ruled that in such countries, for ṣalāh, the west, which is the qiblah direction, lies between those two points. In mathematical terms an arc of 48 degrees between them counts as the direction of the qiblah. Even someone who inclines 24 degrees to the right or left of the actual bearing of the Sacred Mosque is still facing the right way and his prayer is valid, as the commentary on al-Chaghmīnī sets out in detail.

This should expose the ignorance and muddle of those who, on finding some mosques in Pakistan and India two or three degrees off true, have declared the prayers offered in them null and void. Such baseless opinions only betray a wish to sow confusion and bickering among Muslims. The Sharīʿah is for all people and all countries until the Day of Judgement, so its injunctions in every sphere of life have been made easy to practise. Muslims in remote hamlets, mountains, forests or islands must be able to act on them from their own observation and experience, without scientific instruments or mathematical calculation. People east of Makkah may therefore take an arc of 48 degrees as their qiblah, and a deviation of five or ten degrees does not affect the validity of their prayers at all. A hadith al-Tirmidhī reports from Abū Hurayrah makes this plain: "The qiblah lies between the east and the west." It was addressed to the people of Madinah, whose exact qiblah is to the south, somewhere between east and west, but in effect it explains the phrase "towards the Sacred Mosque".

That is the general principle. Still, when laying the foundations of a mosque one should try to make the orientation towards the House of Allah as exact as possible. The Successors of the Companions, and the generations after them, used a simple method. If a town had a mosque built by the Companions, the neighbouring mosques were given the same orientation, and these in turn served as models for the mosques of the surrounding villages and towns, in a chain that kept extending itself. The method for fixing the qiblah far from Makkah has therefore always been this: if an old mosque stands nearby, new mosques should follow its orientation, because in so many towns it was the Companions themselves or their Successors who built the mosques and fixed the direction that later generations followed. The mosques already built are sufficient to determine the orientation, and it is improper to raise needless objections and doubts. The Sharīʿah disapproves of attempts to throw Muslims into perplexity, because such perplexity can lead people to suspect that since the Companions, their Successors and Muslims in general failed to fix a mathematically exact bearing, their prayers were invalid. That thought is not only false but insolent.

For this reason Ibn Rajab, the famous Ḥanbalī scholar of the eighth century after the Hijrah, disapproved of using astronomical instruments and complex calculations to fix the orientation. He wrote that the scholars in general permit learning astronomy insofar as it helps in determining the qiblah or in finding one's way on a journey and the directions of roads. More knowledge than that is not necessary under the Sharīʿah, since it may lead a person to neglect more important matters, and indulgence in complex calculation sometimes breeds vile doubts about the mosques of the Muslims in their towns, a weakness especially common among amateurs of such sciences. It may even lead a person to think that the prayers of the Companions and their Successors in certain towns were invalid, which is wholly false. For this reason, he added, Aḥmad ibn Ḥanbal forbade reliance on the Pole Star in fixing the orientation, since the hadith states only that the qiblah is between east and west.

As for deserted regions, forests, new settlements and the like, where no earlier mosque exists, the Sharīʿah lays down a rule based on the practice of the Companions and their Successors. One should make an approximate determination of the qiblah by the sun, the moon and the Pole Star, phenomena everyone knows well enough, and if one still suspects a slight deviation, ignore it. According to al-Badāʾiʿ, the authoritative work of jurisprudence, in places far from Makkah an approximately correct orientation chosen on such general indications stands in place of the Kaʿbah, and every ruling about the qiblah applies to the direction so chosen. The Sharīʿah offers many illustrations of the principle at work. Sleep is taken to stand for the passing of wind and so invalidates wuḍūʾ (ablution). A journey is taken to represent hardship even when it involves none, and anyone on any kind of journey receives all the concessions the Sharīʿah grants a traveller. The same principle requires that an orientation fixed by general and familiar indications be accepted as the qiblah. The scholar known as Baḥr al-ʿUlūm states the rule in his Rasāʾil al-Arkān: the only condition for facing the qiblah is that the person praying be duly convinced that his face is turned towards the Kaʿbah. The Sharīʿah does not compel us to adopt the exact bearing obtainable only with astronomical instruments, so the scholars in general conclude that a deviation invalidates the prayer only when it is as great as the difference between east and west.

### The courtesy of not asking

In the devotional reading, Allah had let His Prophet ﷺ know that the Real's eye was on him, so that his courtesy would be modelled on the Real's own. Practising that courtesy, he did not ask the Real for his heart's desire. He only gazed at heaven. Then He gave him more than He gives those who do ask. A generous Lord with an exalted servant keeps that servant within courtesy's bounds, shows him the road of deeds and grants him success, then rewards him for the deeds and praises him for his reverence: "How excellent is the reward for those who work ˹righteousness˺" (3:136), and of Sulaymān (Solomon), "what an excellent servant ˹he was˺!"
