(38:30). So He told Muṣṭafā ﷺ: you are in My vision and My exalted witnessing, so take care to recognise what respect the Presence is owed, and let your asking keep within courtesy. When his heart was set on the qiblah he did not show it, out of courtesy. He kept the wish in his heart, and then the Exalted Presence addressed him: We have come to know the wish in your heart and have admired your beautiful courtesy in not asking. We will bestow on you what you approve in the matter of the qiblah. O Muḥammad, all the servants in the world seek My approval, but I seek yours. Everyone searches for Me, but I call for you. Everyone wishes for My caresses, but it is you We caress: "your Lord will give so much to you that you will be pleased" (93:5). Now take the Kaʿbah as the qiblah of your soul and Me as the qiblah of your spirit. When those caresses came from the Presence of Unity, the tongue of his state said in its yearning that when the Beloved's heart reaches out once in love, the suffering of separation becomes easy to bear. Abū Bakr al-Shiblī said that the qiblahs are three: the qiblah of the common people, the qiblah of the elect, and the qiblah of the elect of the elect.

### In short

- The Prophet ﷺ longed for the qiblah of Ibrāhīm and kept looking to the sky without asking. Allah praised that longing, promised a qiblah he would love, and granted it in the same verse (2:142, 2:115, 2:143).
- Wherever Muslims are, they face the Kaʿbah, with exceptions for voluntary prayer on a journey, for battle, and for honest error.
- The People of the Book knew from their own Scripture that this change would come, and most denied it out of envy, though a few like ʿAbdullāh ibn Salām accepted it.
- Saying "the Sacred Mosque" and "its direction" rather than "the Kaʿbah" makes the obligation easy: distant worshippers face the general direction, an arc of about 48 degrees suffices, old mosques set the bearing for new ones, and instruments are not required.
- Inwardly, the Prophet's ﷺ courtesy in not asking won him more than asking could (3:136, 38:30, 93:5).

145.text:
Verse 145 closes the door on any hope that the People of the Book would come round over the qiblah. "Even if you were to bring every proof to the People of the Book, they would not accept your direction ˹of prayer˺, nor would you accept theirs; nor would any of them accept the direction ˹of prayer˺ of another. And if you were to follow their desires after ˹all˺ the knowledge that has come to you, then you would certainly be one of the wrongdoers". Continuing the subject of the divinely ordained orientation, the verse gives yet another instance of their malice.

### Phrase by phrase

**"Even if you were to bring every proof to the People of the Book, they would not accept your direction ˹of prayer˺"**. The Arabic carries the force of an oath: by Allah, even if you brought the Jews and Christians every sign and proof that the change of direction is true, every sign they asked of you, they would not face your qiblah or embrace your religion. Allah describes their disbelief, stubbornness and defiance of what they know to be true about His Messenger ﷺ. Were he to bring forward every proof of what he was sent with, they would never obey him or give up following their desires, as Allah says elsewhere: "Indeed, those against whom Allah’s decree ˹of torment˺ is justified will not believe—even if every sign were to come to them—until they see the painful punishment" (10:96-97). It is not that they demand solid and convincing arguments before accepting the new ruling. Sheer stubbornness keeps them from assenting, and no proof in the world will ever satisfy them. Those who give free rein to their desires never follow the path of reason. In their perversity they seek from denying Allah's signs the kind of satisfaction He wished them to draw from accepting them. Their refusal came from being used to behaving as they pleased, and from romantic notions about the special position of their own people, which they had made the bedrock of their life and creed.

**"nor would you accept theirs"**. You will not face their qiblah after Allah has turned you from it. This is a categorical negation both of the Prophet's ﷺ hope that they would become Muslims and of their hope that he would return to their direction. It shows the vigour with which the Messenger of Allah ﷺ carried out what Allah commanded. As firmly as the Jews cling to their opinions and desires, so firmly does the Prophet ﷺ cling to Allah's commands, obeying Him and following what pleases Him, and he would never adopt their desires under any circumstances. Praying towards Bayt al-Maqdis (Jerusalem) had therefore never been because it was the Jews' qiblah, but because Allah had commanded it. The Prophet ﷺ never departed from the pattern of earlier prophets until he received revelation on the matter. True to that principle, he first made Jerusalem his qiblah, since the prophets from the time of Sulaymān (Solomon) had prayed towards it. Islam's coming was the signal that the Jews were being removed from their post as torch-bearers of the true faith, and the faith itself had to be set apart from Jewish tradition so that it could emerge in a new and unmistakably pure form. That is why he eagerly awaited the instruction to change, which came in the second year after the Hijrah. The phrase also declares that the House of Allah will remain the qiblah until the end of the world. The new qiblah was instituted by divine command and will never be abrogated, which refutes the scoffing allegation that Islamic rulings had no stability and that the Muslims might go back to Bayt al-Maqdis, as al-Baḥr al-Muḥīṭ observes.

**"nor would any of them accept the direction ˹of prayer˺ of another."**. The Jews and the Christians do not follow one another's qiblah either. The Jews took Bayt al-Maqdis, the Christians the east, and each rejects the other's choice. Each group calls the other disbelievers, and each follows its own desires in the matter of the qiblah as in other sacred laws and rulings. The two groups show the same malice towards each other that they show towards the Muslims. Since the Prophet ﷺ can accept neither orientation, there is no prospect of agreement between the People of the Book and the Muslims on this point.

**"And if you were to follow their desires after ˹all˺ the knowledge that has come to you, then you would certainly be one of the wrongdoers"**. If, after being warned, you prayed towards their qiblah, following the whims they call you to, after the revelation that has come to you and the knowledge that the Sacred Precinct is the qiblah of Ibrāhīm (Abraham), then, hypothetically, you would be among the evildoers who harm themselves. Allah warns those who defy the truth knowingly, since the case against a person who knows is stronger than against anyone else. Bayt al-Maqdis had indeed once been instituted by divine command, but that command is now abrogated. Whoever follows an abrogated ruling and ignores the new one that replaced it is disobeying Allah and acting on his own opinion and desire. For the Prophet ﷺ to follow the desires of the People of the Book is naturally impossible. But supposing, purely for argument's sake, that he did so after receiving a definite ruling by revelation, he would be counted among the unjust, those who disobey divine commands. Such a situation can never arise. As a prophet he is sinless and so cannot be among the unjust, and it follows that it is impossible for him to favour their desires and adopt their qiblah as his own. The warning is outwardly addressed to the Prophet ﷺ, whom Allah has protected from ever doing such a thing, but it is really meant for his Ummah, which is being made to realise the gravity of ignoring or disobeying the ruling that has finally fixed the House of Allah as the qiblah of the Muslims.

### A barrier between the two

In the devotional reading, devotion to the path of the Real was already the Prophet's ﷺ by the eternal decree, just as it was decreed that his enemies would fall by the wayside. Between the two sides stands a barrier, a barzakh, like the one between the two seas: "He merges the two bodies of ˹fresh and salt˺ water, yet between them is a barrier that they never cross" (55:19-20). They will not follow his qiblah even if he showed them evidence clearer than suns and moons, and he will not follow theirs whatever stratagems they bring. In that lies a decree from Allah from pre-eternity.

### In short

- No proof would ever bring the People of the Book to accept the new qiblah, for their refusal comes from obstinacy and desire, not lack of evidence (10:96-97).
- The Prophet ﷺ will never return to their direction. His earlier facing of Jerusalem was obedience to Allah, not deference to the Jews, and the Kaʿbah is now the qiblah until the end of time.
- Jews and Christians reject each other's qiblah too, so no agreement is possible.
- Following their desires after revealed knowledge would be wrongdoing. The Prophet ﷺ is protected from it, and the warning is really for his Ummah.
- Inwardly, an unbridgeable barrier was decreed between the two sides (55:19-20).

146.text:
Verses 144 and 145 contrast inward knowledge with public denial. The People of the Book knew that Allah had commanded the Muslims to face His House. Verse 146 shows that their conduct towards the Prophet ﷺ himself was just as dishonest. "Those We have given the Scripture recognize this ˹Prophet˺ as they recognize their own children. Yet a group of them hides the truth knowingly". The Torah and the Injīl (Gospel) had foretold his coming and set down the signs by which people would know him. Their Sacred Books provided decisive evidence about the promised Last Prophet ﷺ. Jews and Christians recognised him from that evidence, yet many stubbornly refused acknowledgment.

### Phrase by phrase

**"Those We have given the Scripture"**. The scholars of the Jews and the Christians, those given knowledge of the Torah. ʿAbd Allāh ibn Salām and his companions are the believing recipients connected with its revelation. They belonged to the People of the Book and knew the Messenger of Allah ﷺ through the description, traits and mission set out in their Scripture.

**"recognize this ˹Prophet˺ as they recognize their own children."**. They know Muḥammad ﷺ by his description and traits as surely as a man knows his own son among other children. The pronoun may also refer to the Kaʿbah at Makkah as the true qiblah. The scholars recognised the truth of the Messenger's ﷺ mission with the same ease as their own children. Arabs use this comparison for something unmistakable. In a hadith, the Messenger of Allah ﷺ asked a man who had a boy with him whether the boy was his son. The man said yes, and testified to it. The Prophet ﷺ remarked that he would not wrong the boy, nor would the boy wrong him. ʿAbd Allāh ibn Salām said that he recognised the Prophet ﷺ the moment he saw him as he would his own son, and that his recognition of Muḥammad ﷺ was the more intense of the two. In al-Qurṭubī's account, ʿUmar asked him whether he knew Muḥammad ﷺ as he knew his own son. He replied: yes, and more, for the Trustworthy One came down from heaven to the Trustworthy One on earth with his description, and by it I recognised him, whereas I know nothing of his mother's story. In another version, ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb asked him how that could be. He answered that he bore witness truly and with certainty that Muḥammad ﷺ is the Messenger of Allah, but could not bear witness with the same certainty that his son was his, since he had no knowledge of what women do. ʿUmar said: may Allah give you success, O son of Salām!

A word on the simile. When a comparison brings two things together it does not involve every aspect of both, only those relevant to the occasion. One should not let the imagination wander into illegitimate cases. The point is simple and obvious: a son grows from infancy to manhood under his parents' eyes, so his face and general appearance are enough for his father to know him without doubt or hesitation. The Jews and the Christians enjoyed the same ease, or even certainty, in recognising the Last Prophet ﷺ. Persisting in denial was therefore as dishonest as a man refusing to recognise his own son.

**"Yet a group of them hides the truth knowingly"**. A party of the People of the Book conceal his description and traits, knowing them to be in their Book, and conceal from people what they find there about him, which is the truth that you, Muḥammad ﷺ, follow. They do it out of envy, fully aware that it is the truth. This was gross dishonesty. Some of them denied the truth themselves and also tried to keep it hidden from others, knowing perfectly well that it had been established by revelation from Allah Himself, including the new ruling on the qiblah.

### Why clear truth is still denied

Whenever Allah reveals a truth to the world it comes supported by clear arguments, so that no one can fail to recognise it as the truth. In this argument, refusing that truth reveals a failure to know Allah. Genuine knowledge of Him would bring recognition of His word. Those who find words to reject the truth imagine they have discovered strong arguments and are standing on firm logical ground. Soon enough they find that those words were imaginary props, devised by themselves to give their egos a false satisfaction. In the devotional reading, their hidden envy breeds haughtiness about what they necessarily know. Whoever has been defeated in the darkness of his lower self throws off the cloak of bashfulness. Censuring him is useless, for words will not rein in his abandon.

### In short

- The scholars of the Jews and Christians knew the Prophet ﷺ from the description in their own Scriptures as surely as a father knows his son among other boys, which is why ʿAbd Allāh ibn Salām said his certainty about the Prophet ﷺ exceeded his certainty about his own son.
- The simile makes one point only: recognition without doubt, so denial was deliberate dishonesty.
- A party of them hid his description, and the truth about the qiblah, out of envy, knowing full well it was true.

147.text:
Verse 147 turns from the deniers to the Prophet ﷺ and his followers. "˹This is˺ the truth from your Lord, so do not ever be one of those who doubt". After exposing concealment by the People of the Book, Allah reassures His Prophet ﷺ and the believers. What the Prophet ﷺ brought is true, beyond doubt.

### Phrase by phrase

**"˹This is˺ the truth from your Lord"**. That you are a Prophet sent by Allah, and that the Kaʿbah at Makkah is the qiblah, is the truth from your Lord. The phrase can also be read in a general sense as a definition of truth itself: only that is truth which comes from Allah. Whoever grasps this can never allow himself to doubt this particular truth, or any other truth Allah has revealed to a prophet.

**"so do not ever be one of those who doubt"**. Do not be among those who waver, who doubt whether they really know. The Arabic says "be not of the doubters". It does not simply say "do not waver": it warns against having that disposition at all. Make absolutely certain, O Messenger, that you are not among those who doubt its truth. The address is to the Prophet ﷺ, but the community is intended by it. In the devotional reading: after the suns of certainty have risen for you, do not give way to the results of mere guessing.

### In short

- What the Prophet ﷺ brought, including the qiblah, is the truth from his Lord, and truth by definition is what comes from Allah.
- The command not to be "of the doubters" forbids even the disposition to waver. It is addressed to the Prophet ﷺ and meant for his Ummah.

148.text:
Religious orientation matters enormously to any community, so verse 148 continues the theme of the qiblah and adds a further reason for the change. "Everyone turns to their own direction ˹of prayer˺. So compete with one another in doing good. Wherever you are, Allah will bring you all together ˹for judgment˺. Surely Allah is Most Capable of everything". The verse introduces the subject with the word wijhah, which literally means the thing one turns one's face towards. Ibn ʿAbbās explained it as the qiblah, and the reading of Ubayy ibn Kaʿb actually has the word qiblah in its place, which removes any ambiguity.

### Phrase by phrase

**"Everyone turns to their own direction ˹of prayer˺."**. Every person of every community has a direction he faces in prayer. The verb is also read in the passive, "he is made to turn to it". Ibn ʿAbbās, in al-ʿAwfī's report, said this speaks of the followers of the various religions: every nation and tribe has a qiblah it has chosen, while the qiblah Allah appointed is the one the believers face. Abū al-ʿĀliyah said that the Jew has a direction he faces and the Christian has a direction he faces, and Allah has guided this Ummah to the true qiblah. Mujāhid, ʿAṭāʾ, aḍ-Ḍaḥḥāk, al-Rabīʿ ibn Anas, as-Suddī and others said the same. Another gloss takes it to mean that every prophet had a qiblah, the Kaʿbah, which he was ordered to face. One reading has each adherent of a religion facing a direction according to his own whim. Nations differ in their directions of prayer as in their sacred laws, and there is nothing wrong in that when it is by Allah's command, just as He says: "To each of you We have ordained a code of law and a way of life. If Allah had willed, He would have made you one community, but His Will is to test you with what He has given ˹each of˺ you. So compete with one another in doing good" (5:48). Every religious community has had its particular orientation. Some directions were appointed by Allah and others chosen by the community. Why then should anyone object, or wonder, that Allah has given the Islamic Ummah a qiblah peculiar to it? It is a distinct religious community in its own right, in fact the last of them all, which makes a distinct qiblah all the more necessary. The People of the Book have no right to object to the Kaʿbah being divinely chosen for the Muslims.

**"So compete with one another in doing good."**. Hasten, O community of Muḥammad ﷺ, to perform acts of obedience, outdoing every other nation and striving in the good deeds you have been commanded. Once the divine command has gone out, the Muslims need not trouble themselves about the objections or ridicule of others. Their concern should be the doing of good deeds as Allah and His Prophet ﷺ define them. They should abandon fruitless controversies and strive to excel in good, since they must appear before Allah on the Day of Judgement to be rewarded or punished for their deeds. The Muslims can be certain of their right to a distinct qiblah. With no expectation that the People of the Book will accept the reasoning, Allah directs them away from futile disputes. The Qur'an discourages unnecessary argument, because it distracts a person from his real task, which is to prepare for death and the next world.

**"Wherever you are, Allah will bring you all together ˹for judgment˺."**. On land or at sea, wherever you may be, He will gather you on the Day of Resurrection and reward you for the good you did. The verse ends with this reminder, suggesting that the wish to be safe from others' criticism, and the anxiety to win arguments, only betray attachment to this passing world. Wisdom lies in caring more for what lasts for ever.

**"Surely Allah is Most Capable of everything"**. He can gather you from the earth even after your bodies and flesh have decayed and scattered. Bringing you all together and rewarding you is not hard for Him.

### Hastening to good deeds, including prayer on time

The command to compete in good also means that one should hurry to do a good deed, whether ṣalāh, ṣawm (fasting), the Hajj or zakāh, as soon as the opportunity arises. The ability to do good is a favour from Allah, and neglecting it is ingratitude and disrespect towards Him. There is reason to fear that putting it off may be punished by the withdrawal of that favour, so that the person loses the ability to do good altogether. May Allah protect us from such a fate. Another verse makes the point explicit: "O believers! Respond to Allah and His Messenger when he calls you to that which gives you life. And know that Allah stands between a person and their heart" (8:24).

Some jurists infer from this expression a preference for praying at the start of each prescribed time, or as early as possible. They cite hadiths in support. Ash-Shāfiʿī shares this view. Abū Ḥanīfah and Mālik hold that certain prayers are better offered somewhat late, as the Prophet ﷺ indicated by word or deed, while the rest should be offered as early as possible within their time. Al-Bukhārī reports from Anas the superior merit of praying ʿIshāʾ rather late in the night, and Abū Hurayrah too reports this preference on the Prophet's ﷺ part, as al-Qurṭubī notes. Al-Bukhārī and al-Tirmidhī report from Abū Dharr that on a journey Bilāl wanted to call the adhān as soon as the time of Ẓuhr began, but the Prophet ﷺ told him to wait until it was cooler, remarking that the heat of midday is part of the fire of Hell. Evidently he preferred Ẓuhr to be offered late in summer. On the basis of such hadiths Abū Ḥanīfah and Mālik concluded that where no instruction to delay exists, as with Maghrib, it is better to pray as soon as the time begins, but where a specific indication exists one should pray somewhat later within the prescribed time. They add that whoever wishes to act on "compete in doing good" even in the latter case can do so only by not delaying once the recommended (mustaḥabb) time has arrived. In short, by the consensus of the jurists verse 148 establishes the principle that when the time of a prescribed prayer has come, one should not delay it without a valid excuse, which may be a clear specification of the Sharīʿah of the kind just described, or a physical disability such as illness.

### Five qiblahs and one Friend

In the devotional reading, created beings have five qiblahs: the Throne, the Footstool, the Inhabited House, the Holy House in Jerusalem, and the Kaʿbah. The Throne is the qiblah of the angels who bear it, the Footstool that of the cherubim, the Inhabited House that of the spiritual beings, the Holy House that of the prophets, and the Kaʿbah that of the faithful. Light makes up the Throne, gold the Footstool, carnelian the Inhabited House, marble the Holy House, and plain stone the Kaʿbah. The allusion for the faithful servant is this: if you cannot reach the Throne to circumambulate it, the Footstool to visit it, the Inhabited House to worship there or the Holy House to serve there, you can at least turn your face five times a day to this stone, the qiblah of the faithful, and receive the reward of all of them. One of the masters said the allusion is that every person has been distracted from Allah by something that came between them, so, O faithful, belong to Me and be through Me. All the people have turned away from Me and grown familiar with others, making their sweetheart someone other than Me. Those claiming friendship on the Path are called to look away from all that is below Allah, including even the highest paradise. This brings straight following of Muṣṭafā ﷺ in Sunnah and conduct, giving that paragon his due through emulation. Greatest among prophets, he turned his gaze from created beings. Unity alone was his refuge and chosen resting place. When a man wears his spirit down on passion's road, he had best incline to none but the Friend, and think of neither hell nor paradise. Whoever sets himself right in following Muṣṭafā ﷺ will find the candle of friendship with the Real lit on his road, and will never fall away from friendship's avenue.

### In short

- Every community has its own direction of prayer, so the Islamic Ummah, the last of them, is entitled to its own (5:48). Objections should be ignored, not debated.
- The real task is to outdo one another in good deeds, for Allah will gather everyone, wherever they died, for judgement.
- "Compete in good" also means hastening to good works as soon as they are possible (8:24), including praying when the time comes, with the schools differing only over the prayers the Prophet ﷺ himself delayed.
- Inwardly, the Kaʿbah of stone earns the faithful the reward of the four higher qiblahs, and the believer is called to turn from everything but Allah in the footsteps of Muṣṭafā ﷺ.

149.text:
Verse 149 repeats the command of verse 144 with a new phrase at its head. "Wherever you are ˹O Prophet˺, turn your face towards the Sacred Mosque. This is certainly the truth from your Lord. And Allah is never unaware of what you ˹all˺ do". The Arabic says "from whatever place you set out", which shows that the ruling now covers the state of a journey. The repetition points out that the stipulation applies equally whether one is travelling or not.

### Phrase by phrase

**"Wherever you are ˹O Prophet˺, turn your face towards the Sacred Mosque."**. From whatever place you set out on a journey, O Muḥammad ﷺ, and wherever you are, you and your followers face the Sacred Mosque, the Kaʿbah at Makkah, when you pray. The reasoning given in this passage requires the Muslims, at home or on the road, to turn towards the Sacred Mosque, for that is beyond doubt the qiblah appointed for them by divine command. Obeying it, like every other command, is obligatory.

**"This is certainly the truth from your Lord."**. The Sacred Mosque is the qiblah of Ibrāhīm (Abraham), and the truth revealed to you from your Lord. In the first command (2:144) Allah recorded the fulfilment of His Prophet's ﷺ wish and ordered him to face the qiblah he loved. In this second command He adds that the change is also the truth from Him, raising the matter a step above the first verse. There Allah granted what His Prophet ﷺ wished for. Here He declares that this is the truth He Himself loves and approves.

**"And Allah is never unaware of what you ˹all˺ do"**. The verb is read "you do" and also "they do", as in 2:144. He is not heedless of what the People of the Book conceal about the qiblah of Ibrāhīm, nor of anything else. He is aware of all you do and will reward you accordingly. Muslims should obey, bearing in mind that Allah is not unaware of what people do.

### Why the command is given three times

Allah commands the facing of the Sacred Mosque three times in verses 144, 149 and 150. One explanation is that the ruling is tied to what comes before it and what comes after it. In the first instance Allah fulfilled the Prophet's ﷺ wish. In the second He stated that the change is the truth from Him. The third answers the Jews' objection about his following their qiblah. Their Books told them that his commanded direction would be Ibrāhīm's Kaʿbah. Facing it also removed the Arab disbelievers' objection. This qiblah was more honoured than that of the Jews. The Arabs revered the Kaʿbah and were pleased that the Messenger ﷺ was told to face it.

In announcing the change, verses 144 to 150 address the listeners three times in the singular and twice in the plural. In a general way the repetition is for emphasis. The new qiblah not only gave the opponents of Islam an occasion for glee, it was also a sudden and conspicuous change in the Muslims' own observances, and without such emphatic repetition their hearts would have stayed unsettled. The reiteration also signals that this is the final and definite decision, and that no further change is to be expected. Al-Qurṭubī, however, explains the repetition so that each phrase acquires a new implication. The commands in the singular are addressed to the Prophet ﷺ himself and those in the plural to the Companions and Muslims in general. Verse 144 concerns those in Madinah or in their own home town, whatever it may be, making clear that the ruling is not peculiar to the Prophet's ﷺ mosque but applies to every town, village and quarter. Verse 149 repeats the command with "from wherever you set out", which refers to the state of travel. Because a journey involves different situations, unbroken travel for days at a time, or a short or long stay somewhere along the way, verse 150 repeats the injunction once more to cover them all.

Many people today, especially those with a Western education, approach the Qur'an as they would a book by a human author who keeps to what commonly passes for logic and sequential argument. The repeated wording of Allah's Book embarrasses or confuses them. Unable to explain what appears redundant, even some who wish to serve Islam today may begin to doubt. They overlook an elementary fact: the Word of Allah is not bound by the rules of philosophical or literary composition, and the repetition of words, phrases and even whole sequences of sentences is a regular mode of expression in all the Sacred Books of the world. The great orthodox commentators, those who adhere unfailingly to the Qur'an and Sunnah, have each tried to suggest the reasons for this device and to explain the implications of each instance. Maulānā Muḥammad Idrīs summarised the explanations for these verses in five points. First, the first declaration addresses the residents of Makkah, the second the people of the Arabian peninsula, and the third all people anywhere in the world. Second, the first covers all situations and states, the second all places, and the third all periods of time. Third, the passage gives three reasons for the change of orientation, and the command is affirmed afresh alongside each reason. Fourth, this was the first occasion in the Islamic Sharīʿah on which a new command came to abrogate an earlier one, so repetition was needed to impress the manifold significance of the occasion on people's minds. Fifth, the abrogation of any command tends to raise all kinds of doubts and to produce internal or external disorder, and the naive cannot grasp the why and how of a divine command being abrogated, which makes emphatic reiteration all the more essential.

The devotional reading joins bodily orientation with inward approach. Wherever the body faces the qiblah, near or far, the heart should seek nearness to Allah. This applies both in good fortune received from Him and in affliction.

### In short

- The command of 2:144 is repeated for the traveller: from wherever one sets out, the Sacred Mosque is the qiblah.
- Here Allah adds that the change is the truth from Him, not merely a wish granted.
- The threefold command (144, 149, 150) answers three objections and covers home, journey and every state, and the repetition itself seals the ruling as final. Repetition is a normal mode of divine speech, not redundancy.
- Inwardly, as the body turns to the qiblah from any distance, the heart should turn to Allah in every state.

150.text:
Verse 150 gives the command for the third time and states the third reason for the change. "Wherever you are ˹O Prophet˺, turn your face towards the Sacred Mosque. And wherever you ˹believers˺ are, face towards it, so that people will have no argument against you, except the wrongdoers among them. Do not fear them; fear Me, so that I may ˹continue to˺ perfect My favour upon you and so you may be ˹rightly˺ guided". This is the third command from Allah to face the Sacred Mosque from every part of the world in prayer.

### Phrase by phrase

**"Wherever you are ˹O Prophet˺, turn your face towards the Sacred Mosque. And wherever you ˹believers˺ are, face towards it"**. From wherever you set out, O Prophet ﷺ, turn towards the direction of the Sacred Mosque when you pray, and wherever you may be, O believers, on land or at sea, turn your faces towards it in prayer. All of this is repeated for emphasis.

**"so that people will have no argument against you"**. So that neither the Jews nor the idolaters have any ground for contention over the change of direction. The description of the Muslim Ummah known to the People of the Book included a command to face the Kaʿbah. Had the Muslims not matched this description, the Jews would have used the fact against them. Had they stayed on the qiblah of Bayt al-Maqdis (Jerusalem), which was also the Jews' qiblah, that too could have served the Jews as an argument against others. Both the Torah and the Injīl identified the Kaʿbah as the future qiblah of the promised Last Prophet ﷺ. Had the Muslims gone on facing Bayt al-Maqdis, the opponents of Islam would have had an excuse for denying the Prophet ﷺ. The new command cuts the ground from under their feet, and at least the fair-minded among them can no longer raise this objection. The change silences two arguments at once: the Jews' claim that he rejected their religion yet followed their qiblah, and the idolaters' claim that he professed the creed of Ibrāhīm (Abraham) yet contravened Ibrāhīm's qiblah. "People" here, on one reading, means ʿAbdullāh ibn Salām and his companions, who knew from their Scripture that the Sacred Mosque was the qiblah of Ibrāhīm. Once you pray towards it, they have no argument against you.

**"except the wrongdoers among them."**. The stubborn and malicious will still carp. Those who transgress with their words, such as Kaʿb ibn al-Ashraf and the Arab idolaters, retain their contention. The phrase indicates the mushrikīn of Quraysh, whose unsound reasoning ran: this man claims to follow the religion of Ibrāhīm, so if facing Bayt al-Maqdis was part of that religion, why did he change it? The answer is that Allah chose, for a wisdom of His own, to have His Prophet ﷺ face Bayt al-Maqdis first, and he obeyed. Then Allah changed the qiblah to that of Ibrāhīm, the Kaʿbah, and he obeyed again. He obeys Allah in every case and never defies Him for an instant, and his Ummah follows him in this. The obstinate also said that he changed direction only out of a natural inclination towards the idolatrous religion of his forefathers, or that Bayt al-Maqdis rather than the Kaʿbah had been the qiblah of the earlier prophets, so that adopting the Kaʿbah broke with established prophetic tradition. The exception is a continuous one: no one will have anything to say against you except what these people say, and they will go on arguing with the weakest of arguments.

**"Do not fear them; fear Me"**. Do not fear their arguing with you over the change, nor the doubts raised by unjust and stubborn people. Fear Allah alone, by complying with His command, following His instructions and keeping away from what He has forbidden, for He alone deserves to be feared. The Muslims need not worry about defending Islam against baseless objections. The only thing that can harm them is not the hostility of people but disobedience to, or disregard of, divine commands. Fearing Allah alone is the only way to remain true to the guidance they have received, which is Islam.

**"so that I may ˹continue to˺ perfect My favour upon you"**. This connects with "so that people will have no argument against you". I will perfect My bounty on you by legislating that you face the Kaʿbah, so that the Sharīʿah is complete in every respect, just as I have completed your religion for you. Allah instructed the believers to face the Kaʿbah to perfect His blessings on them, to distinguish them from all other communities and to guide them to the noblest direction of prayer, the principal rituals of their religion. Steadfastness in this is itself a blessing from Allah, and the blessing will appear in its full glory in the next world, when the Muslims are admitted to Paradise as the reward of their faithfulness.

**"and so you may be ˹rightly˺ guided"**. Guided to the truth and to the qiblah of Ibrāhīm, directed to what the other nations were led astray from. Allah guided this Ummah to it and favoured it with it, which is why this Ummah is the best and most honoured of nations.

### The change of qiblah as the completion of guidance

After the Kaʿbah became the qiblah, the People of the Book debated whether Allah's direction was east or west. Reducing the matter to direction alone misunderstood it. The appointment of His House signalled more than a prayer bearing. It marked the time for His greatest favour to humanity to be disclosed. It had been decided long before, in answer to the prayer of Ibrāhīm and Ismāʿīl (Ishmael) for a messenger to be raised from their descendants (2:129), that Allah would send a final Prophet to the world. The path to everlasting life was now being thrown open to all. Bringing religion to its final perfection in Islam does not mean the earlier religions were incomplete. They were complete in themselves, but none was preserved in its original and authentic form. True religion had repeatedly been revealed, only to meet human rebellion, distortion or neglect. Now its revelation took the final form that could not be erased. Divine religion that had degenerated into a set of mythological tales was now incorporated into history as solid fact. Previously no pattern of true religion had remained intact for posterity. It was now presented as a lasting reality, lived and practised. Thus the qiblah change disclosed the completion of Allah's guidance to humanity, not simply a move to a more sacred bearing.

In the devotional reading: if you want no one to have a pathway against you, no shadow from any created thing to fall on you and no hand to reach you with harm, then from whatever place you set out, wherever you are and whatever your state, be for Us and be from Us, for nothing can reach those who occupy themselves exclusively with Us. "Do not fear them": when they have been effaced from their engendered existence as so many mortal remains, and Our decrees flow over them, why should there be any fear of them? The perfection of grace is to add unveiling to kindness. The one whom He suffices through the demands of His generosity stands below the one whom He enriches by the rightful due of His existence. The lovers picture perfect happiness that is complete only through the beloved. Their one remaining lack is the beloved's absence while they themselves remain present.

### In short

- The third command adds the third reason: facing the Kaʿbah fulfils the description of the Last Prophet ﷺ in the earlier Scriptures, leaving fair-minded people no argument, and refuting both the Jews' and the idolaters' objections.
- Only the obstinate, like Kaʿb ibn al-Ashraf and the Quraysh idolaters, go on carping. Their objection is answered by the Prophet's ﷺ obedience in both directions.
- Muslims are to fear Allah, not critics, for only disobedience can harm them. The qiblah perfects Allah's favour and completes the Sharīʿah.
- The change marks the completion of divine guidance promised in answer to Ibrāhīm's prayer (2:129), not a mere swap of directions.
- Inwardly, whoever is wholly for Allah, wherever he is, is beyond the reach of any created harm.

151.text:
Verse 151 closes the long discussion of the qiblah by returning to the prayer with which it began. "Since We have sent you a messenger from among yourselves—reciting to you Our revelations, purifying you, teaching you the Book and wisdom, and teaching you what you never knew—". When Ibrāhīm (Abraham) and Ismāʿīl (Ishmael) raised the Kaʿbah they prayed for two things (verses 127 to 129): that Allah accept their founding of the House, and that He raise among their descendants a messenger from among themselves. The qiblah passage has already shown that the first request was granted. Verse 151 now declares that the second was granted too, and the sentence runs on into verse 152, where the response Allah asks for is spelled out.

### Phrase by phrase

**"Since We have sent you a messenger from among yourselves"**. The verse opens with "as" or "just as", the Arabic letter kāf that compares two things. On one reading it connects with the previous verse: just as I perfect My favour on you by giving you the qiblah, so too I have sent among you a Messenger of your own, Muḥammad ﷺ, and the sending of the Messenger is itself part of the perfecting of My grace. Al-Qurṭubī instead connects the comparison with the first words of verse 152, "remember Me", so that the two verses together mean: the ability to remember Allah is as great a blessing as the new qiblah and the coming of the Last Prophet ﷺ, and people must therefore thank Allah so that His favours continue. Mujāhid likewise explained the verse as meaning: so remember Me in gratitude for My favour. The founder of the Kaʿbah prayed for this Prophet ﷺ. His being sent in answer explains why the House became his qiblah. Allah reminds His believing servants of what He gave them by sending Muḥammad ﷺ as a Messenger, and the Messenger is from their own lineage, one of themselves.

**"reciting to you Our revelations"**. He recites to them the clear verses of the Qur'an, with its commands and prohibitions. This is the first of the attributes Ibrāhīm named in his prayer, and verse 151 lists them in order: he recites the verses, he teaches the Book and the wisdom, he purifies, and he teaches what his listeners did not know.

**"purifying you"**. He cleanses them of sin, of idolatry and of the worst kinds of behaviour, the ills of the soul and the practices of the Jāhiliyyah, the age of ignorance before Islam. He causes them to grow by directing them to virtue and goodness, by belief in the Oneness of Allah, by zakāh and by charity, and by forbidding them evil and wrong. He takes them out of the darkness of disbelief into the light of faith.

**"teaching you the Book and wisdom"**. The Book is the Qur'an, and the wisdom (ḥikmah) is his Sunnah, the rulings of the Qur'an, the lawful and the prohibited, and the understanding of religion (fiqh).

**"and teaching you what you never knew"**. He teaches them legal rulings, the prescribed punishments, the stories of bygone nations and both worldly and sacred knowledge that they had no access to before the revelation of the Qur'an and the coming of Muḥammad ﷺ, things that could not be found in the earlier divine Books or worked out by individual reason. In the days of ignorance they used to utter foolish things. The blessing of the Prophet's ﷺ message raised them to the rank of the awliyāʾ, the loyal friends of Allah, and the rank of the scholars, so that they came to have the deepest knowledge among people, the most pious hearts and the most truthful tongues. A parallel verse says: "Indeed, Allah has done the believers a ˹great˺ favour by raising a messenger from among them—reciting to them His revelations, purifying them, and teaching them the Book and wisdom. For indeed they had previously been clearly astray" (3:164). Allah also censures those who failed to value this bounty: "Have you not seen those ˹disbelievers˺ who meet Allah's favours with ingratitude and lead their own people to their doom" (14:28). Ibn ʿAbbās said that the favour of Allah in that verse means Muḥammad ﷺ.

### The answered prayer and the sign of the qiblah

While building the Kaʿbah, Ibrāhīm and Ismāʿīl asked Allah to raise a prophet among Makkah's people. Acceptance of that prayer decreed the arrival of the final Prophet ﷺ with Makkah as his focus. Later messengers foretold him. His arrival was then signalled by making Makkah's Kaʿbah the direction of prayer for every nation. The sincere needed no further proof, but even a sign as conclusive as this did not silence those who gave no thought to Allah. It is those who fear Allah who are guided along the path to Him.

The devotional reading connects the sending of the Messenger with opened gates of attainment. Allah already knew His friends would thirst for meeting Him. Access to Him comes only through His messengers. Their sending charges some people with the Law's burdens. For others it bestows the honour of learning to draw near. The reading stresses the difference between these responses.

### In short

- The verse announces that Ibrāhīm's second prayer (2:129) has been answered: a Messenger from the people's own stock has been sent, which also explains why his qiblah is the Kaʿbah.
- His four tasks are those Ibrāhīm named: reciting the verses, purifying, teaching the Book and the wisdom (the Sunnah), and teaching what no one could otherwise know (cf. 3:164).
- The comparison "as We have sent" links either to the perfecting of favour in verse 150 or to "remember Me" in verse 152: the Prophet ﷺ is the favour, and remembrance and gratitude are the response (14:28).

152.text:
Having sent the Messenger in answer to Ibrāhīm's prayer, Allah tells people how to respond to so great a gift. "remember Me; I will remember you. And thank Me, and never be ungrateful". People are to remember Allah as the Supreme Benefactor and to thank Him by obeying Him. As long as they do so, He will remember them by showering material and spiritual blessings on them, and the verse ends with the warning not to deny His blessings or disobey Him.

### Phrase by phrase

**"remember Me; I will remember you."**. Remember Me through prayer, glorification, acts of obedience and the like, and I will reward you. Al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī explained: remember Me in what I have commanded you, and I will remember you in what I have bound Myself to do for you, meaning His rewards and forgiveness. One reading is: remember Me in times of ease and I will remember you in times of hardship. Another: remember Me through obedience and I will remember you by granting you Paradise. The remembrance asked for engages the heart and the whole person, and its reward is Allah's approval and protection, since each is repaid according to his deeds. Al-Bukhārī records a ḥadīth qudsī also reported by Imām Aḥmad from Anas. It promises that private remembrance by the son of Adam is answered privately by Allah. Remembrance in an assembly is answered in an assembly of angels, or a better assembly. Drawing near by a hand's span is met by a forearm's length. A forearm's approach is met by an arm's length. Coming on foot is met by Allah coming at a run.

**"And thank Me"**. Be grateful for the countless favours I have bestowed on you, and show it by obedience. Allah commands that He be thanked and promises still more for thanking Him, as another verse says: "And ˹remember˺ when your Lord proclaimed, 'If you are grateful, I will certainly give you more. But if you are ungrateful, surely My punishment is severe.'" (14:7). Abū Rajāʾ al-ʿUṭāridī related that ʿImrān ibn Ḥuṣayn once came to them wearing a fine silk garment they had never seen him wear before or after, and explained that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ had said that Allah likes His favour to be visible in the person receiving it. The wording refers to His creation, or to His servant in the transmission of the narrator Rūḥ.

**"and never be ungrateful"**. Do not be ungrateful through disobedience, do not stop giving thanks for these blessings, and do not deny them or use them in prohibited ways. Allah is reproaching those who did not give the bounty of the Prophet ﷺ its due, and commanding the believers to affirm that favour and appreciate it by thanking and remembering Him.

### What remembrance is

Dhikr, remembrance, belongs essentially to the heart. Since the tongue is the heart's interpreter, reciting a divine Name or a verse of the Qur'an aloud is also called dhikr, but oral dhikr truly deserves the name only when the heart remembers along with it. The poet Rūmī observed that repeating a divine Name has no efficacy if one is thinking of cows and donkeys while mechanically pronouncing it. Even so, mechanical dhikr without the heart is not altogether futile. When a man complained to the Sufi Abū ʿUthmān of exactly this, he replied that one should thank Allah even for the favour of having drawn at least one organ, the tongue, into His service. Al-Qurṭubī records both anecdotes.

The merits of dhikr are innumerable, and the greatest of them is the assurance given here, that when a person remembers Allah, Allah remembers him. Abū ʿUthmān once claimed to know the moment at which Allah remembers His servants. When his hearers asked how he could know such a thing, he answered from this very promise: a Muslim who remembers Allah is at once remembered by Him, so everyone can know for himself that the instant he turns to Allah in remembrance, Allah remembers him.

### Remembrance as obedience

The remembrance described here includes obedience to Allah's commands. His answering remembrance brings forgiveness and reward. Saʿīd ibn Jubayr took the remembrance of Allah to mean obedience and submission to Him, saying that whoever has not obeyed Him has not remembered Him, even if he keeps himself outwardly busy with supererogatory (nafl) prayers and recitations of His praise. A hadith supports this fully. Al-Qurṭubī cites it from the Aḥkām al-Qurʾān of Ibn Khuwayz Mandādh: the Prophet ﷺ said that whoever obeys Allah, keeping to the rules of the lawful (ḥalāl) and the unlawful (ḥarām), has truly remembered Him even if he falls short in nafl prayers and fasting, while whoever disobeys the divine commands has in fact forgotten Allah, however many hours he spends in nafl prayer, fasting and praise.

The Sufi master Dhū al-Nūn al-Miṣrī said that whoever remembers Allah in the full sense forgets everything else, and that in return for such total absorption Allah Himself takes charge of all his concerns and gives him something far more valuable for everything he loses. The Companion Muʿādh remarked that for winning deliverance from divine wrath no deed of a human being compares with dhikr. Abū Hurayrah reported a hadith in which Allah Himself declares that He stays with His servant for as long as the servant goes on remembering Him with lips moving in dhikr. Only those who are filled with fear of Allah are free of fear of everything besides Him, and Allah remembers those who remember Him.

### Remembrance of the Friend

The devotional reading describes remembrance of the lovingly kind Friend as nourishment for the spirit and comfort for the heart. In its polo image, remembrance is the ball struck by the bat of familiarity with Him. Yearning is its steed and love its field, burning for Him is the rose and recognising Him the garden. Such remembrance makes the Real apparent, for it is joined to the Reality and separate from mortal nature. It is the watering place of the tree of tawḥīd, whose fruit is friendship with the Real, which is why the Lord of the Worlds said that His servant does not cease remembering Him, and He remembering the servant, until the servant is passionate for Him and He for the servant. This is not the remembrance of the tongue that everyone knows. It lives inside the spirit. In later life Abū Yazīd used little spoken remembrance. Asked why, he expressed wonder at remembrance by the tongue and still greater wonder at the stranger's presence. What place did a stranger have there? Remembrance belonged within the spirit. One master, in a whispered prayer, asked his Lord how he could possibly remember Him while He Himself was doing the remembering and the servant was crying out from his own forgetfulness. He is both the remembrance and the remembered, and only He helps anyone find Him. Whoever reaches You is done with sorrows, whoever sees You, his spirit laughs. Who in the two worlds has more joy than the one who remembers You?

To the poor man the warning is: you are remembering yourself, so what do you know of remembering Him? Never having travelled, what do you know of the way stations? Never having seen the Friend, how can you know His name and mark? You worship yourself, for whatever you do, you do for your own sake. Entering the spirit brings dignity. The image then leads the traveller into the street of the Reality, remembering Him within the secret core. What is disclosed has never been seen by an eye, heard by an ear or conceived in a mortal heart. One of Allah's scriptures is reported to say: My servant, you will remember Me once you have tried out the others, for I am better for you than anyone else. When you have seen and tested them, you will know My worth and My rightful due. Once you have grasped their lack of loving kindness and My kindness and loyalty, you will know that I am more lovingly kind and more useful to you than anyone else. The address reminds the servant that Allah's remembrance and love came first. Divine desire preceded the servant's desire. It asks whether shame before Him has led the servant to turn elsewhere, and where that wandering leads. His door remains open, and His gifts continue to reach the servant. As someone put it, all your brightness is from Me, you wander about and then you come back to Me. A single step on His path is pictured as meeting a thousand gifts of generosity. The servant's small service receives abundant blessing, and a little obedience meets immense mercy. The Prophet ﷺ alluded to this in the saying from Allah already quoted, that whoever remembers Him in himself is remembered by Him in Himself, whoever remembers Him in an assembly is remembered in a better assembly, and whoever comes to Him walking is met by Him rushing. As for "thank Me", it has been said that gratitude is what arises when one sees the blessings and is grateful in respect of one's own activity.

### In short

- Remembering Allah through obedience, prayer and glorification is met by His remembering the servant with reward, forgiveness, approval and protection, as the ḥadīth qudsī of the hand's span and the forearm promises (al-Bukhārī).
- Gratitude brings increase (14:7) and Allah loves to see the effect of His bounty on His servant. Ingratitude means disobedience or denying and misusing the blessings.
- True dhikr is of the heart, with the tongue as its interpreter. Saʿīd ibn Jubayr and the hadith cited by al-Qurṭubī make obedience in ḥalāl and ḥarām the real test of remembrance, above nafl worship.
- Dhū al-Nūn, Muʿādh and Abū Hurayrah's hadith show its fruits: Allah takes charge of the one absorbed in Him, nothing saves from His wrath like dhikr, and He is with the servant whose lips move in remembrance.
- Inwardly, Allah remembered and loved the servant first. Remembrance in the spirit, not merely on the tongue, leads to friendship with Him.

153.text:
The enemies of Islam had objected to the change of qiblah in the hope of planting doubts about the religion itself. The preceding verses answered them, but some simply ignored the answers and persisted in their hostility, and that was likely to dishearten the Muslims. Verse 153 forestalls such a reaction by prescribing the way to overcome grief and anxiety. "O believers! Seek comfort in patience and prayer. Allah is truly with those who are patient". Having commanded that He be thanked (verse 152), Allah now ordains patience and prayer, for a servant is always either enjoying a bounty he should be thankful for or suffering a hardship he should meet with patience. A hadith describes the believer's condition as remarkable: every divine decree brings him good. Receiving a blessing, he responds gratefully and benefits through that gratitude. Facing affliction, he remains patient and benefits through that patience.

### Phrase by phrase

**"O believers! Seek comfort in patience and prayer."**. You who have faith in Allah and follow His Messenger ﷺ, ask Allah's help in everything, for this world and the Hereafter, through the beauty of patience and by establishing the prayer as He has instructed. Patience here means steadfastness in fulfilling Allah's obligations and in abstaining from violations and shameful deeds, and patience under affliction. Prayer is singled out for mention because of how often it is performed and how great it is, and it includes abundant supererogatory prayers by night and day, which cleanse a person of sin. Patience and prayer are the best means of easing the effects of affliction, as the earlier verse said: "And seek help through patience and prayer. Indeed, it is a burden except for the humble—" (2:45). The Qur'an states the remedy in a deliberately general form, "seek help", without specifying the situation, which shows that it works for all the ills that are part of human existence, whether wants and needs or anxiety and suffering. The promise applies above all to those who pray, whether the obligatory (farḍ) or the voluntary (nafl) prayer, since prayer is the supreme form of worship.

**"Allah is truly with those who are patient"**. He helps them, protects them from shameful deeds and gives them success. This phrase holds the secret of how patience saves a person from every kind of trouble. The reward of patience is the honour of Allah's company, and once the might of the Lord of the Worlds has come to a person's aid, what pain can overwhelm him, and who can stop his affairs from prospering?

### What patience (ṣabr) means

The Arabic ṣabr is far wider than the English "patience". Its root meaning is restraining oneself, keeping oneself under control. In the usage of the Qur'an and hadith it has three modes. The first is holding back from whatever the Sharīʿah has declared unlawful (ḥarām). The second is forcing oneself to be regular in the forms of worship and steadfast in obeying Allah and His Messenger ﷺ, and this kind brings more reward than the first. The third is enduring every kind of trouble and pain, understanding that it is Allah's will that one should suffer and hoping for a reward for it, and this kind is mandatory, just as repentance is. Saʿīd ibn Jubayr is cited for the point that a word of grief or a sigh of pain that one cannot hold back does not contradict ṣabr or nullify it. ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Zayd ibn Aslam divided ṣabr into two parts: patience for Allah's sake in what pleases Him, even if it is hard on heart and body, and patience in avoiding what He dislikes, even if it is desired. Whoever acquires both will, Allah willing, be among the patient whom Allah greets when they meet Him, as Sūrat al-Aḥzāb says: "Their greeting on the Day they meet Him will be, 'Peace!' And He has prepared for them an honourable reward" (33:44).

People commonly identify ṣabr with the third mode alone and overlook the first two, which are in fact the more basic. All three are equally obligatory, and every Muslim is required to practise them all. In the language of the Qur'an and hadith, al-Ṣābirūn is the title of those who are steadfast in all three with equal rigour. A hadith says that on the Day of Judgement a call will go out, "Where are the Ṣābirūn?", and those who kept to the three forms of patience will rise and be admitted to Paradise without having to render an account of their deeds. The Qur'an itself corroborates this: "Only those who endure patiently will be given their reward without limit" (39:10).

### Why prayer is named separately

Ṣabr, as just defined, already covers every form of worship, prayer included, since all of them are its branches. Ṣalāh is nevertheless mentioned on its own because it is the most perfect model of ṣabr. In prayer a person binds himself to obedience and worship and restrains himself not only from everything sinful but even from what is otherwise permissible, such as eating, drinking and talking. Prayer is thus a visible demonstration of what ṣabr means: keeping oneself under control, shunning everything sinful and submitting wholly to obedience.

Prayer also has a special power to release a person from every kind of trouble and to fulfil his needs. This may not be explicable rationally, but the efficacy is a characteristic quality in the very nature of prayer, as it is in certain medicines. It shows itself, however, only when prayer is offered properly, with the physical and spiritual etiquette the Sharīʿah lays down. If our prayers seem fruitless, it is because we have been careless of that etiquette and have not turned to Allah with single-minded devotion and total submission. According to hadith, whenever the Prophet ﷺ faced a grave problem of any kind he hastened to offer nafl prayers, and through the blessing (barakah) of prayer Allah came to his aid and resolved it.

### The world as a testing ground

Whoever has adopted religion in the real sense has truly discovered Allah. He lives in permanent thanksgiving and remembrance of his Lord, and that life alone is a source of peace and happiness. Peace and happiness, however, will materialise completely only in the eternal world to come. This world was not created for reward but for the trial of humankind. Because it is a testing ground, Allah's servants meet obstacles on their path, so that the earnest can be told apart from those who are not serious. The obstacles come in ordinary situations: human temptations, family demands, worldly interests, social pressure. These are the real tests of life. The person must recognise the test being faced. Remembering Allah and giving thanks for life's blessings then helps avoid its pitfalls. There is only one way to succeed, and that is patience and prayer, which means attaching oneself to Allah and sticking conscientiously to the path of truth while enduring every setback. Those who do not waver from the path despite its difficulties, who stay with Allah even when no worldly benefit seems to come of it, are the ones who will finally emerge successful. Allah has reserved the eternal blessings of the next life for those willing to sacrifice this life for it.

### The blessing that comes through patience

In the devotional reading, "seek help through patience and prayer" is also read as: seek Allah's blessing (ṣalāt) through patience, for one becomes worthy of the Lord's blessing by bearing patiently the flow of His decrees. That is why this passage says "give good tidings to the patient" (verse 155) and then "upon those rest blessings and mercy from their Lord" (verse 157). One explanation connects the patient's highest ranks and ultimate treasures with divine company, maʿiyyah. Allah says, "Allah is truly with those who are patient".

### In short

- When opponents persist despite every answer, the believer's remedy for grief is patience and prayer (cf. 2:45), a remedy stated generally because it suits every trouble.
- Ṣabr has three obligatory modes: abstaining from the ḥarām, steadfastness in worship and obedience, and enduring hardship. The Ṣābirūn who keep all three enter Paradise without reckoning (39:10, 33:44).
- Prayer is named separately as the most perfect form of self-restraint and because of its special efficacy when performed with proper etiquette, as the Prophet ﷺ did in every crisis.
- "Allah is with the patient" is the secret: His company brings help, protection and success, and the world's trials are the means by which the earnest are distinguished.

154.text:
Verse 153 inculcated patience in the face of an unpleasant situation. The verses that follow mention harsher trials, and they put war with the disbelievers first for two reasons: the sacrifice of life is the greatest sacrifice, and whoever endures that loss steadfastly will manage lesser losses, and it was also relevant to the moment, since those who objected to the new qiblah were the same people the Muslims were facing in battle. "Never say that those martyred in the cause of Allah are dead—in fact, they are alive! But you do not perceive it". The hypocrites used to say of the martyrs of Badr, Uḥud and the other battles that so-and-so had died and lost all comfort and happiness, in order to distress sincere believers. Allah answers them here.

### Phrase by phrase

**"Never say that those martyred in the cause of Allah are dead"**. Do not say, O believers, of those killed in obedience to Allah, striving in His path at Badr or in any other battle, that they are dead like other people who die. One who dies in the cause of Allah is a shahīd, a martyr, and although it is correct and even permitted to call him dead, we are forbidden to regard his death like ordinary deaths.

**"in fact, they are alive!"**. They are alive with their Lord, living as those in Paradise live, provided with comfort and bounties and receiving their sustenance. Muslim reports in his Ṣaḥīḥ that the souls of the martyrs are inside green birds that move about in Paradise wherever they wish and then take refuge in lamps hanging beneath the Throne. Their Lord looked at them and asked what they wished for, and they replied: what more could we wish for, when You have favoured us as You have favoured none of Your creation? The question was repeated until they understood that an answer was required. They asked to return to earthly life for another opportunity to fight for Allah and be killed for Him again. The Lord said: I have written that they shall not be returned to it. Imām Aḥmad reports that ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Kaʿb ibn Mālik related from his father that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said that the believer's soul is a bird feeding on the trees of Paradise until Allah returns it to its body on the day of resurrection. That hadith includes all believers in its general sense, so the Qur'an's singling out of the martyrs serves to honour and favour them, even though other believers share in the rewards they enjoy.

**"But you do not perceive it"**. You are not aware of the honour bestowed on them or of their real state, because the manner of their life can be known only through revelation from Allah. With these words the Qur'an asserts that life in the barzakh transcends all sensory perception.

### Life in the barzakh

According to the teachings of Islam, the dead are given a kind of new life in the barzakh, the intermediate stage that begins with death and lasts until the Day of Resurrection, and this life develops in them a sensitivity to punishment and reward. Believer or disbeliever, virtuous or vicious, everyone receives this taste of life in the barzakh. It has many grades, however: one for people in general, and others for prophets and the righteous, which differ in degree of excellence. Many scholars have gathered material on the subject, and the balanced view of Maulānā Ashraf ʿAlī of Thānā Bhawan, which agrees closely with the Qur'an and the teaching of the Prophet ﷺ, can be summarised as follows.

Life in the barzakh is given to everyone and gives perception of reward and punishment, but the martyr's life there is qualitatively different. His perception is keener and deeper, as life is present both in the fingertips and in the heels but the fingertips are far more sensitive. The finer life of the martyr in the barzakh even reaches his physical body, whereas ordinary bodies are unaffected. Consequently a martyr's body does not waste away, decay or mingle with the dust, but keeps its freshness and a semblance of life, as hadiths and observation confirm. The martyrs are therefore described as living, and we are forbidden to call them dead. For all worldly purposes, however, they are treated like the dead: their property is divided and their widows may remarry. The prophets' life in the barzakh has a further distinction. Their life-sensitivity is finer still, their bodies retain the quality of life, and in some ways it extends into this world, so that their property is not divided and their widows may not remarry. The strongest in retaining this quality of life are the prophets, then the martyrs, then ordinary people. Some hadiths indicate that certain friends of Allah and righteous people share this excellence with the martyrs, apparently those who die while exercising severe discipline over their lower selves. So although the verse speaks specifically of martyrs, it does not exclude the virtuous and the truthful.

If a martyr's body does return to dust as ordinary bodies do, the chances are that the person did not actually die in the cause of Allah, which is the sole criterion of martyrdom (shahādah). Where someone fulfilled all the requirements of martyrdom beyond any doubt, a hadith establishes that his body must not return to dust. If it nevertheless mingles with the earth, which is what made the author of Rūḥ al-Maʿānī wonder how a martyr's body could be eaten away despite the hadiths, the explanation is that the hadith denies the earth's consuming the body but not decomposition from other causes such as chemical reaction, enzymes and bacteria. Weapons, medicines, food and the elements of water, fire and air undoubtedly affected the bodies of the prophets in this world, and the martyr's life in the barzakh is not superior to the prophets' life in this world, so if such agents act on martyrs' bodies it does not contradict the hadiths that say their bodies are forbidden to the earth. Another answer is that the martyrs' distinction appears in their bodies remaining unspoiled for a very long time, even if disintegration in the long run remains possible, for preservation over a long period is in itself a departure from the normal behaviour of dead bodies, just as eternal preservation would be.

### Alive in the Friend

In the devotional reading, the life of this world has left the martyrs behind, but they have reached endless life. Release from this world's abasement is no loss to them. They have gained union with their exalted Patron. The lover asks that death be described as receiving life in the Friend who took him. True life depends on Him rather than on the spirit alone. The life received in the Friend does not end. The Pīr of the Path prayed: O Lord, if someone is occupied with You, how could his occupation end? When someone lives through You, how could he ever die? A spirit in a body that is deprived of You is like an imprisoned corpse. Truly alive is he who lives with You. Praise be to Allah for the slain of whom the King says that they are alive. Awe is pictured as their cloak. Beneath the Tremendous Throne they find intimate rest, while their spirits repose in the Presence of the Real's majesty, "at the Seat of Honour in the presence of the Most Powerful Sovereign" (54:55).

### In short

- The martyrs of Badr, Uḥud and every battle are not to be called dead as others are dead. They live with their Lord and are provided for, their souls in green birds in Paradise (Muslim), and their one wish is to return and be killed again.
- All the dead have some life in the barzakh, but the martyr's is keener, so that even his body resists decay, and the prophets' is higher still. For worldly rulings, however, martyrs are treated as dead.
- Decay of a body indicates either that the person was not truly a martyr or that natural agents, not the earth's consuming, were at work. In any case long preservation is itself extraordinary.
- "You do not perceive it": this life is beyond the senses and known only by revelation.

155.text:
Having spoken of those who give their lives, Allah now tells the believers plainly that they will be tested. "We will certainly test you with a touch of fear and famine and loss of property, life, and crops. Give good news to those who patiently endure—". Allah tests and tries His servants, as He says elsewhere: "We will certainly test you ˹believers˺ until We prove those of you who ˹truly˺ struggle ˹in Allah's cause˺ and remain steadfast, and reveal how you conduct yourselves" (47:31). Sometimes He tests with bounty and sometimes with the afflictions of fear and hunger. In another verse He speaks of a secure and prosperous town whose people were ungrateful, "so Allah made them taste the clutches of hunger and fear for their misdeeds" (16:112). The frightened and the hungry show the effects of their affliction outwardly, which is why that verse calls fear and hunger a garment (libās) that is put on.

### Phrase by phrase

**"We will certainly test you with a touch of fear and famine"**. "A touch", literally "something", means a little of each. The fear is fear of the enemy, and the hunger comes in years of drought and scarcity of food. Allah tests people with different kinds of hardship, and the test is to see whether they practise patience or not.

**"and loss of property, life, and crops."**. Some wealth will be destroyed or lost, or become hard to earn. Loss of life means losing friends, relatives and loved ones to killing, death and illness, and includes being martyred for Allah's sake. Loss of crops means that gardens and farms fail to yield what is usual or expected, through crop damage and a lack of produce from the earth.

**"Give good news to those who patiently endure—"**. The Prophet ﷺ is to say that Paradise awaits those who endure these calamities patiently. The promise brings happiness here and in the Hereafter. The next verse then describes who these patient ones are. Since the entire Ummah is addressed, it should understand that the world is a place of hardship, labour and ordeal. Accidents of any magnitude are unnerving, but knowing in advance that they are coming makes them easier to bear, and it is no failure of patience to be shaken by them so long as one does not regard them as strange or unlikely.

### The price of the Path

Calling people to truth requires the greatest sacrifices for Allah. Suffering is his lot, because his hearers respond badly to the criticism and admonition that are inseparable from such preaching, and few people in this world are willing to be reproved and warned. The sincere preacher also earns the hostility of mercenary people who do brisk business in the name of religion, since his sincerity threatens the standing of hypocrites. Taking up the task of preaching Allah's word is like putting one's hand into a fire. It exposes a person to prejudice, economic ruin and even expulsion from his own land, and places his life and property in the utmost peril. Persecution in this world is inevitable for one who follows Allah's path. Yet losing everything for Allah is pictured as true finding. Those surrendering their lives to Him receive life without end. For those who do not try to build their paradise in this fleeting world, Allah has prepared an eternal paradise in the next.

### Harshness followed by caress

In the devotional reading, it is the custom of the Lord that whenever He threatens the servant or shows severity in a verse, He caresses him and gives him hope right after it or just before it. In this verse He breaks the servant by naming these harsh things and varieties of trial, and then He gives good news: "give good news to those who patiently endure". And at the head of the passage He said, "Allah is truly with those who are patient" (verse 153). Glory be to Him, how gentle and merciful He is to His servants! His tests include fear and dread, poverty and hunger. They may appear as outward affliction or sorrow within the heart. The outward trial is in fact the easy part, for it comes and goes, like the trial of Ibrāhīm (Abraham) and the trial of Ayyūb (Job). The complete trial is inward sorrow, which never leaves its place for a moment. The nearer someone is, the more worthy of friendship and the more fit for union, the greater his sorrow. Such was the sorrow of Muṣṭafā ﷺ. He had no capacity for it on the highest horizon and no rest from it on the breadth of the earth. He was like a moth before a lamp, unable to stay with the flame and unable to stay away from it. The state of the moth with the candle is that it burns in separation and burns in union. Everyone who seeks union and proximity with Allah must shoulder the burden of tribulation and taste the drink of sorrow.

Āsiya, the wife of Pharaoh, sought the neighbourhood of the Real and asked for His proximity: "My Lord! Build me a house in Paradise near You" (66:11). She wanted a room in the street of the Friend, and was told that it is beautiful indeed but its price is very high, for everything else is sold for gold and silver while this is sold for spirit and heart. She answered that there was nothing to fear in that, and that if the price were a thousand spirits instead of one she would not hold back. So they crucified Āsiyah and drove iron nails into her eyes, and in that torment she was laughing and happy. In the image, a thorn chosen by the Heart-taker is preferable to a thousand dates. Bishr al-Ḥāfī told how he passed through the bazaar of Baghdad where a man was being given a thousand lashes without letting out a sigh. He followed him to prison and asked why he had been beaten, and the man said: because I am entranced by passion. Asked why he had not wept so that they might lighten the blows, he replied that his beloved had been watching, and he was so drowned in contemplating her that he had no thought for weeping. Bishr asked how it would have been had he been gazing on the Greatest Beloved. The man cried out once and died. With true passion, trial assumes the appearance of blessing. This great good fortune comes through the Beloved's beauty giving access to Him. Contemplation then transforms the experience of severity into gentleness. Yet no mere straw can approach Him. Bearing grief for Him requires genuine strength.

### In short

- Allah tests the believers (47:31) with a little fear, hunger, loss of wealth, loss of loved ones and failure of crops, so that patience may be proven, and fear and hunger show outwardly like a garment (16:112).
- The Prophet ﷺ is to give the patient good news of Paradise, and knowing beforehand that this world is a place of trial makes its blows easier to bear.
- Those who preach the truth pay the heaviest price in this world, but those who lose all for Allah are the true finders.
- Inwardly, the hardest trial is the sorrow of the heart that accompanies nearness, as with Muṣṭafā ﷺ, Āsiyah (66:11) and the lover in Bishr al-Ḥāfī's story, and love turns trial into blessing.

156.text:
Verse 156 explains who the patient people praised in the previous verse are. "who, when faced with a disaster, say, 'Surely to Allah we belong and to Him we will ˹all˺ return.'" They are the people who, struck by one of the hardships just mentioned, console themselves with this statement, known as the istirjāʿ. They know that they belong to Allah, who does what He wills with His servants, and that not a single deed, even the weight of an atom, will be lost with Him on the Day of Resurrection. These facts compel them to confess that they are His servants and that their return is to Him in the Hereafter.

### Phrase by phrase

**"who, when faced with a disaster"**. When any calamity of the kinds just listed strikes them.

**"say, 'Surely to Allah we belong and to Him we will ˹all˺ return.'"**. They say, in acceptance, that we are Allah's possession and His slaves, with whom He does as He pleases, that all power belongs to Him, that He created us and showered blessings on us, and that we return to Him after death, when He will requite us. One gloss connects the two approvals: refusal to accept His decree prevents our works from receiving His approval. The reciting of this formula by the patient is in fact the teaching of a principle of virtue. It is what the patient should say, because it brings excellent reward, lifts the burden of sorrow and suffering and effectively consoles the grieving heart. The Ummah's patient conduct brings a shared reward of mercy to those striving for patience. Individuals differ in its degree and quality, however. Each therefore receives a reward corresponding to the patience actually shown.

### The reward of saying istirjāʿ

Several hadiths describe the reward of this confession. Imām Aḥmad reports from Umm Salamah that Abū Salamah once came home from the Messenger of Allah ﷺ delighted by something he had heard him say: no Muslim is struck by an affliction and says the istirjāʿ when it strikes, adding "O Allah, reward me for my loss and give me what is better than it", without Allah doing exactly that. Umm Salamah said she memorised the words. When Abū Salamah died she said the istirjāʿ and asked Allah to compensate her and give her something better, and then thought to herself, who could be better than Abū Salamah?
