When her ʿiddah, the waiting period before a widow may remarry, was over, the Messenger of Allah ﷺ asked permission to see her while she was dyeing a skin. She washed her hands, let him in and gave him a cushion to sit on, and he asked for her hand in marriage. She answered that it was not that she did not want him, but that she was very jealous and feared he might see some fault in her for which Allah would punish her, and that she was old and had children. He replied that Allah would remove the jealousy she spoke of, that as for age he had suffered what she had suffered, and that her children were his children too. She said that she surrendered to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, and he married her. Umm Salamah later said that Allah had compensated her with someone better than Abū Salamah, the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. Muslim reports a shorter version. Another hadith says simply that whoever pronounces the istirjāʿ when an affliction befalls him will be rewarded and compensated with something better. Abū Dāwūd reports, in his section on mursal reports, that when the Prophet's ﷺ lamp once blew out he said the istirjāʿ, and ʿĀʾishah remarked that it was only a lamp, to which he replied that whatever bothers a believer is an affliction of a kind.

### Death as a reminder

The death of a loved one puts a person in a state of prayerfulness, deep thought and contemplation. It reminds him that very little time is at his disposal and that death can come calling at any moment. Yet we are so absorbed in worldly things that we never pause to think of the day that is fast approaching. The Prophet Muḥammad ﷺ said that people are asleep and will wake up only when they die. Death suddenly brings a person before Allah for an account of every deed. The difference between the life actually lived and the life that should have been lived then becomes clear. The Prophet ﷺ also said that on the Day of Judgement no one's feet will move until four questions are answered: where his money came from, the way he spent it, the use he made of his youth, and what he did with his knowledge. The Creator has divided human life into two parts, before death and after it. The first is very short, like the tip of an iceberg, compared with the second, which is eternal, and it is the preparatory phase in which one becomes eligible to enter Paradise. This worldly life is a test for everyone, poor or rich, powerful or powerless, strong or weak, and it is passed by living a need-based life rather than one driven by desire and greed, so that in the Hereafter Allah admits a person to Paradise to live for ever close to his Creator.

On the death of a loved one, then, one should not sink into mourning. The Qur'an gives great hope in moments of grief and loss, saying that Allah will reunite the righteous members of a family in Paradise, and that if one member has reached a higher level, the other righteous members will be raised to it, so that all of them enjoy eternal bliss and nearness to Allah. This idea gives great solace, and it is an incentive to good work and a pious life. The Prophet Muḥammad ﷺ described three things continuing to benefit a person after death: ongoing charity, beneficial knowledge and righteous children praying for him. Other connections are cut off.

### The demands of the unseen

In the devotional reading, Allah tried them with blessings to make their gratitude manifest and with tribulation to make their patience manifest. He brought into existence what He already knew of their state, marking them with the record He had decreed. He tried them with fear, which cleared their breasts, with hunger, which cleansed their bodies, and with loss of goods, which purified their material blessings. Through the afflictions of their lower selves their wages before Allah were magnified, and through the blight of their fruits their recompense was doubled. The patient are those who do not oppose His decree in what He brings to pass. It is also said that He asked them to fear in seeking to avoid His punishment, to hunger in desiring His nearness and generosity, to lose goods through almsgiving in the hope of something better, which is knowledge of Him, to give their lives in submission to His worship, and to give up their fruits by abandoning hope of abundant material blessings. The demands of the unseen (ghayb) come either through wealth, through the self or through near relations. Whoever devotes wealth to Allah will have salvation. Whoever exerts himself for His decree will be raised in degrees. Patience with afflictions involving close relations receives reward and stations near Him. Refusing to withhold the spirit from Allah brings intimate communication without end. Those struck by affliction meet it with patience, even with gratitude, and some with exultation. Whoever sees things as the property of the Real sees himself as a stranger standing between Him and His decree. The Creator, after all, has a greater right over the things He made than they have over themselves.

### In short

- The patient are those who answer disaster with the istirjāʿ, confessing that they are Allah's property and will return to Him, which consoles the heart and brings reward measured by the quality of each person's patience.
- Umm Salamah's story shows the promise in action: whoever says it and asks Allah for something better receives it, and Allah gave her the Messenger of Allah ﷺ in place of Abū Salamah (Aḥmad, Muslim). Even a lamp going out counts as an affliction (Abū Dāwūd).
- Death of a loved one should wake a person to his own short preparatory life, not plunge him into mourning, for Allah reunites righteous families in Paradise and three things outlast the dead.
- Inwardly, each trial purifies something, and the demands of the unseen on wealth, self and kin are repaid with salvation, degrees, nearness and intimacy.

157.text:
Verse 157 states what the patient receive. "They are the ones who will receive Allah's blessings and mercy. And it is they who are ˹rightly˺ guided". Allah's praise and mercy are with them, and they are the ones guided to the path of truth. Allah's blessing here follows from the patience spoken of in verses 153 and 155, for one becomes worthy of the Lord's blessing by bearing His decrees patiently.

### Phrase by phrase

**"They are the ones who will receive Allah's blessings and mercy."**. Those who possess these traits receive blessings (ṣalawāt) from their Lord, meaning His praise and forgiveness in this world, and mercy, meaning that they are not tormented in the Hereafter. Saʿīd ibn Jubayr explained the mercy as safety from the punishment. Allah praises them in the highest gathering of the angels, and mercy descends on them.

**"And it is they who are ˹rightly˺ guided"**. They are guided to rectitude, and guided to remember that we belong to Allah and to Him we return. ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb commented: what righteous things, and what heights! The blessings and the mercy from their Lord are the two righteous things, and being guided is the heights. The heights means further reward, so these people are given their reward and more besides.

### Guidance that begins with mercy

In the devotional reading, the patient obtained their patience and their power to withstand the demands of the divine decree from Allah's prior blessings on them. It was not their patience or endurance that brought them to His blessings. Had it not been for His pre-eternal mercy, their obedience could never have arisen in the condition of servanthood, for His prior solicitude is what brought them pure guidance. They are the rightly guided because He blessed them at the beginning, and so they were guided at the end.

### Mercy whose doors stay open

The mercy promised here has a long history among the family of the Kaʿbah. Ibrāhīm (Abraham), a native of Iraq, left his wife Hājar and his infant son Ismāʿīl (Ishmael) at Allah's command in the uninhabited, waterless place that is now Makkah. Thirst drove Hājar to run back and forth between the hills of Ṣafā and Marwah, and after seven unsuccessful attempts she returned to find the spring of Zamzam flowing from the ground. The event shows how Allah looks after His servants. Whoever persists in His service until there is nothing beneath his feet but burning sand will find that Allah in His mercy causes a refreshing spring to gush from the dryness of the desert, and the pilgrims to Makkah repeat her quest between the hills to commemorate what it means for everyone who struggles in Allah's path. The Jewish religious leaders of Madinah, by contrast, denied the Prophet Muḥammad ﷺ although Allah's signs were displayed clearly in his life and teaching. They feared that accepting an Arab prophet would end their religious hegemony, that people would stop looking to them as leaders, and that the old traditions and the interests bound up with them, of which they were the main beneficiaries, would be destroyed. They thought it wise to conceal the truth lest they lose their worldly status, when it would have been far wiser to proclaim it. They forgot that Allah's servants are required to put truth before worldly interest. Whoever becomes destitute for the sake of the Lord draws succour from the inexhaustible treasures of divine grace. Allah keeps the way to mercy open for His servants. Whoever recognises his error, reforms his conduct and declares the truth as commanded can receive forgiveness. Only those who persist in disbelief until the day they die are deprived of His mercy.

### In short

- The patient who say the istirjāʿ receive Allah's praise and forgiveness in this world and His mercy, meaning safety from punishment, in the next (Saʿīd ibn Jubayr).
- ʿUmar called the blessings and mercy "two righteous things" and the guidance "the heights", that is, reward and more.
- Their patience itself was a gift of Allah's prior mercy: blessed at the beginning, they were guided at the end.
- Hājar's spring shows that Allah's mercy meets those who persist for Him, and its doors stay open to all who turn back, closing only on those who die in disbelief.

158.text:
The subject of the Kaʿbah began back in verse 124, "And when his Lord put Ibrāhīm to a test", continued with the House being made a place of return, a sanctuary and a centre of worship (verse 125), and then with the prayer of Ibrāhīm (Abraham) asking to be taught the rites of worship (verses 126 to 129), which include the Hajj and the ʿUmrah. The centrality of the House was then expressed by making it the qiblah of every ṣalāh wherever it is performed, and its importance was established by making it the goal of the Hajj and ʿUmrah. Verse 158 now turns to a rite performed beside it. "Indeed, ˹the hills of˺ Ṣafa and Marwah are among the symbols of Allah. So whoever performs the pilgrimage or minor pilgrimage, let them walk between ˹the two hills˺." The verse concludes: "And whoever does good willingly, Allah is truly Appreciative, All-Knowing". Earlier the objection of the disbelievers to the Kaʿbah as the qiblah was removed. Here a doubt of the Muslims themselves is removed. It concerned the propriety of the saʿy, the brisk walk between the two hills, in the Hajj and ʿUmrah of which the Kaʿbah is the hub. The passage is thus closely bound together.

### Phrase by phrase

**"Indeed, ˹the hills of˺ Ṣafa and Marwah are among the symbols of Allah."**. Ṣafā and Marwah are two hills adjoining the Kaʿbah in Makkah. Shaʿāʾir is the plural of shaʿīrah, a sign, mark or token, so the symbols of Allah are what He has determined to be the marks of His religion, the rites and ceremonies of the Hajj that He has commanded and the landmarks of His clear sacred law. Going between Ṣafā and Marwah is among the acts Allah legislated for the Hajj in the time of Prophet Ibrāhīm. Pilgrims walk briskly between the two hills after the ṭawāf of the Kaʿbah, and the Qur'an elects to call this "going round" them.

**"So whoever performs the pilgrimage or minor pilgrimage, let them walk between ˹the two hills˺."**. Literally the Arabic says that there is no sin on whoever makes the Hajj to the House, or the ʿUmrah, in going round them. Hajj means in origin to aim or intend, and in the usage of the Qur'an and hadith it is the act of setting out solely to visit the House of Allah and performing the required rites there. ʿUmrah means in origin a visit, and in the Sharīʿah it is the visit to al-Masjid al-Ḥarām with ṭawāf and saʿy. The verb for going round them has an assimilated letter, and the act is the pacing (saʿy) between the two hills seven times. The verse was revealed when the Muslims were averse to it because the pagan Arabs used to go between the hills, each of which had an idol on top that they used to stroke. Allah's declaring that there is no fault in it comforted those Muslims who had been avoiding the walk for fear that it was an unacceptable custom of the time of ignorance, and made clear that it is an accepted act of the Hajj.

**"And whoever does good willingly"**. Whoever volunteers any good deed not obligatory on him, whether ṭawāf or something else. One view is that this refers to performing ṭawāf more than seven times, another that it means a voluntary ʿUmrah or Hajj, and a third, which al-Rāzī states and which is attributed to al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī, that it means volunteering good works in general. Allah knows best. A variant reading of the verb has its letters assimilated.

**"Allah is truly Appreciative, All-Knowing"**. He accepts such works and knows your intentions. His reward for a small deed is immense, and He knows exactly what reward is sufficient, so He never gives anyone less than their due: "Indeed, Allah never wrongs ˹anyone˺—even by an atom's weight. And if it is a good deed, He will multiply it many times over and will give a great reward out of His grace" (4:40). He accepts the smallest of your works, and His reward is abundant.

### Why the verse says "no sin"

ʿUrwah asked ʿĀʾishah about this verse and suggested that, by Allah, there would be no sin on a person who did not go between the two hills. She replied that what he had said was the worst of readings, O my nephew. Had that been the meaning, the verse would have read "there is no sin on one who does not go round them". Rather, she said, the verse was revealed about the Anṣār. Before Islam they used to enter iḥrām at Mushallal for the idol Manāt that they worshipped, and those who did so used to hesitate to go between Ṣafā and Marwah. After Islam they asked the Messenger of Allah ﷺ about this hesitation of theirs from the days of ignorance, and Allah revealed the verse. ʿĀʾishah added that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ made going between the hills part of the Sunnah, and no one should abandon it. The hadith is in the Ṣaḥīḥayn. In another version ʿUrwah later mentioned ʿĀʾishah's statement to Abū Bakr ibn ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn al-Ḥārith ibn Hishām. He said he had not heard this. He had, however, heard learned men say that everyone except those ʿĀʾishah mentioned used to call going between the two hills a practice of the Jāhiliyyah, while others among the Anṣār said they had been commanded to make ṭawāf of the Kaʿbah but not between Ṣafā and Marwah. Abū Bakr ibn ʿAbd al-Raḥmān concluded that the verse seems to have been revealed about both groups. Al-Bukhārī has a similar narration from Anas, who said: we disliked going between Ṣafā and Marwah because they were shrines of Quraysh in the pre-Islamic period, so we abandoned them in Islam, and then Allah revealed this verse.

The reports on the occasion of revelation come through several chains. One runs through Muṣʿab ibn ʿAbd Allāh al-Zubayrī from Mālik from Hishām from his father ʿUrwah from ʿĀʾishah, who said the verse was revealed about the Helpers, who used to make pilgrimage to Manāt near Qudayd and avoided going between Ṣafā and Marwah until they asked the Messenger of Allah ﷺ about it when Islam came. Al-Bukhārī narrates this from ʿAbd Allāh ibn Yūsuf from Mālik. Another chain, through Yaḥyā and ʿAbd al-Raḥmān from Hishām from his father, has ʿĀʾishah say that it concerned a group of the Helpers who before Islam made pilgrimage to Manāt and were forbidden to go between the hills, and who raised the matter when they went on pilgrimage with the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. Muslim narrates it from Abū Bakr ibn Abī Shaybah from Abū Usāmah from Hishām from his father from ʿĀʾishah.

ʿUmar ibn Ḥubshī asked Ibn ʿUmar about the verse and was sent to Ibn ʿAbbās, who explained that each hill had carried an idol, a male figure called Isāf on Ṣafā and a female figure called Nāʾilah on Marwah. According to a claim of the People of the Book, the two had committed adultery inside the Kaʿbah, were turned to stone by Allah, and were set on the two hills so that people might take heed. With the passage of time they came to be worshipped instead of Allah, and the people of the Jāhiliyyah stroked them whenever they passed between the hills. After embracing Islam and seeing the idols destroyed, the Muslims still hesitated over the walk because of its association with those idols. Al-Shaʿbī reported the same, that Isāf was on Ṣafā and Nāʾilah on Marwah and that people used to touch them, so that after Islam they were hesitant about the walk until this verse came down.

The wording "no sin", then, must be read in the light of the question it answers. One might think the Qur'an merely says that the saʿy is "no sin", which at most would make it one of many permitted acts. But the question was about the idols on the two hills and the fact that the people of the Jāhiliyyah did the saʿy to show devotion to them, which seemed to make the practice forbidden (ḥarām). It is in answer to that doubt that Allah declared it free of sin. Since it is the real and authentic tradition of Ibrāhīm, there is no reason to think it tainted, and the malpractice of a pagan band in the intervening period does not turn what is good in the sight of Allah into a sin. The expression "no sin" therefore does not go against the saʿy being obligatory. A reported view of Ibn ʿAbbās makes the walk optional, understanding the absence of sin as allowing choice. Al-Shāfiʿī and others instead regard it as a pillar of the Hajj. The Prophet ﷺ made the requirement clear.

### The ruling and the Prophet's ﷺ practice

Muslim records Jābir's long hadith about the pilgrimage. After completing ṭawāf, the Messenger of Allah ﷺ returned to the corner and kissed the Black Stone. He left through the door near Ṣafā, reciting "Indeed, Ṣafā and Marwah are among the symbols of Allah". He said that his starting point would be what Allah had commanded him to begin with. In al-Nasāʾī's narration he said: begin with what Allah began with, meaning Ṣafā. Imām Aḥmad reports Ḥabībah bint Abī Tajrah's observation of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ performing saʿy. The people walked ahead of him between Ṣafā and Marwah. His pace was fast enough to twist his garment around his knees. He instructed them to perform saʿy because Allah had prescribed it for them. Al-Bayhaqī and others also report this saying. The hadith is used as proof that the saʿy is a pillar (rukn) of the Hajj. It has also been said that it is obligatory (wājib) rather than a pillar, so that whoever omits it, by mistake or deliberately, can make up the shortcoming with a sacrifice (dam). The positions of the schools are that the saʿy is a commendable practice of the Prophet ﷺ according to Imām Aḥmad, an absolute obligation (farḍ) according to Mālik and al-Shāfiʿī, and a necessity (wājib) according to Abū Ḥanīfah, which means that one who abandons it must slaughter a goat in compensation. The details of how the Hajj, the ʿUmrah and the saʿy are performed are readily available in the books of fiqh.

### Hājar's search and the pilgrim's state of heart

Ibn ʿAbbās related, in a hadith mentioned earlier, that the origin of this rite is the going back and forth of Hājar, the wife of Ibrāhīm, between Ṣafā and Marwah in search of water for her son Ismāʿīl (Ishmael). Ibrāhīm, a native of Iraq, had left them at Allah's command in the place now known as Makkah, where there was neither habitation nor water. When Hājar feared her son would die she stood up, begged Allah for help and kept going between the two hills, humble, fearful and meek before Him. After seven unsuccessful attempts she returned to find the spring of Zamzam flowing from the ground. Allah had answered her prayer, relieved her loneliness, ended her plight and given her water that is nourishing food and a cure for sickness. The event is a sign of how Allah looks after His servants. Whoever persists in His service until there is nothing but burning sand beneath his feet will find Allah in His mercy bringing a refreshing spring out of the dry desert. When Muslims make the pilgrimage they repeat Hājar's historic quest between the hills and so commemorate what it means for everyone who struggles in Allah's path.

Whoever performs the saʿy, therefore, should remember his own meekness and humility and his need of Allah to guide his heart, to bring his affairs to success and to forgive his sins. He should want Allah to remove his shortcomings and errors, to guide him to the straight path, to keep him firm on it until he dies, and to change his condition from one of sin to one of perfection and forgiveness, the very providence that was granted to Hājar.

### Honoured for the neighbour's sake

In the devotional reading, these sites and relics, these ruins and remains, are extolled and visited because they are the ruins of the lovers, where the traces still gleam. The passions of houses belong to those who lived in them, and there is no concern or joy in the house itself. Even the dust of the lovers' footprints has tremendous value for those who love them, and the smallest grain of dust on the edge of their path is more precious than the most fragrant musk, simply because the beloved once walked beside it. Ṣafā and Marwah were favoured by being close to the House. Running between them became a prescribed rite alongside circling the House. Both that running and the ṭawāf hold a principal place in pilgrimage. The neighbour is honoured for the sake of the neighbour.

### In short

- Ṣafā and Marwah are among the marks of Allah's religion, and the saʿy between them belongs to the rites Allah gave Ibrāhīm, continuing the Kaʿbah theme that began at verse 124.
- "No sin" answers the Muslims' fear that the walk was a pagan practice because of the idols Isāf and Nāʾilah. ʿĀʾishah insisted it does not mean the walk is optional, and the Prophet ﷺ made it part of the Sunnah (Ṣaḥīḥayn, al-Bukhārī from Anas).
- The Prophet ﷺ began at Ṣafā "with what Allah began with" (Muslim, al-Nasāʾī) and said Allah had prescribed the saʿy (Aḥmad, al-Bayhaqī). It is a pillar or farḍ for Mālik and al-Shāfiʿī, wājib for Abū Ḥanīfah, and commendable for Aḥmad.
- The rite re-enacts Hājar's search for water, and the pilgrim should perform it with her humility and need, asking Allah for guidance, steadfastness and forgiveness.
- Voluntary good of every kind is accepted and rewarded in full by the Appreciative, All-Knowing (4:40).

159.text:
Several verses earlier, in the debate over the qiblah, verse 146 pointed out that the People of the Book recognise the Prophet ﷺ as they recognise their own sons, and that a group of them conceals the truth knowingly. Verse 159 concludes that subject with a stern warning to those who not only hide the truth but persist obstinately in doing so. "Those who hide the clear proofs and guidance that We have revealed—after We made it clear for humanity in the Book—will be condemned by Allah and ˹all˺ those who condemn". Abū al-ʿĀliyah connects these verses with concealment of Muḥammad's ﷺ description by recipients of Scripture. Another report concerns their scholars hiding both his description and the verse prescribing stoning for married adulterers.

### Phrase by phrase

**"Those who hide the clear proofs and guidance that We have revealed"**. The clear proofs are the signs the messengers were sent with, which guide to the correct path, together with the commands and prohibitions mentioned in the Torah. The guidance is what benefits hearts, and in particular the description of Muḥammad ﷺ and his features given in the Torah. The Jews and Christians who hid the proofs showing the truth of the Prophet ﷺ and what he brought are the first people meant.

**"after We made it clear for humanity in the Book"**. Allah had made all this plain to His servants through the Books He revealed to His messengers, and to the Children of Israel in the Torah, so there was no excuse of ignorance.

**"will be condemned by Allah and ˹all˺ those who condemn"**. Allah removes them far from His mercy, and one reading adds that He torments them in the grave. Abū al-ʿĀliyah, al-Rabīʿ ibn Anas and Qatādah said that "those who condemn" are the angels and the believers. Others include the prophets, or every single thing, which curses them when it prays that they be cursed, or all created beings other than humans and jinn, who curse them when they hear their screams from the grave. The contrast is with creation's prayers for a scholar's forgiveness, including those of fish and birds. Concealing knowledge instead brings Allah's curse and the curse of those who condemn. Mujāhid said that when drought strikes the earth the animals say that this is because of the sinners among the children of Adam, and ask Allah to curse them. Mujāhid and ʿIkrimah noted that the verse leaves the cursers unspecified, which suggests that everything and every living being curses such people, animals and insects included, because their misdeeds harm all created life. A hadith from al-Barāʾ ibn ʿĀzib, which al-Qurṭubī cites from Ibn Mājah, has the Prophet ﷺ say that "those who curse" are all the creatures that move on the earth. The warning thus encompasses this life and resurrection. Allah, angels, humanity and every other condemning being curse the concealers, each according to its own manner. Allah knows best.

### The duty to pass on religious knowledge

Concealing the clear signs and guidance Allah has revealed is a terrible crime that earns the curse of Allah and of His whole creation. Several rulings follow from this. First, it is forbidden to conceal knowledge that must be disclosed and spread. The Musnad records, through several chains that strengthen one another, that Abū Hurayrah related the Prophet's ﷺ saying that whoever is asked about knowledge he possesses and hides it will have a bridle of fire fastened on his mouth on the Day of Resurrection. Al-Qurṭubī gives it from Abū Hurayrah and ʿAmr ibn al-ʿĀṣ as reported by Ibn Mājah. The jurists say this warning applies to a person who is the only knowledgeable one available in a given situation. If others are present, he may suggest that the question be put to a scholar who knows, as al-Qurṭubī and al-Jaṣṣāṣ explain. Second, one who lacks sound knowledge of religious rulings should not try to explain them. Third, answers to intricate religious questions beyond the grasp of ordinary people should not be set before them, lest they fall into misunderstanding. This is not concealment of knowledge, since what is forbidden is hiding the clear guidance of the Qur'an and Sunnah, which must be spread widely, and the verse's phrase "clear proofs and guidance" strongly suggests this limit. It was of such questions that the Companion ʿAbd Allāh ibn Masʿūd said that reciting hadiths which people do not fully understand throws them into a nest of discord. Al-Bukhārī reports ʿAlī as saying: disclose to people only as much knowledge as they have the capacity to understand, or do you want them to deny Allah and His Messenger ﷺ? Anything beyond their comprehension breeds doubt and may lead them to reject it.

A scholar or guide is therefore responsible for assessing people's ability to receive what he communicates, and sensitive questions should not be raised before someone likely to fall into error. This is why jurists, when discussing such questions in writing, close with a standard warning that the matter is delicate and should be kept to the scholar's own understanding rather than broadcast. A saying attributed to the Prophet ﷺ warns against withholding wisdom from a deserving person or offering it to someone unfit to receive it. The first wrongs the person. The second wrongs wisdom itself. Al-Qurṭubī draws a limit for teaching Islamic disciplines to opponents. A disbeliever engaged in polemics, or someone promoting misleading religious ideas, should receive such teaching only when its correcting effect is certain. Likewise, rulers should not be given rulings they could misuse to terrorise their citizens, and the concessions (rukhṣah) and legal stratagems (ḥiyal) should not be aired in public unnecessarily, lest people grow used to seeking excuses in practising the faith.

### Hadith falls under the same warning

Al-Bukhārī records that Abū Hurayrah said: were it not for a verse in the Book of Allah, I would not have narrated a single hadith to anyone, and he then recited this verse. Other Companions are reported to have said similar things while narrating hadith. These reports show that in the Companions' view the hadith of the Prophet ﷺ shares some of the privileges stated for the Qur'an. The verse itself warns those who conceal what was revealed in the Qur'an and does not mention hadith, but the Companions ruled that the Prophet's ﷺ hadith was covered by the reference, so that concealing hadith would bring the same warning upon them.

### Stinginess with the knowledge of the Path

The devotional reading concerns knowledge of the Path's proper conduct unveiled by the Real. Some recipients then become reluctant to share it with aspirants seeking counsel and guidance. At that moment they become deserving of wrath, and one fears that the blessing will be removed from their knowledge, since they fell short in it just as they held back from imparting it to the deserving.

### In short

- The verse condemns the People of the Book who hid the Torah's description of the Prophet ﷺ and the stoning verse, concluding the theme of verse 146.
- They are cursed by Allah and by all who curse: angels, believers, prophets and, as Mujāhid, ʿIkrimah and the hadith of al-Barāʾ indicate, every creature harmed by their sin.
- Hiding needed religious knowledge brings a bridle of fire (Abū Hurayrah, Ibn Mājah), yet knowledge must be matched to the hearer's capacity (ʿAlī in al-Bukhārī, Ibn Masʿūd), and al-Qurṭubī draws further limits for polemicists, rulers and concessions.
- Abū Hurayrah narrated hadith because of this verse, showing that the Companions held hadith to fall under the same duty of disclosure.

160.text:
The fate of those who persist in concealment is obvious, yet Allah still holds out His mercy. "As for those who repent, mend their ways, and let the truth be known, they are the ones to whom I will turn ˹in forgiveness˺, for I am the Accepter of Repentance, Most Merciful". Allah excludes from the curse everyone who repents to Him, regrets what he has been doing, corrects his conduct and makes known to people what he had hidden.

### Phrase by phrase

**"As for those who repent"**. Those who turn back from such deeds and ask forgiveness, regretting that they hid the clear signs. For the People of the Book, the explanation here means turning from Judaism and accepting Islam. Belief in Allah and His Prophet ﷺ then demonstrates an honest change of heart.

**"mend their ways"**. They make amends in their actions, correcting what they do outwardly and inwardly, and worship Allah alone without ascribing partners to Him.

**"and let the truth be known"**. They show clearly what they used to conceal, the truth and guidance they had hidden, and in particular the traits and description of Muḥammad ﷺ. To demonstrate their changed stand they come forward and state the truth clearly and publicly.

**"they are the ones to whom I will turn ˹in forgiveness˺"**. Allah accepts their repentance and overlooks their past transgressions. He turns to those who turn to Him asking forgiveness and regretting what they did. The verse also shows that those who used to call people to innovation, or even to disbelief, are forgiven by Allah if they repent to Him.

**"for I am the Accepter of Repentance, Most Merciful"**. He is the Relenting towards those who repent and the Merciful towards the believers, and towards whoever dies in a state of repentance.

### Making amends by guiding others

In the devotional reading, those excepted are the ones who make up for their past negligence by graciously turning back and taking on the task of advising the aspirants. They show them clearly the goodness of keeping to certain modes of behaviour, explaining and demonstrating it beautifully. The clearest proof of the sincerity of your actions, and the truest testimony to the message by which you call people to Allah, is that your behaviour does not contradict what you allude to in your speech. As the prophet Shuʿayb said to his people: "I do not want to do what I am forbidding you from" (11:88).

### In short

- The curse of verse 159 is lifted from whoever repents, reforms his conduct and openly declares the truth he concealed, which for the People of the Book means embracing Islam.
- Even those who once preached innovation or disbelief are forgiven on sincere repentance, for Allah is the Accepter of Repentance and Most Merciful.
- Inwardly, amends for withholding guidance are made by guiding others, and one's conduct must match one's words (11:88).

161.text:
After the exception for those who repent, Allah states the fate of those who do not. "Surely those who disbelieve and die as disbelievers are condemned by Allah, the angels, and all of humanity". Those who disbelieve in Allah and His Messenger ﷺ and remain in that state until they die, without repenting, deserve this curse in this life and the next.

### Phrase by phrase

**"Surely those who disbelieve and die as disbelievers"**. The phrase "while they are disbelievers" is a circumstantial clause: the curse falls on those whose disbelief lasts until death.

**"are condemned by Allah, the angels, and all of humanity"**. The curse of Allah is His torment and His removing them from His mercy. The angels curse them, and so do people, whether this means people in general or the believers, all of whom call for them to be excluded from Allah's mercy. One gloss adds that the curses believers direct at one another end up falling on these disbelievers.

### Cursing in general and cursing by name

There is no disagreement that cursing the disbelievers as a class is lawful. During qunūt in prayer, and at other times, ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb invoked a curse on the disbelievers. Later imams continued that practice. Cursing a specific disbeliever is another matter. Some scholars held it impermissible, because we do not know how Allah will bring about his end. Others allowed it, citing the story of the man repeatedly brought for punishment for drinking: when someone said "may Allah curse him, how often he is brought", the Messenger of Allah ﷺ forbade that curse because the man loved Allah and His Messenger. They understood the reply to permit cursing someone who lacked that love. Allah knows best. From the words "and die as disbelievers", al-Jaṣṣāṣ, al-Qurṭubī and others concluded that it is not permissible to curse a disbeliever about whom it is not certain that he will die in disbelief. Since we have no way of knowing in what state a person will die, we are bound by the ruling that cursing a disbeliever by name is not permitted. That the Prophet ﷺ cursed some disbelievers by name is explained by the fact that their death in disbelief was revealed to him. Cursing the disbelievers as a whole, including tyrants and the unjust, without specifying anyone, is technically correct.

It follows that cursing is so grave that it is disallowed even against a disbeliever whose end is uncertain. How then could it be permissible against a Muslim, or even against an animal? Ordinary people in Muslim societies neglect this aspect of proper conduct, and women in particular are prone to very hard language about acquaintances they dislike. Cursing is not confined to the word "curse": every synonym falls under the same ruling. Laʿnah means being driven away from the mercy of Allah, so all damning language, whatever its shade, circumstance or tongue, counts as laʿnah.

### In short

- Those who die in disbelief without repenting are cursed by Allah, the angels and all people, in this world and the next.
- Cursing disbelievers in general, as ʿUmar did in the qunūt, is lawful. Cursing a named person is not, since no one knows how he will die (al-Jaṣṣāṣ, al-Qurṭubī), and the Prophet's ﷺ naming of some was by revelation.
- Cursing is grave enough that it is forbidden even against an uncertain disbeliever, let alone a Muslim or an animal, and every form of damning speech counts.

162.text:
Verse 162 describes how long the curse lasts. "They will be in Hell forever. Their punishment will not be lightened, nor will they be delayed ˹from it˺". Those who die in disbelief suffer the eternal curse until the Day of Resurrection and after it in the fire of Jahannam.

### Phrase by phrase

**"They will be in Hell forever."**. They abide for ever in the curse and in the Fire, which the next words indicate.

**"Their punishment will not be lightened"**. It will not be lifted, decreased or reduced, not even for a day or for the blink of an eye.

**"nor will they be delayed ˹from it˺"**. Their torment will not be deferred, changed or tempered even for an hour. They are given no respite in which to repent or excuse themselves, and no extra time on the Day of Judgement. It is continuous and eternal. We seek refuge with Allah from such an end.

### Those who turn back from the Path

In the devotional reading, verses 161 and 162 allude to those who travel the path of spiritual desire but then choose a return to habitual life. They die while caught in that estrangement. They are the companions of separation. There is no drawing near for their spirits, no setting right of their calamity, and no one to ask mercy for them. They have lost in this world and the Hereafter, cursed by the gnats in the air and the stagnation in the water. "Abiding" means that they remain for ever in their contemptible position, insignificant, with no lessening of it and no relief, without kindness or favour.

### In short

- The curse on those who die disbelieving is eternal: in Hell their punishment is neither reduced nor postponed, and no respite is given for repentance or excuse.
- Inwardly, the warning is for those who abandon the Path for the life of habit and die in that estrangement, the companions of separation.

163.text:
Verse 163 follows the warning to those who die in disbelief by declaring the truth they denied. "Your God is ˹only˺ One God. There is no god ˹worthy of worship˺ except Him—the Most Compassionate, Most Merciful". When the idolaters (mushrikīn) of Arabia heard "your God is one God", so contrary to their belief, they were puzzled how there could be a single object of worship for the whole wide world, and felt that so serious a claim needed proof. That proof is given tersely in this verse and the next. One report says the verse was revealed when they asked Muḥammad ﷺ to describe his Lord.

### Phrase by phrase

**"Your God is ˹only˺ One God."**. The One deserving of your worship is one God, without son or partner, without equal in essence or attributes, unique in both. He is the One and Only, the Sustainer, with no partners or equals.

**"There is no god ˹worthy of worship˺ except Him"**. No one else has the right to be worshipped. Allah declares His Oneness here because the disbelievers denied it.

**"the Most Compassionate, Most Merciful"**. He is al-Raḥmān, the Most Gracious, the Tender, whose mercy is vast, and al-Raḥīm, the Most Merciful, compassionate with His creation and surrounding them with blessings. These two Names were explained at the beginning of Sūrat al-Fātiḥah. Shahr ibn Ḥawshab reported from Asmāʾ bint Yazīd ibn al-Sakan that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said that Allah's Greatest Name is contained in two verses: this one, and the opening of Sūrat Āl ʿImrān, "Alif-Lām-Mīm" (3:1) followed by "Allah! There is no god except Him, the Ever-Living, the Sustainer of all". Allah then goes on, in the next verse, to mention some of the proofs that He alone is God, for He created the heavens and the earth and all the creatures between them, and all of them testify to His Oneness.

### Tawḥīd in its wider sense

Tawḥīd, the cardinal principle of the faith, is proved repeatedly in the Qur'an, so a summary suffices here. First, He is One in His being: nothing in the universe of His creation is like Him, He has no duplicate, replica, equal or parallel, and so unshared is His station that He alone deserves to be called al-Wāḥid, the One. Second, He is One in the right to be worshipped: given the nature of His Being, the completeness of His perfect attributes and the wonder of His creation and nurture of it, all human obedience and all worship (ʿibādah) must be for Him alone. Third, He is One in being free of any composition: He has no parts, segments, organs, substances, elements, atoms or particles, and cannot be analysed, divided or resolved. Fourth, He is One in being the first and the last: He existed when nothing else did and will exist when nothing else does. Who then, if not He, should be called the only One? This summary is al-Jaṣṣāṣ's.

Humanity has only one God, and He is the only worthy focus of a person's attention. Our very existence on earth and all the benefits we draw from the world around us are manifestations of His boundless grace and mercy. Our response should be devoted service. Life and death should be for Him, with every hope directed towards His eternal favour. A person owes everything to his Creator. Once he becomes conscious of that debt, his Lord comes to mean everything to him, the way a mother is everything to her infant.

### One in everything

In the devotional reading, the verse describes the one Lord, who is God and King. His oneness shows in magnanimity and in governance, in forbearance and in beautiful doing, in generosity and in peerlessness, in loving kindness and in the caressing of His servants. Every magnificence is the mantle of His majesty and every tremendousness the shawl of His lordship, and in these He is one. He is one in Essence, in attributes, in deed and mark, in loyalty and covenant, in gentleness, in love and friendship. On the day the portions were apportioned, who was there but He, the One? Before it, who was there? That same One. After it, who handed over the portions, who shows, who adorns? That same One. He surpasses every apparent thing in manifestation and every hidden thing in hiddenness. His oneness remains in both. The address pictures Him as most directly present yet most concealed, farther than the servants imagine yet nearer than the spirit's vein. It censures the child of Adam who fails to value this declaration and its exalted connection. The wonder is not that He ascribed the servants to Himself and said, "My servants" (15:42). The greater wonder is His connecting Himself with His servants. He joins His name to theirs in the words "Your God". This is not because His lordship must be joined to their servanthood, or because they deserve it, but because in generosity and loving kindness He is unique and one. In the presence of our Heart-taker's beauty we are not suited for Him. He is suited for us. There was no world and no Adam, no tracks and no traces, no one in the house, and your God was one God.

### In short

- Against the idolaters' astonishment, the verse declares that God is one, without partner, son or equal, and alone has the right to worship. The next verse gives the proof from creation.
- The Greatest Name of Allah lies in this verse and the opening of Āl ʿImrān (3:1), according to the hadith of Asmāʾ bint Yazīd.
- Tawḥīd means He is one in being, in the right to worship, in freedom from composition, and in being first and last (al-Jaṣṣāṣ).
- Inwardly, the wonder is that the One joined His name to His servants' name, "your God", out of pure generosity (cf. 15:42).

164.text:
The idolaters had asked for proof of the claim in verse 163 that God is one, and this verse answers with a series of signs that the learned and the unlettered can grasp alike. "Indeed, in the creation of the heavens and the earth; the alternation of the day and the night; the ships that sail the sea for the benefit of humanity;" then "the rain sent down by Allah from the skies, reviving the earth after its death; the scattering of all kinds of creatures throughout;" and finally "the shifting of the winds; and the clouds drifting between the heavens and the earth—˹in all of this˺ are surely signs for people of understanding". The message is simple and clear: the origination and continuance of all these things is the work of His perfect power alone, and no being other than He can take the credit.

### Phrase by phrase

**"Indeed, in the creation of the heavens and the earth;"**. The sky with its height, its intricate design, its vastness and the heavenly bodies in their orbits, and the earth with its density, its lowlands, mountains, seas, deserts and valleys and all the useful things it holds. The sign lies in their making, or in the making of the marvels they contain. Who can bypass the wonder of the creation of the heavens and the earth?

**"the alternation of the day and the night;"**. One comes and goes and the other follows without delaying an instant, as Allah says: "It is not for the sun to catch up with the moon, nor does the night outrun the day. Each is travelling in an orbit of their own" (36:40). Sometimes the day shortens and the night lengthens, sometimes the reverse, each taking from the length of the other: "He merges the night into day and the day into night" (57:6). The alternation is understood by some to include the passing of life and death, happiness and sorrow, wealth and poverty.

**"the ships that sail the sea for the benefit of humanity;"**. Allah shaped the sea so that it can carry ships from one shore to another, and the ships run on it without cracking and sinking, so that people enjoy what other regions have and export their own goods in return, food, clothing and merchandise of every kind. It is a formidable sign of His power that water, so liquid and fluid, lifts on its back ships carrying tons of weight from East to West. Had water not been given the state in which its particles move freely while remaining one mass, no maritime activity would exist, and even with that fluidity the help of the winds was needed to cross thousands of miles of sea: "If He wills, He can calm the wind, leaving the ships motionless on the water. Surely in this are signs for whoever is steadfast, grateful" (42:33). "For the benefit of humanity" points to the countless benefits people gain from trading their goods by sea, benefits that vary from country to country and from age to age.

**"the rain sent down by Allah from the skies, reviving the earth after its death;"**. He revives the earth with vegetation after drought has dried it out: "There is a sign for them in the dead earth: We give it life, producing grain from it for them to eat" (36:33), down to "Glory be to the One Who created all ˹things in˺ pairs—˹be it˺ what the earth produces, their genders, or what they do not know" (36:36). The water descends drop by drop, in a measure and manner that harms nothing, for if it always came as a flood nothing would survive. Nor is the raining the whole marvel. The storage of water on earth baffles human ingenuity. If everyone were asked to store a six-month quota of water for personal use, how would anyone manage it, and how could it be kept drinkable and clean all that time? Allah in His mercy took care of this too: "We send down rain from the sky in perfect measure, causing it to soak into the earth. And We are surely able to take it away" (23:18). Water is stored openly in ponds and lakes for people and animals, lowered under mountains and valleys into a hidden network accessible to anyone who digs, and kept as a vast sea of ice on the mountain ranges, safe from spoiling and melting slowly to reach the world through nature's own water lines.

**"the scattering of all kinds of creatures throughout;"**. He creates and spreads living things of every shape, colour, use and size, male and female, dividing them across the earth where the vegetation gives them fertile pasture. Allah knows them all, sustains them, and nothing is hidden from Him: "There is no moving creature on earth whose provision is not guaranteed by Allah. And He knows where it lives and where it is laid to rest. All is ˹written˺ in a perfect Record" (11:6), that is, in the Preserved Tablet (al-Lawḥ al-Maḥfūẓ).

**"the shifting of the winds;"**. Allah harnesses the winds to serve humanity and in His wisdom keeps changing their direction, to right and to left, from south to north and from cold to warm. Sometimes the wind brings mercy and sometimes torment. Sometimes it announces the clouds that follow it, sometimes it leads them, herding, scattering or directing them. It blows from the north, from the south, from the east striking the front of the Kaʿbah, and from the west striking its back. Many books have been written about winds, rain, stars and the rules concerning them, but this is not the place to elaborate.

**"and the clouds drifting between the heavens and the earth"**. The clouds are compelled and subjected by Allah's command, running between sky and earth to whatever lands He wills without being attached to either.

**"˹in all of this˺ are surely signs for people of understanding"**. All these things are clear signs testifying to Allah's Oneness for those who comprehend and contemplate, who understand evidence and proof and who believe that these things come from Him. Allah says likewise: "Indeed, in the creation of the heavens and the earth and the alternation of the day and night there are signs for people of reason" (3:190), "˹They are˺ those who remember Allah while standing, sitting, and lying on their sides, and reflect on the creation of the heavens and the earth" (3:191).

### The universe as an introduction to its Maker

The vast universe spread out before us is a magnificent introduction to Allah. A limitless world of earth and heavens proves that a Creator stands behind it. Its apparently different and contrasting elements work together in complete harmony, which shows that their Creator and Sustainer is one and only one God. Every single thing benefits the rest of the universe in some way, which shows that all of it is designed on a definite and fully conscious plan. Seemingly lifeless things are given life through natural processes, showing that death here is only a temporary phase always followed by new life. Every kind of living creature flourishes in huge numbers, all sustained by varied forms of the same food and drink, a token of Allah's unfathomable power. The atmosphere wrapping the whole earth shows that human life lies entirely in the Creator's hands, and the fact that everything in the universe has been tamed to serve human needs, with every requirement provided before a person is even born, shows that the Creator is deeply compassionate. These signs are reflections of the Creator in His creation. The universe displays His existence and His oneness on so vast a scale, combining every aspect of perfection, that no one with any vision or a grain of intelligence can fail to discover Him in it. Yet the signs serve as proofs only for the one who reflects on them sincerely. To reach the truth one must search for it sincerely, rise above worldly considerations before drawing conclusions, and be absorbed not in externals but in the inner reality beneath the surface of things. Allah's Oneness is thus proved by citing some manifestations of His perfect power, a subject that al-Jaṣṣāṣ, al-Qurṭubī and others treat in great detail.

### Three gazes

In the devotional reading, the Lord of the universe here shows people in general the road to Himself, so that they may gaze on the wonders of the dominion of heaven and earth and the artisanry of land and sea, recognise the Artisan and attest to His oneness. Ibn ʿAṭāʾ said that He made Himself known to the common people through His creation, to the elect through His attributes, and to the prophets and the elect of the elect through His Essence. The gaze of ordinary believers rests on the artisanry, and from the artisanry they reach the Artisan. The elect among the faithful know the attributes, and from the attributes reach the One described, from the name the Named. So when the Children of Israel were told, "Allah commands you to sacrifice a cow" (2:67), they did not recognise it until the cow had been described to them, and then they sacrificed it. The prophets and the sincerely truthful recognise Him through Him and not through anything else. They look from Him to Him, not from the other to Him. Allah alludes to this state in the words, "Have you not seen how your Lord extends the shade" (25:45). The instruction was not to look at the shadow in order to see His artisanry. It was to look at Him, and so see His artisanry. The paragon of the world is told not to fix on Gabriel's coming but on the One who sends him, looking from Allah to the angel rather than from the angel to Allah. Consider the women who were the companions of Joseph. When the very being of Joseph was unveiled to them, they were annihilated from themselves and became oblivious even of Joseph's attributes.

### In short

- As proof that God is one, the verse points to seven signs: the heavens and earth, the alternation of night and day (36:40, 57:6), ships on the sea (42:33), rain reviving the dead earth and stored in the ground (36:33, 23:18), the spread of living creatures (11:6), the shifting winds and the suspended clouds.
- Each sign shows a single power, knowledge and wisdom at work, for only one Creator could make contrasting elements serve one harmonious plan centred on human need.
- The signs convince only those who reflect sincerely, rising above worldly motives (3:190-191).
- Inwardly, the common people know Allah through His works, the elect through His attributes, and the prophets through Himself (Ibn ʿAṭāʾ, cf. 2:67, 25:45).

165.text:
The preceding verses set out Allah's Oneness strongly and positively, with its proofs. Verse 165 turns to the error of those who, despite such clear signs, give others a share in His divinity and treat them as the caretakers of their needs. "Still there are some who take others as Allah's equal—they love them as they should love Allah—but the ˹true˺ believers love Allah even more." The verse continues: "If only the wrongdoers could see the ˹horrible˺ punishment ˹awaiting them˺, they would certainly realize that all power belongs to Allah and that Allah is indeed severe in punishment". Here Allah describes the condition of the polytheists in this life, before turning in the next verses to their destination in the Hereafter.

### Phrase by phrase

**"Still there are some who take others as Allah's equal"**. Among people are disbelievers who set up rivals and equals to Allah, idols that they worship alongside Him, magnifying them and submitting to them. Yet Allah alone is worthy of worship, and He has neither rival nor opponent nor partner. The Ṣaḥīḥayn record that ʿAbd Allāh ibn Masʿūd asked the Messenger of Allah ﷺ which sin is the greatest, and he answered: to set up a rival to Allah when He alone created you. One view is that the verse refers to leaders whom people took as gods. Another connects its revelation with hypocrites hiding precious wealth, whether burying gold and silver or concealing it in caves.

**"they love them as they should love Allah"**. Their attachment to these objects reaches the proportions of the love that is due to Allah alone, a love like the love sincere believers have for Allah.

**"but the ˹true˺ believers love Allah even more."**. The believers' love for Allah is more intense and more lasting than the disbelievers' love for their idols. Because they love Him, know His greatness, revere Him and believe in His Oneness, they associate nothing with Him in worship but worship Him alone, depend on Him and seek His help in every need. A polytheist may turn away from his self-made god when loss threatens, and when things go badly such people call on Allah alone. The believer trusts Allah in gain and loss alike, keeps His love and pleasure as his lasting possession, and never leaves his Creator whatever the odds. The believers never reject Allah, whereas the others soon abandon their idols for Him when hardship comes.

**"If only the wrongdoers could see the ˹horrible˺ punishment ˹awaiting them˺"**. If those who wronged themselves by taking equals to Allah could see the torment on the Day of Judgement, they would behold a terrible sight. The verb "see" (yarā) is read as active or passive, "they see" or "they are made to see", and on one reading its subject is the listener, on another the wrongdoers themselves, in which case it carries the sense of knowing. The response to "if only" is left unstated. If these people knew the terrible punishment that awaits them for their disbelief and shirk, they would shun the deviation they live by.

**"they would certainly realize that all power belongs to Allah and that Allah is indeed severe in punishment"**. All might, power and the ability to vanquish belong to Allah, and His punishment in the Hereafter is severe. At resurrection the idolaters will directly see this truth. Had they possessed that certainty here, they would have believed rather than appoint rivals to Allah. The verse also contains a subtle hint: the opportunity to correct themselves was there. Their frustrations with their gods could have taught them that these were helpless and that real power rests with Allah. They missed it, and must now learn the hard way, hence the stern warning.

### How people make gods

By nature and circumstance human beings look for an external support, a being that compensates for their helplessness and gives them confidence. To give someone this place in one's life is in effect to accept that being as a deity, and whatever becomes the focus of a person's love, devotion and reverence is held to be his god. Since Allah remains invisible in this world, those who judge by appearances tend to grant a visible being the status that belongs only to the Almighty, usually leaders who become the centre of public attention through some mark of distinction. The vacuum in human nature was meant to be filled by Allah, but many fill it with something else, impressed by visible pomp and splendour, by special talents, by seats sanctified by centuries of tradition, by a large following, or by the halo of legend around public figures, and so come to regard certain persons as possessing extraordinary power. In truth, no one in Allah's universe possesses any power or greatness but Allah. A human being can hold the status of divinity only so long as Allah remains unseen. When He appears on the Day of Judgement everything will change so drastically that people will flee from one another. Those who take pride today in their devotion to great men, thinking they are clinging to a firm rock that will help them in the Hereafter, will find that attachment meaningless, as if it had never existed, and will be left to look back on their lives in helpless regret.

### A love that never turns away

The devotional reading finds complete honour for the faithful and Allah's friends in this verse alone. Even without another verse about them, this declaration would establish their eminence. The Lord of the Worlds describes their love for Him as deeper and fuller than the unbelievers' love for their idols. Every so often the unbelievers set up another idol. Like poor people they are content with something carved of wood, and when they can afford it they take the wooden one down and make another of silver or gold. If their love were real, why would they turn from one to another? A man once met a woman among the recognisers of Allah and told her that his all was busy with her all and that he had lost himself in love for her. She asked why he did not look at her sister, who was more beautiful. He asked where the sister was, wanting to see her. Her answer was to send him away as an idler for whom passion was no fit occupation, since a man whose claim of love was true would have had no interest in anyone else. The love of the faithful is not like that. They never turn away from Allah and never incline to another, for if they did they would never find His like however much they sought. Poor man, Allah has many servants like you, and if something bad is to happen to you it will happen, but how can you turn away, when you will not find a Lord like Him? Shiblī traced a lesson in Sufism to a dog asleep outside a house. Driven away repeatedly by the owner, it repeatedly returned. He thought the dog base. In the story Allah then enabled it to speak, asking where else it could go when this man was its owner. The lover will not leave the Friend for a hundred cruelties, and even if they increase he will not be troubled, for he chose Him over everyone else and would have no excuse for complaining.

### In short

- Despite the signs, some give to others the love that is due to Allah alone, and setting up a rival to Him is the greatest sin (Ibn Masʿūd, Ṣaḥīḥayn).
- The believers love Allah more, because they love Him in hardship and ease and never turn away, while the idolater abandons his god when trouble comes.
- Had the wrongdoers seen in this world what they will see on the Day of Judgement, that all power is Allah's and His punishment severe, they would never have taken equals.
- People deify visible leaders and traditions to fill a need meant for Allah, but every such attachment dissolves on the Day of Judgement.
- Inwardly, true love is constancy: the faithful never exchange the Friend for another, as Shiblī learned from the dog that would not leave its master's door.

166.text:
Verse 165 ended by saying that Allah is severe in punishment. How severe will now be shown. "˹Consider the Day˺ when those who misled others will disown their followers—when they face the torment—and the bonds that united them will be cut off". The severity of the punishment will unfold when the leaders whom the polytheists followed disown their own devotees, when both witness the torment, and when every bond of leading and following between them is snapped.

### Phrase by phrase

**"˹Consider the Day˺ when those who misled others will disown their followers"**. The leaders who were followed in disbelief will reject the weak and lowly people who followed them, denying that they ever misled them, once they see the terrors of the Day of Judgement. It is much like what happens in this world when accomplices in a crime wriggle out of it on arrest, going so far as to deny recognising one another. The angels whom the idolaters claimed to worship will declare their innocence of them: "We disassociate ourselves ˹from them˺ before You. It was not us that they used to worship" (28:63), and "Glory be to You! Our loyalty is to You, not them. In fact, they ˹only˺ followed the ˹temptations of evil˺ jinn, in whom most of them had faith" (34:41). The angels thus declare themselves Allah's walī, His loyal protected ones, and not the idolaters'. The jinn too will disown those who worshipped them: "And when ˹such˺ people will be gathered together, those ˹gods˺ will be their enemies and will disown their worship" (46:6), for who could be more astray than one who calls on what cannot answer until the Day of Judgement (46:5). The false gods "will deny their worship and turn against them" (19:81-82). Prophet Ibrāhīm (Abraham) told his people that they had taken idols only to keep harmony among themselves in this life, "But on the Day of Judgment you will disown and curse one another. Your home will be the Fire, and you will have no helper!" (29:25). The lowly will say to the arrogant, "Had it not been for you, we would certainly have been believers", and the arrogant will reply, "Did we ever hinder you from guidance after it came to you? In fact, you were wicked ˹on your own˺" (34:31-33). Satan himself will say after the judgement, "I did not have any authority over you. I only called you, and you responded to me. So do not blame me; blame yourselves" (14:22).

**"when they face the torment"**. Both the leaders and the lowly behold the punishment in the Hereafter.

**"and the bonds that united them will be cut off"**. The pledges and affection, the ties of friendship and kinship that existed between them on earth, collapse. ʿAṭāʾ reported that Ibn ʿAbbās explained the bonds as the friendship, and Mujāhid said the same in a narration of Ibn Abī Najīḥ. When they see Allah's torment, their power and every means of salvation are cut off, with no way of making amends and no escape from the Fire.

### Why the idolaters' love fails and the believers' love holds

In the devotional reading, the unbelievers loved their idols in keeping with caprice and nature, not reality. At resurrection, the first sight of punishment exposes their lack of any secure support. They then abandon their idols. The friendship of the faithful, by contrast, is the fruit of the Real's own friendship, as He says: "who love Him and are loved by Him" (5:54). Difficult paths and trials therefore do not diminish their love or turn them from the Real. They first endure the pains of dying. Their pure spirit is then taken, and years pass while they lie in the dust. Then they are frightened again and again at the resurrection in its various stations, rebuked and shown severity of many kinds, and some are kept for a time in hell. Despite all these tribulations, at every moment they fall further into passion and spend their spirits and hearts even more in friendship for the Real, saying in the language of their state: if You are happy with my grief, give me grief upon grief, and away with a passion that lessens under a hundred cruelties. That is why He said that those who have faith are more intense in love for Allah.

### In short

- The punishment of shirk begins with betrayal: the leaders and false gods, whether angels, jinn, idols or Satan, disown those who followed them (28:63, 34:41, 46:6, 19:82, 29:25, 34:31-33, 14:22).
- Every tie of friendship, kinship and loyalty between leader and led is severed before their eyes, and with it every means of escape (Ibn ʿAbbās, Mujāhid).
- Inwardly, a love founded on caprice collapses at the first sight of torment, while a love born of Allah's love (5:54) only deepens under trial.

167.text:
The followers now face the leaders who abandoned them. They cry, "If only we could have a second chance, we would disown them as they disowned us." Their wish cannot undo the choices made in earthly life. The verse turns from that futile hope to the regret their deeds now bring.

### Phrase by phrase

**"The ˹misled˺ followers will cry, 'If only we could have a second chance, we would disown them as they disowned us.'"** The weak followers wish to return to the world. They would refuse the allegiance their leaders once demanded and turn the rejection back upon them. They also claim they would abandon the idols and worship Allah alone.

**"And so Allah will make them remorseful of their misdeeds."** Their past actions appear as causes of anguish rather than resources for rescue. Seeing the punishment and their mutual rejection makes the consequences of following falsehood plain.

**"And they will never ˹be able to˺ leave the Fire"** The warning includes leaders and followers alike. For the shirk described here, associating others with Allah, the punishment is an enduring stay. Neither group can escape by blaming the other.

### Why would a return not repair their choices?

The words if only express a wish, with we would disown as its imagined result. The followers want another chance partly to settle the account with those who used them. The explanation also reads their promise of exclusive worship as false: if returned, they would go back to the forbidden conduct.

Their distress therefore does not establish a transformed purpose. The opportunity for obedient choice belonged to the life they have already spent. Regret at the result cannot now replace those deeds.

### How are the lost deeds pictured?

The explanation recalls (25:23), where apparent good is reduced to scattered dust. In (14:18), the deeds of those denying their Lord resemble ashes swept away by a storm. The mirage in (24:39) promises water but yields nothing when approached.

Each comparison reveals a failure at the moment of need. What seemed usable cannot provide the hoped-for benefit. The followers now see not only the punishment but the emptiness of the actions in which they had placed confidence.

### What does the inward reading emphasise?

The devotional reflection speaks of tasting the bitterness of attachment to created things. The companionship once trusted now brings only anguish. Distance from Allah cannot be repaired by the very relationships that helped produce it.

The leaders' rejection reveals that dependence, while the followers' desired revenge remains powerless. Neither offers a way out of the final consequence.

### In short

- The followers wish to reject the leaders who have abandoned them.
- Their promised change is not accepted as proof that they would obey if returned.
- Their deeds are pictured as dust, ashes and a mirage at the time of need.
- Neither leaders nor followers escape the Fire through shifting blame.

168.text:
Having declared that He alone is God and the Creator of everything, Allah now presents Himself as the Sustainer of all His creation and mentions one of His favours. "O humanity! Eat from what is lawful and good on the earth and do not follow Satan's footsteps. He is truly your sworn enemy". The verse was revealed when some people declared it unlawful to use a camel that had been let loose for the idols. Al-Kalbī, reporting from Abū Ṣāliḥ, said it came down about the tribes of Thaqīf, Khuzāʿah and ʿĀmir ibn Ṣaʿṣaʿah, who forbade themselves certain foods and meats, namely the baḥīrah, al-sāʾibah, al-waṣīlah and al-ḥāmiyah.

### Phrase by phrase

**"O humanity! Eat from what is lawful and good on the earth"**. O people, and in the first place O people of Makkah, eat of the meat, vegetables and fruits of the earth, of what is cultivated and of the cattle you raise, everything pure and lawful that Allah has not prohibited and that does no harm to body or mind. The root of ḥalāl means to open a knot, so what is made ḥalāl is something whose restriction has been untied. Ṭayyib, good, covers the clean and the pure in both senses, lawful and naturally wholesome and delicious. The Companion Sahl ibn ʿAbd Allāh said that salvation depends on three things: eating ḥalāl, fulfilling the divine obligations, and following the Sunnah of the Prophet ﷺ.

**"and do not follow Satan's footsteps."**. Khuṭuwāt is the plural of khuṭwah, the distance between the feet in striding, so Satan's footsteps are his ways and methods, the temptations he embellishes and the whisperings by which he misguides his followers, here his suggestion that cultivating land and raising cattle, or certain animals, are unlawful. The Jāhiliyyah practices meant are the baḥīrah, a she-camel whose milk was reserved for the idols so that no one might milk her, the sāʾibah, a she-camel set loose to pasture freely for the idols with nothing allowed to be carried on her, and the waṣīlah, a she-camel freed for the idols because she gave birth to a female at her first and again at her second delivery, together with everything else Satan made attractive to them. Muslim records from ʿIyāḍ ibn Ḥimār that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ related Allah's words: every kind of wealth I have given My servants is lawful for them, and I created My servants upright (ḥunafāʾ), but the devils came to them, led them away from their religion and forbade them what I had allowed. Qatādah and al-Suddī said that every act of disobedience to Allah is among Satan's footsteps, and ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd reports Ibn ʿAbbās as saying that any vow or oath made in anger is among Satan's footsteps, and its expiation is that of a vow.

**"He is truly your sworn enemy"**. His enmity towards you is plain, and no one with sense follows an enemy who wants to harm and mislead him. Allah warns elsewhere: "Surely Satan is an enemy to you, so take him as an enemy. He only invites his followers to become inmates of the Blaze" (35:6), and, of Iblīs and his offspring, "Would you then take him and his descendants as patrons instead of Me, although they are your enemy? What an evil alternative for the wrongdoers ˹to choose˺" (18:50).

### Rulings drawn from the verse

Dedicating animals to idols, or to a saint or anyone other than Allah, is declared unlawful in verse 173 that follows. This verse does not deny the unlawfulness of such a dedicated animal, as some have wrongly supposed. The point is to reject turning permitted animals into forbidden ones through dedication to idols. Leave them as they are and use them for your own benefit. Inventing prohibitions on one's own authority is a grave sin. Dedication to someone other than Allah makes the thing impure, and that impurity makes it unlawful. If someone dedicates an animal to other than Allah out of ignorance or carelessness and wishes to put it right, he should resolve to withdraw from the deed and repent of it, and then the meat of that animal becomes lawful for him.

Polytheism is the worship of something other than Allah in order to satisfy one's feelings of devotion and veneration. Allah is the human being's greatest and most essential need. The desire to worship Him belongs to human nature so deeply that life cannot dispense with Him. Going astray does not mean abandoning God altogether. The real God is replaced by a false one. That is why the Islamic law holds unlawful everything that in any degree diverts a person's natural desire for God in another direction. The polytheists set animals free in the name of their deities and did not use them for food or work, which is tantamount to granting divinity to an object, a prerogative of none but Allah, and dilutes the reverence that should be reserved for Him alone. Satan encourages people to channel their awe and reverence along other paths so that their attachment to Allah is weakened.

In the devotional reading, what is forbidden, however pleasing now, is contaminated in the end, and what is permitted, however hateful now, is wholesome in the end. The pure and permitted is what is acquired without forgetting the Real, what the gatherer obtains for His sake while witnessing Him in every state, and anything that makes you forget the Real or disobey Him is from Satan's footsteps.

### In short

- Allah, the sole Creator, is also the Sustainer, and He has made the good things of the earth lawful. Tribes like Thaqīf and Khuzāʿah had forbidden themselves animals such as the baḥīrah and sāʾibah, and the verse was revealed against this.
- Satan's footsteps are his ways of misguidance, including inventing prohibitions (Muslim from ʿIyāḍ ibn Ḥimār), every act of disobedience (Qatādah, al-Suddī) and angry oaths (Ibn ʿAbbās). He is a declared enemy (35:6, 18:50).
- Dedicating animals to other than Allah is forbidden (verse 173), and the believer's duty is not to make lawful things unlawful on his own authority. Repentance restores the lawfulness of a wrongly dedicated animal.
- Shirk replaces the true God with a false one, and the law blocks everything that diverts devotion from Allah.

169.text:
Verse 169 explains what following Satan's footsteps leads to. "He only incites you to commit evil and indecency, and to claim against Allah what you do not know". Your enemy Satan commands only what harms you, and worse.

### Phrase by phrase

**"He only incites you to commit evil and indecency"**. Sūʾ, evil, is whatever troubles a good and reasonable person, and includes sinful and harmful acts and disobedience that brings hardship. Faḥshāʾ, indecency, is what is immodest and what the Law abhors, such as adultery, and some have said that sūʾ means sin in general and faḥshāʾ the major sins. "He only incites you" refers to instigating a suggestion in the heart. A hadith from ʿAbd Allāh ibn Masʿūd has the Prophet ﷺ say that the son of Adam is subject to a suggestion from Satan and a suggestion from the angel. Satan's suggestion offers the expedient advantages of evil, opening a way towards denial of truth. The angel's suggestion promises success and reward for good deeds, leaving the heart at peace in its acknowledgment of truth.

**"and to claim against Allah what you do not know"**. He commands what is even worse than indecency, speaking about Allah without knowledge, telling lies about Him and His religion, forbidding what He has not forbidden, and saying things about faith and sacred law that neither Allah nor His Prophet ﷺ have taught. This includes every innovator and every disbeliever. In the devotional reading, it is because of his own audacity towards Allah that Satan induces people to speak falsely about Him.

### In short

- Satan's suggestions lead only to harmful sin and to indecency, and his whisper in the heart is opposed by the angel's (Ibn Masʿūd).
- Worst of all, he leads people to speak about Allah without knowledge, inventing prohibitions and beliefs, which is the mark of innovators and disbelievers.

170.text:
The idolaters receive a call to Allah's revelation through His Messenger ﷺ. Asked to leave ignorance and misguidance, they instead invoke ancestral practice. "When it is said to them, 'Follow what Allah has revealed,' they reply, 'No! We ˹only˺ follow what we found our forefathers practicing.'" The verse ends: "˹Would they still do so,˺ even if their forefathers had ˹absolutely˺ no understanding or guidance". Ibn Isḥāq reports Ibn ʿAbbās's account of a group of Jews invited to Islam by the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. They refused. Their response was to say that they preferred the practice inherited from their fathers.

### Phrase by phrase

**"When it is said to them, 'Follow what Allah has revealed,'"**. When the disbelievers, and the Arab idolaters (mushrikīn) in particular, are told to follow the guidance and light Allah has sent down, the affirmation of His Oneness and the lawfulness He has declared of what is cultivated and of the cattle people raise.

**"they reply, 'No! We ˹only˺ follow what we found our forefathers practicing.'"**. They resist stubbornly, insisting on the customary practice inherited from their fathers, the worship of idols and false deities and the forbidding of the camel let loose and the slitting of the camel's ear for the baḥīrah, because they assumed their forebears had been divinely appointed to follow that way.

**"˹Would they still do so,˺ even if their forefathers had ˹absolutely˺ no understanding or guidance"**. The question is one of repudiation. How could they go on following their fathers in all conditions and to the exclusion of every other way, even if those fathers understood nothing of religion and had no guidance to the practice of any prophet?
