One reading makes it: even if their fathers understood nothing about the affairs of this world either. Those they imitate had no sound understanding and no guidance to the truth that Allah accepts.

### Blind following and legitimate following

The verse censures the blind following of forefathers, but it also lays down, in the words "no understanding or guidance", the condition that distinguishes forbidden following from the permissible kind. Following the forefathers is censured because they lacked reason and guidance. Guidance means the injunctions revealed openly and clearly by Allah, and reason here means the binding guidance deduced by ijtihād from the recognised sources of the Sharīʿah. Those named in the verse cannot be followed because they had neither a revealed law from Allah nor the ability to derive rulings from His Word. There is a subtle hint in this. If one is satisfied that a certain scholar has perfect knowledge of the Qur'an and Sunnah, and that where no clear and direct text exists he has the expertise of a mujtahid to derive rulings from them by analogy, it is permissible to follow such a scholar. This does not mean obeying his injunctions or his person. It means obeying the injunctions of Allah alone, but since direct and trustworthy knowledge of those injunctions in all their ramifications is not available to most people, they must follow a mujtahid scholar in order to act in accordance with them. Those who hasten to quote verses like this one against following the great mujtahid imams are themselves unaware of their proven meaning.

Al-Qurṭubī said in his comments on this verse that the prohibition refers to following forefathers in false beliefs and deeds. Following them in correct beliefs and good deeds is not included, for Sūrat Yūsuf presents it clearly in the words of Yūsuf (Joseph): "I have shunned the faith of a people who disbelieve in Allah and deny the Hereafter" and "I follow the faith of my fathers: Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob" (12:37-38). Following forefathers in falsehood is forbidden, while in truth it is permissible and indeed desirable. Al-Qurṭubī also took up the question of following the mujtahid imams here, noting that some quote this verse to criticise taqlīd. He agreed that following falsehood was wrong. Following truth was a different matter: it is fundamental to religion and helps protect the Muslims' faith. Someone unable to exercise ijtihād must follow qualified guidance in religious matters.

The devotional reading describes eyes fixed on people of matching form, class, kind and ancestry. Their settled path leads them into the fire. Recognising their ancestors' lack of restraining intelligence and unifying guidance would have led them to resist that hostile example. They would have seen its opposition to Allah's command. Instead, insight was taken from them, along with the proofs that bring certainty.

### In short

- Called to Allah's revelation, the disbelievers, including a group of Jews (Ibn ʿAbbās via Ibn Isḥāq), plead the custom of their fathers, who had neither understanding nor guidance.
- The verse condemns following ancestors in falsehood, not following the guided, as Yūsuf's example shows (12:37-38). Following a qualified mujtahid is really obedience to Allah's law for those who cannot derive it themselves (al-Qurṭubī).
- Inwardly, those who cannot look beyond their own kind lose the light of insight.

171.text:
Allah now gives a parable of the disbelievers in relation to the one who calls them. "The example of the disbelievers ˹not responding to the Messenger's warning˺ is like a flock not comprehending the calls and cries of the shepherd." The verse concludes: "˹They are wilfully˺ deaf, dumb and blind so they have no understanding". Just as Allah says elsewhere that to those who disbelieve in the Hereafter belong all evil qualities (16:60), so here He likens them to animals.

### Phrase by phrase

**"The example of the disbelievers ˹not responding to the Messenger's warning˺ is like a flock not comprehending the calls and cries of the shepherd."**. In their injustice, misguidance and ignorance, and in their stubborn following of the path of their fathers, the disbelievers and mushrik idolaters facing Muḥammad ﷺ are like wandering camels and sheep. When the shepherd calls them to what benefits them, telling them for instance to eat or drink, they hear only unintelligible sound, a shout and a cry, and understand nothing of what is said. In the same way the disbelievers who listen to an admonition hear the voice but not the meaning that is meant to correct them. Ibn ʿAbbās and Abū al-ʿĀliyah give this explanation, alongside Mujāhid and ʿIkrimah. It is also related from ʿAṭāʾ and al-Ḥasan, Qatādah and ʿAṭāʾ al-Khurāsānī, and al-Rabīʿ ibn Anas. The comparison joins the caller and the unresponsive disbelievers. They correspond to a shepherd and a flock that hears the sound without understanding it.

**"˹They are wilfully˺ deaf, dumb and blind"**. They are deaf because they do not hear the truth so as to benefit from it, dumb because they do not utter it and are tight-lipped when it comes to accepting it, and blind because they do not see or recognise its path and way, nor their own benefit and loss. They pretend to be deaf, dumb and blind where the truth and guidance are concerned.

**"so they have no understanding"**. With their vital senses so dulled they comprehend no admonition. They fail to understand Allah's command and the Prophet's ﷺ call. Camels and cattle similarly hear a shepherd without comprehending his words.

### How superstition hardens into deafness

Once something that is not God is accepted as God through a superstitious attitude, many other evils follow. People may assign an animal supernatural powers belonging to Allah alone. They then treat it as a means of nearness to Him and a giver of blessings. A later generation inherits these superstitions as settled beliefs and zealously defends them as the ancestors' sacred way. Rational examination of their beliefs then meets resistance. Each generation deepens the resistance until arguments can no longer be heard or understood. They behave as though sight, hearing and thought were unavailable for considering what is put before them.

In the devotional reading, without the ears of comprehension and acceptance their bodily hearing did them no good. They sank to the level of animals, incapable of attainment, and whoever is content to be like an animal does not have much worth.

### In short

- The disbelievers who ignore the Messenger's ﷺ call are like a flock that hears the shepherd's voice but grasps nothing of it, a reading shared by Ibn ʿAbbās, Mujāhid, Qatādah and others (cf. 16:60).
- They are deaf to the truth, dumb in confessing it and blind to its path, and so understand nothing.
- Inherited superstition hardens generation by generation until people lose the very capacity to weigh an argument, and one content to live like an animal has little worth.

172.text:
The previous verses corrected the error of the idolaters who made unlawful what Allah had made good and permissible. Verse 172 now warns the believers against falling into the same error, reminds them of Allah's blessings and teaches them gratitude. "O believers! Eat from the good things We have provided for you. And give thanks to Allah if you ˹truly˺ worship Him ˹alone˺". Allah commands His believing servants to eat from the pure things He has created for them and to thank Him for them, if they are truly His servants.

### Phrase by phrase

**"O believers! Eat from the good things We have provided for you."**. You who have faith in Allah and follow His Messenger ﷺ, eat of the lawful things He has given you, what is cultivated on the land and the meat of cattle. The ḥalāl is that which carries no bad consequence, and the ṭayyib, the good thing, is that whose blessing is not attributed to any created thing. When a servant finds food that combines both qualities, it is permitted and good.

**"And give thanks to Allah"**. Thank Him outwardly and inwardly for what He has made lawful and for the overwhelming blessings He has given you. Gratitude includes undivided devotion to Allah and restraint from disobedience. The true meaning of thankfulness is that you do not draw a breath in anything but the pleasure of the Real for as long as the energy from that permitted and good food remains in you.

**"if you ˹truly˺ worship Him ˹alone˺"**. If it is really He whom you worship, and nothing besides Him. One reading takes it as a rebuke to those who thought they were serving Allah by declaring good things unlawful: if you truly intend to worship Allah, do not declare them unlawful, for worshipping Him entails treating them as lawful.

### Lawful food and answered prayer

Pure nourishment helps bring acceptance of prayer and worship. Impure nourishment obstructs that acceptance. Imām Aḥmad records, and Muslim and al-Tirmidhī also, that Abū Hurayrah related the Messenger of Allah ﷺ saying: O people, Allah is Ṭayyib, pure and good, and accepts only what is ṭayyib. He has commanded the believers with what He commanded the messengers, saying "O messengers! Eat from what is good and lawful, and act righteously. Indeed, I fully know what you do" (23:51), and "O believers! Eat from the good things We have provided for you". The Prophet ﷺ then described a man on a long journey, dishevelled and dust-covered, who stretches his hands to the sky crying "O Lord, O Lord", Yet unlawful provision supplies his food, drink and clothes. What has nourished him is unlawful too. How, he asked, could such a man's supplication be answered?

Eating ḥarām promotes evil instincts, kills the taste for worship and makes prayers ineffective. Eating ḥalāl generates inner light, creates a distaste for evil, leads towards high morals and produces a state in which the heart welcomes worship, finds the very thought of sin sickening, and has its prayers answered. That is why Allah told all His prophets to eat from what is good and to do what is righteous (23:51). Living by the ḥalāl helps a prayer to be answered, and living by the ḥarām destroys that chance.

### Gratitude rather than superstition

Human beings should feel thankful and obedient to Allah while eating and drinking, saying in effect that in accordance with His command they eat and drink what He has provided. Such feelings evoke true devotion to the Maker. Under self-made beliefs the psychology changes: attention shifts to the supposed properties of the things consumed, and the very blessing meant to produce thanksgiving produces veneration for material objects instead, until the created is given the position of the Creator. When Allah makes something unlawful, it is not because the thing is sacred but because it is impure or the divine law has testified to its uncleanness, as the next verse shows with carrion, blood, swine and what is sacrificed to idols.

### In short

- Having censured the idolaters for forbidding good things, Allah commands the believers to enjoy the lawful and good things He provides and to thank Him, for that is what worshipping Him alone entails.
- Lawful food is a condition of answered prayer: the Prophet's ﷺ hadith of the dusty traveller shows that one nourished on ḥarām cannot expect his supplication to be heard (Abū Hurayrah, in Aḥmad, Muslim and al-Tirmidhī, cf. 23:51).
- Ḥalāl food brings inner light and love of worship, while ḥarām deadens the heart.
- Gratitude keeps food a blessing from Allah, whereas superstition turns it into an object of veneration.

173.text:
Verse 173 specifies what Allah has in fact forbidden, so that the prohibited may remain prohibited and nothing else be added to it. "He has only forbidden you ˹to eat˺ carrion, blood, swine, and what is slaughtered in the name of any other than Allah." The verse continues: "But if someone is compelled by necessity—neither driven by desire nor exceeding immediate need—they will not be sinful. Surely Allah is All-Forgiving, Most Merciful". The idolaters used to eat carrion and animals slaughtered in a name other than Allah's while treating other animals as forbidden. The verse corrects both errors at once: the prohibited must never be treated as lawful, and it is an error to declare any animal forbidden beyond those specified.

### Phrase by phrase

**"He has only forbidden you ˹to eat˺"**. "Only" (innamā) is a restrictive particle, so the sense is that Allah has forbidden only the things named and nothing else. Sūrat al-Anʿām states the same thing more plainly: "Say, ˹O Prophet,˺ 'I do not find in what has been revealed to me anything forbidden to eat except carrion, running blood, swine—which is impure—or a sinful offering in the name of any other than Allah'" (6:145). This raises a problem, since many other things are proved unlawful by other verses and by hadith. The answer is that ḥalāl and ḥarām are not being discussed here in the absolute sense but with reference to the animals that the idolaters of Makkah treated as lawful or unlawful on the basis of their pagan beliefs. The previous verse censured their forbidding of lawful animals, and in contrast this verse tells them that they fail to keep away from the very animals Allah has forbidden while shunning those He has allowed. The restriction is therefore relative, directed against polytheistic beliefs, not absolute. The prohibition concerns consumption, which is the subject of the passage, and the Sunnah adds that whatever is cut from a living animal counts as carrion too.

**"carrion"**. Maytah, the dead animal, is in the terminology of the Sharīʿah any animal not slaughtered according to its requirements, whether it dies of itself or is killed by strangling, a violent blow, a fall, goring, or being partly eaten by a wild beast. Dead creatures of the sea are excluded, as Allah says: "It is lawful for you to hunt and eat seafood, as a provision for you and for travellers" (5:96), and as the hadith of the whale in the Ṣaḥīḥ shows. The Musnad, al-Muwaṭṭaʾ and the Sunan record the Prophet's ﷺ saying about the sea that its water is pure and its dead are permissible. Al-Shāfiʿī, Aḥmad, Ibn Mājah and al-Dāraquṭnī report from Ibn ʿUmar that the Prophet ﷺ said two dead things and two kinds of blood have been made lawful for us: fish and locusts, and liver and spleen. Fish and locusts are therefore ḥalāl without slaughter even if they die on their own or are killed, though a fish that has decomposed and floats on the surface is ḥarām. The subject returns in Sūrat al-Māʾidah.

**"blood"**. Blood is forbidden here absolutely, but 6:145 qualifies it as blood that flows, so the jurists agree that congealed blood such as the liver and the spleen is clean and permissible.

**"swine"**. The flesh of the pig is forbidden whether the animal is slaughtered or not, and this includes its fat, either by implication, because the term laḥm (flesh) covers it, or by analogy. The meat is singled out because it is the part people mostly seek, and every other part is implied.

**"and what is slaughtered in the name of any other than Allah."**. This is whatever is slaughtered in a name other than His, for monuments, idols, divination arrows or the other practices of the Jāhiliyyah. Ihlāl is the raising of the voice, which the Arabs used to do when sacrificing to their gods. Al-Qurṭubī mentions that ʿĀʾishah was asked about what non-Muslims slaughter for their festivals and then send to Muslims as gifts, and she said: do not eat what has been slaughtered for that day, but eat from their vegetables.

**"But if someone is compelled by necessity—neither driven by desire nor exceeding immediate need—they will not be sinful."**. Allah permits these things when they are needed for survival and no permissible food is available. The muḍṭarr, the one compelled, is in the terminology of the Sharīʿah a person whose life is in danger. Ordinary pain or need does not qualify. Such a person may eat on two conditions: his aim must be to save his life and not to enjoy the food, and he must eat only as much as will keep him alive, for filling the stomach remains prohibited even then. Mujāhid explained that the permission applies to one who, if he did not eat, would be driven to highway robbery, rebellion against the rulers or some other disobedience, but not to one who eats transgressing the limits, or continually, or in a state of disobedience to Allah, even if he is in dire need. Saʿīd ibn Jubayr said the same, and he and Muqātil ibn Ḥayyān also explained "not driven by desire" as not believing it to be permissible. Ibn ʿAbbās is reported to have said that it means eating the dead animal without continuing to do so, and Qatādah that it means not eating carrion when the lawful is available. The person compelled must eat without taking his fill and without carrying anything away. Al-Shāfiʿī held that the rebel and the transgressor are excluded from the dispensation, and that whoever sets out on a journey in disobedience, such as a fugitive or an unjust tax collector, may not eat any of these things unless he repents.

**"Surely Allah is All-Forgiving, Most Merciful"**. Muqātil ibn Ḥayyān said this refers to what is eaten out of necessity. Saʿīd ibn Jubayr said that Allah is forgiving towards what has been eaten of the unlawful and merciful in allowing the prohibited in times of necessity. He forgives even one who ate more than he strictly needed, and it is from His mercy that He granted this dispensation. Masrūq said that whoever is in dire need but refuses to eat or drink until he dies will enter the Fire, which shows that eating carrion to survive is not merely permitted but required.

### Rulings on carrion

Hunting is governed by the same principle. An animal out of reach of the hunter's knife becomes lawful without slaughter if the hunter, after saying bismillāh, wounds it with a sharp-edged weapon such as an arrow. Mere wounding is not enough. The wound must be inflicted by a sharp edge. An animal shot and killed by a gun before it can be slaughtered is therefore treated like one killed by a blow from a stick or stone, which 5:3 calls mawqūdhah and classes as ḥarām, though if it is slaughtered before it dies it becomes lawful. Some scholars regard the conical bullet as a kind of arrow, but the majority hold that a bullet bores and tears the flesh by explosive force rather than cutting it, so game killed by it is not permissible without slaughter.

Carrion is forbidden absolutely, so everything about it is forbidden: eating it, buying it and selling it. The same applies to all impurities, whose use, sale and benefit are all unlawful, so much so that one may not deliberately feed carrion or anything impure even to an animal, though if it is left somewhere and a dog or cat eats it of its own accord there is no harm. The prohibition appears general here, but 6:145 clarifies that it is the edible parts that are forbidden, so the bones and hair of a dead animal, which are not food, are clean and may be used, and another verse of Sūrat al-Naḥl permits the use of animal hair without any condition of slaughter. The hide carries impurities such as blood and is forbidden until tanned, after which it is permissible. The fat of a dead animal and everything made from it is forbidden, including its sale. Avoiding soap made from animal fat is a good precaution, but since it is seldom possible to be sure that fat from dead animals was used, there is some leeway, and Companions such as Ibn ʿUmar, Abū Saʿīd al-Khudrī and Abū Mūsā al-Ashʿarī ruled that such fat is forbidden only as food and permitted its external use and sale.

According to al-Shāfiʿī and others, the milk and eggs inside an unslaughtered dead animal are impure because they are part of it. Mālik, in one narration, held them pure in themselves but rendered impure by their location. There is a similar difference about cheese made from the milk of dead animals. The popular view is that it is impure, yet the Companions ate the cheeses of the Magians, and al-Qurṭubī commented that since only a tiny part of the dead animal is mixed into it, it is permissible, because a minute impurity does not matter in a large quantity of liquid. Rennet (infaḥah), the lining taken from the stomachs of suckling lambs and kids to curdle milk, is unobjectionable if it comes from an animal slaughtered in the name of Allah. If it comes from an animal not slaughtered Islamically, Abū Ḥanīfah and Mālik consider it clean while Abū Yūsuf, Muḥammad, al-Thawrī and others call it impure. Since cheese made in non-Muslim countries is very likely to contain such rennet, caution favours avoiding it, although the position of Abū Ḥanīfah and Mālik gives leeway. Cheeses that contain pork fat, which may be shown on the wrapper, are absolutely ḥarām and impure. Ibn Mājah reports that Salmān said the Messenger of Allah ﷺ was asked about butter, cheese and fur, and replied: the lawful is what Allah has made lawful in His Book, the forbidden is what He has forbidden in His Book, and what He has not mentioned is part of what He has pardoned.

### Rulings on blood, including transfusion

Since only flowing blood is forbidden, the blood remaining on the flesh after slaughter is clean, by agreement of the jurists, the Companions and their successors and the Ummah in general. By the same analogy the blood of mosquitoes, flies and bedbugs is not unclean, though a significant amount should be washed off. Because eating and drinking blood is forbidden absolutely, its external use, its sale and any income from it are forbidden too.

Human blood is part of the human body and, once outside it, is rated impure, so transfusing it from one person to another might seem ḥarām for two reasons: respect for the human body forbids such use, and blood is a heavy impurity whose use is not permitted. But the concessions the Sharīʿah allows under compulsion and in the treatment of disease lead to another conclusion. Transfusion needs no surgery, since blood is drawn with a syringe and transferred by the same means, which makes it comparable to milk, which forms in one human body and becomes part of another. The Sharīʿah, in view of the infant's need, made milk its first food and obliged mothers to nurse while married, and after divorce made the father responsible for arranging a wet-nurse or paying the mother to continue: "And if they nurse your child, compensate them" (65:6). Milk is even used medically for adults, and the Fatāwā ʿĀlamgīriyyah states that there is no harm in dropping a woman's milk into a man's nose or giving it orally as medicine, a subject treated in al-Mughnī of Ibn Qudāmah in the chapter on hunting (Kitāb al-Ṣayd). Milk is an altered form of blood and shares with it the quality of being part of the human person, the only difference being that milk is clean and blood is not. The first reason against transfusion therefore falls away, and as to impurity, some jurists have permitted the use of blood on medical grounds. The correct position is that transfusion is not permissible under normal conditions but is doubtless permissible under compulsion, that is, where the patient faces death, no effective drug is available and there is a strong likelihood that the transfusion will save his life. The authority is this very verse, which permits saving one's life by eating carrion. Where there is no such compulsion, or other treatments would work, the jurists differ, some permitting and others not.

### Swine and the consecrated animal

Al-Qurṭubī explains that mentioning the "flesh" of swine is not meant to restrict the prohibition to the meat. All parts of the pig, bones, skin, hair and ligaments, are forbidden by consensus of the Muslim community. The word laḥm is used to show that the pig is unlike other prohibited animals, which slaughter purifies even if eating them stays forbidden. The pig's flesh is not purified by slaughter, because it is absolutely impure and unlawful, although the use of its bristles for stitching leather has been permitted in hadith.

The animal dedicated to other than Allah takes three known forms. First, an animal slaughtered to please someone other than Allah with that name called over it is forbidden by consensus. It is carrion, and no benefit may be taken from any part of it, which is what the verse plainly means. Second, an animal slaughtered to please someone other than Allah even though Allah's name was pronounced over it. Many ignorant Muslims do this when they slaughter goats, sheep or even chickens to please elders and leaders while saying bismillāh. The jurists agree that this too is ḥarām and the animal is a carcass, differing only over the reason. Some hold that the verse itself covers this case. The glosses on al-Bayḍāwī state that every animal over which a name other than Allah's was invoked is ḥarām even if slaughtered in Allah's name, and that scholars agree a Muslim who slaughters intending to please other than Allah becomes an apostate, so that his animal is one slaughtered by an apostate. Al-Durr al-Mukhtār, in its chapter on slaughtered animals, says that slaughtering an animal to celebrate the arrival of a dignitary is ḥarām because it falls under what is dedicated to other than Allah even when His name is mentioned, and al-Shāmī concurs. Others consider it a strain on the Arabic to read the phrase as covering this case directly, and forbid it instead by the commonality of cause, the intention of pleasing someone other than Allah. One scholar judged this the soundest and most cautious view. A further verse supports the prohibition: the phrase in 5:3 about "what is sacrificed on altars" (nuṣub), meaning everything falsely worshipped, stands in contrast to "what is slaughtered in the name of any other than Allah" earlier in the same verse. Since the latter already covers slaughter with a false name pronounced, the former must mean slaughter intended to please idols, which includes animals slaughtered for someone other than Allah even though His name was recited over them. This observation comes from Maulānā Ashraf ʿAlī Thānawī. Al-Qurṭubī takes the same approach in his commentary, noting that it was the Arabs' custom to call aloud the name of the one for whom they slaughtered, and that this was so prevalent that the real cause of the prohibition, their intention to please other than Allah, was identified in the verse with the call itself. He bases this on the rulings of ʿAlī and ʿĀʾishah. In ʿAlī's time Ghālib, the father of the poet Farazdaq, slaughtered a camel, and although there is no report that any name other than Allah's was mentioned over it, ʿAlī ruled that it fell under what is dedicated to other than Allah and was ḥarām, and the Companions accepted his verdict. Al-Qurṭubī also reports, through Yaḥyā ibn Yaḥyā, the teacher of Imām Muslim, a long hadith from ʿĀʾishah in which a woman asked her about non-Arab foster relatives who constantly celebrated festivals and sent gifts, and ʿĀʾishah replied: do not eat what was slaughtered for that day, but eat from the fruit of their trees. In sum, slaughter intended for someone other than Allah is forbidden both by commonality of cause and by 5:3.

Third, an animal released after slitting its ear or branding it, as an object of reverence to someone other than Allah, neither worked nor meant for slaughter. Such animals, the baḥīrah and sāʾibah, are not covered by this verse or by 5:3. The practice of releasing them is ḥarām by the Qur'an, as a later verse shows, but neither the practice nor the false belief makes the animal itself unlawful. To treat it as forbidden would be to endorse the false belief, so it is lawful like any other animal, and by the principles of the law it never leaves its owner's possession, whatever he imagines. If he sells or gives it away, it is lawful for the recipient. People in some countries endow goats or cows in the name of their gods and leave them with temple keepers who may sell them, even to Muslims, and some ignorant Muslims do the same at shrines and graveyards, leaving a goat or a cockerel with keepers who sell it. Whoever buys such livestock or poultry from keepers authorised by the owners may lawfully buy, slaughter, eat or resell it.

A fourth situation concerns things other than animals: food or sweets offered in fulfilment of vows to someone other than Allah, by Hindus in their temples or by ignorant Muslims at shrines. Such a nadhr for other than Allah is ḥarām by the same commonality of cause, so eating, feeding, buying and selling it are all forbidden, as detailed in works of fiqh such as al-Baḥr al-Rāʾiq. The ruling rests on analogy with the animals the Qur'an names expressly.

### Compulsion, and the forbidden as medicine

Even under compulsion the Qur'an does not make these things lawful. It says only that there is no sin on the one who eats, so they remain ḥarām and the sin of using them is forgiven because of necessity. There is a world of difference between making something lawful and forgiving a sin. Had the aim been to make these things lawful under need, a simple exception from the prohibition would have sufficed. Instead the text adds that Allah is Forgiving and Merciful, making the point that what is ḥarām remains ḥarām and its use remains a sin, but the compelled person is forgiven.

The verse also proves that a person whose life is in danger may use what is forbidden as medicine, under conditions hinted at in the text. There must be a state of compulsion with danger to life, not ordinary pain or sickness. No lawful treatment must work or be available. It must be normally certain that the forbidden medicine will save life, just as a couple of morsels of unlawful meat are enough to save the starving, for a medicine that merely seems useful without certainty of cure does not fall under the exception. And, as the verse states, enjoyment must not be the aim and no more than needed may be used. Given these five conditions, any unlawful or impure medicine may be used internally or externally by the consensus of the jurists. Using impure or ḥarām medicine in ordinary illnesses is disputed. Most jurists forbid it short of compulsion, because the Prophet ﷺ, as reported in al-Bukhārī, said that Allah has not placed the cure of the Muslims in what He has forbidden. Some permit it on the strength of the episode of the ʿUraynah tribesmen, reported in all the hadith collections, whom the Prophet ﷺ allowed to drink the milk and urine of camels, which cured them. But that episode admits of several explanations, so the sound original position is that without the conditions of extreme necessity, ḥarām medicine is not permissible in common diseases. Later jurists, considering the flood of unlawful and impure medicines in modern times and people's weakness, have permitted forbidden medicine when no lawful and pure one is effective or available. Al-Durr al-Mukhtār notes the disagreement, says the apparent ruling forbids it as al-Baḥr al-Rāʾiq states in the chapter on fosterage, but reports from al-Ḥāwī al-Qudsī that some scholars permitted the forbidden as medicine when the cure is certain and no alternative exists, like the permission given to one dying of thirst to take a sip of wine. Modern medicines from Europe and America in which alcohol is certainly used as a base or solvent, or other impure ingredients are certainly present, fall under these rules. Where the presence of impure ingredients cannot be ascertained there is a little more leeway, but precaution is best, especially when the need is not pressing. Allah knows best.

### Hunger and the garden

Someone in dire straits who finds both carrion and other people's food that he could take without risking his hands or causing harm may not eat the carrion. Ibn Mājah reports that ʿAbbād ibn Shuraḥbīl al-Ghubarī said that in a year of famine he came to al-Madīnah, entered a garden, rubbed some grain clean and ate it, and put some in his garment. The owner beat him and took his garment. He went to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, who told the owner: you did not feed him when he was hungry, or he said starving, nor did you teach him if he was ignorant. He ordered the garment returned and a wasq, around 180 kilograms, or half a wasq, of food given to him. The chain is sufficiently strong and other reports support it, such as the hadith of ʿAmr ibn Shuʿayb from his father from his grandfather that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ was asked about hanging clusters of dates and said there was no harm in a needy person taking some in his mouth without putting any in his garment.

In the devotional reading, Allah has forbidden in outward matters these specific things dedicated to other than Him, and He has forbidden to the innermost hearts companionship with anything other than Him, and even witnessing anything other than Him. The one who is "compelled", who has not found the means to annihilation in the realities of the Real, should travel only by way of the law: either effaced in Allah, or standing by means of Allah, or acting for Allah. Otherwise he is a foolish man of no account.

### In short

- Only four things are forbidden here, relative to the idolaters' inventions: carrion, flowing blood, swine, and what is slaughtered for other than Allah (cf. 6:145, 5:3). Fish and locusts, liver and spleen are excepted (Ibn ʿUmar), and sea creatures are lawful (5:96).
- Carrion and all impurities may not be eaten, sold or used, except non-edible parts such as bones, hair and tanned hide. The jurists differ on fat for external use, on milk, eggs and rennet from unslaughtered animals.
- Flowing blood is forbidden in every use, and transfusion is permitted only under life-threatening compulsion, by analogy with milk and on the authority of this verse.
- Every part of the pig is forbidden and slaughter does not purify it. Slaughter for other than Allah is forbidden even when His name is pronounced (ʿAlī, ʿĀʾishah, al-Qurṭubī), while released animals like the baḥīrah remain lawful, and vow offerings to other than Allah are ḥarām by analogy.
- The one whose life is at risk must eat the forbidden, without desire and without excess (Mujāhid, Saʿīd ibn Jubayr, Masrūq). The sin is forgiven, not the thing made lawful, and the same conditions govern forbidden medicine.
- The starving may take from others' food in need, and the owner who refuses is at fault (ʿAbbād ibn Shuraḥbīl, Ibn Mājah).

174.text:
The earlier verses dealt with unlawful things that are tangible. The verses that follow take up intangible deeds that are unlawful, evil deeds inner and outer, beginning with the religious scholars of the Jews who sold false verdicts and distorted the Torah for those who paid them. "Indeed, those who hide Allah's revelations, trading them for a fleeting gain consume nothing but fire into their bellies. Allah will neither speak to them on the Day of Judgment, nor will He purify them. And they will suffer a painful punishment". Al-Kalbī, reporting from Abū Ṣāliḥ from Ibn ʿAbbās, said the verse was revealed about the leaders and doctors of the Jews, who received gifts and surpluses from ordinary Jews and had hoped the new prophet would be sent from among them. When he was sent from among others they feared losing their income and their leadership, so they altered the traits of Muḥammad ﷺ in the Torah and told people that the prophet to be sent at the end of time would look like this, and did not resemble the prophet in Makkah. Ordinary people compared the altered description with Muḥammad ﷺ, found it different, and did not believe in him. Another report names Kaʿb ibn al-Ashraf, Ḥuyayy ibn Akhṭab and Judayy ibn Akhṭab as the people concerned.

### Phrase by phrase

**"Indeed, those who hide Allah's revelations"**. The Jews, and the Christians likewise, who concealed what their Books said in description of Muḥammad ﷺ, all of which testified to his truth as a Messenger and Prophet, and more generally the signs of truth and prophethood revealed in the Scriptures.

**"trading them for a fleeting gain"**. They took a small price in exchange, the joys and delights of this earthly life: leadership, status, money, and the gifts and honour the Arabs gave them. They feared losing followers if they disclosed their knowledge of Muḥammad ﷺ. Concealment protected their small income at the cost of their souls. They preferred it to guidance, to following the truth and believing in the Messenger ﷺ, and so profited only failure and loss in this life and the next. Nevertheless, Allah disclosed the truth of His Messenger ﷺ here through clear signs and decisive proofs. The people whose allegiance they feared losing followed him and supported him against them. Their conduct brought further anger upon the wrath already incurred.

**"consume nothing but fire into their bellies."**. Whatever they eat in return for hiding the truth will become a raging fire in their stomachs on the Day of Resurrection, or, on another reading, they eat nothing but the unlawful, and the Fire is their journey's end. Allah says similarly: "Indeed, those who unjustly consume orphans' wealth ˹in fact˺ consume nothing but fire into their bellies. And they will be burned in a blazing Hell" (4:10), and an authentic hadith says that those who eat or drink from gold or silver vessels are filling their stomachs with the fire of Jahannam.

**"Allah will neither speak to them on the Day of Judgment, nor will He purify them."**. Because Allah is furious with them for concealing the truth, He will not speak to them kindly or with words that bring them joy, nor look at them, nor cleanse them of the filth of their sins by forgiving them, nor praise or commend them in any way. They will hear only what grieves them.

**"And they will suffer a painful punishment"**. That is the Fire, a torment that reaches into their hearts.

### A warning to the scholars of this Ummah

Concealing Allah's Book for trifling worldly profit breaches a trust. The account describes the resulting consumption as eating fire. On the Day of Qiyāmah Allah will not speak to them affectionately or purify them by forgiving their sins, and their punishment will be terrible. The warning also reaches the ʿulamāʾ of the Last Prophet's ﷺ community. These religious scholars must avoid the same practices. Money or personal advantage must never prevent faithful disclosure of Allah's injunctions. Whoever changes an injunction of the Sharīʿah out of greed for worldly gain should know that what he consumes is like embers of fire stored in his stomach, because that is the end of such deeds. Some perceptive scholars regard unlawful wealth as Hell's fire in reality. Its nature is not sensed during this life. After death, they explain, the deeds appear as fire.

The public may accept invented prohibitions as sacred religion. Scholars can then fear losing the popularity that depends on that public. They may lack the courage to state openly that those beliefs do not belong to true religion. They may revel in compromises that bring them wealth and honour, but in Allah's eyes they are the worst of offenders. Hiding the truth for worldly considerations is not among the offences Allah overlooks in the Hereafter. It is a crime that deprives a person of His mercy.

The devotional reading assigns distinct trusts. Scholars must communicate the evidence of knowledge. Allah's friends must safeguard what is entrusted as secret. If the scholars conceal the proofs of knowledge they will be bridled with a bridle of fire, and if the friends divulge even a sliver of the secret they are at once distanced from the secrets and stripped of the lights they were given. To each there is a limit, and to each a command.

### In short

- The verse condemns the Jewish scholars who altered and hid the Torah's description of the Prophet ﷺ to keep their gifts and leadership (Ibn ʿAbbās via al-Kalbī, naming Kaʿb ibn al-Ashraf and the sons of Akhṭab).
- What they earned by concealment is fire in their bellies (cf. 4:10), and on the Day of Judgement Allah will not speak to them, purify them or praise them.
- It is a warning to the scholars of every age, including this Ummah, never to hide or bend Allah's rulings for money or popularity, for unlawful wealth is itself the fire of Hell.
- Inwardly, scholars must publish their proofs while the friends of Allah must guard their secrets, each within his limit.

175.text:
Verse 175 describes the bargain those concealers made. "They are the ones who trade guidance for misguidance and forgiveness for punishment. How persistent are they in pursuit of the Fire". In their mortal life they abandoned guidance and adopted error, and in the Hereafter they will miss forgiveness and deserve punishment.

### Phrase by phrase

**"They are the ones who trade guidance for misguidance"**. The guidance was to announce the Prophet's ﷺ description found in their Books, the news of his prophethood and the glad tidings of his coming proclaimed by earlier prophets, and then to believe in him and follow him. Instead they preferred misguidance, denying and rejecting him and concealing his description. They bought disbelief at the price of faith and Judaism at the price of Islam, taking error in place of guidance in this world.

**"and forgiveness for punishment."**. Concealment and the sins accompanying it lead them towards torment. Without that concealment, pardon would have awaited them in the Hereafter. They chose what leads to the Fire instead of what leads to Paradise.

**"How persistent are they in pursuit of the Fire"**. How bold they are to plunge into the Fire, and how great their endurance seems. The statement is meant to provoke amazement in the believers at the indifference with which the disbelievers commit sins that must bring them the Fire, as if they did not realise what suffering it contains, for in reality they will have no patience whatever to endure it. Those who see them in their severe and painful torment will be amazed that they can bear such punishment. Other readings ask what made them so bold as to enter the Fire, or how deeply they indulge in the works of the people of the Fire. We seek refuge with Allah from such an end.

### What does the exchange mean inwardly?

In the devotional reading, those who prefer the other to the unseen (ghayb), the creation to the Real, and the lower self (nafs) to intimacy with Allah, how hard are their hearts, how shameless what they love and seek, how cheap their worth, and how disgraceful in the eyes of those who can see.

### In short

- The concealers of truth exchanged guidance for misguidance by rejecting the Prophet ﷺ they recognised, and forfeited the forgiveness awaiting them for punishment.
- Their boldness in sinning their way to the Fire is held up as a cause of amazement, since they could never endure it.
- Inwardly, this is the hardness of a heart that prefers creation to the Creator and the self to intimacy with Him.

176.text:
Verse 176 gives the reason for the punishment just described. "That is because Allah has revealed the Book in truth. And surely those who differ regarding it are totally engrossed in opposition". All of this befalls them because they chose to stray from the Book of Allah, which is so clear and true.

### Phrase by phrase

**"That is because Allah has revealed the Book in truth."**. The torment of eating fire and what follows it is deserved because Allah sent down the Books to His Messenger Muḥammad ﷺ and to the prophets before him, bringing Gabriel with the Qur'an as He had sent the Torah, and these revelations establish the truth and expose falsehood. Their Books commanded them to announce the truth and spread knowledge, since what Allah reveals in truth must be made clear and not hidden, yet they defied that knowledge and rejected it. The Final Messenger ﷺ called them to Allah, commanded righteousness and forbade evil, and they rejected him, denied him and hid what they knew about him, thereby mocking the signs Allah had revealed to His messengers.

**"And surely those who differ regarding it are totally engrossed in opposition"**. Those who dispute about the Book, believing in parts of it and disbelieving in and concealing other parts, in particular the Jews who contravened what it said of the traits of Muḥammad ﷺ and then hid them, are in schism far removed from the truth and in deep disagreement with guidance. Some say the verse refers to the idolaters, who differed over the Qur'an, some calling it poetry, some sorcery and some divination. Either way, people in such intransigence can expect a matching punishment.

### The road away from return

Worse than those who merely fail to accept the truth are those who, when it is presented to them, start meaningless discussions instead. They develop a propensity to divisiveness and in the end stray so far from the truth that no chance of return remains. In the devotional reading, Allah revealed the Book in truth and made its decree come to pass in sincerity, bringing each party to what He had prepared for them and establishing them on the way He fashioned for them.

### In short

- The punishment follows from the fact that Allah's Books were revealed in truth and commanded to be proclaimed, and these people hid and mocked them instead.
- Those who pick and choose within the Book, or dispute its nature as the idolaters did, have drifted into schism far from the truth.
- Quarrelling with the truth rather than accepting it leads step by step to a point of no return.

177.text:
With this verse Sūrat al-Baqarah reaches its halfway mark and changes direction. Until now the message was addressed mostly to those who denied the Qur'an: its truth was established, those who accepted and rejected it were described, Allah's Oneness and the prophethood were proved, His favours on the descendants of Ibrāhīm were recounted up to the words "when Abraham was tested by his Lord" (2:124), and then the issue of the qiblah ran on until it was settled by the identification of Ṣafā and Marwah as a sign of Allah (verse 158), followed by the refutation of shirk in its roots and branches. The second half of the sūrah is primarily education of the Muslims in the principles and details of their religion, and it opens with the comprehensive concept of birr, righteousness. "Righteousness is not in turning your faces towards the east or the west. Rather, the righteous are those who believe in Allah, the Last Day, the angels, the Books, and the prophets;" then "who give charity out of their cherished wealth to relatives, orphans, the poor, ˹needy˺ travellers, beggars, and for freeing captives;" then "who establish prayer, pay alms-tax, and keep the pledges they make; and who are patient in times of suffering, adversity, and in ˹the heat of˺ battle." The verse ends: "It is they who are true ˹in faith˺, and it is they who are mindful ˹of Allah˺". This verse contains many great wisdoms, encompassing rulings and correct beliefs, and what follows to the end of the sūrah is an elaboration of it.

### Phrase by phrase

**"Righteousness is not in turning your faces towards the east or the west."**. Allah first commanded the believers to face Bayt al-Maqdis and then the Kaʿbah, and the change was hard for some of the People of the Book and even for some Muslims. This verse clarifies the wisdom behind the command: the objective is obedience to Allah, adherence to His commands, facing wherever He commands and implementing whatever He legislates. That is birr, taqwā and complete faith. Facing east or west is not in itself righteousness or obedience unless Allah has legislated it, just as He says of the sacrificial animals: "Neither their meat nor blood reaches Allah. Rather, it is your piety that reaches Him" (22:37). Abū al-ʿĀliyah said that the Jews faced west in prayer and the Christians east, and Allah answered the claims both made. Al-Ḥasan and al-Rabīʿ ibn Anas said the same. The debate over the qiblah is thus closed in a unique way: faith cannot be reduced to turning west or east, for these are mere directions and cannot be made the whole object of faith to the exclusion of the other injunctions of the Sharīʿah. The address may be to Jews, Christians and Muslims together: real righteousness and reward lie in obedience to Allah, and whatever direction He appoints becomes correct and meritorious by that fact alone. While the command was to face Bayt al-Maqdis, obeying it earned reward, and now that the command is to face the House of Allah in Makkah, obeying this earns reward. One reading takes "righteousness" here to mean faith, and another to mean "all of righteousness". Al-birr is also read al-barr, the dutiful person.

**"Rather, the righteous are those who believe in Allah, the Last Day, the angels, the Books, and the prophets;"**. Al-Thawrī recited this phrase and said that what follows it are the types of birr, and he spoke truly, for whoever acquires the qualities named embraces all of Islam and every kind of righteousness. Believing in Allah is believing that He alone deserves worship and trusting Him in the full sense. Believing in the Last Day is believing in resurrection after death and giving the Hereafter priority over this world. The angels are the emissaries between Allah and His messengers, running the world at His command. The Books are the revealed Scriptures given to the prophets, finalised by the most honourable of them, the Qur'an, which supersedes and abrogates all earlier Books, contains every type of righteousness and the way to happiness in both worlds, and testifies to all the prophets from the first to the last, Muḥammad ﷺ. Believing in the prophets is accepting these mortals as Allah's chosen messengers, all of them without distinction. Faith in these matters must so pervade a believer that it issues in the deeds that follow.

**"who give charity out of their cherished wealth"**. They give money away while desiring it and loving it, and often while having little of it. The Ṣaḥīḥayn record that Abū Hurayrah related the Prophet's ﷺ saying that the best charity is what you give while healthy and thrifty, hoping to become rich and fearing poverty. Allah praises those who "give food—despite their desire for it—to the poor, the orphan, and the captive" (76:8), saying "We feed you only for the sake of Allah, seeking neither reward nor thanks from you" (76:9), and says: "You will never achieve righteousness until you donate some of what you cherish" (3:92). The Anṣār who "give ˹the emigrants˺ preference over themselves even though they may be in need" (59:9) represent a still higher rank, since they give away what they themselves need, whereas those described here give what they covet. The phrase "out of love for it" (ʿalā ḥubbihi) has three possible meanings. The pronoun may refer to Allah, in which case spending must not be driven by material motives or display but by love for Allah, with the perfect sincerity (ikhlāṣ) His majesty requires. It may refer to the wealth, in which case only the part of one's possessions that one loves earns merit, and giving away cast-offs in the name of charity is no charity, though giving them to someone who can use them is better than throwing them away. Or it may refer to the act of giving, meaning that the heart should be fully content with what is spent, rather than the hand giving while the heart aches. Al-Jaṣṣāṣ suggested that all three meanings may be included.

**"to relatives, orphans, the poor, ˹needy˺ travellers, beggars, and for freeing captives;"**. Relatives have the first right to one's charity, as the hadith says: ṣadaqah to the poor is charity, but ṣadaqah to relatives is both charity and the nurturing of kinship, for they are the most deserving of your kindness. Orphans are children who have lost their fathers while still young and weak, before the age of work, with no one to look after them. The miskīn (plural al-masākīn) is one who lacks sufficient food, clothing or shelter and should be given enough to meet his needs. The Ṣaḥīḥayn record from Abū Hurayrah that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said the miskīn is not the one who goes around and is satisfied with a date or two or a bite or two, but the one who does not have enough and whom people do not notice so as to give him charity. He is the one who shies away from asking. The wayfarer is the traveller who runs out of money and is given what will take him home, and whoever sets out on a permissible journey is given what he needs for the journey and the return. Guests are included: ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭalḥah reported Ibn ʿAbbās as saying that the son of the road is the guest hosted by Muslims, and Mujāhid, Saʿīd ibn Jubayr, Abū Jaʿfar al-Bāqir, al-Ḥasan, Qatādah, aḍ-Ḍaḥḥāk, al-Zuhrī, al-Rabīʿ ibn Anas and Muqātil ibn Ḥayyān said similarly. Those who ask are those who beg and are given from zakāh and general charity. Freeing captives means slaves who seek to buy their freedom by contract but cannot find the money, as well as captives, and one reading adds those who fight in Allah's way. The first five recipients are introduced in one way and this last head in another, with the preposition "in", to show that the money does not pass into the slave's hands as his own to spend at will, but is spent on buying slaves from their masters and setting them free.

**"who establish prayer, pay alms-tax"**. Those who pray on time and give the prayer its due of bowing, prostration, attention and humility, perfecting the five daily prayers. The zakāh is the obligatory charity due on wealth, as Saʿīd ibn Jubayr and Muqātil ibn Ḥayyān stated, and the term also covers what was given as charity before zakāh was made obligatory. Two forms of spending other than zakāh have been mentioned before zakāh itself, perhaps because of the common negligence of those rights on the assumption that paying zakāh is enough. Financial obligations do not end with zakāh, as al-Jaṣṣāṣ and al-Qurṭubī note. Spending on relatives who have a valid excuse for not earning is necessary, and if a needy person is dying of poverty after you have paid your zakāh, it becomes obligatory to save his life on the spot. Building mosques and schools for religious education also belongs to these obligations. The difference is that zakāh has its own detailed law that must be followed in all conditions, whereas these other duties depend on need: where there is need, spending is obligatory, and where there is none, it is not.

**"and keep the pledges they make;"**. They fulfil their covenants with their Lord and with other people, as in "those who honour Allah's covenant, never breaking the pledge" (13:20). The opposite is hypocrisy, for a hadith says the signs of a hypocrite are three: when he speaks he lies, when he promises he breaks his promise, and when he is entrusted he betrays the trust, and in another version, when he vows he breaks his vow and when he disputes he is foul. Here the style changes from verbs to nouns, which signifies a continuing habit of keeping one's word, since an occasional fulfilment, which even a disbeliever or sinner manages now and then, does not qualify a person for this list. Keeping promises is chosen to represent all dealings with people because abiding by one's undertakings is the essence of every transaction, buying and selling, leasing, renting and partnership. The true believer treats a contract with people as a covenant with Allah.

**"and who are patient in times of suffering, adversity, and in ˹the heat of˺ battle."**. Patient in extreme poverty, fear and hardship, in illness, pain and hunger, and on the battlefield when facing the enemy without fleeing, as Ibn Masʿūd and Ibn ʿAbbās explained, along with Abū al-ʿĀliyah, Murrah al-Hamdānī and Mujāhid, and likewise Saʿīd ibn Jubayr, al-Ḥasan and Qatādah, with the same view from al-Rabīʿ ibn Anas, al-Suddī, Muqātil ibn Ḥayyān, Abū Mālik, aḍ-Ḍaḥḥāk and others. Of all the inner qualities only ṣabr is named, because patience means controlling the self and guarding it from evil, and that is the essence of every inner deed, the means by which high morals are gained and low ones removed. The word for "the patient" is in the accusative of praise (naṣb ʿalā al-madḥ) rather than following the pattern of the preceding phrase, which means that among the righteous the patient deserve special praise, since patience gives special power for righteous deeds, and the suffering that accompanies these situations makes it all the more important.

**"It is they who are true ˹in faith˺, and it is they who are mindful ˹of Allah˺"**. Whoever acquires these qualities is truthful in his faith and in his claim to righteousness, having realised faith in the heart, on the tongue and in deed. They are the muttaqūn, the God-fearing, because they avoid what is forbidden and perform what is commanded, keeping their pledges and refraining from breaking them.

### The chapters of righteousness

Birr is an umbrella word in Arabic for what is good in the absolute sense, combining every act of righteousness and obedience, inward and outward, and its essence is obedience. The verse stresses belief, charity, keeping promises and patience, which together contain the principles behind all the injunctions of the Qur'an: the articles of faith, the deeds that follow from them, and morals. These three departments are all housed in the verse. The articles of faith come first, under belief in Allah and the rest. Then comes acting on them, in worship, up to the payment of zakāh, and in dealings with people, under keeping pledges, concluding with morals under patience. The final statement is that those who follow all of this are true Muslims and the ones who may be called God-fearing. From here to the end of the sūrah the details of this comprehensive attribute unfold as needed: retaliation, bequests, fasting, jihād, Hajj, spending, menstruation, the oath of abstention, divorce, marriage, the waiting period (ʿiddah) and dower (mahr), with jihād and spending in Allah's way stressed again, some aspects of trade and witnessing, and a finale of good tidings and the promise of mercy and forgiveness.

A religious act is in essence aimed at discovering Allah as the light of the heavens and the earth, who is closer to a person than his jugular vein. What brings a person close to Him is not mere adherence to outward forms but actions done in total sincerity for His sake alone, until He becomes part and parcel of one's being and one's attachment to Him is so strong that one does not waver from the straight path even in the most trying circumstances. His pleasure is earned by true faithfulness, not by turning the face in one direction or another. Whoever has these qualities earns Allah's blessing in this world and the next.

### The wage-earner and the recogniser

In the devotional reading, the outward meaning of the verse is what the Sharīʿah stipulates. Its inner meaning concerns the Ḥaqīqah, which is to the Sharīʿah as the spirit is to the body, for what is a body without a spirit? The Sharīʿah is the house of the servitors, where all the people gather and keep it flourishing with service and worship. The Ḥaqīqah is the house of the sanctuary, where the recognisers gather and keep it flourishing with veneration and contemplation. The distance between the two is the distance from familiarity to love: familiarity is the attribute of wage-earners, love the attribute of recognisers. The wage-earner brings all the kinds of piety named in the verse and then worries that if the wind blows against them or anything is taken away he will lose his wage. The recogniser performs all of it exactly as stipulated and then fears that if any of it remains to his account he will be held back from good fortune. Any talk that keeps you from the road, be it unbelief or faith, and any picture that holds you back from the Friend, be it ugly or beautiful, is an obstacle. The wage-earner says, my prayer, my fasting, my almsgiving, my patience in trials, my loyalty to covenants. The recogniser says in the tongue of abasement: who am I to wear the cloak of loyalty to You, or to speak of You with a spirit's scent on my lips? The Pīr of the Path said: how should I have known that the wage-earner's share is everlasting paradise, while the recogniser hopes for one glance? The wage-earner wishes for houris and palaces, and the recogniser is drowned in light in the sea of face-to-face vision. When Abū ʿAlī Rūdbārī lay dying he told his sister Fāṭimah that the doors of heaven had opened, the Gardens had been adorned and the maidservants were calling from the battlements that all of it had been built for him. The tongue of his state answered: O God, how could I be happy with paradise and houris? Give me one breath and from that breath I will build a paradise. Your rightful due is that I look on no one with the eye of love until I see You.

### In short

- The verse closes the qiblah dispute by relocating righteousness from directions to obedience: whatever Allah commands is the merit, not east or west (22:37, Abū al-ʿĀliyah).
- It is a summary of the whole religion, as al-Thawrī observed: belief in Allah, the Last Day, angels, Books and prophets, then charity from cherished wealth (3:92, 76:8-9, 59:9) to relatives, orphans, the poor, travellers, beggars and for freeing slaves, then prayer and zakāh, keeping covenants (13:20), and patience in poverty, illness and battle.
- Financial duty does not end with zakāh (al-Jaṣṣāṣ, al-Qurṭubī), keeping one's word is the essence of all dealings, and patience is the essence of all inner virtue and receives special praise.
- Those who combine these are the truthful and the God-fearing, and the rest of the sūrah elaborates the chapters of this birr.
- Inwardly, the wage-earner serves for paradise, while the recogniser, like Abū ʿAlī Rūdbārī, wants nothing but the Friend.

178.text:
After the brief introduction to the nature of righteousness in verse 177, the text turns to its subsidiary injunctions, and the first is the law of qiṣāṣ, equal retaliation. "O believers! ˹The law of˺ retaliation is set for you in cases of murder—a free man for a free man, a slave for a slave, and a female for a female." The verse continues: "But if the offender is pardoned by the victim's guardian, then blood-money should be decided fairly and payment should be made courteously. This is a concession and a mercy from your Lord. But whoever transgresses after that will suffer a painful punishment". The killer is to be killed whatever the status of the parties. If the aggrieved party relents and forgoes retaliation without forgiving the offence entirely, the killer must pay the fixed blood-money (diyah) fairly and promptly, and the claimant must pursue it in a recognised manner without harassment. This law of pardon and blood-money is a relief granted by Allah's grace, for otherwise nothing but death would face the killer. Whoever crosses Allah's limits after that, by filing a false or doubtful murder charge or by reopening a case after pardon, is severely punished.

### Phrase by phrase

**"O believers! ˹The law of˺ retaliation is set for you in cases of murder"**. Qiṣāṣ means likeness, and in usage returning like for like. As a term of the Sharīʿah it is the equal retaliation for an aggression against a person's body, allowed only on condition that the principle of like for like is strictly observed, as verse 194 of this sūrah says more plainly, "aggress against him in the like manner as he did against you", and as the end of Sūrat al-Naḥl says: "If you retaliate, then let it be equivalent to what you have suffered" (16:126). It applies exclusively to culpable homicide, where someone is killed deliberately with a lethal weapon. The believers are told not to transgress the limits as nations before them did, changing what Allah ordained. In the Jāhiliyyah the Jewish tribe of Banū al-Naḍīr had defeated Qurayẓah and made it a rule that a Naḍīr man who killed a Qurayẓah man was not killed but paid a hundred wasq of dates, while a Qurayẓah man who killed a Naḍīr man was killed, or, if Naḍīr chose ransom, paid two hundred wasq. Allah commanded justice in the penal law and the avoidance of the path of the misguided who alter His commands in disbelief and transgression.

**"a free man for a free man, a slave for a slave, and a female for a female."**. These words refer to the event behind the revelation. Just before Islam, war broke out between two Arab tribes and many men and women, free and slave, were killed on both sides. The case was still unsettled when both tribes entered Islam and began to discuss retaliation. The stronger tribe insisted on nothing less than a free man for their slave and a man for their woman from the other side, even if he was not the killer. The verse refutes this barbaric demand: the one who killed is the one to be killed, and an innocent free man or man may not be killed for a killer who was a slave or a woman. The verse does not mean that no retaliation is taken from a man who kills a woman or a free man who kills a slave. Its opening words prescribe retaliation "in cases of murder" generally, and other verses state it more explicitly, such as "a life for a life" (5:45), which is said to abrogate the earlier wording. The Sunnah makes clear that a man is killed for a woman, and that religion is taken into account, so that a Muslim is not killed for a disbeliever even if the Muslim is a slave and the disbeliever free. Al-Bukhārī reports from ʿAlī that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said a Muslim is not killed for a disbeliever, and no sound opinion or authentic hadith contradicts it, though Abū Ḥanīfah held that a Muslim may be killed for a disbeliever on the general wording of 5:45 in Sūrat al-Māʾidah. The four imams, Abū Ḥanīfah, Mālik, al-Shāfiʿī and Aḥmad, and the majority hold that a group is killed for one person they murder. ʿUmar said of a boy killed by seven men that if all the people of Ṣanʿāʾ had joined in killing him he would have killed them all, and no Companion disagreed, which amounts to a near consensus (ijmāʿ). One opinion attributed to Aḥmad is that only one person is killed for one, and Ibn al-Mundhir attributes this also to Muʿādh, Ibn al-Zubayr, ʿAbd al-Malik ibn Marwān, al-Zuhrī, Ibn Sīrīn and Ḥabīb ibn Abī Thābit.

**"But if the offender is pardoned by the victim's guardian"**. This refers to accepting blood-money in cases of intentional murder, as Abū al-ʿĀliyah, Abū al-Shaʿthāʾ, Mujāhid, Saʿīd ibn Jubayr, ʿAṭāʾ, al-Ḥasan, Qatādah and Muqātil ibn Ḥayyān held. Aḍ-Ḍaḥḥāk reported Ibn ʿAbbās as explaining that pardon means the victim's relative accepting the diyah after capital punishment has become due. The pardon may also be the victim's own, before death. The indefinite "anything" of the blood implies that even a partial pardon by the heirs waives retaliation, and the mention of "his brother" is a gentle entreaty to pardon and a reminder that killing does not sever the brotherhood of faith.

**"then blood-money should be decided fairly and payment should be made courteously."**. The relative who accepts blood-money should collect his right with kindness and without force, insult or injury, and the killer should pay it in a good way, without delay, fraud, resistance or further harm, so that no one needs to go to court. One reading describes the customary instalments: three years for a full diyah, two for half, one for a third. The diyah in the Sharīʿah is one hundred camels, or one thousand dinars, or ten thousand dirhams, roughly nineteen pounds of silver by current measures. Because the pursuit follows from the pardon, one of al-Shāfiʿī's two opinions is that the blood-money is itself a duty, while the other, which is preferred, is that retaliation is the duty and the blood-money merely compensation for forgoing it, so that if someone pardons without naming blood-money nothing is owed.

**"This is a concession and a mercy from your Lord."**. Allowing blood-money for intentional murder lightens what was required of earlier nations. Saʿīd ibn Manṣūr reports Ibn ʿAbbās as saying that the Children of Israel were bound to apply retaliation and were not permitted to pardon for blood-money, while Allah allowed this Ummah to do so, and Ibn Ḥibbān records this in his Ṣaḥīḥ. Qatādah said that Allah had mercy on this Ummah by giving them the diyah, which no nation before had: the people of the Torah could execute or pardon but could not take blood-money, the people of the Gospel were required to pardon with no diyah legislated, and this Ummah may execute, or pardon and accept blood-money. Saʿīd ibn Jubayr, Muqātil ibn Ḥayyān and al-Rabīʿ ibn Anas said the same. Allah gave latitude and did not impose a single course as He made retaliation obligatory for the Jews and pardon for the Christians.

**"But whoever transgresses after that will suffer a painful punishment"**. Whoever kills the killer after taking or agreeing to the blood-money will suffer a painful and severe torment from Allah, as Ibn ʿAbbās, Mujāhid, ʿAṭāʾ, ʿIkrimah, al-Ḥasan, Qatādah, al-Rabīʿ ibn Anas, al-Suddī and Muqātil ibn Ḥayyān said. One reading adds that such a person is himself killed and is neither forgiven nor allowed to pay blood-money. The punishment is the Fire in the Hereafter or execution in this world.

### Further rulings

If the murderer is fully pardoned, for example when both surviving sons of the victim forgo their right, he is free of any claim. If the pardon is partial, one son pardoning and the other not, the killer is released from retaliation but the son who did not pardon is entitled to half the diyah. Likewise a settlement between the parties on an agreed sum cancels retaliation and makes payment of that sum obligatory, subject to conditions set out in the books of fiqh. The heirs of the victim, however many, inherit the right to retaliation and blood-money according to their shares in the estate. Blood-money taken is divided among them by those shares, and if retaliation is chosen the right is held by all in common. Since retaliation is indivisible, a pardon by any one heir is effective and covers the retaliation rights of the others, who then receive blood-money according to their shares. Although the right of retaliation belongs to the heirs, by the consensus of the Muslim community they may not carry it out themselves. They must obtain it through a Muslim ruler or his deputy, because the details of qiṣāṣ are intricate and beyond the ordinary person, and heirs ignorant of when retaliation does or does not apply might commit excesses in the heat of anger. By unanimous agreement the right must be secured through the agency of an Islamic government, as al-Qurṭubī notes.

Islam's principle of retaliation in like measure, an eye for an eye and a tooth for a tooth, means that a killer forfeits his own life. This effectively discourages the taking of life, since fear of losing one's own life deters one from taking another's, so that the lives of all members of society are protected. The object of qiṣāṣ is the protection of society, not revenge. It also cools the vengeful feelings of the victim's family and so forestalls further violence. Yet Islam permits a settlement between the killer and the bereaved, who may demand execution, accept blood-money or forgive outright. These alternatives aim to keep brotherly feeling alive in Muslim society and to prevent an atmosphere of rivalry, and blood-money has the further advantage of compensating the family for its loss.

### The law of friendship

In the devotional reading, the verse addresses the body, heart and spirit together: O totality of the servant, if you want to step into the street of friendship, first detach your heart from life and throw away everything you know of states and deeds, for in the law of friendship your life will be taken as retaliation and all your knowledge will be the blood-money, and even more is needed. If you are the man for the work, enter. Otherwise nothing is accomplished with self-love and defilement. In the tracks of manliness the plane tree lives long, and in the tracks of defilement the jasmine fades fast. In the world, whenever someone is killed, retaliation or blood-money is due from the killer. In the law of friendship both are due from the one who is killed. The Pīr of the Path said: how should I have known that there is retaliation for those slain by friendship, or that friendship is sheer resurrection and the slain of friendship must ask for the blood-money? He burns some and kills some, and none who is burned regrets it and none who is killed turns away. How You kill us, and how we love You, how we love the Killer! One is burnt and left unsettled, another slain and bewildered in the field of solitude, one hangs on reports while another is mingled with face-to-face vision, one is in a whirlpool and another longs for water, yet the drowned is not sated and the thirsty cannot sleep.

### In short

- Qiṣāṣ, like-for-like retaliation (cf. 16:126, 5:45), is prescribed for deliberate murder: the killer himself is executed, whether free, slave, man or woman, and the verse's wording refutes a tribe's demand for a free man or a man in place of a slave or woman who had killed.
- A Muslim is not executed for a disbeliever (ʿAlī, al-Bukhārī), though Abū Ḥanīfah differed, and a group is executed for one victim (ʿUmar, near-ijmāʿ).
- The heirs may pardon in exchange for diyah, collected and paid with courtesy, a mercy not granted to the Jews (retaliation only) or the Christians (pardon only). Killing after accepting diyah brings painful punishment.
- Partial pardon or settlement ends retaliation and transfers the claim to blood-money, and the right must be exercised through the ruler, not privately (al-Qurṭubī).
- Inwardly, the law of friendship demands the lover's own life as retaliation, and none so slain regrets it.

179.text:
Verse 179 states the wisdom of the law just laid down. "There is ˹security of˺ life for you in ˹the law of˺ retaliation, O people of reason, so that you may become mindful ˹of Allah˺". The law of equal retaliation is presented to people of reason as preserving life, not merely taking it. Fear of the punishment deters killing and thereby saves lives.

### Phrase by phrase

**"There is ˹security of˺ life for you in ˹the law of˺ retaliation"**. The explanation finds great benefit in prescribing execution for murder. A would-be killer who expects that penalty holds back. Both his life and his intended victim's are thereby preserved, protecting the sanctity of life. Blood is spared and further attacks between people stopped, and there is a continuation of existence and a lesson in it. The earlier Books contained the saying that killing stops killing, and the Qur'an expresses the idea with far greater clarity and eloquence. Abū al-ʿĀliyah said that Allah made retaliation a life, for how many a man who thought of killing was stopped by this law for fear of being killed in turn. Mujāhid and Saʿīd ibn Jubayr give similar explanations, as do Abū Mālik and al-Ḥasan. The same view comes from Qatādah, al-Rabīʿ ibn Anas and Muqātil ibn Ḥayyān.

**"O people of reason"**. You who have sound minds, comprehension and understanding grasp this.

**"so that you may become mindful ˹of Allah˺"**. Perhaps by this you will be compelled to refrain from Allah's prohibitions and from what He counts as sin, warding off the killing of one another for fear of retaliation. Taqwā means doing all acts of obedience and refraining from all that is forbidden, keeping to His sacred law and doing as He instructs.

### The greater life

The devotional reading first recognises the same deterrence. Expecting execution, the would-be killer refrains, and both parties remain alive. By the allusive explanation, however, there is a greater life in abandoning retaliation, for when someone has been annihilated in Allah, He becomes his successor, and life from Him is more perfect than remaining with oneself. In the image, Allah inherits from them and becomes their successor. The Successor's abiding is dearer than the annihilated person's former life.

### In short

- Retaliation preserves life: certainty of execution deters the would-be killer and so protects both him and his intended victim (Abū al-ʿĀliyah, Mujāhid and others).
- The Qur'an states this with more eloquence than the older maxim that killing stops killing.
- The law is addressed to people of reason and aims at taqwā, keeping people from Allah's prohibitions.
- Inwardly, the greatest life belongs to the one annihilated in Allah, whose place He Himself takes.

180.text:
The next injunction concerns the will. "It is prescribed that when death approaches any of you—if they leave something of value—a will should be made in favour of parents and immediate family with fairness. ˹This is˺ an obligation on those who are mindful ˹of Allah˺". The verse commanded that parents and relatives be included in the will, and this was obligatory, on the soundest view, before the verse of inheritance came down. Once Allah legislated fixed shares for the deserving heirs, they took their portions without needing to be named in a will or to be reminded of the dead person's favour.

### Phrase by phrase

**"It is prescribed that when death approaches any of you"**. Literally al-waṣiyyah is an order to do something, whether during the lifetime of the one who gives it or after his death, but in accepted usage it refers to what must be done after death, so it may be translated as will or bequest. "When death approaches" means when its causes appear. The verse is read as prescribing the will for the moment death draws near, so that the dying person should make his testament.

**"if they leave something of value"**. Among the many meanings of the Arabic word khayr is wealth, as in the verse which says of man that he is passionate in his love for good things, where it is agreed to mean wealth. One reading takes it as a large amount of wealth.

**"a will should be made in favour of parents and immediate family with fairness."**. In early Islam, when shares of inheritance were not yet fixed, a dying person could bequeath up to a third of his estate to his parents and relatives in whatever proportions he chose. That third was their right and the rest went to the children. The obligation had three aspects: no shares except those of the children were fixed, so the other relatives' portions were determined by the will. Making such a will was obligatory on the dying person. Bequeathing more than a third was not permitted. "With fairness" means justly, more generously towards the parents, not exceeding the allotted third and not preferring the richer relative.

**"˹This is˺ an obligation on those who are mindful ˹of Allah˺"**. The word rendered "obligation" emphasises what precedes it. The duty is a firm one on the muttaqīn, the God-fearing who ascribe no partner to Allah, and the will is to follow the sacred law (Sharīʿah).

### What was abrogated and what remains

The first of the three aspects was abrogated by the verse of inheritance according to most of the Companions and their successors. Ibn ʿAbbās is reported as saying that the bequest to parents and next of kin was abrogated by the verse "For men there is a share in what their parents and close relatives leave, and for women there is a share in what their parents and close relatives leave—whether it is little or much. ˹These are˺ obligatory shares" (4:7).
