Ibn Abī Ḥātim relates the same from Ibn ʿUmar and Abū Mūsā, from Saʿīd ibn al-Musayyib and al-Ḥasan, from Mujāhid, ʿAṭāʾ and Saʿīd ibn Jubayr, and from Muḥammad ibn Sīrīn, ʿIkrimah, Zayd ibn Aslam and al-Rabīʿ ibn Anas, and adds that the abrogation by 4:7 was also stated by Qatādah, al-Suddī, Muqātil ibn Ḥayyān, Ṭāwūs, Ibrāhīm al-Nakhaʿī, Shurayḥ, aḍ-Ḍaḥḥāk and al-Zuhrī. Imam Aḥmad records from Muḥammad ibn Sīrīn that Ibn ʿAbbās recited Sūrat al-Baqarah until he reached this verse and then said that it had been abrogated, which Saʿīd ibn Manṣūr and al-Ḥākim also record, al-Ḥākim grading it ṣaḥīḥ by the criteria of al-Bukhārī and Muslim. In another narration from Ibn ʿAbbās the verse of inheritance abrogated the will in favour of those who have fixed shares, while the command to bequeath to relatives without a share still held, as al-Jaṣṣāṣ and al-Qurṭubī note. By the consensus of the Ummah, however, it is not obligatory to bequeath to relatives who have no fixed share, so the obligatory character of the will in their favour is abrogated too, and such a bequest is now only desirable (mustaḥabb), and that subject to their need.

The second aspect, the obligation itself, was abrogated by the famous mutawātir hadith, transmitted through unbroken chains from many sides whose narrators could not have agreed on a lie, delivered in the sermon before some one hundred and fifty thousand Companions at the Farewell Ḥajj: Allah has Himself given everyone who has a right his right, so there is no will for any heir (al-Tirmidhī, also recorded in the Sunan from ʿAmr ibn Khārijah). The narration from Ibn ʿAbbās adds: unless all the heirs permit it. Since Allah fixed the heirs' shares, the testator need not, and indeed may not, make a will in favour of an heir, though if the other heirs allow it, it becomes permissible. Al-Jaṣṣāṣ says the hadith is reported from a group of Companions and accepted unanimously by the jurists, so it counts as an assured report capable of abrogating a verse. Al-Qurṭubī says that scholars agree that an injunction known with full certainty from the Prophet ﷺ, as with mutawātir and well-known reports, is on a par with the Qur'an and must be taken as Allah's command, so abrogation of a verse by such a hadith is no cause for doubt. Although the hadith invalidating a will for an heir is formally a solitary report (al-khabar al-wāḥid), its proclamation at the Farewell Ḥajj before the largest ever gathering of Companions, together with their consensus and that of the Ummah, shows that they regarded it as absolutely proven. Had they felt the slightest doubt they would never have abandoned a verse of the Qur'an for it.

The third aspect still holds by unanimous approval: no more than a third may be bequeathed, unless the heirs permit more, even the whole. It is recorded in the Ṣaḥīḥayn that Saʿd ibn Abī Waqqāṣ (Abū Waqqāṣ's son) asked the Prophet ﷺ whether, having wealth and only a daughter to inherit, he might bequeath all his property, then half, and was refused each time, and was then told a third, and even a third is too much, since it is better to leave one's heirs wealthy than poor and begging from others. Al-Bukhārī records that Ibn ʿAbbās recommended that people reduce their bequests from a third to a quarter because of these words. The will should therefore be fair, giving relatives a portion without injustice to the qualified heirs and without extravagance or stinginess.

### Rulings

A will is no longer needed for relatives whose shares the Qur'an fixed, and is not permitted for them without the other heirs' consent, but relatives with no legal share may be bequeathed up to a third. The specific will described in this verse is abrogated, yet making a will remains necessary, especially for someone who owes debts or holds things in trust, which must be covered in it. It is recorded in the Ṣaḥīḥayn from Ibn ʿUmar that the Prophet ﷺ said it is not permissible for a Muslim who has something to bequeath to pass two nights without his written will ready beside him, and Ibn ʿUmar said that no night passed after he heard this without his will being ready. Another wording speaks of three nights for one against whom others hold rights. It is recommended, on the general sense of this verse, to bequeath up to a third to relatives who do not inherit, and many verses and hadiths command kindness and generosity to kin. A person may alter or cancel his will concerning the third during his lifetime. After a death the question arises how to deal with the wealth left, and the Islamic rule is to distribute it justly among the heirs, which the God-fearing should do in a spirit of fairness, creating a brotherly atmosphere and preventing litigation and quarrels. Where a family member such as an orphaned grandson does not inherit under the scheme of inheritance, the testator may provide for him from the third, for Islam approves of every lawful device for keeping society free of disputes.

### The testament of the poor

In the devotional reading, the testament of the lords of wealth is one thing and that of the lords of spiritual states another. The rich give out a third of their wealth at the end of their lives, while the poor give out limpidness of states and truthfulness of deeds. As much as the disobedient man fears for himself because of his bad deeds, the recogniser fears ten times more because of the truthfulness of his deeds and the limpidness of his states. The difference is that the disobedient fears the outcome and dreads punishment, while the recogniser fears the majesty and awareness of the Real. The fear of the recognisers is called awe, and that of the disobedient fear. Fear arises from reports and awe from face-to-face vision. Awe is a fear that places no veil before supplication, no blindfold over insight and no wall before hope, a fear that melts and kills, and until he hears the call "Do not fear, nor grieve" (29:33) its owner finds no ease. He is shown generosity yet burns in dread of losing it, his light is increased and the terror of alteration is cast into him. Abū Saʿīd Abī al-Khayr was in this state at death, and was asked to say some words of reminder. When he laid his head on the pillow of death and was asked, as the qiblah of the burnt, the model of the yearners and the sun of the world, to give some reminder to those he was leaving, the Shaykh said only that his two eyes were full of water, his liver full of fire, his hands full of wind and his head full of dust. Bishr al-Ḥāfī had the same state at his departure.

### In short

- Before the verse of inheritance, a dying person had to bequeath up to a third to parents and relatives in fair proportions.
- The verse was abrogated by 4:7 (Ibn ʿAbbās and many successors) and by the Farewell Ḥajj hadith "there is no will for an heir" (al-Tirmidhī), which the Ummah unanimously accepted (al-Jaṣṣāṣ, al-Qurṭubī).
- What remains: no bequest to an heir without the other heirs' consent, up to a third for non-inheriting relatives (recommended, not obligatory), and no more than a third in all (the hadith of Saʿd, the Ṣaḥīḥayn).
- A will covering debts and trusts should always be kept ready (Ibn ʿUmar).
- Inwardly, the poor bequeath pure states rather than wealth, and the recogniser's fear is awe born of vision.

181.text:
Having prescribed the will, the passage protects it. "But whoever changes the will after hearing it, the blame will only be on those who made the change. Indeed, Allah is All-Hearing, All-Knowing".

### Phrase by phrase

**"But whoever changes the will after hearing it"**. Whoever alters the testament of the deceased after hearing it and knowing what it contains, whether a witness or a trustee, by adding to it, taking from it, stopping something in it or, obviously, concealing it altogether, falls under this verse.

**"the blame will only be on those who made the change."**. The sin resulting from the altered will rests on those who changed it, while the one who made the will bears no responsibility for what they did. Ibn ʿAbbās and others said that the dead person's reward is preserved for him by Allah and the sin is earned by those who change the will. Here the explicit subject, "those who made the change", stands in place of the pronoun, which emphasises who bears the burden.

**"Indeed, Allah is All-Hearing, All-Knowing"**. Allah hears the words and the will of the testator and knows the deeds of the trustee, what the beneficiaries or others have altered, and every detail of their situations, and He requites each accordingly. It is also said that He knows the deed of the testator himself, whether he transgressed in his will. Because of the fear of this sin, people used to execute a dead person's will exactly as it stood even when he had exceeded the limits in it, until the following verse was revealed.

### The weight of a will

ʿAbd al-Razzāq reports from Abū Hurayrah that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said that a man may do the works of the righteous for seventy years and then commit injustice when dictating his will, so that his life ends with the worst of his deeds and he enters the Fire, while another may do the works of the wicked for seventy years and then dictate a just will, so that he ends with the best of his deeds and enters Paradise. Abū Hurayrah then told his listeners to read, if they wished, the verse ending "These are the limits set by Allah, so do not transgress them. And whoever transgresses the limits of Allah, they are the ˹true˺ wrongdoers" (2:229). Changing the provisions of a will is unlawful unless the aim is the fair settlement described next.

In the devotional reading, whoever distorts an utterance takes its evil and harm upon himself, and his punishment is to be denied the fragrance of sincerity. Whoever aids the religion is aided by Allah, and whoever gives aid against it is forsaken by Him.

### In short

- Altering, cutting, adding to or hiding a will after hearing it is a sin borne by the alterer alone, and the deceased keeps his reward (Ibn ʿAbbās).
- Allah hears the testator's words and knows the trustee's deeds, and will requite each.
- A will can decide a life's end for good or ill (Abū Hurayrah, with 2:229).
- Distorting words costs the distorter the fragrance of sincerity.

182.text:
Verse 182 states the exception to the prohibition on changing a will. "Whoever suspects an error or an injustice in the will and brings about a ˹fair˺ settlement among the parties will not be sinful. Surely Allah is All-Forgiving, Most Merciful".

### Phrase by phrase

**"Whoever suspects an error or an injustice in the will"**. Ibn ʿAbbās, Abū al-ʿĀliyah, Mujāhid, aḍ-Ḍaḥḥāk, al-Rabīʿ ibn Anas and al-Suddī explained the first word as error. Error here is straying from what is right unintentionally, and injustice or sin is deliberately exceeding the third or singling out a rich person. The errors include cases where an heir indirectly gains more than his fair share, for instance when the will directs that a certain item be sold to him, or where the testator names his daughter's son in the legacy in order to increase the daughter's portion. Such things may arise from softness of heart without thought of the consequences, or from sinful intent. "Suspects" here means knows that the testator has purposely committed a mistake or transgression.

**"and brings about a ˹fair˺ settlement among the parties"**. The executor is permitted to correct the errors and replace the unjust provisions with a better arrangement, so that both Islamic law and the dead person's wishes are respected. He makes peace between the heirs and the testator, or between the testator and the trustee, by commanding that justice be done, advising the testator and rectifying the wrong, and reconciling those who disagree about it, reducing any bequest to no more than a third. This is not counted as altering the will, which is why Allah mentioned it separately, excluding it from the prohibition of the previous verse.

**"will not be sinful."**. There is no blame on him for this. Rather, he is rewarded for setting things right.

**"Surely Allah is All-Forgiving, Most Merciful"**. He forgives the deceased who erred or transgressed in his will, and is merciful regarding the testator's deed. It is also said that His mercy appears in granting the dispensation to reduce bequests to a third and so commanding adherence to fairness. He is forgiving towards every servant who repents to Him and compassionate with them.

### Kindness to beginners

In the devotional reading, the verse alludes to one who recognises a weakness in an aspirant or sees a slackness of purpose in a novice, or to a counsellor who speaks with pure sincerity to someone who lacks the capacity for it. Such a person treats the aspirant with indulgence, encouragement, persuasion and leniency, and this is not objectionable, for urging people towards pure sincerity and encouraging what is not yet firmly established in them carries ample reward. Kindness to beginners helps put things right. Their resolve may still be weak and their effort not yet sincere, so they need this patient treatment.

### In short

- Where a will contains an error or a deliberate injustice, such as favouring one heir indirectly or exceeding the third, the executor may correct it and reconcile the parties without sin, and is rewarded for it.
- This correction is not the forbidden alteration of verse 181.
- Allah forgives the testator's error and shows mercy in permitting the adjustment to a third.
- Inwardly, gentle indulgence towards weak novices is part of making things right.

183.text:
From the will the passage moves to the fast. "O believers! Fasting is prescribed for you—as it was for those before you—so perhaps you will become mindful ˹of Allah˺". Allah addresses this Ummah's believers with the command to fast. They must leave food, drink and sexual relations with an intention sincere to Him alone. Fasting purifies the soul of evil and bad behaviour.

### Phrase by phrase

**"O believers! Fasting is prescribed for you"**. Literally ṣawm means to abstain. In the terminology of Islamic law it is abstention from eating, drinking and sexual intercourse, continuously from dawn to sunset, with the intention of fasting. If someone eats or drinks even a minute before sunset the fast is invalid, and if someone abstains all day without the intention there is no fast either. Ṣawm is an act of worship (ʿibādah) regarded as a pillar and sign of Islam, and its merits are too many to list here. One early reading recalls abstention beginning with sleep before dawn, or with the dawn prayer. It describes food and intimacy as forbidden after the night prayer or after sleeping. Later verses abrogated that rule. They permit relations on fasting nights and food and drink until dawn's white thread becomes distinct from the black.

**"as it was for those before you"**. The command is accompanied by the statement that the obligation is not peculiar to the Muslims, for fasting was enjoined on the earlier communities too, who are an example in this, so the Muslims should perform the duty more vigorously and obediently than the nations before them. The reference shows the importance of fasting and encourages the Muslims: whatever inconvenience fasting involves was faced by earlier communities as well, and a hardship shared by many is easier to bear. "Those before you" is general, covering every religious community from Ādam to the last of the Prophets ﷺ, so that fasting, like ṣalāh, was prescribed to the Ummah of every prophet without exception. Those who take it to mean the Christians or the People of the Book give an example rather than excluding others. Nor does the verse imply that the earlier fasts were identical in every respect, for there were differences in number and timing. The thought resembles "To each of you We have ordained a code of law and a way of life" (5:48).

**"so perhaps you will become mindful ˹of Allah˺"**. The fast purifies the body and restricts Shayṭān's avenues. In the Ṣaḥīḥayn the Prophet ﷺ tells young men who can afford marriage to marry, and those who cannot to fast, for it will be a shield for them. Fasting curbs the desires that prompt disobedience and grows in a person the power to control his desires, which is the foundation of taqwā, the special Qur'anic term tentatively translated as fear of Allah, abstinence and warding off evil. So one guards oneself against sin and against His punishment by good deeds, of which fasting is among the best.

### The spirit of the fast

The main aim of fasting is to reduce dependence on material things and strengthen spiritual resolve so that a person may enter the higher realms of faith and piety. Ramaḍān offers a special occasion for good deeds and avoidance of evil. It brings joy to the believer's heart and peace to his mind. Though the fast is prescribed for one month a year, its spirit endures, teaching a person to withdraw from the world while remaining part of it and to fulfil his spiritual obligations amid the turmoil of a materialistic world. Ramaḍān is the month of heightened God-consciousness. Instead of gossip, lying, slander and other marks of bad character, the believer concentrates on cultivating good habits, and his inner self moves day by day towards righteousness, devotion and piety. This is the path the Prophet Muḥammad ﷺ himself laid down, spending Ramaḍān in prayer and praise, especially at sunset when breaking the fast, the moment when the believer feels closest to his Creator. Perhaps for this reason he counted the fasting person at the time of breaking the fast among the five whose supplications are never turned down, with the just ruler, the oppressed, the parent praying for his children and the traveller in Allah's cause.

### The guests of the Real

The allusive reading presents the faithful as future guests of the Real. Their prescribed fast prepares them to arrive hungry at Paradise's banquet. The generous like their guests to arrive hungry so that the feast is sweeter to them, and the Lord of the Worlds created Paradise and all within it for the faithful, needing none of it Himself. A Sufi master once sent out an invitation and nobody came. He raised his hands and said that if the Lord sent His servants to the Fire tomorrow, Paradise and its bliss would be like his own empty table, for a table's value lies in people sitting and eating at it. Allah created all the treasuries of blessing for the faithful who eat, while He Himself does not eat. That is why He says that fasting belongs to Him and He Himself rewards it. One of the masters explained: self-sufficiency belongs to Me, I neither eat nor drink, and I reward those who fast without reckoning, for by not eating they sought conformity with Me, and the first station of friendship is conformity. The report speaks of past and future sins being forgiven through conformity with the angels in saying "Āmīn" after the Fātiḥah. The image then points to the nobility of heart and religion through conformity with Allah in not eating. It preserves the distinction: the servant abstains temporarily and with effort. Allah's attribute is beginningless. It is also said that He ascribed fasting to Himself so that the hands of claimants would not reach it: at the Resurrection, when those you wronged gather round and carry off your acts of worship in settlement, the Lord will keep your fasting in the treasury of His bounty and tell them that it is His and they have no share in it.

### In short

- Ṣawm is abstention from food, drink and intimacy from dawn to sunset with intention, a pillar of Islam.
- It was prescribed for every earlier community (cf. 5:48), which both dignifies it and makes its hardship easier to bear, though details differed.
- Its purpose is taqwā: it shields against desire (the hadith of the young men) and builds self-control.
- Ramaḍān trains character and brings closeness to Allah, and the faster's prayer at ifṭār is answered.
- Inwardly, the faithful fast as hungry guests invited to the banquet of Paradise, and fasting belongs to Allah alone.

184.text:
Verse 184 sets the measure of the fast and its concessions. "˹Fast a˺ prescribed number of days. But whoever of you is ill or on a journey, then ˹let them fast˺ an equal number of days ˹after Ramaḍân˺." It continues: "For those who can only fast with extreme difficulty, compensation can be made by feeding a needy person ˹for every day not fasted˺. But whoever volunteers to give more, it is better for them. And to fast is better for you, if only you knew". The fast falls on a fixed number of days so that it does not weigh on hearts and weaken their resolve and endurance.

### Phrase by phrase

**"˹Fast a˺ prescribed number of days."**. The days are few and specified, those of Ramaḍān, thirty days, and Allah fixed a small number to make things easy for those under the obligation.

**"But whoever of you is ill or on a journey, then ˹let them fast˺ an equal number of days ˹after Ramaḍân˺."**. The sick person meant is one who cannot fast without unbearable hardship or strongly fears that his illness will worsen, as the words "Allah intends ease for you, not hardship" in verse 185 indicate, and the jurists agree on this. The text says "on a journey" rather than "a traveller" to show that merely leaving home is not enough: one must have embarked on a journey, not gone five or ten miles. The Qur'an does not fix the distance, but guided by the Prophet's ﷺ words and the Companions' practice, Abū Ḥanīfah and many jurists set it at three days' walking in three daily stages, which later jurists put at forty-eight miles. One is exempt only while the journey continues. A short halt does not end it, but an intended stay of fifteen days at one place, a period fixed by a statement of the Prophet ﷺ, removes one from the status of being on a journey, while someone who intends to spend fifteen days moving between different places remains a traveller and keeps the concession. "An equal number of days" means that the sick person and the traveller must fast other days to match those missed, so that fasts abandoned under compulsion are made up by qaḍāʾ. The phrasing suggests that the obligation arises only once the sick person recovers and the traveller returns home and lives long enough to make them up, so one who dies before that owes no qaḍāʾ and need not leave a will for a fidyah. The make-up fasts may be consecutive or spread out, in any order, since the wording leaves the choice open.

**"For those who can only fast with extreme difficulty, compensation can be made by feeding a needy person ˹for every day not fasted˺."**. In the early days of Islam those who had the strength to fast but did not wish to could pay a ransom in charity instead, with the reminder that fasting was better. The aim was to accustom people to fasting. Al-Bukhārī and Muslim record from ʿĀʾishah that ʿĀshūrāʾ had been a day of fasting, and that when Ramaḍān was made obligatory whoever wished fasted and whoever wished did not, and al-Bukhārī records the same from Ibn ʿUmar and Ibn Masʿūd. Muʿādh said that at first whoever wished fasted and whoever wished fed a poor person for each day. Al-Bukhārī records from Salamah ibn al-Akwaʿ that when this verse came down those who did not wish to fast paid the fidyah until verse 185 abrogated it, and Muslim, Abū Dāwūd, al-Nasāʾī, al-Tirmidhī, al-Ṭabarānī and others report it from him as well. Ibn ʿUmar said it was abrogated, and ʿAbdullāh ibn Masʿūd, as al-Suddī reports from Murrah, explained the phrase as those who find fasting difficult. The abrogation by "So whoever is present this month, let them fast" (2:185) applies to the healthy resident who must fast. According to the consensus of the Ummah the ransom remains for the very old and for those with a permanent illness and no hope of recovery, as al-Jaṣṣāṣ and al-Maẓharī state. Al-Bukhārī reports that ʿAṭāʾ heard Ibn ʿAbbās recite the verse and say that it was not abrogated but applies to the old man and woman who can fast only with difficulty and choose to feed a poor person for each day. Such a person does not have to fast other days, since he is unlikely to improve, and pays a fidyah per day. Al-Bukhārī held the same, citing Anas, who for a year or two after growing old fed bread and meat to a poor person for each day, and Abū Yaʿlā al-Mawṣilī gives it with a connected chain from Ayyūb ibn Abī Tamīmah: Anas could no longer fast, so he prepared a dish of tharīd and invited thirty poor people and fed them. The same applies to pregnant and nursing women who fear for themselves or their children. Ibn ʿAbbās said the verse remains valid for these two and is not abrogated, and they pay the fidyah without making up the days.

**"But whoever volunteers to give more, it is better for them."**. Whoever feeds an extra poor person, or gives more than the minimum ransom, does good that is good for him in reward.

**"And to fast is better for you, if only you knew"**. Fasting is better than breaking the fast and paying the ransom, if you knew the goodness in it, so do it. This was the first of Allah's rulings on fasting, and afterwards He made the fast a duty on every able person who has reached puberty.

### The stages of the fast

A long hadith from Muʿādh ibn Jabal in the Musnad of Aḥmad describes three changes in ṣalāh and three in ṣawm in the early period. When the Prophet ﷺ came to Madīnah he fasted three days each month and the tenth of Muḥarram. Then Ramaḍān was ordained with the option of fasting or paying ransom, fasting being preferred. Then the verse of witnessing the month removed the option for those with strength, the ransom remaining for the very old. The third change concerned the nights: at first eating, drinking and intimacy after ifṭār were allowed only until one slept, sleep marking the start of the next fast, until the verse making relations lawful on the nights of the fast permitted all three until dawn, and suḥūr soon after rising became the sunnah, as hadiths in al-Bukhārī, Muslim and Abū Dāwūd confirm.

### Rulings on the ransom

The ransom for one missed fast is half a ṣāʿ of wheat, about 1.632 kilograms, or its market value, given to a poor person, roughly the amount a person eats in a day, or one mudd of the staple food of the town. It should not be given as part of the wages of those who serve a mosque or madrasah. The ransom for one fast should not be split between two recipients, and as a precaution the ransom for several fasts should not be given to one person on a single day, though some scholars permit it and the payment counts if the precaution is not observed. Whoever cannot even pay the ransom should seek forgiveness through istighfār and intend in his heart to pay when he can.

### Fasting for Allah and through Allah

In the devotional reading, whoever is present in the month fasts for Allah, and whoever is present with the Creator of the month fasts through Allah. The fast for Him leads to recompense and the fast through Him to nearness. The first is the fulfilment of worship and belongs to every worshipper (ʿābid), the second is the healing of spiritual desire (irādah) and belongs to every seeker. The first is performed by the outward self and the second by the innermost selves. The first abstains according to the plain expressions of the Sharīʿah, the second according to the allusions of reality (al-ḥaqīqah). Whoever is present in Ramaḍān abstains from what breaks the fast, while whoever is present with the Real abstains at all times from witnessing created things. Whoever fasts with his lower self drinks of Salsabīl and Zanjabīl, whoever fasts in his heart drinks of what brings love through the blessing of Allah's approval, and those who fast with their innermost selves are those of whom He says "their Lord will give them a purifying drink" (76:21), a drink not turned about in the hand but appearing from His kindness, a drink of intimacy and not from a cup. The sick person and the traveller allude to the one whose spiritual desire loses its vigour so that he turns back to other than Him, whether through a permissive interpretation, a lack of strength and endurance or weakness in bearing the decrees of reality.

### In short

- The fast is a small, fixed number of days, the thirty of Ramaḍān.
- The genuinely sick and those on a real journey (three stages, later reckoned as forty-eight miles, not a stay of fifteen days) may break the fast and make up the days later in any order.
- The option of ransom for the able was the first stage, abrogated by 2:185 (Salamah ibn al-Akwaʿ, ʿĀʾishah, Ibn ʿUmar), but remains for the permanently unable, the aged (Ibn ʿAbbās, Anas) and nursing or pregnant women who fear harm.
- The ransom is half a ṣāʿ of wheat or its value per day, given to the poor, and giving more is better, while fasting is better still.
- Inwardly, the worshipper fasts for Allah and the seeker fasts through Him, and the fast of the innermost self is rewarded with the pure drink of 76:21.

185.text:
Verse 185 extends the brief verse before it and asserts the great merit of Ramaḍān. "Ramaḍân is the month in which the Quran was revealed as a guide for humanity with clear proofs of guidance and the standard ˹to distinguish between right and wrong˺. So whoever is present this month, let them fast." It goes on: "But whoever is ill or on a journey, then ˹let them fast˺ an equal number of days ˹after Ramaḍân˺. Allah intends ease for you, not hardship, so that you may complete the prescribed period and proclaim the greatness of Allah for guiding you, and perhaps you will be grateful". The "prescribed number of days" of verse 184 was somewhat vague, and this verse explains that the days meant are those of the month of Ramaḍān.

### Phrase by phrase

**"Ramaḍân is the month in which the Quran was revealed"**. Allah honoured Ramaḍān above the other months by choosing it for sending down the glorious Qur'an, as He did for all the Books He revealed to the prophets. Imam Aḥmad records from Wāthilah ibn al-Asqaʿ that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said that the scrolls of Ibrāhīm came down on the first night of Ramaḍān, the Torah on the sixth, the Injīl on the thirteenth and the Qur'an on the twenty-fourth, while a narration from Jābir places the Psalms on the twelfth and the Injīl on the eighteenth. The earlier Books came down whole on those dates. The Qur'an's peculiarity is that it was sent in its entirety from the Preserved Tablet to the heaven of this world on one night of Ramaḍān, and then revealed to the Prophet ﷺ gradually over twenty-three years. One account says that Gabriel brought the whole Qur'an to the first heaven, dictated it to the angelic scribes, and then brought it down to Muḥammad ﷺ day after day, sometimes one, two or three verses and sometimes a whole sūrah. That night was Laylat al-Qadr, the Night of Power, as the Qur'an itself says that it was revealed in the Night of Power. The hadith puts it on the twenty-fourth, and since al-Ḥasan held that Laylat al-Qadr falls on the night of the twenty-fourth the two agree, but if that alignment is not accepted the Qur'an's statement prevails, and whichever night is the Night of Power is the one intended.

**"as a guide for humanity with clear proofs of guidance and the standard ˹to distinguish between right and wrong˺."**. Allah praises the Qur'an as guidance for the hearts of those who believe in it and keep its commands, leading people away from error. Its clear proofs are plain, unambiguous signs for those who understand, testifying to its truth and guidance as opposed to misguidance, to the straight path as opposed to the crooked, and to the distinction between truth and falsehood and between the lawful and the forbidden, including legal rulings, punishments and the avoidance of doubtful matters.

**"So whoever is present this month, let them fast."**. The word shahida comes from shuhūd, presence, and al-shahr here means Ramaḍān, so whoever is present in the month must fast throughout it. This requires the healthy person who witnesses the start of the month while resident in his land to fast, and it abrogated the general choice of paying ransom instead, leaving fasting as the only option. Being present means finding Ramaḍān with the ability to fast: being Muslim, sane, of age, resident and free of impurities including menstruation and post-natal bleeding. Those who lack the basic ability, the disbeliever, the minor and the insane, are not addressed by the obligation, while those who have the ability but are prevented at some point by a valid excuse, a menstruating or post-natal woman, a sick person or a traveller, have found the month in a state of ability, so the command applies to them, relief is granted for the time of the excuse and qaḍāʾ is required later.

**"But whoever is ill or on a journey, then ˹let them fast˺ an equal number of days ˹after Ramaḍân˺."**. Having ordered the fast, Allah repeats the permission for the sick person who cannot fast or fears harm, and the traveller, to break the fast and make up the days. The concession had already appeared in the previous verse, but since the option of ransom had now been cancelled, a doubt might arise that the concession for the sick and travelling had been abrogated as well, or swallowed by the general words "whoever is present", so it was positively repeated. The authentic Sunnah records that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ travelled in Ramaḍān for the conquest of Makkah, marched as far as Kadīd, then broke his fast and ordered those with him to do the same, as the Two Ṣaḥīḥs record. That order did not make breaking the fast compulsory, for the Companions used to travel with him in Ramaḍān with some fasting and some not, neither group criticising the other, and he would have criticised those who fasted had it been required. He himself sometimes fasted on journeys: Abū al-Dardāʾ relates in the Two Ṣaḥīḥs that on one Ramaḍān journey the heat was so intense that men put their hands on their heads, and only the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and ʿAbdullāh ibn Rawāḥah were fasting. Still, using the permission is better, for he said that those who did not fast had done well and there was no harm on those who fasted, and in another hadith he told people to hold to the permission Allah had granted. Some scholars hold the two equal, since ʿĀʾishah relates in the Two Ṣaḥīḥs that Ḥamzah ibn ʿAmr al-Aslamī, who fasted a great deal, asked whether to fast when travelling and was told to fast or not as he wished. When fasting becomes hard, breaking it is better: Jābir relates that the Prophet ﷺ saw a man being shaded by others, was told he was fasting, and said that it is not piety to fast while travelling, as al-Bukhārī and Muslim record. Those who ignore the Sunnah and believe breaking the fast on a journey to be disliked must break it and may not fast. Making up the days need not be consecutive, for consecutive fasting is required only in Ramaḍān itself and afterwards what matters is simply the number, which is why Allah said "an equal number of days".

**"Allah intends ease for you, not hardship"**. Out of mercy He allowed the sick and the travelling to break the fast while keeping it binding on the healthy resident, this ease being the very reason He commanded the fast as He did. One reading takes it as His wish that the traveller take the dispensation and not bear the hardship of fasting on the road. Imam Aḥmad records from Anas ibn Mālik, and the Two Ṣaḥīḥs confirm, that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said to treat people with ease and not hardness, giving glad tidings and not driving people away, and the Ṣaḥīḥayn record that he said the same to Muʿādh and Abū Mūsā when sending them to Yemen. The Sunan and Musnad compilers record his words that he was sent with the easy Ḥanīfiyyah.

**"so that you may complete the prescribed period"**. You were allowed to break the fast when ill or travelling because Allah wanted ease for you, and He commanded the make-up only so that you complete the days of a full month once you are home and well.

**"and proclaim the greatness of Allah for guiding you"**. Remember Allah upon completing the act of worship, as in "When you have fulfilled your sacred rites, praise Allah" (2:200), "Once the prayer is over, disperse throughout the land and seek the bounty of Allah. And remember Allah often" (62:10) and "glorify Him during part of the night and after the prayers" (50:39-40). Hence the Sunnah encourages tasbīḥ, taḥmīd and takbīr after the obligatory prayers, and Ibn ʿAbbās said that they used to know the Messenger of Allah ﷺ had finished the prayer by the takbīr. Several scholars hold that the takbīr of ʿĪd al-Fiṭr is derived from this verse, magnifying Allah on the day of ʿĪd for guiding you to His religion and the principal rites of His religion.

**"and perhaps you will be grateful"**. If you keep to what Allah commanded, performing the obligations, leaving the prohibitions and observing His limits, you may be among the grateful, thankful for the dispensation and for being guided to the religion He approved for you.

### Rulings

Fasting Ramaḍān becomes obligatory on condition that one finds the month in a state of ability. Whoever finds the whole month fasts the whole month and whoever finds less fasts the days he finds, so a disbeliever who embraces Islam or a minor who comes of age in mid-Ramaḍān fasts from then on without qaḍāʾ for the earlier days. The insane person, being a Muslim adult, has the basic ability, so if he regains sanity during the month he must make up the earlier days, and the same applies to a woman purified in mid-Ramaḍān, a sick person who recovers or a traveller who becomes resident. The month is established in Islamic law in one of three ways: sighting the new moon oneself, proof of the sighting through a trustworthy witness, or, failing both, completing thirty days of Shaʿbān. If on the eve of the twenty-ninth of Shaʿbān clouds or bad weather hide the horizon and no admissible witness appears, the next day is the day of doubt (yawm al-shakk), for the moon may or may not have been there. Fasting that day is not obligatory but makrūh, forbidden in the hadith so that farḍ and nafl are not confused, as al-Jaṣṣāṣ notes. In lands where day or night lasts for months, finding Ramaḍān plainly does not apply and such people would not fast. As for ṣalāh, the Ḥanafī jurists al-Ḥuluwānī and al-Qabālī ruled that they pray according to their own day and night, so that where dawn follows immediately on maghrib ʿishāʾ is not obligatory, and where a day lasts six months there would be only five prayers in that period and no Ramaḍān, hence no obligatory fast, the position also taken in Imdād al-Fatāwā.

### Fasting as training in gratitude

Fasting trains the believer in two things at once, thanksgiving and the fear of Allah. Food and water are great blessings whose worth people fail to appreciate. The one who fasts goes hungry and thirsty all day and then eats and drinks his fill at sunset in a state of extreme need, and through his own experience realises how great these blessings are, which produces boundless gratitude towards his Lord. At the same time total abstention from food and drink from dawn to sunset is an exercise in making Allah one's guardian and a training for a God-fearing life that abstains from everything He has forbidden. The whole life of the believer is a life of fasting: in Ramaḍān he abstains temporarily from certain things so that for the rest of his life he may permanently renounce whatever Allah disapproves of. The Qur'an is a great blessing, and through fasting a person becomes truly thankful and able to live by its teachings.

### A month that washes and burns

In the devotional reading, Ramaḍān has turned towards the friends. It is a month that both washes and burns: it washes the hearts of sinners with the water of repentance and burns the bodies of the servants with the fire of hunger. The name Ramaḍān is derived either from ramḍāʾ, the hot stone that burns whatever is laid on it, or from ramaḍī, the rain that washes whatever it meets. Asked what Ramaḍān is, Muṣṭafā ﷺ replied that in it Allah burns the sins of the faithful and forgives them. Anas ibn Mālik heard the Messenger of Allah ﷺ say that when Ramaḍān comes the gates of the Garden are opened, the gates of the Fire shut and the devils fettered, and that if someone reaches Ramaḍān and is not forgiven, then when will he be. He also said that if Allah gave the heavens and the earth leave to speak they would give those who fast in Ramaḍān the good news of the Garden. Poor man, you do not know the worth of this blessing: eminence has been set down beside you and you are unaware. Islam, the highest of creeds, is your religion. The Qur'an, the most exalted of books, is your Book. Muṣṭafā ﷺ, master of the children of Ādam, the eye and lamp of the kingdom and leader of the world's folk at the Resurrection, is your messenger. The Kaʿbah, the most eminent of spots, is your qiblah. And Ramaḍān, the most excellent of months, is your month and the season of your practice, a month in which acts of disobedience are forgiven, the devils subdued, Paradise adorned with its doors open and the doors of Hell shut, in which the market of the corrupt is broken, the deeds of the obedient are joined with self-purification and past sins and recorded stains are burned away. The Commander of the Faithful ʿAlī said that had Allah wished to chastise Muḥammad's community He would not have given them the month of Ramaḍān nor the sūrah "Say: He is Allah, One" (112).

### In short

- Ramaḍān was chosen for the revelation of the Qur'an, sent down whole to the lowest heaven on Laylat al-Qadr and then revealed gradually over twenty-three years, as the earlier Books also came down in this month (Wāthilah ibn al-Asqaʿ, Jābir).
- Whoever finds the month with the ability to fast must fast it. This ended the option of ransom for the able.
- The concession for the sick and travelling is repeated so no one thinks it abrogated. Breaking the fast on a journey is permitted and often better (the march to Makkah, Jābir), though the Prophet ﷺ himself sometimes fasted (Abū al-Dardāʾ), and missed days are made up in any order.
- Allah intends ease, as the Prophet's ﷺ instructions to Muʿādh and Abū Mūsā show. The fast ends with takbīr, as worship generally ends in remembrance (2:200, 62:10, 50:39-40), the root of the ʿĪd takbīr.
- The month is fixed by sighting, testimony or completing Shaʿbān. Fasting the day of doubt is makrūh. Converts and new adults fast from when they qualify, while the recovered, the purified and the returned traveller make up earlier days.
- Fasting teaches gratitude for food and drink and trains a God-fearing life, and inwardly Ramaḍān washes hearts and burns sins (ʿAlī, Anas).

186.text:
Between the injunctions of fasting in the three previous verses and the long verse on fasting and iʿtikāf that follows, this brief verse is placed to persuade Allah's servants to obey His commands by recognising how, in His special grace, He hears and answers their prayers. "When My servants ask you ˹O Prophet˺ about Me: I am truly near. I respond to one's prayer when they call upon Me. So let them respond ˹with obedience˺ to Me and believe in Me, perhaps they will be guided ˹to the Right Way˺". Fasting is undoubtedly a difficult obligation despite its many concessions, and to make the trial bearable Allah mentions His special grace: I am near My servants, and when they pray I answer and take care of their needs. Under such conditions it is fitting that servants bear the hardships that come with carrying out His injunctions.

### Phrase by phrase

**"When My servants ask you ˹O Prophet˺ about Me: I am truly near."**. A group of the Prophet's ﷺ followers asked him whether their Lord was near, so that they should speak to Him quietly, or far, so that they should call out to Him, and this verse came down. A villager is also reported to have put the question in these words. One reading has the question coming from the People of the Book. The answer is that Allah is near to them in His knowledge, aware of everything about them, and near in answering. From "I am near" comes the ruling that prayer should be made slowly and quietly, and that raising the voice in supplication is not desirable. Imam Aḥmad records from Abū Mūsā al-Ashʿarī that during a battle the Companions shouted "Allāhu akbar" whenever they climbed a hill or went down into a valley, and the Prophet ﷺ came to them and told them to be gentle with themselves, since they were not calling upon one who is deaf or absent but upon the All-Hearing, All-Seeing, who is closer to each of them than the neck of his mount. He then asked ʿAbdullāh ibn Qays, which was Abū Mūsā's name, whether he should teach him a phrase that is a treasure of Paradise, "lā ḥawla wa lā quwwata illā billāh". The Two Ṣaḥīḥs record this, and Abū Dāwūd, al-Nasāʾī, al-Tirmidhī and Ibn Mājah have similar wordings. Imam Aḥmad also records from Anas that the Prophet ﷺ related Allah's words: I am as My servant thinks of Me, and I am with him whenever he calls on Me.

**"I respond to one's prayer when they call upon Me."**. Allah answers the one who calls on Him sincerely, without mediator or intercessor and without raised voices, granting his request. Imam Aḥmad records from Abū Saʿīd that the Prophet ﷺ said that no Muslim makes a duʿāʾ free of sin and of severing kinship without Allah granting him one of three things: a swift answer, a reward stored up for the Hereafter, or an equal measure of evil turned away from him, and when the Companions said they would then pray more, he said that Allah has more. ʿUbādah ibn al-Ṣāmit relates similarly, as recorded by ʿAbdullāh the son of Imam Aḥmad and by al-Tirmidhī, that no Muslim on earth supplicates without Allah granting it or averting an equal harm, so long as he asks for no sin or breaking of kinship. Imam Mālik records from Abū Hurayrah that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said a person's supplication is answered so long as he does not grow impatient and say that he prayed and was not answered, which the Two Ṣaḥīḥs record from Mālik in al-Bukhārī's wording. Muslim's version adds the conditions of asking for no sin or severing of kinship, and explains impatience as saying that one has prayed and prayed without seeing an answer, and so losing interest and giving up supplication. In the Musnad of Aḥmad and the Sunan of al-Tirmidhī, al-Nasāʾī and Ibn Mājah, Abū Hurayrah relates that three are never refused: the just ruler, the fasting person until he breaks his fast, and the oppressed, whose prayer Allah raises above the clouds, opening the gates of heaven for it and swearing by His might that He will help him, even if after a while. Placing this verse amid the rulings of fasting also hints that the prayer made at the completion of a fast is accepted, so one should be particular about praying then, for the Prophet ﷺ said that the fasting person's prayer at the time of ifṭār is accepted, and ʿAbdullāh ibn ʿUmar used to gather his family around him at ifṭār and pray.

**"So let them respond ˹with obedience˺ to Me and believe in Me"**. Let them answer My call to obedience, obeying My Messenger and devoting themselves to Me and My sacred law, and let them persevere in faith in Me and in My Messenger before they ask, for that is the surest route to being answered.

**"perhaps they will be guided ˹to the Right Way˺"**. So that they may be guided in worldly and sacred matters and have their prayers answered.

### Open a door

In the devotional reading, the servants who ask about Him are those who hold the ring of veneration for Him, who have fled to His street, put aside everything less than Him, undertaken His service, believed in Him and cut themselves off from secondary causes, wrapping the turban of trial round their heads and buying His love with spirit and heart. They came into existence with passion and leave with passion. To such servants He says that He is near: near uncalled and unsought, near unhoped for and unperceived, near by His firstness and His attributes, self-standing, near not by the servant's worthiness but by His own description. This is what He said to Moses on that pitch-black night at the edge of the Mount when he "was called from the bush in the sacred ground to the right side of the valley" (28:30), for after Ādam no one heard the speech of the Real with the ears of his head except Moses. Hearing the call, Moses was unsettled and his patience fled, since love always snatches away the hand of patience, and in his burning he asked where he should seek the One who had made him hear. The answer came: seek as you wish, for I am with you, nearer to you than your spirit is to your body, your life-vein to you and your speech to your mouth. In allusion it is as if the Exalted Lord said: I am near to you through knowledge but far from your imagination. The lovers have Me as their share, while the wage-earners receive their wages from Me. To remember Me is delight and to love Me is celebration. Whoever recognises Me holds the kingdom, whoever finds Me has joy, whoever keeps My company gives his spirit rest, and whoever is near Me has light. For the friends I stand in place of the spirit, and for the recognisers I am a resurrection that needs no Trumpet.

He says further: I am near to My servants and love the near ones. Those who call Me are answered, those who seek Me are given access, and those who reach proximity to Me have My good pleasure. My servant, draw near so that I may draw near, for whoever approaches Me by a span finds Me approaching by a cubit. If you call Me I will respond, and I also call you, to the aid of My religion and the acceptance of My messenger's message, so respond to Me. Open a door so that I may open a door. Open the door of supplication and I open the door of response: "Call upon Me, I will respond to you" (40:60). Open the door of turning back and I open the door of good news, as those "turning to Allah ˹alone˺, will have good news" (39:17). Open the door of spending and I open the door of replacement: "whatever you spend in charity, He will compensate ˹you˺ for it" (34:39). Open the door of struggle and I open the door of guidance: "those who struggle in Our cause, We will surely guide them along Our Way" (29:69). Open the door of trust and I open the door of sufficiency: "whoever puts their trust in Allah, then He ˹alone˺ is sufficient for them" (65:3). Open the door of asking forgiveness and I open the door of forgiveness, for whoever "seeks Allah's forgiveness will certainly find Allah All-Forgiving, Most Merciful" (4:110).

### In short

- Asked whether their Lord was near or far, the believers were told He is near in knowledge and in answering, so supplication, especially at ifṭār in Ramaḍān, should be quiet (the hadith of Abū Mūsā).
- Every sinless prayer is answered in one of three ways (Abū Saʿīd, ʿUbādah ibn al-Ṣāmit), provided one does not grow impatient (Abū Hurayrah), and the just ruler, the faster at ifṭār and the oppressed are never refused.
- The condition is to answer Allah's own call with obedience and firm faith, which leads to guidance.
- Inwardly, Allah is nearer to the lover than his life-vein, as He told Moses (28:30), and every door the servant opens He answers with another (40:60, 39:17, 34:39, 29:69, 65:3, 4:110).

This long verse explains the remaining injunctions of fasting, including iʿtikāf. "It has been made permissible for you to be intimate with your wives during the nights preceding the fast. Your spouses are a garment for you as you are for them. Allah knows that you were deceiving yourselves. So He has accepted your repentance and pardoned you." It continues: "So now you may be intimate with them and seek what Allah has prescribed for you. ˹You may˺ eat and drink until you see the light of dawn breaking the darkness of night, then complete the fast until nightfall." And it closes: "Do not be intimate with your spouses while you are meditating in the mosques. These are the limits set by Allah, so do not exceed them. This is how Allah makes His revelations clear to people, so they may become mindful ˹of Him˺". The verse brings relief from Allah by ending a practice of the early years, when Muslims could eat, drink and approach their wives only until the ʿishāʾ prayer, or until they slept. Whoever slept or prayed ʿishāʾ was barred from all three until the next night, and the Muslims found this hard.

### Phrase by phrase

**"It has been made permissible for you to be intimate with your wives during the nights preceding the fast."**. The opening words, uḥilla lakum, show that what is now made lawful was unlawful before. The word rafath literally covers everything a husband says or does in seeking his wife's consent, but the Ummah agrees that here it means intercourse, as Ibn ʿAbbās, ʿAṭāʾ and Mujāhid explained, with the same from Saʿīd ibn Jubayr, Ṭāwūs and Sālim ibn ʿAbdullāh, from ʿAmr ibn Dīnār, al-Ḥasan and Qatādah, and from al-Zuhrī, aḍ-Ḍaḥḥāk, Ibrāhīm al-Nakhaʿī, al-Suddī, ʿAṭāʾ al-Khurāsānī and Muqātil ibn Ḥayyān. Al-Bukhārī records through Abū Isḥāq from al-Barāʾ ibn ʿĀzib that when Ramaḍān was first ordained the permission to eat, drink and approach one's wife was conditional on not sleeping after ifṭār, so that a nap after breaking the fast made all three unlawful until the next evening. Qays ibn Ṣirmah al-Anṣārī had worked all day on his land and came home at ifṭār to find nothing to eat. His wife went out to find him something, and being exhausted he fell asleep before she returned, so that when she came back she cried out that he had slept. He fasted the next day in that state and fainted in the middle of the day, and when the matter was mentioned to the Prophet ﷺ this verse was revealed, down to the words about dawn. In another wording from al-Barāʾ, when the fast of Ramaḍān was ordained the men abstained from their wives all month, but some deceived themselves, and the verse came down. Al-Walibī reports from Ibn ʿAbbās that after ʿishāʾ in Ramaḍān the Muslims were forbidden food and intimacy until the following night, and that some, among them ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb, approached their wives or ate after ʿishāʾ, complained to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, and Allah sent down the verse. ʿUmar had gone in to his wife after finding her asleep, and told the Prophet ﷺ what he had done. The Muslims were very happy at the revelation. The rule abrogated here, the unlawfulness of eating and intimacy after sleeping, appears nowhere in the Qur'an. The Companions observed it as set by the Prophet ﷺ, as Aḥmad narrates in his Musnad, and the verse first confirms that rule as a divine command and then abrogates it for ease. This shows that rules established by the Sunnah can be abrogated through the Qur'an, and that in Islamic law the Messenger's ﷺ ruling carries the same authority as a Qur'anic injunction. The permission was then extended further when suḥūr, eaten towards the end of the night after rising from sleep, was declared a sunnah.

**"Your spouses are a garment for you as you are for them."**. Ibn ʿAbbās, Mujāhid, Saʿīd ibn Jubayr, al-Ḥasan, Qatādah, al-Suddī and Muqātil ibn Ḥayyān explained that your wives are a resort for you and you for them, and al-Rabīʿ ibn Anas said they are your cover and you theirs. The image is a metaphor for embrace and for the need of each for the other: husband and wife are intimate with one another, which is why intimacy was permitted on the nights of Ramaḍān to make things easier. Each protects the other and keeps the other pure.

**"Allah knows that you were deceiving yourselves. So He has accepted your repentance and pardoned you."**. You were betraying yourselves by approaching your wives on the nights of the fast, as happened with ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb and others, who apologised to the Prophet ﷺ. Allah relented towards you before you even turned in repentance, forgave you, relieved you of your self-deception and did not punish you.

**"So now you may be intimate with them and seek what Allah has prescribed for you."**. Now that it is lawful, lie with them and seek what Allah has decreed for you, meaning offspring, as Abū Hurayrah, Ibn ʿAbbās and Anas said, together with Shurayḥ the judge, Mujāhid, ʿIkrimah and Saʿīd ibn Jubayr, and also ʿAṭāʾ, al-Rabīʿ ibn Anas, al-Suddī and Zayd ibn Aslam, and Ḥakam ibn ʿUtbah, Muqātil ibn Ḥayyān, al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī, aḍ-Ḍaḥḥāk, Qatādah and others. Qatādah also explained it as seeking the permission Allah has granted you. A righteous child is the gift sought.

**"˹You may˺ eat and drink until you see the light of dawn breaking the darkness of night"**. Eating, drinking and intimacy are allowed during any part of the night until the light of dawn is distinct from the darkness. The Arabic likens the darkness of night to a black thread and the light of dawn to a white one, as the two stretch along the horizon, and then makes it plain by adding "of dawn". Al-Bukhārī records from Sahl ibn Saʿd that when the words about the white and black threads were revealed without "of dawn", some who meant to fast tied black and white threads to their legs and went on eating until they could tell them apart, until the words "of dawn" came down and they understood that night and day were meant. Al-Bukhārī also records from al-Shaʿbī that ʿAdī ibn Ḥātim put a black string and a white one under his pillow and watched them all night without being able to distinguish them, and when he told the Prophet ﷺ in the morning he said that his pillow must be very wide, or in another wording that the back of his neck was wide. Some took this to mean that ʿAdī was slow-witted, a weak view, for al-Bukhārī's fuller narration has ʿAdī asking whether the two threads were real threads and being told that his neck would be wide indeed if he could see them, since they are the blackness of night and the whiteness of day. The qualifier "distinct" guards against extremes: one should not, like the chronically doubtful, treat eating as unlawful before dawn has broken, nor be so heedless as to go on eating once certain that it has. Certainty of daybreak is the dividing line. Before it, eating is not ḥarām, and after it even a minute's indulgence is ḥarām and spoils the fast. Reports of Companions who continued eating well past the usual time are explained by their not yet being certain of dawn and refusing to stop merely on others' caution.

**"then complete the fast until nightfall."**. Fast from daybreak until the night arrives with the setting of the sun, and break the fast then. The Two Ṣaḥīḥs record from ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said that when night comes from the east and day departs from the west, the fasting person breaks his fast. Sahl ibn Saʿd al-Sāʿidī relates that people will retain goodness so long as they hasten to break the fast, and Imam Aḥmad records from Abū Hurayrah, in a hadith al-Tirmidhī calls ḥasan gharīb, that Allah said the dearest of His servants to Him are those who hasten most to break the fast. One reading says the verse about completing the fast was revealed concerning Ṣirmah ibn Mālik ibn ʿAdiyy.

**"Do not be intimate with your spouses while you are meditating in the mosques."**. Literally iʿtikāf is to stay in a place in seclusion, and in the terminology of the Qur'an and Sunnah it is staying in a mosque under particular conditions. ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭalḥah reports Ibn ʿAbbās as saying that the verse concerns the man in iʿtikāf in the mosque in Ramaḍān or any other month, who is forbidden to approach women by night or day until he finishes. Aḍ-Ḍaḥḥāk said that formerly a man in iʿtikāf would leave the mosque and, if he wished, be with his wife, and Allah forbade touching one's wife during iʿtikāf whether inside the mosque or outside it. Mujāhid, Qatādah and others say the same, and Ibn Abī Ḥātim reports this explanation from Ibn Masʿūd, Muḥammad ibn Kaʿb, Mujāhid, ʿAṭāʾ and al-Ḥasan, as well as from Qatādah, aḍ-Ḍaḥḥāk, al-Suddī, al-Rabīʿ ibn Anas and Muqātil. One account says the verse was revealed about a group of Companions including ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib and ʿAmmār ibn Yāsir who, while in retreat in the mosque, would go to their wives when they needed, bathe and return, and were then forbidden. This is the agreed practice: whoever is in iʿtikāf may not have intercourse, and if he must leave the mosque to relieve himself or to eat he may not kiss or embrace his wife or busy himself with anything other than his retreat, not even visiting the sick, though he may ask after them in passing. Eating and drinking at night remain lawful for the one in retreat as for everyone else, but intimacy is forbidden even at night, which is why the verse states the rule separately. The generality of "in the mosques" shows that iʿtikāf may be performed in any mosque. The juristic condition that it be a mosque where congregational prayer is regularly held, and not a deserted one, derives from the very meaning of a mosque, whose main purpose is congregational prayer, since individual prayer can be offered in a house or shop. Other rules, such as fasting during iʿtikāf and not leaving the mosque without a need recognised by the law, derive partly from the word itself and partly from the Prophet's ﷺ words and deeds, and the jurists explain them after the rules of fasting, just as the Qur'an mentions the two together. By mentioning iʿtikāf after fasting Allah draws attention to practising it in the month of fasting, especially its last part. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ kept iʿtikāf in the last ten nights of Ramaḍān until he died, and his wives did so after him, as the Two Ṣaḥīḥs record from ʿĀʾishah. The Two Ṣaḥīḥs also record that Ṣafiyyah bint Ḥuyayy visited him in the mosque during his retreat, and when she rose to go home at night he walked her back to her lodging in the house of Usāmah ibn Zayd on the edge of al-Madīnah. Two Anṣārī men passed them hurriedly, shy of disturbing him, and he called them back, told them she was Ṣafiyyah bint Ḥuyayy, and when they protested their innocence of any suspicion he said that Shayṭān runs in a person wherever the blood runs and that he feared he might cast an evil thought into their minds. Imam al-Shāfiʿī commented that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ was teaching his Ummah to remove any evil thought at once so as not to fall into what is forbidden, for those two men feared Allah too much to think ill of him. The verse forbids intercourse and whatever leads to it, such as kissing and embracing, during iʿtikāf, but a wife may attend to her husband: ʿĀʾishah said in the Two Ṣaḥīḥs that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ would lean his head into her room so that she could comb his hair while she was menstruating, and that he entered the house only for a human need.

**"These are the limits set by Allah, so do not exceed them."**. This is what Allah has explained, ordained, specified, allowed and forbidden concerning the fast, its objectives, what is permitted in it and what it requires, limits He has legislated and made clear so that you neither approach nor overstep them. ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Zayd ibn Aslam said that the limits are the four stated in this verse, and that his father and others would recite the verse and say the same. "Do not approach them" is stronger than "do not overstep them" used elsewhere, for whoever comes near the limits is close to falling into what is prohibited. The prohibitions of eating, drinking and intimacy while fasting are Allah's limits, and one should not even go near them for fear of crossing them. For this reason excessive gargling while fasting is makrūh, since water may slip down the throat, as is placing medicine in the mouth and kissing or embracing one's wife. It is also better to stop eating a couple of minutes before the end of suḥūr and to delay ifṭār a couple of minutes as a precaution, since carelessness in these matters goes against this command.

**"This is how Allah makes His revelations clear to people, so they may become mindful ˹of Him˺"**. Just as He explains the fast and its rulings, He explains His other rulings, His commands and prohibitions, through the words of His servant and Messenger Muḥammad ﷺ, so that people know how to attain true guidance and how to worship Him, doing what He commands and avoiding what He forbids. Similarly He says, "He is the One Who sends down clear revelations to His servant to bring you out of darkness and into light" (57:9).

### Suḥūr and the true dawn

Allowing food and drink until dawn is itself proof that suḥūr is encouraged, for it is a concession (rukhṣah), and Allah loves His concessions to be accepted. The Two Ṣaḥīḥs record from Anas that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said to eat suḥūr because there is blessing in it. Muslim records from ʿAmr ibn al-ʿĀṣ that the difference between our fast and that of the People of the Book is the meal of suḥūr. Imam Aḥmad records from Abū Saʿīd that suḥūr is a blessed meal not to be abandoned even if one only sips water, for Allah and His angels send blessings on those who eat it, and several hadiths call it the blessed meal. It is preferable to delay it until near dawn. The Two Ṣaḥīḥs record that Zayd ibn Thābit ate suḥūr with the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and then went to pray, and when Anas asked how long there had been between the adhān and the meal, he said the time it takes to recite fifty verses. Imam Aḥmad records from Abū Dharr that the Ummah will keep its goodness as long as it hastens ifṭār and delays suḥūr. Many of the Salaf allowed suḥūr to continue until close to fajr: this is reported from Abū Bakr and ʿUmar, from ʿAlī and Ibn Masʿūd, from Ḥudhayfah and Abū Hurayrah, and from Ibn ʿUmar, Ibn ʿAbbās and Zayd ibn Thābit, and among the Tābiʿīn from Muḥammad ibn ʿAlī ibn Ḥusayn and Abū Mijlaz, from Ibrāhīm al-Nakhaʿī and Abū al-Ḍuḥā, and from Abū Wāʾil and other companions of Ibn Masʿūd. It is also the view of ʿAṭāʾ, al-Ḥasan and Ḥakam ibn ʿUyaynah, of Mujāhid and ʿUrwah ibn al-Zubayr, and of Abū al-Shaʿthāʾ Jābir ibn Zayd, al-Aʿmash and Maʿmar ibn Rāshid. The Two Ṣaḥīḥs record from al-Qāsim from ʿĀʾishah that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said that Bilāl's adhān should not stop anyone from suḥūr, because he calls it at night, so people should eat and drink until they hear the adhān of Ibn Umm Maktūm, who does not call until dawn, in al-Bukhārī's wording. Imam Aḥmad records from Qays ibn Ṭalq from his father that dawn is not the ascending white glow but the red light spreading along the horizon, and Abū Dāwūd and al-Tirmidhī have the wording that people should eat and drink without being hurried by the rising whiteness, until the redness appears. Ibn Jarīr and Muslim record from Samurah ibn Jundub that people should not be stopped by Bilāl's adhān or by the whiteness until it spreads. Because this hadith is sometimes reported only in part, some contemporaries have misunderstood it, suggesting that one may go on eating for a while after the fajr adhān and that someone who wakes late during the adhān may hurry and eat something. The hadith in fact clearly requires stopping at the adhān of Ibn Umm Maktūm, which was called precisely at daybreak, and the Qur'an itself fixes the deadline at the certainty of dawn, so that permitting even one minute beyond it contravenes the text. The reports from the Companions and early elders about latitude in suḥūr and ifṭār are to be understood, in the light of the text, as discouraging excessive precaution well before one is certain of dawn, as has also been explained of them, for no ordinary Muslim, let alone a Companion, would openly contravene the Qur'anic command, especially when the verse ends by stressing precaution with "do not approach them".

Those who can see the horizon with their own eyes, with a clear sky and the ability to recognise the first light, must act by looking at it directly. Where the horizon is hidden or unclear, or a person cannot recognise daybreak, the time is fixed by other signs or by calculation, and there will be a period when certainty is lacking. Al-Jaṣṣāṣ answers in his Aḥkām al-Qur'ān that in such doubt it is preferable not to eat or drink deliberately, but one who eats in a state of doubt well before certainty is not a sinner, though if it later proves that dawn had broken, a make-up fast becomes due. Likewise if the new moon is not sighted on the eve of Ramaḍān and people do not fast, and witnesses later establish that it was sighted on the twenty-ninth, those who missed the day thinking it the thirtieth of Shaʿbān are not sinners but owe qaḍāʾ by unanimous agreement, and someone who breaks his fast near sunset on a cloudy day and then finds the sun still up is not a sinner but must make the fast up. It follows that one who wakes late while the usual adhāns are being called, which makes dawn certain, and knowingly eats is both a sinner and liable to qaḍāʾ, while one who eats in doubt commits the sin with the qaḍāʾ due and a degree of blame.

### Starting the fast junub, and wiṣāl

One benefit of allowing intimacy, food and drink until dawn is that it is permissible to begin the fast in a state of major impurity and to bathe any time after waking, which is the view of the four imams and the majority. Al-Bukhārī and Muslim record from ʿĀʾishah and Umm Salamah that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ would rise junub from intercourse, not from a dream, bathe and fast, and Umm Salamah added that he neither broke that fast nor made it up. Muslim records from ʿĀʾishah that a man asked whether he should fast when dawn found him junub, and the Prophet ﷺ replied that the same happened to him and he fasted. When the man said that the Prophet ﷺ was not like them since his past and future sins were forgiven, he swore by Allah that he hoped to be the most fearful of Allah among them and the most knowledgeable of what taqwā is. Several authentic hadiths forbid wiṣāl, continuing the fast through the night into the next day without eating. Imam Aḥmad and the Ṣaḥīḥayn record from Abū Hurayrah that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ forbade it, and when the people said that he practised it himself he replied that he was not like them, since his Lord gave him food and drink in his sleep. When they refused to stop, he fasted with them two days and two nights until the crescent of Shawwāl appeared, and then said that had it not appeared he would have made them fast longer, as a punishment. Wiṣāl was one of the Prophet's ﷺ special qualities, since he was assisted in it, and the food and drink he received were plainly spiritual rather than material, otherwise it would not have been wiṣāl at all. It is permitted, however, to continue from sunset until suḥūr, for Abū Saʿīd al-Khudrī relates in the Two Ṣaḥīḥs that the Prophet ﷺ forbade wiṣāl but allowed whoever wished to continue until suḥūr, again explaining that he had One who fed him and gave him drink during the night.

### The essence of fasting

Fasting is by nature an act of patience, and patience means putting up with every kind of difficulty to carry out Allah's commandments, which brings a person to the state of mind that draws him near to Allah. Only those find Allah who surrender themselves wholly to Him, and only the words of those reach Him whose wavelength matches His. The command to fast is followed by the command not to consume one another's property unjustly, which shows the essence of fasting: to create such a sense of subservience that when Allah commands abstention from anything one abstains at once. If Allah wishes a person to stay away even from lawful things, he must not hesitate, and one who abstains from the lawful at His command will have no difficulty abstaining from the unlawful.

### The right of the Real and the portion of the servant

In the devotional reading, the verse shows that the customs that characterise human beings are not attributed to Allah. Whether one is engaged in worship (ʿibādah), which is the right of the Real, or in the customs of companionship with one's spouse, which is the aim of the lower self and a worldly concern, both are the same for one's state so long as there is refined conduct (adab). The verse was revealed concerning the lapse of al-Fārūq, and Allah made that lapse the occasion of a dispensation for all Muslims until the Resurrection. Such are the rulings of divine solicitude. It is said that Allah knew there was no escaping worldly concerns for the servant, so He divided the night and day of this month between His right and the servant's portion: for His right, complete the fast until night, and for your portion, eat and drink until the white thread is distinct from the black. The prohibition during retreat states that the place of nearness is sanctified from the pursuit of worldly concerns: when you are occupied with yourselves you are veiled through yourselves, but when your business is with Us, do not turn back from Us to yourselves. The jealousy of the Real comes at the times when serious business is mixed with play. ʿĀʾishah once told the Messenger of Allah ﷺ that she loved him and loved being near him, and he answered: let me be, daughter of Abū Bakr, I am worshipping my Lord, for I have a time in which none but my Lord is permitted to me.

### In short

- The early rule barring food and intimacy after sleep or ʿishāʾ, hard on men like Qays ibn Ṣirmah and ʿUmar, was confirmed as divine and then lifted: the nights of the fast are open until dawn, and spouses are each other's garment.
- Dawn is the moment the white thread of day is distinct from the black of night (Sahl ibn Saʿd, ʿAdī ibn Ḥātim). Certainty of dawn is the dividing line, so suḥūr is a blessed sunnah delayed until near dawn (Anas, Zayd ibn Thābit, the adhān of Ibn Umm Maktūm), but not a minute beyond it.
- Eating in genuine doubt is not a sin but requires qaḍāʾ if dawn had broken (al-Jaṣṣāṣ). The fast ends at sunset and should be broken promptly (ʿUmar, Sahl, Abū Hurayrah).
- One may start the fast junub (ʿĀʾishah, Umm Salamah). Wiṣāl is forbidden except until suḥūr, being a quality peculiar to the Prophet ﷺ. In iʿtikāf, in any mosque of congregation, intimacy and its preliminaries are forbidden day and night, though a wife may serve her husband, and the Prophet ﷺ kept the last ten nights until he died.
- "Do not approach" Allah's limits is stricter than "do not overstep", so even gargling excessively or kissing while fasting is makrūh, and Allah clarifies His rulings so people may fear Him (57:9). Inwardly, the month is divided between Allah's right and the servant's portion, and the place of nearness is kept clear of worldly concerns.

188.text:
The previous verses dealt with fasting, in which the use of lawful things is forbidden for a fixed period, and now the acquisition and use of unlawful wealth is forbidden altogether. "Do not consume one another's wealth unjustly, nor deliberately bribe authorities in order to devour a portion of others' property, knowing that it is a sin". The two themes belong together, since the real purpose of fasting is to train a person to abstain from what is lawful to him, after which abstaining from what is wholly unlawful should come more easily. There is a further link: one must make an effort to break the fast with what is ḥalāl, for whoever endures the rigours of the day and then breaks his fast with ḥarām will find his fast unacceptable to Allah.

### Phrase by phrase

**"Do not consume one another's wealth unjustly"**. The lawful acquisition and use of things was already stressed in verse 168 of this sūrah, which calls mankind to eat of what is lawful and good on earth and not to follow the footsteps of Satan, and again in Sūrat al-Naḥl: "So eat from the good, lawful things which Allah has provided for you, and be grateful for Allah's favours" (16:114). Here the opposite is forbidden. The words are general and cover usurpation, theft and robbery, by which property is taken by force, and also interest, gambling, bribery and every defective sale or transaction that Islamic law disallows even where the parties plainly consent. Money gained by lying or a false oath, or by earnings the law forbids even if one has sweated for them, is all ḥarām and false. Although the verse speaks of eating, it means use in the absolute sense, by eating, drinking, wearing or any other mode, just as one says that so-and-so ate up another's property even where nothing edible was involved. One reading lists oppression, theft, usurpation and perjury among the forbidden means, another extortion and cheating. The Qur'an pointedly says "your wealth", amwālakum, of the wealth of others. This hints that whoever encroaches on another's property should remember that the other loves and cares for his property as the encroacher does for his own, and would be hurt in the same way. It also suggests that when one person encroaches and the practice becomes general, others will encroach on him in turn. Imagine a society in which adulteration becomes common: the dealer who earns a little extra by mixing cheaper fat into butter goes to the milk shop and is given milk watered down, his spices are adulterated, so are his medicines, and the vicious circle goes on without end. The adulterator enjoys the extra in his coffers without noticing the hole beneath, for in reality he keeps none of it. Snatching another's property by false means opens the door to the plundering of one's own.

**"nor deliberately bribe authorities in order to devour a portion of others' property"**. Do not take property cases to the authorities so that through them you eat up some of people's wealth sinfully, nor offer judges bribes or the goods themselves, so as to obtain by their arbitration what belongs to others. This includes filing false cases, taking false oaths and giving or procuring false witness. ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭalḥah reports Ibn ʿAbbās as explaining that the verse concerns a debtor who, when there is no evidence of the loan, denies it and takes the matter before the authorities, though he knows the money is not his and that he is a sinner consuming what is forbidden to him. Mujāhid, Saʿīd ibn Jubayr, ʿIkrimah, al-Ḥasan, Qatādah, al-Suddī, Muqātil ibn Ḥayyān and ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Zayd ibn Aslam said the same: do not go to law when you know you are in the wrong.

**"knowing that it is a sin"**. While you know the falsehood of what you claim and know that Allah has forbidden it. To sin knowingly is the worst of things and carries the greatest punishment. The words also show that someone who claims something through a genuine misunderstanding and goes to court for it is not covered by this warning.

### The occasion of revelation

The verse was revealed over a land dispute between two Companions, Imruʾ al-Qays ibn ʿĀbis al-Kindī and ʿAbdān ibn Ashwaʿ al-Ḥaḍramī, as Muqātil ibn Ḥayyān relates. Imruʾ al-Qays held the land and ʿAbdān was reclaiming it. The plaintiff had no witnesses, so the Prophet ﷺ asked the defendant to swear an oath as the law requires. As he prepared to do so the Prophet ﷺ recited to him, by way of counsel, "Indeed, those who trade Allah's covenant and their oaths for a fleeting gain will have no share in the Hereafter" (3:77). Hearing this warning to those who seize property by a false oath, he abandoned the oath and surrendered the land, so that ʿAbdān received it without a judgment being pronounced. Imruʾ al-Qays admitted taking the money when the verse was revealed. The verse therefore first forbids acquiring property by unlawful means and then warns against false suits, false oaths and false witness.

### A court ruling does not change the truth
