The Two Ṣaḥīḥs record from Umm Salamah that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said that he was only human, that people brought their disputes to him, and that one of them might be more eloquent in presenting his case so that he judged in his favour on the strength of what he heard. Whoever was thus given something of his brother's right should not take it, for he would be allotting him a piece of the Fire. Verse and hadith together prove that the ruling of an authority does not change the reality of the matter. It neither makes the forbidden lawful nor the lawful forbidden, and it holds only as far as it goes, so if the ruling matches the truth there is no harm, and if not, the judge earns his reward while the cheat carries the burden. Qatādah said: son of Ādam, know that the judge's ruling does not permit you what is prohibited or prohibit what is permitted. He rules by his best judgment and the testimony of witnesses, and being human he may err. If he wrongly rules in someone's favour, that person will still face the dispute when the parties meet Allah on the Day of Resurrection, and the wrongdoer will then be judged swiftly and precisely in a way that outweighs whatever he gained by the mistaken judgment in this world. A Muslim judge may, through a misunderstanding, give one party what belongs to the other, but such a judgment does not make it lawful for him, nor does it make unlawful what is lawful for the rightful owner. Whoever grabs another's property through a court by fraud, false witness or a false oath bears the curse of it and should give it up, mindful of the accountability of the Hereafter before the All-Knowing, All-Aware. According to Abū Ḥanīfah, however, in matters of contract and annulment where the qāḍī has authority under Islamic law, his judgment renders the contract or annulment valid even if it rested on a false oath or false testimony, and the rules of lawful and unlawful then follow from it, though the curse of lying and of procuring false witnesses still hangs round the culprit's neck.

### The criterion of lawful earning

The whole world agrees that money and goods are needed and that life depends on them, and it agrees that there are favoured and permissible ways of acquiring them and undesirable, forbidden ways. Nearly everyone looks down on theft, robbery and fraud, yet people lack a sound criterion for deciding which means are permissible, and perhaps cannot devise one, since the matter concerns the well-being of all humanity. A universal, sound and reasonable criterion can only come from the Lord and Creator of all the worlds through revelation. Had human beings been left to forge their own, those framing the law would naturally think first of their own nation or community, and even an international body representing the whole world cannot, as experience shows, satisfy everyone, so that legal injustice ends in war and chaos. The law of the permissible and forbidden enforced by the Sharīʿah of Islam comes directly from revelation or is derived from it, and being reasonable, natural and comprehensive it is the only law that can work for every nation and guarantee peace. Everything of common utility, to which all people have equal claim, such as air, water, vegetation, heat, unowned forests and the growth of uninhabited mountains, is left as the shared property of all, and no one may take it over as owner. Things which, if shared, would disturb society or breed conflict are governed by private ownership. The law of initial ownership of land and its produce differs from the law of transfer, and the whole is so framed that no one is left without the necessities of life provided he makes the effort to earn them, while no one usurps others' rights or inflicts loss on them so as to concentrate capital in a few hands. Under the law of transfer, whether by the divine rules of inheritance or by agreed sale, there must be no fraud or deception and no ambiguity or deficiency that could breed future dispute. Consent must be genuine and not extracted under pressure. Every transaction the law calls void, invalid or sinful has some inherent defect: plain fraud, a return for something unknown, the usurping of a right, gain through another's loss, or the illegal disposal of public rights. Interest, gambling and the like are forbidden chiefly because they harm the public interest, letting a few individuals grow as parasites while the community sinks into poverty, so that even mutual consent cannot make them permissible, since they are a formalised crime against the whole community. This verse covers all such cases.

### Ḥalāl brings blessing and ḥarām produces evil

The Qur'an stresses in many places abstention from the unlawful and the acquisition of the lawful, and points out that human deeds and morals are deeply affected by what one eats, for good conduct can hardly be expected from one who does not eat and drink what is ḥalāl: "O messengers! Eat from what is good and lawful, and act righteously. Indeed, I fully know what you do" (23:51). Here lawful eating is joined to the command to do good, hinting that righteous deeds flow only from lawful food. The Prophet ﷺ explained in a hadith that although the verse addresses the prophets, all Muslims are charged with the same command, and added that the prayer of one who eats the unlawful is not answered, describing people who take great pains in worship and then raise their hands crying "O Lord, O Lord" while their food, drink and clothing are all ḥarām, and asking how such prayer could be answered. A great part of the Prophet's ﷺ teaching was devoted to saving his Ummah from the unlawful. He said that whoever ate ḥalāl, followed the Sunnah and did not harm people would enter Paradise, and when the Companions said that these things were common among the Muslims of his day he replied that in every future age too there would be people who kept to them, a hadith al-Tirmidhī reports and grades ṣaḥīḥ. He told ʿAbdullāh ibn ʿUmar that four traits would suffice a person even if he had nothing else in the world: guarding trusts, telling the truth, good character and care about eating what is ḥalāl. When Saʿd ibn Abī Waqqāṣ asked him to pray that he become one whose prayers are answered, he told Saʿd to make his food pure and lawful and he would be so, swearing by Him in whose hand was Muḥammad's life that when a servant puts a morsel of ḥarām into his stomach no deed of his is accepted for forty days, and that flesh grown from unlawful gain has the Fire as its only destination. ʿAbdullāh ibn Masʿūd reports him swearing that no servant becomes a Muslim until his heart and tongue are Muslim and his neighbours are safe from his harm, and that when a servant acquires the unlawful and gives it in charity it is not accepted, if he spends it it is stripped of blessing, and if he leaves it to his heirs it becomes his provision for the journey to Hell, for Allah does not wash away one evil with another but does wash away an evil deed with a good one.

### The questions of the Day of Resurrection

Muʿādh ibn Jabal reports the Prophet ﷺ as saying that no servant will move a step on the Day of Judgment until he answers four questions: about his life and how he spent it, his youth and how he used it, his wealth and where he earned it and where he spent it, and his knowledge and how far he acted on it, as al-Bayhaqī records. ʿAbdullāh ibn ʿUmar reports a sermon in which the Prophet ﷺ sought refuge with Allah for the Emigrants from five traits. The first was immodesty, for when it spreads among a people they are struck by plagues, epidemics and diseases their elders never heard of. The second was cheating in weights and measures, which brings famine, high prices, crushing labour and oppressive rulers. The third was withholding zakāh, for which rain is withheld. The fourth was breaking the covenant with Allah and His Messenger, after which Allah sets foreign enemies over them who seize what is theirs without right. The fifth was the failure of rulers to judge by the Book of Allah because His revealed injunctions do not suit their fancies, upon which Allah sends mutual hatred and strife among them. Ibn Mājah, al-Bayhaqī and others report this and al-Ḥākim grades it ṣaḥīḥ by the standard of Muslim. May Allah grant us and all Muslims the fullest ability to stay safe from such calamities.

### A life of renunciation

The life of a believer is thus one of renunciation, for throughout his life he must keep away from certain things, and Ramaḍān is the training for it. A month of restraint teaches that the true servant of Allah worships at the level of taqwā and lives in piety and fear of Him, and that Allah answers the call only of those who bring themselves close to Him by a life of sacrifice. In the devotional reading, when you turn to created beings to judge your affairs, know that Allah is watching and His knowledge encompasses you, so stand in shyness before the Real. Created beings know only externals, while the Real governs the innermost secrets of hearts.

### In short

- After the fast's abstention from the lawful comes the ban on the unlawful: usurpation, theft, interest, gambling, bribery, false oaths and every defective transaction, in every mode of use (cf. 2:168, 16:114).
- "Your wealth" reminds the encroacher that others love their property as he loves his, and that wrong invites wrong in return.
- Revealed over the land dispute of Imruʾ al-Qays and ʿAbdān, where 3:77 stopped a false oath, the verse forbids winning others' property through the courts knowingly.
- A judge's ruling cannot make the forbidden lawful (Umm Salamah, Qatādah), though Abū Ḥanīfah holds that it validates contracts and annulments outwardly.
- Only revelation gives a universal criterion of lawful earning, and ḥalāl food is the root of good deeds and answered prayer (23:51, the hadiths of Saʿd and Ibn Masʿūd), while wealth is among the four questions of the Day of Judgment (Muʿādh).

189.text:
The theme of righteousness begun in verse 177 continues. Six injunctions have appeared so far, on retaliation, bequest, fasting, iʿtikāf and abstention from the unlawful, and now come those of Ḥajj and jihād, prefaced by the clarification that lunar months and days govern Ḥajj and the other religious duties. "They ask you ˹O Prophet˺ about the phases of the moon. Say, "They are a means for people to determine time and pilgrimage." Righteousness is not in entering your houses from the back doors." It continues: "Rather, righteousness is to be mindful ˹of Allah˺. So enter your homes through their ˹proper˺ doors, and be mindful of Allah so you may be successful". The verse also erases a custom of the Jāhiliyyah by which people in iḥrām, if they needed to go home, entered from the back, even through a hole bored in the wall, believing it forbidden to use the front door in iḥrām and even counting this as righteousness.

### Phrase by phrase

**"They ask you ˹O Prophet˺ about the phases of the moon."**. Al-ʿAwfī relates from Ibn ʿAbbās that people asked the Messenger of Allah ﷺ about the crescents and this verse was revealed. Ibn ʿAbbās says that the Companions had a distinctive courtesy: out of great respect they asked their Prophet ﷺ very few questions, unlike the communities of earlier prophets who asked many and so failed in the etiquette due to a prophet. He counts fourteen questions from the Companions in the Qur'an. They include verse 186, "when My servants ask you", and this question. Six more occur in Sūrat al-Baqarah and six in other sūrahs. One account says the verse was revealed when Muʿādh ibn Jabal asked about the timing of the pilgrimage. The question concerned the new moon, which unlike the sun begins as a thin crescent, grows slowly to a full circle and then shrinks again. They may have asked about its cause or about the wisdom of its gradual waxing and waning. The answer states the wisdom and benefit. If that was what they asked, the answer matches the question. The alternative is a question about physical causes, regarded here as unlike the Companions' good manners. In that case, answering with benefits rather than physical reality carries a lesson. The reality of heavenly bodies is considered beyond human reach and unnecessary for practical purposes here or hereafter. On this reasoning, it is not worth asking about. What can usefully be asked and explained is the benefit that comes to people from the moon's waning and waxing, its setting and rising.

**"Say, "They are a means for people to determine time and pilgrimage.""**. The crescents mark appointed times, mawāqīt. They regulate transactions, contracts, debt repayments and women's waiting periods, ʿiddah. They also identify fasting and its end, completion of the zakāh year, blood-money deadlines and pilgrimage days. If the new moons always looked the same none of this could be known. ʿAbd al-Razzāq reports Ibn ʿUmar's account of the Messenger's ﷺ words. Allah made crescents signs of periods for people. Begin and end the fast upon sighting them. If the crescent is hidden, count thirty days. Al-Ḥākim records this in his Mustadrak with a ṣaḥīḥ chain, noting that al-Bukhārī and Muslim did not record it. The moon is an almanac of nature set in the sky so that people may plan their worldly affairs and their worship. The superstitious hold the days of the waxing moon auspicious and those of the waning moon inauspicious, but the phases are meant to serve only as measures of time.

**"Righteousness is not in entering your houses from the back doors."**. Al-Bukhārī records from al-Barāʾ that in the Jāhiliyyah people entered their houses from the back after assuming iḥrām, and Allah revealed this. Abū Dāwūd al-Ṭayālisī also transmits al-Barāʾ's report. His wording describes the Anṣār returning from journeys and entering by the rear of their houses. Al-Ḥasan said that when people in the Jāhiliyyah set out on a journey and then decided not to travel, they would not enter by the door but climb over the back wall. One account names a group of Companions from Kinānah and Khuzāʿah who in iḥrām entered their houses from the back or from the roof as had been the pre-Islamic habit. They bored holes to enter and leave, ignoring the doors, and claimed it was piety. Since entering by the door is not forbidden there is nothing to abstain from, so this is neither obedience nor God-fearing.

**"Rather, righteousness is to be mindful ˹of Allah˺."**. Real righteousness lies in abstaining from what Allah has made unlawful and not contravening His commands, in iḥrām avoiding hunting and the like, and it belongs to whoever is mindful of Him outwardly and inwardly. Many people have come to regard mere outward observance as religiosity.

**"So enter your homes through their ˹proper˺ doors"**. Enter by the doors you always used, even in iḥrām, for that is easier and less troublesome, and Allah does not burden you with difficulty.

**"and be mindful of Allah so you may be successful"**. Do what He commands and avoid what He forbids, fearing Him in the state of iḥrām, so that you prosper when you stand before Him tomorrow and He rewards you fully, are spared His anger and punishment, and attain what you hope for and escape what you fear. The centre of all these principles is that people keep fearing Allah so that they may hope for the best of both worlds.

### The lunar calendar

The verse says only that the moon helps count the months and days on which transactions and acts of worship such as Ḥajj depend. Sūrat Yūnus says the same, that Allah made the moon "a reflected light, with precisely ordained phases, so that you may know the number of years and calculation ˹of time˺" (10:5). A verse of Sūrat Banī Isrāʾīl links the count to the sun as well: "We made the sign of the day ˹perfectly˺ bright, so that you may seek the bounty of your Lord and know the number of years and calculation ˹of time˺" (17:12). Years and months can thus be counted by a solar calendar too, yet the Qur'an's words about the moon show that the lunar calendar is the fixed choice of the Sharīʿah, especially in acts of worship tied to a particular month and date. Ramaḍān, the Ḥajj and its days, Muḥarram and Laylat al-Qadr all depend on the sighting of the new moon, for this verse establishes that the lunar reckoning is the one trusted in Allah's sight, though months can be counted by the sun as well. The explanation connects the Sharīʿah's choice with a visible sign on the horizon. Scholars and the unlettered can see it, as can villagers, islanders and mountain-dwellers. In contrast, the solar calendar requires instruments and calculations. These cannot as easily become everyone's personal experience. In worship the lunar calendar is obligatory, and it is favoured in social and business dealings too, as the basis of Islamic worship and a symbol of Islamic identity. The solar calendar is not juristically prohibited, on condition that its use does not spread so far that people forget the lunar one, which would harm obligatory worship such as fasting and Ḥajj. A sample of this is visible today in offices and businesses, public and private, where the solar calendar is used so constantly that many people cannot even name all the Islamic months, a deplorable sign of a lack of will to uphold a matter of religious and national identity with self-respect. The recommendation is to use the solar calendar in office dealings involving non-Muslims. Other correspondence, private dealings and daily needs can follow the lunar calendar. This preserves identity and earns the reward of farḍ ʿalā al-kifāyah. That is an obligation whose performance by some suffices for the rest.

### Making the permissible a sin

The house-entry clause yields a legal principle. Nobody may independently make something necessary, wājib, or an act of worship when the Sharīʿah has not given it that status. Likewise, making a sin of what the law permits is itself sinful. That is exactly what those people did: entering by the door was permissible and they made it a sin, while breaking in through the back wall was not required and they made it necessary, and for this they were admonished. Innovations (bidʿah) in religion are impermissible for the same reason, because they make the unnecessary obligatory, as farḍ or wājib, or the permissible forbidden, and this verse makes clear that doing so is prohibited, giving a guiding rule for thousands of practices in vogue. The following verses carry the injunction on fighting the disbelievers. In Dhū al-Qaʿdah of the year 6 AH the Prophet ﷺ set out for Makkah to perform ʿumrah while the city was still controlled by the idolaters, who refused him and his Companions entry, and after much negotiation it was agreed that the Muslims would perform ʿumrah the next year, the pact known as the Peace of Ḥudaybiyyah. The expression "do not transgress" in those verses means, according to the majority, not to exceed the limit in fighting by killing women and children.

### The waxing and waning of the heart

In the devotional reading, the waxing and waning of the moon allude to the contraction and expansion of the recognisers and the awe and intimacy of the lovers. Contraction and expansion are for the elect what fear and hope are for the common people, and higher than both is awe and intimacy, which belongs to the elect of the elect. These correspond to the stations of the wrongdoers, the moderate and the foremost. The highest limit is the lovers' intimacy. In that state, a man may enter fire without awareness of it. Its heat leaves the repose of intimacy undisturbed. Abū Ḥafṣ al-Ḥaddād was a blacksmith who had lit a fierce fire and put iron in it, as smiths do. Someone passed by reciting a verse of the Qur'an. The shaykh rejoiced at the verse, intimacy overcame him, and he reached into the furnace and drew out the hot iron and held it until his apprentice cried out to ask how he could be holding it. He set it down and left his trade, saying that he had left it many times and come back, but this time the trade had left him.

### In short

- The Companions, who asked few questions, asked about the crescent moon, and were told its benefit rather than its cause: the phases fix the times of debts, waiting periods, fasting, zakāh and Ḥajj (Ibn ʿAbbās, Ibn ʿUmar).
- The lunar calendar is the Sharīʿah's fixed choice for worship (cf. 10:5, 17:12), visible to everyone, and should not be forgotten through overuse of the solar one.
- Entering houses from the back in iḥrām, a Jāhilī custom thought pious (al-Barāʾ, al-Ḥasan), is no righteousness. Righteousness is taqwā.
- Treating the permissible as a sin or the unnecessary as obligatory is the root of bidʿah and is forbidden by this verse.
- Inwardly, the moon's phases mirror the heart's contraction and expansion, and the lovers' intimacy, as the story of Abū Ḥafṣ al-Ḥaddād shows.

190.text:
With the calendar settled, the injunction on fighting follows. "Fight in the cause of Allah ˹only˺ against those who wage war against you, but do not exceed the limits. Allah does not like transgressors". The whole Muslim community agrees that jihād and fighting were prohibited before the emigration to Madīnah. Every verse of that period told the Muslims to bear patiently the pains inflicted by the disbelievers and even to ignore and forgive where they could. After the emigration the first command to fight came through this verse, as al-Rabīʿ ibn Anas and others say. Abū Bakr al-Ṣiddīq instead identifies the verse permitting the wronged to respond to those fighting them. Most Companions and their successors name this Sūrat al-Baqarah verse as the first command to fight. The verse Abū Bakr identifies was also among the earliest on the subject. It may be called the first permission.

### Phrase by phrase

**"Fight in the cause of Allah ˹only˺ against those who wage war against you"**. After the Prophet ﷺ was prevented from visiting the House in the year of Ḥudaybiyyah, he made a pact with the disbelievers that he would return the following year and they would vacate Makkah for three days. As the believers prepared for ʿumrah with him, they feared a broken agreement and an attack by Quraysh. They were reluctant to fight in iḥrām, within the Sacred Precinct or during sacred months. The verse answered those fears. Abū Jaʿfar al-Rāzī conveys al-Rabīʿ ibn Anas's report from Abū al-ʿĀliyah. He identifies this as Madīnah's first verse about fighting. Afterwards, the Messenger of Allah ﷺ fought his attackers and spared non-combatants, until Sūrat Barāʾah was revealed. ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Zayd ibn Aslam said the same and added that the verse was later abrogated by "kill the polytheists ˹who violated their treaties˺ wherever you find them" (9:5), or by the opening verse of immunity in the same sūrah. This is not plausible, however, since "those who wage war against you" simply directs the fighting at the enemies actually fighting Islam and its people, as in "together fight the polytheists as they fight against you together" (9:36). Fighting in the cause of Allah means fighting in obedience to Him to raise His religion and His word, whether in the Sacred Precinct or elsewhere, against the disbelievers who fight you to turn you from His religion. The fighting referred to is that which took place in the Prophet's ﷺ lifetime, when the Makkan opponents, not content with expelling him and his Companions from their home town, prevented them from living and working peacefully in Yathrib and repeatedly attacked them without provocation, so that they had to fight in self-defence. Once aggression has been committed believers are obliged to defend themselves, but initiating hostilities is not permitted, only defensive war, and even that must be openly declared by an established state.

**"but do not exceed the limits."**. Fight for Allah's sake and do not become transgressors by committing what is forbidden. Al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī includes mutilation and theft of spoils among transgressions. He also forbids killing women, children and elderly non-combatants, and killing priests or residents of houses of worship. Burning trees and killing animals without real benefit are included. Ibn ʿAbbās, Muqātil ibn Ḥayyān and ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz share this view, alongside others. Muslim records from Buraydah that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said to fight for Allah's sake against those who disbelieve in Him, but not to steal from the spoils, betray, mutilate, kill a child or kill those who dwell in houses of worship. The Two Ṣaḥīḥs record from Ibn ʿUmar that a woman was found dead in one of the Prophet's ﷺ battles and he then forbade the killing of women and children, and there are many other hadiths to this effect. Since the command is restricted to those who come to fight, people who do not fight may not be killed in jihād: women, children, the very old, priests and monks devoted to quiet religious pursuits, the physically handicapped, and casual labourers who work for the disbelievers but do not go out to fight with them. The jurists therefore also rule that if a woman, an old man or a religious person actually takes part in the fighting or helps the enemy in any way, killing them becomes permissible, because they then fall among "those who wage war against you". The Prophet's ﷺ battle orders explain the injunction well. Abū Dāwūd records Anas's account of instructions to departing Companions. They were to set out in Allah's name, adhering to the Messenger's ﷺ community. They must spare the old and weak, young children and women. Abū Bakr al-Ṣiddīq gave Yazīd ibn Abī Sufyān the same instructions when sending him to Syria, adding the prohibition of killing the devout, the monks and priests, and the labourers employed by the disbelievers, especially when they do not fight.

**"Allah does not like transgressors"**. He does not love those who initiate fighting, in the Sacred Precinct or anywhere else, or who overstep the bounds He has set and made sacred.

### Killed by the sword of struggle

The recognisers and chevaliers read this fighting as a spiritual stage for travellers and a state of lovers. Passing through its gate requires being slain by struggle's sword on the Sharīʿah's path and burned in love's fire. Do not suppose that fire is only the lamp you know or that killing is only the state you know. Those killed by the Real are one thing and those killed by the throat another, and burning in the fire of punishment is one thing and burning in the fire of love another. A great master describes discovering the smoke of a burning brand where he had expected a lamp. In friendship, he says, the sin belongs to the slain, while the judge shelters the adversary. Bewilderment in union is itself the path. Whoever is drowned in Him seeks Him still more. One day Shiblī went into the desert and saw forty men, distracted and impassioned, each lying with a brick under his head and his life at his throat. Moved by tenderness, he asked Allah what He wanted of them. Pain burdened their hearts and their haystacks had been set alight. Would He now slay them all with jealousy's sword? His innermost core was told: I will kill them, and once I have killed them I will pay their blood-money. Asked what that was, the answer came that whoever is killed by the sword of My majesty has the vision of My beauty as his blood-money. The blood-money of one killed by the hand is dinars, and of one killed by passion, seeing.

### In short

- This is the first Madinan command to fight, revealed before the make-up ʿumrah following Ḥudaybiyyah, when Muslims feared treachery from Quraysh (Abū al-ʿĀliyah, al-Rabīʿ ibn Anas). Fighting had been forbidden in Makkah.
- It permits fighting only against those who actually fight the Muslims, and the claim that 9:5 abrogated it is not plausible (cf. 9:36).
- Transgression means mutilation, theft of spoils, and killing women, children, the old, monks and labourers (al-Ḥasan, Buraydah, Ibn ʿUmar), unless they join the fighting.
- Only defensive, declared war is allowed. Allah does not love aggressors.
- Inwardly, the lovers are slain by the sword of struggle, and their blood-money is the vision of His beauty (Shiblī).

191.text:
Verse 191 was revealed after Ḥudaybiyyah, when the Prophet ﷺ decided, under the terms of the treaty, to travel to Makkah with his Companions for the make-up ʿumrah he had been stopped from performing the year before. "Kill them wherever you come upon them and drive them out of the places from which they have driven you out. For persecution is far worse than killing." It continues: "And do not fight them at the Sacred Mosque unless they attack you there. If they do so, then fight them—that is the reward of the disbelievers". On the eve of the journey the Companions worried that the disbelievers could not be trusted to keep a treaty. If they turned aggressive as before, what were the Muslims to do? The verse gave them permission to meet aggression by killing the attackers wherever they found them and, if they could, to drive them out as they themselves had been driven out.

### Phrase by phrase

**"Kill them wherever you come upon them"**. If they start the fight, kill them wherever you find them, in the Sacred Precinct or elsewhere. Spend your energy fighting them as they spend theirs fighting you.

**"and drive them out of the places from which they have driven you out."**. Expel them from Makkah as they expelled you, by way of equal recompense. This was carried out after the conquest of Makkah.

**"For persecution is far worse than killing."**. Throughout the Makkan period, Muslims were restrained from fighting and repeatedly told to forgive. Before this verse, the Companions consequently believed that killing disbelievers was bad and forbidden. The comparison with fitnah corrects that misconception. Killing is a terrible evil. Yet the Makkan disbelievers persisted in kufr and shirk and barred Muslims from religious duties, including Ḥajj and ʿumrah. The permission to kill them is explained as averting this greater evil. The word fitnah here means disbelief and polytheism and the prevention of Muslims from their worship, as al-Jaṣṣāṣ, al-Qurṭubī and others state. Because jihād involves shedding the blood of men, Allah points out that these men are committing disbelief, associating partners with Him and hindering from His path, which is a far greater evil and more disastrous than killing. Abū Mālik explains the comparison as condemning the disbelievers' acts. The explanation that shirk is worse comes from Mujāhid and Saʿīd ibn Jubayr, and from Abū al-ʿĀliyah and ʿIkrimah. Al-Ḥasan and Qatādah give it too, as do al-Rabīʿ ibn Anas and aḍ-Ḍaḥḥāk. Their idolatry is more serious than slaying them in the Sacred Precinct or in iḥrām, the very thing the Muslims so greatly feared. Oppression that stops believers from worshipping and drives them back to disbelief is worse than killing.

**"And do not fight them at the Sacred Mosque unless they attack you there."**. The words "wherever you come upon them" might seem to include killing within the Ḥaram. The next sentence restricts that general wording. Fighting must not begin near the Sacred Mosque, including its Makkan environs, unless the enemy attacks there first. The Two Ṣaḥīḥs record that the Prophet ﷺ said that Allah made this city a sanctuary on the day He created the heavens and the earth, and that it remains sacred by His decree until the Day of Resurrection. He was granted permission to fight there for only one hour of a day. Its trees must not be cut and its grass must not be uprooted. Anyone citing his fighting there must be reminded that Allah permitted His Messenger ﷺ, not them. This refers to the conquest of Makkah by force and the deaths of some polytheists at al-Khandamah. Beforehand, he had announced safety for those who shut their doors. Those entering the Mosque or Abū Sufyān's house were also safe. Within Makkah's Ḥaram, even birds and animals must not be killed, much less human beings. If someone begins killing there, however, the other party may defend itself. The jurists agree on this exception. One legal reading confines this prohibition on initiating combat to the Sacred Mosque and its precincts. Elsewhere, it regards defensive jihād as necessary and initiating jihād as valid.

A different reading permits only defensive war. It places the fighting in the Prophet's ﷺ lifetime, when his Makkan opponents expelled the Muslims and repeatedly attacked their new settlement at Yathrib, Madīnah. On that reading, Muslims must defend themselves against aggression, but may not begin hostilities. Even defensive war must be publicly declared by an established state. Before the make-up ʿumrah in 7 AH, the Companions feared combat within the sacred precincts. They knew fighting there was prohibited. The verse answers that concern: honour the Ḥaram, but defend yourselves if the disbelievers attack within it.

**"If they do so, then fight them—that is the reward of the disbelievers"**. If they attack you there first, you may fight and kill them to stop their aggression, and such killing and expulsion is the requital of disbelievers, for whom death is the reward. A variant reading has "slaying" rather than "fighting" in all three verbs. On this basis the Messenger of Allah ﷺ took the pledge from his Companions under the tree at Ḥudaybiyyah to fight, after Quraysh and their allies Thaqīf and others joined together to stop the Muslims from reaching the Sacred House. Allah then stopped the fighting before it began: "He is the One Who held back their hands from you and your hands from them in the valley of ˹Ḥudaibiyah, near˺ Mecca, after giving you the upper hand over ˹a group of˺ them" (48:24), and He spared Makkah because of "believing men and women, unknown to you" whom the Muslims "might have trampled" (48:25).

### Expel love of the enemy first

In the devotional reading, the command means that it is incumbent on you to show enmity to His enemies just as it is incumbent to befriend and assist His friends, sparing them not even for ties of kinship. Expel first your love and alliance with them from your hearts, and then drive them from the lands of Islam so that they are diminished. "Persecution is worse than killing" also alludes to the heart's ordeal of veiling. This is graver than bodily suffering through spiritual exertion. Losing the heart's life is more serious than losing the body's. Bodies live by what suits and is familiar to them, but the heart lives only through Allah, so remaining apart from Him is far worse than letting go of one's spirit and life. The Sacred Mosque clause also alludes to protecting time with Allah from bodily and lower-self attributes. These may intrude even through voluntary acts of obedience. A distracting preoccupation must be removed by every possible means. No attachment should remain to block the heart from Him.

### In short

- Revealed before the make-up ʿumrah of 7 AH, the verse allowed the Muslims to kill attackers wherever found and to expel the Makkans as they had been expelled, later fulfilled at the conquest.
- Fitnah, meaning kufr, shirk and barring Muslims from worship, is worse than killing (Abū Mālik, Mujāhid, Qatādah), which removed the Companions' scruple about fighting.
- Fighting may not be initiated in the Sacred Mosque and its precincts, a sanctuary since creation in which even animals are safe, except in defence, which the jurists unanimously allow. One legal reading allows initiating jihād elsewhere, while another allows only defensive war declared by an established state.
- The pledge under the tree rested on this permission, but Allah held back both sides (48:24-25).
- Inwardly, expel love of the enemy from the heart first, for separation from Allah is worse than losing one's life.

192.text:
After the permission to fight comes the door to peace. "But if they cease, then surely Allah is All-Forgiving, Most Merciful".

### Phrase by phrase

**"But if they cease"**. The command to stop applies when the polytheists cease their fighting in the Sacred Area and accept Islam in repentance. They turn to Allah, leaving disbelief and the association of partners with Him. The Muslims must then stop fighting them. The Companions had feared Makkan treachery during the ʿumrah of 7 AH, and this verse completes the answer given to them: the fighting permitted in defence ends as soon as the aggressors desist.

**"then surely Allah is All-Forgiving, Most Merciful"**. Allah will forgive them their sins even if they had previously killed Muslims in His Sacred Area, for His forgiveness covers every sin, however enormous, once the sinner repents. He forgives those who turn to Him with regret and asks nothing of them for the disobedience they committed before, and He is merciful to those who die in a state of repentance, compassionate and not quick to punish.

### Quieting the lower self

In the devotional reading, when the clamour of your thoughts and the enemies within your lower self (nafs) cut you off from Allah and jostle you, give up the chatter of the lower self and stop its combative motion, for those who have been asked to guard their innermost secrets should have no business with the exertions of the lower selves in their various forms of opposition.

### In short

- Once the aggressors stop fighting and disbelieving, the Muslims must stop fighting them.
- Allah forgives even those who shed Muslim blood in the Ḥaram if they repent, for no sin exceeds His forgiveness.
- He is merciful to the penitent and slow to punish.
- Inwardly, when the lower self's clamour cuts one off from Allah, its chatter and combat must be stilled.

193.text:
Verse 193 states the goal of the fighting and its limit. "Fight against them ˹if they persecute you˺ until there is no more persecution, and ˹your˺ devotion will be to Allah ˹alone˺. If they stop ˹persecuting you˺, let there be no hostility except against the aggressors".

### Phrase by phrase

**"Fight against them ˹if they persecute you˺ until there is no more persecution"**. Fight them, if they begin fighting you, whether in the Sacred Precinct or not, until fitnah is no more. Fitnah here means shirk, according to Ibn ʿAbbās, Abū al-ʿĀliyah, Mujāhid and al-Ḥasan, and likewise Qatādah, al-Rabīʿ, Muqātil ibn Ḥayyān, al-Suddī and Zayd ibn Aslam: until there is no association of partners with Allah in the Sacred Precinct and no one is prevented from Allah's path. Al-Bukhārī records Nāfiʿ's account of Ibn ʿUmar's refusal to join the conflict involving Ibn al-Zubayr. Two visitors complained of the people's shortcomings. Why, they asked, did the son of ʿUmar, a Companion of the Prophet ﷺ, not go out? He replied that Allah had forbidden him to shed his brother's blood. They invoked the command to fight until persecution ended. He answered that their earlier fighting had ended fitnah and established religion for Allah alone. The visitors instead wanted fighting that would restore fitnah and turn religion towards others. ʿUthmān ibn Ṣāliḥ adds another question addressed to Ibn ʿUmar as Abū ʿAbd al-Raḥmān. Why did he alternate Ḥajj and ʿumrah across the years, yet leave jihād despite Allah's encouragement? Ibn ʿUmar replied that Islam is built on five: faith in Allah and His Messenger, the five prayers, fasting Ramaḍān, paying zakāh and the Ḥajj to the House. The man cited this verse alongside "if two groups of believers fight each other, then make peace between them. But if one of them transgresses against the other, then fight against the transgressing group" (49:9). Ibn ʿUmar recalled their fighting during the Messenger's ﷺ lifetime. Islam was then weak, and believers faced killing or torture for their religion. Once Islam became strong, that fitnah ended. Asked about ʿAlī and ʿUthmān, he affirmed Allah's forgiveness of ʿUthmān. The questioners, he said, disliked that forgiveness. He described ʿAlī as the Messenger's ﷺ cousin and son-in-law. Pointing towards ʿAlī's house, he showed its closeness to the Prophet's ﷺ. Ibn ʿUmar thus explained the verse as referring to the coercive religious system of the ancient world. In this reading, war against fitnah was temporary and tied to a specific purpose. The Islamic revolution replaced religious persecution with intellectual freedom. With that fitnah ended, Qur'anic permission for violence applied only where self-defence became inevitable.

**"and ˹your˺ devotion will be to Allah ˹alone˺."**. So that the religion of Allah prevails over all others, all worship is for Him alone and none is worshipped beside Him, and Islam and the worship of Allah reign in the Sacred Precinct, the path of Allah becoming the dominant way of life. The Two Ṣaḥīḥs convey Abū Mūsā al-Ashʿarī's report of a question put to the Prophet ﷺ. One man fights from bravery, another to show off. Which fights in Allah's cause? His reply identifies the one whose purpose is to make Allah's word uppermost. The Two Ṣaḥīḥs also record his command to fight until people declare that none but Allah has the right to be worshipped. That declaration protects life and property from him, except by the right of the law. Their reckoning remains with Allah.

**"If they stop ˹persecuting you˺, let there be no hostility except against the aggressors"**. If they abandon shirk and their fighting of the believers, cease warfare against them, for whoever fights them afterwards commits injustice, since aggression may only be launched against the unjust. This is the sense of Mujāhid's statement that only combatants are to be fought. Or the meaning is that once they abandon their injustice, which is shirk, no aggression may be started against them, "aggression" here meaning retaliation and fighting, as in "if anyone attacks you, retaliate in the same manner" (2:194), "The reward of an evil deed is its equivalent" (42:40) and "If you retaliate, then let it be equivalent to what you have suffered" (16:126). Those who desist are not wrongdoers and may be shown no enmity. ʿIkrimah and Qatādah said that the wrongdoer is the one who refuses to declare that there is no god but Allah. One reading takes it as those who start the fight against you in the Sacred Precinct, where you are not allowed to kill them once they stop.

### Combat against the lower self

In the devotional reading, the verse alludes to combat against the lower selves, for your worst enemy is the nafs within you. Hold fully to the disciplines of the spiritual path until nothing remains of the traces of carnal humanity. Submit the nafs and the heart, qalb, to Allah. No inward opponent should remain to defend itself or follow the lower self. Nor should it independently manage its affairs or exercise free choice in any state. The vicissitudes of life will then flow over you as He wills and you will be effaced from every choice except what comes with the decree. When the self surrenders there is no enmity except towards the masters of holding back, while those who uphold the right of Allah's command are far from any obligation to compel others.

### In short

- Fighting continues only until fitnah, meaning shirk and religious persecution, ends and worship is for Allah alone (Ibn ʿAbbās, Mujāhid and others).
- Ibn ʿUmar refused to join the strife of Ibn al-Zubayr's time, explaining that fitnah had been fought when Islam was weak and no longer existed (al-Bukhārī, with 49:9).
- Fighting in Allah's cause means fighting so that His word is uppermost (Abū Mūsā), and the declaration of faith protects life and property.
- Once the enemy desists there may be no hostility except against aggressors, retaliation being limited to the equivalent (2:194, 42:40, 16:126).
- Inwardly, the real war is against the nafs, until it surrenders and the servant is effaced in the decree.

194.text:
Having answered the Companions' fear of fighting within the Ḥaram, the passage now answers their fear about the month. "˹There will be retaliation in˺ a sacred month for ˹an offence in˺ a sacred month, and all violations will bring about retaliation. So, if anyone attacks you, retaliate in the same manner. ˹But˺ be mindful of Allah, and know that Allah is with those mindful ˹of Him˺". The make-up ʿumrah was to fall in Dhū al-Qaʿdah, one of the four sacred months in which fighting anyone anywhere was forbidden, and the Muslims wondered how they could fight even defensively if the Makkans attacked. The answer is that just as the need for defence makes an exception to the sanctity of the Ḥaram, it makes an exception to the sanctity of the sacred months.

### Phrase by phrase

**"˹There will be retaliation in˺ a sacred month for ˹an offence in˺ a sacred month"**. Ibn ʿAbbās and Miqsam relate the exclusion from ʿumrah in the sixth Hijrah year. The account also comes from Qatādah and al-Suddī, from ʿAṭāʾ and al-Rabīʿ ibn Anas, and from aḍ-Ḍaḥḥāk. The idolaters barred the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and his Muslim companions from the Sacred House. This happened in the sacred month of Dhū al-Qaʿdah. They agreed to let him enter the following year, and he did so with his Companions, and Allah allowed him to make up for their treatment with these words. Qatādah describes their entry into Makkah in the following Dhū al-Qaʿdah. They performed ʿumrah and stayed three nights. This repaid the idolaters who had boasted about turning them back at Ḥudaybiyyah. The sacred month of the ʿumrah in the seventh year after the Migration was compensation for the sacred month in which they were stopped in the sixth. Just as they fight you in a sacred month, fight them in it, a reply to the Muslims' sense of the gravity of the matter.

**"and all violations will bring about retaliation."**. Sacred things (ḥurumāt), whatever must be treated as inviolable, the sacred land, the sacred month and the state of iḥrām, demand retaliation in kind when they are violated, one in return for another. There are four sacred months, Dhū al-Qaʿdah, Dhū al-Ḥijjah and Muḥarram, which run consecutively, and Rajab. Even before Islam fighting in them was held unlawful and the Makkan disbelievers observed their sanctity, and in the early years of Islam, through 7 AH, the law remained in force, which is why the Companions were perplexed. Later, by the consensus of the Ummah, the prohibition of fighting in these months was abrogated and permission to fight given, though it remains preferable not to initiate fighting in them without the need to defend. Their sanctity has therefore not been wholly abrogated. It stands like the sanctity of the Ḥaram, and both admit an exception for defence. Imam Aḥmad records Jābir ibn ʿAbdullāh's report with an authentic chain. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ refrained from warfare during a sacred month unless attacked first. He then marched out. Otherwise he waited until those months ended. So when he was told at Ḥudaybiyyah that ʿUthmān, whom he had sent as envoy to the polytheists, had been killed, he took the pledge from his Companions under the tree to fight them, fourteen hundred men, and when he learned that ʿUthmān was alive he gave up the fight and returned to peace. Likewise after the battle of Ḥunayn, when Hawāzin took refuge in al-Ṭāʾif, he besieged the city, and Dhū al-Qaʿdah began while the siege continued. Anas relates in the Two Ṣaḥīḥs that forty days passed from the start of Ḥunayn until the Prophet ﷺ returned to al-Madīnah from al-Jiʿrānah. Mounting casualties led him to end the siege without taking al-Ṭāʾif. He returned to Makkah for ʿumrah, starting from al-Jiʿrānah, where the Ḥunayn spoils were divided. This pilgrimage took place in Dhū al-Qaʿdah, in the eighth Hijrah year.

**"So, if anyone attacks you, retaliate in the same manner."**. Whoever commits aggression against you by fighting in the Sacred Enclosure, in iḥrām or in the sacred months, answer him in the manner of his aggression, but do not go beyond what he did. The Muslim response is itself called aggression only because it resembles it in form. This ordains justice even towards the polytheists, as in "If you retaliate, then let it be equivalent to what you have suffered" (16:126). Combat is forbidden within Makkah's sacred precincts and during the sacred months. An attack there permits believers to defend themselves. Defence still excludes atrocities and breaches of Allah's limits. Great wartime provocation does not remove those restraints.

**"˹But˺ be mindful of Allah"**. Fear Allah when avenging yourselves, renouncing aggression and not exceeding what He has permitted, and obey Him out of taqwā.

**"and know that Allah is with those mindful ˹of Him˺"**. He is with the God-fearing by His aid and support in this life and the Hereafter, giving them victory and success.

### When two rights meet

In the devotional reading, the verse alludes to the case when two of Allah's rights face each other: submit the moment to the ruling of the moment and move with its allusions. Preferring either right for even a small worldly advantage veils you from witnessing the Real. It blinds the heart's sight. The fitting choice is the one that more strongly opposes your whims and stands further from personal attraction and pleasure. Allah is with the God-fearing who fear preferring their own whims over what pleases Him, and when they act for Him rather than for themselves He is with them by His help: "If you stand up for Allah, He will help you" (47:7).

### In short

- The ʿumrah of 7 AH in Dhū al-Qaʿdah repaid the exclusion of 6 AH in the same sacred month (Ibn ʿAbbās, Qatādah).
- Violations of sacred things, the Ḥaram, iḥrām and the four sacred months, may be answered in kind but no further (cf. 16:126).
- The Prophet ﷺ never began fighting in a sacred month (Jābir), as the pledge at Ḥudaybiyyah and the siege of al-Ṭāʾif show. The months' sanctity now admits an exception for defence, like that of the Ḥaram.
- Taqwā governs even retaliation, and Allah is with the God-fearing.
- Inwardly, when two rights of Allah meet, follow the ruling of the moment and never your own portion (47:7).

195.text:
Verse 195 brings the tenth injunction under the theme of righteousness begun in verse 177. "Spend in the cause of Allah and do not let your own hands throw you into destruction ˹by withholding˺. And do good, for Allah certainly loves the good-doers". Muslims are obliged to spend money and materials according to the needs of the jihād commanded in Allah's way. From this the jurists deduce that besides the fixed duty of zakāh Muslims have other financial obligations, neither permanent nor tied to a threshold or quantity, but binding on all as and when the need arises, and lapsing when there is no need. Spending on jihād falls under this provision.

### Phrase by phrase

**"Spend in the cause of Allah"**. Spend your wealth in obedience to Allah, in striving for His sake and in the many areas of obedience and closeness to Him, above all in fighting the enemy and in whatever strengthens the Muslims against him. One account says the verses from "Fight in the cause of Allah" to the end of this verse were revealed about the Companions who were in iḥrām with the Prophet ﷺ on the way to the ʿumrah after the year of Ḥudaybiyyah, so the spending was for that journey. Al-Bukhārī records that Ḥudhayfah said the verse was revealed about spending, and Ibn Abī Ḥātim reports the same from him and adds that Ibn ʿAbbās, Mujāhid, ʿIkrimah, Saʿīd ibn Jubayr, ʿAṭāʾ, aḍ-Ḍaḥḥāk, al-Ḥasan, Qatādah, al-Suddī and Muqātil ibn Ḥayyān said similarly.

**"and do not let your own hands throw you into destruction ˹by withholding˺."**. The plain sense is that Muslims may not throw themselves into ruin by their own choice, and the explanations of what this means differ. Aslam Abū ʿImrān said that at the siege of Constantinople, when ʿUqbah ibn ʿĀmir led the Egyptian forces and Faḍālah ibn ʿUbayd the Syrians, a huge Byzantine column came out of the city and the Muslims lined up against it. A man of the Anṣār charged the Roman lines alone, broke through and came back, and people cried out that he was throwing himself to destruction. Abū Ayyūb al-Anṣārī, who was present, said that they were explaining the verse wrongly, for it was revealed about the Anṣār themselves, the Companions who fought beside the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and supported him. When Islam became strong and its following grew, they said to one another that Allah had honoured them with the Prophet's ﷺ companionship and victory, that they had neglected their families, estates and children, and that now that warfare had ceased they might go home and attend to them. Then this verse came down, and the destruction it speaks of is staying with one's family and estate and abandoning jihād. Abū Dāwūd, al-Tirmidhī, al-Nasāʾī, ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd, Ibn Abī Ḥātim, Ibn Jarīr, Ibn Marduwayh, al-Ḥāfiẓ Abū Yaʿlā in his Musnad, Ibn Ḥibbān and al-Ḥākim record this, al-Tirmidhī grading it ḥasan ṣaḥīḥ gharīb and al-Ḥākim saying it meets the criteria of al-Bukhārī and Muslim though they did not record it. This proves that banishing jihād from Muslim life is the cause of their degradation and destruction, and Abū Ayyūb accordingly spent his whole life in jihād away from his home in Madīnah, dying at Constantinople, where he was buried. The same understanding is reported from the earliest authorities, Ibn ʿAbbās, Ḥudhayfah, Qatādah, Mujāhid and aḍ-Ḍaḥḥāk. Abū Bakr ibn ʿAyyāsh reports from Abū Isḥāq al-Subayʿī that a man asked al-Barāʾ ibn ʿĀzib whether he would be throwing himself to destruction if he charged the enemy alone and was killed, and al-Barāʾ said no, since Allah had told His Messenger ﷺ "So fight in the cause of Allah ˹O Prophet˺. You are accountable for none but yourself" (4:84), and this verse concerned withholding spending. Ibn Marduwayh and al-Ḥākim record this, al-Ḥākim again noting that it meets the criteria of the Two Shaykhs. Al-Thawrī and Qays ibn al-Rabīʿ relate it from al-Barāʾ with the addition that destruction is a man sinning and refusing to repent. Al-Barāʾ also said that to lose hope in Allah's mercy and forgiveness is to go voluntarily to one's destruction, so despair of forgiveness is forbidden. Ibn ʿAbbās said the verse is not about fighting but about refraining from spending for Allah's sake, by which a person throws himself into ruin. Others say that spending in Allah's way so excessively that the rights of one's family suffer is the destruction meant, so that such excess is impermissible, and others that the verse forbids throwing oneself into an attack when it is already plain that one can achieve nothing against the enemy but death at their hands. Al-Jaṣṣāṣ reconciles these views by saying that all these rules can be drawn from the verse. Withholding the funds needed for the struggle, or abandoning it altogether, gives the enemy the advantage. More than anything else the struggle for Allah's cause demands the spending of money, and it is the sacrifice of wealth that people find hardest. The Qur'an therefore tells us to treat Allah's cause as our own and to spend generously on it. Failing this invites destruction in this world and the next, for if a person will not surrender what he has to Allah, why should Allah give him what He has? People imagine that wealth is best spent on themselves and their families, but the Qur'an calls that the way to destruction. Wealth is properly used in generous spending for the religion, which earns divine help in this world and Paradise in the Hereafter.

**"And do good, for Allah certainly loves the good-doers"**. Allah commands excellence (iḥsān), the highest of the acts of obedience, as an incentive to do everything well, in worship, dealings and conduct. Where iḥsān concerns worship, the Prophet ﷺ explained it in the well-known hadith of Jibrīl: worship Allah as if you see Him, and if you cannot reach that perception, know that He sees you. Where it concerns social dealings, he explained it, as the Musnad of Aḥmad reports from Muʿādh, as liking for others what you like for yourself and disliking for them what you dislike for yourself. One reading takes the good here as spending well in Allah's way, or as having a good opinion of Him. Allah loves those who do good, rewarding them generously and leading them to true guidance.

### Spending wallets, hearts and spirits

In the devotional reading, the rich remove money from their wallets, the poor remove the rich from their hearts, and the voicers of tawḥīd remove all creatures from their secret cores, to which He alludes in "Say, ˹O Prophet,˺ "Allah ˹revealed it˺!" Then leave them" (6:91). The rich let wealth go for the reward of the next world, the poor let the rich go for the sake of the Lord's religion, and the recognisers let creatures go for the sake of seeing the Glorified. The rich spend their possessions in zakāh and charity to escape Hell, the worshippers spend their souls in the duties of worship to reach Paradise, and the recognisers spend their spirits and hearts in the realities of witnessing to reach union with the Real. Muṣṭafā ﷺ said that beautiful doing is to worship Allah as if you see Him, for if you do not see Him, He sees you: to worship in wakefulness and awareness as if gazing on Him. This hadith alludes to the heart's encounter with the Real, the secret core's meeting with the Unseen and the spirit's contemplation of its Patron, and it urges purity in deeds, the curtailing of wishes and loyalty to what was accepted on the First Day, when the spirits heard "Am I not your Lord?" and answered "Yes, You are!" (7:172). Loyalty to that acceptance is serving the Protector, wishes are curtailed in "as if you see Him", and deeds are purified in "He sees you". When an eye has seen Him, how can it busy itself glancing at others? When a spirit has found His companionship, how will it make do with water and dust? The call "Return to your Lord" (89:28) is addressed to the pure spirit, which cannot make its home in a frame of clay. Whoever is used to that Presence will not long endure the abasement of the veil, nor will the ruler of his own city spend his life in exile. The attribute of the spirit is subsistence while water and dust undergo annihilation, and he who lives in the Real is not like him who lives in this world. The realiser knows the secret that the Real can be seen, and "as if you see Him" bears witness to it.

### In short

- Spending for jihād is obligatory as the need arises, over and above zakāh.
- "Destruction" means above all abandoning jihād to sit with one's family and estate, as Abū Ayyūb al-Anṣārī explained at Constantinople, and also withholding spending (Ibn ʿAbbās, Ḥudhayfah), despairing of mercy or refusing to repent (al-Barāʾ), reckless excess in giving, or a hopeless attack. Al-Jaṣṣāṣ accepts all of these.
- A lone charge against the enemy is not self-destruction (al-Barāʾ, with 4:84).
- Iḥsān in worship is to worship as if seeing Allah, and in dealings to wish for others what one wishes for oneself (the hadith of Jibrīl, Muʿādh).
- Inwardly, the rich spend wealth, the poor spend their attachment to the rich, and the recognisers spend their very spirits to reach the Real (6:91, 7:172, 89:28).

196.text:
After the rulings of fasting and jihād, Allah explains the rites, and the eleventh injunction in the series on righteousness that began in verse 177 concerns the Ḥajj. "Complete the pilgrimage and minor pilgrimage for Allah. But if prevented ˹from proceeding˺, then ˹offer˺ whatever sacrificial animals you can afford. And do not shave your heads until the sacrificial animal reaches its destination." The verse continues: "But if any of you is ill or has a scalp ailment ˹requiring shaving˺, then compensate either by fasting, charity, or a sacrificial offering. In times of peace, you may combine the pilgrimage and minor pilgrimage then make the sacrificial offering you can afford." And it ends: "Whoever cannot afford that ˹offering˺, let them fast three days during pilgrimage and seven after returning ˹home˺—completing ten. These offerings are for those who do not live near the Sacred House. And be mindful of Allah, and know that Allah is severe in punishment". Because the Ḥajj is tied to Makkah al-Mukarramah and the Kaʿbah, some related questions were covered under the subject of the qiblah in verses 125 to 128 of this sūrah, and the saʿy between Ṣafā and Marwah was taken up in verse 158 as a corollary. Now verses 196 to 203, eight consecutive verses, present the injunctions and questions of Ḥajj and ʿumrah.

### Phrase by phrase

**"Complete the pilgrimage and minor pilgrimage for Allah."**. By the strong consensus of the Ummah the Ḥajj is a cardinal pillar of Islam, emphasised in many verses and numerous authentic hadiths. According to the majority it became obligatory in the third year of the Hijrah, the year of Uḥud, through the verse of Sūrat Āl ʿImrān which makes the pilgrimage to the House a right of Allah upon people, stating its conditions and sternly warning those who neglect it despite ability. The present verse was revealed, by agreement, about the event of Ḥudaybiyyah, so its purpose is not to declare the obligation, already stated, but to convey special rulings governing Ḥajj and ʿumrah. To complete them means to finish their rites once begun, which is why the verse goes on to speak of being prevented, and the scholars agree that beginning Ḥajj or ʿumrah makes finishing them binding, just as voluntary prayers and fasts must be completed once started. Sūrat Āl ʿImrān mentions only Ḥajj, and this verse mentions ʿumrah without saying whether it is obligatory in itself, so the question is not settled here. Jābir asked the Prophet ﷺ whether ʿumrah was wājib and he replied that it was not, but that performing it was better and meritorious, a report of al-Tirmidhī, who grades it ḥasan ṣaḥīḥ, Aḥmad and al-Bayhaqī, and on this basis Abū Ḥanīfah, Mālik and others hold ʿumrah to be a sunnah rather than wājib. Makḥūl said that completing means beginning them from the mīqāt, the stations the Prophet ﷺ appointed for assuming iḥrām. ʿAbd al-Razzāq relates from al-Zuhrī that ʿUmar explained it as performing each separately, with ʿumrah outside the months of Ḥajj, since Allah says the Ḥajj is in the well-known months. Al-Suddī took it as maintaining their performance, and Ibn ʿAbbās said that Ḥajj is ʿArafāt and ʿumrah is ṭawāf. Al-Aʿmash relates from Ibrāhīm that ʿAlqamah cited Ibn Masʿūd's reading "complete the Ḥajj and ʿumrah to the House", so that one does not go beyond the House during the ʿumrah, and Ibrāhīm added that Saʿīd ibn Jubayr attributed the same to Ibn ʿAbbās, while Sufyān and al-Thawrī relate the reading "perform the Ḥajj and ʿumrah to the House" from Ibrāhīm and ʿAlqamah. "For Allah" means with sincerity, so that He accepts them, carrying the Ḥajj to full completion and the ʿumrah to the Sacred House. Ḥajj takes place once a year in Dhū al-Ḥijjah, while ʿumrah may be performed at any time, and any worship done purely for Allah is valuable in His sight.

**"But if prevented ˹from proceeding˺, then ˹offer˺ whatever sacrificial animals you can afford."**. These words came down in the sixth year of the Hijrah, the year of Ḥudaybiyyah, when the polytheists of Quraysh stopped the Messenger of Allah ﷺ from reaching the House and Sūrat al-Fatḥ was revealed. The Muslims were allowed to slaughter the sacrificial animals they had with them, seventy camels, and to shave their heads and leave iḥrām. When the Prophet ﷺ ordered them to shave and leave iḥrām they hesitated, expecting the order to be abrogated, until they saw him go out having shaved his head, and then followed him. Some only shortened their hair, which is why he prayed for Allah's mercy on those who shaved, and only at the third asking added those who shortened. Every seven men shared one camel. They were fourteen hundred, camped at Ḥudaybiyyah outside the Sacred Area, though it is also said they were within its boundary, and Allah knows best. The ransom for release from iḥrām is thus the sacrifice of whatever animal is easy to obtain, a goat or sheep, a cow or a camel. Imam Mālik reports that ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib used to say the offering includes a sheep. Ibn ʿAbbās said that the hady comprises eight kinds of animal, camels, cows, goats and sheep, and ʿAbd al-Razzāq relates from him that it means as much as one can afford, al-ʿAwfī relating from him camels for one who can, otherwise cows or sheep, while Hishām ibn ʿUrwah relates from his father that it depends on the price. The proof that a sheep suffices when one is prevented is that Allah required whatever hady is available, and the hady is any kind of cattle, which is the view of Ibn ʿAbbās, the Prophet's ﷺ cousin and the scholar of tafsīr, and the Two Ṣaḥīḥs record from ʿĀʾishah that the Prophet ﷺ once offered sheep as hady. Being prevented (ḥaṣr) is not confined to enemy action. Imam Aḥmad records from al-Ḥajjāj ibn ʿAmr al-Anṣārī that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said that whoever suffers a broken bone or lameness has left iḥrām and must perform Ḥajj again, and that when he mentioned this to Ibn ʿAbbās and Abū Hurayrah they confirmed it. The Four Collections report it, the versions of Abū Dāwūd and Ibn Mājah adding illness. Ibn Abī Ḥātim relates that Ibn Masʿūd, Ibn al-Zubayr, ʿAlqamah, Saʿīd ibn al-Musayyib and ʿUrwah ibn al-Zubayr, as well as Mujāhid, al-Nakhaʿī, ʿAṭāʾ and Muqātil ibn Ḥayyān, held that prevention covers an enemy, illness or a fracture, and al-Thawrī said it covers everything that harms a person. Abū Ḥanīfah and other jurists likewise hold that one unable to complete the rites through sickness may use this concession, since "if prevented" is general. The Two Ṣaḥīḥs record from ʿĀʾishah that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ visited Ḍubāʿah bint al-Zubayr ibn ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib, who said she wished to perform Ḥajj but was ill, and told her to perform it and stipulate that her place of release would be wherever Allah halted her, and Muslim records the like from Ibn ʿAbbās, so making such a condition is permitted. The Prophet's ﷺ own practice shows that although one may leave iḥrām after the sacrifice in such an emergency, it remains obligatory to perform the Ḥajj or ʿumrah afresh as qaḍāʾ when circumstances allow, which is why he and his Companions performed the ʿumrah the following year in place of the one missed at Ḥudaybiyyah.

**"And do not shave your heads until the sacrificial animal reaches its destination."**. This clause continues "Complete the pilgrimage and minor pilgrimage" and does not depend on the clause about being prevented, as Ibn Jarīr mistakenly held. In the year of Ḥudaybiyyah the Prophet ﷺ and his Companions shaved and sacrificed outside the Ḥaram, but in normal conditions, when the House can be reached safely, no one may shave until the hady reaches its place of sacrifice, after which the rites of Ḥajj, ʿumrah or both are concluded. The Two Ṣaḥīḥs record that Ḥafṣah asked the Messenger of Allah ﷺ why the people had left their iḥrām for ʿumrah while he had not, and he replied that he had matted his hair and garlanded his hady and would not leave iḥrām until he had sacrificed. Since release from iḥrām is lawful only after shaving or close-trimming the hair, the verse makes shaving the signal of release and so proves that shaving or trimming in iḥrām is forbidden. "Reaching its destination" means, according to Abū Ḥanīfah, that the animal is taken into the sacred precincts and slaughtered there, personally or through someone authorised to act on one's behalf. Al-Shāfiʿī likewise places the sacrifice within the enclosure, made with the intention of release and divided among the needy, after which the head is shaved. Another view is that one prevented from entering the Sanctuary sacrifices wherever he has been stopped, but if he can enter he does so on the Day of Sacrifice, the tenth of Dhū al-Ḥijjah, or at least within the days of tashrīq, the eleventh, twelfth and thirteenth.

**"But if any of you is ill or has a scalp ailment ˹requiring shaving˺, then compensate either by fasting, charity, or a sacrificial offering."**. If one is forced by sickness or by irritating lice to shave the head or any part of the body, one may do so to the extent of the need but must redeem it by fasting, charity (ṣadaqah) or sacrifice. Al-Bukhārī records from ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn al-Aṣbahānī that ʿAbdullāh ibn Maʿqil sat with Kaʿb ibn ʿUjrah in the mosque of Kūfah and asked him about the fidyah of fasting. Kaʿb said the verse was revealed about his own case in particular but applied to everyone in general: he was carried to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ with lice falling thickly on his face, and the Prophet ﷺ said he had not imagined his suffering had reached such a point, asked whether he could afford a sheep, and when he said no, told him to fast three days or feed six poor people half a ṣāʿ each and shave his head. So a general ruling was derived from a particular case. Imam Aḥmad records Kaʿb saying that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ passed him while he was lighting a fire under a pot with lice falling from his head or eyelids, asked whether they troubled him, and told him to shave and then fast three days, feed six poor people or sacrifice an animal, the narrator Ayyūb noting that he did not know which option was mentioned first. The Qur'an lists the options from the easiest to the hardest, fasting, feeding, sacrifice, while the Prophet ﷺ advised Kaʿb beginning with the most rewarding, a sheep, then feeding six, then three fasts, and each text suits its place. The sacrifice must be offered within the Ḥaram, where the feeding is also directed to the poor of the Sanctuary, whereas fasting and charity have no fixed place. The Qur'an does not state the number of fasts or the amount of charity, but the hadith of Kaʿb fixes three days or half a ṣāʿ of wheat to each of six needy persons, about 1.632 kilograms or its value, also reckoned as three cubic measures of the staple food of the town. The word "or" shows free choice. The case of one who shaves without excuse is included all the more, and redemption is likewise due from one who, with or without excuse, enjoys such things as scent, clothing or oils in iḥrām even without shaving. One reading adds that a sick person unable to remain where he is may return home before his offering reaches its place.

**"In times of peace, you may combine the pilgrimage and minor pilgrimage then make the sacrificial offering you can afford."**. When you are secure from the enemy and recovered from sickness, and able to complete the rites, whoever joins ʿumrah to Ḥajj must offer whatever animal is available, the least being a sheep or a seventh share of a camel or cow. One reading takes "in safety" as the command to make up the following year what Allah made obligatory, whether Ḥajj or ʿumrah. Before Islam the Arabs would not combine Ḥajj and ʿumrah in the months of Ḥajj, from the start of Shawwāl, thinking it a sin, and this verse corrects their misconception. Combining them takes two forms. In the first, one enters iḥrām for both from the mīqāt and remains in it until the last day of Ḥajj, which the hadith calls qirān. In the second, one enters iḥrām for ʿumrah alone, performs its rites in Makkah, leaves iḥrām, and then on the eighth of Dhū al-Ḥijjah, when setting out for Minā, enters iḥrām for Ḥajj from within the Ḥaram, which is tamattuʿ in the technical sense. Literally tamattuʿ means enjoying the benefit of combining the two, so the Qur'anic words cover both methods, and the authentic hadiths show both, some narrators saying the Prophet ﷺ performed tamattuʿ and others qirān, with no difference between them concerning the hady. Between the ʿumrah and the Ḥajj the pilgrim enjoys what is forbidden in iḥrām, scent and clothing, until he enters iḥrām for Ḥajj in its months. The offering is then sacrificed after entering iḥrām, ideally on the Day of Sacrifice. Those who combine the two must show gratitude for being allowed two acts of worship in one journey, and the sacrifice is that expression. A cow is permitted as well, for al-Awzāʿī reports from Abū Hurayrah that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ slaughtered cows on behalf of his wives when they performed tamattuʿ, as Abū Bakr ibn Marduwyah records, and this proves that tamattuʿ is legislated. The Two Ṣaḥīḥs record that ʿImrān ibn Ḥuṣayn said they performed tamattuʿ in the Prophet's ﷺ lifetime, that the Qur'an was revealed about it, that nothing came down forbidding it and he did not forbid it until he died, and that a certain man then said what he wished by his own opinion, al-Bukhārī noting that he meant ʿUmar. It is authentically reported that ʿUmar discouraged tamattuʿ, saying that if they followed Allah's Book they should complete the pilgrimage, yet he never called it unlawful. He only wished people to visit the House more often, making Ḥajj in its months and ʿumrah through the rest of the year, as he himself explained.

**"Whoever cannot afford that ˹offering˺, let them fast three days during pilgrimage and seven after returning ˹home˺—completing ten."**. Whoever finds no animal, because none is available or he lacks the means, fasts three days in the Ḥajj season, in a state of iḥrām, completing them by the ninth of Dhū al-Ḥijjah. Al-ʿAwfī relates from Ibn ʿAbbās that the three days are fasted before the day of ʿArafah, and if ʿArafah is the third day the fast is complete, with seven more on returning home. Abū Isḥāq relates from Wabarah from Ibn ʿUmar that one fasts the day before Tarwiyah, the day of Tarwiyah, which is the eighth, and the day of ʿArafah, the ninth, and Jaʿfar ibn Muḥammad relates the same from his father from ʿAlī. For this reason one should enter iḥrām before the seventh of Dhū al-Ḥijjah, and ideally before the sixth, since fasting on ʿArafah is discouraged. Whoever has not fasted the three days, or some of them, before the Day of ʿĪd may fast them in the days of tashrīq. ʿĀʾishah and Ibn ʿUmar said, as al-Bukhārī reports, that fasting the days of tashrīq was allowed only for those who had no hady, and ʿAlī said that whoever did not fast the three days during Ḥajj should fast them in tashrīq, a view shared by ʿUbayd ibn ʿUmayr al-Laythī, ʿIkrimah, al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī and ʿUrwah ibn al-Zubayr on the general wording. Muslim's report from Qutaybah al-Hudhalī that the days of tashrīq are days of eating, drinking and remembering Allah is general, while the report of ʿĀʾishah and Ibn ʿUmar is specific. In the view of the Companions and Abū Ḥanīfah, one who fails to fast the three days during Ḥajj must offer a sacrifice instead, arranged in the Ḥaram through someone he knows as soon as possible, as al-Jaṣṣāṣ notes. As for the seven, there are two opinions: when one returns to the camping grounds, or when one reaches home. ʿAbd al-Razzāq relates from Sālim that Ibn ʿUmar explained it as going back to one's family, and the same is reported from Saʿīd ibn Jubayr, Abū al-ʿĀliyah and Mujāhid, from ʿAṭāʾ, ʿIkrimah and al-Ḥasan, and from Qatādah, al-Zuhrī and al-Rabīʿ ibn Anas, though the seven may also be completed in Makkah or on the way home at a time of one's choosing. Al-Bukhārī records from Sālim ibn ʿAbdullāh that Ibn ʿUmar described the Farewell Ḥajj: the Messenger of Allah ﷺ performed tamattuʿ, joining ʿumrah to Ḥajj, drove his hady from Dhū al-Ḥulayfah, began with iḥrām for ʿumrah and then for Ḥajj, and the people did the same, some bringing animals and some not. On reaching Makkah he told whoever had brought a hady not to leave iḥrām until completing the Ḥajj, and whoever had not to perform ṭawāf of the Kaʿbah and between al-Ṣafā and al-Marwah, shave or shorten the hair, leave iḥrām, and later assume iḥrām for Ḥajj and offer a sacrifice, fasting three days during Ḥajj and seven on returning home if he could not afford one, as the Two Ṣaḥīḥs record. The words "completing ten" emphasise the ruling in the Arabic manner of saying "I saw with my eyes, heard with my ears and wrote with my hand", as in "winged birds soaring in the sky" (6:38), "nor could you write at all" (29:48) and "thirty nights then added another ten—completing his Lord's term of forty nights" (7:142). It is also said that the phrase stresses that ten days, no fewer, must be fasted.

**"These offerings are for those who do not live near the Sacred House."**. This concerns the residents of the Ḥaram area, who do not perform tamattuʿ. ʿAbd al-Razzāq relates from Ṭāwūs that tamattuʿ is for those whose families do not live in the Ḥaram and not for the people of Makkah, and that Ibn ʿAbbās said the same. Residents have no need of it, since they are constantly there and can perform ʿumrah and ṭawāf freely at any other time of year. The prohibition on combining Ḥajj and ʿumrah in the Ḥajj months is thus restricted to those living within the limits of the mīqāt, who can easily return for ʿumrah after the season, while for those coming from beyond the mīqāt it is permitted, since a separate journey for ʿumrah from such distances is not easy. The mīqāt are the stations appointed by Allah on every route to Makkah, at which everyone proceeding for Ḥajj or ʿumrah must assume iḥrām, and passing them without iḥrām is a sin. "Those who do not live near the Sacred House" means those whose families live outside these stations.

**"And be mindful of Allah, and know that Allah is severe in punishment"**. Fear Allah in what He commands and forbids, following His sacred law and respecting His limits. Taqwā, a Qur'anic term with no English equivalent, denotes fearing and abstaining from anything against the rules Allah has set. The warning is that His punishment is severe for whoever knowingly acts against His injunctions. Pilgrims today are widely negligent of this: many make no effort to learn the rules of Ḥajj and ʿumrah, and many who know them do not follow them strictly, while bad guides or careless companions make them miss even obligatory acts, let alone the sunnah and etiquette of the pilgrimage. May Allah grant us all the ability to correct what we do. Pilgrims carry provisions for the road, but the best provision is to live in fear of Allah, for taqwā is not the observance of outward forms but a state of heightened consciousness in which the mind is filled with Allah's greatness and beauty. A believer does not live for his desires but for the goal of abstaining from everything Allah has forbidden and from misdeeds and quarrels with his fellows, and the Ḥajj serves this moral training.

### The House and its guests

In the devotional reading, Wahb ibn Munabbih relates that Allah revealed to Ādam: I am the Lord of the world and its folk, the Creator of all, the King who does what He desires. I am the Lord of Bakkah, and those who dwell there are My neighbours. Those who visit it are My delegates and guests under My protection. I will people this spot with the folk of heaven and earth, who will come in droves from every direction, their hair dishevelled and their faces dusty from the hardship of the road, crying "Allah is greater" and "Here I am", the earth coloured with the blood of sacrifice. Whoever visits this House in purity is My guest and one of those near to Me, and it befits My majesty to honour him and bring him to forgiveness through the gift of mercy. Among your children is a prophet named Ibrāhīm, My bosom friend, by whose hand I will establish it and whom I will command to build it, making its eminence appear, bringing its watering place to light, marking its sanctuary and teaching him how to worship Me there. After him the world's folk will keep it inhabited with reverence in their hearts, and then will come the turn of Muḥammad the Arab, Seal of the Prophets and lamp of heaven and earth, whose birthplace and origin it will be, the place where revelation falls on him and the home of his honour, its watering place, deputyship and rule placed in his hand.
