After that, love for it will be set by Me in the hearts of the faithful in every corner of the earth, and they will come bareheaded and barefoot, their goods set aside and their lives in their hands, to circle the House and ask My forgiveness. If anyone asks what I will do with them, say that I am with them in knowledge, found by their souls and present in their hearts, the cure of their pain, hidden from their eyes but face to face with their spirits.

The ḥajj of the common people is one thing and the ḥajj of the elect another. The first sets out for the street of the Friend and the second for the face of the Friend. One goes to the Friend's house, the other to the Friend. The common people go with their souls and see doors and walls, while the elect go with their spirits and find conversation and vision. Whoever goes with the soul finds suffering and carries burdens to circle the Kaʿbah, and whoever goes with the spirit finds rest and ease, and the Kaʿbah itself circles his house. Hence the story of Ibrāhīm Khawāṣṣ, who in his deprivation once found himself wandering bewildered in Byzantium, as the Men of the Path fall anywhere. The news there was that the king's daughter had gone mad and her father had bound her as madmen are bound, the physicians helpless, while she sometimes breathed a cold sigh and rained hot tears, now weeping, now laughing. He went to the king's door and said he had come to cure the sick girl. The king asked if he was a physician. He said he had a Lord who was a physician. The king pointed to the battlements, where severed heads were set, and said that this was the recompense of anyone who failed to cure her, and Ibrāhīm said he had nothing to fear, for how can a lover fear his own destruction? The king sent him to his daughter's room, and before he had set foot inside he heard the words "Tell the believing men to lower their gaze" (24:30). He stood still, bewildered by her state, and heard another call: son of Khawāṣṣ, a drink that increases nothing but thirst, a food that increases nothing but consternation! From behind the curtain he asked her what this state and this ecstasy were. She told him that she had been sitting in joy among her slave girls and friends when suddenly a pain fell into her heart and a sorrow reached her spirit, so that she was annihilated from herself and enraptured, and before she returned to her room the pain had taken hold and the work was complete. When she came to some ease she found herself in chains, approved His judgment and was content with His decree, knowing that He wants no evil for His friends. Ibrāhīm proposed that they contrive a way for her to reach the Abode of Islam and cultivate the faith there, since it would be a shame to leave one so dear in the Abode of Unbelief. She answered that there was no manliness, son of Khawāṣṣ, in tending the faith where faith already reigned. The true man, she said, embraces Islam in the land of unbelief and nurtures it there in spirit and heart.

### In short

- Once begun, Ḥajj and ʿumrah must be completed. Ḥajj is a pillar made obligatory in 3 AH, while ʿumrah is a sunnah according to Abū Ḥanīfah and Mālik (the hadith of Jābir).
- Revealed at Ḥudaybiyyah, the verse allows one prevented by an enemy, and by extension illness or injury (al-Ḥajjāj ibn ʿAmr, al-Thawrī, Abū Ḥanīfah), to sacrifice whatever animal he can, even a sheep, and leave iḥrām, making up the rite later. A condition may be stipulated at iḥrām (Ḍubāʿah).
- No shaving before the offering reaches its place, so shaving in iḥrām is forbidden, and one forced to shave by illness or lice redeems it by three fasts, feeding six poor people half a ṣāʿ each, or a sheep (Kaʿb ibn ʿUjrah).
- Tamattuʿ and qirān, combining ʿumrah with Ḥajj in the Ḥajj months, are lawful for those from beyond the mīqāt, not for Makkans, and require a sacrifice or ten fasts, three in Ḥajj before ʿArafah or in tashrīq and seven after returning (the Farewell Ḥajj of Ibn ʿUmar, ʿImrān ibn Ḥuṣayn). ʿUmar discouraged tamattuʿ without forbidding it.
- Taqwā is the pilgrim's best provision, and inwardly the pilgrims are Allah's guests, the common people reaching His house and the elect His face (Wahb ibn Munabbih, Ibrāhīm Khawāṣṣ).

197.text:
The second of the eight verses on the rules of Ḥajj fixes its time and its etiquette. "˹Commitment to˺ pilgrimage is made in appointed months. Whoever commits to ˹performing˺ pilgrimage, let them stay away from intimate relations, foul language, and arguments during pilgrimage." It continues: "Whatever good you do, Allah ˹fully˺ knows of it. Take ˹necessary˺ provisions ˹for the journey˺—surely the best provision is righteousness. And be mindful of Me, O people of reason". The previous verse required whoever enters iḥrām for Ḥajj or ʿumrah to complete it. ʿUmrah has no fixed date and may be done at any time of year, but for Ḥajj the months, dates and timings of each act are fixed, and so this verse opens by stating that Ḥajj has known months.

### Phrase by phrase

**"˹Commitment to˺ pilgrimage is made in appointed months."**. The word ashhur is the plural of shahr, month. Al-Bukhārī relates that Ibn ʿUmar identified the months as Shawwāl, Dhū al-Qaʿdah and the first ten days of Dhū al-Ḥijjah, a report whose chain Ibn Jarīr completed and declared authentic and which al-Ḥākim records as meeting the criteria of the Two Shaykhs. Abū Umāmah narrates the same, and they have been the months of Ḥajj since the Jāhiliyyah. The same is reported from ʿUmar, ʿAlī and Ibn Masʿūd, from ʿAbdullāh ibn al-Zubayr and Ibn ʿAbbās, from ʿAṭāʾ, Ṭāwūs and Mujāhid, from Ibrāhīm al-Nakhaʿī, al-Shaʿbī, al-Ḥasan and Ibn Sīrīn, and from Makḥūl, Qatādah, aḍ-Ḍaḥḥāk ibn Muzāḥim, al-Rabīʿ ibn Anas and Muqātil ibn Ḥayyān. Some say the whole of Dhū al-Ḥijjah is included. Ibn Jarīr preferred the first view, noting that it is common usage to call two months and part of a third "months", just as an Arab says he visited someone this year or this day though he was there for only part of it, and just as the Qur'an speaks of hastening away from Minā in two days when it is really a day and a half. The verse shows that iḥrām for Ḥajj is assumed only in these months, as reported from Ibn ʿAbbās, Jābir, ʿAṭāʾ, Ṭāwūs and Mujāhid, for a Ḥajj in specified months cannot be entered before them, just as prayer has a fixed time before which it is not valid. Al-Shāfiʿī records Ibn ʿAbbās saying that no one should assume iḥrām for Ḥajj before its months because of this verse, and Ibn Khuzaymah records him saying that it is of the Sunnah of Ḥajj to assume iḥrām in its months, an authentic report, and a Companion's statement that something is "of the Sunnah" counts as a hadith of the Prophet ﷺ for the majority, all the more when it comes from Ibn ʿAbbās, the interpreter of the Qur'an. Ibn Marduwayh relates from Jābir that the Prophet ﷺ said no one should assume iḥrām for Ḥajj except in its months, with a reasonable chain, and al-Shāfiʿī and al-Bayhaqī record through Ibn Jurayj that Abū al-Zubayr heard Jābir ibn ʿAbdullāh asked whether one enters iḥrām for Ḥajj before its months and answer no, which is more reliable than the marfūʿ version. Since the months begin with Shawwāl, iḥrām for Ḥajj before Shawwāl is not permitted. Some imams hold such a Ḥajj simply invalid, while Abū Ḥanīfah rules it valid but makrūh.

**"Whoever commits to ˹performing˺ pilgrimage"**. Whoever assumes iḥrām in these months, taking the duty upon himself, is bound to complete the rites. Ibn Jarīr relates from al-ʿAwfī that the scholars agree that "commits" here means making it a binding obligation. ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭalḥah relates from Ibn ʿAbbās that it refers to those who assume iḥrām for Ḥajj and ʿumrah, ʿAṭāʾ said it means assuming iḥrām, and Ibrāhīm, aḍ-Ḍaḥḥāk and others said the like.

**"let them stay away from intimate relations"**. Those in iḥrām for Ḥajj or ʿumrah must avoid rafath, meaning intercourse, as in "It has been made permissible for you to be intimate with your wives during the nights preceding the fast" (2:187), together with whatever leads to it, such as embracing, kissing and speaking to women of such things. Ibn Jarīr relates from Nāfiʿ that ʿAbdullāh ibn ʿUmar said rafath is intercourse or mentioning it with the tongue, by men or women. ʿAṭāʾ ibn Abī Rabāḥ said it is intercourse and foul speech, which is also the view of ʿAmr ibn Dīnār, and ʿAṭāʾ added that they used to forbid even hinting at the subject. Ṭāwūs and Abū al-ʿĀliyah said it includes telling one's wife that one will be with her once iḥrām ends. ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭalḥah relates from Ibn ʿAbbās that it covers intercourse, kissing, fondling and foul words to one's wife. That rafath means relations with women is the view of Ibn ʿAbbās and Ibn ʿUmar, of Saʿīd ibn Jubayr, ʿIkrimah and Mujāhid, of Ibrāhīm al-Nakhaʿī and Abū al-ʿĀliyah, who related it from ʿAṭāʾ and Makḥūl, of ʿAṭāʾ al-Khurāsānī, ʿAṭāʾ ibn Yasār and ʿAṭiyyah, of al-Rabīʿ, al-Zuhrī and al-Suddī, of Mālik ibn Anas, Muqātil ibn Ḥayyān and ʿAbd al-Karīm ibn Mālik, and of al-Ḥasan, Qatādah, aḍ-Ḍaḥḥāk and others. Rafath is a comprehensive word covering intercourse, its preliminaries and open talk of love-making, all forbidden in iḥrām, though an indirect or implied reference is not prohibited.

**"foul language"**. Literally fusūq means transgression, and in the Qur'an's usage disobedience, which in its general sense includes every sin. Miqsam and others relate from Ibn ʿAbbās that it is disobedience, and this is the view of ʿAṭāʾ, Mujāhid, Ṭāwūs and ʿIkrimah, of Saʿīd ibn Jubayr, Muḥammad ibn Kaʿb and al-Ḥasan, and of Qatādah, Ibrāhīm al-Nakhaʿī, al-Zuhrī, al-Rabīʿ ibn Anas, ʿAṭāʾ ibn Yasār, ʿAṭāʾ al-Khurāsānī and Muqātil ibn Ḥayyān. Ibn Wahb relates from Nāfiʿ that ʿAbdullāh ibn ʿUmar took it to mean the acts Allah has forbidden in the Sacred Area, that is, what is prohibited specifically in iḥrām, an interpretation well suited to the occasion, since sins in general are forbidden in every state. Others say it means cursing, citing the authentic hadith that cursing a Muslim is fusūq and fighting him is kufr. ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Zayd ibn Aslam said it means slaughtering for idols, as in "a sinful offering in the name of any other than Allah" (6:145), and aḍ-Ḍaḥḥāk said it is insulting one another with bad nicknames. Those who take it as all kinds of disobedience are correct, for Allah forbids wrongdoing in the Ḥajj months in particular though it is forbidden all year, saying of the sacred months, "So do not wrong one another during these months" (9:36), and of the Sacred Area, "whoever intends to deviate by doing wrong in it, We will cause them to taste a painful punishment" (22:25). The Two Ṣaḥīḥs record from Abū Hurayrah that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said that whoever performs Ḥajj to this House without rafath or fusūq returns as sinless as on the day his mother bore him. Things that are not sins in themselves but become impermissible through iḥrām are six: intercourse with its preliminaries and love talk, hunting land game or guiding a hunter, cutting hair or nails, and using perfume, which apply equally to men and women, and for men wearing stitched clothing and covering the head and face, while Abū Ḥanīfah and Mālik also forbid women to cover the face in iḥrām. Intercourse, though included in fusūq, is named separately as rafath to stress its gravity, because the other prohibitions can be amended by expiation, whereas intercourse before the standing at ʿArafāt nullifies the Ḥajj itself, requires the sacrifice of a cow or camel and obliges the pilgrim to perform the Ḥajj again.

**"and arguments during pilgrimage."**. Jidāl is the effort to overturn an adversary, hence a rough altercation. Ibn Jarīr relates from ʿAbdullāh ibn Masʿūd that it means arguing with one's companion until one angers him, which Miqsam and aḍ-Ḍaḥḥāk relate from Ibn ʿAbbās and which is also reported from Abū al-ʿĀliyah, ʿAṭāʾ, Mujāhid and Saʿīd ibn Jubayr, from ʿIkrimah, Jābir ibn Zayd, ʿAṭāʾ al-Khurāsānī and Makḥūl, from al-Suddī, Muqātil ibn Ḥayyān, ʿAmr ibn Dīnār and aḍ-Ḍaḥḥāk, and from al-Rabīʿ ibn Anas, Ibrāhīm al-Nakhaʿī, ʿAṭāʾ ibn Yasār, al-Ḥasan, Qatādah and al-Zuhrī. Some take the word in its general sense, while others, mindful of the place and the state of iḥrām, relate it to a particular quarrel. In the age of ignorance people differed over the place of the standing: some held ʿArafāt necessary, others insisted on Muzdalifah and claimed that Ibrāhīm had stood there, and they differed over the time too, some performing Ḥajj in Dhū al-Ḥijjah and others earlier in Dhū al-Qaʿdah, each side accusing the other of error. The Qur'an said "no arguing" and ended all such quarrels, proclaiming the truth that the obligatory standing is at ʿArafāt, the necessary stay at Muzdalifah, and the Ḥajj in no days but those of Dhū al-Ḥijjah, and once the divine command is given quarrelling is forbidden. One reading mentions heated argument about the obligatoriness of the pilgrimage. In one of the recited variants the three nouns are read in the accusative, fa-lā rafatha wa-lā fusūqa, an absolute negation, while in the other the first two take the nominative, and the sense is the same. On this interpretation the prohibitions are confined to acts otherwise permissible but forbidden by iḥrām, just as eating and drinking are forbidden only in fasting and prayer. Those who take fusūq and jidāl generally reply that although sin and quarrelling are deplorable everywhere, they are graver in iḥrām: in those blessed days and in the sacred land, where everyone comes to worship at his best, chanting labbayk and clothed in a garment that constantly reminds him that he is devoted to worship in Allah's sight, any sin or dispute becomes sinfulness at its worst. The wisdom of forbidding these three in particular is that the time and place of Ḥajj expose people to them: long absence from family in iḥrām and the mingling of men and women in their thousands at the maṭāf, the masʿā, ʿArafāt, Muzdalifah and Minā make desire hard to control, so obscenity is forbidden first, the crowds devoted to their rites give occasion for sins such as theft, hence "no sin", and the crush of space breeds quarrels, hence "no arguing". The Qur'an's eloquence appears in the phrasing: instead of commanding "do not be obscene, do not sin, do not quarrel", it negates them outright, hinting that such things have no place in Ḥajj and cannot even be imagined there.

**"Whatever good you do, Allah ˹fully˺ knows of it."**. Having forbidden evil in deed and speech, Allah encourages righteous deeds, including voluntary charity, stating that He knows the good they do and will reward them with the best rewards on the Day of Resurrection. Abstaining from sin and from the violations of iḥrām is not enough. The pilgrim should treat the occasion as one that comes once in a lifetime and devote himself to worship, remembrance (dhikr) of Allah and good deeds, assured that every act of virtue is known to Allah and generously rewarded. Whatever one abstains from in the Sacred Precinct, Allah accepts.

**"Take ˹necessary˺ provisions ˹for the journey˺—surely the best provision is righteousness."**. Al-Bukhārī and Abū Dāwūd record from Ibn ʿAbbās, and ʿIkrimah relates from him, that the people of Yemen used to go to Ḥajj without enough supplies, saying they were the people of tawakkul, reliance on Allah, and then begged in Makkah, so Allah revealed this verse. ʿAṭāʾ ibn Abī Rabāḥ said people would travel and lay their burden on others. One account says they took provisions wrongfully from the settlements on their way and were forbidden to do so. Ibn Jarīr and Ibn Marduwayh relate from Ibn ʿUmar that when people assumed iḥrām they would throw away their provisions and seek others, and Allah forbade this and required them to carry flour and sawīq. The verse corrects those who set out for Ḥajj and ʿumrah unprepared in the name of trust in Allah and then have to ask for help, or suffer privation and trouble others. Taking provisions is not against tawakkul but is its essence, which is to gather the means Allah has provided to the best of one's ability and then place one's trust in Him, as the Prophet ﷺ explained it. Abandoning all effort to acquire the means of subsistence and calling it tawakkul is sheer ignorance. Having required people to provide for the journeys of this life, Allah directs them to the provision needed for the Hereafter, taqwā, as He says, "the best clothing is righteousness" (7:26), mentioning the material covering first and then the spiritual covering of humility, obedience and taqwā, and declaring the latter better and more beneficial. Taqwā literally means guarding, and with it one guards against asking others. One reading adds that the best provision in this world is trust in Allah, and another that taqwā here is restraint from begging, so that the pilgrim travels at his own expense and burdens no one.

**"And be mindful of Me, O people of reason"**. Fear My torment, punishment and affliction, which fall on those who defy Me and disregard My commands, O people of intellect and understanding, fearing Me above all in the Sacred Precinct.

### The pilgrimage of the heart

In the devotional reading, the pilgrimage of the bodily selves is in known months. Iḥrām binds only in them, and whoever lets that time pass has missed the pilgrimage. Likewise the pilgrimage of hearts has known times and is fitting only in them: these are the days of youth, for one who has no spiritual desire (irādah) in his youth has no communion in old age. The one whose season of quest and desire has passed is suited only to the worship whose outcome is the Garden, not the desire whose outcome is communion. The prohibition of lewdness, wickedness and disputing alludes to the traveller on the path of desire, who stops at nothing on the way and mixes nothing with his desire. Whoever argues with him, opposes him or is rude to him, he yields to them all, disputing with no one for this world and competing with no one for worldly fortune, self or honour, as Allah says of His servants that "when the foolish address them ˹improperly˺, they only respond with peace" (25:63). Content with Allah's knowledge and judgment, he has no need to be seen, judged or known by creatures. The piety of ordinary people is the avoidance of errors, and the piety of the elect is the avoidance of anything other than Allah in the inner secrets of their hearts.

### In short

- Iḥrām for Ḥajj is valid only in its months, Shawwāl, Dhū al-Qaʿdah and the first ten days of Dhū al-Ḥijjah (Ibn ʿUmar, Ibn ʿAbbās, Jābir). Abū Ḥanīfah holds an earlier iḥrām valid but makrūh.
- Once committed, the pilgrim must shun rafath (intercourse, its preliminaries and talk of it), fusūq (sin, especially the violations of iḥrām) and jidāl (angry quarrelling, including the old disputes over the place and time of the standing), and a Ḥajj free of these returns him sinless (Abū Hurayrah).
- Intercourse before ʿArafāt nullifies the Ḥajj, which is why it is named separately from the other five iḥrām prohibitions.
- Good deeds are known and rewarded. Provisions must be taken, for tawakkul means using the means and then trusting Allah (the Yemenis, Ibn ʿAbbās), and the best provision is taqwā (7:26).
- Inwardly, the heart's pilgrimage has its season in youth, and the elect's piety is to keep the heart's secret free of all but Allah (25:63).

198.text:
Verse 198 removes a scruple about earning during the pilgrimage and then turns to the central rites. "There is no blame on you for seeking the bounty of your Lord ˹during this journey˺. When you return from 'Arafât, praise Allah near the sacred place and praise Him for having guided you, for surely before this ˹guidance˺ you were astray".

### Phrase by phrase

**"There is no blame on you for seeking the bounty of your Lord ˹during this journey˺."**. Al-Bukhārī records from Ibn ʿAbbās that ʿUkāẓ, Mijannah and Dhū al-Majāz were trading posts in the Jāhiliyyah, and that after Islam people disliked trading during the Ḥajj season until this verse came down. Abū Dāwūd and others record from him that they avoided business during the Ḥajj, saying these were days of dhikr, and Mujāhid relates the same from him, the verse meaning "do engage in trade". This is also the explanation of Mujāhid, Saʿīd ibn Jubayr and ʿIkrimah, of Manṣūr ibn al-Muʿtamir and Qatādah, and of Ibrāhīm al-Nakhaʿī, al-Rabīʿ ibn Anas and others. Ibn Jarīr relates with a strong chain that when Ibn ʿUmar was asked about trade during Ḥajj he recited this verse, and Aḥmad records from Abū Umāmah al-Taymī that he told Ibn ʿUmar that they hired out their camels to pilgrims and walked with them, that they had long done so, and that some claimed their Ḥajj was invalid. Ibn ʿUmar asked whether they did not chant the talbiyah, circle the House, go between Ṣafā and Marwah, stand at ʿArafāt, throw the pebbles and shave their heads, and when he said yes, told him that a man had asked the Prophet ﷺ the same question and received no answer until Jibrīl came down with this verse, whereupon the Prophet ﷺ summoned the man and told him that they were pilgrims indeed. Ibn Jarīr relates that Abū Ṣāliḥ asked ʿUmar, as Leader of the Faithful, whether they used to trade during Ḥajj, and he replied that their livelihood came from nothing else. In the Jāhiliyyah the Arabs had distorted worship and dealings with absurd customs, turning devotion into amusement and not sparing even the Ḥajj, setting up bazaars, exhibitions and trade promotions at the great gathering of Minā. When Islam swept these away the Companions, ready to stake anything for Allah's pleasure, began to suspect even trading and working for wages during the Ḥajj days as a relic of ignorance that Islam might forbid outright. The verse makes clear that one who earns a profit by trade or wages by work incurs no sin. Yet the two words "the bounty of your Lord" reform the old trade fair: earn if you must, but treat the earning as Allah's favour and be grateful, never making the pilgrimage an exercise in minting money, and "no blame" hints that avoiding such occupation where possible is better still, since it touches the perfect sincerity the Ḥajj deserves. Everything turns on intention. If the basic aim is to earn, with the Ḥajj as an adjunct, or if both aims weigh equally, this is contrary to sincerity and reduces the reward and blessings of the Ḥajj. If one sets out intending the Ḥajj and unforeseen difficulties leave him short of funds, some earning by trade or employment to cover his needs does no harm to sincerity, though even then it is far better to keep the five special days of the rites free of trade and employment and devote them wholly to worship and dhikr, for which reason some scholars have ruled trade in those days forbidden. In the devotional reading, whatever one seeks of Allah's bounty within what He has decreed is praiseworthy if it carries a portion for the Muslims or strengthens the religion, while whatever is sought solely for one's own worldly fortune is flawed.

**"When you return from 'Arafât"**. ʿArafāt, grammatically a plural, is the name of a well-known plain outside the limits of the Ḥaram. It is the place of the standing and a pillar of the rites. Imam Aḥmad and the Sunan compilers record from ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Yaʿmar al-Diylī that he heard the Messenger of Allah ﷺ say three times that Ḥajj is ʿArafāt, that whoever stands at ʿArafāt before dawn has performed the Ḥajj, and that the days of Minā are three, with no sin on whoever leaves after two or stays. The time of standing runs from noon on the day of ʿArafah until dawn on the Day of Sacrifice, the tenth of Dhū al-Ḥijjah. At the Farewell Ḥajj the Prophet ﷺ stood after praying ẓuhr until sunset and told the people to learn their rites from him. ʿUrwah ibn Muḍarris ibn Ḥārithah ibn Lām al-Ṭāʾī came to him at Muzdalifah at the time of prayer and said that he had come from the two mountains of Ṭayyiʾ, exhausting himself and his mount, and had stood on every hill he passed, and asked whether his Ḥajj was valid. The Prophet ﷺ replied that whoever prayed this prayer with them, stood with them until they moved on, and had stood at ʿArafāt before that by day or night, had completed his Ḥajj and its rites, a hadith of Aḥmad and the Sunan compilers that al-Tirmidhī graded ṣaḥīḥ. All pilgrims must reach the plain and stay there between noon and sunset. It is the most important obligation of Ḥajj, for which, if missed, there is no substitute by expiation or ransom. As for the name, ʿAbd al-Razzāq relates from ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib that Allah sent Jibrīl to Ibrāhīm to teach him the rites, and when Ibrāhīm reached ʿArafāt he said "ʿaraftu", I know this place, having been there before, and so it was named. Ibn al-Mubārak relates from ʿAṭāʾ that Jibrīl taught Ibrāhīm the rites and he kept saying "ʿaraftu, ʿaraftu", and the like is attributed to Ibn ʿAbbās, Ibn ʿUmar and Abū Mijlaz. A clearer explanation is that ʿArafāt is the plain where man comes to know his Lord and learns through worship and dhikr how to draw near to Him, and where Muslims from East and West meet and know one another. ʿArafāt is also called al-Mashʿar al-Ḥarām, al-Mashʿar al-Aqṣā and Ilāl, and the hill in its middle is Jabal al-Raḥmah, the Mount of Mercy. Ibn Abī Ḥātim relates from Ibn ʿAbbās that in the Jāhiliyyah people left ʿArafāt when the sun sat on the mountain tops like a turban on a man's head, whereas the Messenger of Allah ﷺ delayed until sunset, and Ibn Marduwayh adds, with a ḥasan chain, that he then stood at Muzdalifah, prayed fajr early and moved on when dawn had broken. In the long hadith of Jābir ibn ʿAbdullāh in Muslim, the Prophet ﷺ remained standing until the sun had set, its yellow glow had faded and its disc had vanished. He then seated Usāmah behind him and drew the nose-rope of al-Qaṣwāʾ so tight that her head touched the saddle, gesturing with his right hand and calling on the people to proceed calmly, and whenever he came to a rise of sand he slackened the rope a little until she climbed it, and so they reached Muzdalifah. There he led maghrib and ʿishāʾ with one adhān and two iqāmahs, offering no voluntary prayer between them, lay down until dawn, prayed fajr with adhān and iqāmah when the light was clear, mounted al-Qaṣwāʾ again, and at al-Mashʿar al-Ḥarām faced the qiblah, supplicating, glorifying Allah and saying lā ilāha illā Allāh, until the daylight was very bright, and then moved quickly before sunrise. The Two Ṣaḥīḥs record that Usāmah ibn Zayd was asked about the Prophet's ﷺ pace and said it was slow, quickening a little when he found room. Pilgrims should press on together from where the multitude streams forth, with no feeling of superiority over one another.

**"praise Allah near the sacred place"**. On the way back from ʿArafāt it is necessary (wājib) to spend the night at Muzdalifah and remember Allah there, particularly as He has taught. Al-Mashʿar al-Ḥarām is the name of a mountain in Muzdalifah, also called Quzaḥ, at its far end. Al-mashʿar means a sign or waymark and ḥarām sacred, so the name marks it as a sacred monument of Islam, and the adjoining plain is Muzdalifah. ʿAbd al-Razzāq relates from Ibn ʿUmar that all of Muzdalifah is al-Mashʿar al-Ḥarām, and he also described it as the mount and its surroundings, while Ibn ʿAbbās, Saʿīd ibn Jubayr, ʿIkrimah, Mujāhid, al-Suddī, al-Rabīʿ ibn Anas, al-Ḥasan and Qatādah said it is the area between the two mountains. Imam Aḥmad records from Jubayr ibn Muṭʿim that the Prophet ﷺ said that all of ʿArafāt is a standing place except ʿUranah, all of Muzdalifah is a standing place except the bottom of Muḥassir, all of Makkah is a place of sacrifice, and all the days of tashrīq are days of sacrifice. In a hadith of Muslim he stood there remembering Allah and supplicating until his face began to glow. The remembrance includes every kind of dhikr, with heart and tongue, the talbiyah "labbayka Allāhumma labbayk", the tahlīl and supplication, but it refers particularly to offering maghrib and ʿishāʾ together at Muzdalifah, the act of worship peculiar to that plain, which the next words seem to indicate.

**"and praise Him for having guided you"**. Remember Him in the manner He has taught, without adulterating it with personal opinion, for personal reasoning would demand that maghrib be prayed at its own time and ʿishāʾ at its own, whereas on that night Allah prefers maghrib delayed and joined with ʿishāʾ. From this emerges the basic ruling that man is not independent in worship and remembrance: he may not worship as he wishes or remember Allah as he chooses, but every act of worship and dhikr has its etiquette and must be performed as stipulated. Allah does not like addition, subtraction or change of time or place, even if the change seems to increase the worship. People tend to add features to voluntary prayers and charity without any reason approved by the Sharīʿah, then treat these as necessary though Allah and His Messenger ﷺ did not, and even regard those who omit them as in error. This verse exposes their position, for such invented forms of worship reflect the Jāhiliyyah, when the disbelievers concocted rites from their own opinions and reduced a serious act to a few customs. The verse reminds the Muslims of Allah's favour in teaching them the rites of Ḥajj according to the guidance of Ibrāhīm al-Khalīl, the principal rites of His religion and the rituals of His pilgrimage, the particle "as" giving the reason for the remembrance.

**"for surely before this ˹guidance˺ you were astray"**. Before the guidance, the Qur'an, the Messenger ﷺ and Islam, you were among the misguided and the disbelievers, unaware of the sacred laws, and each of these meanings is correct. In the devotional reading, having gone so far as to perform what He asked, remember His favour, for had He not desired you, you would not have desired Him, and had He not chosen you, you would not have preferred His good pleasure.

### The spirit of the rites

The sequence of the verse follows the sequence of the days. The standing at ʿArafāt falls on the ninth of Dhū al-Ḥijjah, the night that follows is spent at Muzdalifah, and the morning of the tenth, the Day of Sacrifice, begins with the remembrance at al-Mashʿar al-Ḥarām before the pilgrims move on to Minā. Each station has its own act: the standing and supplication at ʿArafāt, the combined prayers and the night at Muzdalifah, and the dhikr at the sacred waymark until the light is bright. Fear of Allah is the basic element of worship, and as long as the pilgrim keeps that frame of mind it does not matter if he mistakes the order of a rite or attends to some private business in the holy land. What matters is entering into the spirit of the pilgrimage, fear of Allah, remembrance, prayerfulness, thanksgiving and wholehearted submission, and doing nothing that runs counter to it, for the lesson of the Ḥajj is the equality of all before the one supreme God, and whoever does not absorb it there is unlikely to apply it in the rest of his life.

### In short

- Trading and working for wages during Ḥajj are lawful (Ibn ʿAbbās on the fairs of ʿUkāẓ and Dhū al-Majāz, Ibn ʿUmar and the camel-hirers), but earnings should be received as Allah's bounty, and the days of the rites are best kept free for worship.
- Ḥajj is ʿArafāt (ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Yaʿmar, ʿUrwah ibn Muḍarris): the standing from noon to sunset on the ninth, with no substitute if missed, named from Ibrāhīm's "ʿaraftu".
- The Prophet ﷺ left ʿArafāt only after sunset, unlike the Jāhiliyyah, and at Muzdalifah joined maghrib and ʿishāʾ, stayed the night and stood at al-Mashʿar al-Ḥarām in remembrance until just before sunrise (Jābir, Usāmah).
- Dhikr there must follow the form Allah taught, which shows that worship may not be altered by personal opinion, the mark of Jāhilī religion.
- This guidance, after former misguidance, is Allah's favour, and inwardly the servant desired Him only because He first desired the servant.

199.text:
The third verse on the rules of Ḥajj was revealed against a particular background. "Then go forth with the rest of the pilgrims. And seek Allah's forgiveness. Surely Allah is All-Forgiving, Most Merciful". Having commanded the remembrance at al-Mashʿar al-Ḥarām after the return from ʿArafāt, Allah now insists that everyone, without exception, must first go to ʿArafāt and come back from there with the multitude.

### Phrase by phrase

**"Then go forth with the rest of the pilgrims."**. The Quraysh, as custodians of the Kaʿbah, enjoyed a unique position of influence in Arabia. In the Jāhiliyyah, other pilgrims went to ʿArafāt. Quraysh and their religious allies, the Ḥums, instead remained at Muzdalifah. They argued that custodians of the Ḥaram should not leave its boundaries. Muzdalifah is inside those boundaries, whereas ʿArafāt is outside. They used this distinction to justify standing and departing from Muzdalifah. They claimed special standing as inhabitants of Allah's town and servants of His House. Al-Bukhārī records ʿĀʾishah's account of this distinction. The Ḥums stayed at Muzdalifah while the other Arabs stood at ʿArafāt. Islam brought the command for the Prophet ﷺ to stand with them at ʿArafāt and depart from there. She identifies that command as the meaning of this verse. Abū Bakr ibn Khaythamah relates a report through Sufyān ibn ʿUyaynah and ʿAmr ibn Dīnār. Muḥammad ibn Jubayr ibn Muṭʿim describes his father losing a camel on the day of ʿArafah. Searching for it, he saw the Messenger of Allah ﷺ standing among the people there. He wondered why a man of the Ḥums was standing at that place. The hadith is in the Two Ṣaḥīḥs, Muslim recording it through ʿAmr al-Nāqid from Ibn ʿUyaynah. Abū Sufyān explains aḥmas as someone particularly strict in religious observance. Quraysh were known as the Ḥums. Satan misled them with a whisper about their Sacred Precinct. Honouring another place, he suggested, would make others think less of their own. The truth was that they loved to display their pride and kept the common people at a distance. So Allah commanded them to go where everyone goes, into the plain of ʿArafāt, and return from there with everyone else. The word afīḍū, rendered here "go forth", literally means to flow or pour out, suggesting the mingling with the multitude that the Quraysh had shunned. That the place meant is ʿArafāt is the explanation of Ibn ʿAbbās, Mujāhid, ʿAṭāʾ, Qatādah, al-Suddī and others, and Ibn Jarīr chose it and reported consensus (ijmāʿ) on it. One early report takes the words to mean returning from where the people of Yemen returned, and says the verse was revealed about the Ḥamsiyyūn who refused to press on from the Sacred Mosque to ʿArafāt. Al-Bukhārī also records from Ibn ʿAbbās a second application, that the going forth refers to proceeding from Muzdalifah to Minā to stone the pillars, and Allah knows best. The pilgrims are thus told to leave ʿArafāt as Ibrāhīm used to, without omitting the standing there as the people of ignorance did.

**"And seek Allah's forgiveness."**. Those who wanted a distinct status by staying at Muzdalifah were told that their act was a sin for which they must seek forgiveness, so that Allah might pardon them and grant His mercy. The pilgrim also asks forgiveness for any defects in his performance of the Ḥajj and for his sins generally, for Allah frequently orders His remembrance when acts of worship are finished. Muslim records that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ used to ask forgiveness three times after finishing the prayer, and the Two Ṣaḥīḥs record that he encouraged tasbīḥ, taḥmīd and takbīr, saying subḥān Allāh, al-ḥamdu lillāh and Allāhu akbar thirty-three times each after it. Ibn Marduwayh collects the hadith that al-Bukhārī records from Shaddād ibn Aws, in which the Prophet ﷺ taught the master supplication for forgiveness: the servant acknowledges Allah as his Lord beside whom there is no god, as his Creator whose servant he is, declares that he holds to His covenant and promise as far as he is able, seeks refuge with Him from the evil he has done, admits His favour and his own fault, and asks forgiveness since none forgives sins but He. Whoever says this at night and dies that night enters Paradise, and whoever says it by day and dies that day enters Paradise. The Two Ṣaḥīḥs also record from ʿAbdullāh ibn ʿAmr that Abū Bakr asked the Messenger of Allah ﷺ to teach him a supplication for his prayer, and was told to say that he had wronged himself greatly, that none forgives sins but Allah, and to ask for a forgiveness from Allah's own presence and for mercy, since He is the Forgiving, the Merciful. There are many other hadiths on this subject.

**"Surely Allah is All-Forgiving, Most Merciful"**. He forgives those who repent and is merciful to those who die in a state of repentance, merciful to the believers.

### Human equality in practice

Claiming special standing by keeping apart from others is arrogance. It should always be avoided, especially during Ḥajj. Iḥrām and the shared place and purpose teach human equality. Wealth, learning and social importance give no exemption from that lesson. A display of assumed distinction, and in iḥrām at that, makes the offence worse. The verse also teaches a social principle. People of higher standing should not isolate themselves from those below them. Eating, staying and travelling as one family builds brotherhood, concern and love. It removes barriers between rich and poor and between employers and employees. In his sermon at the Farewell Ḥajj the Prophet ﷺ declared for all time that no Arab is superior to a non-Arab and no white person to a black, and that superiority depends on taqwā and obedience. The devotional reading rejects distinction based on patched clothing, dress or another outward quality. The pilgrim should see himself simply among humanity. A thought of independent achievement or of events happening through him or for him calls for repentance. He should seek forgiveness and renew faith, because the reading identifies such self-regard as hidden shirk in the heart.

### In short

- The Quraysh and the Ḥums stood at Muzdalifah out of pride, inside the Ḥaram, while everyone else stood at ʿArafāt (ʿĀʾishah in al-Bukhārī, Jubayr ibn Muṭʿim's surprise at seeing the Prophet ﷺ at ʿArafah).
- All pilgrims must stand at ʿArafāt and flow back from there with the multitude (Ibn ʿAbbās, Mujāhid, ʿAṭāʾ, Qatādah, al-Suddī, consensus per Ibn Jarīr), or, in a second reading, from Muzdalifah to Minā.
- Seeking forgiveness after worship is the Prophet's ﷺ practice: three times after prayer, the master supplication for forgiveness (Shaddād ibn Aws), Abū Bakr's prayer.
- The Ḥajj teaches human equality: no Arab over non-Arab, no white over black, only taqwā counts, and even the sense of having achieved something is a hidden shirk to be repented of.

200.text:
Verses 199 to 201 correct several customs of the Jāhiliyyah, and this verse deals with what the Arabs did once the rites were over. "When you have fulfilled your sacred rites, praise Allah as you used to praise your forefathers ˹before Islam˺, or even more passionately. There are some who say, "Our Lord! Grant us ˹Your bounties˺ in this world," but they will have no share in the Hereafter".

### Phrase by phrase

**"When you have fulfilled your sacred rites,"**. When you have completed the devotions of your pilgrimage, having stoned Jamrat al-ʿAqabah, performed the ṭawāf and the sacrifice and settled at Minā, remember Allah. Allah commands that He be remembered after the rituals are performed. The devotional reading distinguishes the due, ḥaqq, of servanthood, ʿubūdiyyah, from the due of love. The rites fulfil servanthood through the self, nafs. Remembrance fulfils love through the heart, qalb, for Allah's sake. That undertaking continues through each moment and throughout life.

**"praise Allah as you used to praise your forefathers ˹before Islam˺, or even more passionately."**. Saʿīd ibn Jubayr relates Ibn ʿAbbās's account of ancestral boasting during the Jāhiliyyah pilgrimage season. People recalled fathers who fed the poor, paid to settle disputes or supplied blood money, diyah. Recounting such deeds was their only dhikr. Allah revealed this verse to Muhammad ﷺ in response. Mujāhid said that in the season of pilgrimage the people of the Jāhiliyyah recalled their fathers, their exploits and their lineages and boasted of them to each other, and al-Ḥasan said that when the bedouins related anything they would swear by one's father that they had done this and that. After the rites at ʿArafāt and Muzdalifah, the ṭawāf and sacrifice, they settled at Minā. There they gathered for poetry and praise of ancestral achievements. These gatherings lacked remembrance of Allah. They wasted blessed days on matters unrelated to the purpose of pilgrimage. So they were told that as soon as they had completed the rites of iḥrām and come to stay at Minā they should devote their stay to the remembrance of Allah, in tahlīl and takbīr, and abandon the reminiscences and boastful claims about their forefathers. Better still was to remember Allah, not them, and with greater attachment and fervour. The "or" does not express doubt about which is greater but urges people to remember Him more than they ever remembered their fathers, as in "like a rock or even harder" (2:74), "feared those ˹hostile˺ people as Allah should be feared—or even more" (4:77), "at least one hundred thousand people" (37:147) and "two arms-lengths away or even less" (53:9). Grammatically, "more intensely" qualifies the remembrance that is the object of the command. One early explanation is that one should say "O Allah" as one used to say "father", or remember Allah for the blessings He showered on one as one used to recall the kindness of one's fathers. Another explanation develops the childhood analogy. A child remembers the father on whom everything depends. An adult's continuing dependence on Allah is greater still. Real honour therefore comes through dhikr of Allah rather than pride in ancestry. In the same vein the devotional reading offers a series of comparisons: just as others boast of their fathers, let your boasting and delight be in Us. If your fathers have a right over you for raising and educating you, Our right is more binding, since Our favours are more perfect. Your ancestors may have glorious deeds, but Our sublimity is beyond anything in the best of their states. If you never weary of remembering your father, remember Us continually without weariness, boredom or forgetfulness. If you are not pleased when someone speaks ill of your lineage, do not listen to those who err about Us, but defend Us. A father is remembered with respect and deference, so remember Us with awe, even as you also remember the kindness of nearness and the best of caring. He said "fathers" and not "mothers" because the father is remembered out of respect and the mother out of compassion, and Allah shows mercy and does not receive it. And "yet more intensely" because the Real (al-ḥaqq) is more deserving (aḥaqq): one may become estranged from a father, whereas no one who knows Allah can think of opposing what He has made obligatory in the smallest way.

### Wasting the days of Ḥajj

The Qur'an thus guides the Muslims to shun the customs of the age of ignorance, especially in the great days of Ḥajj, which are reserved for worship and dhikr, have merits of their own, and are a gift that may not come again if lost through carelessness. Ḥajj requires a demanding journey and absence from family and business. It costs both time and money. Even after such effort, unforeseen circumstances may prevent it. If Allah in His grace has removed every obstacle and allowed one to complete the obligation, the occasion calls for gratitude, which demands keeping busy in remembering Him and avoiding wasteful gatherings and conversations. Dhikr is all radiance and benefit for this world and the Hereafter, whereas the forefather tales of the Jāhiliyyah profited no one here or there. Muslims today hold no poetic recitals in praise of their family trees, but thousands from all over the world still spend these precious days in idle gatherings, entertainments, amusements, shopping and similar pursuits of personal satisfaction, and this verse is enough to warn them.

### The one-sided prayer

**"There are some who say, "Our Lord! Grant us ˹Your bounties˺ in this world,""**. Allah encourages supplication following remembrance, which helps its acceptance. He also criticises requests concerned only with this life. Ignoring the Hereafter is an example others are warned not to imitate. Saʿīd ibn Jubayr relates from Ibn ʿAbbās that some bedouins would come to the standing place and pray for a year of rain, fertility and good child-bearing, never mentioning anything of the Hereafter, and the verse was revealed about them. The old reports describe their requests as camels, cows, sheep, slaves and wealth. Some people of the Jāhiliyyah performed devotional acts yet prayed only for comfort, wealth and honour. Their requests showed no concern for the life to come. The verse corrects using the great occasion of Ḥajj for small present gains while forgetting the Hereafter. Such people are given their lot in this world. Their prayer notably omits the word "good". Material desire seeks constant satisfaction without considering what is truly beneficial. They do not ask whether the object is good or bad, properly or improperly obtained, or how others regard their conduct.

**"but they will have no share in the Hereafter"**. They have no portion in the Hereafter, no share of Paradise through their pilgrimage, because their conduct shows that they went through the obligation merely in a formal manner or to earn prestige in their society, and pleasing Allah and salvation in the Hereafter are objectives alien to them. The explanation identifies disbelievers whose belief and requests are confined to worldly life. They ask for health, wealth and children. Attachment to this life and neglect of the next leave them without the Hereafter's gifts prepared for Allah's faithful servants.

### In short

- After the rites, at Minā, the pilgrim must fill his time with remembrance of Allah, not the ancestral boasting of the Jāhiliyyah (Ibn ʿAbbās, Mujāhid, al-Ḥasan).
- "Or even more passionately" means more than you ever remembered your fathers, like the "or" of 2:74, 4:77, 37:147 and 53:9, and Allah's claim on remembrance far exceeds any father's.
- Wasting the days of Ḥajj on idle talk, amusement and shopping is the modern form of the same error.
- Those who pray at the standing place only for rain, herds and wealth, as some bedouins did, are given their lot here and have no share in the Hereafter.

201.text:
Against the one-sided prayer of the previous verse, Allah describes His virtuous and favoured servants, some of whom may be less prosperous in material terms. "Yet there are others who say, "Our Lord! Grant us the good of this world and the Hereafter, and protect us from the torment of the Fire."".

### Phrase by phrase

**"Yet there are others who say, "Our Lord! Grant us the good of this world"**. The earlier statement depicts the manner of the idolaters and this one the way of the believers, and the contrast is meant to encourage people to ask for good in both abodes, for which a reward is promised. The word ḥasanah includes everything good, inward and outward. Worldly good includes health for oneself and family, and a lawful livelihood with increase and barakah, blessing. It includes fulfilled needs, beneficial knowledge, virtuous deeds and sound morals. Honour and prestige are mentioned alongside strong faith, straight guidance and complete sincerity in worship. Other descriptions list well-being, a spacious dwelling, a pleasing spouse, sufficient provision, a good profession, a comfortable mount and good repute, all of which are only part of the good sought in this life, and the early reports mention knowledge, worship, preservation from sins, martyrdom and booty. The devotional reading gathers worldly good into knowledge and worship, witnessing mysteries and successful service. It also includes purification through obedience, the Sunnah and community, firmly established faith and the sweetness of obeying Allah.

**"and the Hereafter,"**. The Hereafter's good includes Paradise and its innumerable blessings without end. It extends to Allah's pleasure and the privilege of seeing Him. Its best part is Paradise, which includes safety from the greatest terror at the place of gathering, a light reckoning and the other favours of that life. In the devotional reading, the beautiful thing of the next world is Paradise and the vision, seeing with the eyes, the realisation of union, deliverance from burning and separation, the encounter, and the "serenity, fragrance, and a Garden of Bliss" (56:89). This reading joins good here with obedient deeds, and good there with the pain of recognition. A long road separates the stage of deeds from that pain. Deeds win houris and palaces, while the one who carries this pain is drowned in light in the ocean of seeing face to face.

**"and protect us from the torment of the Fire.""**. Safety from the Fire includes being guided in this world to what leads to that good end, such as avoiding the prohibitions, sins of every kind and doubtful matters. The early reports gloss it as being spared the torment of the grave and the torment of Hell, and the request is that Allah not make one enter the Fire. The prayer is thus a compendium of all prayers, encompassing the whole range of man's worldly and other-worldly objectives: peace in this world, peace in the Hereafter and, at the end, safety from the punishment of the Fire. Al-Qāsim ibn ʿAbd al-Raḥmān said that whoever is given a grateful heart, a remembering tongue and a patient body has been given good in this life, good in the Hereafter and safety from the Fire. This is why the Sunnah encourages reciting this duʿāʾ. Al-Bukhārī and Muslim record from Anas ibn Mālik that the Prophet ﷺ used to pray very frequently in these words, and it is masnūn to say it particularly during ṭawāf. Aḥmad records, and Muslim too, that Anas said the Messenger of Allah ﷺ visited a Muslim who had wasted away until he was as weak as a sick chick, and asked whether he had been praying for anything. The man said he used to ask Allah to give him in this life whatever punishment was stored up for him in the Hereafter. The Prophet ﷺ exclaimed that he could not bear that, and told him he should have asked for good in this world and good in the Hereafter and protection from the torment of the Fire. The man began reciting this prayer and was cured. There is a subtle point here: whoever wants this world alone is held back from the reward of the next, for Allah says that such a one "would have no share in the Hereafter" (2:102), and the Prophet ﷺ said that whoever loves this world harms his next world, and whoever loves his next world harms this world, so prefer what subsists to what perishes. But whoever wants both this world and the Hereafter is not held back from either, for Allah gives him what he wants. It is reported that Allah is ashamed that a servant should lift his hands to Him and be disappointed, and that He is ashamed to refuse a grey-haired person who observes propriety and holds to the Sunnah.

### Moderation in religious and worldly pursuits

Prayers, especially those offered on the pilgrimage, are the outward expression of an inward state. Prayer expresses what the heart values. Attachment to worldly riches and grandeur leaves little room for other requests. Seeking the next world instead places it at the centre of devotion. The believer's prayer is not a request for worldly riches, for material gain is only part of the test paper, and no one would ask to make his test harder. It is rather a request that Allah give him what is best for him in Allah's sight in this world and what is best in the Hereafter, and save him from eternal doom. The verse is a serious warning to Muslims who, even at the unique time of Ḥajj and in such sacred places, pray chiefly for material ends. Many rich people pray, or ask those they respect to pray, not for deliverance from the reckoning of the Hereafter but for increase in wealth and growth in business. Many who multiply litanies and voluntary acts of worship come to believe themselves very devout and special, while the same love of this world hides behind the facade. Others keep up relations with pious elders and revere departed saints mainly in the hope that their prayers and charms will keep worldly hardship away and bless their belongings. The whole affair rests with Allah, the All-Knowing and All-Aware. Everyone must examine deeds and intentions during Ḥajj or ziyārah. This includes litanies, voluntary prayer, supplication and ṣalāh. At the same time, the verse corrects those ignorant dervishes who think real worship lies in praying for the Hereafter alone and claim not to care about this world. The claim is false, for man depends on the fulfilment of his worldly needs not only to live but to perform his worship and obedience, without which the objectives of faith cannot be served. The blessed practice of the prophets was to pray for the good of both worlds, and whoever thinks that asking Allah for worldly needs is beneath piety is unaware of the station of prophethood and of man's role in this world. What is required is not to treat material needs as the purpose of life, but to show far more concern for the Hereafter alongside them and to pray for it. In the devotional reading there remains a further group, who have recognised the reality of approval, surrendered to Allah's decree and are content with His determination. They do not turn from praising Him to asking of Him, and seek neither this world nor the next, and of them the Lord of the Worlds says that whoever is kept from asking by remembering Him is given the most excellent of what He gives those who ask.

### In short

- The believers' prayer asks for ḥasanah in both worlds: health, lawful provision, knowledge, good character and sincerity here, and Paradise, Allah's pleasure and His vision there, plus safety from the Fire.
- It is a compendium of all supplication, the Prophet's ﷺ most frequent prayer (Anas, al-Bukhārī and Muslim), masnūn in ṭawāf, and he taught it to a man wasting away who had asked for his punishment in this life.
- Prayer reveals the heart: asking only for wealth, even behind a show of piety, betrays love of this world, while refusing to ask for worldly needs at all is false asceticism, for the prophets prayed for both.
- Whoever wants this world alone forfeits the next (2:102), whoever wants both is given both, and those content with Allah's decree receive better than what the askers receive.

202.text:
Allah promises a return to those who ask for good in both lives: "It is they who will receive a ˹heavenly˺ reward for the good they have done. Surely Allah is swift in reckoning." Their prayer belongs with their righteous conduct. Neither the good they sought nor the work they performed is lost from His knowledge.

### Phrase by phrase

**"It is they who will receive a ˹heavenly˺ reward for the good they have done."** They receive a share from their pilgrimage, deeds and supplication. The explanation describes reward in both worlds and a great portion in Paradise. Allah praises the people whose request embraces this life and the next.

**"Surely Allah is swift in reckoning"** His knowledge and power do not depend on calculations or instruments. He can assess everyone's lifelong deeds and dispense their return without difficulty. The coming account is therefore not delayed by the size of creation.

### Does working for passage to pilgrimage prevent reward?

Al-Hakim records from Sa'id ibn Jubayr that a man asked Ibn 'Abbas about an agreement with his employers. Part of his wages was that they would take him to perform hajj. He wanted to know whether this was acceptable.

Ibn 'Abbas included him among those receiving a share for what they had earned. The circumstance of his passage did not exclude him from the promise. Al-Hakim calls the report authentic according to the criteria of the Two Shaykhs, while noting they did not record it.

### What meanings are given to swift reckoning?

One hadith describes the account of all creation taking half a worldly day. The statement reinforces the ease of the task for Allah, not dependence upon human machinery.

Other explanations understand the words through His swift protection or the severity of punishment for those displaying devotion to be admired. The familiar final reckoning occurs at judgment, while the elect are pictured as accounting for their conduct at every breath.

The distinct explanations all keep the person's action under divine attention. Good receives its return, and evil remains answerable.

### What further group is pictured inwardly?

The passage names those asking only for this world and those asking for both worlds. The devotional reading adds an unmentioned group: people content with Allah's decree who surrender every request.

It also connects the portion with what was earned. Good brings a good portion, while something else brings another outcome. Contentment in the further allusion does not erase the praise given to the prayer actually described.

### In short

- Those seeking good in both worlds receive their share from deeds and prayer.
- Ibn 'Abbas includes the worker whose wages provided passage to hajj.
- Allah needs no instruments to reckon with creation.
- The inward reading joins constant self-accounting with contentment in His decree.

203.text:
The last of the eight verses on the rules of Ḥajj asks the pilgrims to fill the final days with remembrance of Allah, so that the Ḥajj ends perfectly and the life after it becomes correct and fruitful. "And remember Allah during ˹these˺ appointed days. Whoever departs swiftly on the second day is not sinful, neither are those who stay behind ˹till the third—seeking additional reward˺, so long as they are mindful ˹of their Lord˺." It closes: "And be mindful of Allah, and know that to Him you will ˹all˺ be gathered".

### Phrase by phrase

**"And remember Allah during ˹these˺ appointed days."** Ibn ʿAbbās identifies the appointed days with tashrīq: the eleventh, twelfth and thirteenth of Dhū al-Ḥijjah. He distinguishes them from the "known days", the month's first ten.

ʿIkrimah explains remembrance here through takbīr after obligatory prayers. The jurists regard this takbīr as wājib, necessary. Other descriptions include tahlīl and tasbīḥ alongside takbīr. One account extends the period to five days: ʿArafah, the Day of Sacrifice and the three following days.

Imam Aḥmad records ʿUqbah ibn ʿAmr's report that these days are Islam's festival, for eating and drinking. Aḥmad also records Nubayshah al-Hudhalī's account, transmitted by Muslim too. It describes tashrīq as days for food, drink and remembrance of Allah.

Ibn Jarīr records a report from Abū Hurayrah about days of eating and dhikr. The Prophet ﷺ sent ʿAbdullāh ibn Ḥudhāfah to announce this at Minā. His proclamation also forbade fasting on those days.

Jubayr ibn Muṭʿim's hadith includes all tashrīq days within the days of sacrifice. The report of ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Yaʿmar al-Diylī gives three days for Minā.

Miqsam conveys another explanation from Ibn ʿAbbās: four appointed days, beginning with the Day of Sacrifice. Ibn al-Zubayr, Ibn ʿUmar and Abū Mūsā also give this view. It comes from Mujāhid and ʿAṭāʾ, and from Saʿīd ibn Jubayr and ʿIkrimah. Ibrāhīm al-Nakhaʿī and Abū Mālik are named alongside al-Ḥasan and Yaḥyā ibn Abī Kathīr. Further holders include al-Zuhrī, al-Suddī, Qatādah and al-Rabīʿ ibn Anas. The view is also given by Muqātil ibn Ḥayyān and aḍ-Ḍaḥḥāk, by Mālik ibn Anas and ʿAṭāʾ al-Khurāsānī, and by others. The following permission to hasten away in two days supports this reading. Those words concern the three days after sacrifice.

The verse directs dhikr at slaughter, after prayers and in supplication generally. It also includes takbīr with each day's pebbles at the Jamarāt. Abū Dāwūd and others record a hadith connecting these rites with remembrance. Ṭawāf, saʿy between al-Ṣafā and al-Marwah, and casting pebbles were prescribed so that Allah would be remembered.

**"Whoever departs swiftly on the second day is not sinful, neither are those who stay behind ˹till the third—seeking additional reward˺,"**. Next comes a clarification of the length of the stay at Minā and the deadline for stoning the three pillars, an issue the people of the Jāhiliyyah debated. Some held it necessary to stay until the thirteenth and stone on that day, calling anyone who returned on the twelfth a sinner, while others held return on the twelfth necessary and staying through the thirteenth a sin. Both were corrected: whoever hurries away on the second of the days of tashrīq, after casting his stones, commits no sin, and whoever delays, staying for the third night and casting his stones, commits no sin either. The pilgrim has the choice, and sin is precluded in both cases, though it is better and preferable to stay through the thirteenth, which was the practice of the Prophet ﷺ. The jurists say that one who leaves Minā before sunset on the twelfth need not perform the stoning of the third day, but if the sun sets while he is still in Minā he may no longer leave until he has stoned for the third day, for which there is a special concession allowing it between the morning and noon. One early reading takes "no sin" on the one who delays to mean that he leaves with his sins forgiven, and another makes the hastening the right of one who avoids hunting until the third day.

**"so long as they are mindful ˹of their Lord˺."**. Permission to leave on either day eases the pilgrimage for those fearing and obeying Allah. Such people truly deserve the Ḥajj. The Qur'an elsewhere limits acceptance to the God-fearing. Whoever was steeped in sins long before the Ḥajj, remained negligent during it and did not abstain from sin afterwards gains no benefit from it, although the formal obligation is validly discharged and he is cleared of the crime of not having performed it. The one who fears Allah during his pilgrimage and performs it as instructed is the true pilgrim.

**"And be mindful of Allah, and know that to Him you will ˹all˺ be gathered"**. This closing line is the essence of all the Ḥajj injunctions. The first procession was from ʿArafāt. The second disperses the gathered pilgrims towards their homes. Allah links these assemblies with the final gathering before Him: "to Him you will ˹all˺ be gathered" (23:79). There, hidden and open deeds are accounted for and recompensed. During the special days, the pilgrim must guard against shortcomings in prescribed acts. Afterwards, fear of Allah should prevent pride in the achievement and a return to sin. When deeds are weighed, sins can consume the good deeds. A hadith says that one who returns from a completed Ḥajj is as cleansed of sin as on the day he was born, which is why pilgrims are told to maintain taqwā. Purification should be followed by careful avoidance of temptation. That safeguards good in both worlds. Returning to a life of sin forfeits the benefit of that earlier forgiveness. The scholars have said that one who returns from Ḥajj with his heart free of the love of this world and drawn to concern for the Hereafter has had his Ḥajj accepted, his sins forgiven and his prayers answered. Throughout the Ḥajj people pledge obedience to Allah before His House, and such pledges should not be thoughtlessly broken afterwards. A pious elder recalled temptation after returning from Ḥajj. A voice from the unseen twice asked whether he had not performed the pilgrimage. That reminder became a barrier between him and the sin. By contrast, a pious man from Turkey, a disciple of Mawlānā Jāmī, used to see a halo of light over his head, went on Ḥajj and found on his return that the state was gone. His master told him that before the Ḥajj he had the gift of humility and wept before Allah thinking himself a sinner, and after it he had grown proud and put on the airs of someone righteous, so that the very Ḥajj had become the cause of his pride and the loss of his radiance. The final emphasis on taqwā also guards against self-righteousness. Satan can introduce that thought after a great act of worship and spoil its deeds. Fear and obedience are therefore necessary before, during and especially after Ḥajj. Otherwise the worship risks being wasted. "You shall be gathered before Him" is the greatest lesson of the pilgrimage, given on the plain of ʿArafāt where millions gather every year, a gathering that symbolises the final assembly of all mankind on the Day of Judgment. Practical results come from actions, not words.

### The two sanctuaries

In the devotional reading, there are three sorts of remembrance: the remembrance of habit, which has no worth, for it is the heedlessness of the inmost core, the remembrance of calculation, which has no adornment, for it seeks a wage, and the remembrance of companionship. The fearful remember from dread of being cut off and cling to supplication, the hopeful from wishing to find what they seek and cling to praise, and the lovers from the tenderness of burning, having heard the call beforehand with the ear of love. There are two sanctuaries, the outward one surrounding the Kaʿbah and the inward one surrounding the heart of the believer. In the midst of the outward sanctuary stands the Kaʿbah, the qiblah of the faithful, and in the midst of the inward one a Kaʿbah that is the target of the All-Merciful's gaze, the goal of the pilgrims in the first case and the locus of lights in the second, "so they are enlightened by their Lord" (39:22). The outward sanctuary is kept free from the hands of evil-doers and unbelievers, the inward from seeing and thinking of others. An article found in the outward sanctuary is left where it lies until its owner appears, but what is found in the inward sanctuary cannot be pursued, for it is nothing but Allah's secret.

### In short

- The appointed days are the days of tashrīq, the eleventh to thirteenth of Dhū al-Ḥijjah (Ibn ʿAbbās), days of eating, drinking and dhikr that may not be fasted (ʿUqbah ibn ʿAmr, Nubayshah al-Hudhalī, Abū Hurayrah), with takbīr after the prayers, at the slaughter and at the Jamarāt.
- Leaving Minā on the twelfth after stoning or staying for the thirteenth are both sinless, ending the Jāhilī quarrel, though staying is better, and one still in Minā at sunset on the twelfth must stone on the thirteenth.
- The concession is for the God-fearing, whose Ḥajj alone is truly accepted.
- Taqwā after the Ḥajj matters most, guarding the cleansed pilgrim against relapse and against pride in his achievement (the voice from the unseen, Jāmī's disciple), and the gathering at ʿArafāt foreshadows the gathering before Allah (23:79).
- Inwardly, remembrance may be of habit, of calculation or of companionship, and the believer's heart is a second sanctuary with its own Kaʿbah, the object of Allah's gaze (39:22).

204.text:
The previous verses distinguished two kinds of people who pray, those who want everything here and those who ask for the good of both worlds. The same two kinds now appear as the hypocrite and the sincere believer. "There are some ˹hypocrites˺ who impress you with their views regarding worldly affairs and openly call upon Allah to witness what is in their hearts, yet they are your worst adversaries".

### Phrase by phrase

**"There are some ˹hypocrites˺ who impress you with their views regarding worldly affairs"**. Al-Suddī said that these verses were revealed about al-Akhnas ibn Sharīq al-Thaqafī, an ally of Banū Zuhrah, who came to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ in al-Madīnah and announced his Islam while his heart concealed otherwise. He was eloquent and good-looking, and the Prophet ﷺ liked his speech. He claimed to have embraced Islam sincerely, invoking Allah as witness. He professed love for the Prophet ﷺ and support both privately and publicly. Frequent visits and oaths reinforced that profession. Away from the Prophet ﷺ, however, he promptly turned to mischief against the Muslims. Ibn ʿAbbās said the verses were revealed about some hypocrites who criticised Khubayb and his companions killed at al-Rajīʿ, after which Allah condemned the hypocrites and praised Khubayb and his companions. It was also said that they describe the hypocrites and the believers in general, the view of Qatādah, Mujāhid, al-Rabīʿ ibn Anas and several others, and this is correct. Such a man's speech, words and outward appearance please you in this life, though they would not please you in the Hereafter, since they contradict what he really believes. Ibn Jarīr conveys al-Quraẓī's report of Nawf al-Bikālī, a reader of the earlier Books. Nawf found a description there of some members of this ummah who exploit religion for profit. Their words surpass honey in sweetness, but their hearts surpass aloes in bitterness. They look like sheep while concealing wolves' viciousness. The reported divine address asks how they dare challenge Him while being deceived by Him. It includes an oath by Himself to bring a fitnah upon them. That trial will bewilder even the wise. Nawf said that he then found these people described in the Qur'an in this very verse, and al-Quraẓī's statement is ḥasan ṣaḥīḥ.

**"and openly call upon Allah to witness what is in their hearts,"**. He swears by Allah that he loves and follows you. Such people pretend to be Muslims while defying Allah through the disbelief and hypocrisy hidden in their hearts, as He says of them, "They try to hide ˹their deception˺ from people, but they can never hide it from Allah" (4:108), an explanation Ibn Isḥāq relates from Ibn ʿAbbās. It was also said that when such people announce their Islam they swear that what is in their hearts matches what their tongues say, which is also correct, the choice of ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Zayd ibn Aslam and of Ibn Jarīr, who relates it from Ibn ʿAbbās and Mujāhid, and Allah knows best. The hypocrite uses professions of faith to protect himself and his finances. He falsely invokes Allah as witness to inward faith and goodness. His actual disposition is hostility and hatred towards the Muslims.

**"yet they are your worst adversaries"**. The word aladd literally means wicked, and here most quarrelsome, from the same root as the "contentious" people of "warn those who are contentious" (19:97). The hypocrite lies, twists the truth when he argues and cares nothing for it, deviating, deceiving and disputing stubbornly on account of his enmity towards the Prophet ﷺ and his followers, arguing for falsehood as a staunch opponent. The Ṣaḥīḥ records that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said the signs of a hypocrite are three: when he speaks he lies, when he promises he breaks it, and when he disputes he is most quarrelsome. Al-Bukhārī records from ʿĀʾishah that the Prophet ﷺ said the most hateful of people to Allah is the one who is aladd and khaṣim, the bitterly quarrelsome.

### Words and deeds

Those who have made opportunism their religion can always impress people with words, because it serves their interest to do so. Right and wrong do not matter to them and no fixed standard guides them, only what is calculated to make a good impression on the listener. They have no difficulty painting a glowing picture outside while their hearts lack the warmth of sincerity, for they owe loyalty to nothing but their own interests. His speech suggests a great reformer, but his actions spread corruption. The contradiction lies within him. He professes love of truth while pursuing personal advantage at others' expense. Promises of peace and reconciliation give way to actions breeding conflict. He manipulates emotions and seeks popularity without regard for the actual situation. Such people have sold themselves for this world. Even when the truth is made plain they do not follow it, seeing no gain in it, and they uphold it only when there is enough profit to be had. Behind an obsequious exterior they hide a proud ego, which is why they can never acknowledge a truth that comes from a preacher they consider beneath them. The devotional reading contrasts skill in speech with hearts deprived of divine attention. Their hearts are pictured as bound by deprivation and covered in ignorance. Nothing inward supports their outward appearance. Their words lack weight, and their fidelity cannot be trusted. The allusion is to the people of externals who have not been helped by the lights of insight and have no faith in this kind of discourse, from whom secrets must be kept since they receive them only with disapproval. Peaceable ordinary people who respect and fully believe in this path are nearer to it. Those claiming to be elect while lacking faith in it are farther away.

### In short

- The verse describes the hypocrite, revealed about al-Akhnas ibn Sharīq (al-Suddī), about the hypocrites who mocked Khubayb's companions (Ibn ʿAbbās), or hypocrites in general (Qatādah, Mujāhid, al-Rabīʿ).
- Sweet speech and oaths of sincerity mask disbelief, as 4:108 says, and the earlier Books described such men as sheep outwardly and wolves within (Nawf al-Bikālī).
- Aladd means bitterly quarrelsome (compare 19:97), and the most hateful person to Allah is the stubborn disputant (ʿĀʾishah), quarrelsomeness being one of the three signs of a hypocrite.
- Opportunists impress with words but corrupt with deeds, follow truth only when it pays, and hide a proud ego behind flattery.

205.text:
Fine words are tested by what follows them: "And when they leave ˹you˺, they strive throughout the land to spread mischief in it and destroy crops and cattle. Allah does not like mischief." The person's conduct away from the Prophet ﷺ exposes the corruption hidden beneath the speech.

### Phrase by phrase

**"And when they leave ˹you˺, they strive throughout the land to spread mischief in it"** The explanation understands the departure as turning away, and another gloss connects it with anger. The person then acts through transgression. False words, corrupt belief and evil deeds belong to the same portrait.

**"and destroy crops and cattle."** The harm reaches cultivated land, animals and what people depend upon for livelihood. Burning grain and fields or killing livestock damages more than the owner's immediate property.

**"Allah does not like mischief"** He rejects such corruption and the conduct of those practising it. Religious and worldly affairs alike can be ruined by the actions described.

### What is reported about al-Akhnas?

Al-Suddi says al-Akhnas left the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and passed a Muslim field and some donkeys. He burned the field and hamstrung the animals. The verse is connected with those acts.

Another account says he saw the crops and livestock, then returned at night to burn and slaughter. The alternatives differ in timing, while both illustrate destruction concealed behind plausible speech.

Mujahid gives another aspect: corruption brings the withholding of rain, so crops and offspring perish. The explanation thus includes harm directly committed and the wider consequence of the corrupt conduct.

### Does striving mean running?

Sa'a means striving or intending. The same word describes Pharaoh turning away in (79:22). In (62:9), believers are called towards Friday remembrance with related language.

The latter command means setting out for prayer, not running to the mosque. The sunnah instead teaches walking calmly and with dignity. The same verb therefore takes its moral character from the purpose towards which the person strives.

### What inward corruption is pictured?

The devotional reading describes ties to religion weakening while attachment to worldly gain grows stronger. Desire becomes woven around forbidden acquisitions. Private planning then follows worldly advantage rather than sound judgment.

Such people enlist helpers whose inner sight has been removed. The account joins this loss of discernment with outward damage: both religious affairs and the proper order of worldly life suffer.

The warning therefore looks beyond a single destructive incident. It asks what the person's ambitions and private choices are doing to the bonds of obedience.

### In short

- The person's actions expose what fine speech concealed.
- Reports connect al-Akhnas with burning crops and harming livestock.
- Striving takes its meaning from its aim, and the Friday command does not require running.
- The inward reading contrasts weakened devotion with tightening attachment to worldly gain.

206.text:
Advice reveals the pride behind the corruption: "When it is said to them, "Fear Allah," pride carries them off to sin." Rather than turn back, the hypocrite takes offence and continues the wrong. The verse names Hell as the outcome of that refusal.

### Phrase by phrase

**"When it is said to them, "Fear Allah," pride carries them off to sin."** The advice asks for restraint and adherence to truth. Pride answers with anger. The person makes the very correction an occasion for further sin instead of repentance.

**"Hell will be their proper place. What an evil place to rest"** The Fire suffices as punishment. Its description as a resting place or cradle makes the destination terrible rather than comforting. Corruption joined to refusal of correction receives this warning.

### Why does advice provoke more wrongdoing?

Habitual evil makes the hypocrite resent being corrected. Rage and self-importance carry him further into what he was asked to avoid. He protects his pride instead of examining his conduct.

The explanation compares (22:72), where those rejecting revelation show rage when it is recited. They appear ready to attack the people reciting it. Here too, the response to a truthful warning exposes the refusal to receive it.

### How does the inward reading describe the adviser?

The proud person asks how anyone dares address someone like him. He then reverses the advice, accusing the adviser of needing correction instead. Hostility can remain in the heart for years.

Divine mercy would have helped him recognise his faults and receive the warning humbly. That recognition is itself a favour. Without it, pride makes fair criticism seem an insult.

### What punishment is already felt inwardly?

The devotional reading sees estrangement, darkness in the lower self and narrowed choice as an earlier chastisement. Desire repeatedly drives the person before the greater punishment arrives.

It connects this with (32:21), which describes a lesser torment before the major one. The inward application does not replace the outward warning of Hell. It describes a present foretaste alongside the final consequence.

One early report alleges that al-Akhnas ibn Shurayq burned another person's crops and killed a donkey. It connects the three verses with that conduct. The account's reported character is retained rather than raised to certainty.

### In short

- Pride turns a call to fear Allah into an occasion for more sin.
- The hypocrite attacks the advice instead of examining the fault.
- Recognising one's errors and accepting correction is a divine favour.
- Inward estrangement is pictured as a foretaste of the greater punishment.

207.text:
