After exposing hypocrisy, the passage honours sincere sacrifice: "And there are those who would dedicate their lives to Allah's pleasure." Such people prefer obedience to personal gain. The closing words connect their devotion with Allah's graciousness towards His servants.

### Phrase by phrase

**"And there are those who would dedicate their lives to Allah's pleasure."** The image is of someone selling himself, spending his life in obedience for Allah's approval. Ṣuhayb ibn Sinān al-Rūmī is central to accounts of revelation, but the meaning also embraces other forms of costly faithfulness.

**"And Allah is Ever Gracious to ˹His˺ servants"** Allah gently guides His servants towards what pleases Him. His mercy is vast. Their ability to surrender themselves is a gift of that gentleness, not a claim that obliges Him to favour them.

### What did Ṣuhayb surrender?

The connection with Ṣuhayb is given by Ibn ʿAbbās and Anas, together with Saʿīd ibn al-Musayyab and Abū ʿUthmān al-Nahdī. ʿIkrimah and others also give it. Al-Ḥākim, Ibn Jarīr and Ibn Abī Ḥātim report it with sound chains.

Ṣuhayb embraced Islam in Makkah and sought to emigrate. Quraysh would not let him take his wealth away. He chose to leave the wealth rather than give up migration.

Saʿīd ibn al-Musayyab relates that pursuers caught him after he left Makkah. Ṣuhayb dismounted and prepared his bow and arrows. He reminded them of his skill as an archer and swore to resist with arrows, then his sword, while able. Alternatively, he would disclose where his money was if they promised to let him go.

They accepted that bargain, and he gave them the information. On reaching al-Madīnah safely, he told the Prophet ﷺ what had happened. The Prophet ﷺ twice congratulated Abū Yaḥyā, Ṣuhayb's kunyah, on the profitable exchange. The verse confirmed that praise.

Other accounts describe capture and torture. In them, Ṣuhayb argued that he was an old man who would not harm the Makkans by staying or leaving. He offered his money in return for being left with his religion. They accepted and even supplied a mount and provisions.

ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb, Abū Bakr and other Companions met him at al-Ḥarrah, the black stony ground outside al-Madīnah. They congratulated him on his trade. He wished that theirs too would prosper and asked what they meant. They answered by reciting the verse revealed about him.

### Who else falls within the meaning?

Similar events involving other Companions are also cited. One early account joins Ṣuhayb with his companions and connects the closing words with Yāsir and Sumayyah. They were ʿAmmār ibn Yāsir's parents and were among those killed by the Makkan idolaters.

The meaning extends to fighters who give themselves for Allah. The exchange of believers' lives and wealth for Paradise is also described in (9:111). When Hishām ibn ʿĀmir advanced into the enemy's ranks, some criticised him. ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb and Abū Hurayrah answered them with this verse.

Al-Ḥasan gives another application. A Muslim invites a disbeliever to affirm Allah's oneness, offering safety for his blood and property. When the invitation is refused, the Muslim pledges his own life for Allah and fights until killed.

Another explanation concerns commanding good and forbidding evil. Abū al-Khalīl relates that ʿUmar heard the verse recited and uttered the words of return to Allah. He identified a man killed while carrying out that duty.

### What is the inward meaning of the exchange?

Sincerity places Allah's command ahead of the demands of the self. It may require relinquishing wealth, popularity or inherited religious custom to follow the truth. Hostility does not change that standard.

The devotional reading describes servants favoured by mercy and raised through divine predetermination. They prefer the Real's pleasure to themselves and surrender to their mawlā, their Protector. His gentleness brings them to those states. The states do not first earn that gentleness as a debt.

### In short

- Ṣuhayb's surrender of wealth for emigration illustrates the profitable exchange of personal advantage for Allah's pleasure.
- The accounts also include martyrs, fighters and those killed while commanding good.
- Sincerity obeys Allah despite the cost in possessions, status or life.
- Divine graciousness enables devotion rather than becoming something devotion can demand.

208.text:
Sincere intention does not make every religious addition right. The verse calls for complete acceptance of Islam: "O believers! Enter into Islam wholeheartedly and do not follow Satan's footsteps." It warns against both omitting its commands and adding practices as religion beyond the Sharīʿah and Sunnah.

### Phrase by phrase

**"O believers! Enter into Islam wholeheartedly"** Al-silm, also read al-salm, can mean peace or Islam. Here the Companions and their successors understood Islam. Kāffah expresses completeness: the whole person is to submit, and all of Islam is to be accepted.

**"and do not follow Satan's footsteps."** The warning rejects Satan's temptations, divisive suggestions and apparently pious additions that contradict guidance. He may also whisper that sound conduct and abandoning harmful inclinations are beyond one's ability.

**"Surely he is your sworn enemy"** Satan's hostility is evident. His suggestions must not be followed simply because they appear to offer greater devotion.

### Why did keeping earlier practices become a problem?

ʿAṭāʾ relates from Ibn ʿAbbās an occasion involving ʿAbdullāh ibn Salām and his companions, formerly learned Jews. They wished to continue honouring the Sabbath and avoiding camel meat and milk after becoming Muslims.

Their reasoning was that Moses' law required the Sabbath, while Islam did not command its dishonouring. They could believe camel meat lawful without eating it, since eating it was not obligatory. Combining the practices seemed to them a stronger obedience to divine law without opposing Muhammad's ﷺ Sharīʿah.

When reproached, they defended the possibility of observing both. They also asked the Prophet ﷺ for permission to follow the Torah, recognising it as Allah's Book. The verse corrected their proposed combination.

The distinction concerns counting an unnecessary practice as part of the faith. Islam's completeness does not depend on adding requirements from the earlier law. Sincerity that exceeds the limits of Sharīʿah and Sunnah becomes bidʿah. Such a satanic lapse can merit punishment more severe than ordinary wrongdoing.

Ibn Abī Ḥātim relates Ibn ʿAbbās's explanation concerning believers who still kept parts of the Torah and earlier revelation. They were told to accept Muhammad's ﷺ religion completely, omit none of it and cease that adherence to the Torah.

### What does completeness include?

Al-ʿAwfī conveys Ibn ʿAbbās's explanation of al-silm. The same sense is given by Mujāhid and Ṭāwūs, by aḍ-Ḍaḥḥāk and ʿIkrimah, and by Qatādah, al-Suddī and Ibn Zayd.

Kāffah functions as a ḥāl, a qualification of state. It may qualify the people entering Islam. On that reading, hands, feet, eyes and ears must agree with the heart, thought and feeling in obedience. Outward observance without inward acceptance is incomplete. So is inward approval that does not govern action.

Alternatively, it qualifies Islam itself. Then the command requires acceptance of every injunction rather than selection among them. The two readings converge on sincere and comprehensive obedience.

Abū al-ʿĀliyah and al-Rabīʿ ibn Anas explain the completeness alongside Ibn ʿAbbās and Mujāhid. Others include Muqātil ibn Ḥayyān, ʿIkrimah, al-Suddī, Qatādah and aḍ-Ḍaḥḥāk. Mujāhid includes the performance of good and pious deeds, especially addressing converts from the People of the Scripture.

Obedience includes all commands within one's ability and restraint from prohibitions. Its scope includes belief and worship, social dealings and personal rights, business and trade, industry, government and politics. The Qur'an and Sunnah provide a unified way of life, not disconnected permissions to choose.

### Why is ritual alone not enough?

The warning especially challenges those who confine religion to the mosque and prescribed worship. Neglecting social and commercial duties does not remove them from Islam. The discussion censures religious people who neither learn those duties systematically nor intend to act on them.

The occasion also calls Muslims to keep Islam's teaching as their religious standard rather than depend on other religions and nations. Earlier recipients of Scripture accepted some parts and denied others. Believers must not reproduce that partial acceptance.

### What are Satan's inward footsteps?

The commands to avoid Satan also connect with his incitement to evil and unsupported claims against Allah in (2:169). His invitation to the Blaze appears in (35:6). A suggestion may resemble faith while leading away from it.

The devotional reading asks the believer to make peace with others but not with the opposing lower self. Making peace with that self weakens spiritual effort and lets the seeker's interest fade.

Satan whispers that obedience and the abandonment of unwise inclinations cannot be maintained. The contrasting image is Moses' mother in (28:7). She is told to place him in the river when afraid, and Allah returns him safely. Trust in His direction is set against the whisper of inability.

### In short

- The occasion concerns converts wishing to retain Sabbath observance and avoidance of camel meat as religion.
- Completeness requires inward and outward obedience, and acceptance of Islam's whole teaching.
- Social rights and commercial duties belong with worship, not outside religion.
- Satan can disguise deviation as added piety or discourage obedience through whispers of inability.

209.text:
Clear proofs leave no excuse for deliberately turning away. The verse warns: "If you falter after receiving the clear proofs, then know that Allah is indeed Almighty, All-Wise". Accepting Islam means following its commands, not preserving only the parts that suit one's interests.

### Phrase by phrase

**"If you falter after receiving the clear proofs,"** Slipping here means turning from the precepts of Islam after their truth has been established. The proofs include the Prophet ﷺ, the Qur'an and Islam itself. For the former Jews addressed in an account of revelation, they also include the explanations in their own Scripture.

**"then know that Allah is indeed Almighty, All-Wise"** Allah cannot be defeated, nor can anyone escape His punishment. His decisions, actions and laws are governed by wisdom. A delay in punishment therefore does not mean that wrongdoing has been overlooked.

### What does wholehearted acceptance require?

One early report connects the verse with ʿAbdullāh ibn Salām and his companions. They retained attachment to the Sabbath and an aversion to camel meat and other things. The warning concerns resistance after guidance has become clear.

The contrast is between two ways of accepting Islam. One person follows its commands and prohibitions without making personal advantage the condition of obedience. Another accepts it only where it fits ordinary life and protects existing interests. Habits, cherished beliefs, desired profits, honour and leadership then become barriers to change.

Initial enthusiasm may fade when obedience requires a change of thinking or the surrender of a preference. The person keeps the Muslim name but prevents Islam from directing life. The warning calls for more than such conditional acceptance.

### Why is a later slip more serious?

Turning away after proof is a graver matter than making an ordinary mistake. The inward reading contrasts a single lapse after disclosure with many lapses before it. Once treachery has become known, trust cannot simply be assumed. It also pictures the punishment for the worst sins as uprooting those who persist in them.

This is not a reason to treat divine patience as permission. Allah's might means that nothing can block His judgment against rejection of His Messenger ﷺ. His wisdom governs when that judgment arrives.

Abū al-ʿĀliyah, Qatādah and al-Rabīʿ ibn Anas connect His might with retribution and His wisdom with decree. That wisdom also governs the sacred laws He establishes and the replacement of earlier nations' laws. Believers should fear Him and honour His greatness.

### In short

- Clear proofs make deliberate withdrawal from guidance especially serious.
- Wholehearted Islam allows its commands to change one's habits and interests.
- Allah's power cannot be resisted, and His wisdom determines the timing of judgment.

210.text:
The verse challenges those who postpone acceptance of clear guidance: "Are they waiting for Allah ˹Himself˺ to come to them in the shade of clouds, along with the angels?" At the final judgment, a sudden profession of belief cannot reopen a life whose test has ended.

### Phrase by phrase

**"Are they waiting for Allah ˹Himself˺ to come to them in the shade of clouds, along with the angels?"** The question concerns those who do not enter Islam completely, those following Satan and, in another explanation, the people of Makkah. The scene belongs to the Day of Resurrection, when Allah judges the earliest and latest generations and angels surround them.

**"˹If He did˺, then the matter would be settled ˹at once˺."** Judgment would have been completed. Another explanation emphasises the completion of their destruction. The people of Paradise and Hell would already have their appointed destinations.

**"And to Allah ˹all˺ matters will be returned ˹for judgment˺"** Every outcome returns to Him in the Hereafter. Reward and punishment rest with Him alone. No competing power remains to alter His judgment.

### How is the coming described?

Ẓulal is the plural of ẓullah, meaning a shade or canopy. Abū Jaʿfar al-Rāzī conveys Abū al-ʿĀliyah's explanation: angels descend in the clouds' shadows, and Allah comes as He wills. A reading places both Allah and the angels within that description. The descent of angels with the clouds is also described in (25:25).

Another explanation takes the coming as the arrival of Allah's command or chastisement. The account also describes it as befitting His majesty and without modality, bilā kayf.

The discussion places this coming among the mutashābihāt, whose reality exceeds human understanding. The majority of the Companions, their successors and the revered elders of the ummah affirmed the statement without attempting to determine how it occurs. Human reason cannot establish the nature of Allah's Being and attributes.

### What does the inward reading emphasise?

People may imagine the Hour far away. Its terrible events disclose the gravity of Allah's affair and the working of His power. In this reading, the described acts express those events rather than a change in His locality.

Hearts illumined by insight into divine oneness do not need to seek taʾwīl here. They recognise the Real as beyond fading, movement, a particular place or time, and appearing before human beings. When the matter is determined, the veil of the unseen is removed and divine preordination becomes clear.

### Why is waiting until then futile?

Arguments for belief have already been given. For someone seeking signs, the universe itself lies before him. Refusing clear arguments does not become reasonable merely by demanding further miracles.

The purpose of this world's test is faith without seeing Allah, on the strength of His proofs. Seeing the final judgment and only then believing does not fulfil that test. The passage beginning in (89:21) describes the crushed earth, the angels in ranks and Hell brought near. Its warning asks what use remembrance will have once that moment arrives. The same loss of opportunity for belated belief appears in (6:158).

### What returns to Allah?

Al-umūr means the matters or affairs whose consequences return to Allah. The verb has a passive reading, describing their being returned, and an active reading, describing their return. Both place the final decision with Him and connect it with each person's deeds.

The contrast also reaches those who put personal interests ahead of Islam. Their material advantage may encourage contempt for wholehearted believers who lack it. But that advantage lasts only through the present order. In the next, those apparently great are lowered and those considered lowly receive high places.

### In short

- The final judgment is not a further chance to postpone faith until Allah is seen.
- The accounts preserve differing explanations of the coming and affirm the limit of human knowledge about its manner.
- The inward reading denies movement or confinement in place to the Real.
- All affairs return to Allah, and temporary worldly superiority does not determine the final ranks.

211.text:
The Children of Israel provide an example of rejecting guidance after receiving clear signs. "Ask the Children of Israel how many clear signs We have given them." The question rebukes ingratitude. It also introduces a general warning about exchanging Allah's favour for disbelief.

### Phrase by phrase

**"Ask the Children of Israel how many clear signs We have given them."** The Prophet ﷺ is instructed to question the children of Jacob about the manifest proofs they received. Allah honoured them with religion and gave commands and prohibitions in the time of Moses. The question requires acknowledgment, not fresh proof of something doubtful.

**"And whoever trades Allah's favour—after receiving it—˹for disbelief˺"** The favour includes signs that lead towards guidance, Allah's religion and His Scripture. Rejecting these after they arrive reverses their intended use. The explanation also includes refusing the guidance brought by Muhammad ﷺ.

**"should know that Allah is indeed severe in punishment"** Allah has power to punish denial. The warning is not restricted to one people or one incident. Losing a blessing after its value has become clear is itself a severe consequence.

### Which signs had they received?

Moses brought signs that included his shining hand, the divided sea and water flowing from the rock he struck. Clouds sheltered the people from intense heat. Manna and quails supplied their food. Such gifts testified to the Creator and to the truth of His messenger.

Yet many preferred disbelief to faith and turned from these blessings. The grammatical discussion treats "how many" as an interrogative expression. It links the second object of the command to ask with the object and specification of what Allah gave.

The inward reading emphasises the purpose of asking. The Messenger ﷺ did not need to resolve doubt about an established proof. Those addressed needed to admit what the proof had already shown.

### What happened when blessings were rejected?

The account links particular favours with particular acts of ingratitude. They received the Torah but denied what deserved acceptance, and were threatened by the mountain above them. They heard Allah's word but entertained doubts, and lightning struck them.

The parted sea delivered them from Pharaoh. Instead of gratitude, they turned to the calf and suffered killing. Disobedience spoiled the food supplied as manna and quails. Their further distaste ended that provision and left them to grow food through their own labour.

Prophets raised among them should have brought satisfaction and guidance. Killing those prophets was followed by loss of power. Several of these episodes appear earlier in the surah. The sequence shows repeated rejection, not a shortage of signs.

### Why does the warning extend beyond them?

The same principle is applied to the disbelievers of Quraysh in (14:28-29). There, ingratitude for Allah's gifts brings a people and their followers to ruin. Receiving favour does not protect anyone who deliberately exchanges it for denial.

The devotional reading dwells on withdrawal of grace. Its worth may become apparent only after it is taken away, when those who rejected it mourn what they cannot recover. The poetic image is of an abandoned beloved who can no longer be found when sought again.

### In short

- The Children of Israel received many signs through Moses but repeatedly rejected their meaning.
- The account connects rejected favours with punishment and loss.
- The warning applies to anyone who exchanges received guidance for disbelief.
- Losing grace can reveal its worth too late.

212.text:
Love of wealth and comfort can turn into contempt for people who put faith first. "The life of this world has been made appealing to the disbelievers, and they mock the believers." The verse reverses that apparent superiority: the mindful will stand above their mockers at judgment, and provision belongs to Allah.

### Phrase by phrase

**"The life of this world has been made appealing to the disbelievers,"** The comforts of worldly life attract those satisfied with them. They accumulate wealth but refuse the spending that would earn Allah's pleasure. The explanation identifies the disbelievers of Makkah, including Abū Jahl and his circle.

**"and they mock the believers."** Poor believers are ridiculed for not placing worldly gain first. Those mentioned include Salmān al-Fārisī, Bilāl ibn Rabāḥ al-Ḥabashī, ʿAmmār ibn Yāsir and Ṣuhayb al-Rūmī. Their spending seeks their Lord's pleasure rather than the approval of wealthy mockers.

**"Those who are mindful ˹of Allah˺ will rank above them on the Day of Judgment."** Those who reject kufr and shirk will have the better state at resurrection. The believers enter Jannah, while the disbelievers enter Jahannam. Their final ranks overturn the judgments made from wealth alone.

**"And Allah provides for whoever He wills without limit"** Provision may mean abundant wealth here or ample gifts in Paradise. Another explanation includes the mocked believers eventually gaining control of their mockers' property and lives. None of these readings makes possessions a proof of honour before Allah.

### How does worldly attachment produce mockery?

When material gain rules a person's outlook, faith may be abandoned whenever it interferes with that gain. The same outlook treats practising believers as foolish. Chiefs among the Israelites and ignorant polytheists are included in this pattern of ridicule.

The inward reading describes people deceived without recognising their deception. Their vision grows dark, and they deride Allah's friends. Their attitude reveals what they value, not the real worth of those they mock.

Those who put personal interests before Islam often possess the visible splendours of life. Those who accept Islam without conditions may lack them. This difference tempts the former to assume superiority. But the present order is temporary. The next order lowers those once thought great and raises those once considered insignificant.

The believers' spending for Allah's Face secures happiness at the return to Him. They are exalted at the gathering, resurrection and final abode. The account contrasts their high ranks with the depths of the Fire. One early report also gives them superiority here through a stronger argument and the standing they attain.

When people testify on that Day and ignorance clears from their hearts, the true losers will become evident.

### Why does wealth not establish honour?

Provision depends on Allah's decree, not merely on personal ability or influence. Respect based on possessions is not necessarily valid in His sight. To claim honour from wealth and despise the poor confuses temporary resources with lasting worth.

A report from ʿAlī warns against despising a Muslim man or woman for hunger. Allah will disgrace the offender before the gathering of all people. It also warns against falsely alleging a weakness in a Muslim: the accuser will be set on a high mound until the words are withdrawn.

### What remains of a person's possessions?

A hadith qudsī promises divine provision to the son of Adam who spends. The Prophet ﷺ likewise encouraged Bilāl to give without fearing deprivation from the Owner of the Throne. The promise of replacement also appears in (34:39), which calls Allah the Best Provider.

The Ṣaḥīḥ records two angels descending each day. One asks Allah to replace the gifts of those who spend in His cause. The other asks for destruction of the miser's wealth.

Another recorded saying challenges the repeated claim, "my money, my money". A person's effective possession is what is eaten and consumed, worn and worn out, or given in charity and preserved in the record of deeds. What remains passes to the heirs.

Imam Aḥmad records a further warning from the Prophet ﷺ. It pictures this world as a home and wealth for those who lack a true home and wealth, gathered by people without sound understanding. The point is not to mistake temporary accumulation for lasting security.

### In short

- Attachment to worldly gain can lead people to ridicule devoted believers.
- The final ranks of believers and disbelievers reverse appearances based on wealth.
- Provision is Allah's gift, not a certificate of honour.
- Spending for Allah brings replacement and preserves what accumulation alone cannot keep.

213.text:
The preceding verses traced opposition to the truth to love of this world. This verse points out that throughout history Allah has shown clear signs to establish the true faith, while seekers of worldly benefit have worked against it to protect their material interests. "Humanity had once been one community ˹of believers before they lost faith˺. Then Allah raised prophets as deliverers of good news and as warners, and revealed to them the Scriptures in truth to judge among people regarding their disputes." It continues: "And no one disputed the Scriptures except the very people who received them after clear proofs had come to them—out of jealousy. Then Allah, by His grace, has guided the believers to the truth regarding those disputes. And Allah guides whoever He wills to the Straight Path".

### Phrase by phrase

**"Humanity had once been one community ˹of believers before they lost faith˺."**. There was a time when all human beings belonged to a single community with a common religion and belief, a faith true and natural. Then differences of temperament and taste, opinion and thought produced contradictory beliefs, until the true could no longer be told from the false, and it was to make truth distinct from error and show people the straight path that Allah sent prophets with Books and revelations. Al-Rāghib al-Iṣfahānī says in al-Mufradāt that ummah denotes a set of people gathered together by faith, time or place, so the unity may be one of beliefs and ideas, of presence in a region at a given time, or of descent, language, colour and the like. Two questions arise: what sort of unity is meant, and when did it exist. The first is settled by the end of the verse, which mentions the later differences and says the prophets were sent to determine the true way among many. Prophets and Scriptures were plainly not sent to resolve differences of descent, language, colour, country or period, but differences of ideas and beliefs, so the unity meant is unity of belief. Was that shared belief the Oneness of God, or a shared state of disbelief and error? Ibn ʿAbbās, as Ibn Jarīr records, said that there were ten generations between Adam and Nūḥ, all on the religion of truth, that they later disputed, and that Allah then sent the prophets as warners and bearers of good news, adding that ʿAbdullāh ibn Masʿūd read the verse as "the people were one community, and then they disputed". Al-Ḥākim records this in his Mustadrak with a ṣaḥīḥ chain not recorded by al-Bukhārī and Muslim. Abū Jaʿfar al-Rāzī relates from Abū al-ʿĀliyah that Ubayy ibn Kaʿb read it the same way, and Qatādah said they all had guidance, then disputed, and Allah sent the prophets, the first of them Nūḥ. One early gloss takes it to mean that in the times of Nūḥ and Ibrāhīm people were one community of disbelievers, though it also records that in the time of Ibrāhīm there were followers of the true religion, and the weightier view of the majority is that all were united on the Oneness of God. Other verses point the same way: "Humanity was once nothing but a single community ˹of believers˺, but then they differed. Had it not been for a prior decree from your Lord, their differences would have been settled ˹at once˺" (10:19), the decree being that truth and falsehood, good and bad, should exist side by side in this world, and the addresses to the prophets, "Indeed, this religion of yours is ˹only˺ one, and I am your Lord, so worship Me ˹alone˺" (21:92), and "Surely this religion of yours is ˹only˺ one, and I am your Lord, so fear Me ˹alone˺" (23:52). As to the period, Ubayy ibn Kaʿb and Ibn Zayd placed it in pre-eternity, when the spirits of all human beings were created and asked whether He was not their Lord, and every soul without exception answered yes, so that all were on the one true belief whose name is Islam. Ibn ʿAbbās placed it in the time when Adam came into the world with his wife and their children multiplied, all believing in Adam's religion and following his teaching of God's Oneness, all obedient to the religious law except Qābīl. In the Musnad of al-Bazzār an addition to his statement says this unity of belief lasted from Adam to Idrīs, ten qarns, and if qarn means a century that is a thousand years, during which all followed Islam and tawḥīd. Others date it to the flood of Nūḥ, which swept away all but those in the ark, so that the survivors were all Muslims and monotheists. The three statements do not contradict one another, for in each of these periods people were one community on the true faith. People were agreed and guided on the way of their father Adam until Satan misled them and they split into believers and disbelievers.

**"Then Allah raised prophets as deliverers of good news and as warners,"**. The first sentence says that mankind was one community, and the second that Allah sent prophets and Books to resolve disputes, and the two do not seem to fit, because the reason for sending prophets is people's disputing, which did not exist at the time. The answer is plain: in the early period people held to one true faith, later differences crept in and led to disputes, and then came the need for prophets and Books. Why, then, is the appearance of differences not mentioned? Those with insight into the Qur'an's style know that in relating past events it never tells the whole story but omits what can be understood from context. In the story of Yūsuf, the released prisoner proposes to the king that he be sent to Yūsuf for the interpretation of the royal dream, and the next thing related is his addressing Yūsuf, without any statement that the king approved, that he went to the prison and arrived there. Likewise the onset of differences after the single community did not need stating, since the world has always known disputes. What needed to be said was that before all these disputes there was a time when all human beings followed one true religion, and, very pointedly, that Allah provided for the removal of the disputes through guidance. The prophets, raised from the children of Nūḥ and Ibrāhīm, brought good news of Paradise and eternal peace to those who follow the true faith and warning of the Fire to those who turn away. Religion as revealed by Allah is one religion, yet men put a variety of interpretations on it to suit their own mental make-up, so that differing viewpoints arise, all claiming allegiance to one Scripture. When this happens Allah chooses one of His servants to proclaim the truth on earth. He speaks in human language and looks no different from anyone else, but those bent on finding truth recognise the divine quality in his words, forget their differences and flock to his standard, while others cling stubbornly to their self-made interpretations, asking why they should accept teaching from another, and their claim to a monopoly on truth makes them so proud and prejudiced that they deny the very truth they claimed to own.

**"and revealed to them the Scriptures in truth to judge among people regarding their disputes."**. Allah supported the prophets with revelations and Books sent down with Jibrīl, expounding what is true and what is false in matters of belief and idea, so that each prophet might judge by his Scripture between people in their religious differences. "In truth" is connected grammatically to "revealed". Some say the sense is that the Scripture serves as the final authority, or that the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ rules the people by it. The purpose of sending prophets and Books was nothing other than to gather people who had left the single ummah and branched into sects back into one community. Whenever people strayed, Allah sent a prophet and a Book, and when they strayed again another prophet and another Book, to put them back on the straight path. It is like health, which is one, compared with diseases, which are many: each disease called for its own medicine and regimen. Finally came the most comprehensive prescription of all, effective against every disease for as long as Allah keeps this world going, the most complete of all earlier prescriptions and one that pre-empts all future treatments, namely Islam, with the last of the prophets and the Qur'an. The recurring problem of interpolated Scriptures and lost prophetic teachings, which had required new prophets and Books in the past, was removed when Allah Himself undertook to protect the Qur'an from alteration, and promised to raise and sustain within the community of Muhammad ﷺ a group that would always hold to the true faith and circulate the correct teachings of the Qur'an and Sunnah among Muslims everywhere, unflinching before any hostility. After that the doors of prophethood and revelation had to be closed for ever, and so came the proclamation of the end of prophethood. The coming of prophets and Books was never a source of division between people. All of them aimed at gathering people around the one true faith to which they had originally adhered.

**"And no one disputed the Scriptures except the very people who received them after clear proofs had come to them—out of jealousy."**. Despite prophets and Books bearing open truths, the world split into two groups. Some did not accept the clear guidance, and strangely the first to deny it were the very people to whom the prophets and verses were sent, the Jews and the Christians, so that some believed and others disbelieved. More astonishing still, there was no room for doubt in Scriptures that were neither beyond their understanding nor likely to confuse them. They knew and understood, yet their lust for taking the opposite stand made them deny. Those given the Torah differed about Muhammad ﷺ and his message, despite its clarity and the clear proofs in their own Scripture, out of injustice, resentful envy and insolence towards one another, and for this they disbelieved. Grammatically, "after clear proofs had come to them" belongs with "they differed" and is to be understood before the exception. The second group were enabled by Allah to follow the straight path and said yes to the prophets, messengers and divine Books sincerely and wholeheartedly. The two groups are the ones named in Sūrat al-Taghābun: "He is the One Who created you, yet some of you are disbelievers while some are believers" (64:2). So the gist is that all human beings were at first followers of the true faith. Then temperamental diversity gave way to self-interest, disputes surfaced, beliefs themselves were disputed, and the line between true and false was blurred. Allah sent prophets and Books to bring people back to the faith they had held, and despite all guidance and clear signs some followed dutifully while others, out of obstinacy and hostility, took the road of denial.

**"Then Allah, by His grace, has guided the believers to the truth regarding those disputes."**. ʿAbd al-Razzāq relates that Abū Hurayrah explained this with the Prophet's ﷺ words that the Muslims are the last nation but the first on the Day of Resurrection and the first to enter Paradise, although the Jews and Christians were given the Book before them, that Allah guided them to the truth wherever the others disputed, and that Friday is the day they disputed over and Allah guided this ummah to it, so the others follow, the Jews with the next day and the Christians with the day after. Ibn Wahb relates from ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Zayd ibn Aslam that his father listed the disputes. They differed over the day of congregation, the Jews taking Saturday and the Christians Sunday, and Allah guided the ummah of Muhammad ﷺ to Friday. They differed over the qiblah, the Christians facing east and the Jews Bayt al-Maqdis, and Allah guided this ummah to the Kaʿbah in Makkah. They differed over prayer, some bowing without prostrating and others prostrating without bowing, some praying while talking and some while walking, and over fasting, some fasting part of the day and others abstaining from certain foods, and Allah guided this ummah to the truth in both. They differed over Ibrāhīm, whom the Jews called a Jew and the Christians a Christian, when Allah made him a ḥanīf and a Muslim, and over ʿĪsā, whom the Jews rejected while accusing his mother of a grave sin and the Christians made a god and the son of God, when Allah made him by His word and a spirit from Him, and in each case guided this ummah to the truth. "By His leave" means, according to Ibn Jarīr, by His knowledge of them and by what He directed and guided them to, that is, by His will. Allah guided the believers through the prophets to the truth of what others disputed in religion, or protected them through the prophets from those disputes and turned them from falsehood to the truth, enabling them to tell guidance from misguidance.

**"And Allah guides whoever He wills to the Straight Path"**. He guides whom He wills of His creation, whoever deserves it, or holds firm by His grace whomever He wills, to the path of truth, an established religion with which He is pleased, the path of faith, and He commands the decision and the clear proof. Al-Bukhārī and Muslim record from ʿĀʾishah that when the Messenger of Allah ﷺ rose to pray at night he would address Allah as the Lord of Jibrīl, Mīkāʾīl and Isrāfīl, Creator of the heavens and the earth, Knower of the unseen and the seen, who judges between His servants in what they dispute, and ask to be guided by His leave to the truth in what is disputed, since He guides whom He wills to a straight path. Another supplication asks Allah to show us the truth as truth and grant us to follow it, to show us falsehood as falsehood and keep us from it, not to let it become confused for us so that we go astray, and to make us leaders of the believers.

### Lessons of the verse

Three lessons follow. First, the verse supports the identification of nationhood on the basis of religion, the two-nation view of Muslim and non-Muslim, and shows that its real foundation is the united nationhood that flourished at the beginning, based not on country of origin but on believing the truth and following the straight path. There was real unity at the start of the world when people followed the true faith, disputes came later, and the prophets called people back to that unity. Those who rejected the call cut themselves off from it and became a separate nation. Second, evil people have always chosen to oppose every prophet and every Book and have been eager to muster their maximum forces against them. Since Allah has allowed this to be the customary state of affairs, people with strength of faith should not be dismayed by the chronic intrigues and hostility of the wicked. Just as the disbelievers follow their elders in denial and hostility to the prophets, true Muslims should follow their own elders, the prophets, in bearing injuries patiently while continuing to call to the faith with wisdom, sound advice and good grace, which is perhaps why the next verse counsels forbearance and patience in distress. Third, in the devotional reading the verse carries another intimation. When Allah first created creatures He created them in the veiling wrap of createdness, the darknesses of created attributes surrounding them, all one group in the curtain of obscurity, gathered in the darkness of absence, captive to their own make-up. Then a courier came from the infinite world to their tininess, of which the Prophet ﷺ reported that Allah created the creatures in darkness and then cast upon them something of His light, and whoever the light struck was guided and whoever it missed went astray. When that messenger turned its face towards them they all became aware, captive to desire and subject to will, their ears fixed on their own lot, asking what would be decreed for them. Then the hand of predetermination divided them into two groups, the fortunate, of whom He said that they belong to the Garden and He does not care, and the unfortunate, of whom He said that they belong to the Fire and He does not care, meaning that He fears no blame and has no regrets, that He gains nothing from loyalty and loses nothing from disloyalty, and that whoever gains faith is himself the one who profits while He remains as He was, without equal or need.

### In short

- Mankind was first one community of believers in God's Oneness, in pre-eternity (Ubayy, Ibn Zayd), from Adam to Idrīs (Ibn ʿAbbās, ten generations, al-Bazzār), or after the flood, and only later split, as 10:19, 21:92 and 23:52 confirm.
- Prophets with good news and warning, and Books to judge disputes, were sent to gather people back to that one faith, like remedies for successive diseases, until the final, protected prescription of the Qur'an closed prophethood.
- The very recipients of Scripture disputed it out of envy after clear proofs, splitting mankind into believers and disbelievers (64:2).
- Allah guided this ummah to the truth in what they disputed, Friday, the qiblah, prayer, fasting, Ibrāhīm and ʿĪsā (Abū Hurayrah, Zayd ibn Aslam), and the Prophet ﷺ prayed nightly for that guidance (ʿĀʾishah).
- Lessons: nationhood by faith, the constancy of hostility to prophets and the patience it calls for, and the inward truth that guidance is the light Allah casts.

214.text:
The earlier warning about hostility now recalls the suffering of past believers. "Do you think you will be admitted into Paradise without being tested like those before you?" The verse encourages patient effort for the Hereafter. It also reassures those who cry for help that Allah's promised relief is near.

### Phrase by phrase

**"Do you think you will be admitted into Paradise without being tested like those before you?"** Earlier communities met trials that believers should be prepared to endure. One early report addresses ʿUthmān ibn ʿAffān and his fellow believers after a trying experience. Their suffering is not a new feature of faith.

**"They were afflicted with suffering and adversity"** Al-baʾsāʾ is explained as poverty, and aḍ-ḍarrāʾ as ailments. Ibn ʿAbbās gives the latter sense, which includes illness and pain. The description also covers disasters, fear, calamities, hardship and hunger.

**"and were so ˹violently˺ shaken"** Fear of the enemy and repeated afflictions shook them as an earthquake would. Their trial reached an extreme intensity.

**"that ˹even˺ the Messenger and the believers with him cried out, “When will Allah's help come?”"** The cry asks for the promised help to arrive soon. It does not deny the promise or express doubt about Allah. The verb has the readings yaqūla and yaqūlu.

**"Indeed, Allah's help is ˹always˺ near"** Allah answers with the nearness of help, victory over the enemy and safety. Those who trust Him are reassured. The conjunction of hardship and ease also appears in (94:5-6).

### Why does faith demand sacrifice?

Clear proofs do not always overcome resistance. People may fear losing the comfortable life, interests and honour they have built. Accepting the truth requires willingness to surrender those protections when they conflict with it.

The road to Paradise can therefore appear dangerous. Its price is the self: habits, thought and action must be reshaped according to Allah's direction. Calling others to good and criticising wrongdoing also invites resistance. Teachers of truth need patience with their hearers' adverse reactions.

Earlier peoples and their fate are recalled in (43:8). The testing of those who claim belief is described in (29:1-3). These references locate the present trial within an established pattern.

### Does this exclude entry through mercy?

Other Qur'anic passages and sayings of the Prophet ﷺ show that sinners may enter Paradise through divine grace and forgiveness, without undergoing hardship. The explanation distinguishes degrees of trial rather than denying that mercy.

The lowest degree is resisting the desiring self and Satan, or defending the foundations of belief against hostile forces. Every Muslim can face that kind of effort. Beyond it are intermediate and higher degrees. The level of strenuous effort corresponds to the level of entry into Paradise. None is altogether untouched by struggle.

A saying of the Prophet ﷺ gives the prophets the hardest trials, followed by those closest to them.

### What did earlier believers endure?

The poverty reading is given by Ibn Masʿūd and Ibn ʿAbbās, along with Abū al-ʿĀliyah and Mujāhid. Other holders include Saʿīd ibn Jubayr and Murrah al-Hamdānī, al-Ḥasan and Qatādah, aḍ-Ḍaḥḥāk and al-Rabīʿ, al-Suddī and Muqātil ibn Ḥayyān.

An authentic hadith describes Khabbāb ibn al-Aratt and others asking the Messenger of Allah ﷺ to pray for divine support. He recalled earlier believers sawn from the head downwards or torn between flesh and bone with iron combs. Even those ordeals did not make them abandon religion.

He swore that the religion would be established until someone could ride between Ṣanʿāʾ and Ḥaḍramawt without fearing anyone but Allah, apart from a wolf threatening his sheep. He reproached their haste.

The Companions experienced severe shaking at al-Aḥzāb. Their terror and conflicting thoughts are described in (33:10-12). When Heraclius asked Abū Sufyān about the fighting with the Prophet ﷺ, he heard that each side sometimes lost. He recognised the pattern of prophets being tested before their final victory.

### Why is asking for help not a failure of trust?

The prophets and their followers knew Allah had promised support. Its time and place were not specified. Their cry arose from distress and longing for deliverance, not doubt incompatible with their station.

Earnest supplication does not contradict tawakkul. Allah loves His servants' sincere prayers, and prophets and pious believers have the strongest claim to that devotion. Asking for early relief remains an expression of dependence on Him.

### What do the inward images teach?

The devotional reading contrasts wishful speech with the courage to face difficulty. The moth meets the candle through burning. The candle gives light by losing its own head. Joining, life and fulfilled desire are pictured through relinquishment.

Firdaws is a sweet garden approached through thorns. Muṣṭafā ﷺ describes the Garden as surrounded by disliked things. The comparison between those who know and those who do not appears in (39:9).

Another image places precious pearls beneath an ocean guarded by sharks and great fish. Two seekers arrive. One retreats before the dangers, exposing a wish without adequate resolve. The Sharīʿah rejects reaching religion through mere wishes and self-display. A poetic comparison makes his mismatch like a black crow seeking a white falcon.

The other seeker is so drawn by the pearl that fear no longer rules him. He plunges into the water. If felicity assists him, he wins the pearl. Otherwise the sharks take his life, and his name enters the register of "I do not care". His state is likened to that of two thousand lovers killed each month without a sigh. These images press the distinction between desire alone and costly commitment.

### In short

- Earlier believers faced severe trials, and present believers should not expect faith without effort.
- Degrees of trial differ, and the account preserves entry through Allah's mercy.
- The cry for help expresses longing for promised relief, not a denial of tawakkul.
- Allah's help is near, while the inward images warn against seeking the pearl through wishes alone.

215.text:
The previous verses gave emphatic commands: leave disbelief and hypocrisy and enter Islam completely, heed no one against the command of Allah, spend wealth and give life for His pleasure, and show fortitude in every hardship. From here the surah turns to details of that obedience concerning wealth, life, marriage and divorce, all within the continuing theme of righteousness. "They ask you ˹O Prophet in˺ what ˹way˺ they should donate. Say, "Whatever donations you give are for parents, relatives, orphans, the poor, and ˹needy˺ travellers. Whatever good you do is certainly well known to Allah."".

### Phrase by phrase

**"They ask you ˹O Prophet in˺ what ˹way˺ they should donate."**. These details answer the Companions' questions to the Prophet ﷺ. Allah gives the answer through him, so the fatwā is effectively divine. The same attribution appears in "They ask you ˹O Prophet˺ regarding women. Say, "It is Allah Who instructs you regarding them"" (4:127). There Allah attributes the ruling to Himself. One may also say the rulings are the Prophet's ﷺ, conveyed to him by revelation. Such question-and-answer injunctions occur at nearly seventeen places in the Qur'an. Nine questions come from the Companions: seven in al-Baqarah and one each in al-Māʾidah and al-Anfāl. Six come from disbelievers: two in al-Aʿrāf and one each in Banī Isrāʾīl, al-Kahf, Ṭā Hā and al-Nāziʿāt. The Qur'an answers them all. Ibn ʿAbbās praised the Companions as the best people he had seen. Despite their devotion and closeness to the Prophet ﷺ, their questions were few. He counted about thirteen matters answered in the Qur'an. They asked only when necessary. The question here, "what they should spend", is repeated in the same words in verse 219, yet the two answers differ, and the wisdom of this appears from the backgrounds. Ibn al-Mundhir connects the revelation with ʿAmr ibn al-Jamūḥ, an elderly wealthy man. He asked the Prophet ﷺ what to give and to whom. Ibn Jarīr instead reports a question from the Muslims generally. It therefore has two parts, what and how much to spend, and where it should go. The question in verse 219, as Ibn Abī Ḥātim relates, arose when the command to spend in the way of Allah was revealed and some Companions asked for an elaboration of what money or thing they should spend, a single point of inquiry. The answer here gives more weight to the second part, the recipients, which is answered frontally and clearly, while the first part is answered as a corollary, and the later verse, restricted to what should be spent, is answered with "the surplus". Muqātil ibn Ḥayyān said this verse was revealed about voluntary charity, and Ibn ʿAbbās and Mujāhid explained the question as how they should spend. One early report notes that this was before the verse of inheritance was revealed.

**"Say, "Whatever donations you give are for parents, relatives, orphans, the poor, and ˹needy˺ travellers."**. "Of good" explains "whatever", covering small and large amounts, and this concerns the half of the question represented by the giver, after which Allah addresses the other half, the receiver. Permissible, pure wealth should reach the recipients with the strongest claim. They include parents and needy relatives, orphans in need and the destitute. They also include travellers separated from home and family, and guests who arrive along the way. A hadith lists those with the greatest claim on one's generosity as one's mother, father, sister and brother, then the nearest and then the next nearest relatives. Maymūn ibn Mihrān once recited this verse and remarked that these are the proper channels of spending, and that Allah did not mention among them drums, pipes, wooden images or the hangings that cover walls. One early report says that giving charity to parents was later abrogated by the verse of inheritance. Several rulings follow. First, the two verses concern voluntary charities, al-ṣadaqāt al-nāfilah, not obligatory zakāh. The Prophet ﷺ fixed zakāh's threshold and rate. Neither is specified here. This also removes the doubt raised by the inclusion of parents, to whom zakāh may not be given under the Prophet's ﷺ teaching, since the verses have nothing to do with zakāh. Second, even a gift given or food served to parents and other near relatives counts as spending in the way of Allah and earns reward with Him if the intention is to obey Him. Third, voluntary charity should come only from what is surplus to personal needs. Spending in a way that hurts one's own family, overrides their rights and reduces them to straitened circumstances is no act of merit, and one who leaves his debts unpaid while squandering money on voluntary charities is not liked in the sight of Allah. Abū Dharr al-Ghifārī and others regarded spending the surplus, al-ʿafw, as obligatory. They held that money or goods beyond one's needs could not be retained even after zakāh and other dues. Giving all the remainder as ṣadaqah was therefore wājib in their view. The majority of the Companions, their successors and the great imams read the requirement differently. What is given should come from surplus, but giving all surplus is not obligatory. The Companions' consistent practice supports that distinction.

**"Whatever good you do is certainly well known to Allah.""**. Whatever good works you perform, by spending on these or otherwise, Allah knows them, as He knows your intention, and will reward you for them in the best manner, no one being wronged even by the weight of an atom. Nothing is hidden from Him, however small. The words also answer the first part of the question as a corollary: Allah has placed no restriction on the amount, and whatever you spend according to your capacity will earn a matching reward with Him.

### Spending for others

People readily devote life and wealth to family benefit, personal desires and ambitions. Islam urges him to spend for the cause of Allah, which is a quite different form of expenditure, spending on others rather than on oneself. Another tendency is to pour all one's energy into attaining a high worldly position, something visible, whereas the everlasting reward, which cannot yet be seen, ought to be the chief goal. What man dislikes may please Allah, and only that will benefit him in the next, infinitely vaster world. In Allah's sight evil lies in preferring one's own pleasure to the pleasure of one's Creator, and what profits a man here may only harm him there. The devotional reading contrasts two kinds of relinquishment. Giving wealth on the Sharīʿah's path is beautiful. Surrendering the spirit in the field of Ḥaqīqah, detached from others in contemplation, is portrayed as greater. Fulfilling loyalty is beautiful too, but relinquishing self for the carpet of limpidness is placed beyond it. One person asks how he should spend his property, and the Sharīʿah answers: from 200 dirhams, 5 dirhams, and from 20 dinars, half a dinar. Another asks, and the Ḥaqīqah answers that he will not be with Him along with body and spirit. The story of the wage-earners is one thing and the story of the recognisers another: the wage-earner's recognition reaches as far as recognising the spirit, while the recogniser's reaches throwing the spirit away. Those fortunate Companions asked how to spend not because they had failed to find their way to poverty, but in the hope of receiving this caress from the Exalted Presence, that whatever they had given and would give, the Lord knew. It is like Moses, called by name on that pitch-black night in the desert of the Mount. Burning with the pleasure of the address, he asked who was speaking to him, not from ignorance but drowned in yearning for the vision of the Real, hoping to be called again and perhaps to light up, and when asked whether he did not know who was calling, he said that he knew but was waiting for the caller to say, "It is truly I. I am Allah—the Lord of all worlds" (28:30). The corresponding address here reassures the asker that Allah already knows what has been said. The servant may ask without shame or dread. The verse at the beginning of this section alludes to the worshippers' spending of their wealth in order to reach recognition, and the verse at its end to the recognisers' spending of their lives in struggle in order to reach the Recognised.

### In short

- The verse answers ʿAmr ibn al-Jamūḥ's question (Ibn al-Mundhir), or the Muslims' generally (Ibn Jarīr), about what to spend and on whom, one of the few questions the Companions asked (Ibn ʿAbbās), and its twin in verse 219 asks only what.
- Voluntary charity (Muqātil ibn Ḥayyān) goes first to parents, relatives, orphans, the poor and travellers, the nearest having the first claim, not to drums, pipes and wall hangings (Maymūn ibn Mihrān).
- It is not zakāh, which has fixed thresholds and may not be given to parents, and gifts to kin made for Allah's sake are rewarded.
- Give from surplus without harming one's family or neglecting debts, and the majority, against Abū Dharr, hold that giving away all surplus is not wājib.
- Allah knows every good deed and intention and rewards without limit, and inwardly the lover spends not wealth but his very spirit (28:30).

216.text:
Verse 216 moves from spending possessions to risking life. "Fighting has been made obligatory upon you ˹believers˺, though you dislike it." The verse acknowledges that burden, then contrasts limited human judgment with Allah's knowledge of what truly benefits people.

### Phrase by phrase

**"Fighting has been made obligatory upon you ˹believers˺,"** The explanation concerns jihād against enemies transgressing against Islam. Its legal discussion distinguishes a collective obligation from circumstances making it binding on individuals.

**"though you dislike it."** Fighting naturally burdens the heart. It involves travel, struggle, wounds and death, and risks both life and wealth. Acknowledging that reluctance does not remove the command.

**"Perhaps you dislike something which is good for you"** Apparent loss can lead to victory, reward or martyrdom. Human assessment of benefit often fails to see the outcome.

**"and like something which is bad for you."** Staying away may seem comfortable but lead to defeat, subjugation and loss. The principle also extends to other choices where desire hides harm.

**"Allah knows and you do not know"** Allah knows the consequences in this life and the Hereafter. His command, rather than personal liking, must guide the believer's judgment and conduct.

### What occasions are mentioned?

One early report connects the verse with Saʿd ibn Abī Waqqāṣ, al-Miqdād ibn al-Aswad and their associates. It relates the command to a general summons with the Prophet ﷺ.

The same account places verse 217 with ʿAbdullāh ibn Jaḥsh and his companions. They killed ʿAmr ibn al-Ḥaḍramī on what they reckoned to be the final afternoon of Jumādā al-Ukhirah, day 30. They had not seen the moon of Rajab. Quraysh reproached them for fighting during a sacred month. The fuller discussion of that incident belongs to the next verse.

### How is the collective obligation explained?

Al-Zuhrī says that everyone has a duty of support according to need. Those who stay behind must supply help when required and march when summoned. If their participation is unnecessary, they remain behind.

The Ṣaḥīḥ records a warning about dying without having fought or sincerely intended to fight, describing such a death as Jāhiliyyah. At al-Fatḥ, the conquest of Makkah, the Prophet ﷺ said migration from Makkah to al-Madīnah had ended. Jihād and intention remained, and those summoned were to march.

The wording of the verse might initially suggest an absolute duty on every Muslim. Other verses and sayings qualify that impression. In ordinary conditions it is farḍ ʿalā al-kifāyah, a collective obligation, rather than farḍ ʿayn on each individual. When a sufficient group discharges it, the others are released. If nobody does so in a country or period, all bear responsibility for abandoning it.

A hadith speaks of a group continuing this duty until the Day of Judgment. The discussion also cites (4:95). There, those who strive have higher ranks, but a good reward is promised to those with valid reasons for remaining. These include compelling excuses and engagement in other religious service. Such a promise supports the distinction from an unconditional individual duty.

The division between those marching and those acquiring religious knowledge in (9:122) makes the same point. Both forms of service remain possible within a collective duty.

Al-Bukhārī and Muslim record a man asking to join the Prophet's ﷺ jihād. His parents were alive, so he was directed to serve them and earn reward through that service. Those not needed by a group already carrying out the duty can attend to other religious responsibilities.

### When does the duty become individual?

The Imām may issue a general summons because of pressing need. Then the duty becomes binding on all, as illustrated by the rebuke for clinging to the land in (9:38).

The discussion also considers invasion of an Islamic country. If the defenders are too few or weak, responsibility reaches neighbouring Muslims. If they too cannot repel the attack, it extends farther and may ultimately bind every individual Muslim.

The majority of jurists and hadith scholars therefore distinguish these circumstances from the normal collective obligation. While it remains farḍ kifāyah, children need parental permission to go, and a debtor must first clear the debt. When a general call or aggressive encirclement makes it farḍ ʿayn, those conditions no longer apply. The account includes the permissions of parents, a husband and a creditor in that distinction.

### Why can reluctance misjudge benefit?

The explanation lists possible outcomes of fighting: defeat of the enemy, victory and dominance, possession of lands, wealth and offspring, booty, martyrdom and reward. These belong to its historical account of the command and its consequences.

Even an intelligent person can confuse benefit with harm. Looking back may reveal that something eagerly pursued was damaging, while something avoided proved helpful. What seemed loss in Allah's way can be disclosed as gain and lasting peace.

Conversely, avoiding the duty can lead to the enemy taking land and government, impoverishment and subjugation. It can also forfeit spoils, martyrdom and reward. The desiring soul may reject the obligation that brings happiness and seek what brings destruction.

### How does the principle reach ordinary conduct?

People may prefer unrestricted freedom when Allah's limits are better for them. They may welcome flattering friends instead of critics who kindly expose faults. Saving face before people can tempt them to defy truth, although real honour comes from upholding it before Allah.

A religion promising Paradise without sacrifice may be attractive. The explanation instead stresses struggle and sacrifice, and warns against becoming absorbed in the present while neglecting life beyond death.

The inward reading distinguishes the lower self from the heart. Discipline defers the self's comforts, while nearness brings the heart immediate consolation. Happiness requires resisting the self's opposition and following the heart's approach to Allah. Trust in the Real's promise of ease is preferable to the self's fearful forecasts.

### In short

- The legal discussion ordinarily treats jihād as a collective obligation, qualified by need and other religious duties.
- A general summons or an invasion beyond the defenders' capacity can make the duty individual.
- Permission and debt requirements differ between those circumstances.
- Natural reluctance and apparent advantage cannot replace Allah's knowledge as the standard of obedience.

217.text:
This verse opens with a question raised by disbelievers of Quraysh after a raiding party of Companions killed a man on a day that turned out to belong to a sacred month. "They ask you ˹O Prophet˺ about fighting in the sacred months." The answer begins: "Fighting during these months is a great sin. But hindering ˹others˺ from the Path of Allah, rejecting Him, and expelling the worshippers from the Sacred Mosque is ˹a˺ greater ˹sin˺ in the sight of Allah. For persecution is far worse than killing." It continues: "And they will not stop fighting you until they turn you away from your faith—if they can. And whoever among you renounces their own faith and dies a disbeliever, their deeds will become void in this life and in the Hereafter. It is they who will be the residents of the Fire. They will be there forever."

### Phrase by phrase

**"They ask you ˹O Prophet˺ about fighting in the sacred months."**. Ibn Abī Ḥātim relates from Jundub ibn ʿAbdullāh that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ assembled a party under Abū ʿUbaydah ibn al-Jarrāḥ, who wept at the thought of parting from him, so the Prophet ﷺ relieved him and appointed ʿAbdullāh ibn Jaḥsh instead, giving him a sealed letter not to be opened until he reached a certain place and telling him to compel none of his men to go on. When ʿAbdullāh read it he said the words of istirjāʿ, "Surely to Allah we belong and to Him we will ˹all˺ return" (2:156), declared that he heard and obeyed Allah and His Messenger, and read it to his companions, two of whom turned back while the rest went on. They came upon Ibn al-Ḥaḍramī of Quraysh and killed him, not knowing whether the day was in Rajab or in Jumādā, and the polytheists accused the Muslims of murder in the sacred month, whereupon this verse was revealed. Ibn Isḥāq al-Madanī, as transmitted by Ziyād al-Bakkāʾī to ʿAbd al-Malik ibn Hishām, gives the fuller account. In Rajab, after returning from the first expedition of Badr, the Prophet ﷺ sent ʿAbdullāh ibn Jaḥsh ibn Riʾāb al-Asadī with eight men, all Emigrants and none of the Anṣār, ordering him to march two days before reading his instructions and to force no one to accompany him. From Banū ʿAbd Shams ibn ʿAbd Manāf there was Abū Ḥudhayfah ibn ʿUtbah ibn Rabīʿah, and of their allies ʿAbdullāh ibn Jaḥsh himself, the commander, and ʿUkkāshah ibn Miḥṣan of Banū Asad ibn Khuzaymah. ʿUtbah ibn Ghazwān ibn Jābir was an ally of Banū Nawfal ibn ʿAbd Manāf, Saʿd ibn Abī Waqqāṣ was of Banū Zuhrah ibn Kilāb, and the allies of Banū Kaʿb included ʿĀdī ibn ʿAmr ibn al-Rabīʿah, who was not of the line of Ibn Wāʾil, Wāqid ibn ʿAbdullāh ibn ʿAbd Manāf ibn ʿArīn ibn Thaʿlabah ibn Yarbūʿ of Banū Tamīm, and Khālid ibn Bukayr of Banū Saʿd ibn Layth, while Suhayl ibn Bayḍāʾ of Banū al-Ḥārith ibn Fihr was also with them. After two days' march ʿAbdullāh opened the letter and found the order to go on to Nakhlah, between Makkah and al-Ṭāʾif, and there to watch the caravan of Quraysh and gather news of them. He said that he heard and obeyed, told his companions that he had been forbidden to force anyone, that those who sought martyrdom should come with him and those who disliked it should turn back, and that he himself would carry out the command, and not one of them turned back. In the Ḥijāz, at Buḥrān near al-Furuʿ, Saʿd ibn Abī Waqqāṣ and ʿUtbah ibn Ghazwān lost the camel they rode by turns and went back to look for it, while the rest reached Nakhlah. There a caravan of Quraysh passed carrying raisins, provisions and merchandise, with ʿAmr ibn al-Ḥaḍramī, whose name was ʿAbdullāh ibn ʿAbbād, ʿUthmān ibn ʿAbdullāh ibn al-Mughīrah and his brother Nawfal of Makhzūm, and al-Ḥakam ibn Kaysān, a freedman of Hishām ibn al-Mughīrah. The travellers were alarmed at the sight of the Companions until they noticed ʿUkkāshah's shaven head and concluded that these were pilgrims for ʿumrah with nothing to fear. The Companions conferred. It was, they believed, the last day of Rajab, and they said that if they let the caravan pass it would reach the Sacred Area and be safe from them, while if they attacked they would be killing in the sacred month. They hesitated, then encouraged one another and resolved to kill whom they could and seize what the caravan carried. Wāqid ibn ʿAbdullāh al-Tamīmī shot ʿAmr ibn al-Ḥaḍramī dead with an arrow, ʿUthmān and al-Ḥakam surrendered, and Nawfal escaped, and the party returned to al-Madīnah with the caravan and the two prisoners. Ibn Isḥāq adds, from the family of ʿAbdullāh ibn Jaḥsh, that ʿAbdullāh set aside a fifth of the booty for the Messenger of Allah ﷺ before the fifth had been prescribed and divided the rest among his men. When they arrived the Prophet ﷺ told them he had not commanded them to fight in the sacred month, and he left the caravan and the prisoners untouched and took no share. The raiders were stricken and thought themselves ruined, their Muslim brethren reproached them, and the Quraysh declared that Muhammad ﷺ and his Companions had violated the sacred month, shedding blood, seizing property and taking captives in it, while the Muslims still in Makkah answered that it had happened in Shaʿbān. The Jews rejoiced and read omens in the names: ʿAmr meant the war had begun, al-Ḥaḍramī that war had come, and Wāqid that it had flared up, but Allah turned all of this against them. Al-Zuhrī relates from ʿUrwah ibn al-Zubayr that the day was the last of the sacred month, that some of the party said they knew for certain the day belonged to the sacred month and should not be violated out of greed, but that the view of those who wanted worldly gain prevailed, that Ibn al-Ḥaḍramī was the first man killed in fighting between Muslims and disbelievers, and that the Quraysh sent a delegation to ask the Prophet ﷺ whether he permitted fighting in the sacred month. Al-Zuhrī also names the killer as ʿAbdullāh ibn Wāqid al-Laythī and dates the killing to the last day of Rajab. Another account says the Muslims thought it the thirtieth of Jumādā al-Thānī, but that month had only twenty-nine days that year, so the new moon had risen the evening before and it was in fact the first of Rajab, in the year 2 AH. One early gloss confines the question to warfare in Rajab. Arab feeling ran high over the age-old respect for the sacred months, and this unintentional violation let the opponents taunt the Prophet ﷺ and his followers for not respecting even them.

**"Fighting during these months is a great sin."**. Fighting in Rajab, Dhū al-Qaʿdah, Dhū al-Ḥijjah and Muḥarram is a grave matter, heinous in sin and deserving great punishment. In the grammar, "fighting in it" is an inclusive substitution for "the sacred month", "fighting" is the subject and "great" its predicate. The Muslims had not acted deliberately, but through a misunderstanding about the date, and the verse concedes the principle while refuting the accusers. This verse proves that fighting is forbidden in the four sacred months, as do other verses, such as "of which four are sacred. That is the Right Way" (9:36), and the Prophet's ﷺ words in the sermon of the Farewell Ḥajj that four of the months are sacred, three consecutive and the fourth the Rajab of Muḍar. ʿAṭāʾ ibn Abī Rabāḥ swore that this injunction stands for ever, and several other Successors regard it as unabrogated, but according to al-Jaṣṣāṣ the majority of jurists hold it abrogated by consensus, so that fighting is no longer forbidden in any month. They differ over what abrogates it: some name "fight the polytheists together" in 9:36, many the verse "kill the polytheists ˹who violated their treaties˺ wherever you find them" (9:5), taking "wherever" to include whatever month or time, and others the Prophet's ﷺ own conduct, since he besieged al-Ṭāʾif in the sacred months and sent Abū ʿĀmir al-Ashʿarī on the expedition of Awṭās during them. Al-Bayḍāwī, on the opening of Sūrat al-Barāʾah, and Rūḥ al-Maʿānī on this verse report consensus on the abrogation. Al-Maẓharī answers all these arguments: the sanctity of the sacred months is plainly affirmed in the very Verse of the Sword, which states that the months with Allah are twelve, of which four are sacred, and the Farewell Sermon, delivered only eighty days before the Prophet ﷺ died, affirmed it clearly, so these verses cannot be its abrogators, and the siege of al-Ṭāʾif took place in Shawwāl, not Dhū al-Qaʿdah. What can be conceded is that the absolute prohibition admits an exception allowing Muslims to defend themselves and counter-attack if the disbelievers start fighting in these months, and this much is abrogated and clarified by "a sacred month for ˹an offence in˺ a sacred month" (2:194). The gist is that initiating fighting in these months is forbidden for ever, but if disbelievers attack, the Muslims may fight back in defence. Al-Jaṣṣāṣ reports from Jābir ibn ʿAbdullāh that the Prophet ﷺ never fought in a sacred month unless the disbelievers began the fighting.

**"But hindering ˹others˺ from the Path of Allah, rejecting Him, and expelling the worshippers from the Sacred Mosque is ˹a˺ greater ˹sin˺ in the sight of Allah."**. If the Muslims had killed in the sacred month, the disbelievers of Quraysh had hindered people from the path of Allah, His religion and obedience, disbelieved in Him, barred the believers from the Sacred Mosque and expelled its own people, the Prophet ﷺ and the believers, from it, which is a greater sin with Allah than killing the man they killed, deserving a greater punishment than the killing of ʿAmr ibn al-Ḥaḍramī. Disbelief, setting up idols in the Holy Mosque and driving the Muslims out of it are a greater evil than killing a disbeliever in a state of war. Nothing is more abhorrent to Allah than a man steeped in great crimes trying to discredit another by magnifying his minor mistake. When the call to truth was raised among the Quraysh they not only denied it but sought to stop others following it, closing the doors of Allah's House to His servants, turning the Prophet's ﷺ followers out of their homes and tormenting them with extreme cruelty to force them to forsake their faith.

**"For persecution is far worse than killing."**. Al-fitnah, trying to force the Muslims back into disbelief after they had believed, is worse with Allah than killing, and the idolatry of the Quraysh is worse than the slaying of ʿAmr. Persecuting a person for his faith is a crime worse than any other in the eyes of Allah. In the devotional reading, some acts of disobedience are worse and more intractable than others, and bad manners at the door do not carry the consequences they do on the intimate carpet. When the lower self errs its punishment is deferred, the burning of the Hereafter, but when the heart errs the punishment is immediate, separation, and heedlessness in hearts is graver than the harm of error to the lower self, for the lower self is kept from its good fortune while the heart is kept from the Real.

**"And they will not stop fighting you until they turn you away from your faith—if they can."**. The people of Makkah will go on fighting with unrelenting viciousness in order to turn the believers from Islam to disbelief, from the path of truth to their false path, if they are able. In the devotional reading, this alludes to the people of heedlessness who seek to lure you towards their heedlessness and are content only when you break the pact of your spiritual desire by returning to your former state, and whoever breaks his pledge to Allah deforms his heart.

**"And whoever among you renounces their own faith and dies a disbeliever, their deeds will become void in this life and in the Hereafter."**. Whoever renounces Islam and dies in disbelief has his works thwarted and his good deeds rejected, so that they count for nothing and yield no reward. Death in disbelief is specified as the condition because, according to al-Shāfiʿī, one who returns to Islam does not have his earlier deeds invalidated, is rewarded for them and need not repeat such deeds as the Ḥajj. Several rulings concern apostates. Deeds going to waste in this world means that the apostate's wife passes out of the bond of marriage, that he inherits nothing from a relative who dies a Muslim, that all the prayers and fasts of his Muslim years are reduced to nothing, and that no funeral prayer is offered for him and he is not buried in the Muslims' graveyard, while in the Hereafter it means no reward for his worship and eternal Hell. If an apostate becomes a Muslim again, he can at least hope to be saved from Hell and the injunctions of Islam apply to him for the rest of his life, but the jurists differ over whether a man who has already performed Ḥajj must repeat it if able, and whether the reward of his earlier prayers and fasts returns to him in the Hereafter: Abū Ḥanīfah holds that he must repeat the Ḥajj and does not accept that he is rewarded for his earlier worship, while al-Shāfiʿī differs on both points. For an original disbeliever, the reward of good deeds done in disbelief is held in abeyance: if he embraces Islam he receives a matching reward for them, as the hadith says that one embraces Islam with all the good one did before, but if he dies a disbeliever everything is lost. The fate of the apostate is thus worse than that of the original disbeliever, which is why jizyah may be accepted from the latter while a male apostate who does not return to Islam is killed and a female apostate imprisoned for life, since their conduct insults Islam and an insult to so binding an authority deserves no lesser punishment.

**"It is they who will be the residents of the Fire. They will be there forever."**. They are the people of Hell, abiding in it for ever, neither dying nor leaving it.

### In short

- The raid of ʿAbdullāh ibn Jaḥsh at Nakhlah, in which Wāqid ibn ʿAbdullāh killed ʿAmr ibn al-Ḥaḍramī and two prisoners and a caravan were taken, fell on a day the raiders took for the end of Jumādā but which was in Rajab, and the Quraysh accused the Muslims of violating the sacred month (Jundub, Ibn Isḥāq, ʿUrwah via al-Zuhrī).
- Fighting in the four sacred months is a grave sin, and whether the ban is abrogated (al-Jaṣṣāṣ on the majority, 9:5, 9:36, al-Ṭāʾif and Awṭās) or stands with an exception for self-defence (ʿAṭāʾ, al-Maẓharī, 2:194, Jābir) is disputed, the latter view holding that only initiating fighting remains forbidden.
- The Quraysh's own crimes, barring the path of Allah, disbelief, expelling the people of the Sacred Mosque and persecuting believers for their faith, are far graver than the killing.
- The disbelievers will never stop trying to turn the believers from their religion, and an apostate who dies in disbelief loses everything in both worlds, with the rulings on marriage, inheritance, burial, repeated Ḥajj (Abū Ḥanīfah against al-Shāfiʿī) and penalty that follow.

218.text:
The raiders of Nakhlah were relieved of their fear of sin but still asked whether their action earned reward. This verse gave them hope: "Surely those who have believed, emigrated, and struggled in the Way of Allah" may expect His mercy. Forgiveness and reward remain in Allah's hands.

### Phrase by phrase
