### How do the jurists organise the two categories?

Al-Razi distinguishes riba in loans from riba in trade. Al-Jassas distinguishes the buying-and-selling category from the category without sale, identifying the latter with the time-based increase on loans known in the age of ignorance.

Ibn Rushd describes the prohibition of profit on loans as established through Qur'an, sunnah and the community's agreement. Al-Tahawi likewise says the Qur'anic riba plainly concerned loans, while the other category became known through prophetic statements. Differences arose in some of the latter's details.

Shah Waliullah distinguishes primary riba from transactions annexed to its prohibition. He explains Al-Bukhari's saying that riba is only in nasi'ah through the primary loan category, not as permission for every unequal barter prohibited elsewhere.

The discussion names primary riba as riba al-Qard, the riba of loans, or riba al-Qur'an. It says its unlawfulness was never disputed in the Muslim community. Juristic disagreements over the added category do not displace that agreement.

It supports the prohibition through seven Qur'anic verses, more than forty hadiths and consensus. Those counts describe the argument's evidentiary scope. They do not introduce verse numbers not supplied in this job.

### Why avoid doubtful means as well?

The shariah blocks means leading to what is unlawful. Conversely, something without which an obligation cannot be completed becomes required for that purpose. Both principles concern the practical path into an act, not merely its final name.

The Two Sahihs record from An-Nu'man bin Bashir that lawful and unlawful matters are clear, with doubtful matters between them. Avoiding the doubtful protects religion and honour. Indulging them resembles a shepherd grazing beside a restricted pasture and likely to enter it.

Al-Hasan bin 'Ali reports in the Sunan that the Prophet ﷺ advised leaving what causes doubt for what does not. The counsel supports caution where knowledge is insufficient. It does not claim all trading questions are doubtful or that ordinary lawful trade must cease.

Ibn Majah records from Abu Hurayrah a warning describing seventy kinds of riba, with the least likened to intercourse with one's mother. The shocking comparison conveys its seriousness. No grading beyond what the discussion provides is added.

### Can a formal contract make a forbidden act lawful?

Ahmad records from 'A'ishah that when the riba verses were revealed, the Prophet ﷺ recited them in the mosque and prohibited trade in alcohol. The discussion says the six collections record the report except At-Tirmidhi.

The Two Sahihs also record a condemnation of people who, after being forbidden animal fat, melted and sold it and consumed the price. Changing the form did not remove the underlying wrong. The account refers specifically to that evasion rather than supplying a judgment about unrelated people.

'Ali and Ibn Mas'ud report the curse upon the one consuming riba, the one paying it, the two witnesses and the scribe recording it. Witnesses and paperwork can make the agreement look legitimate to observers, but the ruling concerns its reality. Intention and substance cannot be repaired by a respectable-looking form.

That principle matters throughout the discussion of modern arrangements. An old wrongdoing does not become acceptable merely because institutions make it appear refined, orderly or beneficial.

### Must a prohibited practice have no benefits at all?

The economic reflection first rejects that test. Harmful creatures and poisons can have uses, and even theft, bribery and robbery give someone an advantage. A benefit somewhere does not settle the moral balance.

The comparison is with intoxicants and gambling, which have some benefit but greater harm. Riba may likewise bring an immediate gain to its recipient while imposing a heavier worldly and spiritual cost. A transitory personal advantage is not equal to lasting welfare.

A robber's gain is obvious, but the community loses security. No sound judgment would call the act beneficial simply because the robber prospers. In the same way, the reflection insists that riba be examined through its effects beyond the lender.

The religious argument also includes the Hereafter. A brief profit followed by an enduring loss cannot be judged solely through the brief profit. An economic calculation excluding that consequence is already narrower than the verse's judgment.

### Why can custom conceal harm?

The reflection compares habitual practice with an anaesthetic. Familiarity can make people insensitive to harms they would notice in an unfamiliar setting. Once a system becomes fashionable, its smallest apparent gains can overshadow its gravest effects.

It describes modern riba as an epidemic mistaken for a cure. A reformer may be dismissed because the practice seems indispensable. But a physician who calls disease health merely because treatment is difficult has failed the patient.

Prophets similarly call towards reform without waiting until everyone promises obedience. Were acceptance a condition for speaking truth, unbelief, kufr, and association of partners, shirk, would remain unchallenged. The preaching of Allah's oneness began despite widespread opposition.

The reflection therefore distinguishes popularity from rightness. This is its reason for continuing the warning even when banking and commerce appear built around interest. Practical difficulty requires effort, not a reversal of the ruling.

### Why is the prosperity of some countries not the whole answer?

The argument criticises pointing only to wealthy marketplaces in the United States or the European economic community as evidence of the system's universal benefit. It says the costs borne by less fortunate peoples must also be examined.

A stark analogy compares observing the prosperity of man-eaters with ignoring their victims. The comparison is rhetorical, aimed at judging a gain only where it is enjoyed. Its point is not an independently demonstrated description of every foreign market.

The reflection contends that some capitalists grow through resources drawn from a wider community, while poverty, hunger and crises fall upon others. Its criticism follows the distinction already made between individual gain and collective harm.

These are the economic claims advanced in the discussion, not a new statistical survey. Their moral use is to resist assuming that a prosperous beneficiary proves the justice of the whole arrangement.

### How does the banking critique describe concentration of wealth?

The account contrasts individual moneylending with joint-stock banks pooling many people's deposits. Supporters say this lets people lacking skill or sufficient capital receive a small interest return and enables larger businesses to obtain loans.

The critique answers that small deposit returns do not ordinarily maintain a household. Depositors still seek labour or employment, while their accumulated resources become available to borrowers with large assets and strong credit. The small saver does not receive comparable access.

Its example is a borrower owning one hundred thousand who operates a business of one million through nine hundred thousand borrowed. A one-percent business return represents ten percent of the borrower's own capital. Someone trading only with the same personal hundred thousand receives merely the one-percent return on that amount, before considering expenses.

The purpose is to show how access to pooled capital magnifies the large borrower's opportunity. It is an illustration of the mechanism described, not a complete balance sheet incorporating every financing cost.

Large buyers also obtain discounts on raw materials unavailable to small competitors. The account says dominant firms may even force a temporary market fall to drive an entrant out, accepting a loss they can survive but the entrant cannot. In that way business becomes concentrated rather than universally accessible.

### What harms are claimed for competition and prices?

The first claimed harm is exclusion from independent enterprise. People who supplied the pooled savings become dependent upon employment and whatever return the large holders choose to offer.

The second concerns control of commodity prices. Dominant holders can sell high or restrict sale to raise prices further. The wider community then pays through reduced purchasing power while the few increase their holdings.

The proposed contrast is a wider field of businesses operating from personal capital. More independent enterprises would support more workers and broaden participation in profit. Competition would give sellers a reason to reduce margins and improve availability.

The reflection does not supply a separate technical model proving every outcome. It identifies the feared concentration and presents dispersed enterprise as its desired corrective. The claim must remain attached to that argument rather than being silently converted into a universal empirical law.

### Why does the account emphasise losses as well as profits?

Another example describes a business of one hundred thousand supported by ten thousand personal capital and ninety thousand borrowed. When the business collapses, the account says the borrower's own contribution forms only a tenth of the lost resources, while the greater exposure belongs to pooled community funds.

It criticises a pattern in which profit is privately enjoyed but institutional losses return to the public. Writing off a loss at a bank does not make the missing resources disappear from society's burden.

At the same time, the failed borrower suffers personal ruin and an unpayable debt. The reflection contrasts that with losing only personal capital in an interest-free enterprise, where the person may become penniless without the same added borrowing burden. Those are two sides of the described risk, not mutually exclusive claims that the borrower never suffers.

### What example is given from Pakistan's cotton trade?

The account cites the cotton crisis of 1954. It says traders had invested mainly borrowed bank funds with comparatively little personal capital. Prices fell from 125 rupees to ten, leaving traders unable to cover bank margins.

The market was closed and government assistance sought. The government then bought stocks at ninety rupees instead of the depressed ten, absorbing losses counted in millions. The discussion asks whose money financed the rescue and answers that it belonged to the nation, including the poor.

This is the historical example supplied for muhaq, destructive loss. It is retained as the account gives it, without outside correction or a claim of independent verification. Its role is to illustrate the public bearing of a private venture's losses.

### How are insurance and the stock exchange criticised?

The discussion says losses arise through calamities such as a ship burning or sinking, and through prices falling below purchase costs. It views insurance and stock-market arrangements as institutions used to shift those exposures further towards pooled public resources.

Its criticism of insurance focuses on who receives the large payments and the use of communal premiums. It mentions fraudulent damage or theft claims for vehicles and contrasts substantial capitalist recoveries with a small number of ordinary accident beneficiaries.

Its criticism of the stock exchange describes speculative arrangements as spreading losses from price slumps across many people. Both criticisms concern the shifting of burdens in the economic picture already presented.

The passages contain strong rhetorical condemnation. They do not supply every legal distinction among insurance contracts or every form of share ownership. Such distinctions should not be invented here, nor should the criticism be represented as a new comprehensive financial ruling beyond what is stated.

### Why is high taxation said not to cure the problem?

The account recognises governments trying to reverse concentration through very high income-tax rates, sometimes approaching the whole income. It says businesses then resorted to fictional accounts and concealment of capital.

The result, in its argument, was continuing private concentration rather than recovery of the resources for public benefit. A poetic comparison pictures locking the door while overlooking an enemy already inside the house.

The diagnosis therefore remains interest-oriented concentration, not merely insufficient taxation. The reflection calls for changing the underlying arrangement rather than repeatedly treating the surface result. Its proposed principle is enterprise using one's own capital instead of private command over a nation's pooled capital through interest borrowing.

### Would ending interest simply freeze money in chests?

An objection asks what would happen to savings if banks did not offer interest. Even a small return appears better than money buried and useless to everyone.

The answer pairs prohibition of riba with zakah. Qualifying idle wealth remains subject to a recurring fortieth each year. Hoarding does not exempt it. This gives its owner a reason to place it in useful enterprise rather than watch the holdings diminish.

Proper payment simultaneously helps poor and needy people. The discussion therefore proposes a double effect: prompting investment and sharing resources. It does not present the prohibition as an isolated command without any other institution of economic life.

It expects wider enterprise when large and small owners alike seek productive uses for their own capital. Profit and work would be distributed among more participants, while the poor also receive the required zakah. That is the positive alternative advanced against the buried-chest objection.

### Is interest-free banking said to be impossible?

The discussion acknowledges that abruptly abandoning a widespread system is difficult. It rejects the conclusion that difficulty makes the prohibition false or commerce necessarily impossible.

It recalls (22:78), which denies a burden of hardship in religion. It argues that a way must be sought to preserve national and international commerce while avoiding riba. Patience, courage and steady reform are required, just as treatment of an epidemic can be difficult without being useless.

The proposed task is cooperation between experts in shariah and banking to reconstruct operating principles. The institution of a bank need not be identified with every interest-based rule currently governing it. Banking could remain and become more beneficial through a different design.

A note describes an earlier draft of interest-free banking prepared with scholars and considered practical by some experts. Attempts to implement it did not endure because of businessmen's apathy and absence of government sanction. The detailed operating rules are not supplied in this passage and are not invented here.

### How are emergency needs to be met?

The discussion distinguishes commercial borrowing from accidental necessities faced by poor people. For the latter it proposes properly functioning zakah and obligatory charities.

It criticises complete nonpayment, inaccurate calculation and merely handing money away without identifying entitled recipients. Proper payment requires finding deserving people and transferring ownership into their hands. Removing money from one's pocket is not the complete duty.

The argument claims that full and correct observance would eliminate Muslims' need for interest-bearing emergency loans. It then describes a just Islamic government collecting relevant zakah in a Baytul-Mal, a public treasury.

That treasury could meet needs, provide larger loans without interest and help unemployed people run shops or enter productive work. A remark from an unnamed European expert praises the potential of the zakah system. No name or further external authority is added to it.

The proposed remedy thus joins personal compliance, sound distribution and institutions. It does not rest on telling a distressed individual merely to endure while the community ignores its obligations.

### What moral harm is described?

Sacrifice and generosity allow someone to accept personal discomfort to ease another's distress. The reflection says habitual dependence on interest weakens that refinement. The lender begins to see need as an opportunity for extraction rather than mercy.

It also describes jealousy of others' independent rise, reluctance to share and increasing intoxication with wealth. Greed then narrows judgment until the person no longer attends to right, wrong or the final consequence.

These descriptions explain why the warning reaches character as well as accounting. Riba opposes the preceding pattern of charitable mercy not only in the direction of money but in the habits it can cultivate.

### Why distinguish committing a sin from declaring it lawful?

The discussion acknowledges that individuals can struggle to escape an entrenched system unless a government, nation or determined group undertakes sustained reform. That is a call for organised responsibility, not a justification of riba in principle.

At minimum, the person should recognise the ruling truthfully. Taking or paying interest is a sin in this account. Trying to establish it as halal, lawful, is a further and greater wrong against belief and knowledge.

Confessing the practical wrong does not itself close a business. It leaves the way open to repentance and the search for a lawful arrangement. Defending the wrong as right obstructs that return and turns one offence into two.

The warning even describes people observing tahajjud, pre-dawn voluntary salah, and dhikr, remembrance, yet entering a shop or factory without recognising interest and gambling as sin. Visible devotion does not make financial conduct exempt from obedience.

### What is the inward warning about self-authorised interpretations?

The allusive reading criticises ta'wil used to excuse turning from the command. Such licence produces neither secure independence now nor recovery later. Its paired expressions contrast loss in the immediate life, 'ajilihim, with no profit in the coming life, ajilihim.

Those responding to admonition restrain the bridle of desire instead of letting it run freely. They receive respite and an opportunity to change. Returning to the blameworthy state renews exposure to sudden uprooting and punishment.

The image returns the economic debate to the servant's own response. Institutions may need reform, but the heart must not use their complexity to silence a clear warning. Acknowledgment, restraint and a sincere return begin there.

### In short

- Allah distinguishes permitted trade from riba despite their shared appearance of gain.
- The primary loan increase is treated as clear, while some added barter applications require juristic interpretation.
- The warning reaches consumers, payers and helpers, and formal paperwork cannot legalise the substance.
- The extensive economic reflection criticises concentrated gain, transferred losses and the corruption of mercy by greed.
- Repentance, lawful reform and properly functioning zakah are proposed responses, not declaring the forbidden lawful.

276.text:
The apparent arithmetic of gain and loss is reversed: "Allah has made interest fruitless and charity fruitful." Riba can increase a balance while taking away its benefit and blessing. Sadaqah, charity, can reduce what is held while increasing lasting good. The verse asks the reader to judge wealth through its relation to Allah, not its visible quantity alone.

### Phrase by phrase

**"Allah has made interest fruitless"** The explanation includes actual loss of the property and removal of barakah, its blessed benefit. Riba can also become a cause of punishment here and at resurrection. Increase in an account does not prove increase before Allah.

**"and charity fruitful."** He accepts sincere obligatory and voluntary charity, blesses the giver and multiplies the reward. The return may be tenfold, seven hundredfold or more. Its fruit is not confined to an immediate replacement of the money spent.

**"And Allah does not like any ungrateful evildoer"** The ending is connected with the beginning. Someone dissatisfied with lawful provision seeks other people's wealth by prohibited means. The discussion distinguishes kufr, disbelief expressed through denying the prohibition, from the sin of someone who recognises it as haram, unlawful, but still practises it.

### Why are riba and charity placed together?

Their nature, aims and outcomes are opposed. Charity gives what one owns without demanding a material return from the recipient. Riba takes an increase from another without the countervalue required by the account of lawful exchange.

The charitable giver accepts a reduction for Allah's pleasure and the Hereafter's reward. The riba-taker seeks a prohibited addition to existing capital. Allah can frustrate that greed while making the willingly reduced property fruitful.

The contradiction concerns more than outward possession. Wealth exists to support life, comfort, dignity and those dependent upon a person. Losing its useful effects is a form of loss even when the number remains large. Receiving benefit from modest resources is a form of increase even when the balance is smaller.

### What other references explain the distinction?

The comparison of Al-Khabith, evil or impure things, with At-Tayyib, good and pure things, is recalled in (5:100). Their abundance does not make them equal. The gathering and casting away of evil in (8:37) further shows that quantity alone does not secure acceptance.

In (30:39), a gift aimed at obtaining a greater return from other people's property has no increase with Allah. These references distinguish the purpose and quality of an act from its apparent expansion.

Ibn Jarir compares the statement with Ibn Mas'ud's saying that riba ends in less even when substantial. Ahmad records a similar statement in Al-Musnad. The discussion also gives the prophetic warning that however much riba increases, it ultimately decreases, citing Ahmad and Ibn Majah.

### What happens to a small pure gift?

Al-Bukhari records from Abu Hurayrah that the Prophet ﷺ described giving even the equivalent of a date from honest resources. Allah accepts only the good and pure. He accepts such charity with His right Hand and raises it for the giver as a person raises an animal until it becomes mountain-sized.

The image gives growth a different measure from compound monetary gain. The starting amount is small, but its accepted return is immense. The purity of its acquisition is expressly part of the promise.

No new explanation of the divine attribute is supplied here. The account preserves the hadith's description without adding a doctrine absent from the material.

### Is the destruction only in the Hereafter?

One explanation emphasises that riba brings no benefit at the final return and may become a curse, while charity becomes an enduring blessing. That consequence is certain within the discussion.

The fuller explanation also sees traces in this life. Wealth may collapse outright, or its pleasures and benefits may be removed. Ma'mar reports hearing from elders that forty years hardly pass before a riba-consumer's wealth is overtaken by muhaq, major destructive loss.

The discussion cites market collapses and failed fortunes as examples, while acknowledging ordinary loss in lawful trade too. Its strongest contrast associates catastrophic reversal particularly with riba and speculative markets. These are the claims of the economic reflection, not an independently established forecast about every person's fortune.

The argument does not require each wrongful account to become visibly empty on the same day. Removal of benefit offers another explanation where outward possession continues.

### Can articles of comfort guarantee comfort?

Gold and silver do not themselves relieve hunger, cool a room or warm a body. They obtain things serving those purposes. The real benefit lies in what a person can use and enjoy, not merely in the metal or balance.

The reflection compares swollen wealth without benefit with swelling in a body. Growth exists, but it is not healthy growth. No one would value bodily swelling simply because measurements increased.

A comfortable house, carefully arranged bed, good mattress, heating and cooling can be purchased. Sleep cannot be bought directly. Illness or anxiety may prevent it despite all those aids. The account mentions a report claiming seventy percent of Americans needed sleeping pills, and notes that even medication can fail.

That figure belongs to the report cited in the reflection, not a current medical statistic established here. Its purpose is to distinguish purchased equipment from the mercy, rahmah, of actual rest.

The same distinction applies to eating, family enjoyment and peace of mind. Someone absorbed in turning ten million into fifteen and then twenty may have little time to enjoy any of it. Factories, ships and business worries occupy the night and day that the wealth was meant to make comfortable.

### Why is wealth not the same as honour?

The social criticism describes lenders who make a livelihood from exploiting poverty. It cites historical moneylenders in India and Jewish lenders in Syria as examples of wealthy people resented for such conduct. The criticism concerns the exploitative acts described, not an inherent quality of an ethnic or religious population.

The account links resentment between labour and capital with socialism, communism and violent confrontation. It argues that outwardly prosperous circles cannot be judged apart from people bearing the costs. A severe man-eater analogy again contrasts the well-fed beneficiary with victims elsewhere.

Those are the reflection's historical and economic claims. Their moral point is that extracting wealth at others' expense does not produce genuine respect. Charity, by contrast, can bring tranquillity to someone with fewer luxury goods and goodwill from those helped.

The account also warns that inherited riba wealth may be lost or fail to bring benefit to descendants. It rejects assuming that a flourishing next generation settles the whole question of blessing.

### What additional warnings are gathered here?

The discussion presents ten prophetic sayings to reinforce the prohibition, without supplying collectors and grades for each one. Those absent details are not added.

One names seven destructive offences: association of partners with Allah, sorcery, unlawful killing, consuming riba, exploiting an orphan's property, fleeing at battle and slandering chaste, unsuspecting believing women. Riba appears among offences of grave religious and social harm.

Another describes the dream of a river of blood where a man trying to emerge is driven back by a stone thrown into his mouth. The explanation identifies him with consuming riba. The full named dream narration has been treated under the preceding verse, while this collection repeats its warning.

Another curses the recipient, payer, writer and witnesses of riba, calling them alike in responsibility for the prohibited arrangement. Helpers who formalise it are not excused merely because they did not consume the added payment.

A further warning names four kinds of people denied admission to Paradise and its bliss: addiction to wine, taking riba, exploiting an orphan's property and disobedience to parents. Another compares a dirham received as riba with thirty-three acts of fornication or adultery, emphasising its severity.

The collection also prohibits sale of fruits before they are fit to eat and says widespread adultery and riba invite punishment upon a town. It associates prevalent riba with famine and prevalent bribery with fear.

An Ascension account describes reaching the seventh heaven and seeing thunder and lightning, followed by people whose stomachs resembled houses containing visible snakes. Jibra'il explained that they had consumed riba. No additional collector or authenticity assessment is provided in this passage.

Another warning calls for abstention from embezzlement of spoils and riba, using severe language about unforgiven sins and the embezzler carrying the stolen property at judgment. The collection finally says a creditor must not accept a gift from the debtor because of the loan.

The point of gathering these warnings is awakening, not supplying a new chain or grading from memory. Recognising the sin as sin is the first protection against calling it lawful. The account describes its wider discussion as supported by seven verses and these ten sayings, while directing fuller research elsewhere.

### What is the inward difference between growth and loss?

Permitted conduct is described as accompanied by good and blessings. Conduct arising from unchecked desire ends in loss. The contrast asks not merely whether resources grow but what sort of life is being formed through acquiring and spending them.

A person was not sent into the world simply to hoard. The trial concerns developing qualities fitting for Paradise. Charity gives resources to needy people for Allah, while usury uses them to exploit. Their different aims cannot be assumed to lead to the same final condition.

### In short

- Riba can lose its property, benefit or blessing despite apparent increase.
- Allah grows sincere charity, even when the starting gift is small.
- Comfort and honour cannot be measured by the luxury goods money purchases.
- The collected warnings reach those assisting riba as well as consuming it.
- The contrast concerns the character and final destination formed through the use of wealth.

277.text:
After the severe warning comes a promise for obedient believers: "Indeed, those who believe, do good, establish prayer, and pay alms-tax will receive their reward from their Lord." Faith is joined to a life of worship and care. The promised peace answers the fear and disgrace described for prohibited gain.

### Phrase by phrase

**"Indeed, those who believe,"** They acknowledge Allah, His messengers and scriptures, and accept His commands, including the prohibition of riba. Gratitude recognises His provision rather than seeking more through rebellion.

**"do good,"** Righteous action puts that recognition into practice. It includes kindness to creation and refraining from prohibited conduct. Faith is not presented here as a substitute for obedience.

**"establish prayer,"** They fulfil salah, particularly the five daily prayers, with what is required for their completion. Establishing it means more than claiming an attachment to its name.

**"and pay alms-tax"** They discharge zakah on their property and direct it to those entitled to receive it. The act joins acknowledgment of Allah's right with help for His servants.

**"will receive their reward from their Lord,"** The honour is kept with Him, in Paradise, rather than exhausted in a temporary reputation. The assurance stands beside the preceding account of rejected gain.

**"and there will be no fear for them, nor will they grieve"** They are freed from fear concerning the future and sadness over worldly losses. A reported gloss pictures death slain and the Fire closed, when the promise of safety becomes manifest.

### Why join belief, worship and giving?

The verse gathers inward acknowledgment, righteous conduct, bodily devotion and financial responsibility. It does not make one outward accomplishment excuse deliberate neglect of the rest.

The person thanking Allah through obedience is contrasted with the person refusing His limits to accumulate more. Proper giving seeks the world of Paradise, while exploitation fixes its aim on amassing here. Different purposes form different lives and different final outcomes.

The image of charity raised by Allah, recorded by Al-Bukhari from Abu Hurayrah, belongs fully to the preceding verse's explanation. Here the resulting assurance is gathered into the promise of reward for the believing and practising person.

### What inward consolation is given?

The allusive reading recalls (18:30), the assurance that the wage of those doing beautiful deeds is not wasted. Taking refuge at the gate of divine generosity is pictured as entering shade. A step towards Allah finds a gift, and attachment to His generosity leaves the chamber of sorrows.

The language contrasts communion with the darkness of separation. A spirit recognising the Lord's favour laughs in relief. The Pir of the Tariqah marvels at care appearing in every breath and asks who could have a patron or friend like Allah.

The present signs are described as a message, with the full celebration still to come. The promised robe of honour is the reward with their Lord and freedom from fear and grief. The reflection joins it with repose and ease in (56:89), and the appointed time of union with the Beloved.

Poetry longs for separation to strike its tent and depart from the spirit's desert. The closing image recalls Gabriel with six hundred peacock-like wings unable to go beyond the Lote Tree alongside the Prophet ﷺ. It expresses the exceptional reach described in the reflection without adding an outside narrative or collector.

### In short

- Belief joins righteous conduct, complete prayer and proper zakah.
- The Lord's reward answers the previous warning with hope and security.
- Gratitude is shown through obedience and kindness, not hoarding alone.
- The inward reading celebrates divine care now and the fuller consolation to come.

278.text:
The prohibition reaches claims still awaiting payment: "O believers! Fear Allah, and give up outstanding interest if you are ˹true˺ believers." A transaction's having begun earlier does not justify collecting its prohibited increase after the command. Faith is tested in surrendering a claim that can seem valuable to its holder.

### Phrase by phrase

**"O believers! Fear Allah,"** Taqwa means guarding conduct through obedience and remembering His watchfulness. The command prepares the heart before announcing a rule that may be difficult to accept. A financial claim must be judged before Allah, not only by its owner's preference.

**"and give up outstanding interest"** Leave the unpaid riba still held against other people. The permission concerning past receipts does not extend to collecting an addition that remains unpaid. Principal and interest must be separated.

**"if you are ˹true˺ believers"** Iman, faith, requires accepting His permitted trade and prohibited riba. The opening appeal to fear and closing appeal to belief surround the practical rule. The account treats them as preparation for obedience, not merely ornament around a legal formula.

### What dispute prompted the instruction?

Zayd bin Aslam, As-Suddi, Ibn Jurayj and Muqatil bin Hayyan connect it with Bani 'Amr bin 'Umayr of Thaqif and Bani Al-Mughirah of Bani Makhzum. Outstanding riba transactions remained from the age of ignorance.

Thaqif claimed payment, while Bani Al-Mughirah refused to pay riba after accepting Islam. The matter was referred to 'Attab bin Usayd, the Prophet's deputy in Makkah. He wrote for guidance, and the Prophet ﷺ sent the revealed command back to him.

They then declared repentance, abandoned their unpaid riba and recognised that they could not face war with Allah and His Messenger. The instruction was therefore implemented in a concrete dispute, not left as a general sentiment.

A fuller account identifies the claimants as sons of 'Amr ibn 'Umayr ibn 'Awf al-Thaqafi: Rabi'ah, 'Abd Yalayl, Hubayb and Mas'ud. The brothers' demands were subject to the same rule as everyone else's.

### How do the accounts differ in detail?

Ibn 'Abbas's report through al-Kalbi begins with a reservation: this was what they had heard, and Allah knew best. It says Banu'l-Mughirah complained that others' interest had been cancelled while they were still expected to pay. The claimants relied on their treaty as requiring payment to them.

Another discussion places the dispute after the conquest and describes mutual peace arrangements. It names Mu'adh as governor in one report and 'Attab ibn 'Asid in another. The account elsewhere uses 'Attab bin Usayd. These reported alternatives are retained without inventing a single resolution of the names.

The underlying point is that accepting the relevant Islamic law through a treaty did not preserve a special right to riba. The cancellation governed both Muslim claimants and others bound by that agreement.

### What other reported occasion is given?

'Ata and 'Ikrimah connect the verse with Al-'Abbas ibn 'Abd al-Muttalib and 'Uthman ibn 'Affan lending dates. When repayment fell due, the owner said paying everything would leave too little for himself and his dependants.

He proposed paying half then and increasing the interest on the rest. They agreed, and later asked for the agreed payment. The Prophet ﷺ heard and warned them against proceeding. That report concerns an added charge for postponement, while the tribal account concerns disputed outstanding claims.

Both expose the same problem: need or a previous arrangement does not authorise collecting the forbidden addition. The verse demands abandoning it once the instruction is received.

### Why begin cancellation with the Prophet's uncle?

In the Farewell Hajj address, the Prophet ﷺ declared the riba of ignorance abandoned and began with the large claims of Al-'Abbas. The announcement allowed principal but no increase.

That example removed the appearance that the law served a private financial interest. Muslim claims against others were cancelled too. The purpose was reform for humanity, not a rule that transferred advantage to the messenger's household or community.

The detailed Farewell report and the rule protecting principal belong to the following verse. Here its relevance is the relinquishment of an outstanding claim even where the claimant has a close connection with the Prophet ﷺ.

### What choice does the inward reading describe?

The contrast is between maw'ud, what the Lord promises, and maqsud, what the lower self seeks. Contentment with the divine promise is better than attaching the heart to an acquisition desired by the self.

The self's demand can deceive, while the Real's promise is secure. Letting go of riba becomes an instance of that wider discipline: the heart trusts Allah's return rather than treating its immediate desire as indispensable.

### In short

- Outstanding interest must be abandoned, not collected because an agreement began earlier.
- The reported disputes show the prohibition applied to concrete financial claims.
- Cancellation did not exempt the Prophet's family or favour Muslim creditors.
- Faith and taqwa prepare the heart to obey even when relinquishing a claim is difficult.
- The inward lesson prefers Allah's promise to the lower self's demands.

279.text:
The warning is uncompromising, but repentance remains possible: "If you do not, then beware of a war with Allah and His Messenger!" Those who abandon riba may recover principal without oppressing the debtor or having their own right erased. The rule opposes injustice on both sides.

### Phrase by phrase

**"If you do not,"** If the outstanding riba is not abandoned, the person is knowingly refusing the command. The warning follows a clear opportunity to stop.

**"then beware of a war with Allah and His Messenger!"** Ibn 'Abbas explains this as certainty of war. He also describes riba-consumers being told at resurrection to take up arms. Another gloss joins punishment in the Hereafter with coercive enforcement by the messenger in this life.

**"But if you repent,"** Stop and resolve not to return. The condition is more than a verbal claim while continuing the same conduct. The discussion distinguishes practical sin from denying the prohibition and confronting lawful authority.

**"you may retain your principal"** The original amount lent remains due in the ordinary repentant case. 'Amr bin Al-Ahwas reports the Prophet's Farewell Hajj announcement cancelling every pre-Islamic riba claim and beginning with Al-'Abbas bin 'Abd al-Muttalib. Ibn Abi Hatim records that account.

**"neither inflicting nor suffering harm"** Taking more than principal wrongs the debtor. Returning less wrongs the creditor. Another explanation extends the words generally to not harming others and not being harmed through the debt.

### Why is this warning so severe?

The discussion describes the declaration of war as an exceptional warning, surpassed only by the warnings concerning kufr, disbelief. Riba is not a harmless private preference where another party has agreed under pressure.

The inward reading says wilful persistence carries no standing or dignity before Allah. Miqdar and akhtar, measure and honoured standing, are denied to that defiance. An impressive account or worldly position does not neutralise it.

Ibn 'Abbas also gives a historical enforcement ruling: the Muslim ruler requires a persistent offender to repent and, if refusal continues, applies the severe penalty described. The passage specifies execution in that ruling. It is an account of public authority's enforcement, not permission for individuals to attack a creditor.

### What distinctions are made about withholding principal?

One legal view asks why getting back the principal is linked to repentance. If refusal arises from declaring riba halal, lawful, it treats that denial as apostasy. It gives two rules for the property. What was earned while Muslim passes to Muslim heirs. What was earned after apostasy goes to the Baytul-Mal, the state's treasury.

Another case concerns a person who knows riba is haram but rebels against the Islamic government. The same account says the state takes the property and holds it in trust until repentance. These special cases concern the person's status and defiance of public authority. They give no general right to steal from a sinful lender.

The broader justice explanation stresses that wrongdoing in one field does not erase rights in other fields. The offender's prohibited interest is withheld, but capital is returned. The two points are distinct. The usual debt rule protects principal. The further legal cases concern apostasy or armed rebellion, judged by public authority.

### What does repentance restore?

It removes the prohibited demand and preserves the rightful amount. The debtor is not required to pay a penalty disguised as interest, and the lender is not required to surrender principal merely because interest had once been stipulated.

The subsequent instruction adds mercy where actual repayment is impossible. It does not contradict the right described here, but governs its exercise during hardship.

### In short

- Refusal to abandon riba receives a severe warning of war with Allah and His Messenger.
- Repentance leaves the original principal due without the forbidden increase.
- Justice protects the debtor and the creditor's rightful claim together.
- The additional enforcement rulings concern historical public authority, not private violence.

280.text:
The protection of principal does not justify tormenting an insolvent debtor: "If it is difficult for someone to repay a debt, postpone it until a time of ease." Allah requires respite during genuine hardship and encourages forgiving the debt as charity. The creditor's opportunity is to show mercy, not to turn helplessness into another charge.

### Phrase by phrase

**"If it is difficult for someone to repay a debt,"** The person lacks means rather than merely refusing an affordable payment. The explanation connects the case with Banu Makhzum, whose creditors had now abandoned riba and asked for principal.

**"postpone it until a time of ease."** Wait until repayment becomes possible. The readings maysara and maysura both concern ease. Unlike the pre-Islamic choice between immediate payment and added interest, the delay is not sold to the distressed person.

**"And if you waive it as an act of charity,"** Forgiving all, or in another explanation part, of the debt becomes sadaqah. The charitable act is the released claim itself. The creditor need not first extract the money and then hand it back to make the relief real.

**"it will be better for you, if only you knew"** Its benefit before Allah exceeds the apparent loss. Respite is required in the hardship described, while remission is offered as a greater good. The instruction asks the creditor to recognise a return beyond immediate collection.

### What reported dispute is connected with respite?

Al-Kalbi says Banu 'Amr ibn 'Umayr told Banu'l-Mughirah to return the principal and they would forgo its interest. The debtors asked for time until harvest because circumstances were difficult.

The report then describes refusal and revelation of this instruction. Its final attribution of the refusal names Banu'l-Mughirah, although the preceding dialogue makes them the requesting debtors. That wording is a textual difficulty, not a basis for inventing a new sequence. The essential connection is the request for respite in hardship.

### How can cancellation be better than recovery?

One answer concerns the enduring blessings of Paradise in place of a temporary gain. Another concerns barakah in what remains. A small amount may meet many needs without a numerical increase.

The reflection contrasts that with money whose intended benefit never arrives or which must be spent on distress, treatment and consultation. It gives health and effective ordinary treatment as examples of blessing. It does not make illness proof of wrongdoing or claim all poor people are always healthy.

The general social effect is also beneficial. Compassion, sympathy and goodwill grow when weakness is not punished. Justice protects principal, while mercy governs its exercise and may go further by relinquishing it.

### What reward is given for postponement?

Ahmad records through Sulayman bin Buraydah that his father heard the Prophet ﷺ promise charity equal to the debt for each day of time granted. He also heard a promise of twice that amount and asked about the difference.

The explanation distinguishes the periods. Before the repayment term ends, the daily reward is the equivalent amount. Once it ends and further time is granted because of hardship, the daily reward is doubled.

The account values waiting as an act rather than inactivity. Keeping the distressed person free from harassment is a continuing form of good even where no money is newly transferred.

### Why did Abu Qatadah forgive a debt?

Ahmad records that Abu Qatadah sought a man owing him money who repeatedly hid. A boy revealed that the man was inside eating, and Abu Qatadah called him out. Asked why he hid, the debtor said he had no money and faced hardship.

Abu Qatadah asked him to confirm it by Allah, then wept. He recalled the Prophet ﷺ saying that someone granting respite or forgiving debt would receive shade of Allah's Throne at resurrection. Muslim also records the hadith.

The episode joins verification with compassion. The creditor did not simply dismiss the claim as an excuse, and the confirmation moved him towards mercy instead of another demand.

Al-Tabarani's Mu'jim also contains the encouragement for someone desiring divine shade to give lenience, deferment or forgiveness. A similar saying is recorded by Muslim. Another saying encourages respite for the person seeking an answered prayer or removal of misfortune, without supplying an additional collector here.

### What happened to the lenient merchant?

Abu Ya'la Al-Mawsili records from Hudhayfah a saying of the Prophet ﷺ about a servant summoned for account. He first says he has no deed equal even to an atom to offer, repeating his answer. He then remembers his dealings as a wealthy merchant.

He gave easy terms to those who could pay and time to those in difficulty. Allah declared Himself more worthy of lenience and admitted him to Paradise. Al-Bukhari, Muslim and Ibn Majah also record the account from Hudhayfah. Muslim gives a related wording from 'Uqbah bin 'Amir and Abu Mas'ud Al-Badri.

The story does not present a licence to neglect every other duty. It reveals the value of mercy that its doer had barely counted among good works. Lenience in business can be a decisive act of obedience.

### What follows when insolvency is proved before a judge?

The legal and inward discussion says continued detention is not permissible once the detained person's insolvency is established. Proof of that condition is retained in connection with the adversary's claim, but the debtor receives respite.

It asks what profit or commercial transformation can be expected from a person without goods or capital. Jurists say a healthy person should seek work, while bodily weakness limits what can be required. Someone bankrupt in strength as well as money must rely on the provision appointed for debtors.

The reflection connects this with Allah's knowledge of human weakness, difficulty and sincere need. His mercy is not detached from those realities. The legal demand should likewise distinguish unwillingness from incapacity.

### In short

- Genuine inability to repay requires postponement without charging for the delay.
- Waiving the debt is a greater charity, with benefit beyond the amount surrendered.
- Prophetic reports promise continuing reward and divine shade for lenience.
- Proven insolvency limits detention and demands attention to actual capacity.
- Mercy in financial dealings nurtures both personal reward and communal goodwill.

281.text:
The financial commands end by returning every transaction to its final account: "Be mindful of the Day when you will ˹all˺ be returned to Allah." Claims, repayments and gifts all belong to a life that ends. On that day neither apparent success nor an incomplete worldly record will conceal what a soul has earned.

### Phrase by phrase

**"Be mindful of the Day"** Taqwa directs present conduct towards the reality of judgment. The warning closes the riba instruction with accountability rather than leaving it as an external regulation alone.

**"when you will ˹all˺ be returned to Allah,"** The event is resurrection. The readings turja'una and tarji'una express being returned and returning. Neither leaves anyone outside the encounter.

**"then every soul will be paid in full for what it has done,"** Believer and disbeliever receive the recompense of good and evil. The wealth of this life will vanish, but responsibility for its use will not.

**"and none will be wronged"** No good deed is diminished and no extra sin added. The account is complete and just. The command to avoid injustice in debt therefore ends in assurance of Allah's perfect justice.

### Is this described as the last revelation?

An-Nasa'i records from Ibn 'Abbas that this was the final verse revealed. Ad-Dahhak and Al-'Awfi also transmit that account from him.

One discussion says the Prophet ﷺ died thirty-one days later. Other reports give only nine days. The alternatives are preserved rather than forcing one chronology. Their common effect is to place the return to Allah at the close of the revealed instruction.

### Why is law alone not enough?

The social reflection says reform requires people willing to uphold a system. Even a secular order depends on a degree of public character and acceptance. An Islamic order likewise cannot be fully produced by imposing regulations on people without taqwa.

The Qur'an therefore addresses faith, fear of Allah and concern for the Hereafter alongside legal commands. It works upon the individual who must choose to obey when an opportunity for evasion appears.

In this explanation, personal reform is the direct aim and social reform its collective manifestation. A community changes as its members develop the required spirit. Law has a place, but cannot substitute for that inward willingness.

### Why discuss other riba passages here?

The extended review brings the instruction into a wider Qur'anic perspective. It counts seven relevant verses in Al-Baqarah, one in Al 'Imran and two in al-Nisa. A verse in al-Rum has differing interpretations. Its totals reflect whether that last verse is included, rather than announcing an additional undisclosed ruling.

The review's purpose is to clarify whether the prohibition depends upon an extreme rate or compounding, and whether every use of the word riba concerns the same practice. Those questions affect how the financial commands are received.

### Does multiplied interest alone fall under the prohibition?

The discussion cites verse 130 of Al 'Imran, warning against riba multiplied many times. Mujahid's account describes the familiar pattern: when a loan fell due and could not be paid, an extension added another charge, followed by further increases at subsequent deadlines.

The phrase condemns that prevailing method. It is not a condition making a smaller increase lawful. Other passages prohibit riba without that qualification.

An analogy is the warning against taking a paltry price for divine signs. Even a whole worldly kingdom would be paltry compared with revelation. The wording does not mean a sufficiently large price would make the exchange permissible.

The review also notes how apparently simple interest can become repeated increase when receipts are added to the creditor's funds and lent again. Reinvestment can multiply the gain even without calling the initial arrangement compound interest. Its conclusion is that neither simple nor compound interest escapes the prohibition described.

### What is recalled concerning earlier law?

Verses 160 and 161 of al-Nisa are discussed as describing people who obstructed Allah's way, took riba despite its prohibition and consumed others' property falsely. The consequence included good things previously permitted becoming forbidden and a painful punishment for disbelievers among them.

The explanation connects the prohibition with the law of Musa (Moses). It describes transgression by the people in the passage, not an inherent quality of all their descendants. The point is that riba was not a newly incomprehensible practice first named for this community.

These are the verse numbers and chapter names supplied by the review. No additional corrected references are imported from memory.

### What are the two readings of the verse in al-Rum?

The discussion cites (30:39). One reading concerns interest that appears to increase property but does not increase it with Allah. It contrasts that with zakah and sadaqah, whose apparent reduction produces multiplied good.

The bodily analogy compares swelling with unhealthy increase and therapeutic cleansing or bloodletting with an apparent reduction that can benefit health. The contrast concerns useful results, not approving growth or condemning reduction merely by quantity.

Another reading takes riba there as a gift offered to obtain a larger gift in return. The discussion gives gifts at marriage ceremonies as an example. Such giving aims at personal advantage rather than Allah's pleasure and therefore receives no reward as expenditure in His cause.

It connects that meaning with (74:6), an instruction to the Prophet ﷺ not to give a favour for an increased return. The verse then concerns self-interested gifts rather than directly legislating loan interest.

### Why is the gift interpretation preferred in that discussion?

Al-Rum is Makki, connected with revelation in Makkah, while the specific prohibition of riba came in Madinah. Not every verse in a Makki chapter must have that origin, but the classification supplies a strong presumption unless evidence shows otherwise.

The preceding subject also concerns giving relatives, poor people and travellers their due while seeking Allah's pleasure. The next distinction naturally clarifies that expecting a bigger personal return is not the same purpose.

The discussion therefore considers the gift reading weightier here. It does not use that interpretation to cancel the explicit prohibition elsewhere. The added nuance concerns this particular verse's meaning, not a permission for loan interest.

The review of those passages consequently leaves the central conclusion unchanged: riba is haram, unlawful, whether doubled, repeatedly multiplied or initially simple. The declaration of war against defiance remains part of that conclusion.

### What inward return occurs before death?

The allusive reading distinguishes the future return of bodily selves from the heart's return in every breath. The latter is pictured as payment made now rather than a promise deferred to resurrection.

Immediate attentiveness to Allah's claim is described as more fitting for the intimate servant than waiting until the final reckoning to recognise it. It contrasts the ordinary call to fear a day with the direct call in (2:41) to fear Allah Himself.

This does not deny the future return. It draws a present discipline from it: remember the Lord now, fulfil duties now and do not postpone the heart's obedience until death makes new action impossible.

### In short

- Every soul returns for a complete account without injustice.
- Reports identify this as the final revelation while differing over the days until the Prophet's death.
- Faith and taqwa make financial law part of personal obedience rather than mere external compliance.
- The wider review rejects limiting the prohibition to extreme or compound interest.
- Present inward return prepares the servant for the unavoidable final return.

282.text:
Trust and practical safeguards belong together: "O believers! When you contract a loan for a fixed period of time, commit it to writing." The verse gives detailed rules for recording obligations, taking witnesses and protecting those who assist. Clear evidence serves justice before a dispute arises and helps preserve relationships when memory fails.

### Phrase by phrase

**"O believers! When you contract a loan for a fixed period of time, commit it to writing."** The instruction includes loans and deferred transactions such as payment now for later delivery. The amount, description and due date need clarity. Recording them protects rights beyond the moment when both parties remember the agreement.

**"Let the scribe maintain justice between the parties."** The writer must record what was agreed without adding, omitting or favouring one side. Skill must not become a means of exploiting a party unable to check the record.

**"The scribe should not refuse to write as Allah has taught them to write."** Knowledge is a divine gift to be used in helping others. The repeated command to write emphasises that duty. Mujahid and 'Ata say a requested scribe is required to record the terms.

**"They will write what the debtor dictates, bearing Allah in mind and not defrauding the debt."** The person against whom the claim stands acknowledges it through dictation. They must not hide any part, diminish the value or alter its description. Taqwa guards the record from dishonesty even where manipulation might pass unnoticed.

**"If the debtor is incompetent, weak, or unable to dictate, let their guardian dictate for them with justice."** The cases include reckless handling of wealth, minority, incapacity, old age, illness, inability to speak or a language barrier. A wali, guardian or authorised representative, supplies the dictation without abusing that position.

**"Call upon two of your men to witness."** The explanation requires mature, sane, upright Muslim men. Some glosses also expressly mention free status. The witnesses preserve the agreement in addition to its written form.

**"If two men cannot be found, then one man and two women of your choice will witness"** The specified alternative concerns financial contracts, directly or indirectly involving property. Trustworthiness and approved character remain necessary. One man alone or only two women are not the combination described for ordinary dealings here.

**"so if one of the women forgets the other may remind her."** The explanation concerns error or forgetfulness corrected through the other's reminder. Readings of the verb for reminding and of the conditional clause give grammatical variations while retaining that stated purpose.

**"The witnesses must not refuse when they are summoned."** The interpretations distinguish being asked initially to witness from being called later to testify. All emphasise preserving the truth rather than suppressing known evidence.

**"You must not be against writing ˹contracts˺ for a fixed period—whether the sum is small or great."** Do not become weary of documenting a modest debt. A small amount can also produce disagreement, and the term matters alongside the sum.

**"This is more just ˹for you˺ in the sight of Allah, and more convenient to establish evidence and remove doubts."** The document supports witnesses' recollection and ends disagreement over what was promised. Their handwriting or signatures can help them remember the transaction.

**"However, if you conduct an immediate transaction among yourselves, then there is no need for you to record it,"** An exchange completed on the spot does not carry the same deferred obligation. Its omission from writing is not sinful merely because a record was not made.

**"but call upon witnesses when a deal is finalized."** Witnesses provide an additional safeguard even in immediate trade. The discussion gives different explanations of whether this is obligatory or recommended, particularly in light of the following verse's permission to rely on trust.

**"Let no harm come to the scribe or witnesses."** Their assistance must not expose them to wrongful burden. Another reading also directs them not to cause harm through falsified records or distorted testimony. Both sides of the transaction deserve protection.

**"If you do, then you have gravely exceeded ˹your limits˺."** Causing the prohibited harm is sin, not merely a breach of etiquette. Protecting one's own claim does not authorise violating another person's rights.

**"Be mindful of Allah, for Allah ˹is the One Who˺ teaches you."** He teaches conduct beneficial here and in the Hereafter. Awareness of Him should govern both receiving the instruction and acting upon it.

**"And Allah has ˹perfect˺ knowledge of all things"** Amounts, descriptions, consequences and intentions are known to Him. A technical pretext cannot make a deception invisible to the Lord.

This is the Qur'an's longest verse. Abu Ja'far bin Jarir records Sa'id bin Al-Musayyib's report that he had been told the debt verse was the last revealed from above the Throne. That report differs from the earlier identification of the verse about the final return as the last revelation. It is retained as a reported view, not merged into one chronology.

### Why specify the term rather than leave it vague?

The legal explanation requires a determined due date without ambiguity. Merely saying at harvest is not sufficiently precise, because weather may change when harvesting takes place. A date and month remove that uncertainty.

The Two Sahihs record from Ibn 'Abbas that on arriving in Al-Madinah the Prophet ﷺ found people paying ahead for fruit to be delivered after one or two years. He instructed that such payment be for a specified measure, weight and delivery term.

The allowance therefore does not permit an undefined obligation. Clear quantities and timing protect the parties from later disagreement. Written terms preserve that clarity when the transaction remains open for a long period.

### Is writing a strict requirement in every case?

One account treats it as initially necessary, then relaxed by the following permission to entrust one another. That view is transmitted from Ibn Zayd, Ar-Rabi' bin Anas, Al-Hasan, Ash-Sha'bi, Abu Sa'id and Ibn Jurayj.

Another explanation treats taking witnesses as recommended rather than universally obligatory. Both discussions preserve the practical value of documentation. Relaxation where genuine trust exists is not a claim that evidence is useless.

Ibn Jurayj distinguishes writing terms when borrowing from taking witnesses when buying. The common aim is securing rights and reducing disputes, not encouraging suspicion for its own sake.

### Why is writing itself a form of service?

The scribe received a capacity others may lack. Using it to assist an unlettered person can be charity, just as a hadith describes helping a worker or doing what a weak person cannot do.

Another hadith warns of a fiery bridle for someone who withholds knowledge. The account uses these sayings to discourage selfish refusal, without adding collectors or grades not supplied for them.

The writer must also refuse dishonesty. Helping one party obtain a passing advantage by falsifying terms causes lasting harm to the writer's own moral account. Gratitude for skill therefore means service joined to fairness, not compliance with every request regardless of truth.

### Who may dictate when the debtor cannot?

The guardian can be a parent, executor, custodian or interpreter, depending on the incapacity. A representative can assist someone whose language the scribe does not understand. The word wali is broad enough in the discussion to cover guardianship and authorised representation.

One gloss identifies the guardian of the debtor's financial interests with the creditor. Others emphasise the person in charge of the debtor's affairs. Whichever role is described, justice is explicit: no extra amount may be added because the person cannot dictate.

The debtor's own dictation is otherwise preferred because the record then expresses the acknowledgment from the liable party. Guardianship repairs a genuine inability rather than removing the person's responsibility without cause.

### Why require the stated witness combination?

The explanation connects two women's testimony in the described financial cases with the provision for one to remind the other. Muslim records from Abu Hurayrah the Prophet's address urging women towards charity and forgiveness, with a warning about frequent cursing and ingratitude towards husbands.

When a woman asked about his reference to shortcomings in mind and religion, he explained the first through the stated witness rule and the second through nights without prayer and the interruption of fasting during Ramadan. The report also remarks on women's influence over men of otherwise sound minds.

Those are the explanation and examples supplied in the hadith. The passage should not be expanded into an unsupported claim about every woman's intelligence, honesty or capacity in every subject. Here its legal application is specified financial evidence, alongside the requirement that approved witnesses be trustworthy.

The reminder provision matters because preserving a right includes correcting forgetfulness, not merely counting names. The account notes readings fa-tudhakkira and fa-tudhkira, and a conditional reading giving the reminder as the response if error occurs.

### When must a witness come forward?

Qatadah and Ar-Rabi' bin Anas apply the command to accepting the role when called. Ibn 'Abbas and Al-Hasan Al-Basri are reported as including both initial witnessing and subsequent testimony.

Mujahid and Abu Mijlaz distinguish them: one may choose whether to become a witness, but someone who has witnessed must come forward when testimony is needed. The majority explanation in the discussion particularly understands the verse through testifying to what is already known.

Some describe the initial duty as fard kifayah, a communal obligation fulfilled by enough suitable people in the ummah, the Muslim community. Later testimony can likewise become communal if the needed evidence has already been properly supplied. Otherwise the knowledgeable witness must not leave a right unsupported.

### What happened in the horse transaction?

Ahmad records through the family of Khuzaymah bin Thabit Al-Ansari an account of the Prophet ﷺ agreeing to buy a horse from a Bedouin. He went ahead to obtain its price while the seller followed.

Other men, unaware of the agreement, offered more. The seller then told the Prophet ﷺ to buy or he would sell elsewhere. When the Prophet ﷺ affirmed that he had already bought it, the seller denied the sale and demanded a witness.

Khuzaymah Al-Ansari testified that the horse had been sold to him. Asked his basis, he said his trust in the messenger. The Prophet ﷺ made Khuzaymah's testimony equivalent to two men's. Abu Dawud and An-Nasa also record the account.

The discussion uses the transaction to support the view that witnesses are not always a condition required before a sale can occur. The exceptional status granted to Khuzaymah is part of that report, not a permission for everyone to claim observation of events they never saw.

### Why protect scribes and witnesses from burdens?

If service routinely means unpaid cost, humiliation or repeated disruption, truthful people become reluctant to assist. The shariah discussion therefore permits a scribe's requested wage and a witness's legitimate return travel expense. Refusing such dues can be part of the prohibited harm.

The social criticism describes witnesses kept waiting for hours by police, treated as criminals or repeatedly summoned as hearings are postponed. Work, family needs and livelihoods suffer, while threats of arrest make avoidance harder.

It argues that such treatment deters honest witnesses and leaves professional witnesses willing to say either truth or falsehood. The remedy joins the duty to testify with safeguards against unnecessary harm. Justice should not be preserved for the disputants by destroying it for those helping them.

Al-Hasan and Qatadah also apply the prohibition to the helpers' own conduct. The scribe must not record something other than dictated, and the witness must not substitute false evidence or suppress what was heard.

### How does taqwa strengthen this system?

The verse begins and ends legal detail with awareness of Allah. Some jurists draw twenty important rulings from it, but the rules still depend on people willing to apply them honestly.

The link between taqwa and being taught is illustrated through (8:29), the gift of a criterion distinguishing right from wrong, and (57:28), mercy and light by which to walk. Allah's guidance includes insight as well as an external document.

The inward reading calls this caution an expression of mercy. Allah teaches particulars of transactions, strengthens rights and calls for witnesses both at the outset and through execution so that people do not become adversaries. Sidq, sincerity and truthfulness, is its underlying character.

### In short

- Record deferred obligations with clear amounts, descriptions and due dates.
- Fair dictation, competent witnesses and accurate writing protect both parties.
- Interpretations distinguish obligatory safeguards from permissions where genuine trust exists.
- Those providing records or testimony must neither cause harm nor be wrongfully burdened.
- Taqwa makes the evidence system an expression of truth and mercy rather than a tool of manipulation.

283.text:
When the usual written safeguard is unavailable, another can secure the debt: "If you are on a journey and a scribe cannot be found, then a security can be taken." But even a pledge is not required where the parties rely on genuine trust. The responsibility to repay and to speak truth remains, with or without documents or collateral.

### Phrase by phrase

**"If you are on a journey and a scribe cannot be found,"** The situation particularly concerns a deferred debt during travel. Ibn 'Abbas includes lack of paper, ink or pen even when a person who can write is present. The need is for a usable means of recording, not merely a literate companion.

**"then a security can be taken."** Rahn is a pledge held to secure the claim. The readings ruhun and rihan are its plural forms. Being taken into possession is explained as a condition of validity and assurance for the creditor or representative.

**"If you trust one another, then ˹there is no need for a security, but˺ the debtor should honour this trust ˹by repaying the debt˺"** Trust allows omission of the pledge. Ash-Sha'bi also permits omission of writing and witnesses in that case. The absence of a safeguard does not remove the obligation itself.

**"and let them fear Allah, their Lord."** The trusted debtor must not deny the debt or exploit the creditor's confidence. Taqwa guards a right that may lack easily produced external proof.

**"And do not conceal the testimony,"** A person knowing the truth must not hide it when called. If trust is betrayed by denial, the knowledgeable witness must come forward rather than help the wrong through silence.

**"for whoever conceals it, their hearts are indeed sinful."** The heart is where the decision to conceal begins. The wrong is not merely an idle tongue. As-Suddi explains it as being a sinner inwardly too.

**"And Allah ˹fully˺ knows what you do"** He knows whether the trust was discharged and whether testimony was given or hidden. A lack of human evidence does not create a gap in His knowledge.

### Is a pledge allowed only during travel?

The sunnah also permits pledges in towns where writers are available. Travel is singled out because obtaining a record can be harder and security more urgent there. The circumstance explains the example without restricting every permissible use to it.

The Two Sahihs record from Anas that the Prophet ﷺ died while his shield was pledged to a Jewish person for barley bought on credit to provide for his household. Another wording places the creditor among the Jews of Al-Madinah.

The supplied account describes thirty Wasq and gives an approximate weight of 180 kilograms. Those are its stated unit and estimate, retained without silently substituting a different unit from outside knowledge.

The example shows that securing a genuine debt did not contradict trust in Allah. It also gives a concrete settled-town case, beside the journey mentioned in the verse.

### May the creditor benefit from pledged property?

The legal explanation limits the creditor to holding it until the debt is paid. Benefits arising from it remain the original owner's right. Taking it into possession is security, not a transfer of ownership or an unrestricted licence to profit from it.

The distinction protects the debtor even while protecting the creditor's claim. A debt safeguard should not become another extraction beyond what was lent.

### How does trust affect the earlier commands?

Ibn Abi Hatim records with a sound chain Abu Sa'id Al-Khudri's view that this verse abrogated the prior requirement to record and have witnesses. Other explanations describe trust as a permission not to use those means.

In either account, the relaxation concerns the external safeguards, not honesty or repayment. The debtor remains responsible for what was taken. Ahmad and the Sunan record from Samurah, through Al-Hasan and Qatadah, the saying that the hand bears what it took until it returns it.

No interpretation here says that an unwritten debt can be denied lawfully. The creditor's choice to trust is precisely why faithfulness is required of the debtor.

### Why is concealed testimony a heart offence?

Someone might think only the tongue failed to perform a duty. But an inward choice usually directed that silence. Prestige, fear of losing advantage or attachment to someone can make the person withhold the truth.

The discussion places false evidence and hiding true evidence among the gravest sins. It recalls (5:106), a pledge not to hide testimony, and (4:135), the duty to stand for justice even against oneself, parents or relatives, and regardless of wealth or poverty.

That reference also rejects following desire through distortion or refusal. Justice cannot depend on whether the witness prefers the person who would benefit from the evidence.

The social reflection calls concealment a retreat from the believer's role in making just decisions. Conscience asks for truth to be acknowledged and falsehood exposed. A person hiding evidence for worldly standing becomes implicated through the silence chosen.

### What does the shared reflection add about human freedom?

The world from particles to stars follows Allah's command. Human beings appear able to choose different paths, but their freedom is a test rather than independence from Him.

The application here is voluntary fidelity. Other creation follows its appointed course, while the person must choose restraint and obedience. Feeling unobserved is not proof of being outside the Lord's watch.

That shared principle continues into the next verses concerning inward knowledge and belief. Here it guards the entrusted debt and the testimony that might otherwise remain hidden.

### In short

- A pledge can secure a debt when recording is unavailable, and is also permitted beyond travel.
- Trust allows fewer external safeguards but never cancels repayment.
- The creditor's possession of security does not authorise taking its benefits.
- Concealing evidence is an inward decision as well as a failure of speech.
- Allah's knowledge protects the truth even where human records are incomplete.

284.text:
The truth hidden from a court or neighbour is not hidden from its Lord: "To Allah ˹alone˺ belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth." His ownership and knowledge embrace outward action and the heart. The warning therefore completes the instruction against concealing evidence and also reaches the sincerity underlying every duty.

### Phrase by phrase

**"To Allah ˹alone˺ belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth."** He created, owns and governs everything. His ownership comes from bringing things into existence, not acquiring them from someone else. No part of creation falls outside His authority.

**"Whether you reveal what is in your hearts or conceal it, Allah will call you to account for it."** Concealment from people is not concealment from Allah. One interpretation particularly concerns knowingly suppressing evidence. The broader explanation includes chosen beliefs, intentions and inward conduct as well as outward deeds.

**"He forgives whoever He wills, and punishes whoever He wills."** Forgiveness comes through His grace and mercy, punishment through His wisdom and justice. A gloss distinguishes someone repenting from someone refusing repentance. Reckoning does not itself mean every item will end in punishment.

**"And Allah is Most Capable of everything"** His power includes disclosure, accounting, forgiveness and recompense. The readings of the preceding verbs differ over whether they are joined grammatically to the conditional clause or begin a new statement. Both affirm His authority.

### Why were the Companions worried?

Ahmad records from Abu Hurayrah that the Companions came to the Prophet ﷺ and knelt in distress when they heard the verse. They could bear prayer, fasting, jihad and charity, but felt unable to control everything occurring in the heart.

The Prophet ﷺ asked whether they wished to repeat the response of the people of the two Scriptures who said they heard and disobeyed. The account recalls (2:93), with one narration's reservation about the exact quotation. He taught them instead to acknowledge hearing and obedience, seek forgiveness and affirm return to Allah.
